review_text: I received my unit today, December 21,2022. Similar to Reviewer "R1", in his November 2022 review, (See "Top Critical Review", above, the box had clearly been opened, several times. When I removed the unit, it was dirty, fingerprinted, and clearly a used, Customer return. Unlike the Amazon product description picture, instead of a simple, opaque plastic red power off/reset switch, it was a translucent, lens-type switch, (see attached photo), the kind that normally have a led light embedded in them, that illuminates, to indicate strip power is on. When plugged in, the switch did not illuminate, in "power on" position. Since this is a surge suppressor type of power strip, what that normally means, is that someone blew the surge stopper circuit, (they are usually "one shot" metal oxide varisters (MOV's), that will protect, by shunting excess voltage to the ground wire, from a bad surge, but just once), then returned the item. These strips are designed so that the led no longer illuminates, once the surge protection MOV is completely blown out, so the user is warned to replace the unit, to regain surge protection. With minor surges, a MOV may last for years, but one bad surge event is all you get, on the cheaper strips. I quickly checked all of the AC outlets, with a plug-in lamp, and the two regular USB outlets, with my Kindle and a charger cord, and they do still work. I did not have a usb-c male to usb-c male cord handy, to check that third outlet, since that is not a standard configuration, most usb-c devices still use a cord with the familiar, bigger, old "usb-a" connector, on the power plug-in side. So, the bottom line is dirty, used, and no power surge protection, but the outlets do work. It's that busy, "right before Xmas" time, I need it only to plug in Xmas lights and decoration stuff, so I probably won't hassle with a return, as I just don't have time. But I feel really sorry, for someone who gets one to plug in expensive equipment, thinking they have surge protection, and has their pricey equipment ruined. Since this is obviously a repetitive problem, and also a particularly nasty sleight of hand, by a disreputable seller, to pull on consumers, (due to the lack of promised electrical protection), I would not recommend buying, either this product, or anything else from this seller. Hopefully, they'll get thrown off of the platform soon, before anyone suffers electrical damage, or a fire, etc. From what I've seen, Amazon really does care about their reputation, and is usually pretty good, about policing the "bad apples", like these guys, right out the door, and quickly.

I mounted a GoPro Hero 5 in a Luxebell housing to this mount, which I installed on an ICE VTX racing trike. On the positive side, the clamp area opens completely, so the clamp can be installed without having to remove other components. However, even tightened as far as I could, the mount dropped when I went over bumps or rough pavement. After about 25 miles of cycling, the mount vibrated off the arm to which it was mounted, sending my GoPro tumbling along the shoulder of the freeway. (There is a section of freeway in San Diego County where cyclists can use the shoulder). I like the mount, so I applied DAP RapidFuse to the bottom of the rubber, placed it on the mount, and then glued the KOM mount to the rubber. It's solid as a rock now. But, that didn't completely solve the problem. On rough roads or speed bumps the GoPro mount will start to turn out of the KOM arm, leaving the GoPro dangling precariously. Today, I purchased M3 x.5 20mm screws and replaced the hardware, so that the mount no longer swivels or comes off. I remove the camera by opening the back of the Luxebell housing. In sum, it makes a lightweight and adjustable mount for a GoPro, but it may take some work to get a firm mount, and it won't be removable if you want to ride fast over rough pavement.

The EarFun Air Pro 3 Wireless Earbuds offer an impressive array of features and sound quality at an affordable price point, making them an attractive option for budget-conscious consumers. However, while they excel in many areas, there are some drawbacks to consider.On the positive side, these earbuds deliver exceptional sound quality thanks to their Hybrid Active Noise Cancelling technology and 11mm wool drivers. Whether you're listening to music, podcasts, or taking calls, you can expect rich, immersive sound with deep bass and crisp highs. Additionally, the Bluetooth 5.3 connectivity ensures a stable and seamless wireless connection, allowing you to enjoy your audio content without interruption.Despite these strengths, one area where the EarFun Air Pro 3 earbuds fall short is in their microphone performance, particularly in open environments. While the 6 built-in microphones and CVC8.0 noise reduction technology excel in quiet settings, they struggle to deliver clear call quality in noisy environments. This can be particularly frustrating for users who rely on their earbuds for phone calls while on the go or in crowded spaces.However, it's essential to consider that these limitations are somewhat expected given the earbuds' affordable price point. For users primarily interested in high-quality audio playback and ANC performance, the EarFun Air Pro 3 earbuds offer excellent value for money.In conclusion, while the EarFun Air Pro 3 Wireless Earbuds have some drawbacks, such as subpar microphone performance in open environments, they still offer a compelling package of features and sound quality at an affordable price. If you can overlook this minor flaw, these earbuds provide a solid option for budget-conscious consumers looking for a reliable audio solution.

Second, the measuring of distance is way, way, way off. I walk to work every day, and i know that my walk is exactly .75 miles. When i would use the tracker on this watch, it would be ridiculously off--usually way over-estimating the distance. I never had a day where it recorded less than 1 mile for this walk, and sometimes it would say as high as 2.5 miles! I have no idea what it was measuring, since it is supposedly connected through GPS on my iphone (which of course correctly measured .75 miles). it wasn't just wildly off on short city walks either. Third, the battery life is horrible, especially if you use it to track a workout. I routinely go on 30-35 mile bike rides that take me about 3 to 3.5 hours. I used this tracker on 4 occasions to record my workout. Each time the watch was fully charged or almost fully charged (ie: over 85%). On three of the four workouts, the watch died before i could complete the 30-35 mile ride, so of course, it didn't complete the tracking. I went out and bought an apple watch (for not much more than this), and it is 400% better than this useless tracker.

review_text: I have an aging, custom shaped earphones, namely LZ Big Dipper ($680), which has not been used for about 3 years because of its big size and atrocious fitting for a small-eared individual like me. I have attempted using variety of third-party eartips, including the trusted Sony Hybrids eartips, and none of them worked out. I heard the product from Head-fi and intrigued with the praises of it. I was interested to try the novel Xelastec eartips made of the TPE because it can conform to the shape of one’s ear canal just like Comply. I tried the Xelastec on medium size and first impression was that it fitted securely and sealed perfectly, but felt the fitting was too big. I noticed the eartips did not conform much to the shape of my ears, which is unlike of Comply. On the second attempt with the smaller size (MS) , the ear tip wouldn't insert in because the tip felt dry (or tacky like many say). It did not have that slippery feeling of the regular silicone tips, which helps the insertion of earphones into the ear canal. So, I had to apply the ear lubricant Oto-Ease before each fitting. Then, I had to readjust every 5 mins because of the suction issue, and finally my ears became irritated after 30 mins of listening. I tried with other earphones (JVC FXT90) if Xelastec gives the fit issues but found my ears had already gotten sore and numb after using the Xelastec eartips. Frustated that I couldn't listen with my other earphones, I had to listen through a full-sized headphone instead. I have attempted trying out the eartips on three different days, 30 minutes to 1 hour listening session with 6 hours between attempts because of the irritability it causes, and decided I had to stop using it before it harms my ears. I would not risk another attempts buying and trying out the smaller size either because of the dry, tacky characteristic of the eartips. Based on this experience, I believe the Xelastec might not for everyone. Some may have wetter ears, some may have drier ears. It appears I might have dry ears. Later on, I found some pair of comply tips found in my stash, and finally found the best fit which maximizes the sound capability of the LZ Big Dipper. Biased by the trade-off effect of the Comply (sound gets compensated for the maximum comfort), I wasted three years for not realizing this. Shame on me!

I finally decided to get the CS-9080 for a less 'boomy' quiet watching environment. Well... this thing BOOMs. I set the sub volume knob halfway, and it has plenty of LFE to fill my large room. What I like about it, though is that I can more easily adjust the volume sweep compared to my Klipsch (that one needs a gentle touch, and it's awkward to reach). So, the subwoofer is certainly a contender. Most people wouldn't even need a dedicated subwoofer with this speaker. Center channel audio: Clarity of the voices is more natural sounding to my ears compared to the 8060. There's a smoother round-off in the upper mids, and the balance is much more "full". This is probably due to the larger 5.25" mid drivers compared to the 8060's 4.5". I notice a difference. I'm glad I finally pulled the trigger and went for this monster. I now have the Klipsch sub turned off most of the time, and will fire it up for those "special occassions" when it's movie day/night with friends. Heck, I might even experiment with a 2-sub setup, but not sure if they'll match well... but I'll give it a go some day. Current gear: Marantz SR-7011 receiver 5.1.4 Atmos setup. L/R speakers Definitive Technology SM65, Rear speakers SM55, and ceiling speakers are the SM45s. Center speaker is... you guessed it! The CS-9080!

The PoE Texas Gigabit PoE Splitter in-Wall Receptacle with Fast 5V USB Charging and PoE Output is a good product, but the spacing between the two ports is too close for many use cases. Accordingly, I am giving it 3 stars. I like PoE Texas as a company; they sell a lot of great Power-over-Ethernet products, including some cutting edge ones. This product is fairly unique on the market right now because it supplies Gigabit PoE (802.3af) and does 2.4A (5V / 12W) of charging as well. The product only comes in white and I wish they had other color options such as black and gray. However, for my intended use case, white was all right. My specific use case was to hang a Flair Puck (ASIN B07TPRLYS1) on my wall. Flair makes smart vents so you can have the vents automatically open or close based on thermostat integration, plus its own wireless thermostat to control individual rooms and vents, and to serve as a Wi-Fi gateway between the vents and your Internet connection. The vents are powered by 24VAC or 3VDC, while the Flair Pucks are powered by 5VDC or 3VDC. Unfortunately, Flair's somewhat convoluted design requires that the "Gateway Puck", the puck that acts as the Wi-Fi bridge, be powered by 5VDC over USB. I tried to use hardwired 3VDC via the battery terminals and the firmware refuses to let the puck operate: a message pops up saying that it has to be connected by 5VDC USB. I also tried to use 3VDC on the 5VDC USB input, but the Puck refuses to boot up. So, it really does require 5VDC. Flair recently came out with a USB Mount (directly on flair.co, not on Amazon) that acts as a right-angle micro-USB 2.0 male to USB-A 2.0 male adapter, so you can stick a Puck right on a horizontally-mounted USB-A 2.0 female port. This PoE Texas PoE Splitter perfectly fits the bill! One excellent feature of this splitter is that the USB-A 2.0 female receptacle is reversible. You can stick a USB-A 2.0 male plug into it in either direction, and it will work. The "tongue" in the middle feels extremely sturdy and I have confidence that it will last over repeated insertions. There are other reversible USB 2.0 products on the market, but the other ones I have seen (both male and female) do not feel nearly this sturdy. PoE Texas should play this feature up in its marketing. That is where the party comes to an end. As my pictures show, the Flair Puck obstructs the Ethernet port, rendering that port useless. The overhang is only about 0.5cm (5mm). PoE Texas should really redesign this product to have more space between the RJ45 port and the USB port, by moving the RJ45 port up and (perhaps) the USB port down. Also, the LED could be placed in the middle of the device rather than at the top so that more distance can be obtained between the two ports. I wish the LED could be turned off via a manual switch, or obscured (as would be the case if I put a Flair Puck on top of it), since not everybody wants to see an LED on 24/7. PoE Texas probably did not have the Flair Puck in mind when they designed this product. However, there are many "USB warts" out there, and this product's design makes them incompatible with a large set of them. Another example is a round RGB novelty USB light that I happen to have lying around. This one barely fits. I recommend this concept of this product in general, but if you are planning on putting something permanent in your wall I suggest that you wait for a revision.

Maybe another firmware update will come along and fix this, someday before the router slips into "unsupported" designation.

review_text: I have tried several 4-port HDMI KVM switches from Amazon that are about half the price of this one. Although they were usable, and one I have been using for about 6 months, I was not happy with the build quality, especially the switching buttons. So I kept looking, and decided to try this one. It is by far more expensive than the budget models, but I feel it is worth it and this will become my new HDMI KVM. This review is for the 4-port HDMI USB 3.0 version. BUILD QUALITY: Firstly, this is a solid device with excellent build quality. No cheap feeling that some of the others I have tried have had. The connectors for the cables are all solid and the 4 buttons for device selection are easy to press and make contact the first time. FEATURES: This KVM has more features than the others. Firstly, it has a USB 3.0 switcher, rather than USB 2.0 as most have. It has multiple configurable ways to switch devices (buttons on the front, wired remote controller, mouse or keyboard shortcuts which can be changed). You can also enable/disable the beep upon device switching. You can also turn on and off the keyboard shortcut recognition through a dedicated button on the front of the device. Some of the other models require a key sequence to accomplish this. There is also an audio output on the front which mirrors the audio coming through the HDMI port. There is apparently an auto-scan feature but I did not try that feature. AUDIO: I thought the audio output would appear on each computer as a new sound device via USB, but it isn't. It takes the audio being sent to the HDMI output and routes it to this jack. The manual says to set each computer's default audio device to the HDMI output, and then plug your speakers into the jack on the KVM. (Note, the audio is still routed to your monitor over HDMI so you don't lose that, even if you're not using the audio output on the front). This is neat, but it seems to me that the audio out jack is not very high quality, it seems to be missing some of the high frequency content. If your monitor has a headphone jack you could accomplish the same thing by utilizing that. The audio that is output through the audio jack is only the audio of the selected system. A nice additional feature might be to have the option of mixing the audio from all four systems together, no matter if they are selected or not, so that you wouldn't lose audio from non-selected systems. REMOTE: This particular model has a wired remote control. The manual says that if you plug it in, the front panel buttons are disabled. However, I found that to be false. I can use either the remote or the front panel buttons. The remote has lights on it to show you which device is selected. This is a nice feature if you've got the KVM mounted on the back of a workbench, you can bring the controls out to the front of the bench, MONITOR HANDLING: The cheaper KVM switches that I tried would completely disconnect the monitor from the systems not in use. This meant that when you switch from one system to another, the system you were switching away from would "lose" the HDMI monitor and the system you were switching to would "add" it. This switch works differently - all systems always see your monitor as being connected, and the switch just throws away the video from the systems that are not the selected device. I find this to be much more reliable as your systems are not constantly losing and adding a monitor. It also makes for faster switching. KEYBOARD/MOUSE: This switch is supposed to be compatible with wireless keyboards and mice, and I see no reason why it would not be. However, there can be an issue with some keyboards that are not just plain keyboards. For example, my HyperX Alloy Elite does not always work as expected. I have my mouse (wireless) receiver connected into the back of the keyboard, and the keyboard has two cables - one for the keyboard and one for the USB port on the back of the keyboard that my mouse receiver is in. I have these two cables plugged into the KVM in the appropriate connection jacks. Although sometimes switching does work correctly, I have also had instances where the mouse will not be recognized on the system I'm switching to without unplugging the USB cable for the mouse and plugging it back in. The manual does state that some gaming keyboards may have issues and to disable the keyboard shortcut switching. The manual says to use keyboard shortcuts to do this, but since this model also has the front switch for this purpose, I tried that. Once keyboard shortcuts were disabled, I have not had an issue switching between systems with recognition of my keyboard or mouse. I do however lose the capability of using keyboard shortcuts to switch systems, which I don't need anyway. I do plan to try and plug the wireless mouse receiver directly into the KVM but because the keyboard and mouse USB jacks are so close together, I will need a USB extension cable to accomplish this. PERFORMANCE: This KVM performs quite well. Switching between systems is fast. However, because of the way Windows 7 handles USB (slowly) when switching to a Windows 7 system it could possibly take a little more time for your keyboard and/or mouse to be re-recognized. This may not be true on all Windows 7 systems however, but it is what I have experienced. My Windows 10 systems switch quickly and flawlessly. I find having the HDMI monitor not disappear when switching away is a huge plus for this KVM. PACKAGE: This is a complete package. You get 4 HDMI cables, 4 USB 3.0 A to B cables, a power adapter (which seems to not be necessary as the switch can get its power from the connected system(s)), and wired remote + cable. You just need to supply your own HDMI to connect to the output monitor and your own keyboard and mouse connection cable(s) or dongles. Not as I mentioned above the jacks for keyboard and mouse are close together and I was not able to fit a USB cable and a direct connected Logitech unified receiver without using a USB extender cable. PROS: * Excellent build quality * Button, wired remote, or configurable key/mouse shortcut switching modes * All cables included * Can turn switching beep on/off * Auto scan mode * Wired remote with lights works in addition to front panel buttons * Rubber feet on bottom of device * Front button to turn off keyboard switching shortcuts * Audio output jack replicates HDMI audio * Fast switching * No loss of HDMI monitor identification when system is not in use * Supports USB 3.0 devices to switch to selected device * Compact size, and unit has good weight CONS: * Can be finicky to work with gaming keyboards, but can disable shortcuts as a workaround * No mounting holds on bottom of device. Could use Velcro to mount/secure it * Device is small, so lots of cables all connected to one small unit * No lights to show USB or HDMI status of conencted systems(s). Only lights to show selected system CONCLUSION: I did not initially buy this model because of the price, and thought some of the other units that were half the price would be as good or workable. However, now I wish I had just "bitten but bullet" and bought this one to start with. So, if you want a 4 port HDMI KVM with USB 3.0 (even if you really don't need USB 3.0) just get this one.

If you plan on using these at the gym, on campus, or anywhere where there are many other people simultaneously using Bluetooth, you will be very disappointed. I’ve tried these, AirPods Pro, Sennheiser Momentum 2, Skullcandy Crusher ANC, and Lypertek Tevis. Every single one of those EXCEPT the AirPods Pro cut out in highly saturated areas, but the AirPods Pro hurt my ears for some reason so I am unable to use them. With these being the latest and greatest in Bluetooth technology, I was certain they wouldn’t have connectivity issues. I was very wrong, and I’m super annoyed about it. If there are more than about 40 people using Bluetooth around you, they will cut in and out guaranteed. A quick word on Bluetooth: Bluetooth Classic has 79 channels (different frequencies) to transmit data over, and Bluetooth devices will switch channels if they encounter over saturation of their current channel- this is why when you enter an area with other Bluetooth devices your audio might cut our temporarily until your device finds an open channel. Each channel on Bluetooth 5.2 can transmit around 2000Kbps of data at a time, so if an area is so saturated that there are no more available channels, devices will begin to share channels. Now, do the math here with me. Most music streaming services stream audio at 128 or 192Kbps, but we will go with the higher end just to be safe. Let’s say you’re streaming super high quality audio at 320Kbps: that means you should be able to stream roughly 6 streams per channel before that 2000Kbps is fully saturated and you begin to drop packets. 6 x 37 channels (we can go with Bluetooth LE just to be safe) = over 200 Bluetooth streams before anyone’s audio should cut out. Subtract any Wi-Fi interference (since Wi-Fi uses the same frequencies as Bluetooth) and a possible microwave or two running (maybe an employee is making a hot pocket) and let’s say we lose another half of those packets. That means we should still be able to have 100 simultaneous high quality streams ASSUMING the Bluetooth devices have the processing power and speed to efficiently switch between channels and find openings. HOWEVER this isn’t the case with these earbuds! They cut out worse than every other device I have except the Sennheisers, and those get a pass for trying to transmit audiophile quality sound. I’m so sick of dinking around with crappy Bluetooth devices! All I want is to slam out fat sets at the gym without having my audio cut out constantly.

Case is cheap feeling plastic, and opens "upside down" from the way you put the headphones in, though this is minor. What cannot be overlooked is the awful issues with the bluetooth connection. these headphones frequently cut out, and frequently enter a state where only one of the earbuds works at a time. Oh, what a long, strange and frustrating journey this whole mesh WiFi trip has been. No, I’m not talking about this Eero Pro system. Eero is amazing! I’m talking about what it’s taken to get here. You see, I’ve been a long and very happy user of an Apple Extreme network for years. Years of never having to even think about whether my wireless system would work. It just did. Always and without fail. But now that Apple has discontinued their wireless routers and I’ve added more and smarter accessories to the network, it’s become painfully obvious that my old trusty Apple network is no longer up to the task. So I started my journey to find a similarly trouble-free replacement but in a mesh configuration. My first foray was Netgear’s Orbi system. I had read many good reviews about this product and purchased a three-unit system at my local Costco when it went on sale. It worked like a charm…for about 24 hours. After that, it was like playing whack-a-mole but with no compensating prize at the end. One node would need to be reset, then another, then the entire network rebooted…over, and over and over again. My internet connection would go down randomly even though nothing was wrong with my internet service. Enough. I knew from experience that it shouldn’t be this difficult to maintain a wireless network, so back to Costco it went. The old Apple network was reinstated. My next try was purchasing an Arris Surfboard Max mesh system. This manufacturer touts itself as ready for what the future will bring with WiFi 6 and who doesn’t want to be on the cutting edge of that? But alas, being on the cutting edge meant bleeding blood, sweat and tears because as with the Orbi, one quarter to one-half of my smart devices would randomly drop from the network for no discernable reason, although I never did lose internet connection so that was an improvement over the Orbi. How was it possible for everything to be connected to the network before I went to bed only to have them fall off by the next morning? It too was sent back and once again the Apple network was put back into service. But I knew in my heart that somewhere over the rainbow someone had to make a mesh network that just worked. And Hallelujah it exists and its name is Eero Pro! It has now been two weeks since I installed my three-pack Eero Pro system. Everything works flawlessly. Instead of HomeKit displaying a sea of red notices that one or more of my devices or scenes is unreachable, all appears as it should: my Hue bulbs are always reachable; my Lutron switches never fail to work; my smart plugs, Ecobee thermostat, wireless garage door opener, wireless weather station, smart locks, security system, Rachio sprinkler boxes, Amazon Echoes, iPhones, iPads, HomePods, Apple TVs, Airplay enabled Airport Expresses, iMacs, DirectTV box, Denon receiver---all stay connected to the network! Bliss, pure utter bliss! If you’re an Apple user who’s been searching for a stress-free, whole-house mesh WiFi system to replace your aging and overburdened Airport Extreme, then this is the mesh network you want. Trust me on this.

I bought this radio because my wife and I were relocating from California to Florida (making it a road trip) and I thought it would be nice to not have to use cell phone just to reach each other. When I first received the device, it looks very rugged and slick looking like any other Cobra product and that is as good as it gets. On initial testing, the product sounded really good, as long as we were in close proximity and up to about 100 feet. At a range of 300 feet, audio clarity started to drop from good to more static/white noise. With a fairly good amount of tree in our neighborhood plus our metal woofing, we thought those elements were distorting the carrier signal thereby effecting the advertised range. Three weeks later we started our trip and ready to put the device to a real test. Fired the radio up, did a quick radio check at 30 feet, clear as day (love'n it. Did a radio check again at 800 feet, still clear as day (Wow, good bye neighborhood, hello open road) . After we've reached flat open terrain out of the mountain in California, mostly flat farming terrain with zero tall buildings in site, and clear skies, I decided to do one more test to see if the device's reported range holds water. Sent my wife out 3/4 mile out from the cargo truck that I was driving, pressed the push-to-talk button and poke, she could not hear a thing. I could clearly see the vehicle ahead of me. In fact I could almost make out some detail of the vehicle, so it couldn't have been too far out of range. At each button press/release and talk still nothing. She eventually dropped back to about 1/2 mile in order to regain audio. We eventually tried the long range several time with different settings just to have the same result plus a lot of static at each settings. In the end, we decided 1/2 mile is the best we can get out this model, accepted it and move on with our travel days. The girls were disappointed so they ended up using their phones instead, and leave the Cobra for discussion about breaking and refueling strategies. I don't know how Cobra could advertise 38 miles or even 3.8 miles range on this device, where in reality it is way less than. Not very happy with the outcome, but it is now too late to return the device. I eventually gave them to my girls so they can play around on our 5 acres property. I won't tell anyone not to buy this product. But I will say, do your homework and test it before you fully commit.

Reviewing the DDR4 version. Overall, very pleased with this motherboard (MB hereafter). Mostly well-thought-out design, good features, and does what it's supposed to. A few details: Pros: Four (4!) NVMe SSD connections on the MB. I only needed one to start (Samsung 980 EVO Pro 2 TB), but it’s good to have room for expansion. NVMe slots are well-designed. built-in heavy-duty heat sinks, and excellent screw-less hold-downs. In fact, good heat sinks all over the MG. None of them got in the way. Nice wireless antennas for the back. You must angle them a bit to get at all the USB connections, but not a big deal. Works well. Nice debug LEDs on the MB to tell you which components aren't working correctly. Fortunately, didn't need them this build, but who knows what future upgrades will bring. Drivers come on a cute little flash drive (good) but the only thing on there is an ISO image. You have to mount it to be able to use it (not difficult, but WHY? Weird). Back plate for connectors comes mounted to the MB. No fiddly attempts to get it snapped into the case first and then trying to align the MB with the connector holes. Much easier this way. Everything was nicely labeled right on the MB itself, such as jumper connections, fan connectors, etc. Didn't really need to refer to the manual much. Things to be aware of: Flashing the BIOS is a little bit of a pain since you must do it from the BIOS screen. No In-Windows utility to do it from there. Installing Windows 11 is a small pain because it requires a network connection during the install process, and the wireless connection using this MB is not available at that time (Windows installer can't find it). You'll need a wired connection to the internet, or as I did, a USB wireless network adapter to plug in during the installation. Once the install gets past connecting you to the internet and finds drivers for the wireless on the MB, everything should be fine. I did note that the basic drivers installed for the wireless during the initial Windows 11 install did not get me a very good wireless connection - about 80 Mbps down. Once I completed all the Windows updates and correct driver installs, that connection shot up to about 370 Mbps, so all was well eventually. BIOS settings documentation could be a lot better. Worked out fine, but I would have liked to see it be a little clearer (or exist at all). Overall, a solid recommended. I am a highly experienced computer user and have been building and rebuilding systems for more than 35 years. This machine was not refurbished very well. Here is why: 1. The PC came with a 480gb SSD rather than the 512gb drive. And this is not a result of the formatted size vs. actual. The starting size of the drive is 480gb, the formatted size is 446gb. 2. The PC was DOA, but because I could immediately tell from the BIOS beeps that the RAM was not installed properly. I removed all the memory and reinstalled correctly, and it booted up fine after that. This required completely dissembling the PC components and reassembling it. I figured that was easier and faster than returning it. 3. Two of the RAM modules appeared to be corroded. After removing and reinstalling, it ran fine so I am leaving them installed for now. I have some extra 4gb modules so I can replace them if they fail prematurely. 4. The 2.5in SSD was not installed properly. It was stuck with double-sided tape to the hard drive mount inside the PC. Cosmetically, it was fine for a refurb. The following are more design issues that did not have a bearing on my rating. A couple of things to keep in mind about this model/form factor. If you have a full size HDD installed, there is no room for SSDs. I ended up moving the SSD to the expansion slot area since I needed the HDD space. I just used the double stick tape and stuck them to the blue plastic slot braced against the expansion card holder. There are three SATA connectors on the motherboard, but only two SATA power cords. One for a drive and one for the DVDRW. I had to get a power splitter to install two SSDs and one HDD. I opted to move the DVD drive to an external case since I rarely use it. This model has one VGA port and two DisplayPorts so I had to get an adapter to connect to my second monitor. This was cheaper and easier than getting a new monitor with a DisplayPort. This unit will not fit RAM with heat sinks because the drive bay is right above the DIMMs. It works fine if you are able to take the heat sinks off two of the four DIMMs. Overall I like the PC and it works well. Full Windows 10 Pro on it.

What I like most about this scanner is ease of use. With my old Bearcat I had to look up the frequencies I wanted and then punch them in. Time consuming. With the Uniden BCD436HP all you have to do is punch in your zip code . It will list catagories like police , fire rescue, air, ambulances, schools , businesses, railroad, military , Ham , pretty much everything except CB. So I clicked on all of them. It was a mistake . The traffic was huge so I went back and unchecked some of the uninteresting categories . Now listening is more pleasurable. The range on this radio is huge. I get clear reception up to 40 miles. Could it be further? Maybe because it only lists my zip codes nearby frequencies. You can punch in whatever though. The rechargeable batteries last a long time. The radio starts beeping when it get weak . Then I just plug it in my laptop via USB to recharge. It has an earphone jack which I use a lot so as not to annoy the family . The radio has a port for an option GPS. Something you would use to find frequencies if you travel a lot A nice feature on the radio is the avoid button. Sometimes the scanner stops on a fringe signal with a lot of static. Pressing the avoid button will remove that frequency till the next time you turn on the radio. As you can see from my photo the screen is a bit tough to see. There is a button to illuminate it but it is limited to 10 seconds. Obviously to save battery life My take on this radio is that it has everything you could want in a scanner. A little pricy but well worth the money as you will have this radio for a long time.

review_text: I bought this primarily to help with online input lag, noticeable evident when playing sports, fighting and shooters online. I was currently connected to Verizon G3100 router via 1GB internet, however I was still having input lag issues. After changing to this router, the improvement was very noticeable, the only disadvantage is that you have to do a reboot at least once per week to keep it operating at its optimum performance level. Rebooting routers, especially gaming routers is not unheard of, so its not a disadvantage that would remove any star from its review. I know some people may wonder how did I get it to work with Verizon, but there is nothing much to it. Simply replace the existing router with this one, if you are not getting any signal internet signal from the ONT (thats the Verizon box outside your house where the fiber optics cable is terminated and from where the ethernet cable/network cable runs inside your house to the existing Verizon router), simply have Verizon activate the ethernet port, mine was already activated, but some may not be. After replacing the Verizon router with this one, thats it. However, if you have cable from Verizon you can will no longer have the channel guide, to fix this you can simply connect the Verizon router to your Netgear Nighthawk router via ethernet cable or buy a Moca adapter if you want to send back the Verizon router and stop paying for it each month.

I’m not an avid adventurer but I do like to take short videos and pictures of a lot of the outdoor activities I participate in. I’ve been looking at action cameras for some time and have been turned off by the price. I really like the GO Pro Hero 5 but just couldn’t justify the cost for what I would use it for. So, I started looking at the lower cost devices on Amazon and other various sources and I came across the Akaso Brave 6. It seemed to have some very good reviews, so I figured I’d give it a try. I’m glad I did. It's about half the cost of a Go Pro but comes loaded with extras that you end up paying more for with a Go Pro. Overall build quality seems very good. The camera is a bit light weight, but in the case, it has a solid feel to it. The quality of the multitude of accessories seems good as well and they feel durable enough for what I will be using them for. Set-up was easy. I charged both batteries with the included two slot battery charger. They charged pretty quickly. Then put one of the batteries in the camera and started it up. I initially got a SD card error but was finally able to get the camera to format it correctly. After playing with the various settings and adjusting them to my liking, I decided to take the camera out for a test drive. Image capture was quite easy and the 20MP images seem sharp and clear. I don’t have any 4k equipment so I set video quality to 1080 60 fps and video quality seems to be very sharp. Colors look good in both the photos and the videos. The included wrist strap remote is an excellent addition, especially when I use the Brave 6 on my kayak. It’s mounted a little too far out of reach so I can simply use the remote to take the pictures or videos. Definitely a plus. Like I mentioned the kit came with a bunch of mounting hardware and accessories so I was able to set up a similar mount on my wife’s kayak in case she wanted to use the camera. There is also a handlebar mount for mounting it on my bike. My only complaint is the app that Akaso uses to link up with the camera. Its crap and the reviews point that out. It crashes frequently on both my iPhone 11 Pro Max and my Google Pixel 3XL, both running up to date operating systems. Devs definitely need to work out the bugs. So, after a few hours of playing with the Brave 6, I can say it’s a good, low cost alternative to the GoPro, especially for the casual user like me. I’ll update my review from time to time during the long term use.

I have resisted getting an Apple Watch for years as quite frankly I don't want the ability to see all my calls and receive or reply to messages at all times but as a fitness fanatic, I did want the ability to track my workouts / heartrate / activity etc. So I settled on a Fitbit Versa 2. However, with the release of the new Fitbit sense with advanced features I went back and forth between that and the Apple Watch 6 - especially as the price gap was not exactly huge; and ultimately went with Apple for the simple reason that I am a huge Peloton fan and this is compatible with that app so I can get workout metrics when on the road. It is sleek and stylish , though personally and this is just a me thing - I have tiny wrists and would have preferred a slightly smaller screen as it takes up near the entire side of my wrist and its not as comfortable as it could be. Set up is relatively easy; most of the set up guide is embedded in the Tips App on Apple or you can just google it. I found it had a bunch of redundant apps already preloaded so I spent some time erasing some and adding others - everyone wants different things - I don't want a world clock, an app to make emojis or multiple stop watches, but I loved the fact that I could add Starbucks, Peloton and Calm - even though it has its own mindfulness app. The only two things I could really see that the Sense has and this does not, is the skin temperature sensor and electrodermal activity assessor which helps track and manage stress levels. The new Apple watch now has monitoring for blood oxygen saturation which is very accurate and as an avid hiker I love this but I can also see that now, more than ever with Covid, this could be a very useful tool; and has added a sleep tracking feature. The electrocardiogram feature is fascinating too. I am not sure I love the associated Fitness app - it shows active calories burned, exercise and how much time you stand, but I dislike the fact that you cannot add specific workouts that you have done, at least not that I can see - its pretty uninspired. I prefer the basic health app that comes on the phone - this is very comprehensive and after using with the watch, it becomes a comprehensive roadmap to your health . The heart health in particular shows your heart rate, ECG, variability, resting heart rate and walking heart rate average and you can set up notifications for low and high heart rate as well as irregular rhythm. The sleep tracker is far more accurate for me with this watch and it includes sleep graphs and analysis, a wake up phase, and you could also add in the premium app which is free for 7 days then $30 a year thereafter ., includes trends, sleep notes, store detection, a sleep aid and online back up of your data. I think personally, if Peloton had compatibility with the Fitbit I might have gone that route, but that said, there is so much this can do, it might just take time to get used to and figure out all the features. Overall I am a fan think there is lots more to discover about this watch

Disclaimer: A pair of these were bought solely for the purpose of a home theater set-up for a guest room and that’s how they’ll be reviewed. PROS: (This part’s quite short) These speakers sound fantastic for the size. They definitely punch above their weight. Even without the sub, the bass delivered from a stereo pair is adequate and punchy although not as low-frequency as one would hope. Mids and treble are distinct generally until around 90% volume after which distortion occurs. Will that’s it for the pros. CONS: As a “home theatre” alternative this is HORRIBLE. Maintaining connection is a major issue. Again these are in stereo pair and a home theater created with my fire stick 4K. Multiple times during the week one speaker in the pair will stop playing. I’d have to tap the physical volume button or unplug the speakers to get them working. In the 2.5 months playing these I’ve also had to delete and re-add my Amazon home theatre set up over two dozen times to get them playing again. The hardware of these speakers is impressive but honestly the software is a tremendous deal breaker. The software also occasionally affects the audio quality. On multiple occasions there’s been a quite noticeable and horrible reverb from the speakers making it sound as though there was an echo in the room. Now let’s talk Dolby Atmos. You may be tempted to buy these as an Atmos system based on the price. I’d definitely avoid that option (note, Atmos is only available wirelessly through your fire TV and not through optical). I’ve played Atmos content from multiple streaming services and there IS NO DISCERNIBLE BETWEEN ATMOS AND STEREO CONTENT! Quite frankly the fact that these speakers are listed as Atmos, is laughable at best. OPTICAL? Yes indeed. These are connected to the TV (LG NANO Cell) via a toslink to mini toslink adapter. That reverb I mentioned earlier, we’ll that always happens when I use the optical connection, no matter what audio options I use on the TV. This happened to a buddy of mine too so I know it’s not just my speakers. The only place where this sort of shined is as an optical output for my Xbox series X. The audio quality and consistency far exceeded that of Amazon’s bogus “wireless home theatre”. It wasn’t without issues however as there was a bit of a lag between the Xbox’s video and the audio. VERDICT: If you’re looking for a smart speaker that packs a bit of a punch (DEFINITELY WAY MORE THAN A HOME POD) then this may be for you. But as a home theatre, this is a definite flop!

review_text: I’m coming from an Epson Home Cinema 3500. Had it for 4-5 years and ran into the “auto iris error” which seems to be somewhat common with some Epson models. I am looking to get it repaired, however I was hoping to take the opportunity to try out a different brand while I sent my Epson in for repair. After a lot of research and watching several video reviews, I settled on the Benq HT3550. This true 4K projector looked legit and everybody raved about it. I was very excited to give it a try. I’ve never experienced light leakage from a projector before but almost everybody talked about how it was an issue in the previous model, but Benq got it right with this one. I have to tell you, in my opinion this is a pretty big deal. Call me OCD if you want but to me there’s no reason for any projector to be putting out such a distracting light border. I included a picture but please know the image cannot capture the prevalence of the border. In person, it is extremely noticeable. I marked how far out the border goes with the yellow line in the picture. You can see it better without the image on the screen, but it looks like I simply need to keystone the image and zoom in to fit the screen, right? That’s why I included the image of the picture on the screen so that you could see the image fills the screen, keystone is great, but you still have the light leakage. To be fair, my wife says that it doesn’t bother her and when you are watching something on the screen, you don’t really notice the leakage as much. However, I do notice it and it really bothers me. Have a mentioned in the review yet that I’m a little bothered by this, ha! Sorry, I just can’t explain how people are overlooking this issue. The best explanation I have read is that all DLP projectors have a little light leakage and people sort of chalk it up to being something you deal with. Bottom line is it is a superb projector and image quality for the price...IF (and it’s a big IF) you are OK with a 6 to 8 inch light border around your screen. I’m not so it’s going back. It’s really unfortunate because I was really excited about the potential of this device.

review_text: Let me start by saying I'm a huge fan of GL.iNet and their products. I've used their travel routers for years, and generally find them to be some of the best on the market in terms of features, size, and performance. Until recently, my primary travel router was the AR750S, which offered perfectly acceptable performance for most hotels in the United States (and abroad). My only real complaint about the 750S - in the world of USB-C - was its microUSB power cable. As a result, I was thrilled to see GL.iNet release a similar router with slightly better specifications but powered by USB-C. Given my recent lack of travel, I didn't pre-order the MT1300 as I usually do, and waited for it to become available on Amazon to save a couple of bucks on shipping. My copy arrived last weekend, and, frankly, it's a bit of a letdown. The main issue to be aware of is size. The MT1300 is significantly larger than the routers it replaces (AR750S, MV1000W) in every dimension, and is noticeably heavier as well. It feels substantial and well built - and while this is something I think would be great for a router sitting at home, the extra size and weight is hard to justify if you're carrying it around the country on a frequent basis. A comparison of the MT1300 (left) with the MV1000W (center) and AR750S (right) in the pictures should give you a good idea of the added bulk. In fact, the MT1300 has the same footprint and almost the same weight as the RavPower WD009 - a router that contains an internal 6700mAh battery! I wouldn't necessarily have a problem with that if there were a significant performance boost, but the modest gains certainly don't offset the extra bulk, in my opinion. In fact, for those looking for speed an MV1000W with a USB wireless dongle is likely a better solution, offering 2x the throughput than the MT1300 and 3x the throughput of the AR750S, albeit at a higher price point. The bottom like for me is that the MT1300 is too big and too heavy in a world where the MV1000W and/or AR750S exist. I would probably carry it instead of the WD009 given its performance and GL.iNet's excellent UI, but it's hard to justify the MT1300 over the other two. In particular, if you have the AR750S and you're considering whether to upgrade - I would pass. If you really need the speed, you're better off with the MV1000W, and if you don't you're probably better off with the AR750S - even if it means carrying along an extra charging cable.

The “Epic Lab Edition Earbuds” from “JLab” are a set of relatively high-end Bluetooth earbuds, designed to deliver excellent sound reproduction and effective background noise cancelling.Initial set up (like most earbuds of this nature) is quick, simple and pretty self-explanatory. Just pair them up to your phone or whatever device you’re using, and away you go. Simple!When being worn, the earbuds feel very comfy in your ear, and not too cumbersome or invasive within your ear canal. They’re also quite lightweight, so although you’ll feel them in your ear (like you would with any earphones or earbuds), they’re not overly noticeable. Look-wise they don’t stick out too much, with the earbuds only protruding a short distance compared with other earbuds.The silicone ear gels that come with the earbuds allow for different sized ears. I use the smallest ear gels that come with them and find these fit my ears perfectly. When in, the earbuds don’t feel like they’ll fall out easily or anything, although I’m not sure I’d go running with them in, as they don’t feel perfectly secure to that degree.As with most modern earbuds, these ones come with a handy hard-plastic charging case. To charge the earbuds you just pop them into the designated little slots within the case, and they’ll instantly start charging. The case holds charge before it too needs charging up. You can of course, have the case plugged into a power source (using the handy integrated USB cable that comes attached to the case) whilst the earbuds are charging – in effect charging the earbuds straight from the source.Sound quality wise, in my opinion these earbuds are excellent. Ok, so they’re not exactly absolute audiophile quality, but to be honest, they’re not far off. There’s a rich, relatively deep bass and they’re able to reproduce complex layers of notes without any particularly noticeable muffling or amalgamation. Acoustic tones are also very well-rounded and provide a natural sound that resonates through each note.The active noise cancelling is excellent too. It successfully blocks out any surrounding noise, with just the music you’re listening too filling the quiet void.All in all, I’ve been incredibly happy and impressed with the earbuds. I use them for walks and commuting, which really works well for me as the active noise cancelling they offer is excellent. Highly recommended.

I got the i3 8GB memory 128GB SSD Platinum version, which at the time of this review is the top of the line model sold on Amazon. THE GOOD It's physically beautiful. It's sleek, thin, lightweight. I'm mostly a Mac guy having left Windows after MS messed around with the start button and tiles with Windows 8. I had tried to come back a couple times here and there, but 8 and 10 seemed so dated after having switched to Mac. Windows 11 changes that for me and makes me open to coming back to Windows. It's beautiful and modern. They've removed a lot of the old Control Panel options that came from XP a long time ago, so that's good. Some are still there I discovered, but for the most part settings is greatly improved.... Windows 11 is great, but not great enough to make this tablet a keeper. THE BAD Really, Microsoft? A goofy proprietary charger? Not sure if the USB-C port just doesn't take a charge or if mine is defective, but I couldn't get a charge with my MacBook Pro USB-C charger/cable or Samsung S21 Ultra charger. Instead, mine only charges with MS's proprietary charger which means now I'm hauling around yet another charger and cable wherever I go instead of just one USB-C charger for all devices. I could almost live with that inconvenience, but what I can't live with is the speed. I understand that there are other Surfaces that have better/faster specs, but they are also bigger. I wanted a small and capable Windows tablet, but alas this one is only small. This may be an unfair comparison, so take this with a grain of salt, but I happened to get a new iPad Mini 6 the same day. I unboxed and fired up both at the same time and was up and running on the iPad in a quarter of the time even with Apple's annoying Apple ID Fort-Knox password verifications. The Surface was slow out of the gate. At first I thought the touch screen didn't work because when prompted for the usual username stuff, the keyboard would not appear..... oh wait, it did.... just 2-3 seconds AFTER taping on the text box. I thought maybe I was doing something wrong since I've never used Windows tablet before, but eventually it became apparent that the tablet was so extremely slow that even typing text would have serious lag. Then there's the usual and annoying Windows updates. Oh well, just part of the ecosystem, but geez! It took 45 minutes from unboxing to being able to even check out the desktop. I downloaded some desktop stock brokerage programs and they took forever to open. So slow. These aren't super resource heavy programs like Photoshop. They are fairly simple, yet they were just too slow to be usable for quick stock market trading. CONCLUSION So beautiful but just too slow for me. The touchscreen seems finicky and programs take forever to load and use. If MS comes out with a supped up version of this, I would definitely take another look. But if this is as fast as it can run, it's a hard pass. I'd hate to see the tablets with lesser processors. Buy if speed isn't a concern. Pass if you value your time.

This is personally my second most liked pair of headphones. Deaccent hardware cursed with bad software.To start Bluetooth connection has been great and connects consistently and quickly. The connection stability has also been great as compared to other headphones its had very few dropped connections or patchy audio, even at a considerable distances.Noise cancelation, these are personally the best noise cancelling headphones as someone who commutes by bus which is very noise these have provided the best performance, even beating out more expensive options such as the soundcore Liberty 4 NC by a margin.The mic has been good, however robotic. What I mean by this calls sound fine but to people on the other side, voice sounds clear and isolated but robotic. There is probably some processing going but over all its not a bad thing as audio is clear despite sounding off.Sound, Unfortunately this is where it begins to falls short. The audio sounds ok, but in my opinion the bass is uncontrolled in the sense its a bit over the top. While rest sounds ok, with deaccent-ish clarity. With anc on vs off the audio does sound very different. The audio out of the box in my option is leaning on the inadequate side compared to what it is really capable of. A few firmware updates and messing in the eq it sounds good. Over all would recommend if your willing to spend a good few mins adjusting things.App. This is where it begins to fall flat. The app was buggy and the connection to the app was not always there which made it a headache to use when trying to use the app. The app if anything was the worst bit about this headphone, Personally I would recommend just to get there to update and adjust eq and change what the buttons do (like anc modes) so you don't need to return back to the software.The Multi-point over all for me was the deal-breaker for me unfortunately. As I work mainly in IT I use a lot of devices. The problem I had with the feature was not stability but choosing which device is connected and this is in part thanks to the app again. So for regular people who will only use 2 devices at most its fine.Comfort, The headphones for me where ok but long periods of time was not very comfortable and the ear tips them selves not a fan but they are fine. The overall shape of the ear bud is probably more suited to larger ears and the stem design, for my ear, at least did not sit well as I thought. Again theses are personal preferences as the person I gifted these on to said the fit was fine. But compared to his ears mine are more flat and soft, this MAY have played a role.Over all this is a ok product as the product was fine, but with app related compilations and the over all lack of clarity in the audio was the deciding factor for me to move to the soundcore 4 nc which is as if the time of writing £20 more. So if your looking for headphones on a tight £50 budget then yes. How ever if your able to spend the additional the amount of great options increase. On a final note the battery life was not the best when anc is on, this is expected but to the extent this happened not good,Note: Firmware update sin my experience have made significant differences so updating is a must and it is possible the issues addressed could be fixed in the future.

I bought this antenna with great expectations. I used LAVA antennas for more than ten years. The first LAVA antenna lasted almost a full ten years before the rotator motor died. It had been wonderful and I was able to receive ALL broadcast stations in Maine, not only those within 30 miles of where I live, but those from southern Maine, the broadcast towers of which are all more than 100 miles away. The new Lava antenna failed. I worked for nearly two months with Lava customer service to try to figure out why the new antenna wouldn't pick-up the relatively near by signals from the NBC affiliate. That signal is the lowest frequency and the new antenna just wouldn't "see" it at all. That antenna JUST DOESN'T WORK. I bought this 5 Star antenna chiefly because of its slightly larger size and antenna component design and placement. The specifications indicated it should work and the added benefit of the rotor is that since some of the signals we were used to receiving were from the opposite direction of others, the results should have been promising. The 5-Star antenna failed just as badly as the LAVA antenna failed. Since I am not an engineer I decided to spend some money and consult with someone who understood all of the physical aspects of over the air tv. The result after lengthy consultation was that while my antenna location and elevation above the ground was fine, the antenna amplfiers in the antennas that I had on hand... a new LAVA antenna AND a 5-Star antenna...were simply not strong enough or of high enough quality to reliably pick up the channels, particularly the low band broadcasts (NBC). So I give up. Despite the excellent results we had originally from 2011-2020, I have come to the decision that these low cost antennas have become of such cheap quality that they are no longer suitable for reliable reception unless one is only a few miles from the broadcast towers. If the antenna is further away from a broadcast tower than ten miles or so, there is no guarantee that it will "see" the television signals. I am returning the 5-Star antenna and I am very disappointed.

My Sangean HDR-16 HD radio is okay, but I hope units like this will work better maybe as soon as 4 years from now. When I saw the pics of this radio online it looked cheaply made to me, but I needed a radio and ordered it anyway. In person the radio looks well made and better than the pictures, and the plastic is not like cheap brittle looking plastic you might see on 99cent store products. I live about 22 miles east of downtown Los Angeles and the radio stations come in fine. My favorite rock station KROQ was coming in even before I extended the antenna; but you should extend the antenna for tuning into stations. The Sangean radio definitely sounds better than my old General Electric radio alarm clock. On the General Electric radio when you tuned into KROQ another station's signal would overlap sometimes. This doesn't happen with the Sangean. I use the Sangean mostly in my bedroom or my home office, so I don't really have it super loud. If you want to blast loud music out of your garage into the neighborhood I don't think this unit is big enough for that. One problem with the radio, and this has only happened once, is that it was playing and then it went silent. It somehow got turned off, but I don't know how that happened. Another problem I had was that I put radio station presets on the Sangean. I unplugged the Sangean from my bedroom and set it up in the kitchen and the presets would not work, and I had to tune in to my station manually. When I plugged in the Sangean back in my bedroom again the presets appeared to be messed up and I had to punch in all the radio station presets again. The presets worked fine in my carport. There might be something weird about my kitchen. You should test your unit in different parts of your house while you can still return it. The Sangean will also work with four C batteries which can be a little bit hard to slide in. I was afraid of breaking the metal contact coil in the battery compartment. I think they should have made the battery compartment door longer so that you can see the batteries fully; not like it is now where you can see 2 batteries and 2/3's of the remaining batteries that you slide in first. Because after you slide in the first 2 batteries it is a struggle to squeeze one of the batteries between the "slid in battery" and the "coil contact"; and like I said I was afraid of breaking off the coil. I have used the Sangean with my LG cellular phone to play MP3s. I connected a cable on my phone where the headphones go and the other end to the Sangean's "AUX IN" input to play songs through the Sangean's speakers. This cable is not included; I used one from an old Timex radio clock. Sometimes I do this when I want to hear MP3s but the desktop PC is running a program that is using a lot of memory and I can't have memory resources diverted for playing MP3's. I like that when you tune into some stations the display will show the song and artist. What you see on the display depends on the radio station. Some will display the song and artist; others will display the show's name and/or DJ; some will display a message to download their listening app; and others won't show anything at all. This is cool like for a classical music station I sometimes tune into and they'll show song and artist information of people like Beethoven, and they'll list if it's the whatever opus or whatever thing in G major, etc. - and I know very little about classical music; so hopefully you'll have an interesting local radio station like that set up with the updated technology. I would like to give this product 2.5 stars, but it will be rounded off to 3 stars, and that's still about right.

The concept is fantastic - add the ability to put another vertical pole in your shortest leg to make both a two way stand, and also an adjustable third leg for uneven surfaces. Despite the high price compared to other stands, I bought one, thrilled by the adaptability. It arrived today. All the good things I expected are present, including the hook/clamp that can hold the second vertical when not in use, or hook batteries and sandbags or camera bags. There are lots of great design features here. Put there are some big negatives. All the locking handles are plastic, instead of metal. If I were using this as a location stand that was moving around a lot, I'd return it for that reason alone. With rough use, those are going to break. There are some other pieces on the top locking rings that appear to be plastic as well. For this price, this should be an all steel stand. Also the low leg, that is also the additional vertical doesn't extend out as far from the body as the short leg on my other C stands. On my flashpoint stand, that leg's foot is 14" from the vertical pole. On the Savage, it's 11" That makes the stand less stable in the two directions around that leg, and it's noticeable. If you push it towards the high leg, it resists tipping much better than if you push it away from it. That difference is a function of the design, and as long as you make sure you're using the stand properly, with the high leg aimed at your subject, it's probably fine, but it's definitely something to be aware of. All in all, you have to consider this stand as big trade-offs, giving up some stability for the novel and useful design. But there's no reason for the use of plastic at this price, and for that reason I'm only giving it three stars. I'll keep it for use in my studio, but I won't travel with it much, and won't be buying any others.

I have Spectrum internet and wanted to get a WiFi router so I would not have to keep paying the router rental fee. I decided on the Speedefy AX450 because it has the newer 802.11ax (WiFi-6) technology at a good price. I was glad to see that it didn't force me to register an account and provide an email like many of the other router manufacturers. I was able to make it work with my Spectrum modem, a Hitron E31H2V1. However, it was difficult, and I don't recommend it unless you are familiar with setting up WiFi routers. A Quick Start Guide (one large sheet of paper (folded) comes in the box. It goes through the basic steps of connecting power and an ethernet cable from the modem. It has nothing on the router settings. It refers you to a phone app or the website for that info. Because of other complaints about the phone app, I decided to do everything with a browser connection (use 192.168.3.1). If you have an existing WiFi router, I recommend you first connect by browser to that router and write down or take photos of all the settings. Since I have over 12 devices connected to WiFi, I decided to change the SSIDs and WiFi password on the AX450 to match the existing ones, so I would not have to reprogram the WiFi on all my devices. Since my existing WiFi already had 2G and 5G radios, I set up the AX450 to maintain separate 2G and 5G logons. The default is a single logon which automatically selects 2G or 5G depending on the device, and that might work for you. For me the router connection type is DHCP, but for some reason I could not get it to work with the Spectrum DNS servers. I ended up using a public DNS server, Google, at 8.8.8.8. Also several times when I made changes to the AX450 settings, it did not seem to respond. What worked for me was to deenergize the modem and the AX450, energize the modem and wait for it to have full internet connectivity, then energize the AX450, and that usually fixed it. I read all the tips on the Speedefy website, but there is no manual that lists all the AX450 settings and what they do. I successfully set up the Guest account and verified that those logged into the Guest account cannot see or access the other devices on the network. I could not verify speed increases, as I only pay for 200 Mbps and both of these WiFi routers reached that number. Based on the WiFi signal strength on my phone, the signal strength was comparable to my old router, perhaps even a little less in spots. I have a 1700 ft2 house, all one level, with the router in the center of the house. In areas far away from the AX450, with less signal strength, the WiFi speed drops off substantially. So I am satisfied with this purchase but it sure would be better to have a manual which explains all the settings on the AX450, like some other manufacturers provide.

review_text: I took a risk and bought this case blind, having been unable to find it on display at my local microcenter. Hope this review helps you. First impressions, in person: it is beautiful. The white matte finish truly looks luxurious, clean and striking. Owing to the fact also that the case is a heavy solid metal chassis, everything feels expensive and sturdy. (I'm coming from a white NZXT H500i which feels cheap and trivial compared to this) There are no plastic parts to the body of the case; it's either solid metal or tempered glass. (I think just the cable covers and power button are hard plastic). The pictures don't do it justice, it really is impressive to look at in person, and even more impressive once it's been built in. What I liked/loved: Beautiful build quality overall. Sturdy, solid and has a heft to it. Feels expensive. PC comes wrapped in a black fabric. White Matte is a beautiful color and update to this case. Once you've finished your build, the RGB effect from the fans + the built in case RGB is subtle but a beautiful accent to your build. Love it. All controllable from MOBO. A lot of thought was put into assembly and disassembly; panels come off in a way that makes logical sense and are easy to figure out and to do so. All the screws, peripherals, etc come in a plastic toolbox, and that itself comes in a beautiful box with 4 HDD cages individually wrapped, and a beautiful glossy manual. Feels expensive and well thought out. Wonderful to build in, lots of room above the motherboard for cable management, and you can take the top off the case to further increase room for big hands. Cable management on the back is also very well planned out, many channels for cables and i have 5 SSDs mounted to the back of the plastic cable covers - i was initially worried - but it actually all functions very well and routing the wires is also easy, even all the sata cables work fine with the cable covers closed. Airflow is way better than my NZXT (but what isn't) - the front has an airflow gap, the top has holes for exhausting air and of course the back has a big hole for the included 140mm RGB fan. Overall, aircooling in this case works great. There is so much room for storage - which is why i bought this case - i haven't even exhausted all the drive slots (maybe halfway) - and i'm out of SATA headers on my motherboard. You can fit 4 3.5 HDDs in the bottom and 9? i think around the back of the mobo + on the cable covers. Vertical GPU slot for my older 2 slot GTX 1080 works great cos it's meant for 3 slot gpus, so it's actually not up against the glass. Temps are fine. What I didn't like/issues: The main reason why i'm not giving this 5 stars is because the door hinges came corroded. So it was very difficult and scary to remove the glass doors. I had to wiggle them upwards vertically to slowly get them off, feeling scared i'd break something in the process. Luckily, reaching out to Phanteks customer support was great and they sent me new hinges rightaway once verifying my purchase - once new hinges were installed, it worked as expected. Not sure how or why those old ones got corroded. There was a dent in my shipping box, so maybe the air exposed it to the elements? I'm also not a big fan of... the fans included for one reason: they make this hum when above 30-40% - the hum gets louder and resounds throughout the case (resonance) and gets really annoying. Solution was to limit the fans. I also gave Phanteks feedback. Cooling is still fine as they are big fans and the case has a lot of room for air to move through it. Other points of concern, as others have pointed out - removing one glass panel makes the case unbalanced if the other glass panel is opened. Not an issue if it is shut, but if you open the other panel, the case will tip over, even with components inside. I couldn't get the built in fan hub to work rightaway, i think on hindsight it was probably me not configuring my mobo to match its settings (PWM) - i can't remember if my motherboard had that particular fan header configured to DC. So i abandoned using it and had my own Deepcool fanhubs that i ended up using. Not a fan of the case's USB C header cable that connects to the motherboard - it sticks out a lot and doesn't stay in easily. Thought about buying an adapter but that costs $15 just for aesthetics so i just let it be. Cable length is also short so it kind of straddles the cable tie region on the back. I also didn't like that the case doesn't come with SSD mounts for behind the MOBO. There are 3 slots here but u can't use them unless you buy more stuff from Phanteks. At this price point, i think at least 1 should be included. Features I haven't tested: Dual system - i don't have an mATX board and also the bracket doesn't come included. I did buy a Phanteks Revolt X for future expansions, so maybe i'll update here one day when i do expand. PSU has been working great though.

As an IT pro of 15+ years, I'm always excited to be on the forefront of the latest technology. I jumped on the Wi-Fi 6(ax) bandwagon last Christmas and have been encouraging others to do the same in order to future proof their in-home wireless experience. Fast forward to Holiday season 2021, and we are now getting our first Wi-Fi 6 USB adapter which will make adoption rates to the new standard much more appealing with a simple plug and play solution. Gone are the days of drivers on discs. I simply plugged in the device and it popped up similar to when you plug in a thumb drive with a setup.exe to install the drivers for the device. I was connected to my D-Link DIR-X5460 Wi-Fi 6 router within minutes and immediately began running some speed test to put it through it's paces. I always use multiple testing sites (speedtest, speakeasy and google fiber) using an internet connection of 600mbps down/10mbps up. On my initial run, my speed results were coming in about ten percent slower than my other Wi-Fi 6 devices all in the same room near my router (but still much faster than my built in WiFi-5 card I have in my laptop) I was sort of shocked and disappointed with my initial findings but I ran a second series of test just to make sure the first run wasn't a fluke. I'm happy to report the second series of tests performed right on par with the other Wi-Fi 6 devices in my house. I also observed that sometimes, the adapter wanted to connect at the older 2.4 GHz radio instead of the 5Ghz radio which had me disconnecting and reconnecting several times in some case to catch the right radio that provides the best performance. To be fair, my One plus 8 phone also does this occasionally so it could be an auto negotiation issue between devices and my router. I'm glad it comes with a stand as the adapter itself is fairly bulky compared to similar devices. While you can plug it directly into your computer, it would most certainly be blocking other ports you would need to access right beside it. $70 is the hefty price tag you would expect for the first of it's kind product which may be hard to justify when you could easily find comparably performing Wi-Fi 5(ac) equipment at a fraction of the cost. If you already have a good Wi-Fi 5 setup, I would certainly hold off on devices like this until A)The new 6E devices are available and B) More companies start offering Wi-Fi 6 USB adapters which should drive the cost to the consumer down in due time. But if you already have a Wi-Fi 6 router, a legacy device using Wi-Fi4(N) or slower and cash to spare, this is best solution on the market to bring you up to date. Pros: -First Wi-Fi 6 USB adapter on the market -Easy to install (drivers are right on the adapter itself) -Can provide blazing speeds when configured optimally -Comes with it's on stand Cons: -Expensive -Bulky (without the stand it will certainly block other ports) -Performance inconsistencies (Dropped it down another star due to this)

review_text: Overall I got what I signed up for. It's a PCIe Gen 3.0 x1 lane adapter, so expect all NVMe M.2 SSDs to be significantly slowed down due to the limitation of the bus itself. Gen 3.0 x1 is rated for a little less than 1GB/s, factor in all the overhead and ecc and you'll get around 800MB/s effective sequential read/write speeds. However, that's not the entire story. Random Q1D1 performance is what matters the most for daily use. And this adapter did not affect that performance AT ALL. I got the same random q1d1 performance compared to when I used the same SSD on a PCIe Gen 3.0 x4 lanes (I had to give that up because I used the slot for something else and hence why I needed this). So expect slower large file copying, but otherwise you get the same performance. My only 1 star loss for this is the annoying green BRIGHT LED.

After trying a couple of smaller, good antennas, with only minor success, I finally broke down and did what I should have done from the beginning, and I bought this big fella. It arrives in a box a good 6' tall or more. The antenna is in three sections inside the box. I watched a number of videos online about assembling the antenna, as well as reading several reviews, here. I installed this in my attic, hanging it only slightly below the rafters (see the attached photo). I used antennaweb.org to see the best source of channels and where to point the antenna. A handy tool to have is a compass app that I downloaded and used to point this in the area listed on the antennaweb.org website. The antenna, when fully assembled, is around 16 feet long, The VHF antenna rods open up and the full span is a good 6'-8' wide. It definitely "explores the space" 😉 But you need those wide rods to pull in the low-VHF and hi-VHF channels cleanly. I am in the Atlanta market, living northwest of town. Per antennaweb I am in the neighborhood of 25-40 miles from the available stations. This thing pulls in LOADS of channels. I used the auto-finder on both of my TVs to populate the channel list, and I am pulling in more than 90 TV channels! Bear in mind, that includes there being multiple channels being broadcast per station. Picture quality is fantastic! Now I need to make a decision upon which streaming service to purchase, as I'm not getting sports channels like ESPN (college football season will be here before we know it). I am SUPER-HAPPY with this antenna. It is pulling in everything spectacularly! Low-VHF, Hi-VHF, all of the UHF channels. This is the one you want.
