review_text: There are already many reviews for this generation of Samsung fitness/smart watch so I'll just hit the highlights of why I like it. First, I find the S3 to be a feature rich and stylish watch. I very much like being able to access the watch's features using the bezel wheel. No tapping the screen or swiping to see information if I don't choose to. I have a Samsung phone so the watch and App were easy for me to set up and understand. The watch's screen is bright, sharp, colorful, and there are many modifiable watch faces available. I don't keep the GPS feature turned on so my battery life is a good 2 days. I have tried a couple of other fitness watches over the years, some with much longer battery life, but I have mostly used a version of Fitbit watch since 2015. Because I wanted to try something new and after watching/reading a number of reviews for this watch, I purchased a renewed one for around $100. I have been having fun with the watch and have nothing bad to say about it except step counts and some fitness info does not match up with my Fitbit watch results. I guess I will have to calculate a fudge factor in my head for the difference. Anyway, I liked the watch enough to buy a renewed S4 {next gen} watch that offers a few more features over the S3 such as an important new OS. Luckily, the Samsung App allows me to enable 2 watches so I can keep 1 watch charged all the time and switch back and forth between them. Samsung has promised 4 years of software updates so I will have plenty of time with these watches to try out the Samsung ecosystem before I have to decide to move on {or not} to their next gen watch. I believe S3 support updates end the Fall of 2023. review_text: I received this turntable yesterday. I bought it to transfer my vinyl records to digital for playing on my iPhone XR. I used a USB stick and the record recorded fine. I then transferred the record to Apple Music on my Mac. It worked fine there but when I tried to transfer it to my iPhone it would not carry over. Called Apple and spent 2 hours on the phone with them. It turns out the sample rate used to record via the turntable is too low (32). It needs to be 44.1 for it to play on my iPhone. I'm not technical but I understood this. So, I now have to use software I was trying to avoid (Audacity) to convert the 32 sample rate to 44.1. It's a small pain but nonetheless it's an extra step I was not anticipating. If someone from DigitNow is reading this, is there a way to change the sample rate for the turntable? If not, this should be explained in your product description. Update: I wrote to DigitNow regarding the iPhone issue. They responded promptly. The turntable does not allow for changing the sample rate. Therefore, beware that you will need to use Audacity to modify your recordings if you want to transfer them to an iPhone.

For the price this camera is just OK. Here's what I've experienced: Daylight performance is good enough. Good motion detection, perhaps just a bit too sensitive but that's something that can be adjusted through the VicoHome app. I'll write more about the app below. I tried both SD and HD quality but couldn't see any real difference in the recorded daylight when viewed on either my phone or tablet. When set to higher motion detection sensitivity every car that drove by on my busy street 90 feet away triggered a recording. At night the b&w images are only good out to 20 feet or so. The included mounting bracket is OK, seems sturdy enough though I have had trouble finding a good place to mount it on my house. That's my problem not the camera's though. I have had it running outdoors for 24 hours and the camera still shows 99% battery. That's much better than expected. I have Alexa in my home but have not found any way to pair the camera with Alexa. If it's possible it's not documented anyplace. Now for the app: PROS- It works and controls the camera well.Viewing the videos from the Internet is handy BUT that feature will only be available during the 30 day trial period. Watching videos recorded to an internal SD card is more cumbersome but it works. CONS-The camera sends your images to a server somewhere in China! I hate that! After the 30 day trial I expect that I'll start getting requests from China for a credit card to keep the service active. That's not going to happen. The app really eats battery power on my Android phone. Most power hungry app I've ever installed. SUMMARY- It's a plus that the camera can work with just an SD card and no subscription though without 100% functionality. Will I mount this camera permanently? That remains to be seen. Will I keep it? Probably, because it's OK for what I paid for it and it's not worth the hassle to return it but I can imagine a time in the future when it just ends up unused in a box with other failed high tech gadgets. Time will tell. Would I buy more or recommend to a friend? No, probably not.

For years I’ve used an Apple airport time machine. I loved that thing but they quit making them in 2013 and also stopped updating the software. The auto backup feature was very nice and reassuring. Over the years I’ve begun to turn my house into a smart home. For a while my airport seemed to be playing nicely with all of my new devices. Then, gradually, newer devices that I purchased started dropping constantly. WiFi switches, WiFi plugs etc. I thought that it was the cheaper brand switches that I was buying and it never occurred to me that it was the router. Enter eero. I don’t even remember what prompted me to look for a new router but I’m so glad I did. I used to have to reset all of my WiFi plugs every few days. They would just lose connection. Not anymore. I have 50+ smart devices in my home. Everything is smart enabled and this little router is able to manage them all. No issues. I’m able to view and manage all of my smart devices with the eero app. It’s very convenient. I get alerts if anything new connects or wants access. It seems very secure. I have the option to create profiles so I can pause groups of devises. I get that this could be helpful for parents with children.. but for me I don’t have much of a use unless I want to use Alexa to mess with my boyfriend and turn off his access. But I would never. d: I do however like that I have the ability to ask Alexa to restart the router although I have yet to find the need to do this so far. My old router had to be restarted all the time. So far so good. My only con it that there are only two Ethernet ports. One in, one out. So I had to purchase a tplink switch for extra ports. My airport time machine had many ports but it was also over 3x the price of the eero originally. The tplink switch was only $16 so not a bad compromise. Overall I am very pleased with this little router.

I have had many Garmin devices over the years and no matter what, every watch always seemed HUGE on my wrist. The watch I was wearing prior to buying this one is the Venu. This watch is much smaller than the Venu and it looks really nice. I didn’t give it 5 stars because there is no built in GPS but it does use your phone as a GPS. It also doesn’t estimate distance when you are not using GPS which I found interesting but over all for what I need it for right now, it does everything I want. If I want GPS built in I will just use my Venu for those activities but right now I am doing more weight lifting training so it works fine for that.

The watch feels premium with a heavy-duty metal frame. It has a nice weight to it and doesn't feel cheap. The screen is nicely curved for easy swiping. One thing that is obvious is the wide bezel around the actual screen. The rotating crown on the right side has only one function and that is press, even though it rotates. The 1.55inch screen looks nice even in bright light conditions. However, there is no auto-brightness. I was not able to find a double tap to activate function and the screen has to be activated with a twist of the wrist or with the crown button. Swiping and tapping is very responsive. The charging port is similar to other TicWatches with a magnetically held charger that has two prongs. The magnets are weak and when the watch is sitting on its back the prongs get easily detached. Even light bumps will release the magnets. It’s too bad that it’s not compatible with other TicWatches, like to TicWatch 3 Pro. The watch takes regular 20mm watch bands and it’s easy to swap them with the quick release. The settings on the watch are limited to the very basics and most of the watch settings can be changed with the Mobvoi app. The Mobvoi app has only a limited and rather poor-quality watch face selection available (obviously this is a personal opinion). I wish there were more customizations on each of the watch faces available, e.g. adding sensor readings. There is only a single barebones watch face available that has most of the readings on it. It takes forever to transfer or update a watch face, most times a minimum of 2min. Even with the phone close to the watch the Bluetooth connection failed occasionally, and I had to reconnect through the software to find the watch. I hope this gets fixed via a firmware update. The notifications are limited which is to be expected with a focus on health tracking. If you are looking for a smart watch then I recommend looking elsewhere. Sensors in no particular order: Sleep: It does not recognize the start of my sleep and therefore is consistently short by 2 hours based on actual sleep. I was wearing three watches on my wrist for comparison (Fitbit Inspire 2 and Galaxy Watch 4). Both of the other watches were within 20min of my actual sleep. Maybe another problem with the Ticwatch GTH Pro on the right wrist rather than the typical left wrist for most uses. Screen capture from G4 and Ticwatch GTH Pro attached. The Ticwatch also reports a majority of deep sleep which rarely happens based on the other two watches which are more consistent between the two. For now, both the length and quality of sleep are unreliably recognized. Heart rate: The heart rate monitor works well and shows values similar to the G4 and Inspire2. Skin temperature: I love that the watch has skin temperature measurements. It seems to fluctuate with my exercise (outside versus inside) and should be a good indicator of the emergence of sickness like flu etc. SpO2: This is rather unreliable and random and fluctuates to extreme values during the day. When activated through the watch and holding still, the values are more reliable. Screen capture attached. Step counter: The step counter is pretty accurate and giving results similar to the other two watches I was wearing. Wellness score or Arty: This is a hit and miss during measurement for me. I often have to try 2-3 times before it reads and very often it tells me that the reading is not consistent. Especially when wearing on my right wrist the readings work only 20% of the time. This is pretty frustrating. The values can’t be compared to other watches and it’s scientific meaning is questionable to me for now, e.g. eCAP and HSX or ArtyAge. My arterial age based on the data ranges between 20-30 and 50-60 in the same time range. I wish I was that young. The inconsistencies are likely coupled to the reading problems with the sensor itself on my right wrist. I am sure that using the watch for a prolonged time there might be value in these measurement results. The scanning is more robust on my left wrist, so my conclusion is that this is working most likely well for lefties. Summary: Some issues in a few places of the software and sensors. This might have to do with me wearing it on my right wrist. The Arty features will take some time to get used to before they can be used reliably to track health, I think. One of the key features compared to expensive smart watches like the Galaxy Watch 4 is the battery life. After 5 days, the battery still had a good 56% left, indicating the promised 7-10 days of battery life. Overall, a pretty solid smart watch for health tracking at a price of just below $100, e.g. heart related features.

Update as of 1/14/22: Well,,, unfortunately my NAS started throwing some power errors. After some research and digging into the hardware, I found that when installing and because of the tight fit, I cut some solder traces and tore off a resistor from the motherboard when installing it. It was so tight, I had to drill out the motherboard bracket grommets, both top and bottom, to get the MoBo out to inspect and ended up tearing off another resistor. $350.00 down the drain. If you do decide to ourchase, take so e precautions and predrill the motherboard bracket grommets out, install the motherboard and then use a small 4/32 x 1/4" machine screws to fasten them back. I should have done this before hand. It is just too tight of a fit to get a real motherboard installed in it without doing this, or damaging any of your components. The layout just doesn't quite make sense. Something the manufacturer should have done instead of using grommets to fasten the pot metal pieces. Good luck!

There is a lot to like here. It's well styled, it has a lot of good heatsink work in place. Good attachment points for most things, dual holes drilled for different cooler types, and a really solid I/O panel in the back. The instruction manual is fairly clear throughout and everything feels well constructed. Generally speaking I really like the board, but it did have some hiccups that I will detail here. Please keep in mind as it stands today (having built this system last week) I would not change my purchase, but I'd like to help people understand a few quirks. First, and it's been a long long time since I've seen this, out of the box no WiFi worked without updating everything and transferring some drivers over from my old PC which I thankfully hadn't gutted. This does create an issue when installing Windows 11 which now REQUIRES an internet connection without some command line work. If you're new to tech or building a PC this is something you can look up online, but this could be a large hurdle for some users. If your office or room isn't near the router you'll need to mess with some settings or get a long cable. Second, the memory DIMM management for anything over stock is extremely unstable with the shipped firmware and UEFI/BIOS flash. I have 64GB of Corsair Vengeance 3200MHz RAM on the board and everything defaults to 2133, but any increase to this (XMP profile or otherwise) while I was still setting up and tuning lead to massive BSOD events until the BIOS was flashed. That being said, the flash is now available (and even as of this month the patch notes for the current version note DIMM stability improvement). The flash process is smooth, another thumb drive moment, but you basically flash it while the system is is a special boot state with a specific USB port and a toggle in the back. Everything went fine here, and at that point the AI Tweaker profiles and XMP were good to go and stable. Lastly, depending on your cooling you may get some errors. There is an AIO_Pump header on the board and a CPU_FAN header (as is pretty normal), quite a few (and growing) numbers of AIO pumps are cutting down on the leads they have coming off the heatsink unit. This is good for cables and power draw, but it does mean there is no CPU Fan lead to run out in the case of my Corsair H150i Elite Capellix Liquid Cooler. This will essentially not let the Motherboard pass a POST without disabling monitoring of this. It can be done with a simple settings toggle you'll have to search for and then you should be good. Other posters here have noted that that creates a situation where you're not seeing CPU temps, that's not at all the case. You still have full access to your CPU core temps in whatever software you choose, you're literally just not monitoring a fan speed or having the motherboard adjust that fan automatically. It will still work with your radiator fans and monitor temps as normal, the BIOS even judges your cooler over time to know how much voltage it can push in the AI Tweaker mode. Everything else mounted easy and was fine to setup. The heatsinks for the M.2 drives are pretty cool, I used the lower 2 of the 4 for my dual NVMe drives as I've heard the upper two can split power off the PCIe GPU rail. My 3080 RTX mounted to the board fine, I did have to reach in and flick the clip in as it did not lock automatically. Also I did notice that the USB 3.1 header plastic was a bit loose on the board, which I'm not sure why that's not mounted in place. I was able to carefully push it back in though, but I have to watch if I ever swap cases because the plastic might come out with the cable. Once the drivers and firmware were updated the WiFi is fantastic. I'm pulling 800+ up and down on my fiber connection over WiFi with minimal latency. TLDR: Have a thumb drive handy, get the drivers before you start building if you can and don't have a DVD drive in the new system. Update the firmware as soon as you can, after that I think you'll really enjoy the MB.

Very good sound quality. Build quality is awesome, the design looks beautiful. However, I chose to return these. --- Pros --- [Sound] The sound is very good. For BT headphones, these have great sound stage and clarity which is what I value. The sound signature is very similar to my DT770 pro 80 ohms which I'm very happy about. I really don't like sound signatures like Bose's or Sony's ones, Bose's sound is not natural and Sony's is too bass-heavy. These 85h are a bit treble emphasized and the base may not be powerful for most of the people. It might make your ear fatigue after a long time listening because it's not something like Sennheiser's warm sound signature. But I'll take it, I like the sound. [Build quality and design] The build quality is first-class. The material they used is very good. And the design looks cool and handsome. It's around 300 grams, so heavier than most of BT headphones. Overall, it's a good looking, quality headphones. --- Cons --- [ANC] I really don't think their ANC is working well. It only decreases a small amount of low frequency, and that's it. The ANC performance is much worse than Sony or Bose. It's even worse than a $60 ANC headphones I bought on Amazon. Just disappointed. [Volumn] The volume is not enough. Trust me I'm not someone loves to play the music to shake the car door. I need to set the volume to 70 - 85 % for the music, and 90% for movies. Yes, 85% is enough for me and I won't go higher for the most of the time, but it makes you feel less confident about the volume and the battery may drain faster than other headphones. [App] The App is really buggy. That's it. --- (Personal) Deal breaker --- [Comfort] I'm 5'9" 155 lbs. I don't think I have a big head. But the headband is not long enough for me, even I extended it all. If I try to place my ear at the center of the earcup, I need to push the headphone downward hard which makes a lot of pressure on the top of my head. After 20 mins wearing, the top of my headphone is in pain. BTW, The earcups are comfortable, not as well as Bose's but they are fine. [No power off button] These headphones use a mechanism that enables to auto turn on and off when you rotate the hinge. So if the right earcup is facing forward, it will be turned off. And if the earcups are facing to each other which is like when you are wearing them, they will be turned on. This is smart. However, for me, I don't want to leave these in the case when not using them. I have a headphone hanger and I used to hang my headphones to make them handy. When I hang these, earcups need to face to each other. For these headphones, I can't turn it off in that way bc there's no power button and it will be always on like that. Why can't there be a power button... --- verdict --- I can't keep these because of the above two deal-breakers. Those are very personal though. I can endure those three Cons because I love the sound and the design of these. What a pity, I think I have to keep looking for my next BT headphones.

I'm glad I took the plunge after a year of research, debating whether or not trying a new driver technology (new to me) would be worth the money - it was [mostly] worth it. The sound quality is fantastic, in my opinion. It's like listening to my full range floor speakers: treble and bass are distinct from each other (thanks to the inherent "speed" of a planar magnetic driver, as opposed to having a dedicated driver for each range). I now know what "sub-bass" means (and, on that note, "speed"). Where my AKG K240S's were unable to give me bass where I knew there should be some, the HiFiMan HE-4XX gave me back my missing bass, without "muddying" the trebles, but, at the same time, the treble doesn't have that "sparkle" (another term I now actually understand after reading all those audiophile forums) that my AKG had. Very well could be because I tore all the foam and mesh out of my AKG to make them more open and airy. I hesitate to make any modifications to the HE-4XX, but I've seen some mods floating around regarding taking out the filters, etc. We'll see - I don't really like the idea of hairs/dust getting into these drivers. Now about that build quality. At first glance it was fine. Headband is okay, materials are pretty nice, metal is sturdy, a bit stiff at first but loosens nicely over time. However, the tension on the headband adjustment points, where the headband connects to the metal frame, is too high, does not adjust smoothly, and is not consistent across the sides - one is more "jumpy" than the other side. Also, neither side stays where I've set them because that tension is too high, so the headphones naturally push down to their shortest fitting if you're not wearing them... and while you're wearing them. I had a rattling in my right ear cup after a few days. Only when I jostled it/moved it just right. I noticed it at first when moving the headphone, then later in a song. I reached out to HiFiMan customer service and they were quick to suggest that I remove the ear pad and check for debris, etc. No debris was found, but looking through the driver with a light, it looked like a wire was touching the drive on the other side (outer side). I asked them if they could do something about it - as well as the rusting screws on the metal pivots at the ear cup connection - and they took all of my information... then went radio silent. I had asked if they would send me a replacement while mine was being worked on, if that was even an option, and, of course, there was no answer to my question (does *any* customer service group actually answer the questions you ask?). Since they took my address down, I assumed they were sending me a box or something, but then I read the actual warranty and it suggests that shipping costs, etc. on on the customer... so it was then that I decided I'd take the grill off and do what I could. I wasn't happy about having to open up my headphone to that extent as soon as I was, but I also wasn't keen on having to box the thing up and pay for shipping, maybe to only get a refurbished-something back, maybe in worse condition, etc. Took the grill off, saw that a wire was making direct contact with the driver between the magnets. Pull the wired up and bent it a bit so that it would lean across the magnets instead of in between. I didn't tell them to cancel the ticket right away. I wanted to see what they would do/say. A week and a half later, I tell them to cancel the ticket. Not that they're listening anyway, right? Then I get a clicking in my *left* ear cup. That's just today. A different sound than the wire thing - sounds like the driver is moving when I press on the ear cup with *any* force - not pressing them into my head like a lunatic or anything, just taking them off/putting them on. Normal usage forces, stock ear pads. I think it might be debris, and I'm over the honeymoon stage/paranoia of opening them up, and... oh, did I mention that the ring on the right grill isn't even flush with the headphone? There's one section that sticks up that shouldn't. Anyway, I open the left ear cup and there's no debris except what was already in there from the factory (not nothing, mind you). But I do notice a little orange debris here and there. Now that I think about it, I saw some on the grill on the other side at some point, figured it was dust. Didn't think it'd be rust (the screws I complained about weren't all that bad - maybe even added character to the headphone). A couple of screws in my left ear cup are rusted to heck. These headphones came like this. My house is dry as a desert in the winter, the heater is always on and I can't even breath at night is how bad it is. I *wish* we had enough moisture in the air to make something like this happen. No, these were rusted when I got them, and I'm only just now finding out. That bit of orange debris here and there was rust, probably. So, I now have a clicking that I can't fix on my end, I don't think, and, taking a closer look, I have a rusted internal screw on the right side, too, but it's not as bad. So, at least 4 rusted screws, two of which are so bad, you can barely tell those are even screws. I've emailed customer service again, asked them to maybe not close the ticket yet, see what they can do for me, send me a pack of replacement screws at the very least so I can swap in clean ones. I'm willing to do that. review_text: So update make sure you use Sigma Outdoor Junction boxes or another brands outdoor junction boxes. The cameras base plate seals best against these so you dont have to silicone around it to seal. I replaced my standard boxes with these junction boxes and have allowed me to get 2 screws into the mounting plate with one at the top so the weight of the camera doesnt pull the base away from junction box. You can get these boxes in grey, white, and a bronze which can help blend into the cameras. These are a must if you plan on mounting any floodlight cameras to a surface mount junction box. These cameras are convenient and easy to setup. My issue with them for being a hardwired camera there is no way to run conduit to it without mounting it to a junction box. Now this in itself wouldnt be an issue if the plastic backing piece actually had a good way to seal and mount to a junction box. Or have a knockout on the camera. Some of the older ones I saw on youtube appeared to have a 1/2 conduit screw between the spotlights you could remove. The ones I received did not. My next issue is the supplied hardware to mount the camera to a junction box doesnt work very well. It gives you a metal crossbar that goes between the two junction box screws with a hole in the middle to mount the camera to. This one mounting point is all that holds it to the juntion box. The camera weighing 5-8lbs when tightened to its plastic backing plate bends and leaves a 1/4"ish gap around the top and sides from weight of it pulling down and the camera being tighten to it. I understand not everyone is going to be mounting it to a junction box and running conduit to it but for the vast majority of people trying to use this with a junction box unless that box is recessed and flush with your siding there really isnt a good way to mount it.

review_text: I have been using Douni bluetooth speaker for my laptop entertainment system for a while, but I needed some more refined sound with better bass, so I decided to give this a try. my first impression was it was solidly built. The small & round control is just wonderful. very discrete and functional that no one will ever know it is the remote / bluetooth control for the speakers. it works marvelously. As for the sound quality, it is very good for what I had paid for. first, it was loud enough, probably up to 50 watts or so. mid was clear and wide and higher frequency also was much more refined than my Douni BT speaker. but the bass was way too much for me. it wasn't flabby & loud bass. It still maintained its tightness and did not bleed over too much to mid, but it seems like Logitech's sound signature was emphasized on the bass. In most of cases, I listen to youtube music, so after researching it for a while, I found out there is a app for Chrome / Youtube equalizer that you can add into each page you open on your laptop. you can just google "equalizer for chrome" and super easy download. once I had that equalizer app on the youtube page, I was able to control the frequencies. THAT was it. now it was perfect. This Logitech bluetooth speaker is probably the best one that I have ever bought in that price range. Great sound, very nice looking and it certainly looks great on my desk.

I have a managed Ubiquiti 24 port switch (non-POE) and am using Ubiquiti access points (AP-LIte and AP-Long Range) around my house and also IP-POE security cams. My cams are on a cheap 4 port POE 100Mbps switch and my access points are powered by Unifi injectors. I wanted to consolidate so I bought this switch because I heard it works with Ubiquiti AP's. I plugged the uplink of this switch into port 24 on the Unifi switch. I then proceeded to plug in my cameras in ports 1-4 and they all fired up and worked. I plugged my Unifi AP's into ports 7+8. Only the one on port 7 lit up and worked. The one on 8 would not power my AP. I thought maybe the AP-LR was not compatible. I then decided to plug it into port 6 and it fired up and worked. So I don't know if port 8 POE isnt working, or just not working with my AP. But I find it odd that the same AP works on ports 6+7 but not 8. I then plugged one of my security cams into port 8 and it too would not fire up. So it seems that port 8 is dead. I dont think it's a power issue because I only have 6 devices connected and they are all below the wattage this switch can supply. I may return it and just spend the money on an Unifi POE 8 port managed switch because right now I bought an 8 port POE but only 7 work.

Although app shows good signal between WiFi and hub, I get popups several times a day when hub goes offline for a few minutes, then comes back up - kind of annoying. Overall - if it continues to work through the winter and batteries last at least 6 months, then this is probably worth the $50. AFTER A COUPLE DAYS: No notifications when mail arrived today. Blue light solid on hub. App says both sensor and bridge offline and no Wifi signal to bridge, no signal to sensor. I tried several times to get a bridge - WiFi connection, but always ended up with blinking blue light even though WiFi working for other things in house. Returned both units. I now agree with all the other 1-star reviews - this is not ready for prime time. If you want a good sensor and hub, try YoLink.

I am a Deaf Magicain and needed a qualtiy Ipad holder for my virtual shows. this one seemed to have good ratings and price was fair. it arrived quickly (yesterday August 2) and I could tell right away that it was heavier then some other tripod stands which gave me hope. I use lots of tripods for cameras and lights for my shows so I am intamately familiar with tri pods Upon opening it was all separate pieces which is not a big deal- until you want to pack it up. Major flaw #1- you have to completely disassemble the tripod including the IPad holder portion to fit it back in the bag. This makes no sense what so ever! You literally have just killed the convenience of having a travel bag for it. Instead of being able to just shrink it down and put it in the back you have to take every piece apart and then store it. Thus this is NOT a design I would want. I guess if you are not planning to take it with you or pack it down often its not that big of a deal but for me or anyone that travels a lot it will drive you nuts and cost you time. Major flaw #2 – it is very top heavy with an iPad. I bought this particular one for the “goose neck” feature. Most iPad stands don’t offer enough tilt to allow me to position the IPad up and be able to tilt it down to see the table when needed. The Goose neck allows that. HOWEVER, the little ball rotate system does not hold. Meaning after you snap the plastic holder on and tighten the plastic knob the IPad won’t stay where I want it. It will slowly slip down and then boink all the way down it goes. Very frustrating. I literally just used it for a live Zoom magic show (august 3, @ 11:20am) and it took me about 10 minutes to play with it to make it work. Being that the ball feature does not do what it should I was not able to get the IPad set exactly as I wanted. This in my opinion is a huge flaw as it completely takes away an important feature. Yes I could tighten it more but in the past using other aimilar holders the plastic screw piece usually splits. The quality of these holders are not the best. I am exploring a few options to help compensate the issue. One last flaw that I want to mention is about how top heavy this stand is. Thus if you do not position it correctly it will simply tip over and crash to the floor. The solution that will help is to make sure one leg of the tri pod is pointing the same way your iPad is leaning from the goose neck. This way the weight is supported by that leg. However if you barely bump it the other direction- say good bye to your IPad. Knowing that this is for an ipad (and mine is just a 10X7 with no case) the weight needs to be considered and either have longer legs or heavier base. As I mentioned if you point one leg the same direction and no one is walking around it you will be fine. Mine stayed just fine for the entire performance but this could pose a problem if you have a pet or kids or any other people around that might bump it. Over all its clearly a better Tri pod than others that I have used for this purpose and the Goose Neck is what might make me keep this one. That feature alone makes me somewhat over look the other flaws. I might have my seamstress make me a bag that actually fits the tripod so that I can quickly pack it without dismantling every single time. Not to mention that would also weaken the ball rotate area which as I already mentioned is not very good. So based on this I would recommend the tripod with consideration to the flaws. If they don’t bother you or you think you can work around it then this is a good bet. I have not decided whether I will keep it or not but will decide by end of this week. I have 3 more shows this week to use it and by then I should have a better idea if this is worth my time and investment. Magically yours Sam

I had some concerns seeing reviews of these phones not lasting long. After only two weeks, those fears are not completely alleviated. But I can give some initial impressions and observations. First off, I have to say the build quality seems pretty solid, and it makes me wonder what people are doing to their phones that they're breaking in half or falling apart. We'll see as time goes on how they hold up. This is my first pair of planar magnetic driver headphones (I'm comparing with Sennheiser HD599 and Grado SR80i). I think there is definitely a break-in period, and the longer I listen to them the more they warm up and sound more natural, less sterile and digital. The first thing I noticed was a huge stereo field, wider than any headphones I've had before. But along with that comes the symptom that anyone nearby can clearly hear what you're listening to. That's open back headphones for you, but these HiFiMan HE4XX seem even more open back than others. I can clearly hear separate instruments in a mix, panned across the stereo field. To some extent it depends on the mix, and mixes with very little panning do sound smaller and more intimate. The second thing I noticed was the balance. Most headphones have at least some noticeable emphasis on certain frequencies. My Sennheiser HD599 certainly have more bass emphasis. The Grado are more neutral. But all the frequencies seem to get the same attention here, and I like that because it gives me the choice to boost the frequencies I want using an EQ, and I feel more confident tracking into my DAW with them. In other words I'm less worried about emphasized frequencies throwing off my perception. The third obvious thing was how the different frequency ranges were presented. The bass, while not emphasized or boosted, is very smooth and clear. It does not sound distorted or mushy at all. The highs, while crisp and clear, are never harsh or hissy. They are sort of rounded in a way, but without going soft. To me that is pretty awesome. Fourth, I found that with other headphones, I find myself turning them up probably a little too loud to hear more details or hear the music better. With the HE4XX, I can just turn up to a comfortable level and hear everything clearly. Less fatigue after an hour or two. If there's a downside to the HE4XX, it's that they take a fair amount of power to drive them. More than my iPad Pro has to give. So when connecting to mobile devices, I have to have an headphone amp in between. I'm currently using a FIO E17K, which offers a good amount of distortion free volume boost along with EQ when needed. With my HX Stomp (used for connecting studio monitors and recording guitar) I don't need a separate amp, but I do need to turn the volume up significantly compared to my other phones. Overall, I love these headphones and they're definitely an upgrade from my previous headphones.

*Edit to A Once Short Novel. After purchasing an antenna, to verify Over The Air broadcast TV signals were available, we bought a 1 TB Recast device. The first 5 months or so, it worked as advertised. Even the Fire TV App. (required) even made connecting the Recast fairly easy. Despite the Recast not having any written instructions, aside from connecting it to the Antenna: Fire TV Stick; and household power, the set-up was easy. The Fire TV App. is REQUIRED for set-up of the Recast. The App. is also supposed to aid in controlling your Fire TV devices. The Alexa voice recognition, works well enough in setting-up future recordings of individual programs or series. The Fire TV App, couldn't seem to stay connected to my Fire TV Sticks. It simply lost connection, with no warning. It could be reconnected, but it often only reconnected for just a few moments, before again disconnecting. The issues we began having with the Recast started a few months back. At first small barely noticeable issues, such as showing the Bell Symbol, that is visible next to the Settings option on the main page, Going to the notice, showed that the Recast device has lost its connection. And initially, didn't seem to make any difference, as both Live TV viewing & our Recorded programs were still accessible & still being recorded. But eventually, when trying to view Live TV, we began having major issues. All, not just some, of the Over The Air broadcast channels, started having Pixel Issues; Buffering Lag: Freezing: & view/voice synchronization issues. These issues weren't with just the channels having weaker signals, but all channels. I first thought it may be a problem with the antenna, since we could still view our recorded DVR Recast programs. But, the antenna worked fine, when not connected to the Recast. Next, we tried performing a restart of the Recast, using our Fire TV Stick. (Settings:/Live TV:/Live TV Sources:/Fire TV Recast:/Restart). But, this only resulted in loosing all contact with the Recast, and an alert, triangle with a (!) In the center, showing just right of where it says Network. Here is where we received an alert notice, to use the Fire TV App, in order to try and re-establish contact with our Recast device. After several failed attempts to reconnect with the App, I reached out to Amazon for some service assistance. In my request I chose the, (be contacted by phone option). And to Amazons credit, I got a call within minutes. After explaining my problem in detail, the tech then walked me through some of the same things I had already tried, on TWO of our different Fire TV Stick devices. This included allowing the tech to remotely access our equipment. After several failed tries of reconnecting with two of our Fire TV Sticks, the tech had me confirm that we were using the same network on both the recast and the Fire TV Sticks. I was able to confirm this using an App. I had previously loaded, from our (ISP) Internet Service Provider (AT&T U-verse). And after confirming we were using the same Network on all of our equipment, the tech suggested that although our (ISP) Network was the same, there are both 2.4 GHz and 5.0 GHz band options, within the same Network. I later found out is basically like having TWO DIFFERENT NETWORKS, and that wasn't just possibly why the connection couldn't be made, it was the exact reason The Recast & Fire TV Stick couldn't stay connected. The selection of which band, 2.4 GHz and 5.0 GHz, to use, isn't an option, using the default settings on the combination Arris BGW210-700 Modem/Router, that AT&T U-verse provides. You can convince/get them to separate the two bands, and split the signal, if you are lucky enough to connect with someone on the phone that actually knows what they are doing. BUT, doing this can weaken the signal strength, along with other possible problems. *Note: The Recast Ad, HERE, where the Recast is sold, only states that Recast devices must be used on the same WiFi Network as your Fire devices, with no mention of WiFi Networks that provide 2.4 GHz and 5.0 GHz band options being any problem. A well informed AT&T U-verse tech, that came out, informed me that even though the 2.4 GHz & 5.0 GHz bands are on the same Network, they essentially like have two separate networks. So, before buying one, make sure you have the ability to connect to the 2.4 GHz or 5.0 GHz bands, with ALL of your Amazon devices. Not doing so, will result in the above problems we experienced. Final thoughts: If you have a few broadcast programs that you want to record, or, not every TV you have is close to a window, so it can use it's own dedicated antenna, A Recast may be an option to consider. I'd first suggest buying a single antenna, flat and amplified, are available here for under $30.00 U.S., to see what broadcast channels are available. Or, see if any of the Apps. Available on Prime TV offer free delayed rebroadcasts, of your favorite network affiliated programs. Also, make sure your (ISP) Internet Service Provider, offers equipment with the ability to select which of the two bands 2.4 GHz or 5.0 GHz, you can connect with. AT&T U-verse uses a combination Modem/Router, that makes this more difficult to accomplish. It is possible, but much more difficult. Using a separate router, that allows you to designate, which device connects to which band, within your network, works much better. I discovered that someone at Amazon does look over these reviews, and sometimes even on the same day that they are made. One such individual, reached out to me and offered to provide a replacement Recast device. And one of their technical support people, even gave me a follow-up call the next day, to confirm my problem was solved.

I've confirmed that the MAXOAK Laptop Power Bank can fully charge a HP Spectre 360x 15-eb0xxx. The laptop power connectors they provide appear to cover most use cases. However, the HP Laptop gets angry when I use the MAXOAK power bank's 20v@5A port to charge the HP Laptop by saying "An incompatible power supply was detected Your computer will run in reduced performance and may not charge. Use of the original power adapter is recommended." The HP user guide reports the laptop using anywhere from 19.5v@2.31A-45W to 19.5v@16.92A-330W. It does charge with the HP power adaptor, but I can't determine at what power level. For the most part I use the MAXOAK's USB ~5v @2.1A to feed the laptop power when I'm outside. However, that's really not enough power to keep the HP Laptop's internal battery happy when I push it with video encoding, upgrades or s/w dev work. Where this power bank battery really fails is it doesn't provide power to a HP laptop in standby mode. The MAXOAK shuts itself off rather than letting a laptop, in standby mode, sip power from it!! That's NOT the behavior I wanted to see. While there is some usefulness to this power bank I don't find myself needing it. To be somewhat fair the idea of laptop "power banks" are somewhat dubious. The MAXOAK is really too heavy to lug around just incase there is no AC outlet where you're at and as others have stated you run the risk of losing it if you try taking it through airport security.

review_text: Needing a data backup drive, I purchased the Western Digital 5TB Elements Portable External Hard Drive (HDD) based on the company’s reputation and the reviews. I connected the drive to my computer, did a quick format (NTFS) and proceeded to perform a backup using the Windows 10 backup utility. The backup failed at about 90% completion. I noticed an intermittent ticking sound coming from the drive. The computer was reading the drive so I was not sure this “ticking” was not normal for this drive. Additionally, every time I connected the drive to the computer, the computer would freeze for almost ten seconds until the drive was recognized which I found troublesome and annoying. I should note this system is a Windows 10 Pro with an i9 processor and 16GB of RAM so there should be no reason why it freezes just recognizing an external hard drive on a USB 3.0 port. Despite this, I decided to see if I could make it work. I did a long format of drive and again attempted to perform a backup and again it failed. I did another long format and then ran a couple of hard drive diagnostic programs against the hard drive but no errors were found. A third attempt to perform a backup failed. I concluded that despite the diagnostic programs not finding errors, the drive was defective due to its erratic performance, failure to backup and the incessant ticking noise which is likely the read/write head not working correctly. The HDD was returned. I have since purchased a Western Digital 6TB My Book. This drive connected without causing freezes of the system and I was able to perform a successful backup to it.

This is what it's advertised as being. It switches two HDMI (or DVI with a suitable cable) monitors, a keyboard, and mouse between two different computers. It also supports sound but I'll get to that in a moment. There are four ways to switch: two buttons on the device itself, a remote control (wired), a weird and unnecessary hijacking of the middle mouse button on your mouse, and some keyboard shortcuts. The latter is easily switched off, but the mouse weirdness is more difficult to avoid. KVMs usually result in a maze of cables. This one is no different but tries to alleviate some of the mess by combining the connections to the computers in a single proprietary cable for each one that splits out near the end into separate HDMI, USB, and audio cables. My desk is still a mess though, in part because the cables are somewhat thick (they look like four cables glued together), but I appreciate the effort. That said, proprietary non-standard cables are difficult to replace, there's no way to order a replacement as a regular Amazon item. Once I had the KVM set up I found it generally worked. I have two monitors, both 1080P, one HDMI and one DVI. Both could be supported with standard cables (the DVI one needing one with HDMI on one end and DVI on the other, they're cheap and available on Amazon.) My main computer has a single HDMI and single DVI port (plus a DisplayPort which this doesn't support), and the switch supports that configuration with the DVI port being for "Video output B" on that because the proprietary cable would needed an adapter, while the other video output could use a regular DVI/HDMI cable I already had. My laptop uses a USB-C Dock that has twin HDMI outputs (and uses DisplayPort internally) - this worked fine. Finally my keyboard itself is mechanical, which is reportedly sometimes a problem with these kinds of device, but it worked fine here. So... it works. But... First issue: As I mentioned above, the KVM hijacks the middle mouse button for its switching protocol. I thought reading the description it only hijacked double-middle-clicks, but it prevents all middle clicks from reaching the computer. There's a workaround that kinda works, the manual suggests plugging the mouse into a port on the front. This worked initially, then stopped working, then worked again after I unplugged and plugged the mouse back in. This is annoying. Middle click is what many of us use to open links in new tabs, and under GNU/Linux it's the default "Paste" button. There's no good reason to hijack it. (Interestingly the keyboard hotkeys can be completely disabled with a button on the front panel) Second issue: The hub supports audio and, to be fair, it's optional whether you use it, but I just don't see any configuration for audio is ever going to work well. Audio routed through the KVM is switched. But if I get alerts on one computer while using the other, I probably want to hear them. I guess technically there may be some circumstance in which I wouldn't want to hear audio from the "other" computer, but I'm struggling to think of any right now. So, to sum up: Pros: - Works. No issues with computers resizing or moving windows when not connected. Mechanical keyboard compatible. - Switches quickly - Two good options for switching inputs (remote and buttons on the front), plus configurable keyboard hotkeys that can be easily disabled - Seems to be reliable - Still a cabling mess despite efforts to reduce it using proprietary combined cables. I have been an audiophile, built my own stereo equipment, and purchased plenty of retail speakers and amps over the years, including the some recent soundbars. We'll see. Right now I am more than pleased with it and would highly recommend it. If anything goes awry after this honeymoon period, I will update the review. Now back to the music from this little gem. UPDATE: The M83 has a software glitch that causes the device to lock up in a mode that prevents it from connecting, playing or ... turning it off. Very frustrating ... unless you know how to fix it, which is easy. There are several reviews here which reference this glitch, and quite a bit of chatter online about it too. But GOOD NEWS ... it is easy to fix and also easy to prevent. FIX IT: When the device locks up, blue light on or blinking all the time, no sound, won't connect and won't turn off: Insert a 3.5mm audio male plug (like the one for your celphone and for most audio devices with a headphone jack, or a speaker output jack) ..... just insert the plug into the audio plug on the M83. This will reset the software and cure the problem immediately. Insert the plug, the front indicator led will turn red for a few seconds, and then back to flashing blue ... now turn the M83 off, and back on, and the unit is reset. It's as easy as that. Keep this note because it is likely to happen to you and this procedure will fix it. As an aside, I am pretty sure I know why this is happening. The M83 has an odd, somewhat clever feature: It allows you to connect two M83's to the same host device .... When you do, the M83 software will split the two speaker sets into the two stereo channels which you can now physically separate (move the speakers away from each other) to get true stereo. And of course, more sound and more bass. Clever. The problem is that this bluetooth feature requires a software routine that has a bug in it. What happens is that if your M83 loses its connection while streaming, or if it is paired with, and talking to, more than one host (say, you have another device in the room that is paired with it, and is running with Bluetooth on) the clever software in the M83 gets caught in a loop and stuck ... locked up. That's when you get the Blue Light of Death ... it won't go out and you won't be able to turn the device off.) Now you know how to unlock it. But you can also prevent the glitch in most cases. One, always start your M83 session the same way. Start with the M83 turned off. Grab the host device and go into its Bluetooth dialog and remove the M83 from the paired list. Turn the Bluetooth off and back on. Re-add the M83, and wait until you have a CONNECT button. Now turn on the M83 and let it find the host. Hit the connect button on the M83 and let it pair and connect. Now you are good to go. When you are done listening to it, turn the M83 off, and then turn off the Bluetooth on the host. Also, while you are doing this, make sure that no other host devices are nearby which have paired with your M83 and might interfere with the pairing/connecting process. It sounds goofy, but if you follow this simple procedure you should have no problems. I cannot advise you about the two-M83 feature because I do not have two M83s and cannot test that. You will have to try that on your own if decide to go down that road. It would be really helpful if the manufacturer would put the reset procedure in the user manual, it is easy to do and works well but only if you know about it. I am going to try to downgrade my rating to 4 stars for this because this glitch is well known and the Bugani gods really need to take care of it. If they do, then we can put back the fifth star. Cheers, PG

This cable let me remove the reset button wire from the led control board, and let me wire my motherboard's ARGB connector directly to the case led controller's VDG connector, and now the Asus Aura software properly controls the case along with the motherboard.

review_text: This router is a perfect solution for me. It's hard-mounted in my Airstream and, since the input is (roughly) 12v, I just have it running off of my Li-ion battery bank. No AC power adapter and associated DC-to-AC-to-DC conversion power loss. When my destination has a wifi connection, I simply connect my GL-AR750S relay to the destination wifi signal, and wire the GL-AR750S LAN out to the WAN input on the LAX20 Nighthawk. The LAX20 will prioritize the WAN signal, and if no WAN connection, it'll failover to the cell networks. Perfect solution. The failover process takes approx 60 seconds, so there is unfortunately downtime when switching. Still automatic, though! Another note: I originally bought the LAX20 for compatibility with Google Fi (uses all three Sprint, T-Mobile, and AT&T). I have since ditched Google Fi for the cheaper and better alternative US Mobile. I took a gamble and went with US Mobile's Verizon plan, which offers "Unlimited All" without data throttling. The LAX20 works with the Verizon network! I read reviews on here that said contrary, but I have first-hand experience that it does indeed work on Verizon. Just be sure to update your the LAX20 APN field to VZWINTERNET. All in all, it's a fast router and serves my needs very well.

I got turned on to the Logitech thumb trackballs about 20 years ago - back when they only had the wired model. After my wired one broke Logitech no longer sold that model and I had to make the switch to the wireless M570. It was just as good as the wired one, but more convenient. I have loved mine, I've had 5 of them now. I buy them because of their ergonomic features and I'm on the computer all of the time for work and at home. But the reason I have to buy new ones is that they ALWAYS fail. Every time it's either the right-click button no longer registering clicks - or the left click double/triple clicking when you press it down. Typically they last me around 2-3 years and then they fail, slowly at first, but it's consistent. They ALWAYS fail. I've now had 5 of them, each of them failed in one of those two ways after 2-3 years. While they work they are fantastic! And originally I kept replacing them with the same model because it was the only thumb-trackball out there on the market. Now there are others, so after my desktop one failed I bought a cheaper off-brand one. Now that my work one has failed (5th one to fail the same way) I'm going to replace it with another off-brand. For the price, I have always hoped/expected that they would last. But now after having it happen over the past 15 years 5 different times, I'm convinced it's not a fluke, one of them I didn't even use it was used by the rest of the family so it can't even by my specific usage. I have loved these trackballs, but I can't keep shelling out $70 for a product that will only last me 3 years max. Time to move on. If you buy it - you'll love it for a while, but I promise, eventually in a few years it's going to break. You'll start to notice the right mouse button has to be pushed down really hard, or the left click will start multiple-clicking when you hold it down. It's probably not going to be obvious at first but after a few weeks, it'll happen. You can change computers with it, try it on a different machine - it won't matter. This makes it unusable for work, or for gaming. I have a bunch of "trophy" balls, as I always keep the ball when I toss the units. At first, I considered them trophies because I thought I was just being too hard on them, now I know it's not me. You can use them on a different machine for gaming/work/personal use, it doesn't matter, it's going to fail.

I loved this when I got it. Hooking everything up was a breeze, the system seemed to work great. I used it successfully a few times to catch some petty crime near my house, but in those cases not much was at stake so the police were content to take cell-videos of my monitor while I played the footage back. Then someone got murdered. The police needed the actual footage. Guess what? This DVR only exports to h265 and avi's IN A FORMAT THAT DOESNT SEEM TO EXIST IN NORTH AMERICA. An entire urban -police tech unit spent more than an hour trying to get the footage playable. I assume they eventually got it, but it wasn't explained to me. Jump to the future: I start trying to pull footage. There are problems: I found record gaps that lasted hours. When I could pull footage, the files weren't playable in Windows 10, chrome, adobe premiere, vlc player, or even via adobe media encoder. I spent days on emailing tech support. To their credit, they were enthusiastically helpful. Unfortunately, the closest thing to a solution they could provide was to send me a copy of a custom video encoder that set off all my security warnings on my PC. I put it on a laptop I wasn't afraid to wipe, and gave it a test. Long story short, it works. But that means that this system can't export video without a custom player to convert it from whatever format the DVR exports into something that American video players can actually play. If that weren't bad enough, I found an even worse issue: although the DVR plays back directly on the device, it chops the files into pieces for export, and shaves a bit of time off of the ends of each piece in doing so. When I was finally able to watch the stitched together video of only a few minutes, there were gaps in every seam. *So this DVR can't export videos that standard US equipment can play *The videos that are exported come with coverage gaps, rendering the footage potentially useless The system also seems unsafe to use on an internet connected network (as explained in other reviews) and the phone app requires permissions that Hiseeu has no business asking for. Two stars because the system (sort of) works. I'm subtracting the last star because I have received more than a dozen bribe requests to pull this review.

If you are athletic, concerned for accurate measures, skip this watch to avoid disappointment. Save up and spend $80+ on a good smart watch with functioning tracking for various sports and activities, and body data. There are other flaws, I'll list them below. APP: The app "Da Fit" seems half-baked, it lags far behind VeryFit Pro (used on previous Chinese smart watch) and other apps. Garmin (for HR+, etc.), Google Fit, LG Health Samsung, etc. all are far superior. It does have the feature allowing it to "Connect" to Google Fit. But data "synced" with Fit is limited. BP: Blood Pressure ALWAYS measures 140/83. Not believable. I'd say claim to show BP is false. This plus Sleep monitoring and GPS mapping of activities were important features for me, and these aren't really working right or there on the watch. Heart rate seems OK, pretty close to what I can measure myself. SPO2 seems plausible but so far typically close to 98%, even if wake up in middle of night. SLEEP: Restful vs Light Sleep -- it sometimes says I'm sleeping when I'm not. Sometimes not sleeping when I am. Restful vs Light seems always a low ratio. I consider it so inaccurate it's next to useless. My old $30 smart watch was far more accurate, and results shown matched how I felt. ACTIVITIES - Step Counter is what I see working. I really wanted Bicycling tracked: time, distance, avg speed, and GPS mapped. Swimming or Kayaking would have been nice too. "Additional Training" is totally blank on my "Da Fit" app. No watch icons for activities other than steps. Again, my old watch did this far better, although it could lose track of satellites in valleys. No hint as to "Calories Burned" as I had on previous watch. Watch Faces - Yep, lots of these, but mostly eye candy. Can't find one that has more than 3 pieces of data. I WANT ALL of the following on one watch face: time + seconds HH:MM:SS, date MM/DD/YY + DDD day of week, BPM, SPO2, BP, Steps, pace & distance (yards, meters, km, miles), # TXT messages, # missed CALLs, # VMAILs. And it all should be accurate. I could design this watch face if user designed watch faces were allowed. ALERTS: I want vibrate or audio alerts if tracked BP goes over a user set amount, for me I'd want 140/80 since it's nearly always lower. That's why I KNOW the BP reading is wrong. I compare with dedicated BP cuffs and it's never right. I want alerts if SPO2 drops under 90. Vibrate or make phone send a text. Something helpful. It would be great if GPS included functions to set waypoints for rides, walks, runs, swims, etc. CALLS: Since my Android phone supports "Screen Calls" function (blue button), I'd like to have that besides the Accept (green)/Decline (red). App likes to "take over" the Speaker function so I have to reset that to Phone or Speaker (on phone) -- should be a preference. Or tied to Activities -- if Active, ask to allow watch to be speaker & microphone as part of activity start. CALENDAR: Calendar alerts, Reminders, Tasks do not show or sync. Thought a smart watch ought to show these basic smart phone features. These were on smart watches I had over 10 years ago. Seems an easy win to have these.

At this point, I have had the Sense 2 for 2 days and I know at least some of my issues will likely be fixed with later software updates. First, the good. I like the form factor. The case is thin and the watch, even with the supplied band, is comfortable. Speaking of the band, as a big guy, I was overjoyed to see the inclusion of a second band that actually fit. Also, changing bands is a snap. Overall, it seems to be relatively high quality. The battery life, so far at least has been fantastic. I am on hour 42 of wearing it after a 99% charge and it is down to 70% battery left. The screen is fairly bright and crisp. An understated advantage of the Sense 2 (and one of the reasons I switched) is that is OS and phone brand agnostic. You can use it with Apple or Android and, unlike the Galaxy Watch, there are no features locked away if you are not using the correct brand of phone. If you are coming from a Galaxy Watch where you could customize the watch face and all sorts of other things and that is important to you, then move along. This watch will not be for you. For now, at least, there is not really much substantive you can do to individualize your user experience. That's not so great. Also not so great is the things that are missing. There is no Google Maps at launch. Also, despite being a Google company, no support for the Google Assistant (Alexa only sadly). There is also no interface to control music on your phone if that is important to you. I found it mildly annoying, but not a deal breaker. In addition, some people will be turned off by the fact that there are features that require a Fitbit paid subscription to get, even though you get six months for free. The real reason I bought this watch was the ECG function. I have had A Fib for a couple of years and used to use (and still do) a Kardia XL to check my rhythm. The Galaxy Watch 4 was nice because it did a reasonable single lead reading and it meant not having to carry another gizmo with me. You simply held still and put a finger on each of the side buttons. Unfortunately, when I switched from a Galaxy phone to a Pixel, I lost the ability to do an ECG. On the Sense 2, the ECG has not been impressive. First, I have big hands and contorting my right one to get my thumb and forefinger on the corner of the glass has been a challenge at time. It often takes several tries to get it right. Second, despite confirming on both my Kardia and my Galaxy Watch, the Sense 2 will never indicate that I am in A Fib. Apparently, if your pulse goes above 120 (which mine frequently does while in A Fib) then the Sense 2 just gives up and won't really check. Even in instances where it was below 120, the Sense will not confirm. I guess we get to settle for inconclusive results instead. Given this feature was the main reason I bought the watch, it may be a deal breaker for me and I may return it for that reason. If this feature is not that important to you, then it may still be a good option. Overall though, it may be a good option for the right person. If you care primarily about health and fitness tracking and want a good battery life, then this is a good option. At the current $300 price point, I still feel like Fitbit may be asking a little too much given the features of the other higher end options on the market.

I believe that this is not a bug. The indicator is merely there for show only. Be warned, people! Don't rely on the indicator; swap in spare batteries on a schedule. 3. The Btech branded CH-5 Charger that's provided will only charge Btech branded batteries, not third-party batteries. That would crimp me except that I have other chargers that I can use instead of the one provided. Again, be warned, people! In closing, all I can say about this average radio is that the price is right and it is "good enough" for now. Or, as the Chinese put it: Chabuduo. Caveat emptor, says I.

The 2.4Ghz Wifi signal & Ethernet routing works impeccably out of the box throughout (and beyond!) my 2-story house and basement. This is a perfect cheap router for basic home use with those intents. There are two oddities relating to the 5 GHz signal, which may or may not be related. 1. Out of the box, the 5 GHz performance is unstable, varies wildly in speed, and sometimes slows down all the way to zero (with perfect signal strength). Changing the 5 GHz network mode to "Wireless N only" and the channel width to "40 MHz only" in the firmware settings resolves this and has resulted in fast & stable performance on the 5 GHz network as well as the 2.4 GHz network. I think (???) this may relate to the fact that... 2. This router allegedly contains the same Mediatek WiFi 5 hardware as the Linksys e5400 router. That is, the hardware is capable of AC (wifi 5, 802.11AC) protocol but is "disabled" by firmware and sold as a cheaper router. I am honestly not sure why anyone needs faster wifi than the 5GHz wireless N, but it feels "dirty" to sell a router capable of going faster but disabling this possibility. However, out of the box, my computer WAS connecting to this router on an AC protocol, even though the box says the router doesn't use an AC protocol! I suspect that the firmware that is supposed to handicap the router is a mess and instead of simply disabling the AC protocol, it is generally effing up the 5 GHz band behavior. It is for this reason I suspect that locking the 5 GHz network to wireless N only and 40 MHz only improved performance radically over the default settings. It is no longer reporting a connection on an AC protocol but is fast and stable on the advertised 5 GHz Wireless N protocol.

I conducted two tests with an original Olympus BLH-1 and the Wasabi and Power2000 fully decoded clones. The first test was a controlled-lighting tripod-mount time lapse on an E-M1.2 at 1 minute intervals with the screen active. The second test was a constant current discharge to 7.2V at a rate which resulted in discharge time roughly matching the number of pictures taken in the first test. The 7.2V cut-off point was chosen as that appears to be when the E-M1.2 powers off - batteries consistently measured around 7.4V after shut-off, which at a 500mA current drops to around 7.2V. As is to be expected, the Olympus BLH-1 matched the best of the two clones that I tested in terms of capacity at around 1500mAh. The Wasabi 2 pack had one battery also measure around 1500mAh while the other was only around 1200mAh. Meanwhile both Power2000 batteries only measured around 800mAh. Despite the Wasabi batteries coming in close to the original BLH-1 in terms of capacity I would not recommend them as a direct replacement. First issue is the disparity in capacity between the two batteries I received. I ended up carefully disassembling the lower capacity battery and measured both cells individually to confirm that they each had 1200mAh usable capacity. This implies that different 18500 cells were used in one battery I received versus the other. Now it could be that all of the cells Wasabi sources are in the 1200-1500mAh usable capacity range, or they could use lower capacity cells as well. There's no way to tell, but having different capacity between two batteries in a 2 pack does not bode well. The second reason why I would not recommend these batteries as a direct replacement is that they lack charge balancing circuitry. These batteries make use of 2 individual lithium ion cells in series to produce the 7.4V nominal output. The original BLH-1 has circuitry which activates when in an OEM charger to charge each of those two cells individually, thus ensuring that they both fully charge. The Wasabi circuitry provides basic over and under voltage protections in addition to the batter status information output to the camera, but it does not have any charge balancing circuitry. The result of such will be a gradual decrease in effective capacity. Small differences between the two cells will cause one to have a higher charge level than the other during the course of discharge - say it ends at 10% while the other is at 9%. When recharged in series without charge balancing circuitry some portion of that difference in charge level will remain - say 100% charged for one cell and 99.5% for the other. This is a compounding issue, so after the next charge cycle it would be 100% and 99% and so on. Key takeaway being that every charge cycle will result in less effective capacity than the last. Now all that said, if you know what you're doing these are great batteries... to carefully disassemble and turn into 18500 cell holders for your Olympus camera. I carefully cut the non-contact end off one of the batteries, removed the cells, slightly modified the circuit board, and added some spring contacts on the end I'd removed. The result being that I can now swap 18500 cells into my camera almost as easily as a battery. This method avoids the recharging shortcoming of the circuitry by avoiding it altogether - I recharge the 18500 cells individually in a normal charger. To be clear, I'm not recommending that this be done, just providing the information that it can be done. (As an electrical engineer familiar with lithium ion cells I was still somewhat wary of disassembling and modifying the circuit board - only did so after fully mapping it out.)

First off, the camera work for what I need. They could, however, work better. Lot better. My biggest gripe is the connectivity issue between the app and the camera. Everything else is minor by comparison. This is an OEM camera, which means someone else makes the camera and Zumimall puts their label on it. There are many brands with the same guts and have the same issues. Cons: * extended live viewing drains the battery fast * motion detection seems delayed (read about it below) * captures AFTER motion is detected * max 30 seconds of video capture * no PC monitoring software, must use app or no access to camera. * uses broadcast packets to find camera (unreliable) instead of the last known IP. * Must have a very strong wifi signal to connect reliably (89% wifi signal is apparently not enough) * 2.4Ghz only. Crowded spectrum, lots of interference from neighbors wifi. * Captured videos live on the camera; cant transfer them without removing the SD card from the camera. Pros: * wireless, no holes to drill through outside wall * decent picture quality (HD) * 3 days @ 14hrs a day of direct sunlight charged camera to full * night vision works well * videos live on the camera's SD card so they're always recorded (good thing given the connectivity issues) So the cameras (I have 2) work but have caveats that people need to know about. One has 100% wifi signal strength (according to the camera) because I moved the router to the other side of the wall. Second camera is forr feet farther down, wifi an interior wall + outside wall between the camera and wiifi router, reports 89% signal strength, and fails to connect 1 in 3 attempts. The failure to connect drive me nuts more than anything else. I mentioned that the motion capture seems delayed. Due to poor documentation, I can't be sure but it seems like the camera "wakes up" and takes a picture to compare to the last time it woke up. Motion sensitivity determines how much of the picture needs to be the same before "motion" is detected. Motion in-between wake ups will be missed. This is seen when the camera captures someone in the yard, but missied them walking onto the yard. Like I said, I can't be sure this is how the camera works but sure seems like it. Once motion is detected, camera takes a snapshot and sends it to the app as an alert. At the same time it starts recording, 10, 20, or 30 seconds max. Then goes through another sleep/wake cycle and will alert/record again. I would rather it record continuously until motion stops but that's not how the camera works. The use of only the 2.4Ghz wifi is an issue where I live. It's a crowded frequency here. There have been times where I couldn't access the camera for a few hours. I will get alerts but can't watch the video since it won't connect. The app uses broadcast packets to find the camera instead of the last known IP; it should try the last known IP first before trying broadcast packets. Upgrades I'd like to see: * use last known IP of camera before trying broadcast packets. This would go a long ways to solving the connectivity issues. * above change would allow me to view camera after I VPN from my tablet to my home router * Video and picture download. You can save a recording or snapshot, but only view them on the app. * Document camera API so 3rd party software can access the camera. * Document the camera setttings AND how they change the camera's behavior.

First, I build and repair a lot of computers and electronics for family and friends. I ALWAYS use Western Digital drives when building or replacing a hard drive. I usually use the "Black" series of drives for performance, durability, and the warranty. These drives last well past their warranties with decent performance for a conventional platter drive. These are the ones to use when you need a large capacity conventional hard drive. I purchased this 5TB gaming external drive to expand the capacity of my PS4. For the first time, I've gone all digital with my PS4 games to reduce the number of game cases and disks around. I also like to have all of the games available without re-downloading, so this makes digital storage capacity at the console critical for me. Hooking up this drive, formatting it, and moving games over from the internal PS4 HD was much easier than I had anticipated. Downloading games from PSN to the external hard drive is also seamless. Running games directly from the portable drive through the USB 3.0 connection doesn't seem to be any slower than launching them from the internal hard drive, at least I haven't noticed any difference in the load times by subjective evaluation. When running continuously, like during a game transfers, the drive gets warm but doesn't seem to get hot enough where I would be concerned. The only major down side to this drive, and it's a flaw with most of the 2.5" based WD portable drives, is that they put the drive's activity light right next to the USB cable connection. I have the drive stacked on top of my PS4 so that i can see the light flash whenever it's reading / writing. I would rather not see the cable, which has to be twisted from the front back around the housing to plug it into the rear PS4 USB port. Depending on how you route the cable, you may not be able to see the light from certain angles if the cable blocks your line of sight. It's not a big deal, but it would be nicer if they had the drive activity light on the other side for a cleaner looking setup. The other down side, which doesn't bother me at all since I'm not planning to tear this thing apart and I haven't verified this info personally, is that according to youtube reviews the drive itself is not a standard 2.5" SATA laptop drive. The actual hard drive is a portable specific build with a different interface board, so you can't disassemble this bad boy and pop the drive into something else or use the enclosure with a different 2.5" HD. I've only had mine for a couple of months, but so far I have no complaints. It does everything I need with no perceivable penalty in performance. The extra storage space (5TB!) is a life saver since I had maxed out my PS4's internal drive, and it had already been upgraded to a 2TB drive. This is a much better option than cutting up the PS4's case to fit the height of a 4TB internal replacement. In addition, Sony did a nice job in making this approach a well supported option for expanding the PS4's storage capacity.
