RCA DB2 update 08/20/20 After a lot os snooping with psSense firewall logs, WireShark and TCP Dump I found a way to add the RCA DB2 to my local network and remain somewhat safe and secure. TLDR: The DB2 talks a lot. Most of the talking is to Amazon EC2 servers, but there is some traffic going to China and Singapore. You can't put the DB2 into a totally isolated network or VLAN with no internet access, the DB2 requires internet access for setup and password setting. A reasonable compromise is to put the DB2 into a wifi guest network with only access to the internet. I really like the DB2, but I'm going to downgrade it to three stars because you have to do a lot of tweaking and snooping with tools to getting working in an acceptable manner. Update #1: My 30 year old mechanical doorbell had a 16VAC 10VA transformer. There is enough power to run the DB2, but not enough poop to ring the indoor mechanical chime. I ended up replacing the transformer with a 24VAC 30VA transformer I got off Amazon. Now, the indoor chime rings with authority. If you just install the DB2 into your regular network with all of your other wifi stuff, it will work fine. You can pull the doorbell video up on your phone, you can talk people at your front door and you will get doorbell and PIR (motion) alarms. But, the DB2 will also be broadcasting on your home wifi network, be using Universal Plug and Play (UPnP) and occasionally be talking to the mothership in China. There is a reason why the US Government and several large companies don't using HikVision (same as RCA, Laview, EZviz and Nelly's), there are too may backdoors and security compromises. My first networking attempt was to put the DB2 into my IoT VLAN with no access outside of the VLAN. My main home VLAN can look into the IoT VLAN, but nothing can be initiated go out of the IoT VLAN. Put the DB2 into an isolated VLAN will let you view the RTSP video stream, but everything else is broken, no PIR alerts, no two way audio, nothing. My next networking attempt was to put the DB2 into my wifi guest VLAN that has internet access only. Everything works, but there is a lot of chatter going onto the network and some cases going to China and Singapore. I decided to use this configuration, but with added pfSense rules and configurations. First, there is no way to setup a static IP address, only DHCP is supported. So, using the DHCP server service in pfSense set DHCP static mappings for: IP Address DNS Server Set to my local Pi-Hole DNS server with updated blocking lists. NTP Server Set to the local pfSense NTP server. Add some rules to pfSense: Block All access to port 1900 or UPnP Block All access to outside DNS servers Block All access to outside NTP servers Allow All access to pfSense NTP server Allow All access to local pi-hole DNS server(s) Allow DB2 ICMP access to gateway (otherwise wifi will restart every minute of so) Block All access to IP Multicast (224.0.0.0/4) Block All access to trusted networks In pfSense turn on pfBlockerNG and block all "bad" places. Use GeoIP blocking to stay out of China and other questionable areas. Setting up video: I'm using Zoneminder and also use the RCA Security app on iOS. You can start up to three RTSP streams in Zoneminder or VLC and still have the RCA Security app work. rtsp://admin:[password]@[ip address]/Streaming/Channels/101/ WARNING: Do not change the default password on the DB2 sticker. If you change wifi networks or reset/restart the DB2, it will revert to the default password. Resources: REMOVE SPACES Hikvision Doorbell 101: https : // docs. google. com /document /d/ 1gt5aH9I_qBwlrDlYE5aS-0HIyGgV5SgF9oP50E7y-jQ/edit Ipcamtalk - New RCA HSDB2A 3MP Doorbell IP Camera: https : // ipcamtalk. com /threads/ new-rca-hsdb2a-3mp-doorbell -ip-camera.31601/ page-253 ----------------------------------------------------- I wanted a doorbell that did not require a subscription or cloud storage. After reading several reviews on the web and on Amazon I settled on the RCA DB2. This is the same doorbell as Nelly's, but $38 cheaper. The initial install would have taken about 10 minutes, but it took me an hour because I had to cut back the beveled siding to fit the top of the doorbell. In retrospect, I should have just hooked up the doorbell, let it dangle and then test to make sure things work. Once the siding was cut, I was committed. After searching the web, I found live video could be viewed by using RTSP. Set your client to rtsp://[IP_Address]/Streaming/Channels/101 In my case I'm using Zoneminder. The image has severe fish eye distortion, but maybe some good image software would fix it. I'm not using the RCA doorbell app, its annoying and there were many false alarms. Setup your zones in Zoneminder and you will be motion alerts when somebody comes to the front door. I don't want or use the talkback feature of the doorbell because it requires too much insecure internet access. As with many of these cheap products made in China, network security is a concern. I tried to the the doorbell in an isolated VLAN, but it didn't work, the doorbell needs internet access to setup and operate. The compromise I reached was to put the doorbell in a VLAN that can access the internet, but not my internal network. Right after setup the doorbell started to contact Amazon AWS and sites in China and Singapore. Please be aware if this doorbell has access to your internal network, there may be big security issues. If you have a good router, like psSense, you can write a rule to limit what access to the internet this doorbell has. So, here is my Pros/Cons summary: Pros: Easy install Works with indoor 16 V indoor mechanical chime Can connect to RTSP stream. Works with Zoneminder. No cloud storage Cons: The RCA app sucks Must have internet access to setup. Wifi disconnects often Severe fish eye image Contacts servers in China and Singapore frequently. If you change the doorbell password, you do a complete factory default setup again. If people can remove the decorative cover, they can push the reset button for 5 seconds and default the doorbell to factory settings. The chime the doorbell emits is super LOUD and can be heard across the street! There is no way to reduce the doorbell chime sound level. No web or ssh access.

This device is intended to prevent over-discharge of the battery (or batteries) in a system like a solar panel-charged battery bank. Rechargeable batteries of any type can be damaged by being overly discharged in use. There are such things as "deep cycle" batteries, which are more resistant to these problems, but they still have a minimum voltage to which they can repeatedly be discharged without causing permanent damage. This module is a very simple, but very capable, device which basically allows the user to set a minimum voltage, and when the battery voltage drops below that value, it cuts off the output of the battery, shutting down the powered system. I set it up in a test circuit with a variable voltage power supply, to see how well it worked, before using it in my actual circuitry, and was able to verify that this module did exactly what it's intended to do. Then I set it up in a battery capacity testing system, to be used to verify the condition of an aircraft battery. I was interested in applying a moderately heavy load to a fully-charged battery. I wanted to discharge the battery to a reasonable point, but then shut off the load so as not to damage the battery. I was interested in monitoring the capacity of the battery to power that load, while not hurting it. I set the module to allow the battery to discharge to 10 volts. The fully charged battery had an open-circuit voltage of 12.6 volts. I then applied a 100W resistive load (just under 8 amps at the beginning). I monitored the time it took to drop from 12.6 to 10 volts, and then looked at the time it took to do that, using another electrical timer. This allowed me to leave the testing setup alone, without worrying that I would over-discharge the battery. It worked exactly as it was supposed to. As the voltage fell about .1 volts below 10 volts, the relay on the unit opened, and shut off the load. The other setting, the "difference value" keeps the circuit from cycling quickly after the load is removed. As the battery hits 10 volts, it shuts off. That immediately allows the voltage on the battery to increase, due to the loss of the load. If it did not have this "difference setting", that alone might allow it to reset and turn the circuit back on again. This would cause it to cycle off-on-off-on for a while, until the battery didn't recover to above the 10 volt setting. This behaved exactly as I needed for my intended use. If one was using this as it's intended for, in a solar system, for example, without the "difference setting", as soon as the battery output was shut off, when solar charging started again, it would immediately turn on the load again, and the battery wouldn't charge. One would use this device to ensure that the battery (or bank of batteries) is charged above the desired voltage before the load was again enabled. For example, as the system was used to power, say a small lighting system, or a waterfall pump, when the battery falls to below the set minimum safe level you choose, say 9 volts for a deep-cycle battery, it would disconnect the load. You could set the "difference value" to 4 volts. The next day, when the sun came out, the battery would charge, without powering the load, until it reached a level of 13 volts. The load would then be enabled, and if needed power would flow again to the load. Then, when the sun goes down, it would continue to power the load, until the battery reached 9 volts again, when the load would again be disconnected, and the cycle would repeat. This device seems to be very stable. It has a voltage display (red LED digits) to show the battery voltage. I found this to be very accurate, at least within .1 volt DC. And the battery/load cutoff is also very accurate, again within no more than .1 volt DC. The same display is used with the two switches to select and set the minimum voltage and the "difference value". You select "min voltage" by holding the left switch until the display flashes, and then use the two switches to set the value, up or down. When you leave it alone for a few seconds, it reverts back to the normal monitoring mode, and indicates the battery voltage again. You do the same thing with the right switch, to set the "difference value". It's pretty easy to set up once you figure this little finger dance out. It's not that tough, and you will likely only need to do it once. There is a small red LED that lights whenever the relay is energized (ON) and the load enabled. When it trips and turns off the relay/load, the LED is off. So you can tell at a glance what the status of the load is, and at the same time, what the battery voltage is at any given moment. Basically, the thing just works. The setting is persistent, in that it stays after power is disconnected until you manually change it. If you have a need for such a module, you can't beat this to control a moderate load. The relay is marked as being rated for a 20A load. It can handle a battery voltage up to 36 volts.

To clear up some things people clearly do not understand. Are you complaining that the storage capacity isn't what is claimed? Wrong. Hard drive storage capacities have historically been rated using power of ten and your operating system reports capacity in binary which gives a lower number when you see the size reported in your OS. As has always been the case for drive storage capacity 1 MB = 1000 kilobytes, not 1024 kilobytes. 1 GB = 1000 MB, not 1024 MB. 1 TB = 1000 GB, not 1024 GB. 2 TB = 2000 GB, not 2048 GB and so on. Example, in the case of a 1 TB drive you will see a reported capacity of ~931 GB in your OS. A 4 TB drive will report a capacity of about 3.63 TB but if you look at details you will see that means typically about 4,000,768,323,584 bytes. There's your 4TB drive. Reported capacity can depend on your OS, partitioning and formatting. Important to remember this and claiming you didn't get the capacity you paid for isn't going to negate the facts. This is how it's been and is how ALL drive manufacturers rate their capacities, every one of them. OEM hard drives are very, very commonly sold to the public and have been for a very long time. They don't come in a box with retail packaging and they come as DRIVE ONLY, no screws, no data cable, no power connector and no instructions. These days they tend to come in plain brown boxes but they use to just come in only the anti-static bag and you might get it wrapped up in some bubble wrap if you were lucky and if really lucky it was packed so it didn't bang around in the box or sit in a vulnerable corner. This has been going on as long as the 30+ years I've been in the game. OEM DOES NOT MEAN YOU DON'T GET A WARRANTY! It MIGHT if the serial number of the drive you received is one from a batch or group that was supposed to actually go to a specific OEM builder and that batch made its way elsewhere somehow. Something like a "mistake", theft or that OEM dumping them back into the product chain improperly. Check your drive when you get it by checking warranty status of your serial number on the manufacturer's site. If it says no warranty (because it was intended to be the burden of the OEM that batch, group, lot was meant for) then return it to Amazon and be very specific as to why. When you buy computer hardware and you are just a consumer without access to certain knowledge and parts you may find some items like a simple hard drive install to be more of a challenge than you thought. You need to know beforehand if you need screws (some cases use screw-less hard drive retention, most don't), a data cable (SATA is the current common standard in use for PCs) and a SATA power cable or extension. Again, you get only a bare, antistat bagged drive when you purchase an OEM drive and unless it states that it's a retail drive or shows a retail box then it's going to be a bare OEM drive most likely.

Let me start with my setup. I have a gaming/personal pc and a work computer. Before I had 2 wired keyboards, 2 wireless mice, and no desk space. This review is for the 5 pack 16GB USB 2.0 flash drives. Full read/write tests on all five found no functional issues. They come formatted as Fat32 as is typical. Actual size is 15,711,830,016 bytes or around 14.6GB when formatted as Fat32. This is somewhat less than advertised, but not faked, just rounded up to the next standard size. They could be using "2nd's or B quality" memory chips that had too many bad cells to meet QC for major brands. Speeds were consistent across all five. The same hardware is listed under several different brand names (prices vary somewhat). On the plus side, they stay cool, have a red LED that flashes with activity, and are inexpensive. The main body is anodized aluminum and they are sleek looking (better than some name brand USB flash drives with poor visual aesthetics). Each comes with an easy to lose dust cap that fits securely on the end. The attachment loop opposite of the USB plug is made out of plastic so I wouldn't recommend these for hanging from a key chain. Sequential reads and writes are similar to other USB 2 drives I've tested, better than some, worse than others. A slight performance gain can achieved by re-formatting as exFat instead of Fat32 (note, verify first that exFat is compatible with your intended devices). They do not appear to be hermetically sealed (some flash drives are), and may not survive full immersion in liquid. Unfortunately, random writes are painfully slow as is often the case with cheap USB 2 drives. Random read/writes may not matter if you are primarily writing large files. I can't speak to longevity, but since they run fairly cool their lifespan should be okay. Heat is the biggest enemy of electronic devices. Digging deeper into the tech... the flash drive reports to Windows a name of "VendorCo ProductCode" with a product revision of 2.00, so in other words, it only has a place holder where the vendor and product name should go. It reports a VID of FFFF and a PID of 5678, again place holder data which is common on generic drives. Examing the physical circuit board, I can see that the controller is a FC1198BC which is made by FirstChip. The placeholder data is consistent with that of other generic drives using this controller reporting the same place holder information to windows. The memory itself was covered by epoxy with labling of JY8T2D-16GB (I found no information on this).

review_text: This tester is very interesting. Once you find the sweet spot on the tester to hold the batteries it works great. I tested some batteries that had failed in a TV remote and a mouse. Both took two AA batteries rated at 1.5 volts. The dead ones tested out at 1.37+/- volts each and the brand new ones tested at 1.57, 1.43, 1.54, and 1.48. Now to me, this means the tester is very sensitive or the remote or mouse are. I put the "dead" batteries in a AA mini-Maglite and they worked. No telling for how long but if this holds true you could save money on throwing away batteries that aren't completely dead.

Update: after using this thing for over a year I am regretting my purchase. The constant disconnects are annoying. It just disconnects for no reason. Also when setting up it is such a hassle. It should remember saved locations but sometimes I have to run through the setup all over again. And this is not really the camp pro's fault, but it can't work magic. If the campground's wifi signal is bad it's only going to connect you to a bad signal. I always seem to get the camping site far away from the campgrounds WiFi antenna. I like to stream video when I camp. And when the signal constantly drops it makes it difficult. So after a long search for WiFi boosters I purchased the Alpha WiFi Camp Pro 2. Included was a multi directional and a single directional antenna for extra long distances. I have yet to try the single directional antenna. There was also the receiver to attach the antenna, a USB cable, and a router. Setting it up was actually easy. I mounted the antenna to a 1 1/2" x 8' PVC pipe and attached it to the camper with 2 plastic clamps on the edge of a slide. Total for all the hardware was under $10. The USB cable I routed through the fridge vent. Setting it up each time only takes about 10 minutes. I first tested the setup in my driveway. I used my cellphone to do the original setup. I thought it was simple. Sitting in my camper I could find 3 WiFi sources and none of them was my home router. After connecting everything I had over 30 sources including my home system. Speed test showed my connection around 25Mbps. I wouldn't expect much more since this is only a 2.4Ghz connection. I then went inside my home and I was still connected to the camp pro router. So it seems to have a better signal than my home router. On the first camping trip I tested the campgrounds WiFi for the first day. It was about 3Mbps but I was getting constant drops. I connected it to the camp pro and tested for the next 24 hours. Now the speed did not really improve but the signal was stable and I experienced no drops. Also the entire family was able to connect to the camp pro. Worked great! For the money spent I am really happy. It does exactly what it is supposed to do. And all in an easy to install all in one simple kit.

review_text: I own an IT Service Provider business and manage over 60 clients. I needed an IP Remote Power Switch that could be configured to reboot the Internet Modem, then reboot the router in a certain sequence with time delay. Also needed to be able to auto reboot one or more Servers if during Microsoft Update reboots, the server hangs on reboot. This switch does perform each of my requirements. The manual is pretty good but just gets you to the interface with basic explanation of screens. The vendor's website does have FAQs and a lot of documentation. You will need to take advantage of their site to fully learn about this device. I was a little concerned reading the other ratings. Lots of single stars and device failure. This device was the only device that seemed to do what I wanted so I purchased one to test. It appears the latest firmware version that came out late 2020 have resolved those issues. I guess time will tell. The main advantage of this switch is the capability of writing easy scripts to control each of the outlets. EVERYONE is looking for the auto restart of the modem then after a time frame reboot the router. There are other IP Remote Switches but the only ones I found, that was preconfigured to perform this function, only had 2 outlets. Fine for home environment but not a business environment with servers. With this device you have full control over how many external URL's or IPs you need to ping to truly determine your Internet connection is dead. ALL of the URL's or IPs must fail before the reboot process will start. There is a document on the vendors website that indicates only one of the listed items needs to fail for the reboot process to start. The engineer I talked too and my testing proved it must be ALL. This is how it should be. There is a email notification section that understand TLS so you can have emails sent to 365 if necessary. I plan to put this device at all my client sites. That's how well this device satisfies my requirements. I'm writing this review to provide an example of the simple script you can call when your Internet Modem and Router need to be reset. I had to review multiple example scripts on the vendors site to figure out how to create a script that works. Put this in the Scripts location and call from the AutoPing section. Simple now that I've figured it out. Hopefully this helps others looking for this capability. Looks like with scripting you can control almost any feature. function reboot_modem_router_withdelay() --Modem on Outlet 1, Router on Outlet 2 outlet[1].off() outlet[2].off() --Turn on Modem after a 5 sec delay delay(5) outlet[1].on() --Now wait for Modem to fully boot. 5 min works delay(300) --Turn on Router outlet[2].on() end

review_text: [[VIDEOID:6f7bdcc0c1ebb06bb2b91caf10f67c13]] BEST COOLER!!! The price and performance while looking very pretty, this cooler is a bang for your buck!!! I can’t give it full stars because it has a teal logo that you can’t just turn off or change the colors. It ruins the whole point of having customizable RGB, especially in color coded builds. But, aside from that this is definitely one of the best coolers that you can get for the price, that looks good, and does good. Performance: The new CPUs that have been dropping lately run pretty hot especially the high end CPUs so you definitely need a 360mm AIO if you have a high end CPU. I have a 13900K in my build and my idle temps are between 35 - 45 degrees celsius and while gaming it never goes above 75 degrees celsius. So overall it is a solid cooler to cool your CPU. This can definitely tame today’s CPUs. You'll hear pump bubbles for the first couple of days which is completely normal it is overall a pretty quiet cooler now that I had it for a couple weeks. I would definitely replace the fans though, they aren’t bad they are quiet for the most part until high RPMs of course. Looks/Design: I cannot justify spending $300 on a 360mm AIO that looks nice! And this cooler is pretty much half the cost, and looks just as nice. It has a unique design with it being square. I am a sucker for infinity mirror designs it just looks super cool, since you can see the RGB from multiple sides just adds to the already beautiful infinity mirror design especially with lighting effects. HOWEVER that teal logo is just HIDEOUS! It doesn’t match with my setup. So of course I had to do some DIY techniques to compliment my PC build aesthetically. The block with the RGB infinity mirrors just goes on top of the actual pump so it makes it very easy to install the pump, pretty sweet design DeepCool. Since I spray painted the block white to match my build and even the teal logo, the teal logo would still light up teal even though it was spray painted. So behind that block if you look in the inside (while its on) there is a very bright white light that shines onto the teal plastic looking part. All you need to do is cover that light. You can stuff anything in there to do that, I used a tape to try and do that. SO NOW the teal light is gone! And it just looks so much better in my PC now. It is a very easy modification, especially thanks to DeepCool with how they designed the block to be separate. I’ve also ordered some white cable sleeves and wrapped it around the tubes, you can find these also on amazon for pretty cheap. So with these simple and easy modifications to how it looks, it is definitely worth it. I had bought the silver version of this cooler since the white one at the time wasn’t in stock and places where they did have it were selling it for almost $200 what the heck. I really needed a new cooler for my build and I didn’t want to wait on backorder. If you can buy the white version of this cooler it would be a lot easier but you would still have to modify the block to not have it light up the teal logo, and would be a better effect to paint the visible part of the teal. TL;DR Very easy to install. If you find it hard to, a tutorial by “The Provoked Prawn” has a very good installation tutorial. Good looks/design and cooling performance tames high end CPUs. DIY to remove the teal logo: Spray paint front visible part of teal. Inside the block, cover the teal part so that it doesn’t receive any light to light it up teal. If you are in the market for a 360mm cooler, this is 100% a solid pick especially considering the price.

I've never owned a smart watch, so this review is with that in mind. I wanted to get one for several reasons. Mostly I wanted to work at being more active, so paying attention to how much I'm moving around each day was important. I have my phone, but I don't carry it with me all the time, especially as I'm moving around the house, so having some kind of fitness tracker seemed like a good idea. After looking at options I realized that it made more sense to spend money on getting a smart watch with fitness tracker features than just getting something that counted steps. After reading a bunch of reviews and looking at what was out there I decided to try the Amazfit GTS. I figured that if it didn't end up working in the end, I wouldn't be out several hundred dollars like I would with an iWatch. I think, as an entry level, this is a good solid option. I've had it for several weeks now and have used it daily, so I've gotten to see how it does with battery life, functions, accuracy, etc. Overall I'm really happy with it! The battery definitely doesn't last me two weeks, but in the past two weeks I've only charged it twice after the initial charge/set up, and it charged to full battery in about 30-45 minutes. When I did charge it I did it the first time when it was at 20% and the last time it was still at about 40%, so it didn't NEED to be charged. I like the Zepp App that works with the watch, though I've noticed the stress monitor isn't giving me any data. Everything else seems to work well. There's a ton in there! Some people mentioned that there were only a few face options - not true. In the app you can tap on your device and the first thing on the menu is "watch face". From there you can choose from over 50 watch faces, or customize your own. Within the watch face you can also decide what you want displayed, etc. The only glitch I've noticed is that a day or so ago the step count wasn't working properly. I would move around and notice that it wasn't adding new steps on, which then affected some of my goal achievements. I was frustrated because I'd only had it two weeks and had seen some reviews of people saying the watch stopped being accurate after a couple weeks. I looked around for info, and went through the app menu to see if I could find anything, update something, etc. In the Settings menu there's a "Behavior tagging" option. If you tap on that you go to a screen where you can choose an activity to monitor. The little "i" for info button said that it's a way to monitor for inaccuracies. I chose the "walk" option, started it on my phone, then just did normal activity where I was moving around in my house for a few minutes. Stopped it, and noticed that after that the step counter was working properly again. It seems as though it helped recalibrate things. Just wanted to share that for anyone who might have the same issue. Overall I'm really happy with my Amazfit GTS and would recommend it if you want a good starter smart watch.

A little pricey but it works well and I’m happy I bought it. I purchased this on a Black Friday Special over Thanksgiving weekend. It was for a Christmas Gift and put into use after Christmas. My initial review was simply - “A little pricey but it works well and I’m happy I bought it.” Two things happened since then. One very good. One terrible. GOOD. After using the keyboard for a few weeks I my thoughts on the product skyrocketed. It is hands down the best design for my ipad 9 (10.2 inch size). I have looked at many other companies products and they all pale in comparison to the Brydge. At least for my uses. This keyboard truly turns it into a mini laptop. Perfect for sitting on the couch working on your lap, lying in bed watching a movie, sitting it on the counter while preparing a meal, etc. etc. etc. This is where most of the other “competitors” to this product fail. They have prop up stands or no ability to adjust the screen angle which make them fine for sitting on a desktop but TERRIBLE for using as I have described. The Brydge also makes it so simple to pull the ipad out and use it as a handheld device easily when you want to. The keyboard typing experience is excellent. The backlit keyboard is a nice touch for late night typing. The battery power is better than I expected. I think I only had to charge it after about two months of use and it should last even longer now that I realize you can turn off the keyboard backlight when you don’t need it. The keys are well laid out. There are dedicated keys for “SIRI” questions. There are many more things I like but I wont ramble on. For my purposes it is perfect. And it even looks good. It garners many compliments when people see it. THE BAD: Early March (approximately two months of use into it) both plastic hinges failed. The plastic simply cracked on both of them and the screen began to flop. Then within a week they broke entirely and one came off. The unit was useless. I have since seen (by looking at the negative / one star reviews) that this is definitely not an isolated problem. It appears many people have had the exact same problem and that the timeline was almost the same as mine - somewhere just short of three months the plastic hinges failed. Their pictures even looked EXACTLY like mine. I was saddened as it was an obvious design flaw. I can’t say for sure but one person postulated that it was due to Brydge’s new partnership with Otterbox. I have to say that basic logic in my head said that very well may be true. The case that goes over the actual IPad looks and feels like a typical Otterbox product and the box that the Brydge comes in touts “OTTERBOX” right on the cover. I actually like the casing for the ipad. Everyone’s opinions may differ but I like Otterbox products and it’s a nice cover for the IPad when you take it off of the keyboard to use it as a handheld. The problem, however, appears to be that the two plastic / magnetic hinges that connect the ipad to the keyboard are also made of the same plastic. And it is obviously not up to the task of the forces put on it when opening and closing the tight hinges on a regular basis. Look at the picture I post along with other peoples posts and you will see exactly what I mean. THE GOOD: back to the good. Amazon started a case when I messaged them and asked me to type out a message that would be sent directly to the Brydge representative and to note whether I was requesting a refund or a replacement. Which I did. I explained as I have above. I also specifically noted that it was an obvious design flaw and that, assuming the flaw had been addressed, and assuming I got a full warranty with any repair or replacement, I would love a replacement as I thought the product, exclusive of the broken hinges, was excellent. The Brydge representative responded promptly the next day, requested I send pictures and serial number and noted that they would send me a replacement once they received the information. They also noted that there is no longer a need to send in the old unit. To simply please recycle it at a electronics recycling center. (My thought about that was - they have given up on that design or been overwhelmed with returns and thus do not need returned units any more). I replied as requested and again specifically noted that I was concerned it was a design flaw and expected that it had been addressed. I got a message a few days later simply nicely noting that they had approved my new keyboard and it would be in the mail within 48 hours. (It was and I am typing on it now). So - they get good credit for being responsive, courteous, prompt, polite, etc. etc. etc. THE BAD: The keyboard and case, upon inspection, appear to be EXACTLY the same. I appreciate the quick replacement and the good customer service. But I have to say that I feel almost certain I am looking at going through this process again in approximately 2-3 months. THE MAYBE: I hope that I am wrong. But I fear that I am not. Only time will tell. But, even though i seldom write reviews longer than three sentences, I feel compelled to write all of this down. For approximately $100-$130 (depending on if you find it on special or not) you should certainly expect a product like this to last for a few years at least problem free. Or with extremely minimal problems. Maybe a loose key that wiggles. But the flaw I describe makes the unit entirely useless. SUMMARY: I just want anyone considering this to know the details before they make a decision. The product is great. I mean great. The initial customer service was responsive. I’m concerned (almost sure) I will have go through this process again. And I assume / expect that they will be equally responsive. However, I also assume that one year from now I will be told I am “Out of Warranty” and that will be the end of that. Like I said - a product like this should have a minimum expectation of a three years of quality use. My guess is that the Ipad, costing just $349, will last for as much as ten years without any problems beyond being old technology. Hopefully BRYDGE is in the process of a redesign of the plastic hinges. If they want to reach out to me I will gladly Update my review with any information they provide. I hope this information is valuable to any potential customers. I’m not telling you to buy it or not to buy it, simply providing information that you might be able to use. (Side notes. 1. I have bought other Brydge products as gifts and they seem excellent. Just not this one with a poor material choice for the plastic hinge. 2. I forgot to thank the Amazon rep that I texted with - they were excellent. )

review_text: I'd been using the Amazon Halo as I wanted a fitness tracker where I wasn't distracted by the screen. As I progressed, I found myself wanting to listen to music while exercising without my phone flapping around in my pocket. After researching watches that could play music to Bluetooth headphones without my phone, I landed here. I haven't used a "smart watch" before, but my wife has, so while my experience is second hand, I can say I'm fairly pleased. First off, the most important thing it seems to most people: The battery. I decided to break it and see what I could really expect. There are only two things I tweaked: 1) Turned off the "Always on watch face" as I didn't feel the need to have a watch face displayed if I wasn't looking at it, and 2) I scheduled the "turn face on when I lift my wrist" to be off from midnight to six am. I didn't think it necessary for my watch to turn on while I toss and turn. I had all of the heart-rate, sleep, etc. all turned on all the time. I used the watch to listen to music through my headphones for 4 different runs, and a little around the house. So I would say other than the "always on" I gave it quite a push. After 7 full days, my watch battery was still at 15%. My wife is using a Versa 3 and for the same time frame she was at 10%-minus the music playing, and she doesn't have constant monitoring turned on. Battery life is great. It's pretty responsive to swiping, but some of the integration in regards to the app are spotty. I'm on Verizon and none of my message alerts come through as I'm using the Message+ and the app only send notifications if I'm using the base SMS in Android. That's kind of a bummer. There's a decent amount of watch faces(30 or so) and you can find one you like. Getting music onto the watch isn't really straight forward. You have to use the app, which wants you to connect to the watch via wifi, but the watch has a unique wifi password that isn't in the manual, and really not easy to find within the app itself. I had to cause it to "error out" trying to connect about 5x before it showed me the wifi password for the watch. I've not taken it into the lake yet for paddle boarding, I'm waiting for my protective covers to get here. It has knocked up against a few things(stucco, door jams, fiddling around under the hood of my car) and not been scraped or scuffed so far. Protectors, replacement bands, and even charging stands are cheap and plentiful on Amazon, so dressing it up a bit won't be an issue. This again is my first experience, and maybe all smart watch apps are lacking in one way or another. My reports on sleeping and heart rate activity are all present and accessible, but not much to really dig deeper. For $130, I'm very pleased.

Okay, so let me begin by saying that I am a shameless Apple sheep, and buy most Apple products that come out. I have an iPhone 13 Pro Max, iPad Pro, MacBook Air, MacBook Mini, and I'm waiting on a Mac Studio to arrive. But for some reason I've resisted Apple's attempts to make a speaker, and I don't like to wear ear bud style headphones, so never purchased any AirPods. I've even experimented with non-Apple music solutions including Tidal, Amazon and Spotify among others. But with the recent price drop, and the fact that I fly a lot, I decided to give these headphones a try. I genuinely thought there was a 80% chance I'd return them, as I currently use the well reviewed Sony MX4s. The wow factor of these is unbelievable. Watching a movie or TV show on my iPad is incredible. I listened to the opening sequence to The Blacklist Season 1 Episode 1, which has some good audio. My wife, who is never that impressed with audio took a listen and was blown away. I got on board with Apple Music, and listened to the lossless music, and also the specially mixed spacial audio. Wow. Wow again. Yeah, I'd pay retail for these. I think the obvious gripes have been made already. The lightening port was a bad call, but I carry those cables for my iPhone anyway, so no biggie. Although I suspect these headphones will be the last of my devices to still require that plug. The case is idiotic, as is the decision to give me no manual control over turning them off. You seriously have to put these things in the horrific case to put them in low power mode, and there is reasonable question as to whether this case would provide any meaningful protection of these expensive headphones. Speaking of lunacy, the steps you have to take to coax the device into updating its firmware is also Apple arrogance at its finest. Why I can't have a standby switch or button and an update firmware option is beyond me. And again, I'm a fanboy here. It's also pretty sad that the design allows the cans to bang together if not handled carefully, which will surely result in scratches at some point. Oh, and want to listen with a wire, enjoy buying that $35 proprietary cable from Apple. Seriously. This is why people hate Apple. But despite these many very reasonable gripes, the bottom line here is that these sound better than every Bose pair I have owned, my Sony MX4s, and several Bang & Olufsen sets I've had. The seamless swiping between Apple products is also pretty sweet. The transparency mode is probably the best on the market too. There is no doubt I'd highly recommend them. Be aware of the need to bend a little to Apple's will, in several areas, but know that the pay off is some pretty stunning results. I'm actually looking forward to going back to work on Monday to hear how they do on the plane. Flying to New Orleans, so should be in the air for around 3 hours. *** UPDATE: Six months later... So these are great headphones. Unfortunately, after six months of use, it's hard to justify a five star rating. Background noise control is great, transparency mode is amazing, the sound quality is excellent. But, they are heavy, you have to plan your entire business trip packing strategy around lugging these heavy and inconvenient items around. I had to buy a third party case to protect them, and use it with the stupid Apple case. They take up a huge chunk of back pack real estate. Then, after five months or so, they started randomly disconnecting. More specifically, it seems like the sensor that decides if I am wearing them isn't functioning correctly. So if I scratch my head or move too suddenly, they shut off, disconnect, and then I have to pull out my iPhone or iPad, force them to reconnect, and continue. Given that these are heavy and not particularly comfortable, you find yourself trying to put off scratching an itch, just to avoid the hassle of reconnecting. My expectations rise with price, so at over $500, by far the most expensive travel headphones I've ever purchased, I do kind of expect flawless. For all their positives, there are a LOT of negatives, which is such a shame. I imagine that version 2 or 3 will be so cool. And, like a total sucker, I'll probably buy them. For now, I'm going to switch to the AirPod Pro 2s, while these headphones are at the Apple Store being repaired. I may even sell them at this point. Such a shame.

The kit comes with 4 mounting arms for the projector, our Epson EF-100 only has 3 mounting points so I just didn't use the 4th and I was able to adjust the angles for a perfect fit! Very versatile. Since our ceiling outlet is centered on the room but the projector lens is not, I have to tilt the arm sideways a little and the projector mount downward. The the fasteners do a great job holding it firmly in place. Very solid design. Cons: none. Any cons I would have would be due to user error or impatience during installation. Advice: make sure that you center the projector before mounting it because the projection angle makes a huge difference to how "square" your image is. Also, don't over tighten the screws. It's tempting but tighten them just enough so the joints don't move. The projector is basically just hanging there anyway, so you just need to tighten the screws enough so it doesn't swing or sway, or to fight gravity if you have to tilt it downward to project where you want it to. Also if you have to make adjustments, loosen the screws first. Forcing it to move while the screws are already tightened will wear out the metal or could break the screw if you have it on too tight.

In replacement, I bought Garmin's entry-level Drive 51. Here's are some of what I have so far discovered about this GPS unit. 1.) The set-up was easy. 2.) Programming destinations [favorites] took a bit of finessing. Yet, failed to sit in memory 3.) The unit's accuracy is really poor. Several times now the unit has failed to recognize the most basic of destinations. For example, the public libraries in my area. 4.) When pressing the favorites icon, the result is a single destination as opposed to the roster of saved favorites. 5.) An enclosed car charger is a closed unit. This means that if the fuse goes out, you'll need to replace the entire charger unit. At present, I'm on the fence as to whether to return it or continue struggling to figure out how to navigate the unit's fickle nature. Garmin has made this introductory-level unit much less attractive or reliable than I had previously experienced. Too bad. - @daFigz™

After initially being very impressed with this 3-1 charger after a few days of use my opinion has changed.I use this mainly as a bedside stand to charge my iPhone 14 Pro, Apple Watch Ultra and Jabra Elite 10s. The earbud charging part works absolutely fine but the watch charger and phone stand is where the issues lie.The watch charger does not work well with the Apple Watch Ultra ( I have the Ocean band) and no matter what angle you place the charging puck at, the watch does not sit well. It will sometimes come away from the charger by itself if you don’t get it quite right and my watch will not charge. It’s far too finicky. Also I think the watch charger is the cheapest feeling and looking part of the charger and I think over time with folding and unfolding will eventually break.The phone stand is far too light for my 14 pro (Which is quite a heavy phone) it’s not very stable and when removing my phone from the stand you have to hold everything in place as it’s far too light. This makes it very awkward to use. I would certainly not bother if you own the larger pro max. I would also like to add that for such an expensive item the supplied Usb C cable is one the worst I have used, it will never straighten out and cheapens the product. A braided cable would have been much better.I am also not quite convinced by Qi2. I have noticed from use that it generates far more heat then official MagSafe. There are several reviews on YouTube mentioning this and as we know too much heat will degrade the battery far quicker. MagSafe chargers also have a memory feature built in so if you have few located in your home the phone will remember how you had stand by mode set up on each charger where Qi2 chargers will not do this.Overall I think this would be a great travel charger but for everyday use as a bedside stand it’s far too light and cramped. Might be ok if you own the 13 mini and smaller Apple Watch.For me £99.99 is too much just for a travel charger. Also the idea of Qi2 was to make magnetic chargers cheaper to buy then official MagSafe but for this price you can buy an official charger.Anyway unfortunately I will be returning this one and probably go back to an official MagSafe charging stand. The 3 stars is for use as a travel charger but if to use as bedside charger I would give it 2 stars.

review_text: Don't believe the hype by reviewers that receive free review units from Garmin and use them for 2 weeks before writing their review. This watch does not work. Pros: - The Golf App is awesome. I can't think of anything that could be done better. - Hardware is mostly great. Screen is daylight readable and Physical buttons are ideal for exercise. - Battery lasts about a week if you exercise every day. - Running and Bike tracking works great Cons: - Garmin frequently updates the software with broken code - Weather App just says "waiting for data". It's quicker to pull out your phone than troubleshoot your watch constantly. - Alarms stopped working as of most recent update. I'm not joking. - Sleep tracking stopped working as of the most recent update. - As I write this all of garmin connect is down. - Garmin Express software stopped working in the last month. - Using 2 digital buttons to scroll around a map is a joke - Using 2 digital buttons to enter a 0-9 pin number before garmin pay is a joke. It's WAY faster to just pull out a credit card. - Proprietary charger is awful and has worn out the pins on a prior fenix model I had in a single year. - Battery is not replaceable. This is a $600 paper weight if anything goes wrong - Garmin support takes days to respond and then replies with 1 sentence responses that are not helpful. - Strength training tracking doesn't work. Heart rate is all over the place. Rep counting is inaccurate. Lift identification is constantly wrong. There's not much else that could be done here based on the limited input options on the watch. I assume that the software in this watch is so terribly broken because Garmin has like 47 different models they have to write updates for. Unlike an Apple Watch, fitbit, or Wear device, you will not receive any of the new feature updates as soon as a new model of the fenix comes out. This means you're paying $650 for a pretty watch that doesn't work, is not serviceable, and will go out of date in 1 year. UPDATE: Garmin Connect went down for 4+ days. They didn't bother telling anyone why but it has become public knowledge that they were hacked. They still haven't made any mention of whether passwords, personal data, etc. could have been accessed by the hackers that broke into the garmin network. I would not trust this company with any data you don't want malicious actors to have access to. Man... what a trash company Garmin is.

Let me count the ways by which I reach such a conclusion. It is noteworthy that others have had better luck with these people and this machine. In some cases (e.g. WIFI limitations and multiple screens) that may be caused by the fact that most people are happy with the thing as delivered. In others (e.g. loud and rattling fan and the hassle of an not-activated operating system), beware no matter how intense your demands of the computer.. (i) The machine was shipped with Windows 10 as promised but in a version or copy that had not been activated (read not legal in the minds of the gods at Microsoft). The cure for such things is to find what is called a product key and to furnish that to Microsoft at which time, if one holds his or her mouth correctly and asks nicely, Microsoft will validate Windows for them. When USTecno (the refurbisher) people were asked about the problem, one could sense some head scratching on the other end. They then said that the product key was on a sticker on the machine but that one had to rub it (this is not a joke) to expose it. Don’t rub it too hard or you will destroy it (no this is not a joke either). I did rub it and was able to interpret the key and soive the problem after the expenditure of perhaps one-and-a-half hours of discovering that the problem existed (through some of my software being sufficiently smart to know that it was about to join a questionable enterprise) and what to do about it (learn how to get the product key so that I could convey it to the gods of Redmond). It also must be said that the attitude of the people at USTecno was decidedly arrogant and rude as though it was my problem that I had obtained a machine with an invalid version of Windows. Ultimately they would be correct in that assertion. It was my problem and a big one! Their attitude led me to resolve both to write this review and to never deal with them again or maybe with any other Amazon refurbisher. (ii) When I tried to connect the computer to a wired connection (RJ-45) it didn’t work. I never solved this problem (read on and know that I gave up) but I expect that the issue is the fact that the old network adapter ran well on Windows 7 and will not run on Windows 10 (know that this core machine is that old and see below). At least this problem may not go back to the halcyon days of XP as described below! And you ask yourself how could a company ignore such a problem--and I would profess not to know short of some unintelligible comment about their competence. A possible cure is to buy a pci card video adapter, install it and hope that it works to recognize multiple monitors. Be ready to spend a couple hundred dollars and several hours of your time and then not to be certain about the Windows 7/10 problem and the form factor of the card until the big moment when you fire it up and learn the truth. (iii) A corollary to the above is that the machine is apparently delivered with a dongle WIFI connector. Mine would only detect my 2.4 network and didn't recognize the 5.0 that I wanted to use (my 2.4 is loaded and the wired connection did not work as previously stated). The reason for this failure is likely either an operating system issue (this machine was originally delivered when new with Windows 7) or a process of simply buying the least expensive thing that would facilitate a WIFI claim and cover over the non-functional wired connector described above. (iv) When the machine was first fired up, I immediately noticed that one or both of the fans (It seems that the model likely has fans in the power supply and over the CPU) was/were very loud with an attendant rattling noise. If you have ever kept an old computer for a while, you will be familiar with the sound and maybe the results. Again one wonders if the people who rebuilt the system ever turned it on. The cure in this case in part is to buy a $135 power supply (price from Amazon) and install it yourself. If that doesn’t sound difficult, it becomes three times more so in a small form factor machine. That does not address the potential fan over the CPU. In any case the loss of a fan in a power supply is usually enough to produce toast. Another alternative is of course to wait until it dies and run the risk of losing the computer and everything on it while maybe smoking up your office or home. (v) When I tried to connect two monitors to the system, it would not recognize and display on the second monitor. It turns out that the driver in this case is very old and was originally designed for Windows XP sometime in the distant past (with apologies to those of you who may not be sufficiently old to remember such things). The problem of the video adapter not working with multiple displays is well-known and discoverable with a bit of web research except perhaps for the people who rebuilt this machine. The cure in this case is to find the right driver in the anals of intel, download it and install it. Good luck with that if you’re not a technical guru with time on your hands. (vi) And finally the ultimate insult. Amazon policy with this particular rebuilder, and maybe all of them, is to invoke a process which consumes one-and-a-half to two weeks before one gets money back or replacement product. If you are accustomed to Amazon’s typical accommodating process, don’t be misled. This is anything but sensible or accommodating. Amazon in this case works with these people to deliver a piece of junk and then tries to make it difficult for the customer to rectify the problem. And this ain't a widget which is obviously bad "out of the box". It takes work and several hours to learn about all these problems. And one strongly suspects that further persistence would only lead to more unpleasant discoveries. Like I said: "Don't even think about it!".

When writing onto the flash drive, speeds varied wildly (1.2 MB/s to 3.53 MB/s) but I averaged ~1.60 MB/s. At 1.60 MB/s speed it takes nearly 11 minutes to put a 1 GB file onto the flash drive. To make matters worse the speeds fall off into the lower hundreds KB/s range when trying to transfer multiple files at once onto the drive. Granted it does have the correct amount of storage of 116 GB (computer using base 1024 rather than the normal base of 1000) and the transfer speeds off the drive is much higher (~17 MB/s) but the write speeds are so low that you realistically can not use that storage as you would a normal flash drive. Edit: I have used it for a few days now and speeds are averaging even lower. Worse files are starting to fully corrupt and some files are corrupted only in random fractions. I will be returning this device.

I received this product at a discounted rate in exchange for my honest opinion through the Insiders. When I first opened the box to this Sony speaker I was like whoa. I mainly wanted to play music from my phone through Bluetooth and that was an easy setup. Once everything was set up I was disappointed by the quality of the sound. The base wasn't quite as punchy as I had hoped the mids were fine and the highs were kind of flat. So then I discovered there was an app that should allow you to tweak these things. It does allow to tweak these things and I was able to get a very good sound, a sound that has punch and carries but doesn't disturb the neighbors around our pool. The app isn't quite intuitive and it kind of bugs me that I need the app to get a good sound. Now that I have the sound I like it's a very excellent speaker with just a few downsides. One downside is the fact that it doesn't have a battery and needs to be plugged in. A lot of other speakers at this price have a built-in battery so this is a slight disappointment. It's not like I didn't know this ahead of time but at this price it would be nice. Probably the biggest downside was the fact that when you first get the unit and it's off it goes into demo mode which the instructions don't tell you how to turn demo mode off. There's a little sticker on top of the unit but that didn't help me at all. I ended up googling how to do it and it turns out you need the remote which you almost never use otherwise! I have to give it to Sony for making a very good looking and stylish speaker. The styling is second to none. Also the lighting is very cool, easy to adjust and turn off if need be. The speaker has a ton of inputs for music, be it CD or USB or line in or Bluetooth or it can act as an amp for a microphone or a guitar. The CD seems kind of dated but I'm sure there's people who still use that. And as long as you have a CD on the unit you might as well have FM which this does which is a nice touch actually. As long as you remember the antenna that is which is included but you have to install it. My kids were giving me a hard time about getting the speaker because they thought my small Bluetooth speaker sounded just as good until I sent them to the other side of the pool where they barely hurt the small Bluetooth speaker yet they heard the Sony speaker clear as day.

It has conversation awareness which if it detects you are speaking it will lower your music volume and turn on transparency mode if not already on. There are loads of customisable features in the iPhone and iPad ecosystem to take advantage of these earbuds. Spatial audio is great too as when you are using a compatible app your headphones make it seem as though the sound is coming from your device all the time even when you turn your head.Swipe gestures to control volume is much better than deciphering different taps, and pinch to answer calls, play/pause and skip track is again much better than trying to tap the right sequence in the right spot.Build in "find my" features on not only the airpods case but the airpods themselves is great if you are prone to losing them. Wireless charging as standard with USB-C charging available too. You can use an apple watch magsafe charger too on it as opposed to a regular QI charger.Case lid snaps shut with a satisfying snap and stays shut to keep the buds protected. Battery life is great and I have not noticed any reduction in quality over my B&O earpods that these have replaced. I am now a wearer of these almost constantly and I carry them literally everywhere.

review_text: The good: The extender actually is far more feature-rich and configurable than the specifications show. Once you get into the advanced configuration options, you can configure as many (or in some cases) more parameters than your average WiFi router. You can also use it as a wired-to-wireless gateway, which is my configuration. The bad: The web interface is a train wreck — terribly designed and hard to navigate. Settings are hard to find, and sometimes in the middle of configuring something the device will stop responding, and you’ll have to completely reset it (using the hardware reset button — hold it down for 8 seconds) and start configuration from scratch. It took me two hours to get it how I wanted it, but only 10 minutes of that is actual configuration — the rest is try, reset, start again. The ugly: Requires at least one reboot every couple days. And there is no setting to automatically reboot. Sometimes it requires REPEATED REBOOTS in sequence before it starts functioning again. I would not have believed it had I not seen it myself!

I wanted to upgrade to a tri band mesh from a dual band traditional wifi. I tried for a few days to get the product to work. Here is the feedback. Product out of the box seems very cool. Compact design and the app looks cool. I had to work to get my six units of Deco access points setup but after a few hours and working with the application, it seemed to all be setup. I am by no means a network guru but I am fairly competent and I can get technical enough to know QoS, Mac addresses, and to know what a DNS is. I am using six units over 3000 square foot which should be under the 3 units in 4500 square feet advertised. The wireless signals don't seem to go through wall well, so I am glad that I got six units instead of settling for 3 units. Signal strength seems to be low to certain devices like my Amazon Fire. I moved the access points and it seemed somewhat stable. Maybe the access points or mesh were conflicting. But then weird issues started to happen. The entire network would just drop. Then come back. Then on all the devices, it would sometimes drop connection. Another weird issue, it wouldn't allow the user to log in with the correct password. After about six tries, it would then accept the correct password. Very frustrating. The app was pretty cool, but without anything to tune, it became a less useful product and was not an upgrade to my existing wifi. It also didn't have any easy way to access event logs so that I could understand what was working. It had a reporting mechanism that showed when devices accessed the network, but it did not update accurately. I tried chat twice, no response. I sent an email but the response time would be 24 hours. I went onto the tech support forum, and there were similar posts like mine. There seemed to be a firmware code that could be applied that was beta but you could only get it from support. I want wifi to just work. We are all working from home including multiple kids trying to school from home. I can't spend two days trying to work and without a product that looks cool but can't meet common reliability standards. I returned the product. I am disappointed because this product advertised would have been an upgrade but it was not as reliable as past Wifi products that I have used and the support was subpar in my opinion.

I bought this 4-pack of AirTags to track my RV in storage, and three other vehicles, one of which my son drives to school. That way I figure I can always track them if they are stolen. Seemed like a good idea but in practice not so much. First, my not too old iPhone XS does not get location updates. It can show the last known location only when my iPhone was close by. However, my Apple Watch 7 shows frequent tracking updates. So, why can't the Watch share that with the iPhone, where I have a larger screen and can see more detail on the map, zoom in etc. I could live with that but the real deal killer, is that even after a year of this feature being requested, Apple still have not added family sharing. So, I can't let my wife's iPhone see where any of the AirTags are. Even worse, every time she gets in one of our vehicles, she gets a notification that another AirTag is tracking her, with no way to ignore that particular AirTag. I'm very disappointed because these AirTags could have been a really useful addition to a family who already has a few Apple devices, but these are just not fit for purpose. review_text: This network mesh router setup works but, man, it's very limited in it's services and features. Easy to setup and works for just internet purposes really well but security is very weak. Pros: Easy setup App is simple enough Allows for physical connections for local devices making it easier for my PS4 and NAS to feel like they are directly connected without running cable all through the house. Great wireless speeds. Works well even when connected to another router. Gigabit and Fast ethernet ports are great for local connections. Cons: No ability to reserve addresses for systems that shouldn't change (NAS or network attached storage). Unable to limit access to network by MAC address for uninvited devices. Security services on this device is extremely lacking (Network Access Control or NAC) No schedule timer to automatically shut off and turn on LEDs. No QOS or quality of service feature. No guest network to limit guests to. Took a little while to separate wireless networks as this system really wants to make both the same password regardless of different names for 2.5 and 5 ghz. App is extremely limited to a few things. Changing the the 5 ghz to auto disrupts the connections of the mesh and for some reason will not set properly. Don't know why... Added 20200604 No ability to manage remotely which really sucks Also I had to connect directly to the modem rather than through my router to the modem because it would all of sudden drop internet access for no reason whatsoever. For that I have lost my more secure router. Unfortunately I can no longer replicate being able to use a different password for each wireless frequency which is silly as I was able to do it before. The list could go on.... Needless to say it works (still). I'm an IT instructor and Network professional so these issues alarm me. I am glad I kept my old previous router for security. Still these devices do what I needed them to do so I am grateful, although, it might have been nice to replace my old router. I guess you get what you pay for. If you want more security than just passwords this set isn't for you unless the other device will be your security. If you simply need it to have better wireless speeds around your home then this will help you. Good but not great product. Depending on your needs, i would recommend this product. I'll keep you posted if something else about this product comes up. I had to downgrade it to 3 stars. Again if you only need basic connections and not worried about making basic modifications to your network this will work for you.

So before I do my complaining, let me start by taking some accountability—these are bluetooth earbuds that cost less than $40 so to have high expectations is a bit of a fool's errand. I actually bought these in a bundle with 3 other pairs of low-end ear buds (pictured) and these were the best ones I got. Here's the good: -sound quality is actually pretty decent! The other two low end pair of ear buds had such a lack of low frequencies I thought maybe something was wrong with my computer. These ones probably had about 50% the bass of Apple AirPods (not bad for $40!) -surprisingly comfortable! I've worn these for 2-3 hours at work without any pain. That's hard to do! Nice work on the ear design. Complaining time: -Ok so as you heard, I also own a pair of Apple AirPods. Now, clearly I've been spoiled to think that when I am listening to my AirPods on my phone and want to switch over to my desktop computer, I'm just a dropdown click away from switching over. OH NO YOU DON'T! Not with these guys. I've tried it half a dozen different ways, but the only way I can get them to transfer from device to device to hold down the cute little white button on the base of the case and literally RE-pair them with whatever new device I want them on. Now, I work in tech so I know that "human error" happens at an alarmingly troubling rate and I'm not ruling out that I'm just a total moron and not doing this the right way—I would call this possible but unlikely. So, if I could speak to the manufacturers of these buds I would say, "why!" and then... "why?" Why can't I just select "E10" on my phone when I want to switch from my computer over to my phone. Instead what happens is that it forces me to delete E10 and then re-integrate. It's very silly and feels like a bug from 2015. 3 stars, so says I.

I used to have a shortwave radio when I was young and thought I'd pick it up again. This shortwave radio has many features for the money. If you're not technically savvy it may take a while to get to learn to use the features, not intuitive. I live in an urban environment. A lot of noise, so it was important to put up an outside antenna. I put up a magnetic loop antenna about 25 feet high. I can pick up some stations pretty well, but there's still a lot of overpowering noise in my area. Using it indoors without an external antenna is useless. I'm sure it would be the same with any shortwave radio. The sound quality is pretty good, but I never use the AM, FM, or air bands. The build quality leaves a bit to be desired. The unit I received has a bent tuning shaft. It makes using the thumb tuning knob pretty useless. If I use the included AC power adapter I get a loud and annoying hum, of course on batteries it's not there (very annoying). Maybe just a bad power adapter. I'm going to see if I can get a replacement AC adapter, or find a better quality power supply. Pros: Lots of features Memory (once you figure it out) Tuning - direct entry, tuning knob, or up/down buttons Large display Cons: Build quality lacking AC supply noisy Instruction manual could be better

Pros: Video/picture quality is good, even at night. Live video feed is good. You can hear people and they can hear you clearly. App is easy to operate. Price was good. Cons: Records everytime the wind blows, or a bug flies past. Hours of useless video. Only records for 10 seconds, so if someone is on your property, it only records them for the first 10 seconds out of 90 seconds... not particularly useful if someone is breaking in to your car. Overall, I wouldn't buy a second one, primarily because of the 10 second recording. I got the camera because someone had broken into our car and stolen items from our property, but I won't be able catch them on camera if it only records for 10 seconds, but then records HOURS of useless video of cars driving past or my neighbors trees across the street blowing in the wind. If you just want a live stream to watch, then it's great.

Any review without a baseline is like make things up. Especially things like sound a subjective subject. I mainly will compare this soundcore q30 to something I own, which is Beyerdynamic DT770 Pro and Sony WH-1000mx3 Sound: First of all, the bass was way too strong, I personally prefer a monitor headphone, flat frequency response. I tried to set eq on soundcore app at -6 db (max) at low end. It still to strong. On PC, I could set it lower, I find -10 db is acceptable for music. But when come to movie, some special effect sound makes me want to go even lower. Compare to DT770, around twice of price to Q30. DT has a lot detail in music, you could hear all different music instrument. There is not other close back wired headphone like DT770 has better soundstage in its price point, according hi-fi community. Q30 was very weak on this regard. It was ok to watch movie, but you will not touch by the sound, since it leaked soundstage and detail. If I have to give a scored to those three headphones in term of sound use DT770 as reference (10/10) and the other would be WH-1000mx3 (8/10) and Q30 (3/10). ANC: I mainly use to cancel out my furnace fan (fan on basement, my room is above it) noise, Q30 able to kill most of it, maybe 90% as soundcore said. But there always a bit left with there is nothing playing, it is noticeable. WH-1000mx3 able to kill every last bit and more. If I have to give a scored to those two headphones in term of ANC use WH-1000mx3 as reference (10/10) and Q30 (5/10). Function, comfort and other: Q30 use memory form which is very soft yet give no support. That is really noticeable on head bend, since it is thin and narrow. It mostly relies on clamp pressure to stay on your head. If there are too much pressure on headband it will actually uncomfortable in period of time, for me it is around 30 mins. Both Beyerdynamic and Sony I have not problem wearing long period of times, just let it air out half hour or so. After all, they all are close back headphone. There is a function on Q30, hold on right earcup for 1-2 sec to activate transparency mode. It only works half of times for me, and occasionally does not work at all. Sony has similar feature and it work every single time without delay. In addition, q30 has three ANC mode: transport, outdoor and indoor. There is not any different within each other. at least not big enough to waste your time to switch. Last minor complain, notification sounds was too loud, it is fixed volume, but I guess will fixed in future firmware update.

review_text: The bag is a good size, I have a Canon R10 with kit lens in the main compartment, and a Canon 220 EX II with an RF 50mm lens in the other compartment. Overall, the bag looks good. However, quite a few things I don't like. 1. the shoulder strap is attached to the bag via 2 buckles that can be easily unclipped with 2 fingers, if you travel to tourist locations where there are thieves, you are just giving stuff away. 2. The front pocket is so tight and close to the main body of the bag, you can only put in flat stuff, not even batteries, as example. 3. There is a shallow zipped pocket on the inside with 4 pockets sized for 4 SD cards?? Really? This is an armature bag, a 256GB SD card can take 10,000 photos. Including the card in the camera, do we really expect the need for 50,000 photos on a trip? I would love it if the pockets can be size to put in some camera batteries instead. 4. There are 2 net pockets on left and right side of the bag. For the compartment where I put my camera, content in the net pocket can interfere with the camera. I feel the designers valued style over function. Aside from just using the main body of the bag to house a camera, a flash and a lens, all the other features of the bag missed the mark. (update 12/30/2022) went on a trip for a week, carried a Canon R10 with the kit lens and took a few 1000's photos. The side of the bag that touches the body became oily and shiny from rubbing against clothing. For walking around, I carried the camera in the main compartment, and a bottle of water plus a glasses case and some batteries in the other compartment. I used twist ties to loop through the buckles so they can't be easily unbuckles by thieves. I wish the bag was slightly bigger, so I can fit a larger lens on the camera. If there was an outside water bottle pocket, that would have been awesome.

Adhesion - 1/5 - it's basically a rubbery mat that you plop on top of the keyboard. Additionally, it levels the tops of the keys. So if you find your home keys by touch, you'll quickly find yourself typing gibberish as your fingers wander. I guess if you're prone to banging on your keyboard this could muffle your typing if you have a cohabitant who's annoyed at the noise. But wow. If you want to write more than a paragraph you will hate, hate, hate this cover. If you prefer totally flat keypads and not being able to feel the edges of keys and sometimes needing to hit a key multiple times to make it register, this baby is 5/5 stars. For everyone else, it's a 2.
