NOW, full disclosure and BIAS, I LOVE MY SONY PCM A10, more than my multitude of ZOOM products I own, so... a bit SPOILED when it comes to their products having had one of their best offerings in my possession (SO MUCH SO I BOUGHT 4). Pro: -Flexibility: This can be as dumb and simple as you want it to be, or you can go in and get fancy with it and really complicate things. -MicroSD support to whatever your heart desires. NORMALLY, I would say 128GB would be good for these, given their size and that will literally yield like 2 continuous days worth in recording at PCM WAV 16bit 44kHz (max best settings) -STEREO LINE IN (AKA MIC IN): Some of these only offer mono line in which is whatever, but what this kind of allows you to do, is either get a dual lav setup going so you can mic you and another person (AND they do make SILLY LONG DUAL LAVS for this purpose, like 10+FT long, also not TERRIBLY expensive at like $40), meaning then you can isolate the tracks, fix them in post through something like AUDACITY (my personal favorite, since it's free). Turning it into a very inexpensive portable podcast on the go. Get a tiny case for it which I think AMAZON sells, chuck in an in ear and the dual lav with it, and you literally have a portable podcast studio in your pocket that you can doctor on your laptop later. -Smart Screen Tech: BLACK AND WHITE OLED, means it can get bright enough (BARELY) for outdoor use, nothing a cupped hand over the display can't make better. -Size: One thing that this has over say, the PCM-A10; is that not only is it smaller, it's UNIFORM in shape. Meaning this will easily slip in to even that tiny weird "key" pocket on jeans. To the point that you'll barely notice it's there. -CLEVER USB: The mechanism is SUPER CLEVER, it covers the port when the USB is retracted. Cons: -Sound Quality; nothing wrong with CD grade sound, but when you can have better, then why not. OH right, the price. Since this is not expensive. (OKAY, well it wasn't when I bought it, $80, now it's double, got to love AMAZON Scalpers). -Built in mics are not great, they look the part, but they're not great. NONE of the Sony Voice Recorders have great built in mics, that I'VE TESTED. Even my PCM-A10 with its fancy articulated mics don't sound good. They're passable for school and meetings, but not for anything PROFESSIONAL or COMMERCIAL. Like if you want to record your band session on a budget, get an external shotgun for not that much that you can plug into this line-in. -Finish: This is a personal one, it has this beautiful satin finish, that's not gross or rubberized but a great expensive and quality finish that also sadly scratches easy due to how fine of a finish it is. Conclusion: There was a lot of praise, but now seeing that this is going for double what I paid for while the 570 (a better, slightly) version is going for $70, pass on this for price. The 570 is similar in size, slightly taller and ever so slightly thicker, but same recording specs as this. It seems to be a newer probably still in production version. As I said, it was a good first recorder at $80, but at $160, you're nearing real options, like proper TASCAMS, Zooms, and whatnot.

Bought the BR1500MS2 Backups Pro to replace my BR1500G Backups Pro ... which is a great UPS, but does not provide the true sine wave battery backup that my new computer needs. Got the MS2, put it into service, the battery would charge up to 97% fairly quickly, then spend the rest of the day slowly creeping up to 99% of charge. The charge function ran continuously. Shut down for the night, boot back up in the morning, the self-test it does on startup knocked 5% off the battery charge. Same fairly quick progression to 97% charge as the previous day, then all day to get to 99%. Rinse, repeat. The UPS supports up to 900W, my computer, monitor and sound system typically take 162W - 182W when loafing along, maxing out at 468W when playing a video game ... all well within the capabilities of the UPS. They warn against a laser printer, but I don't have one, I have an inkjet ... plus it was never run during the first several days of trouble shooting. During this time, the only load on the battery was for the startup self-tests and a couple of self-tests I initiated with their PowerChute Personal Edition software that allows you to interface with the UPS via your computer. After contacting tech support and determining all the potential problems that were not happening, they shipped me a new UPS (not just a new battery as I was expecting). Got the new UPS out of the box, shipped the old one back (free shipping) ... but saw the same problems as with the first UPS. The charger runs continuously. Self-test knocks 5% off the batter charge, a temporary power flicker (under 1 second) that causes a switch to the battery knocks 1% off the battery charge. After getting to 97% charge, it spends the rest of the day getting to 99%. Tech support was decent, we did a bunch of trouble shooting to determine what was not the problem. The replacement UPS arrived quickly, but it has the same issue. Which is kind of mind boggling ... unless they have a bad lot of batteries. The behavior I'm observing is along the line of a bad lead-acid battery, rather than a problem with the UPS itself ... but I can't confirm that with absolute certainty. Bottom line, right now, until APC figures out what the problem is and fixes it ... either with the batteries or with the UPS or possibly both, I can't recommend buying this hardware. If the battery gets fixed (if that's the issue) the UPS itself seems pretty solid, on par with the 1500G it replaced. My old UPS is solid, unfortunately it is not a true sine wave backup power supply and is not suitable for my new computer. After shipping the first UPS back and having the replacement UPS installed, APC sent me an email to see if the problem was resolved. They said the issue would automatically close after 24 hours, but it took longer than that to check out the replacement. Regardless, I responded back that the new UPS had the same issues and that I hoped they would discover what the problem was, fix it, then replace the defective hardware I currently have. To date, I have not heard from them again, by now, the first UPS should have arrived at their warehouse ... but testing, identifying the problem and a fix may take a bit longer. So I can't say they are ignoring me, but it would be nice to know they are working on the problem. Again, for now, I would hold off buying this hardware until they have resolved the problem. 15 May 2022.

review_text: I purchased these for a project I was working on. They arrived in great condition and with screws to secure the cover. The trouble with them is the individual cell size allowance. I installed NiMH rechargeable batteries (brand-spanking-new) and the fit was excessively tight. I had to really work to get the cover on. Oddly enough, I've had this trouble before with Chinese made battery holders (a flashlight for instance). For some reason Chinese batteries are just a smidge smaller than U.S. batteries. Go to Harbor Freight and get some AA's and see for yourself. The other issue I had was the center cell (+) terminal doesn't protrude through the gap far enough to make contact with the AA cell button. Perhaps this is due to the rechargeable batts having a button height lower in relation to the body height than your typical alkaline or lithium AA cell. I had to remove the terminal and lightly tap an awl using a hammer into the "cup" to make it stick out further. I gave it a little teat or nipple protrusion if you will. That solved the problem. Other than generally having to modify most China made stuff I DO like the fact that there is a USB port attached to it! Hard to find these. Keep in mind these are NOT DESIGNED TO BE USED AS A POWER BANK FOR CELL PHONES!!!! Why? Cell phones require a regulated 5V source to plug the cord into. These are 4.5V nominal with AA and 3.6V nominal with rechargeable batteries plus there is no voltage regulator! It'll never work for this usage without serious modification.

review_text: I have 3 Canon cameras and when I attach this, the screw bottoms out before it tightens against the camera. To make it work, I had to remove the screw and add a couple of washers between it and the release plate.I would expect this length to be standard and I have never had an issue mounting Canon cameras to any other quick release plate or tripod, so I'm guessing this screw is just a little longer or the release plate is a little thinner than expected. Using a Micrometer, it measures 6.50mm from the end of the screw to the release plate. Others I have measure 5.25mm and an older Tripod without a release plate measures 4.84mm. It will tighten down on a Canon if you crank on it fairly hard, but the camera can still move with some twisting motion. Adding the washers changed the measurement to 4.80mm and I can easily tighten it to where it does not twist on the plate.

Let me clarify before getting into this: I drank the iJuice early on. I’ve always been an iPhone person, had a MacBook for college, and was gifted the first generation of AirPods which I immediately fell in love with. After 2 long, heavily-used years the first pair finally gave out. Bummer, but as a paralegal I had those things in ALL day, every day, and I’d never had a pair of headphones last me that long before. Naturally I was VERY excited to get these, knew they’d be worth the money, and was excited for all the new features. The noise cancellation is STELLAR. I mean borderline dangerous how little I can hear when it’s activated. Easy to switch on and off and the different sized earbuds they come with let you fit them perfectly. Battery life, as most Apple products in recent years, has improved. It’s not mind blowing, but you can get a solid 3 hours of listening, and the case itself will provide roughly 4-6 charges. Now for the iBummer... I ignored other reviews about this. Don’t make the same mistake. Based on other site’s reviews and discussions with others who have bought the Pros, it is an inevitable issue. The left AirPod, man. At first it dropped off here and there. No biggie, just put them in the case, close & open again, all set. It’s Bluetooth, it’s a piece of technology, it’s not perfect. It started happening more and more, but same fix. I became diligent with charging and cleaning them just to be safe (you’re supposed to clean any pair of headphones about once a week but like... come on), even got a case for the case. I figured a more advanced piece of technology would of course require some more careful maintenance. Then one day this frickin’ AirPod disconnected and has NEVER reconnected again. I’ve restarted, reconnected, rebooted, re-everything. I even got the new iPhone (again, drank the iJuice) amidst the month-long “pleasekeepworkingmamalovesyoudontgiveup” phase and hoped that an updated phone would alleviate. Nope. Apple customer service offered to send a new left earbud but they require a nearly $100 “refundable” (I’m sure they’d find a way to keep that) deposit and from what I’ve seen online it won’t make a difference. It makes me wonder if the case itself malfunctions or if it’s just the left AirPod. Anyways... Long story short: WASTE of $250. I’m returning them, it’s just not worth the trouble anymore and if I’m spending $250 on headphones when the phone already comes with a free, albeit corded, pair... I expect them to... work? I try to be understanding and firmly believe we already ask too much of most technology, but if you’re selling headphones they should at least work as headphones.

In the past, I have configured other routers successfully as access points. The TP-Link AC 1200 doesn’t allow you to access the router setup page if you have a modem-router combo gateway, but always defaults to the gateway IP. And there is no way that I found to temporarily bypass the gateway's router while configuring the new device. Amazon's help agent had no specific knowledge of the TP-Link AC 1200 router in question, nor about how computer networks are configured in general. It is unfair to these employees and to customers to represent that they have strong skills in these areas. My call was a complete waste of time. The manufacturer's "chat help" was even worse. In all I wasted at least 4 hours dealing with these people. The manufacturer's "Tether" app is supposed to make installation easy, but requires you to provide them with your email and password before you can sign in. This lack of security awareness and potential exposure to their marketing spam is unacceptable. The irony is that the router seems to be working perfectly on its default SSID and password, but using it that way exposes your network to any casual hacker. Though I purchased new, it was obvious that this item had been previously returned to Amazon by another customer, as the packaging had been opened and there was handwriting on the instruction pamphlet. Shame on Amazon. I will be returning this router.

My first run at this 55 in 55R635 TV was not good. The screen came cracked even though the package showed no signs of any damage. The second one was better. The legs are way too low, as I need my center channel speaker in front of it to be in line with my other speakers. So I bought a separate stand from Amazon that works well. For its size the TV is actually quite light. I wanted a Roku based TV so I did not have to use a whole bunch of remotes and it did not disappoint. One can label all the HDMI channel connections with their function... Blu-ray player etc. and have them show up as channels in the channel list above the standard list. You still have to use the device remote to work the device functions, but it's great to be able to select that on the combined TV/Roku remote. I connected my Yamaha RVX867 A/V receiver Audio Return HDMI channel ( ARC) out to HDMI 4 in on the TV which is the audio return channel on the TV. Had some problems and had to use the optical cable output from my TV to the AV3 optical input of the Yamaha. I love it that I can use the TV Remote control to adjust the sound coming from my hi-fi system. I can connect my Mac computer and my iPhone to the TV with an HDMI cable directly and get great sound and picture, but it signals that airplay is being used when it is not One can do it by airplay but it is a bit tricky to get both video and sound at the same time. Surprised that few reviews in professional magazines have noted this problem. The user's manual is a total travesty and deserves an F. They don't tell you anything as to how to interface with your independent audio system in detail. Contrast that with my previous Philip's TV from 2008 and its no contest with a manual of 39 pages. The unit has awesome capabilities as I keep finding as I unearth them ( no thanks to the manual of course) and if you have a Ph.D in the science/engineering area, you may be able to figure them out. I would suggest you call their support number on the box and get all your devices ready and have them walk you though connecting with each of them to the TV for both audio and video with and without airplay. Great value for its capabilities but poor effort in communicating those capabilities to the average user. If it were not a Roku based TV I would not have bought it. I get my TV signals for a single antenna in an old house and I need to get it to three TVs with no coax cable setup in the house. I had to use TABLO to resend the antenna signal wirelessly to all the TVs and Roku allows me to select it as a channel in its lineup. If Samsung or Philips or Sony or LD had a current Roku version of their TV, I would have bought any one of them in a heartbeat. Android users should buy the Android version of this TV and not the Roku version. May be I am being too hard and I should give it one more star, but non-tech users will struggle. Why not 5 stars? Great TV but disgraceful manual

The first MB8611 I received was bad modem and it was difficult to diagnose the problem. I would get intermittent drop out and the modem would reboot itself 6 to 8 times a day. It became impossible to watch a movie on Netflix and Amazon Prime Video without interruptions. Originally I believe the problem lied with Comcast. The cable company kept insisting there wasn't a problem with their line and resisted sending out a technician. I put up with the lousy internet service for three months making repeated complaint calls of drops and low speeds to Comcast. Finally, they sent a cable tech out and replace the coaxial cable from the pole to the home because they did notice power levels were low with the upstream. With the new coaxial cable install did improve speeds, the drop outs continued. To add insult to injury, Comcast raised by monthly rate per month and basically strong-armed me to accepting a 800/mbps service for seventy four dollars or keep my existing 200/mbps at one hundred a month. They did not give me the credit for the lousy service I experience for the three months prior to the new coaxial install. I was ready to ditch Comcast for T-Mobile 5G Home service which recently became available in my area. Anyway, I really believed in the Motorola brand and I refused to believe it could be the modem. I owned Motorola modems since the DOCSIS 1.0 days in the early 2000. After searching the web for information regarding the MB8611, there were many complaints about this new modem. So I decided to give Comcast the doubt and ordered a second identical modem. I did so because I really wanted to keep the 2.5Gbit ethernet connection so when the time comes, I can replace my current Ubiquity's Edgerouter X with something with a 2.5Gbit wan port. To my surprise, it was indeed the first MB8611 modem. The new modem did not drop or reboot for two days as of the time I am writing this review. I checked the modem's internal log and connection status to make sure there hadn't been a problem when I wasn't home or at night when I was a sleep. So far, zero incidents. I hope the problem doesn't reappear after I finish this review. Fingers crossed. Long story short, if you experience repeated reboots and intermittent drop outs then consider it may be the modem. Have your cable company do their thing and check the line first to rule that out. If the problem does not get resolved then consider exchanging your mb8611. You might have just gotten a bad one like I did. The second one is solid so far. I am happy I purchased from Amazon because they saved me a lot more aggravation if I had to deal with Motorola's support line. Apparently a company called Zoom Telephonics actually manufactures this modem under the Motorola brand name license. So these modems are not the rock solid modems from the early Motorola generation many of us have become accustomed. I took away two star for the hassle caused by the modem and the aggravation of having to deal with Comcast automated voice hell system to reach a real human every time I had to call them. Of course Comcast could have easily told me it was the modem but refused to look at it since it wasn't company equipment. It was customer owned equipment. I had to hear the same sales pitch on the phone and by the technician as to why I should be using their company's modem instead of owning my own. uh huh, I'm not going to pay a monthly modem rental fee Comcast!

Full disclosure: I bought this with my own money. Without honest, unpaid-for reviews from the Amazon community, I'd never know what's decent and what's junk. I want to contribute to that community, so I would never write a review on anything I didn't pay for myself. One other thing to note here is that the version I received does not have the "universal" outlet shown in the pictures. I included a photo of mine, which has a U.S.-style outlet. That's not a problem for me, since I live in the U.S. and this has too many watt-hours to go in carry-on luggage. This is my second battery-powered portable power station. Amazon is lousy with these things, all with UFO branding, so it's hard to make a decision about which one to buy. (I had never heard of "Powdeom," and I'll bet you haven't either.) The truth is that all of these things are probably all made in the same giant factory town in China--this is neither good nor bad, it's just a reflection of the supply chain and a case study in comparative advantage. Still, if you want to know about a particular model, YouTube is your friend, as there are lots of people whose channels basically just review these things. It can be hard to tell if their reviews are incentivized by the manufacturer or some other entity, so eventually you just have to bite the bullet and pick one. This one looked like it would fit my needs well as a supplement to my original larger power station. In a pinch, it is ideal for charging mobile devices (various types of USB ports), powering a modem and/or router (150W AC outlet is more than ample for this), or providing a modest amount of light for a long time (the small on-board flashlight only draws a few watts, and at 155.4 watt-hours capacity, should power it for over 24 hours straight). Perhaps best of all, it's dirt cheap for what it is. So why get a second power station, you might ask? Well, we recently had a freak wind event here in Kentucky. The gusts took down power lines all over the state and, more importantly, left me without electricity for 41 hours. The power station I already had--a Yaber 300W, 266Wh model that is no longer available on Amazon--worked well to power my 7W modem for a lot of that time. But since I had to use it for the rest of my power needs, it ran out of juice and I had to run up to my work, where there was electricity, to charge it. This left my house without Internet, which sucked, and I wished I had another smaller power station to keep the modem running while I recharged the bigger one. When I had my power back, I scoured Amazon's inventory and found this one on sale with a clippable coupon for about $70 plus tax, making it far and away the best deal on Amazon. For the price, it's got some killer features usually reserved for more expensive power stations: a 65W USB-c PD port, which charges all my household's phones, my Fire tablet, and my Dell XPS laptop at full speed. Even better, this is an in/out port that also charges the power station itself at a good clip (65W, which I confirmed with a USB power meter). Not only that, but you can combine a 65W USB-c charger with the included AC charger and charge this baby from 0 to 80% in only an hour. I couldn't find any other power stations on Amazon that would do that. (Of course, it's a smaller battery than most.) I haven't tested this yet, because I'm happy so far with the rate of charge just using the USB-c. It's so convenient, because I already have tons of those cables and quite a few USB-c wall chargers. The Powdeom also includes 3 USB-A ports (standard rectangular), a QC 3.0 USB port (for quick-charging Qualcomm chip devices), a DC 12V out, and a DC 15V in port (for use with cylindrical barrel connectors). That's an impressive selection of ports for such a cheap device. It would be great if it had two AC outlets, but you can always use a small cube-style power tap to split it into multiple outlets. I would not recommend plugging a surge protector into this thing, because that could interfere with the flow of the power from what is surely a very basic inverter to the device you're trying to power. You're unlikely to damage anything, but it might not work very well. But there shouldn't be anything wrong with using a simple power tap that simply splits one outlet into multiple outlets without adding surge protection. If what you plug into this power station exceeds the 150 watts is capable of, it will simply shut itself off and not power your device. So far, I am really liking the form factor--it is a compact tube shape with rounded edges, and the build quality is suprisingly good. As you can see in my photo, it's not much larger than a 16.9 oz water bottle. The body is metal, probably aluminum, and the front and back seem to be ABS plastic (see photo). There was a little bit of white adhesive sticking out of the faceplate where it joins the body, which I easily scraped away with a toothpick. It probably weighs between 3 and 4 pounds, so just about anyone could carry it, and the leather strap (or leatherette, I'm not sure) is adequate and ergonomic. It has a nice but not overpowering heft. You could easily fit this in a decent-sized backpack or duffel bag. This can't go with you in your carry-on luggage, because TSA limits such devices to 100Wh (which, at 155Wh, this far exceeds). I immediately charged this up to 100%, as recommended by the manual (and long a best practice for lithium ion batteries) and started putting it through its paces. I plan to deplete this to zero and recharge it a few more times to get the battery and capacity meter calibrated. After that, I plan to repeat a full discharge and charge cycle every 3 months or so. This could easily be done by simply turning on the small flashlight and waiting for it to go out, which should take between one and two days. The instruction manual is pretty short, but the power station is intuitive enough to operate that you probably don't need it. There's a power button at the top left which turns on all the ports except for the AC outlet with a single short press. There's another power button on the top right for the light, which turns it on with a single short press. (You must press the main power button first.) Subsequent short presses cycle it through a strobe mode, then an SOS mode, then turns it off. Finally, there's a button on the center left that turns on the AC outlet. When you short-press it, a small light above the button turns green, which means the AC outlet is functioning. Short-press it again to turn it off. If you plug in and turn on a device that exceeds the power station's wattage capacity, the light turns red to let you know. Your device simply won't function at that point, so there shouldn't be any risk of damage to the power station. So far I've charged up my Pixel 7 phone a couple of times, my Fire tablet, my Dell XPS laptop, and had the flashlight on for probably an hour total. It charges all of these devices at full speed. I even plugged my desktop and monitor into the AC outlet with a surge protector (again, not recommended; I was just testing) and ran it for about 5 minutes. The desktop made a buzzing sound, but it otherwise worked fine. This is probably because the AC outlet produces a "stepped" or "squared" sine wave, not a "true" sine wave like a more expensive power station would. This can be a problem for sensitive devices, such as those with motors. (Just make sure you test out the device you want to power before you have an emergency.) Most other devices should work fine. After all of that use, the power station is still at 59%. Consider my expectations exceeded. I hope I don't need this anytime soon, but even if I don't, I'll find plenty of uses for it around the house and on the road. It would even be a great charging station for the house where there's not a convenient outlet. TLDR: This power station is a great value for the money. At 155Wh and with a variety of USB and DC ports in addition to its AC outlet, it has adequate capacity to charge up just about any mobile device or laptop with power to spare, and its variety of ports mean you can probably plug your device into it. It seems well built and it is easy to carry around and store. Since the AC outlet is limited to 150 watts and doesn't produce a true sine wave output, make sure it will meet your needs before purchasing.

Overall, I'm happy. It's relatively inexpensive and can take the massive Noctua NH-D15, which many cases cannot. But I can't give it 5 stars. For the price it's not too bad, but my cheaper Phanteks case has a thicker metal gauge at each end. For reference, my setup is as follows: - Intel Core i5-12600KF - Noctua NH-D15 chromax.Black - MSI MAG Z690 Tomahawk WiFi - Kingston Fury DDR5 4800 32GB (2x16GB) - 1TB Gammix Blade S70 M.2 PCIe 4.0 NMVe SSD - 2TB Sabrent Rocket M.2 2280 PCIe 3.0 NVMe SSD - 1TB 3.5in WD Enterprise HDD - Seasonic Focus 850W 80 Plus Platinum PSU - AMD Radeon 6650XT GPU Things that I like: - Wider than most cases at just over 9 inches (230mm) - Dark tinted tempered glass panel - Panels that positively pop off/into place - No integrated RGB. I don't need it and I only have an RGB fan to visually indicate CPU temps - Great airflow - Good design - Quality feel of *most* materials, especially the removable metal front cover and side panels - Will take 2x 3.5in drives and 2x 2.5in drives, if you need them Things I don't like: - Front filter is not reinforced and gets sucked up against the fans resulting in noise and drag on the fans - Quick fix: stretch some tape between the sides of the front of the frame and then stick the screen to the tape - Too light of metal gauge on front and back ends: - Bends easily in the front and tends to warp the fan frame, causing rubbing of blades on the frame - Quick fix: gently bend the metal until the fans stop making noise and they'll be fine - In the back just be careful in handling until the MB is installed - Cheap DC fans. Not the worst I've seen, but even a cheap PWM fan would be better Another mention is that it seems a little tight between the MB and the top of the case. There is room for fans, possibly a radiator, but you're not getting in there to work if you have a tower cooler like mine. It's not an issue except that it's hard to connect/disconnect the CPU power with the cooler installed.

I bought this version after it was reduced during one of Amazon’s Prime Days. Having tried a Show device before (a Show 5) which I returned after I could not get it to show the time without interruption by completely irrelevant messages from Amazon, I decided to try again, after I bought another Show 5 and the software allowed me to get an acceptable home screen (even though they still refuse to put large clocks numerals on any background). The Show 8 is a very nicely made and finished device. The quality of the materials and controls are excellent. The screen is a very nice and is a high quality display with reasonable viewing angles. The camera is more than adequate (if you use it or can get it to work). I bought mine in white which had a matching power cable and supply (unlike the black which, according to reports but which I cannot verify, uses the same white power supply and cable). All in all a nice package that feels like a hight quality device. The unboxing experience is good (I think Apple are the reason that unboxing these days is a better experience) and setting up the device is very very simple. The device comes registered to your account and Amazon make the whole setup very easy. Well designed and thoughtfully worked out. I am not sure how much more difficult it would be to reset and allocate to a different account, but accessing setup and the configuration process looks straightforward. Once you have set up the device, you can configure it to your personal likes and I immediately turned off all those screen interruptions so that, in its home state, I get the time only with a background. Selecting that background is where my issues start and which I will discuss later. Voice commands are quick and Alexa displays the results on the screen as well as speaking them. I think you can stop that behavior if you do not like it, but I left it set that way. Now to some of the issues I encountered. Because I have an English accent, I set the language to English (UK) so Alexa understands me more easily and I get a warning that some functions may not work. I have no idea what that means or what is affected but I know that when it gives me notifications about Amazon deliveries it warns me that you can not place orders with Amazon. I never use this function so it does not worry me, but it seems to be a strange limitation (if it is a limitation as I never use it). It appears not to have this limitation if you set it to and speak Spanish or US English, of course. The other issue is that it advertises that you can display your photos. What it does not tell you is that it can only display photos if they are upload to Amazon Photos, for which you need a Prime account, and pay for storage if you have more that 5GB of videos. I use Adobe Lightroom and Apple Photos, so I was forced to try and copy them to Amazon Photos which is a mind bogglingly slow process and bug prone process (Amazon Photos crashed several times during the upload process). Then came trying to show them on the Show. In order to do this you have to create Collections of which there is not a single mention in Photos except when you need to have one to display on your Show. There are some defaults such as Groups, People and Places which Amazon Photos creates, but there are no directions about Collections. Funnily it created a Collection called Most recent 500, but how I create it again is a mystery (I since discovered you can create it via the Alexa app, not via Amazon Photos). Anyway the bottom line is that I was not prepared to learn, curate or anything else in Amazon Photos as I have perfectly capable Photo management software elsewhere and the lack of support for anything other than Amazon Photos is a killer, so that beautiful screen displays nothing but Art. The Echo Show 8 is a great piece of hardware spoiled by restrictive and badly designed software, but, as an Echo device with visual prompting it is rather nice. Sound quality is good and adequate (I have Apple Homepods for higher quality sound but the Echo Show 8 is still pleasant and acceptable). We never use the video calling (most of our friends use Apple’s FT and do not have a video Echo device) and it does not appear to support Zoom or Teams etc. The camera is good quality but, again, we do not use it and I cannot get the Alexa app to show live video from the Show 8 (buggy software) which makes it pointless so we shut the camera off. Recommended with strong caveats.

*UPDATE* raising to 3 stars as I found a work around that seems to be helping. I have added a wall powered USB 3.0 splitter between the drive and the Xbox One X. This seems to be giving the drive enough extra power to prevent the Xbox internal power supply from over exerting itself. Tldr: This external drives power demand exceeds the consoles internal power brick capabilities when under load thus leading to choppy cutscenes and eventual abrupt shutdown of the Xbox to avoid heat damage to the xbox. Advice: Get a wall powered external Drive for this application. I recommend the WD My Book. Used for Xbox One for 3 years no problems. I bought this specifically for expanding my new Xbox One X storage capacity and really wanted an SSD and didn't want the "official" expansion drive for the console. I still have the OG Xbox One and have had the WD My Book 6 TB and it has worked great with no issues. I usually take that Xbox to the Parents for the Holidays but am trying to get away from a mechanical HDD to prevent eventual mechanical drive failures from transporting the HDD around. Plus, SSDs are FAST! Right! I didn't see any negative reviews on this particular drive stating I shouldn't use it for this application and was looking for a drive that was small, light and fast. This looked to fit the bill exactly! In fact, I found some reviews saying it even works great for this application! Well, that is partially incorrect. The drive is powered through the connection cable meaning it is getting its power from the console. The console was not designed to power something like this. So, my very clean and dust free console which has had ZERO issues all of the sudden starts abruptly turning off in mid-game when playing games loaded on the drive (Playing Battlefront 2 for reference). When I turn back on the console I am prompted with a message stating the Xbox shut down to avoid heat damage. I immediately start getting Xbox Red Ring of Death PTSD... but, soon learn my Xbox is fine and the problem revolves around the new expansion drive I recently hooked up. The drive seems to work fine under light load but as soon as I start into a demanding game or really any game with cut scenes, the drives power demand begins to overheat the consoles internal power brick trying to support the drives additional power load and off the Xbox goes to avoid damage. Before it shuts off, the cut scenes start to get annoyingly choppy. SUPER BUMMER as I spent a ton of money on this thing and now it is essentially a paperweight as I have no need for this for any other application. Don't be me. See this review and spare yourself the wasted money and time if this is what you intended to use this drive for. As mentioned above, I have the WD My Book on my other console and that wall powered external expansion drive has not caused any issues with 3 years of running use. Just wish that drive was smaller and was an SSD. One last thing - This drive probably works great on a PC with a decent power supply and a USB 3.2 port. Cheers! Hope this helps someone!

I’ve been on a hunt for bass-heavy headphones for a while. I was originally interested in Skullcandy Crusher EVO’s, but ultimately decided against them due to several issues that shouldn’t be present at the pricepoint of $200. After countless hours of reading reviews of bass-heavy headphones, the Soundcore Q10 sounded like it was for me. To start off, the pros: -good sound quality for the price - you won’t het audiophile quality sound here, but for casual music listening, these do the job well -bass in general is solid, but the bass boost button REALLY kicks it up, which I love -battery life is ridiculous - I’ve used these almost daily for almost two weeks now and I’ve just now hit the “low battery” warning - and I haven’t even charged it yet! This was with the charge it came with out of the box. Honestly impressive. -decent sound isolation. No ANC here, but I’ve found myself tuning out outside noises more often than not. -build quality feels sturdy -bluetooth range is plentiful - I haven’t tested it out, but I have noticed I can leave my phone in the kitchen and I can move around the house without the connection being compromised I’m overall satisfied with my purchase, but there are a few things to keep in mind. First - the hissing noise is kinda loud. If the music is quiet, or if it’s in between songs, the hissing is very apparent. Second - for me personally, comfort is kinda odd. The headband hasn’t caused me issues, but i’ve noticed that the earcups aren’t deep enough, and the headphone rest on the outer edges of my ears. This causes a bit of fatigue after wearing it for a few hours. I don’t know how big my ears are in the grand scheme of things, however. Third - the aforementioned hissing noise is not present in aux mode. However, the bass boost option does not work when in aux mode. Overall, I’d say this is more of a 3.7/5 rating. I have read that cheap bluetooth speakers and headphones have a bit of a hiss to them, which I guess can’t be helped. For $45 though, I can look past these flaws and enjoy them for what they are: booming bass headphones. Would I recommend these? Yes, as long as the cons I mentioned aren’t major dealbreakers.

Dropped the R one on the first day. Refused to pair after that. It was difficult to work the volume control. The short: This thing works. It's got multiple shortcomings that are annoying, but aren't deal breakers. There may be a better speaker out there though. The long: The speaker works well. I bought it in August 2018 and it just died on me in October of 2021. That's better than par for the course when it comes to bluetooth speakers that are used regularly. I've had speakers that died after 12 or 18 months, although I used this speaker once every 2-3 days instead of daily. It connects quickly enough, plays just loudly enough, and withstands water splashes just well enough to stay functional. And that's what this thing is for, so that's why it gets 3 stars. Now for the little stuff. BLUETOOTH CONNECTION The bluetooth connection on this thing is good. I usually had the speaker in the shower with me, but had my phone about 12ft away through a door and wall in my bedroom. No quality issues and no dropped connections. The only minor gripe would be that it takes 5-8 seconds for the speaker to connect to my phone. That isn't a long time, but other bluetooth devices (speakers, headsets, in-ear buds) all connect instantaneously or in less than 2 seconds. You've got to wait a few extra seconds for this thing to connect. CHARGING The charging cable is a USB-A to 3.5mm cable. Yea, a stereo headphone jack is the charging connection. There's a female port for it on the side of the speaker, covered by a small rubber stopper to keep the port from getting wet. Who in the hell is using this charging cable? The fact that this is the charging port and adapter is ABSURD. The cord is only 3ft long too, so good luck charging this any distance from the outlet. You can't charge this the random micro-usb ports you likely have laying around the house and you don't have ANY of these types of charging cables laying around unless you've been collecting cheap electronic charging cables for the last 15yrs. With that being said, it takes about 2-3hrs for this thing to get to a full charge. So not too long for the 4-5hrs of play time it gives you. BATTERY The battery life is pretty good (4-5hrs), but there's no way to tell how much charge you have left. Because of that, you're going to be 2 minutes into a 12 minute shower and hear a 4-beep warning sound that lets you know the speaker needs to be charged. The problem there is that the sound will not play every 60 seconds to remind you. It's going to beep every 15 seconds until it dies. When it beeps, your audio is muted for 2 seconds, so you can't even power through it. It's a total distraction, and it would be avoidable if you could see that it was about to die and give it a quick charge. But you can't. Not ideal. SOUND The sound is ok, but it's not great. It's exaggerated around the 250Hz - 800Hz range, which is the WORST possible range to have boosted in what is likely to be an enclosed, reflective space (a bathroom). That gives the sound a heavy, speakerphone sound that isn't great for what's usually audio that is somewhat compromised from streams (music streaming, podcasts, YouTube audio, etc). To combat this, I use an EQ app on my phone that lets me save presets. I created an EQ specifically for this speaker that turns down the problem frequencies and then boosts the overall volume because the volume is slightly underwhelming anyway. But the reduction in problem frequencies drops the volume even further, so you're definitely going to need a volume boost after that. MICROPHONE I never really used this thing as a bluetooth microphone to answer calls, because I was usually in the shower with the vent on as well. It's noisy. So it was hard for the person on the other end (my wife, usually) to hear me clearly. So I can't knock the audio quality on the microphone since I haven't really counted on it. OVERALL So that's why this is a 3/5 star product. Some nice bells & whistles would make it a better product. I can still recommend it as long as you understand its limitations and drawbacks.

This is because these headphones do not recognize audio input / output in "headset" mode, and go to sleep every 10 minutes. You must use headset mode in order to use the build-in mic. Thus, these headphones cannot be used as a headset for a Windows laptop - you will constantly be disconnected from audio during your zoom, skype, and other teleconferencing activities! I contacted customer service about this issue. They gave me a generic response, and after A MONTH are still trying to claim that their "engineers will look into this problem." Useless customer service. When you pay $1,000 for a set of headphones, you expect better. The other major flaw is that the headphones can only be charged when powered down, plugged into a USB C port, and then a button must be held down for two seconds to activate charging. This is ridiculous. If I plug in the headphones, I expect them to start charging. HiFiMan claims that this was done in order to prevent accidentally draining the battery of the device you're plugging into, but any device with a USB C port will have a much larger battery (if it has one at all) than the one in the Ananda. Even after owning these for a couple of months, I still sometimes forget to "turn on" the charging, and start the next day with a totally drained headset. I'll be returning these.

I wanted a controller for PC gaming for the rare title where a controller is really that much better than kb&m controls, but I wasn't about to shell out $80 for an Xbox controller and the adapter needed to use it for PC. This is the one I settled on, and after at least 100 hours of gameplay use from Hades alone I can say it's a quality controller. Note that this does not have rumble capability of any kind, nor does it have some of the fancy speaker/microphone stuff Sony and Microsoft have started adding to their controllers. If you want all the bells and whistles of the expensive controllers - well, you're gonna have to buy one of the expensive controllers. But if you don't really care about that stuff and just want a well built controller with the standard modern Xbox/PS style layout, this one is a great choice. I have never had a game that supports controller input fail to map the controls correctly or anything like that. And if you install Logitech's profiler software, you can fully rebind the controls yourself - allowing you to correct annoying control setups in games that don't have built-in rebindable controller controls, or if you decide you want to use it for a game that doesn't even have controller support you can rebind the buttons to keyboard buttons so as far as the game is concerned you're just using keyboard controls. Not sure exactly how sophisticated the profiler is in terms of macros and the like because I've never bothered to install it, since this controller just works with no fuss for all the games I've tried it with. It even has a toggle switch on the back to switch to directinput if you wanna play some ancient game that lacks xinput support (if you don't know what this means, don't worry about it - xinput has been the standard for years now and any remotely modern game with controller support is gonna use it). All the buttons still feel good after 100+ hours of heavy use. I haven't noticed any issues with thumbstick drift, a problem even the "premium" controllers sometimes have. The d-pad is much higher quality than on most cheap controllers - it has 4 separate switches for the 4 cardinal directions instead of just one in the middle, so it is more reliable and feels better to use). The controller itself feels a bit lighter than an Xbox controller but still feels sturdy and durable. I'll admit I'm a big of a Logitech fan, so maybe I was biased to like this controller - but there's a reason it's one of the most common recommendations for a budget PC controller and the top seller in the PC controllers Amazon category. If you're looking for a cheaper alternative to an Xbox controller, and don't mind a wired controller or lack of rumble support, this is the product you're looking for. At full MSRP of $24.99 it's a very good deal, and if you're patient and look for deals it's not hard to find in the 15-20 range at which point it's an absolute steal. If you want a budget option that is wireless and has rumble support, look into the Logitech F710.

Got this to replace my 2 year old TPLink Kasa Outdoor Cam. Size and quality are about the same (little smaller and lighter) but there is no "wow" to this camera. The main benefit it has over my existing Kasa Cam is that it has continuous recording to the SD card and RTSP so I can tie it into my HomeAssistant server and Frigate. Other than that, it's an average camera. Daytime quality is good, nothing spectacular (didn't get the 2K as RTSP can only do up to 1080p anyway); nighttime is so-so, moving objects tend to blur in low light and night vision. They claim "color night vision" (see pic) but it's not like the starlight sensors of other cams like the Wyze v3. It's more a gimmick of the little LED spotlight which in my opinion just draws attention to the camera. The fact that it only has a magnetic mount (which does hold decently under my eaves), and would be easy to unplug from the USB extension cable; I want to avoid drawing attention to it as it would be easy to take. The person detection is actually pretty good with default settings (especially compared to their doorbell); haven't gotten any false positives, not sure about any false negatives. Setup and install were both very easy. There is nothing about this camera that makes it worth the $80 price (let alone the 2K for $100). I've considered returning it, but I do like that it has RTSP and continuous recording so will most likely keep it for now. If Wyze would get RTSP on their v3, I'd hands down go with Wyze. Or if TPLink would release their new outdoor cam (which may be later this year), I'd go with that as it's supposed to have the starlight sensor. If you are on the fence and want a camera that has continuous recording and RTSP; I'd say wait for this to go on sale OR just get the Eufy Indoor cams (from what I have read, they do well in protected outdoor uses). Even if the Indoor cam lasted 2 years outdoors and you had to replace it, you'd still pay less money. If these drop $25 or so, I'd consider replacing my 2 other Kasa outdoor cams. If RTSP isn't something you need, then go with the Wyze v3. At least there you get true "color night vision" and save a good amount of money. review_text: We currently have this camera outside of our apartment building facing our car . The quality is actually quite good , and on the first night we put it out, it rained pretty heavy outside which gave it its first test . It worked great in the rain but I have a few major complaints .. the biggest complaint being that 2 year battery life is a stretch . Even the app tells you if people are constantly walking by / cars driving by , the batteries will only last a month or so. That’s my first complaint… my second complaint is that this camera is essentially made to be a camera that only creates short clips .. you can set it to record long clips if whatever is in front of the camera is there for a while .. but the default setting is for 10 second clips in order to save battery life. For years I’ve used YI home and it records clips however long they need to be .. if someone is standing in front of that camera for 5 straight minutes , it will record all of it until they move .. this camera feels more like a monitoring device rather than a security camera if that makes sense. This is great if you need to place it in an area that rarely has foot traffic or cars passing by, also if you don’t need large clips of whatever your recording , so this would work well as a door camera . Since this camera runs on batteries , the default settings will be to limit as much recording as possible and keep clips short and if you increase the clips lengths , the camera warns you that you will get little battery life . This is the downside to it not being connected to a power source , you can also get a live view at any time but after using it for even 20 seconds it asks you “continue?” Because it’s really trying to conserve battery as much as possible .. EDIT : Here’s a list of pros and cons after using this camera for over a month . Pros : wireless , good video quality , good size , easy to install , can be set to record at a schedule , can be set to ignore certain spots that are in frame like a tree moving in the wind , works well rain or heat . Cons : where do I begin ? 1. By default this camera will only record in 10 second clips . You can adjust it to record 1 minute clips at the longest , once the camera has finished recording a 1 minute clip , it can not be re triggered to record another clip for at least another 10 seconds . This is a bit of a downside because you could miss something important . Also another thing that bugs me is that sometimes it will stop filming even though there continues to be movement in front of it . For example you can set the clips to be 1 minute long or have the camera automatically stop recording if the movement has stopped before it reaches 1 minute . But if you set it on this , it doesn’t work well . Many times people have walked by and it stops recording while they’re still in frame . 2. We have used this camera for over a month now and we have already replaced the batteries once . It is actually recommended that you use lithium batteries because they last longer but note that they are also a lot more expensive than regular alkaline batteries . A 6 pack of lithium batteries cost about $15-16 dollars (as an example typical batteries cost that much for a pack of 20) . So the cost will add up 3. When it records a little red light turns on and you can hear a small little click , I personally do not like this as I would prefer it to be completely silent and discreet For all the reasons I already mentioned I could see this camera working decent if you place it in a spot that rarely has foot traffic / cars driving by . Possibly as a door camera , maybe garage or if you just need to monitor an area sometimes like when you’re out , it could possibly work . If you need to monitor an area all the time , you will be replacing the batteries often and you might want to go for wired camera

*** original post *** I decided to turn it after few minutes testing. There are two dealbreakers for me. Since this BT speaker doesn’t cache its settings (it resets all settings once be turned off), such as volume and LED lightings. 1. This speaker resets its volume to 40% very time you turn it off. This is too load for most of mine use cases. You can only lower the volume when audio signal starts to stream to this speaker. Turning volume down very time is such a hassle. 2. This speaker resets its LED lighting after being turned off. I don’t need the LED for most cases and to save the battery. But every time you turn it on, you need to click the LED button for 4 times until the LED is off (since LED has several modes, the last mode is the off mode). Caching(remembering) device setting is such a basic feature of all my Bluetooth speaker. Reset everything is a feature defect to me. I don’t know why a 2022 released BT speaker could miss this simple feature. *** Updates 11/2022 *** So Tronsmart team reached out to me with their updates for the problems I mentioned above. They send me a device to test it out. After I updated the device firmware via the Tronsmart app to version 1.2.2, the device no longer has those issues. It is able to cache/remember the device settings(volume level and LED mode) before being turned off now. As there's no more deal breakers any more, after spending some time with it, I think this device would be a keeper for most of the people. Pros: * It sounds pretty good for its price range. Personally, the sound signature is a bit too warm for me, and the clarity could be improved. But gladly the app offers the EQ setting so you can tweak the sound (NOT many product in this price range can do that), and the device does remember the EQ settings. After I set it to my comfort zone, it sounds pretty good to me. The warm signature makes you able to enjoy the music longer without ear fatigue. * I like the volume knob. It's very easy to change the volume so the user won't need to find the volume button to do so. The knob is responsive and intuitive. * Build quality is pretty good. * LED lighting is a bonus. Cons: * [The Battery Life] The battery life can be better regarding its size and weight. This is not a small device, much bigger than a UBL flip 6. I feel the battery life drops quicker than I expected. * [The Bass] The bass could be more "room-filling" with a dedicated woofer plus two passive radiators. The woofer does its job to provide punch bass, but feels like the two passive radiators do not do its job very well. Plus, consider boost the low end at low volume level (lots of brands are doing this, E.g. Earfun, JBL, etc) and I can tell T7 is restricting its bass level at high volume. Probably because of the distortion, but again regarding its size and a dedicated woofer, this could be improved. * [The Size] It can be smaller so to fit the regular cup holder and can be lighter so easier for one hand carrying. One warm suggestion for the team that to consider adding one more level of operation on the volume knob to make it clickable/pressable? The volume knob already resolve the finding-the-volume-bottons issue, why not include the play button? Say one click for play/pause, and there could be 2 or 3 times clicks for skip/reverse the track operations, or even long press for turn on/off. This could be an additional boost for the UX and can eliminate more of the hard-to-find small buttons on its side. And since Tronsmart provides the app, it's even possible to custom the purpose for different knob-click actions. Tronsmart team earns my respect regarding how they react to user's constructive reviews. This manufacture responds on the issue so fast and resolve the problem timely. They really listened.

At the time I bought this, it cost me $25.85. It has five times the storage of Google's storage plan that costs $30 per year. So yeah ... bye, Google. To back up an Android phone, just attach it, then use CX File Explorer (included on Samsungs) or some other file management app to copy over any or all of the files in your internal storage. It's a little slow, so have your phone charged or put it on a wireless charger while you back up. This has three connectors: USB-C, USB-A (for older computers) and micro USB for older mobile devices. (Flip up the USB-A to reveal the micro USB.) The housing seems sturdy and durable. Overall the only change I would make to it would be to include a cover for both ends to help keep dust out of the connectors. With the current design, you can only cover one end at a time.

review_text: Bought this watch a few weeks ago as I've never had a smart watch before and didn't want to start with a super expensive one (I'm learning the ropes first!). This is a good starter watch and it's very pretty! Short list of pros and cons: Pros: - It's gorgeous and I love that you can customize the face. I made my own cherry blossom face for spring and it's so pretty! - I like the sleep tracker, and the fact that you can download the data onto your phone. - You can view messages and app notifications on your watch (although you can't reply back). - The raise-to-wake function is cool, that way I don't drain the battery. It only turns on the clock face when you're looking at it. - The battery power is really good! Mine lasted three weeks without a single charge. - The step counter is handy, and you can set a goal for yourself. - The 'find phone' function is awesome and I've used it numerous times! - I can start and pause and skip music from the music interface. Cons: - The weather function doesn't work correctly (on mine at least). It only updates once in the morning and then stays the same the rest of the day. Yesterday it was 90F and my watch read 66F all day. - The watch is a bit large for my small wrist. I got a round watch because rectangular ones are definitely too big, but it still feels really large. - The watch disconnects a lot, even if I just leave my phone on the counter and walk upstairs for something. It'll immediately break the connection. Then I have to resync it again via the app. Not hard to do, but that means my messages don't come through and the 'find phone' function doesn't work (which is unhandy when the whole point of finding your phone is that you lost it, so you obviously can't sync it!). All in all I'm pretty happy with it, and it's possible that my issues don't happen to everyone. It's a great watch for health tracking (including periods!) and sleep tracking.

First off I had great hopes for this product, however, they were dashed very quickly. The unit will not allow you to disable (SON) so that my SSID's are separate, instead it manages everything and decides what and how devices are attached and in some cases it does not pick the best option/speed. The Wi-Fi performance is not up to speed, just in the floor above the router directly, my connection degraded considerably and this is a fairly newer construction home. From what I read the satellite can be connected via Ethernet Backhaul, which was confirmed by their tech support the first time I called. However, when I checked through the app and the web interface of the MR60 it showed the satellite unit being connected via 5G Wireless, despite the fact that I had it connected via Ethernet. Turns out that in order for the unit to connect via Ethernet Backhaul it has to be connected directly into the MR60 and not through a switch connected to the MR60, which means you can't have any other wired devices connected on your network! This is a known issue that their engineering team is working on resolving. Tech support, is the worst. The first time I called in I spent about 1 hour and 30+ minutes on hold and being transferred between departments till I got connected to the "Expert Technical Support Person" for the product and even then his knowledge was limited. The second time I called, I was transferred twice and got disconnected with no call back (they promise to call back within 60 seconds if the call is disconnected). The third time, I went through the transfers till I got to the Expert only to be told that the Ethernet Backhaul does not work through a switch. So given the poor performance, the inability to assign my devices to different SSID, I am return the units. I am currently awaiting the ASUS ZenWifi AX which has only 1 review, but seems like a solid unit. I will update once I receive that kit.

While the Satechi was significantly less expensive, it didn't have the flexibility I needed, plus the keys were loud and "clicky," which you don't want when recording. So, I guess you get what you pay for. I guess if I had one other complaint, it would be that there is no on/off button. It powers on simply by inserting the batteries. The scope is amazing. For nearby planets you can see the bands of Jupiter pretty well and make the main ring features of Saturn out pretty well. To be fair, your naked eye view is going have the planets look a bit smaller than a pea. You will see Jupiter and a half dozen of its moons in your total view - so that's neat. Deep space options are great views to capture on this scope. You aren't going to see colors and such, but you will see great clusters. If you want the coloring and all, you'll need to also invest in photographic equipment for long exposures. Now the downside. The motors had issues. This of course is a big deal since you need them to move the scope around. They worked great for a first couple of days and then would die after moving for about 3 seconds. Nothing would get them moving against except a hard reboot. The other big issue I had was with wi-fi connectivity just dropping constantly. This was even with having one of my access points with in 20 feet and no obstructions. Needless to say tracking goes crazy or just stops working. I have been using an external drive as local backup for my NAS, unfortunately that drive developed some problems after only 23,000 hours and needed to be replaced. The price of the Avolusion drive was attractive and I thought that with Amazon’s easy return process, it was worth taking the risk of trying one from this new brand. Also, I liked the fact that it could be used in the horizontal position allowing it to conveniently fit on top of my NAS (same as the failed drive, but I did add some self-adhesive rubber feet to the Avolusion to improve ventilation and stop it sliding around). Like any hard drive, before using the Avolusion, I ran a full set of tests on it. It passed an extended test (screen dump attached) during which I was impressed by how quiet it was and how cool it ran. I then ran the short test to make sure it was still OK and that was also fine (attached). I did not check read/write speeds as this was not important for my application. I then checked the drive info (attached) which shows that the drive was brand new at the start (only 24 power-on hours) and that the advertised 12 TB of data had been read during the extended test. Now for the quirk, the drive does not spin down after a period of inactivity, in fact it NEVER spins down, even if you turn off the computer and unplug the cable – the light goes off, but the drive keeps spinning. I contacted the seller to see if they had any fix for this problem; their customer service was very responsive, but they had no remedy. I did, however, figure out a work-around for the problem. I put the power supply for the Avolusion drive on a time switch and have it turn on before the scheduled weekly backup and then turn off several hours after the backup. I can do this because my NAS fortunately has a setting that allows you to automatically eject the drive at the end of the backup. Summarizing, this Avolusion hard drive is good value for backup applications, but order a digital timer at the same time as you place the order for the drive. I will update this review if the drive fails prematurely. Also, for full transparency, I should mention that the first drive sent by Amazon was DOA, but they did immediately replace it and the return process for the bad drive was completely hassle-free.

When it works, this drive works well. It's quick (maxes out at ~2.9 GB/s on my system) and is easy to use. I bought the drive in October of 2019 but the drive started having issues in August of 2020 and fully died in September of 2020, which means it only lasted 11 months and that's where the issues come in. First, PNY doesn’t provide any diagnostics tools. When I first started having issues the S.M.A.R.T. reports all said everything was fine, but Dell's utility was showing issues. However there was no way to do further tests to confirm Dell's utility info. Talking to support was fine, and they gave me an RMA number so I could send the drive back but with two major issues: 1) They would not send a replacement ahead of time. I did an RMA for Western Digital years ago and they took my payment info and sent a new drive with the understanding that if I didn't send back the defective one, they would charge me for the replacement. No such option exists for PNY so I had two choices; Go without a computer for the two weeks needed for the RMA or, buy a replacement myself and… try to re-sell it later? 2) Return shipping is paid by the customer, and not by PNY. This isn't a huge cost, but again, it's a strike against them, especially since the issue is that the drive failed, so it’s not my fault. So, I ordered a cheap temporary drive and it thankfully arrived the day after this drive fully gave up the ghost (again, the day just before that, the S.M.A.R.T. reports all said everything was fine, but Dell's utility said there were issues). I shipped the drive back Monday, it arrived Friday and they shipped the replacement Tuesday and it arrived Saturday. So a total of 13 days for the turnaround from the time I shipped the drive until the replacement came. The replacement is brand new and appears to be an updated version (thinner flash modules and they are only on one side rather than both sides). It's working well and I'm hoping for multiple years of service from it, but I'm not holding my breath. If they paid for return shipping and gave me an option of getting the replacement before shipping back the defective drive, this review would be glowing. But because of those issues, I can’t recommend buying any hard drive from PNY because if you need to use the 5 year warranty, it’s a pain.

It has a beautiful, bright color touch screen, and an intuitive user interface. Coming from the Samsung gear there are two main things that I noticed. 1. ) The weight is significantly lighter on the Garmin. Noticeably. 2.) The battery life on the Garmin is amazing. My Samsung needed to be charged every night. That meant no sleep tracking for me. It's weird, but awesome to not have to worry about battery for days on end. It's a game changer in my opinion. How Garmin pulls that off on a lighter watch, I have no idea. Garmin obviously is one of the best in the business when it comes to health tracking. I've found to the stats to be pretty accurate. I have noticed, that exercising on my elliptical, the calories burned is under reported on the watch, but that can be adjusted after the fact in the Garmin Connect app. Otherwise, health tracking is great. Have respiration and oxygen saturation stats are cool features I didn't have before. I also like the body battery feature. On to the app. The Garmin Connect App is one of the nicest looking health tracking interfaces I've seen. Samsung health has gotten cluttered and sometimes it's hard to find historical data. The Garmin app interfaces is beautiful and motivating. Cons The Venu 2 is not without it's faults. I think it could have a better build quaility, particularly on the glass. My Samsung after 2.5 years didn't have a scratch on it. My Venu, scratched on day 1. I was not pleased. I have since learned that they do sell screen protectors for the Venu 2 which I would highly recommend. Also, on Amazon, Asurion insurance is only about 30 bucks which covers screen damage. Anyway, for $400, I feel like Garmin could use higher quality glass that is more resistant to scratching. They could also raise the outer bezel just a bit, to make that a more prominent contact point over the screen. This is where I dock the Venu 2 just 1 star. I do also wish that Garmin Connect allowed for more third party integration. My Withings scale for example. It would be nice if these companies would allow some back and forth with health data. But I get why they do it. Would I buy it again? Absolutely. I love this watch so far. The weight, the battery life, the interface, the tracking, and the app are all fantastic. I recommend it with the one caveat of protecting it with a screen protector and possibly insurance.

I have a bunch of Anker products and they are all of great functionality and quality so I knew this would be good. It is compact, well designed and functions well. The arrangement works to charge 3 of my Apple products in a space saving design and it also means that I can cut down on the number of cables used either at a desk or whilst travelling.Just to clarify some points ....1) You do not have to use the supplied 40w power brick and/or cable ( it's great to have these included). You can use any other power brick providing the power supplied is sufficient. I personally use an Anker 4 port power brick ( see photos ) which has got a 45w usb c outlet as well as a 20w USB c and 2 other A outlets. This powers the 3-in-1 from the 45w outlet AND my iPad Air from the other usb C outlet. Anker recommends 30w as the minimum requirement to charge all 3 products2) When you plug in the power supply, a blue light will appear next to the socket. This will disappear after a few seconds if it deems there is enough power but will flash if it's not enough.2) .... However, a standard Apple 20w power brick will show the flashing light but will still charge a phone on its own but not the Watch or AirPods. Bizarrely, however, 18w charge will not allow you to charge either the Watch or AirPods on their own without the phone even though the chart on the Amazon listing seems to imply that you can.Despite this last oddity, it is a great product, if a little on the pricey side. Great for travelling and a nice compact fit for a travel tech bag.

Instructions - they give you instructions on how to setup the tripod, which seems obvious, but the cold shoe mounts for the devices are just kinda "here you go." Doesnt come with a diffuser sleeve - for the price they could include this. I bought theirs and it works fine & seems necessary, but also makes changing the colors a hassle. Colors are changed via plastic faceplates, which seems ludicrous to me for an LED light. It should have adjustable color changing LEDs in my opinion. Cold shoes limited to bottom mount - I feel like if all the shoe needs is a short plastic slot, they could have given us mounts at the cardinal and ordinal points around the ring so we could have multiple devices without worrying how they're going to dit next to each other. Power adapter - I assume this is what the velcro strap they included is for- that's what I used it for, anyway- as the adapter's cord that runs from the brick to the ring's control board isnt long enough to let the brick sit on the ground, and I'm not gonna let it hang from its connector like they show on the picture like some kind of nutter. My laptop setup is relatively bluetooth dependent because I use a standing desk and dock - my keyboard, headphones, and sometimes mouse are all bluetooth. The onboard bluetooth of my Macbook Pro is very weak, but I also have to travel with it often, and I break bluetooth adapters pretty frequently. So far I have purchased maybe 5 adapters, which are usually the unbranded Chinese variety at around $5 each. Generally, the performance has been the same for all of them, which is acceptable, and the only difference may be a couple of feet of range. I purchased this adapter to use with my home theater pc and an Xbox controller for family game nights. I chose a slightly more expensive "upgraded" adapter in hopes to reduce input lag, and for multiple household chores like bluetooth speakers and such. While I didn't expect much of a performance boost, I certainly did not anticipate getting less for more money. The TPlink adapter has the worst range of any adapter I have tried. We've had frequent connectivity issues, including the strange problem of the adapter requiring unobstructed line of sight for any sort of connection. NONE of my other adapters were this finicky. Trying to listen via connected headphones was a real frustration with frequent dropouts, and occasionally, if I using both the controller and headphones via this adapter it was cause constant dropped frames and severe input lag. When I break my other bluetooth adapters, I will likely switch back to the cheap stuff and avoid TpLink bluetooth products in the future. In short, avoid this.

The first problem with Tile is that it's unreliable. About one out of five times you try to use the Tile App on your Smartphone, it gives you a "can't find keys message." But your keys with the Tile on it could be lying right next to your phone. The Tile People are aware of this problem and have posted information on their website and a YouTube video on how to deal with it. To solve the problem, you need to find you keys and then futz with the settings on your phone. You have to monkey around with your Bluetooth settings , restart you cellphone a couple of times, or try different things until you finally get your Tile App to start ringing your keys again. Now you are good to go for the next time you want to find your keys. But this defeats the purpose of the Tile. If you are looking for your keys, you have to find them in order to possibly find them next time. The Tile People need to go back to the drawing board to get this product to work reliably. The second problem is the Tile App must always be running in the background on your cellphone and there's no way to make it load automatically. So every time you go turn off and on your phone, you have to go remember to go through the hassle of reloading the Tile App. If you decide to load the Tile App just when you need it instead of keeping it running, you increase the chances that it can't communicate with your the Tile on your keys. To top it off, periodically you get a message from the App that you need to restart your phone for no reason. When I contacted customer support about my problem, Katherine @ Tile didn't take the trouble to respond to my complaint, basically blew me off, copied and pasted in a bunch of irrelevant instructions, and deadlocked the issue after only my second email. I though I would never hear from Tile Customer Care again but to my surprise several days later, Vanessa T. from higher lever customer support contacted me. Alas, it was the same problem all over again, Vanessa ignored my questions, cut and pasted more irrelevant instructions into her email, and refused to address my concern, which was how can I get me phone to consistently and reliably connect to my Tile? Second level support was even more disappointing than first level. It is clear to me that Tile isn't willing to confront the unreliability issue. We all want an App that works silently and smoothly and doesn't require us to tend to its needs. I wish I hadn't invested in this product and have gone back to my old low tech key finder instead. The Tile People should have worked out the bugs before they shipped.

This device claims 2640 square feet of coverage. That is misleading. You cannot assume it will provide coverage throughout a 2640 square foot house. Coverage is in a circular pattern. The area of that circle is pi * R squared. A 2640 square foot circle has a radius of about 29 feet. That assumes line of sight with no barriers. In the real world the coverage is much less. My router is on the main floor and my office is in the basement. All the locations in my basement where the device showed sufficient signal from the router were too far from the PC in my office to give adequate signal. I was getting better connectivity directly to the router than I was getting with this "extender." I am returning this Rockspace AC1200 extender and ordering another more powerful unit. Editing to add: This seller has contacted me eleven times asking me to delete this review. They began by offering a $10 gift card to delete it. I have notified Amazon after the fourth contact, but the seller continues to try to get me to delete it. They have been increasing the offer, and today they offer $50 for me to delete the review. I thought shoppers might want to know.

I noticed immediately that the battery charge indicator lights did NOT turn off when I turned the radio knob to off.
