review_text: I purchased this as a quick way to connect my iPhone to a Nebula projector. That part works and you can show all your own content photos, videos ... HOWEVER, All the major streaming services APPS check for certified Apple hardware and this cable DOES NOT PASS the test. I plugged an Apple HDMI-Lightning Adapter in and the services all streamed on the Nebula projector okay. Apple has some type of hardware-embedded code level handshake that these streaming apps are checking to be sure the streaming content is safe for viewing only on anApple adapter. This adapter cable does not have that secret sauce. If you plan to use this cable for AppleTV+, Prime, Netflix or Disney+ don't waste your time - I tried all of these services and they all refused to connect to the projector.

I was installing 4 units and ordered 4 of these wifi modules. 3 out of 4 could not connect to the network, while the 4th was connecting just fine. So, I returned the 3 bad ones and re-ordered them. The second order arrived and again only 1 out of 3 units works fine connecting on the 1st trial, while the other 2 units do not connect after many troubleshooting and factory reset attempts to the exact same unit and network that the working unit connects with no issues. So, I conclude that between 60 to 75 % of these units are definitely defective. I was not expecting such a poor quality from the quality leader in mini splits - Mitsubishi. Its a shame. Edit: It turns out that the reason why it was not connecting is that the software that handles it is poorly written. It connects fine if the connection is made in a few seconds after the unit powers up, if you delay it by a few seconds, it will report a wrong error code saying that the "wifi is too weak" and refuse to connect. So, the key is to power it up and immediately use the app to connect to it and do the whole thing very quickly, otherwise it will not connect.

review_text: Prebuilt is widely known to cut corners. A year ago, in July, I got this PC at $1,000... Honestly the biggest mistake I ever made with money. After learning more about PCs, I realized I could've built a bigger and better PC that was faster and didn't heat up as this one does. The size is not the same as advertised. It's pretty small. I didn't bother measuring because I just trusted this company I bought a $1000 PC from. The length says 20.1 inches, my case is 14.1... like why? After 20 minutes of playing a game like Red Dead Redemption 2, Rainbow 6, and COD, my GPU overheats and slowed it down at times. I have to turn the fan on high and open the side panel for 30 minutes and this STILL has to be done every now and then. The thing overheats badly. The airflow is terrible, if I have to open the panel and turn the fan on high every 40 minutes or so, it's BAD. I got this based on the top review for this product by Rick Feldman, I compare the pictures and it's clearly a different motherboard and my GPU isn't the same size. I got PNY GeForce GTX 1660 Super Single Fan with mine. Pretty much the same but just smaller to fit this tiny case and not be in the way of the CPU fan (which is a quarter of an INCH away from the GPU). I know all this because since it overheats, the SkyTech customer service told me to run FURMARK, a program that stresses the GPU.. then the GPU died, so I took it into the shop to have it looked at. They told me FURMARK is a horrible program that in some cases can light the GPU on FIRE. It's well known by so many people as a test to not use. It's a terrible test CUSTOMER SERVICE TOLD ME TO RUN. I left the dead GPU at the store and I got the same GPU later because of the size of the case. GPU's cost a lot nowadays, so I lost so much money fixing this. Why did I buy a new one when Sky Tech could replace it? Well, I left the DEAD GPU at the store and SkyTech can't help me because of their warranty. Like dude, YOU BROKE IT! And potentially damaged other parts with FURMARK. On top of that, they had to nerve to say "well that's pretty fast for them to throw it away" like you don't believe me? YOU BROKE IT. (JayzTwoCents is a PC Youtuber with 3 million subscribers who talks about "FURMARK" in his video "FREE programs that EVERY PC should have..." at 12:22) I only added the customer service part into this product review because of the warranty it came with, I believe it's part of the product you purchase. The case is too small to upgrade the GPU if you want to, Micro ATX case. They made the "M" lowercase (mATX Mid-Tower) in the description to hopefully make people not see the "Micro" part and make it look like it's an "ATX Mid-Tower" case. Since case labels vary from company to company, maybe this small Micro ATX is their version of a Mid-Tower BUT here are the product dimensions in their description LxWxH "20.1 x 9.7 x 21 inches". Mines LxWxH is "14.1 x 7.5 x 14.1".. Is this legal? The motherboard costs $60 dollars and is really cheap. (Someday they will change it but just know, they just straight-up lied) I learned that I should've stopped being a nervous wreck and just built my first PC. If you are willing to spend $900 to $1200 on a prebuilt PC, you will honestly build a PC that these kinds of companies would sell for $350 to $500 more than the amount you spent on the parts. When I bought this PC, I knew NOTHING about PC's. There were almost no YouTube videos of beginners building one, so that overwhelmed me. From January 1st, 2021 to today, there have been more videos uploaded of people building their first PC than last year and it looks so fun. I really regret buying this thing. I plan on getting a new case :) a new motherboard :) and better fans :). Gaming gets 4 stars because of the CPU and the GPU, the chore of not letting the PC overheat is annoying. That's literally it. The only two things that are salvageable. Thanks for taking my $1000 for something that'll HAVE to be completely redone. This terrible experience with SkyTech has taught me to just go for it, just build a PC.

review_text: Recently tried out 3 headphones: 1.) Audio-Technica ATH-MX20 ($49) 2.) Koss Porta Pro On Ear Headphones with Case ($35) and 3.) Monoprice Premium Hi-fi DJ Style Over-the-Ear Pro Headphones with Mic (also known by their product number, 8323, $29). I wanted some headphones for listening to music or movies on my computer. For "serious" headphones in a real sound system (over $200) I recommend Sennheiser, they are excellent and I love their balanced sound, but for casual listens on my desktop I wanted something cheap and comfortable. Short answer, the Audio-Technica's were the clear winner, just as you might expect from the higher price point. Read on for a more detailed review of all three. The Monoprice cans were the cheapest, but while the sound quality was inferior to the other 2, it wasn't terribly worse, just not quite as clear overall. The build quality also looked fairly durable, and they had one thing I really loved that the others did not, and that was a jack in the left headphone to plug in or unplug your cord. Since in my experience the cords in headphones are usually the first thing to wear out, this is a really nice feature, and could save you money in the end. They also came with a 3.5mm to 6.35mm (1/8" to 1/4") adapter, which was nice, and two cords, one with a built-in mic and one without. Importantly, BOTH cords were only about 4 feet long (apparently they used to include a longer cord, but no more.) I may have actually kept these but for one FATAL flaw: they were WAY too tight on my head. Now I assure you I don't have a big giant head! My hat size is an average one. I don't know who they are designing these headphones for, but if you're over 5 years old you may have problems. They could be adjusted for ear height, but this did nothing to reduce the pressure on my head. They didn't have enough swivel either. And the "holes" for the earpads were small, my ears fit in there but just barely, and I don't have extra large ears either! So unfortunately I ruled them out. The Koss headphones were better in both sound quality and comfort. Again, not amazingly better, just about the difference you'd expect between $29 and $35 headphones. The bass was a little less muffled, the mids were more easily picked out, though the highs were about the same. But it seemed like they'd sacrificed on durability. In fairness, they ARE supposed to be fold-up, "DJ style" phones, and there was even a soft carrying case (useless for my purposes) so you wouldn't expect them to be very big and bulky. However there's just a thin band of metal going across the top of the head, and they are not over the ear type so no cushion around the ear. They are "on ear", which is fine, but forget any noise cancellation. There was some sort of "comfort" adjustment on both sides from "firm" to "light" (pressure?) but no instructions, and adjusting it did almost nothing that I could tell, just seemed like a gimmick. The whole thing was very lightweight, which was nice, but also appeared sort of flimsy. Could be wrong, but I could imagine them breaking fairly easily. Also the cord was only about 4 feet long, if that matters to you (and it did to me!). Pretty good sound though, for $35! The Audio-Technica sounded better still - yep, about $14 better than the Koss, so just what you'd expect. Bass was clearer though not intrusive (a problem I have with many headphones) and there was a definite improvement in the clarity of the mids and highs over the Koss and Monoprice. Nothing spectacular, but noticeably better, and they had a well-balanced sound. The build quality looked good, the band across the head was well padded, the swivel of the cans was great (so important for comfort) and the holes for my ears were more comfortably sized as well. The cord was about 3 meters long and thicker than the others, and it also came with a 6.35mm to 3.5mm plug adapter. Overall, this seemed like the clear winner for my purposes. Are any of these going to sound near the quality of my Senn 598's? Uh, no. Were they worth their respective prices? Yes, for the most part, with the caveats that I can't speak to longevity at all, and Monoprice needs to seriously redesign their headphones with a larger head in mind...

The CC pot firstly has a massive dead zone at the minimum range, secondly, the output current is dependent on the input voltage. The higher the input voltage the higher the output current will be allowed to rise. So you cannot protect your electronics reliably if your input voltage is all over the place. Which is the case of a battery supply as the input would definitely become problematic. I couldn't get the current to go below 4A on the output and the current just rise more and more as the input voltage goes up. The input current also increases so I have no idea where the CC came from because neither side is constant anything. Edit: The CC function is greatly dependant on the differences between the input voltage and the output voltage. And I have found that if you create too much load on the output and the output potential is too low it will collapse and pump through more of the input voltage. (kinda think of it in terms of how the resonance of the circuit works) if you collapse the resonance you just start pushing through power directly from the input. Maybe if this was a buckboost converter with cc you could mitigate this problem. But from all 4 units this is how it behaved. So I don't think they are defective you just have to be weary about how boost converters work and their pitfalls. The behavior is the same on my other smaller booster too. But not my buck converter, with buck converters the CC function is rock solid. So I'm going to give this a 3 star because through learning more I figured out its less of a problem with this specific design and more of a compromise with any boost converter this simple.

PRO- The watch itself is well made, looks nice and comes (very handily) with a tool to remove links. Very cool! It does monitor BP, pulse, oxigination, etc. but again, you must have the app running on your phone. There's precious little in the way of instructions, for instance the sleep monitor function. I couldn't tell if I had to engage it before sleep or not, the first night I went to the function in the watch, tapped it a couple of times but it didn't acknowledge if it was running or not, but it turned out it was! 2nd night, on purpose did not engage function to see if it was automatic. Next day appeared not to show anything. 3rd day engaged it again, and it showed only 1st and 2nd nights, BUT when I rebooted my phone, all 3 were there! I've been building PC's for about 15 years, and I always buy ASUS motherboards. I've used others (Gigabyte once) but I've always been pleased with ASUS boards, and once one gets used to the way a given brand does things it's just easier to stick with them. This was my first AMD/Ryzen build (I've always used Intel) and I figured that while this seems a little over priced for what it is, given what's happening with CPU and graphics card prices, this is only mildly overpriced. I should say clearly here that I am not a gamer so there are features on this board that aren't as important to me as they would be to gamers (like power handling and the like; what is important to me is lots of SSD connectors that can be used without limiting use of PCIe slots. What I liked most: 1) I have always hated putting in the I/O plate into the case and then sliding the motherboard in so that the connectors meet the I/O plate correctly. I don't know why I'm so bad at it (I assume it's me as I don't hear that many other people complain about it) but I was determined to get a board this time (even if it means buying "more board" than I need). This one has an integrated I/O plate and that works great. 2) It has MB slots for 2 M2.2280 (or smaller) SSD gumsticks. Some competitive boards have 3, but I can live with two. This board supports PCIe 4, but only for one of the two 2280 slots, but again that was OK with me. 3) In addition to the two 2280 slots, it has 8 SATA connectors and that's great for me. I need lots of storage and wanted to build a no-spinning-hard-drive system and since large SSD's are very expensive, all of these connectors let me use 1TB and 2TB drives. Importantly, you can use all of these without messing up your PCIe slot usage. 4) There are two methods by which this board tells you if there's a problem. First, and easiest, is a set of different color LED's that indicate a problem (one for RAM, one for video, etc), so that all you have to do is see the color and you know what's up. There is also a 2-character LED display that can show much more specific indication. (Hold onto the manual as they are all documented in there, though not necessarily very well.) 5) As has been the case with ASUS as long as I've built with them, their BIOS interface is terrific and the multiple BIOS update methods are nice. 6) I can't imagine spending the money for this MB, and an appropriate CPU, and using the free included Ryzen fan/cooler. First, it's obviously going to have to work hard and is clearly too small to be all that effective. I used the new Cooler Master EVO 212 V2, which is a DELIGHT to install compared to the previous generations (where you really needed 3 hands). BUT, if you do use the included free cooler, the backplate on this board is incredibly tough and strong. I felt bad taking it off to replace it with the plastic one that the CM cooler requires. 7) There are a number of FAN headers, and while I usually don't use the MB fan controls for my case fans (just the two CPU fans on the cooler), I like having them. What I don't like: 1) There is a "cover" that conceals the two 2280 drives and under it is a very small fan. That fan is clearly not very effective, as even when the computer is idling, my high-end Samsung 2280's run warmer than they should. They don't run warm enough to worry me, but I'm wondering if I might be better off removing that cover and putting large heat sinks on those two 2280's. 2) When I first booted up the system, I noticed (as expected) that the two fans attached to the cooler (I liked the fan that comes with the cooler and bought a second identical one) and which were attached to the two CPU fan headers on the board, were showing similar but slightly different, speeds. That's what I expect to see. However, I did upgrade the BIOS, and I noticed that they've screwed up something: Whereas the original BIOS (along with the HWMonitor program I always use) called the fans CPU and CPUAUX (I think I'm getting the second name right), after the update, the second fan is now called "CPUFANIN" and always shows the exact same speed as the primary CPU fan. I am certain that they messed up and it's just repeating the info from the primary CPU fan. This doesn't matter to me UNLESS something happens to one of the fans as I won't easily know which it is. Would I buy this board again? Almost certainly, because other than have 2 rather than 3 2280 connections, the SSD capability seems terrific and I've never had an ASUS board fail. Since I've been working from home during this pandemic, I needed a way to have both my work computer and my personal computer setup and usable without having to play the "switch the cables" game every time. After doing some research and talking to a couple of my tech buddies, I settled on the TESmart (4) Dual Monitor KVM switch. Shipping and receiving was fast, and came properly packaged and undamaged. And the setup is mostly easy. And the switch does work, I can definitely flip between both systems and and dual monitors on both. And the small form factor was a definite plus as my desk at home is not very big. The problem, and for me it's fairly major, is that no matter what I do, I cannot get my Razer Ornata Chrome (keyboard) or my Razer Deathadder Elite (mouse) to work. TESmart "says" they will work (the picture on this very page shows a mechanical keyboard + mouse that are similar (in both shape and size) to my Razer devices. I've plugged them into the USB Keyboard and Mouse ports on the switch, nothing. Plugged them into a USB 2.0 hub and then into the USB 2.0 passthrough on the switch, still nothing. Plugged them both in directly to each computer, works just fine. And the TESmart website gives absolutely NOTHING in means of helping to figure out what is the real issue (other than the fact that this model listed is NOT the updated 2020 model, which I feel is very ignorant of TESmart to do... but hey, it's the corporate way to say, "Let's offload our old stock that we know is junk and not provide actual good service to people who are paying $175+ for equipment."). So my only solution is to either buy a new KVM switch and hope it worked, or just buy a different keyboard and mouse. And since I'm already out ~$200, I'll buy a $20 keyboard/mouse combo deal and just hookup the set to my work computer, leave my higher end Razer devices connected to my personal computer, and just switch keyboards and mice as needed. Yes, I'm aware I could return the switch, but I believe I'm outside the return window for this, as I have wasted a LOT of time trying to get this to work on my own. I'm very disappointed in this device, and very much regret buying it. But that being said, if you are using a regular keyboard and mouse, then I'm guessing you will be fine and won't have the same issues I have been having.

review_text: It's just amazing to me that anyone would spend the thousands of dollars that must have gone into product design and development, packaging, advertising graphics, marketing, etc. AND NOT HAVE PAID A DECENT TECHNICAL WRITER A FEW BUCKS TO WRITE INSTRUCTIONS THAT WORK! The instructions are a joke. A joke translated into many languages, presumably equally unhelpful in all of them. They are vague. They leave out important information. And they are wrong. I finally emailed the seller and they told me enough to get it working. Totally different from the written instructions, of course. Update: These work about half the time. The other times when you need to find the keys or the phone, they don't. Bluetooth is just not that reliable. When you finally find the thing by conventional means, you find bluetooth needs to be restarted, or the Cube battery needs to be replaced, or some other glitch. I have 3 of them. Right now, one will not work no matter what I do. The instructions of course are no help. So, I have to email tech support and wait. I think these are the best out there, but the best in this class of things is just not very good. Pity! The customer support from the seller is really fast. So you can get quick answers by email. And if you don't understand the first answer or it doesn't work, the response to a follow-up question is even faster. So, you can get there from here. The product works well as a keyfinder. Other keyfinders had too-short battery life, so when you lose your keys you also find your battery has gone dead and those finders are not help. This one seems to have good battery life and a battery status indicator within the app, so you get some warning that the battery is running low (if you look at it). A spare battery is included (under the packing material in the little box, so don't throw away the box until you find it). It's range is very limited, so you have to look at the map to see where it was when last in range, and then walk around in that area pushing the button until the beeping starts. Like all of these gadgets, the pitch of the beeper is above the hearing range of an old person with typical high-frequency age-related hearing loss. So, first step when you lose your keys is to put your hearing aids in. Even without the auditory signal, just walking around and watching for when the bluetooth connection is made will tell you visually when you are near the lost keys. It would be useless for finding a pet, unless maybe the pet is a turtle. Working it in reverse, using the finder to make the phone ring and flash to find the phone, is very handy and I use it oftener that way than in the reverse. My second complaint is the app. It has a "Pairing Tutuorial." I clicked it, expecting to learn about pairing. It was not about pairing. So I clicked the "+" to add a cube. The "+" is not clickable. It does nothing. So, how does this happen? They forgot to think about people because they were so busy making the nice box and all the pretty advertising graphics? Just mind-boggling. In the end, every product is about people. Instructions and the user interface are not just a minor detal. They are paramount.

review_text: How different could a cat6 ethernet cable be? I bought this one because it was the lowest priced... and got what I deserved for doing so. I tested the wifi connection, the router, even the jack... and then I isolated it to the cable. I pulled out my phone, read the negative reviews, and was furious. As several others noted (but I missed) this is not cat 6 despite what is printed on the cable. It will "work" but not at the level you're expecting. Buyer beware. --- Pros --- - It is a 50 ft long white flat ethernet cable --- Cons --- - It is not Cat 6 and does not transmit data at speeds up to 1000Mbps - I spent an extra 2 days waiting for a replacement cable and an extra hour re-pulling cable through my walls

To begin with, this is the first gps unit I have ever purchased. Have been wanting one for quite some time and after some research, this one piqued my interest. The device arrived on time and both package and unit were in excellent condition. Along with the device I also purchased the Energizer Rechargeable AA and AAA Battery Charger (Recharge Pro) with 4 AA NiMh rechargeable batteries (came with the charger). The charger has installed progress lighting to tell you the charge status and actually chirps when the charging process is complete. I prefer the rechargeable NiMh batteries since they last longer and allow for longer use of the unit, compared to alkaline batteries. I recommend having a minimum of 4 fully charged batteries on hand whenever using this device. Depending on how much you use it, you could go through batteries fairly quick, even with the longer lasting rechargeables. I have also heard and read that using alkaline batteries will sometimes affect the functionality of the device as they tend to discharge faster than NiMh and Li Ion batteries. Along with the batteries and charger I purchased a Garmin carrying case (recommended by Garmin/Amazon) just to have something to put it in when out and about. The unit allows for the use of a 32GB micro SD card for additional storage since the onboard storage only has 4GB of space (about 3.5 GB available with installed operating system). Sandisk microSD is recommended, which I also purchased with the unit but because the delivery date was a week farther out from the delivery of the unit, I purchased a PNY 32GB microSD. It works just fine with the device. Not knowing much about gps units, I sat down with it at my computer, turned it on and started exploring. So far, I am not disappointed. The pre-installed base map sucks, just thought you would like to know. It lacks any true dimension and has very limited info on it. It shows primary streets and seems to be extremely outdated. My device came with the geocaching turned on which annoyed the hell out of me until I figured out how to turn it off. My local area alone had hundreds of pre-programned geocache sites showing and really cluttered the map view. After opening the package and installing the batteries, I got online and began researching how to acquire free maps to upload to the unit. OpenStreetMap (OSM) has quite a few routable maps that can be loaded onto the device if you don't feel like spending a fortune on Garmins maps, which are highly priced. I installed Garmins BaseCamp program on my computer and after some frustrating trials and errors was able to down load several maps onto the device, including OSM topo maps. The OSM maps are pretty functional on the device and far superior to the preinstalled map (I figured out how to remove this map as well as the two or three other Demo maps installed since I had no need for them). Some advice, before deleting any maps or files ftom your device, create a backup folder on your pc and copy what you intend to delete to it. This will allow you to reinstall the files if you ever need to. Through BaseCamp, with the help of google maps, I was able to add multiple waypoints to the installed maps and upload them to the device. One thing to note here, when adding maps to the device I highly recommend having a microSD card installed. This allows many maps to be stored on the device without eating up the small amount of onboard storage. I store all other information in the onboard storage, (waypoints, etc.) which takes up a very small amount of space. The screen on the device is rather small but that is expected. The screen resolution is, in my opinion, well within the limits of acceptance. Unlike cell phones, this screen views well in direct sunlight. The device starts up without any issues, seems to run smoothly and is very functional when navigating both on foot and by car (I use the Hiking profile for these activities). It's compact, feels sturdy in the hand and looks pretty nice! The touch screen is very responsive. You can also adjust the touch sensitivity in the settings if needed. Overall, as a first time gps'er, I find this device to be very useful and am excited to explore all of its functionality as I continue using it. For first time users, I highly recommend downloading the Owners Manual from the website as the quick start guide has very limited information on how to operate the device. If you intend to use BaseCamp I recommend downloading their Owners Manual as well. Don't let the negative reviews on this product deter you. I have found over the years that sometimes you may get a defective item (quality control typicaly checks only 10% of items sold which does not prevent defective products from being released for retail). Sometimes purchasers have higher expectations for products than what the product allows for, resulting in disappointment and unfair reviews. This is a good product and I do recommend it for purchase and use. I am giving only ⭐⭐⭐⭐ at this time and will update once I have more time with the device! Update 4/28/2021 I have been using this GPS unit quite a lot since purchasing it. To date, I am not disappointed. It performs as expected and outside of losing satellite signal (very rare occourance, typically happens inside certain retail facilities) it is a very reliable device. One suggestion, make sure to turn it off when not in use. The constant update of satellites will drain the batteries (even rechargeables). I forgot to stop my tracking one day and after 14 hours (approximately) the batteries went dead. I am bumping my review from 4 stars to 5 as I have found no evidence of any noteable issues with the device. If you decide to purchase one, I hope you enjoy it as much as I do mine.

review_text: Because I was scared to miss the studs in my plastered walls, I had a professional finishing carpenter install this product a few days ago. He did a great job yet encountered a problem with the product. The mount connects the wall to a double bar to a single bar to the adjustable TV holder. The problem is at the "wrist". See first picture with red arrow and second picture with too much zoom. :) The single bar is preassembled with a welded vertical shaft to hold the bolt allowing the TV to fully swivel. On my unit (and I'm guessing most), the welded shaft is not perfectly vertical. I suppose that is why the design allows for a +/- 3 degrees tilt adjustment. And this DOES correct the problem for a SINGLE swivel viewing position. But I bought this product so I could move the TV for viewing in more than one position: straight on by the sofa across adjacent to the wall (third picture of blue/purple TV), or straight on by the sofa across from the wall (fourth picture of red/orange TV), or at an angle by the whole room. The tilt is NOT possible to correct for ALL swivel positions. You might not be able to see how bad this is from the pictures. This is much more noticeable when in the room. The design concept and product marketing is great. So disappointed with the manufacturing quality of this product. Bought it back in 2021. Took me this long to get on the carpenter's schedule. Can't return it. Buyer beware.

[[VIDEOID:3523dd023dbb12f3dc34ee5fb806689b]] Hello friends. My review is intended to give you a realistic view of this product. First the good. I sleep with a Respironics CPAP machine. My pressure is at 11. I do not sleep with the humidifier. I ran my CPAP machine on this fully charged battery for 17 hours over three different days before a Respironics machine shut off due to a low battery input. However I also wanted to test it as if I was camping so I also used it to charge my cell phone for all three nights. I have a note 5 with a pretty good size battery and it was almost dead each day. So I figure it's got two usable days for breathing and charging your phone. That's not bad. On day 3, I was woken up feeling like I was suffocating because of machine shut off. That wasn't cool. But I had to test it. Next some education. This battery has 12 of the 18650 batteries in it. Those batteries are 3200 milliamps each. In order to get the12volt they built it in 3 18650 in a series. When you series 3 18650 together you get More Voltage but the milliamps stays the same. (Side note. 18650 batteries fully dead are at 3 volts but fully charged at 4.2 volts. That's why you get a swing of 9 volts when dead, and 12 volts fully charged.) So because you have 12 batteries that means that you have three 18650s in a series configuration and you have 4 of those series sets in a parallel configuration. (Side note. When you put batteries in parallel the voltage stays the same but the milliamps goes up with each pack you add). For those of you that understand it, it's set up with 3S4P. That means this battery pack only stores potentially 12,800 milliamps. I know a lot about this because I build bike batteries. Also I wanted to tell you when the switch is off the battery will still charge. Also I wanted to tell you that extra cable they tell you to buy if your machine is showing check battery error message is the wrong cable. I purchased a wire that turns this battery pack into a 12 volt cigarette lighter plug and then used the Respironics adapter to plug into a car. And that work. The cable they tell you to purchase won't plug into your Respironics. At least not Mine. Mine's about a year-and-a-half old. Now for the bad. I believe that this seller does not understand this product very well and a lot of the advice he gives, after reading through all the reviews and questions, conflicts with itself. Also because this battery does not offer the high milliamps that it promises I gave it three stars. Also I purchased a charger to charge it from my car cigarette lighter and after driving for 5 hours this battery what's less than 50% charge. But keep in mind that was on a fully dead battery after using it for 2.25 days. Conclusion. This is a well-built, solid unit that is pretty light. If you want to carry it regularly to charge phones or do any mobile things I think it's a good battery pack. However for high drain situations this is the wrong battery. So for its designed purpose it works as a backup for CPAP machine if your power goes out or you need to charge your phone. So as long as you don't expect too much from it it's a good piece of equipment. I will be keeping this one 4 camping and power outages. I hope my review helps

I bought this to replace/upgrade my 6+ year old QNAP 671 NAS unit. Factors figuring into my decision included experience with QNAP, better PLEX performance compared to comparable Synology systems and support for QuTS Hero OS. After installing 2 Samsung 970 SSD's, 8 WD Red Plus 8TB NAS drives and 64GB of Samsung DRAM, the system has performed well. My current configuration is using the SSD's as RAID 1 for the OS and software while using the HD's purely for data. On the downside for this unit, I was surprised to see the hard disk caddies as plastic (the ones in the 671 were metal). The SSD's were a bit tricky to install due to their location. While they do get hot, I chose not to add heat sinks after seeing the operating temperature well within their limits.

After putting in a lot of effort to build an extremely compact SFF ATX build in a Cerberus X with two 240mm radiators and a 120mm radiator, I kept running into BSODs and random shutdowns while gaming. After troubleshooting CPU, Memory and my GPU I finally decided to plug in a separate ATX PSU just to power the PCI-E power cables going to my 3090 FE and had no problems. Turns out I was triggering OCP half the time and the other half was almost triggering OCP and causing a BSOD that couldn't complete the memory dump. Tried another SF750 I wasn't using and also had the same problems. Tried an RMA replacement and also had the same problem. I don't really blame Corsair for this as the RTX 3000 series is built on Samsung 10nm which can't hit very high clock speeds, so Nvidia compensated by making an extremely wide architecture with tons of CUDA cores. That's bound to draw extremely high amounts of power and the power limit can't kick in fast enough to throttle it.

Good soundbar, with a few critical flaws if you need to use corded headphones from time-to-time. Bought this because my pc needs speakers. I've been using it with headphones alone for nearly 6 months (Covid-19 Work-From-Home Build). My WFH setup is in my bedroom, so to avoid disturbing my wife, I use headphones often. However, there are times its nice not to have to wear them, and times where I want to share the audio with her or my kids, or just have background music playing in the room. The SonaVERSE UBR arrived promptly (2nd day via Prime) and was packed inside an oblong Amazon box. Could have included something to prevent the speaker box from moving around in it. Plugged the audio in, audio out and USB into the back of my machine. The soundbar works well - was able to turn up the volume without distortion (didn't take it to max) and it sounded good (I'm no audiophile though). The volume control has a nice blue glow under it - and nice feel - clicks from off to on and then has some resistance and light clicks as you turn the dial - feels very good. The problem I encountered was when I plugged my headphones back into the device. The first thing I noticed is that the volume dial doesn't control the headphone jack volume. So I got blaring full volume into the headphones until I lowered it in windows. That, by itself is really annoying - as I want to turn my windows volume to max, and then control the sound output using the volume control when using the soundbar. Naturally, I'd want the same when I plug my headphones in. Second issue, which was the deal killer, was that there's noise on the headphones line when nothing's playing, or when it's low volume. This might not matter as much when listening to loud music, but when listening to audio or using it for calls, it's horrible. I noticed that when I reached around back to disconnect the audio wires, just moving them caused the the noises to change. This suggests the wires are poorly insulated/balanced. The issue was subdued when I plug the soundbar into alternative audio ports on the front of my box, but it's still there. (plugging the same headphones into either the back or front audio output is completely absent of any noise). I contacted Amazon and they promptly sent me a replacement. Tried it and still getting noise. To make matters worse, the audio port had some play in it and I couldn't get stereo sound out of it without trying repeatedly to adjust the plug in it it. The second box had one of those leaflets saying "STOP - Do not return this product...". It claims Gogrove.com/support offers 24/7 tech support. While I don't think this is serviceable, I decided to try them out. Unfortunately the website informs you that they only offer M-F 8/5 Pacific time. I submitted a ticket, but don't expect to be contacted as it's Sunday. Sending both back. If you need to use headphones with your speakers/soundbar, skip this product.

Context is key - this is a very inexpensive smart watch (~$40). Comparing it to Apple/Google/Samsung/Fitbit is unfair. So let's just talk about what you do get and why it's a good value. --Useful fitness/health tracker: This watch has great heart rate, Sp02 sensor, exercise detection, GPS integration and more. It's also well water-proofed for open water swimming. Honestly, for fitness tracking alone, it's an exceptional value and should be considered for anyone thinking about getting a Fitbit since most of those don't have lots of bells and whistles either. This watch is less expensive and more capable than those competitors. --Helpful extras: Weather, music control, text/call notifications, and Alexa integration - these make the device a "smart watch" and give you some added convenience around the house. Experiment, and you'll find yourself using it - especially if you're in a room without another smart speaker and want to control household devices easily. --Comfortable and attractive: The first thing I noticed out of the box was how comfortable the included silicone band is. It comes in two sizes, so it can definitely fit pretty much any wrist. I think it uses standard wristwatch band connection points as well if you'd like to change it out. You can choose from a variety of watch faces - I showed the one I prefer in pictures because it has most of the relevant status indicators I like. From the outside, it looks and feels like a high-end smart watch. Great build quality. Cons: No review would be complete without discussing cons. This watch has a few - but try and keep in mind the price point. That's why I didn't take any stars away. --Cannot reply to texts - you can read them, but no ability to reply --Cannot see what music is playing - you just get basic controls (volume, play/pause, next/prev track) --No wireless charging - don't lose the included cable --Touch interface is slightly laggy. Not unusable, just not buttery smooth. Probably a trade-off for improved battery life. Bottom line? This is a capable smart watch. I'm amazed it can be sold for such a low price. If you're looking for a fitness/health tracker, I'd say this is for you. If you'd like to dabble in smart watches to see if you like having the extra features on top, this makes for a great entry point. If you find you don't care for using a smart watch, would you rather be out $40 or $300? Easy question in my book.

I knew this was a budget case and so I did not expect perfection, so this does have a lot of Cons, but all budget cases do. The Pros easily outweigh the Cons as the Air Flow is great and the build quality is really good. I can see this case lasting for a long time, especially after I buy some new Thumbscrews for the glass panel. I would buy this case again if I am doing another budget build. I still have high hopes for this camera, which I bought for three reasons: 1. I lugged around a Canon DSLR with a set of lenses including a 100 - 400 zoom on Safari in Africa, so was looking for a lighter rig to serve me on long days in the field. 2. My hands are not as steady as they used to be, and Olympus' in-body image stabilization is said to be the best. 3. I was intrigued by the built-in focus bracketing (which permits focus stacking), which I am eager to use for macro work. Unfortunately, I have not been able to take full advantage of the camera's capabilities in the six weeks that I've had it. Unbelievably, the almost 300 page digital manual for the camera lacks the kind of depth to actually explain how it works. There is almost no mention of focus bracketing/stacking in the manual. To give an example of just how ridiculously shallow the manual is - I was looking up the capacity (mAh) of the battery, and under specs all it said was the model number and that it was a lithium rechargeable. Everything is covered, but just barely. Because the camera is still relatively new, online help in the form of forums etc. remains limited. Pros: 1. Smaller/lighter body/lenses when compared to a full-size DSLR. 2. "World best" image stabilization. 3. Intriguing special features not offered by Canon, Sony, Nikon. 4. Very fast shooting speed. Cons: 1. Significant compromise in image quality, the result not only of a smaller sensor, but also because it's the same sensor Olympus has been using for many years. 2. Huge digital manual, which none-the-less lacks depth. 3. Bewildering array of interdependent menu items, the organization of which makes absolutely no sense to this mostly Canon user. 4. No built-in flash. (Nor does a flash come with the unit). 5. Persistent rumors that manufacturer's days may be numbered.

Since listings can can change but the reviews stay the same, this review is specifically for: Dell Optiplex 7010 Business Desktop Computer (Intel Quad Core i5-3470 3.2GHz, 16GB RAM, 2TB HDD The actual CPU installed is a 3550 which is an upgrade to the advertised processor. The HDD has 57,000 hours on it which is the equivalent of running continuously 24 hours a day 7 days a week for over 6.5 years. If you use your computer 2 hours per day you would have to use it for 78 years to accumulate as much usage on the hard drive. I'm not saying 57,000 hours on a HDD is excessive I'm just putting this into perspective that this is not a "new" HD nor is it particularly speedy. This isn't an issue for me because I'm using an SDD in the machine and it runs very fast with it. The memory was installed incorrectly- in single channel mode. It works in this manner just far below expectations. I removed one of the memory sticks and put it in the next slot over to make the memory dual mode and it benched twice as fast. I've never heard of "Sesame" memory before and can find little about it on the internet. But I posted a shot of the specs as well. Cheap memory is usually the culprit in any computer problem so it's something to keep an eye on. If anybody knows anything about sesame memory feel free to post as a followup comment. review_text: This stand alone unit is of high quality and offers exceptional sound quality when used for regular Alexa functions like podcasts, music, smart home things, etc. What does not work well at all is the home theater function. I use a Fire TV 4k Stick and a Fire TV Stick Max. I own and use a number if Echo devices and an usually a very satisfied customer. However, I have been struggling with the home theater for six months and have now finally given up. The system is not at all reliable. I have had to delete and reset the home theater function at least 30 times. The home theater function will not play audio reliably from my ReCast. It is jumbled and quirky. The system will periodically for no obvious reason just quit working, requiring the user to unpair the theater in the alexa app. Many times the Echo Sub and Echo Studio units will have to be reset from scratch (wiped and restarted) in order to re-establish the home theater. Amazon support has been involved numerous times and been unable to change the outcomes. Please don’t waste your money on these units if you are planning a home theater use. Completely unreliable. I think the root cause of the failure of the concept is too complex - too many moving parts to reliably function. The moving parts are your internet ISP, Amazon’s network, your wifi router and set up, device compatibility issues and the constantly changing audio formats. So anyway, the system just doesn’t work reliably - fair warning.

review_text: This was an extension cable between my gaming headset and my computer. Right after I couldn't return it anymore it started a crakling humming sound, like feedback or a poor connection. I checked the female end of the cable (where my headset plugs in) and found the outer cover for the plug had become loose. I discovered that it was threaded, so I just tightened it. Didn't fix the problem though. I suspect the damage was done already before I discovered that the cover had become loose. Since every cable they make is made in the same fashion, then maybe they need to address an R&D issue. It is a nice looking cable (comparable to u-Green brand except for a rubber cable instead of a braided cover) due to the nice metal caps, so take away the metal caps and it is just another cheap rubber cable. You can see in the picture, that there is nothing under that metal cap except a ground strap. So as long as the cap is on, it should not be causing a problem. The problem must be internal then. That tells me poor Manufacturing. Given that plugging in my headset and then unplugging it causes a lot of static and gently wiggling the plug while it is plugged in can affect whether you get the humming sound or not tells me that the contacts inside the plug are poor quality and not working correctly.

Extremely punchy, clear and detailed sound. The treble is sweet and bright, almost to the point of fatigue but just off. This adds a lot of articulation to speech. Mids are natural, smooth and detailed. Bass is smooth and punchy, as opposed to the sort of smooth but muddy bass of my HD650. I actually like a little bit of mud in my headphones as long as they are detailed, because it makes headphones feel more relaxed, and while these don't do that they have their own character that I quite like. Comparing these to the Moondrop Starfield, I like these a little better. These and the Starfield image a little differently, where the Starfield does 360 positional imaging better, (the Starfield does that ridiculously well) the imaging on the Legacy 3 is enhanced by a depth the Starfield just doesn't have. The Starfield is somewhat veiled to my ear, but they do crank the mid-range detail up quite a bit. It is not a case where you hear more things in the midrange, they just stand out a bit more and so this is less about quality and more about preference. The midrange detail of the Legacy 3 is still nice and if you care about mids like I do you certainly can't go wrong. A good way to describe it is like, the mids are smoother on the Legacy 3 where the mids on the Starfield are a little more textured. Both are quality. Where the mids are slightly more detailed on the Starfield the highs are FAR more detailed on the Legacy 3 and it gives the impression of a lot more clarity than the Starfield. In terms of overall detail they're VERY equal and it's really just about personal preference as to the exact way that detail is presented. The best way to describe it is to put it into numbers, so I will. Legacy 3: Imaging - 8 Soundstage - 7.5 Highs - 8 Mids - 8 Bass - 8 Starfield: Imaging - 10 Soundstage - 5 Highs - 6.5 Mids - 9 Bass - 6.5 Reference: (HD650) Imaging - 8 Soundstage - 6.5 Highs - 8 Mids - 10 Bass - 7.5

review_text: I have had my nest cams for over 2 years. Here is the good, the bad and the ugly. The good: overall, I am satisfied with the resolution. However, you can not acquire an image at night if you place the cam behind a window due to significant glare. The camera otherwise works as it should with good tech support if trouble surfaces. The bad: beware of nest aware. It borders on shady at best. After 5 months of a 12 month paid subscription, my nest aware stopped working. To add insult to injury, nest will auto renew your subscription (and charge whatever credit card it has on file) and choose a random camera to assign the subscription to. It is time consuming to address and requires customers to monitor charges closely. I actually thought this was a fraudulent charge and then realized it was Nest. The ugly: nest has suffered significant security breaches in the last year with hackers doing a variety of ugly things with family cams. Nest has attempted to address this with two factor authentication but in bringing this technology into a home, families have to worry about another layer of cyber security. My general assessment is that while the nest hardware is good, the nest aware needs close monitoring to avoid inappropriate charges. Lastly, cyber security remains a major concern.

TLDR: These headphones sound better than all Marshall's previous sets (which is saying a lot from someone who loves their other headphones), they're also the most comfortable Marshall headphones, the ANC works well, the app/connectivity can be a little buggy (though not enough to keep me from recommending them). I have (and do) owned a lot of headphones, including 3 pairs of different Marshall headphones, these are my favorite of the bunch. I initially chose Marshall over the competition due to the unique styling and simple control method, I hate capacitive buttons and overly complex interfaces. Since my first pair of Marshall headphones I was hooked, not only do they look better than the competition in my opinion, I find the sound profile very appealing for a large variety of music. If you've tried and liked Marshall's other headphones (authentic ones, not replicas which are common), you'll be a fan of these. Pros: 1) These sound very much like the original Monitor Bluetooth, but with better bass depth and more clarity. They are also FAR more comfortable than the original Monitor which was really my only complaint with that set. 2) I also own the Mid ANC, and that set is great as well, but these are much more comfortable. 3) These have a much better sound stage than the original Monitor and Mid ANC (though I still recommend both of those sets for their price ranges). 4) The ANC between these and the Mid ANC is pretty similar with a slight edge going to the Monitor IIs. 5) I'm a big fan of the build quality on not only these, but all Marshall headphones. They're very robust and feel very well built, the Monitor II though, is a step above even the rest of their lineup... I don't see these wearing out anytime soon, and I'm someone who never bothers with carrying cases, my Monitor I and Mid ANC both show very little wear despite being tossed into camera bags and back packs for years without cases. 6) These surprisingly fold up even smaller than the original Monitor, which was already a remarkably small set when folded up, very handy for transport. 7) The monitoring button is excellent, ALL headphones should have this. Being able to touch a button and have my music not only pause, but outside sound amplified into my ears is a game changer. Being able to just touch a button to talk to a co-worker and then touch it again to get back to work is amazing. Now on to the cons list... 1) Though these are a big step up from the original monitor (as noted above), I still don't find them to be perfectly comfortable after long periods of time. I wear my headphones while working for hours at a time, and these will start to make the top of my head a little uncomfortable after about an hour or so, after 2 or 3 hours I have to move them or take them off to give my head a break. My ears however, are never uncomfortable in them which is a huge step up from the old Monitor and the Mid ANC, those I couldn't bare for more than an hour. If you're looking for the most comfort though, I'd look at something else, though for most uses, these are perfectly fine. 2) I'm not a fan of the app. The app mostly works, and I think it's smart to implement as a way to make sure you're getting authentic headphones (there are a lot of fake Marshall headphones out there), but I just don't find it very useful or necessary. If you like to tweak your EQ (and for some reason don't want to do it with a 3rd party app), then it can be useful... and I guess you could use the ANC slider in some situations, but I've not felt the need to mess with it, I just leave it at 100%. The problem with the app though, is it will often take a long time (or fail entirely) to connect to your headphones. It also will say it's made a change, and then when you back up to another screen you see that the change you just made didn't save. I mostly just leave the app alone though, so I don't knock it too much for that. 3) Sometimes when pushing the before mentioned monitor button, when I push it again to return to my music the ANC will activate, but the music will not resume. Then upon entering my music player I see that the music is indeed playing... but I'm not hearing anything. The only thing I've found to resolve this is to disconnect and reconnect the bluetooth... not a deal breaker since it doesn't happen ALL the time, but it is very frustrating when it does happen. Overall, I'm very happy with these headphones and would certainly recommend them to anyone. I have not tried the Bose 700s, but I have used the QC 35ii and Sony 1000xm2, and I find the Monitor 2 sounds better, looks FAR better, has better controls, and about equal ANC... but importantly, with the Marshalls I don't notice that cabin pressure feeling at all and noticed it quite a lot with the Bose and Sony's, your mileage may vary.

I spent the day today comparing the Pixel Buds 2 with the Galaxy Buds, the Buds+, the Jabra Elite 65t and the Jabra Elite 65e. As for sound quality...I was shocked to find that the original Galaxy Buds (with last week's update) have the most balanced, smoothest and most listenable sound of the three standard "buds". The EQ baked into the Buds app makes a HUGE difference in sound and makes them sound "alive". The Elite 65t have a good, well-balanced sound that can be adjusted to your liking so I'd rank them second in sound quality. Next, the Pixel Buds are good but they don't shine in any one area. There well balanced but just, okay. I was hoping for better. The biggest disappointment to my ears were the Buds+. Even with the EQ in the app, they're shrill and unlistenable for long periods of time. Really bad. And finally, the Elite 65e (while in a different category) have the best "musical" sound of the bunch. Great balance overall. I also left messages from all five devices on my work phone. Again, the sound coming from the neckband style Jabra 65e was full and clear. This was followed by the 65T, the original Galaxy Buds (surprised!), the Pixel Buds 2, and finally the Galaxy Buds+. Sound left during the call from the Buds 2 was hollow and sounded mechanical. Overall, I'd rank them in the following order: the neckband style Jabra 65e provided the best overall performance in sound and calling quality. Next I'd place the Galaxy Buds, the Jabra 65T (only the right bud works for calling), the Pixel Buds 2 and the Galaxy Buds+. In conclusion, the Galaxy Buds+ were an unexpected disappointment and they’re already packed to head back to Amazon. The Pixel Buds 2 were decent and if they were released last year, I’d say they were right up there. But sound and calling quality was not up there for a pair costing $180. The biggest surprise were the original Galaxy Buds. They’ve received a couple updates since being released and at least in a quiet office environment, calling quality was really good. And music sounded well balanced with plenty of bass and clear mids and highs. I recommend the “dynamic” EQ setting. One final note regarding apps… the Jabra and Galaxy Buds+ apps work for both Android and iOS. The Pixel and Galaxy Buds app are Android only. Hope this helps somebody.

review_text: I really wanted to love this watch. But... It's very well made. It's not heavy, or overly large on my wrist (I'm 5'9" 210lbs just for reference). I barely notice that it's in once it's been in awhile. The screen is excellent outdoors and not awful indoors. I use the light on it while indoors to read the face. I do wish the light stayed on a little longer, as when I click it, it ends up turning itself off within about 5 seconds. I'm sure this was a power management decision. The device is VERY intuitive. I was worried that since it wasn't a touch screen that it would be a pain to use. Not at all. If that's a concern of yours like it was mine, I can assure you that the people who engineered how this watch works did a phenomenal job. I didn't read any manuals and figured out how to use the device within several days. Seriously, great job Garmin on the user interface. I really thought that I'd end up using the device to it's potential, but tge truth is I don't at all. I do use it daily for my walks and my occasional bike ride. I check the status several times a day on the accompanying application, which is also very very well designed. The sleep tracking, breathing rate, steps, a plethora of information that I do use. The problem is this device does way more than I actually need and I really think I would have been fine buying a device at half the price from Garmin. This isn't their fault at all, but just be aware that if you're looking at this and won't use it for it's intention, you can save literally hundreds of dollars by opting for a cheaper Garmin device that will do most of the basics, and do those basics very well. Some things I don't like. My heart rate tracking is "okay" for a device at this price. For example, I just went on a walk today up a very steep hill and was showing only 98 heart rate. I know that was wrong. My friends watch was showing a substantial difference on his watch. I checked several times and it never went above 105. On the way down the hill I checked and was suddenly at 135, which seemed accurate as I'd only begun the decent shortly before checking. This happens often enough to be concerning, especially considering how much I paid for the device. Another complaint I have is whilek try to use the breathing app, I constantly am missing vibrations for my breathing timer because the vibration just isn't strong enough. I'd I want to use it effectively I have to actually watch my watch face to tell me when to breath, hold breath, etc, kind of defeating the whole purpose of the exercise which is to focus on breathing. Again, this wouldn't be that concerning if I hadn't spent so much money on this. When I purchased this device it was with the understanding that the premium price that I was paying was for THE smart/activity tracking experience to end all experiences. On cheaper devices these inconsistencies would be overlooked but at this price point it's unacceptable. I do love the device even with my several concerns and don't have buyer's remorse per se, but I definitely could have opted for a cheaper device given what I need it for. Just make sure you really need this and check out their other devices before jumping on this one. Hopefully at some point I step up my game to a point that I'll use all the features and I do hope that with firmware updates the vibration and heart rate tracking become a little more consistent.

review_text: This board has seemed decent enough for what I have needed to use it for. I have been happy with the m.2 performance and things work pretty well, other than a few things I will list here. I have not done any benchmarking, but that would be heavily dependent on the other components anyway. The most egregious problem is the lack of wifi and bluetooth despite the product listing saying it has these features. There are two versions of this board which do, B550M DS3H AC and B550M DS3H AC-Y1. But this is not either of those models. If I had known this, I would have bought a different board. I've actually been having a lot of trouble ever since with bluetooth because I have been struggling to find a bluetooth adapter that actually works. Onboard bluetooth has worked great with my devices on other boards, so I know this is the problem. Still the only fault there was incorrect product information. I would return the motherboard, but that would mean having to tear apart my whole computer, go without for awhile, and reactivate Windows. I might still have to do that just because of this problem. It's been quite a struggle. The other issue I have had was with the Q-flash. This is another feature I bought the motherboard for. Knowing that only the more recent bios would support my cpu, and not having any guarantee of having a recent enough BIOS, I went ahead with this one thinking I could just flash it to the most recent using this feature. Unfortunately this feature did not work at all. The power supply was the problem here, most likely, because the board did not receive any power when pressing the required button. I foudn out later you need to have a power supply that supports the Q-flash feature. I don't know whether there is a list anywhere for that, but be aware of this. If the BIOS has been updated to f14 or later (the January 2022 version), you'll have full CPU support. If not, it won't power on and you won't have any way of knowing whether the BIOS is teh wrong version or you have some other problem. This is my first (and only) advanced fitness watch. I had a relatively simple Fitbit previously, so this was quite a step up. So I write this review with the caveat that I'm not an expert in advanced fitness trackers or smartwatches. Having said that, I am really enjoying this watch. I use it predominantly for walking, swimming, running (and once the weather improves, biking). My Fitbit did not support swimming, and I wanted a watch that could do that, but also seamlessly interface with Strava for activity tracking. At first it was a bit overwhelming, but it only took a few days to get used to the features. After a week or so I was comfortably editing the data screens on the watch during activities to show the data I wanted. I love that it is configurable like this. Accuracy during swimming seems very good. The first few times I used it I either "lost" a lap or had an "extra" one recorded, but lately it has been rock solid. Maybe I was obsessing over having it detect the end of a lap, but now I simply touch the wall and don't worry about it and it counts it accurately every time. It does not seem to recognize my strokes that well, but this may be more about my technique that the watch! That doesn't really bother me though. During walks I have noticed that the heart rate monitor has an issue. The uploaded picture illustrates this. It showed my heart rate hovering at about 80bpm (which I know was inaccurate) and then suddenly jumped up to about 113bpm, which was probably accurate. Somehow it was missing one out of every 3 heart beats. I haven't looked too closely at the problem--maybe it's the clothes I'm wearing, but clearly it was not reading the heart rate accurately at the lower bpm because I was definitely exerting myself. I used it on an elliptical trainer this past weekend and the heart rate was dead on in agreement with the elliptical unit's built in sensor heart rate monitor, so I know it has the accuracy with even vigorous movement. The other readings on the elliptical (pace, etc.) were spot on as well. GPS accuracy is excellent, much better than my phone was recording on MapMyRide and native Strava. It is nice to be able to go out without having to carry my phone to get my routes plotted during workouts. And I love the ability to overlay pace and heart rate on the map. The Garmin Connect app is quite good. It has a few UI idiosyncrasies, but overall it's one of the better ones I've used. It keeps track of personal records for my swims (and I assume it will do the same with bike rides once I start riding), although for some reason it does refuse to capture some records, such as Longest Swim and 1000m. I haven't figured that out yet. I do wish that there was an interface to the MapMyFitness set of apps which is where most of my fitness history lies, so basically I am transitioning away from that platform and to Garmin Connect and Strava. A few things I would like to see improved: First, the watch can be set to auto-sync after an activity is completed and within WiFi range. Great! But to get daily step counts to sync, you either have to open the app or use the Sync feature on the phone. This is not a huge deal if you only use the app itself, but I have a third party service that syncs daily step counts from Garmin Connect, so at the end of the day I need to make sure I force a sync. It would be nice to have the watch auto-sync periodically when in range of my phone. Also, in swimming mode, I like to time certain distances (250m, 750m and 1500m). I would be happy with it capturing every 250m, and I'll note that you can set an auto-lap distance for walks (and I presume runs and bike rides too), but that doesn't seem to be an option for swimming. Instead, I can manually press the lap key, which puts it into rest mode, and then hit it a second time to restart. It's not a huge deal--I get what I am looking for, but it would be nice if it were more automatic. Update: I forgot to mention the accuracy of the sleep tracking on this device. Basically it drastically overestimates my sleep. It shows me getting 9-10 hours a night, and I know that on some nights I have been lying awake for almost an hour and the app shows that I was asleep the whole time. This is not a big deal for me, but if you are looking for accurate sleep tracking, that would be something to watch out for with this watch. Overall, I am extremely pleased with this purchase.

I gave this a fair try and here is my review. Overall this mesh network didn’t work very well in my home. It dropped wifi often and some devices couldn’t sign onto the network. My computer has a VPN and the speed wouldn’t go above 10 Mbps. I’m not an IT professional but have more experience than most with networking and set up. I went from having the modem with two extenders. Wifi speeds were great above 100 Mbps. The challenge was going from one side of my 2,700 southwest ft home to the other side the device (phones mostly) wouldn’t switch network and remain on the old network. I was hoping that would solve that issue and it did, however I never got speeds above 70mbps in any case. I tried different locations and figurations but it just didn’t transfer the speeds like it was suppose to do. This made it difficult to say whether the range was good enough as the speed was already poor from 30-60mbps when standing on top of the unit then going far away to test the range. I just never had the consistency to test the distance. The user face/app looked very clean and easy to use, but the more I toyed with it the more I became frustrated because there weren’t limits like you can do on other networks like net gear or wav-link. There was no way of making these connections more secured network. It was easy set up as it came with three units with power chords and one Ethernet cable. Basically plug and play. But it showed 50+ devices connecting to it and I could only account for 20-30 devices. I was able to rename those devices but some I was still unsure. I place them on the blacklist which was a nice feature, and also did have parental controls including setting limits and time restrictions for gaming systems, phones and other devices. Kids quickly complained about time limit. But now with covid and homeschooling, kids need to be on these devices more than 2 hours a day. I was unable to block just Roblox or minecraft. But our PS4 lost connection immediately at 2 hour limit, but PS4 can still be played on some games without internet; so that requires its own limitation management. Pros: home had wifi with no changing of network names. Cons: lost wifi, poor speeds, some devices couldn’t connect.

Having been a Fitbit (Flex) customer in the past, and being low on funds this year, I knew I would not be able to spring for a new Fitbit. With expanded market competition, I decided to try a lower priced option knowing full well that I could easily “get what I paid for.” I reviewed the feedback of current Fitbit models and then I compared three different off-brand lower priced trackers and their reviews and made the decision on this one. I was torn between giving a 3 star or a 4 star review at the end of writing this review because it had more "cons" than "pros" and yet I'm happy to keep it. Here is my review after having worn it since Friday, October 23rd (so I reserve the right to update this initial review). So here goes: First, I would highly suggest watching the product video offered in this Amazon listing. It is pretty good to show you the box, it is unboxing, the size of the watch and many of its features, including the app. It is not complete though and that is why I am providing this feedback. Pros: • Big screen for people who are far-sighted (like me) • Fairly versatile features (touch screen, notifications, heart rate, BP monitor, sleep, etc.) • For runners and walkers, it tracks your GPS movements via the App on your phone • Inexpensive for the features offered • The suggested App allows for custom watch faces (including your own background picture, see my pictures) • Notifications for SMS and social apps work (although this is not what I bought it for) Cons: • Instruction manual provided has very tiny print. Struggled to view “images” shown even with my reading glasses AND a magnifying glass. Ultimately, I used my copier to enlarge the booklet pages and just read the text instructions (which were adequate). • Big screen for people who like their watches on the smaller side. Can be cumbersome for people trying to wear it at night while sleeping. • Says it is waterproof, but not advised to be worn while in hot/humid showery conditions. So, I do not trust that it’s really waterproof. • The app tracks the biggies, but it is not as versatile as the Fitbit app (the product still shot of the sleep feature showing quality of sleep is not reality, see my pictures) • The “sports” feature of the watch has only a limited selection to choose from and aerobics and weightlifting are NOT in the list. These are my two main chosen exercises. • Activating the tracking feature of a “sport” on the watch does NOT seem to carry over into the App’s “Motion” data. If you want your activity tracked day to day, you will need to initiate the tracking from the App on your phone. • I am still trying to find the setting that I can program to keep the watch from lighting up at night as I move while sleeping. Personally, the features I mainly wanted were heart rate, BP monitor, and sleep data. I would really like a more robust set of options and streamlined watch to App “sport” feature to keep track of exercise as well. For the money, I have received what I wanted and will use it and see how long it lasts. It would have been nice to also have the blood oxygen level feature, but that was not a deal breaker for me. If you cannot afford expensive, this watch is pretty good at hitting all the big metrics. It is lackluster on the activity tracking though so if you are BIG into tracking your activity, this may not be the one for you.

There are several things I want to mention in this review. First, I live in East Tennessee in the Appalachian mountains. I am approximately 40 miles from the TV towers, with trees and mountains in between me and them. I researched a lot of antennas before deciding to buy this one. I did not go wrong! When I first got it I just hooked it up to my TV and laid it in a window on top of my dog kennel and scanned for channels. I got over 40 channels like that. As you can see in the picture I put it on a 10-ft pole outside of the house, and I have it connected to two TVs in the house. I pull in 86 channels on one TV, and 82 on the other. I did not have to try to put it way in the air to be able to get these channels. I did use an app that told me which way to point the antenna for the most television stations that are in my area. The rotor works fine, plus I made sure to place the antenna outside where I can see it from a window and am able to tell which way it is rotating. The rotor does change directions at random so you do need to be able to see the antenna if you're going to use the rotor. However, the way I have it pointed it picks up every channel I need so I don't have to rotate it where I'm at. The other channels in different directions around me are too far away and you're just simply unable to pull them in at all no matter what you have. But I am very satisfied with over 80 channels! Make sure when you take it out of the box that you snap it together and it snaps real tight, and when you're tightening the bolts only use hand pressure do not use any type of tools to tighten anything on this antenna with or you will break the antenna. Our antenna has been through thunder and lightning storms, a freeze, and extremely high winds and it's just fine there is no damage to it whatsoever. I have bragged about this antenna so much that one of my cousins and one of my aunts purchased one. They love theirs too!

What I use it for - I am now teleworking and participate in a lot of Zoom and Skye and Teams meetings for work. And I have video calls on my computer with family and friends. Why I am returning - The camera has some physical features (or lack of) that are annoying. The cord is not very long and barely reached from my screen to where my hard drive is placed. The cord is attached off to the side instead of in the back of the unit, and since the camera is physically very lightweight - the cord weight pulled the camera down on one side. The clip that holds the camera on is weak; it balanced OK, but did not feel secure. Any bump to the cord and it would have come off. When received the camera was so out of focus I thought it was broken, I had to turn the focus to the right for about 5 turns to bring in the picture - shouldn't it only go one turn? Maybe it wasn't secured right. There is no on/off light to show you when it has power. All of that I could have worked with, but the picture quality was unacceptable to me. It looked grainy. Also, it was overly light sensitive. I have a window in my home office with shudders on it, when closed not much light comes through except around the very edges of the shudder... but on my screen you could only see a light blob behind me and it looked like the window was open to full sun. The camera interpreted my overhead light with huge contrast on my face. It looked like my forehead was glowing. There is no adjustment for contrast or lighting. I didn't expect one with the price point, but I did expect it to be balanced and not so exaggerated.

I have purchased two other 3-port HDMI 2.1 switches on amazon and both had the same problem. I was hoping this one would be better, since it has an IR port (and others did not), but it seems that the internals of the switch are mostly the same. I can only get port 3 to transmit a 40Gbit/s signal to my TV. The other ports seem to support only a lower bandwidth. I'm guessing it may be 32Gbit/s, as I can get a PS5 to work with port 2 (it sends a maximum of 32Gbit/s at 4K/120/4:2:2/10-bit), but not XBox Series X. The problem is that the switch does not tell the input device that it supports only 32Gbit/s, so the input device relies on what the TV indicates it supports (in my case 40Gbit/s) and so you get a black screen if you connect a device to port 1 or 2 if that device tries to send something more than 32Gbit/s (like 4K/120/4:4:4/10-bit at 40Gbit/s). So, if you are buying this to connect an XBox and a PC both at 4K/120, you will likely have problems. Even if not, I found that sometimes when manually switching to a device, I got a no signal error, and had to switch back and forth one extra time. Also, the "auto-switching" on this switch doesn't seem to work at all (and it did not on the other 2 models I bought and returned). It only works when you physically plug in a new cable, but that doesn't seem very useful. My same setup (same cables, etc.) work properly with 2 different 2-port switches, so I don't believe my devices or cables are at fault; and they are all HDMI 2.1 certified cables (XBox and output to TV), or the cable that came with the devices (PS5). I can't recommend this as it only supports one device at 40Gbit/s or higher, sometimes requires switching back and forth an extra time to get a signal and doesn't properly support auto-switching ability. The marketing of this product and other 3-port HDMI 2.1 switches on Amazon is false as it claims a blanket 48Gbit/s with no limitations mentioned. They should be clear about what the switch supports.
