Thank you for reading this, hopefully my feedback will help you. I work in IT, with over 20 years of experience so whenever I test a new gadget, I take my time with it to make sure that it meets my expectations and solves my problem. Whenever a friend asks me for advice for a 'good WiFi system', I always point it to EERO, however, EERO systems come with a rather hefty price tag and I had not been able to find a good alternative to them... until I came across MeshForce. Also, my house is rather large (~3600 sqft) and I have had quite a few 'dark spots' that I wanted to cover. The entire setup took less than 10 minutes - yes, it's THAT simple. - Unpack - Connect your base to your LAN/Router/Modem - Download and install the app - Scan the QR code on the bottom of your base to connect to the MeshForce's setup WiFi - Setup your "dots" in 'strategic' places - Setup your network/SSID/Options - Done I honestly believe that this is even simpler than setting up an EERO system, because the dots come 'pre-married' to your base station so all you have to do is just plug them in - genius! You also save time since you can use your google account to sign onto the App. I was really impressed by this system, the app is simple yet it does not lack any of the vital features. What I loved: - Setting up and sharing a 'guest' WiFi takes just 2 seconds. - Port forwarding couldn't be easier. - Multiple options to setup your mesh, including bridge mode! <3 - The speed of the station (and the bases) - The dots have a LAN port which you can use to bridge! - The dots also don't hog the entire wall plug (on a double) so you can still use the 2nd plug :) I have a gigabit fiber connection at home, and with my former system (Ubiquiti) I was pretty happy with the throughput (around 200Mbps). The base (and the dots) delivered almost twice that (400Mbps on the base, ~160Mbps on the first dot and ~100Mbps on the 2nd dot) - Keep in mind that if you set this up as a mesh, that's what you'd expect to see, each 'extender' will have half the connection speed as the previous 'hop'. Overall, this system is impressive for the money. I was a bit skeptical at first but it definitely delivers a great experience for an almost unbeatable price!

I've been a loyal Onkyo customer for 20+ years but that company appears to be in the process of mismanaging itself out of business, at least in the US, so unable to buy what I wanted due to lack of availability, I decided to give Denon a try. Before spending what I normally spend on an AVR, I decided to check out a mid range model. You'll find plenty of reviews about the sound quality of this model, so I won't repeat them, but will say I generally agree that this amp provides a pretty good value on that front. What irritated me about this device is the abysmal quality of the firmware. There are many bugs, some of which I could find others complaining about such as powering on to zero volume rather than the configured volume, but there were also others that I didn't see referenced elsewhere such as: - When using HDMI ARC, even with CEC turned off on both the TV and the AVR, turning the TV off changes the source on the AVR from the currently playing source to the TV Audio source. The only way I could stop this from happening was to stop using ARC and use the optical input for TV audio. "CEC off + ARC on" means don't take any control actions on the AVR, just receive the audio, but Denon is reacting to something the TV is sending (perhaps a TV bug, I don't know). - I selected the "hide" option on the Tuner input accidentally ("hide" prevents an unused source from appearing in the list that the source selector knob can choose from). When I changed the setting back, the Tuner refused to output any audio at all. I could see the "tuned" indication, but no sound. I finally had the idea to use the "reset to defaults" (or something similar) option on the Input Assignment screen and that re-enabled the Tuner audio at the expense of erasing my input configuration. - I haven't fully characterized this problem yet, but I have the AVR hooked up to my home automation system and use Denon's control protocol on port 23 to control the AVR. When powering on the AVR the workaround for the zero volume problem (which is to use the "last" setting rather than a preset value) doesn't work. Sending the power-on, source-select, and volume sequences as fast as the AVR will receive them seems to trigger the volume bug. I can watch the AVR power-on, tell me the volume is 49 (as commanded) and then send a volume update to 0 (which I did not command) and then stay there. I literally had to modify the automation software to poll the volume until the 0 showed up and then re-send the desired volume. This only appears to be a bug around the power-on time; once powered on and the volume is reset the AVR behaves normally with respect to volume. UPDATE: The AVR doesn't seem to implement a buffer on the TCP connection. Putting a 500 ms delay between commands fixed these problems. My experience with Onkyo's control protocol was that it buffered the commands and didn't require these delays. I suppose all of this is the result of buying a new AVR so close to its debut. I am still giving it 3 stars because all of the problems are firmware problems and I hope Denon is working on cleaning up them up, otherwise this is my first and last Denon AVR. If the firmware just worked (rather than wasting 2-3 hours of my time figuring out how to work around the problems) it would have been a 4 star AVR. Onkyo, what happened to you, man? Update: One more annoying problem: I have this issue with a TCL Roku TV and can't be sure that it isn't also partly to blame, but if the TV is not powered on (it is either unplugged or in a deep sleep state) when the AVR is powered on and the TV is then turned on later the AVR thinks no monitor is connected and refuses to output anything on the HDMI port. Turning the TV on doesn't cause the Denon to realize a monitor is now attached and the AVR will continue to refuse to output anything on HDMI until the AVR is power cycled with the TV on. The only way I have been able to prevent this from happening is to turn on "Fast Start" mode on the TV which effectively keeps it turned on all the time (but without driving the screen if the TV is "off"). The idle power of the TV changes from less than 1 Watt to 15 Watts in this mode. What a waste of energy just so the Denon will know a TV is always connected! Again, this could be a strange interaction between this brand of TV and the Denon, but this speaks to the lack of interoperability testing. TCL is not an obscure brand of TV and "Fast Start" off is the default mode. The AVR is probably turning HDMI output off when it fails to get an EDID response from the connected, but powered-off, TV. While it is fine for the AVR to require an EDID response during setup, how many people are constantly changing their TV after setup? Simply remember the last configured monitor and keep driving HDMI for that monitor even if you don't detect anything connected. This seems pretty obvious. I'd be interested to hear from others whether the Denon behaves this way will all monitors or if it is just TCL doing this. (It's too much trouble to either move the rack-mounted AVR to another TV or bring another TV to the rack-mounted AVR since all my TVs are attached to walls...) I am keeping the Denon because I have found solutions for all the problems and the sound quality is very good for the price, but I am dismayed at how much effort was required to get everything working.

I left the cover plate off to help with airflow/cooling. The flashing LED is noticeable behind the translucent black plates I put on my PS5. I could put the cover back on, but testing by reliable sources shows installing the cover increases the temperature of the SSD by 5°C. I wish there was a way WD and SONY (considering this is the first ever official SONY licensed SSD) could incorporate the WD dashboard on PS5 to allow us to change the color of the LED, or at the very least, disable the LED altogether. If that happens, I'll gladly add that 5th star to this review.

It works as described, with catches. This product is developed by the company previously known as Elgato. I forget the name of of the company before that. I have used their Tuner on Mac many years ago. They are pretty much the only company making these devices, so there isn't any option. There isn't competition. I purchased this Android adapter before looking deeper into the Manufacturer. Was looking for a simple way to add a HDTV tuner over USB, and here it is. The catch, the software is clunky, the tuner may need an extension cable, and it over heats super easy. If the usb connection shifts at all while in use you will loose signal and it requires physical disconnect. There is no driver so the phone sees this OTG as a a battery that needs to be charged and I cannot change that. To resolve the issue of the plug not fitting my USB-C jack, I purchased an extension. I recommend something 1 no more than 2 inches, but most flexible C to C extensions start at 6 inches and cost the same as 3ft. Next there is the issue of the heat, I took off the plastic snap fit housing, then applied a layer of Phase Change Material to both sides, Over that I pined a few bits of smoothed metal for making video card heat sync shims. Metal office clips hold it all together, and now the device runs for hours as long as the battery in the phone holds out. My phone has a 8000mAh battery, but the Tuner will still run it down in about 2 hours. With the mods it is stable. 1st run: You have to click on the flag in the Channel Search window to find USA. That was confusing. If the channels cant be found, try the bigger antenna. But chances are, it's already over heated and it wont find anything. You will need to let it cool and try again, be quick about it. Don't touch it while it is searching or the software will lockup. If you got lucky and the channels were found, and you started using it but now it says no signal or no channels found, its over heated. The no channels error is almost always its over heated and shut down. If you can self resolve the heat issue, the device will work just fine. Although I did not reach out to the Vendor, I did try to contact the Manufacturer, and of course there was no reply. My suggestion to the Manufacturer is to get more feed back on the Software interface and make it better. Also fix the heat issue on the tuner. I am assuming this an onboard amplifier that is over heating.

The packaging is very nice, like an Apple product. The frame looks nice also, high quality. I like the way the charger is integrated into the little stand, it really looks good and decreases clutter. The interface of the app is nice, but leaves a lot to be desired. My little nephew could have written a better program. I am using it on a newer iPhone. When loading photos, it randomly shows the photos on my phone over more than 10 years. I have no idea how it chooses to show the photo order. Just any photo or video I have on my phone over more than a decade just randomly shows up as I scroll. Even the most recent photos I have taken are somewhere randomly in the middle of 30,000+ photos. I could not figure out if there is a sort function somewhere. Also, loading photos is very very slow. Maybe if I leave it on for an hour, it will go through all of my photos and then decide to sort them by date? No idea!! Seems like this should be figured out in a Beta version 0.001. Next thing I noticed is there is no option in the app or on the frame to rotate a photo, at all!!! So, after picking a few photos from 2010, 2015, 2016, 2020, I had to go out into my iPhone photos app, find the photos, rotate them, come back to the Nixplay app, wait for several minutes as it loaded all of my photos, scroll down to find my photos somewhere, because as I stated, they are just in some sort of random order, select it to upload the new rotated version to the frame. Why in the world is there no option to rotate the photo on the frame?? Especially if this is designed for multiple people to upload to it. If I give access to my siblings for uploading to my parents frame and I cannot even teach my parents to at least rotate the photo when it shows up...what??! The moment I decided to box it up and return it. I have a total of 10 photos uploaded from my iPhone. The app shows that 38% of the frame storage is full!!! What in the world?? Is there a hard drive in this thing from 1982? How in the heck is 38% of the storage full with 10 photos? By my calculations, this thing fits 26 photos total? Something is wrong here. I did not try to upload any more than the 10 photos to actually see how much it can hold because I was already done with it. You really want me to pay $5 a month for a subscription for this thing? In conclusion: I am quite disappointed. I bought this for my 70+ father's birthday, came to town to set it up in their house so they could see family photos the kids upload. My father now has no birthday present because I bought a product which should not yet be released. If the manufacturer wishes to reach out to me, I'd gladly give them some UX/UI advice.

review_text: Firstly, this is a small compact drive that sticks out about as far as a wireless mouse USB adapter (see pics). Format NFTS for program installs. My primary use for this drive is for steam / programs. Pros: Fast read speeds around 135-140/MBs Small and compact Cons: Inconsistinent write speeds, fluctuates from 10/MBs to 60-70/MBs (observed through Task manager), a benchmark tool seems to average this number out to around 30-35/MBs. For me, thats not really an issue, but for some that may be. Space, this one should garner some critical criticism and should be asked why these companies are straight up lying to consumers about it. Formatted this to NFTS at 4096 byte allocation, that being said the system reports it at 494,206,431,232 bytes = 460.265605926514 GB. 512,000,000,000 bytes is 476.837158203125 GB, where are the the other 17,793,568,768 bytes = 16.5715522766113 GB? This means that Sandisk is selling 96.46324% of 512GB claimed capacity. What if you bought a car and got that much of it? It'd be right back on the lot and complaints to the dealer and the manufacturer would flood in. Its not ok and if this wasn't one of the few small profile drives on the market I'd be sending it back, but need necessitates compromise. Overselling and under providing seems to be the new go-to for companies. This is entirely why this drive is getting 3 stars. UPDATE FEBRUARY 26TH 2023 This drive was intended for use as a steam drive for games. It really sucks for that. The random IO is atrocious. A game that was around 50gb took literally days to install. The write speed took a dive and was in the kbs range the entire time. I'm not using it for a steam drive anymore. It's now just storage. Sequential write and read are about the same, but don't expect random IO to be anything but complete garbage.

I recently purchased a MacBook Pro M-1 chip, not that I need but to see how the much extolled computers and software worked. Over many years, I have accumulated computers that run Windows XP, 7, 10, Linux Mint (two releases), Linux MP on lap top or desk top form. I also use many peripherals: three external hard drives, three printers: an old HP Laserjet, a Brother color laser, mouse, keyboard, slots for thumb drives, etc, etc. All the computers have Intel or AMD chips. I can manually connect any of the computers, only one at a time, to all of the peripheirals with a single USB-3 cable to change operating systems through an unpowered USB-3 hub installed backward so that the output slots are used as import slots from the various computers and the single input cord to the hub is actually used as an output to a powered USB-3 hub to which other hubs or perifiasls are connected. I have found the MacBok Pro, powerful as it is, to be severely anemic in respect to the number of USB peripherals I can connect when using a single USB-3 cable before getting the message to disconnet USB peripherals. Added an externally powered USB-C/USB-3 hub does not resolve the problem. This limitation has not be noted in all the praise the MacBook Pro has been received, else I would not have purchased it, and makes it unsuitable for use in a desktop environment because expansion is so limited. I suspect limiting the number of peripherals was intended to extend battery life, but when the MacBook Pro is on external power as it would be when used as a desktop, the limitation should be bypassed. This current limitation should be prominently noted in product literature and advertising so it not discovered by a disappointed buyer after a MacBook Pro is bought.

I like this trackball a lot! After years of dealing with elbow and wrist issues caused by mousing (even with ergonomic mice), I switched to a mouse-style thumb-operated trackball device. Predictably, that change resulted in issues with my thumb from overuse. This device has neither of those issues, as the trackball and all buttons are operated with your fingers. Since I made the switch, my ergonomics issues are gradually resolving on their own. The top surface of the device normally slopes down toward you, but a pair of fold-out legs on the bottom lets you level out the top of the device if that suits you better (as it does me). The supporting software must be downloaded from Kodak, and on my system both Windows 10 and Norton complained about it, so I had to provide Administrator override in order to proceed with installation. The vendor really needs to address this issue. Fortunately the app works just fine and has not caused any problems over a couple of months' use. The ability to program every button on the device, and to save multiple configurations, allows you to rapidly switch between right-handed and left-handed use, as well as to create & save special configurations to speed up working with specific applications if you need to. UPDATE 2021/02/28: the Control Panel app no longer "works just fine". I'm not sure what happened, but now when I run the app it crashes out and leaves the trackball configuration in a default state. To restore your custom configuration you need to have it saved to your Desktop, then uninstall and reinstall the Control Panel, load & apply the configuration, then never touch the app again. So switching configurations on a per-app is not practical. The Control Panel will not start with Windows but the trackball seems to read the last loaded configuration. Seriously, this really needs to get fixed! But I still love the hardware. The little DPI (dots per inch) switch controls the sensitivity of the cursor to trackball movement, and the app supports it strongly by letting you program 5 DPI settings in each stored configuration. A cute feature is that the scroll wheel briefly lights up in different colors when you switch the DPI setting; and in the way-over-the-top category, the app lets you customize these colors with a Windows-style color palette. All in all, a great product. My only gripe is that the trackball does not seem to be removeable, to let you clean accumulated crud off of the rollers or whatever it rests on inside. The ball needs to be thoroughly buffed with a dry soft cloth a couple of times a day, or whenever the trackball movement starts to feel "sticky". I guess also it would be nice if the device were Bluetooth compatible instead of requiring its own USB dongle, but that was not a major issue for me. Update 2022/06/08: Downrating to 4 stars for premature death. I really love this trackball, but unfortunately it died today. Button clicking still works, but pointing with the trackball seems to have permanently died. Still, going to return it and get a replacement. Update 2022/06/15: Downrating to 3 stars. I found out today that the return window for my original order expired 5 weeks after the order date. That doesn't seem reasonable. Again I still love the way the capabilities and feel of the trackball, but now I understand that the cost of ownership is going to be high.

+If you are an individual who is very concerned about your privacy, these trackers are for you. Every Apple iphone will find the location of the tracker, but only you will see it's location on your iphone, and the chances of losing it is very small. By contrast, Tiles are only detected by people who have the Tile app running on their cellphone. In a city at least, this is usually enough to see a lost Tile a few times a day. +There are a lot of third party sellers of things like attachable clip holders and collar cases. i bought the Spring Blossoms Silicone Case for Airtag Sticker. They work fine for cat and dog collars. The same is true of Tiles. -But if you have a family and you want the option of sharing the trackers location with others, buy a Tile. This is handy for pets because our cats lose their collars at least once a week. It's nice for anyone in the family to be able to help find a collar. -And you can't just slap it on and forget it. You have to watch the battery level. if the tracker is lost when the battery is low, you better find it ASAP. And if it's lost after the battery is dead, kiss $35 goodbye. So my daughter owns the tracker information on our shared cat, and i have to constantly remind her to check the battery level. In comparison, Tiles send the user alerts warning them when one of their batteries is running low. - You can trigger a sound on the tag but it's very, very high pitched and low volume, so it's hard to hear. The worst thing about it is that you cannot lock the sound on when you are searching for it. It plays for 10 seconds or so, then shuts off. All Tiles are louder, have more midrange tone, and the sound can be locked on while you search. Tile Pro's are really loud. - When i am trying to find an Apple Airtag, i cannot see any way to see any ranging. The map on Find My only shows the location of my cellphone, or the cellphone that has detected it. But with Tile, the app gives me rough estimate on signal strength, which generally shows me when i am getting closer or farther away when searching for it. i cannot imagine why Apple doesn't do this. Perhaps it's patented. - You cannot see a location history with Apple Airtag. So if it's on a cat or dog, you cannot see where your pet frequents. Conversely Tiles give a complete location history that goes months back. - i get that a lot of people want privacy on a tracker, but i don't get that the user doesn't have a choice. If i want to share a tracker location with someone, i should be able to allow that.

Here is my 2 cents about these headphones. I was excited to receive these headphones and give them a try. I have a Marantz A/V, 7.1 Surround Receiver connected to my Smart TV so the only way I could hook this head set up was to get a 6.35 mm 1/4 inch Male TRS to 2 RCA female splitter stereo audio adapter cable so I can plug it right into the front of my AVR headphone jack. I had to purchase this adapter through Amazon for about 10 dollars. I bought the J & D adapter it works great to connect the RCA cables. The design of these headphones are not typical to other headphones. They are a new design as of this year. The part the covers your ears is smooth all the way across like a pair of ear muffs I wore on those cold winter days growing up in Maine. What I didn't think about when purchasing these headphones was how warm they are going to be when your wearing them. I am of senior age with hyper tension so it doesn't take me much to get all heated up. These headphone were cooking on me, not a good feeling. I could only wear them for a short time and had to take them off to cool my ears down. One other thing, they didn't seem to want to stay on my head very well, I was constantly trying to adjust them for a good fit and it wasn't happening. When I had them on and look down at my feet or just looking down they would fall off my head. It was a constant balancing act trying to keep them on my head, don't look down, keep your head up, look straight ahead and you'll be fine. Some of the good things about these head phones they sound nice at low to medium volume. I was not able to turn my AVR up beyond 60% because all I heard was distortion so these headphone will not take a lot of wattage. My AVR puts out 100 watts per channel so if you like loud music these are not for you. Sennheiser is known for good quality stuff but maybe you need to spend a few hundred dollars more for the higher end ones, I don't know, they don't talk much about connecting these to a Surround Sound System, nobody does. So it's a guessing game for me to figure out what will work best for me and I'm not having much fun doing so. It's easy to return stuff to Amazon but I don't like having to do so. I returned these headphones because it was difficult for me to wear these headphones longer than 30 minutes. It was heating my ears up to much and giving me headaches. Maybe if I was younger leaving back in Maine watching tv on a cold winter night outdoors they would be fine but not for this old Fellah and now I live in Sunny San Diego. I gave these headphones a 3 star rating they are well made but just not for me.

The Firestick Fire TV device is in my opinion the best streaming device money can buy. The wifi is solid, the user interface is extremely fluid, providing lots of information about titles and integrating available selections from Prime Video and other services apps into recommendations and search results. I really enjoy the bluetooth capability which very conveniently allows me to take my Airpods out of their case and most often automatically connect to the FIrestick. The remote is fantastic, with just as many buttons as necessary without leaving out any important functions (like Chromecast does by omitting the fast-forward and rewind controls from the remote.) It is very ergonomic, and I find myself just tucking it into my palm for long periods as it is very comfortable and a fantastic navigation tool. I like how the UI has a "physics" kind of quality where while holding down the left or right buttons and scrolling through titles the selection with move quickly and then when the button is released the cursor will gradually slow down and pass over two or three titles before settling on the last. I have had this device for about a year and half, and it continues to be plagued by an excessive number of bugs: - When you try to pull up the DVR recordings on the Fire TV Stick, it often displays none. (This is a recent defect. Not a good sign.) - When you pull up the DVR recordings in the Fire TV app, it displays all the current recordings, plus additional ones that have been deleted many, many months ago. - Playback is frequently very skippy. This isn't a problem with recording itself, because you can rewind and play the skipped part on the second try. - Channel guide will randomly show "No program information available". - Scheduled recording feature will skip an instance of the program perhaps because it thinks it has already been recorded, when it hasn't. - After watching a program, you cannot delete it immediately, else you will get "Deletion failed". You have to wait several seconds before the deletion will go through. I was expecting Amazon to push firmware updates over time that would address these issues. Instead, the list of bugs persists and continues to grow. EDIT 8/1/2020: Just keeps getting worse. Downgraded to one star. It has spontaneously developed an issue where it won't maintain a Wifi connection, and it won't let me delete a saved recording. EDIT 12/10/2021: Is it possible to give negative stars? I used this device everyday. I work from home and using a device to switch my peripherals between computers is a must. This device worked great for a while, then it started having little issues. If the housing was bumped or moved all devices would disconnect and then reconnect. Sometimes an audio device would randomly start disconnecting then reconnecting rapidly. Then if you so much as touched one of the peripheral cables all peripherals would lose connection and then come back. I don't know what happened as it sits on my desk and doesn't move. It's not covered by anything, never overheated. I took it apart and inspected the PCB. It seems the solder links on the USB ports aren't done very well. When using a magnifying glass and applying slight pressure to the lip of the USB receptacle (with my finger nail) you can observe the solder links are not making a connection when slight pressure is applied. This means an oversized USB cable with a little bit of weight could cause this to occur. This should not be the case and points to poor manufacturing processes. Unfortunately, I can no longer recommend this device. Your friendly neighborhood electrical engineer!

I did not expect the clarity or quality of five hundred dollar headphones with this purchase. I did expect better clarity than a twenty-five dollar pair of earbuds. This is where these headphones performed poorly. First, the build quality. They are all light-weight plastic and pleather (plastic leather). This makes them comfortable out of the box and very lightweight. I appreciated that the ear cups were not huge on my head and fit nicely over my ears with a bit of room to spare. The problem with them fitting loose out of the box is that when I turned to look at a family member, after wearing them for all of two minutes, they slid off my head easily. I had not adjusted them out in any way, so this is the most snug they will get. I don't have a particularly small head. Perhaps these are geared towards someone with a larger head than average. When I purchase hats, I'm a medium to large, if that helps. I purchased both these and the Beyerdynamic DT 770 pro 80 ohm headphones as I couldn't make a decision based solely on reviews and specs. I believe I'm a bit of a novice audiophile and I was looking for headphones which would help muffle the noise of my other half's booming voice while I work on my trilogy. We have a small house, so while I understand switching to working from home during this pandemic, it means we are both in the main living space, which doubles as an office for us. I had determined to try both headphone sets, after much online research and pick my favorite, fully expecting this headphone to be the winner. I was very surprised that for an extra hundred dollars over the DT 700's, the cords with this set were much cheaper quality and I question their long term durability. The box they come in is nice, but I saw no carrying case. There was a flat pouch for the cords but if that is meant for the headphones as well, I wouldn't trust them not to fall out, as it doesn't zip or seal in any way. Now, as for sound quality; I listen to mostly blues, blues inspired rock and symphonic orchestral music. These all have a variety of instruments and pitches, which the headphones were expected to reproduce clearly. These headphones were OK with the low end (bass), but I definitely picked up on some unnatural amplification at that end...making the bass sound digitized, not soundstage or natural. The mids were where this headphone fails for me. All the mid-range sounds were muffled and synthesized sounding, more so than the bass. There was quite a bit of sibilance (hissing and smeared) in the mid-range as well. The highs were muted and unnatural. Basically, as much as I liked the light-weight and low pressure feel of these headphones on, I just couldn't get past the poor quality sound reproduction. If I hadn't ordered the Beyerdynamics at the same time, I might expect this is just what I get for spending less than five hundred. However, the BD's were one hundred dollars less, have more metal and thicker plastic cups and sound a world apart in quality of reproduction. I listened to Larkin and Poe's new album, Buddy Guy, BB King, Lord Huron, Walter Trout, Gary Hoey, Black Eyed Peas, 2 cellos, The Beatles, Beethoven, and Gov Mule as well as a few others on both headphones. In every case, the 700's were crystal clear in the mids, mostly clear in the highs (you have to be an audiophile or looking for the very slight drop) and clear in the lows, with no emphasis. With the classical symphonic, I could hear rustling and throat clearing, as well as breathing they were so clear. This may detract for some, but I appreciate feeling as if I'm in the room with the orchestra. This clarity made my blues shine anew. The AT's on the other hand, muddled every note and made the mids (a large part of blues) sibilant and hazy. I am not impressed. Perhaps these headphones are for those who listen to folk and modern rock more or perhaps those who just want artificially emphasized base notes and don't worry about clarity of the music they listen to. I can only guess. For me, these are going back and the 700's are staying. One last note, I intentionally did not purchase ANC headphones after listening to and reading dozens of reviews stating that white noise negatively impacts the sound reproduction for those who pick up on nuances. Neither of these state they are noise isolating. I expected only some ability to block out voices and was surprised when, once again, the 700's did a noticeably better job of muffling outside voices. I can't imagine true "noise isolating" headphones do any better. The pads are larger around, as the ear cups are larger. They also have slightly thicker pads. These two factors are what lead to them doing a better job of isolating my ears when in use.

I set up my roll desk next to my battle station to play very casual games on the side like The Sims 4, Cookie Clicker, colony simulators, and Disney Dreamlight Valley. This could have been a great headset for sleeping. While it has no noise cancelation, the earbuds isolates fairly well and has a large battery. However, the firmware nearly ruins it. The first problem I noticed with the firmware pertains to incoming calls. When someone calls, instead of the custom ring tone or the registered name being spoken by the phone assistant, the headset cuts all audio and the voice notification reads out the phone number. That is incredibly useless as I have custom ring tones set that can wake me up for emergencies. Next, Ill cover the volume and control issues. This headset does not report as a Bluetooth headset to my phone, but instead is listed as a media device. This probably wouldn't be an issue if it didn't also set the volume to 80%. I typically listen to the earbuds at 35% volume, and my phone doesn't allow other wireless or wired headphones or headsets to go past 60% volume without confirming that I understand the risks to my hearing. This product bypasses that by not reporting properly to the source. If you connect the headset while you have media playing you'll get blasted until you lower the volume which requires repeatedly pressing the volume down button since holding the volume buttons changes tracks! The worst aspect of the headsets firmware involves the battery. This headset is supposed to have 25 hours of battery capacity during active use. Imagine my surprise when I was listening to a podcast while getting my morning coffee and heard all audio cut out and then heard the notification voice say "Battery Low" while the battery was reporting 20% charge. 20% of 25 hours is 5 hours. Yeah, that was really annoying to hear the low battery warning cut through every 5 minutes until I got so frustrated that I turned the headset off an hour later. This meabs that you can only get 2 nights of uninterrupted sleep before having to charge the headset sin you'll be awoken after 4 hours of the third night by the obnoxious warning.

DO THIS IF YOU WANT A GOOD SOUNDING RECORDING!! This 2 minute read will save you HOURS OF TIME....I wish some one wrote this before I started on this project. I bought this due to the positive reviews and that it is made by Jensen and they are supposed to be an audio company right...car stereos anyone. Anyway, I have about 30 cassette tapes from the 1990s that have interviews, my kids talking and playing guitar with friends. I used a $50 boom box with the worlds worst mic(built in to the boombox) for some of the recordings so I did not have the best equipment at the time and did not realize that I would be messing with these 30 years later. I am a computer graphics person, musician and a semipro photographer...so I use computers and software a lot. I baught this recoder and was not happy with it for what I wanted to do with my cassettes. It was hard to use and would not record to the usb after 2 tapes... so sent it back. Do not waste your time with it if you value your cassettes. The Jensen is about $8 more, solidly built and will last. SO buy it as it is easy to operate and you can see the tape moving...big buttons...and it just works like it is supposed to. Even your grandmother can use it. It is the best alternative for doing this project...I spent HOURS trying to find the best option and even considered buying a $200 cassette deck of ebay, but I did not want the cost and the hassle of setting up a big unit that I would not use again once the tapes were recorded. I used the Jensen with a VTOP USB2.0 Analog Audio Capture Card Device Compatible for Windows (price $19). Works much better than the headphone jack. This plugs in to my windows laptop and makes it easy. You can use the headphone jack but this picks up a lot of random noise. The recorder takes 4 C batteries and also comes with a AC power plug. So here is the IMPORTANT part...If you use the power plug(wall outlet) you will get very loud humming/buzzing or electrical interference when you try to listen/record through the computer. So loud it will ruin your recordings. I tried multiple plugs and computers in my house and all had the hum(it is a grounding issue with the recorder itself and it picks up electrical interference which will end up in your recording) It will not do this if you use the batteries and the recording sounds fine. I have a lot of tapes and did not want to mess with buying C batteries or getting a rechargeable kit of batteries($25more). The solution and the answer is this problem is a noise isolator... "Smof Ground Loop Noise Isolator for Car Audio/Home Stereo System (Eliminate The Buzzing Noise Completely) with 3.5mm Audio Cable, Black Ground Loop Noise Isolator for Car Audio/Home Stereo System" The cost is $10 and it removed ALL of the electrical noise and the recording is as good as the tape! If you do not use one of these you will be frustrated and sorry that you are trying to record all those tapes with poor sound quality...the buzzing is so loud that you can not listen to the recording. Any noise isolator will work and a $30 one is not any better than a $10 one as they all do the same thing. So for about $50 I have a good system to digitize my tapes. NO it is twice as much as the cheap China usb recorder, but I know that the time spent recording will not be wasted and the recordings will be as good as the tape....and you will SAVE TIME in the end. I use adobe audacity to capture the recordings as I have a subscription for my work, but most any program will work. A good FREE software is audacity sound software.(audacityteam.org). It is pretty basic and easy to use. When I put a tape in the Jensen to record, I set a timer on the software for the length of the tape, usually 46 minutes for my 90 min tapes, so the recording will auto stop when the tape is over. That way I just load a tape and hit record and it stops recording when the timer is up(I put one in and go to bed). It keeps you from making hours long recordings that you have to edit later....no timer and you have to turn off the record button or sit by the Jensen to stop it(again a time issue if you have lots of tapes). Audicity also has a timer mode and a quick google search will tell you how to set it. ** Also save your recordings as wav files for the original and make a mp3 copy of the file to share. **Also, do a 1minute test recording before you start to record the entire tape so you can set the volume on the Jensen correctly as it acts as the gain for the recording. Failure to do this can result in a recording to low or too high and both will sound bad ***So if your cassette tapes are important to you, do it right the first time and spend a few $$.

I imagine that most mount a TV this size on the wall, however I used the stand instead. The stand had several problems. 1. The stand does not come pre-installed on the TV, but is instead delivered in 2 separate pieces that require 7 screws to attach. This results in an awkward situation on where you are leaving the TV on the outer rim of the screen while you attach the stand. Compounding this, unless you have an 83 inch table conveniently located to have the TV hang off, the only way to install the stand is to rotate the screen 90 degrees so that it is on its short end (putting even more weight on the outer rim), and installing the base on the side. 2. There are no instructions on how to assemble and attach the stand. The delivery person and I took a guess, and the end result was a TV that wasn't stable and would pitch forward. Googling, I found a video that showed that there is a second piece that combines with the other piece to create a stable stand. But one should not need to Google. The instructions for installation should be delivered in the product. And to be honest, I don't know if having the screen on the side is the correct way to install the stand. Other items. When you provide it a 4k source, the picture is beautiful. When you provide SD and HD, not so much. For the near future, most of my sources are probably going to be sub-4k. I also noticed a flickering of the image when I use my PS4. I tried downgrading the image to just 1080 (no HDR), and that didn't help. Speaking in general, for non-4k sources, image distortions most likely due to upscaling are much more visible than anything on saw on my previous HD 60 inch. I assume that is due to a larger screen and potentially weaker upscaling. It should also be noted that watching a movie at 24 FPS isn't ideal when your streaming devices are at 60 FPS. The screen is 120, so once devices catch up, that issue should go away. One final note is that I found the screen to be too bright, so I brought it down a notch by putting it on Energy Saver mode. Never had that problem in a TV before, but easily solved by the above solution. Bottom line, moving to 4k on a huge screen has some challenges, and the picture will not always be better than an older HD TV on a smaller screen. As time goes on, I expect those issues to go away as you get more 4k sources and better upscaling. I still recommend the TV, despite the early challenges.

I set up AiMesh as soon as I got this, mostly to boost the signal in the bedrooms, farthest from the router. Coverage was spotty and eventually we noticed that our devices were connecting to the bedroom RT-AC68U. After some testing we determined that the RT-AC5300's WiFi signal was weak and would frequently disconnect. (Just to be clear on this, I can't get a reliable connection sitting 5 feet away in the same room.) I moved the RT-AC68U to a better location and our WiFi has been reliable ever since -- because of the RT-AC68U, which is rock solid, and not the RT-AC5300, which is garbage. Fortunately the house is small enough that we get full coverage, and I'm able to use a wired backhaul. As a router, the AC5300 works well, and I was impressed that I was able to transparently import settings from an older RT-AC3200. But I'm afraid any praise I might have is overshadowed by my bitter disappointment in the complete failure of what is supposed to be top-notch WiFi. Too late for me to return or exchange it. Unintentionally, the devices I had been using with the Zettaguard 4 Port HDMI Switch were my Roku and my Nintendo Wii (neither supported 4K). Since 2020 was spent almost entirely at home, I decided I would upgrade my Roku to a 4K model and also purchased an XBox One S. Both of those items are 4K devices, so that meant one was going to have to use the Zettaguard 4 Port HDMI Switch as it's input. That's when I noticed that the HDMI splitter that I paid a premium price in order to have it 4K compatible, didn't support 4K devices. I tried numerous HDMI 2.0 and 2.1 cables alternating between the two devices and the four HDMI ports but nothing worked. Sometimes I will get a picture for a brief amount of time until it cuts it off the goes to either a completely black screen or a screen indicating that no input is detected. I know I should have tested the HDMI splitter with both 2K and 4K devices when I first got it, but it wasn't necessary at that particular time, so I just assumed since it was working for the devices I had connected, it was good to go. Unfortunately that was not the case and now I am having to purchase another expensive HDMI splitter so I can switch the picture settings on my XBox One from 1080p back to 4K.

I first want to note that I bought these for octoprint, but without Wi Fi onboard, you're pretty much tethered to some ethernet port unless you get it to connect. The Debian build has no configuration tool for them, but the armbian build does, but I never got it working with my router. So the most foolproof course of action would be an ethernet to wi-fi adapter. On top of having no way to configure wi-fi, the Debian build installs a deprecated build of python3, 3.5.3, I think. Armbian installs 3.10, which is perfect for my use case. As the other one didn't work. Even then, I had to use a 3rd party script to install octoprint and get it working. In short, use the armbian build, not the Debian, or maybe even ubuntu, builds. I actually bought two of these, both for octoprint and maybe Klipper, but I might turn the other one into a wireless AP with nextcloud to replace my linksys router.

The problem was that despite attempting various GPUs in both PCIE slots that I knew worked, the motherboard was insisting that there was no GPU with which it could display video output. The representative identified the issue as a defective PCIE slot, and I could RMA it, a process which would take ~3-4 weeks. I opted to instead return it to the Amazon seller. The seller forced me to pay for return shipping (which cost me ~$25), and I'm quite frankly not optimistic about my odds of getting a refund request approved once it does arrive at their end, given the (quite frankly hostile) wording of their stated refund policy. Edit: I have since received a refund for the original purchase price, but did have to eat the return shipping cost. I ended up buying by a different motherboard (the WIFI-II variant of this one) from a different seller on Amazon.

I gave this machine two stars because it is a very nice looking computer and runs very fast. Opens programs and even the largest photo files effortlessly. Nice performance right out of the box. However, in spite of the advertising which says you can add a hard drive or two, that's not really accurate. There is a second SATA socket on the motherboard next to the one which goes to the optical drive. I don't know if it's functional or not, because I never got that far. After installing a 2.5" SATA hard drive (there are mounts available for two of them), I realized that there is no SATA power available. The optical drive is powered via a two wire SATA micro power cable which plugs into a six pin power socket on the motherboard. However, there are no such sockets for another SATA drive. The 250 watt power supply has no SATA power cables coming from it at all. After being on the phone for two hours with Acer technical support, they finally admitted that they have made no provisions for adding another SATA drive of any kind. The first time I called them, they said that had a cable available for such purposes, that it would plug into the socket on the motherboard and then split to power two SATA devices. I received the cable overnight. It was a duplicate of the same power cable going to the optical drive. That's when I called them back and wasted so much time on the phone with them. Their position is that they don't support expansion on this computer, "if you want another drive you should use an external one". All of this would not matter if you could change out the power supply to a better one with SATA power. However, the tiny power supply on this computer is not a standard size. There are no replacements on the market for it. If you'll look on the Amazon webpage for this computer, you'll see where they have an "Expandability" tab which shows a 3 1/2" and a 2 1/2" hard drive. Also, in the "questions and answers" section, someone asks if you could add another hard drive and an Acer Manufacturer rep answers that you can. They just fail to mention that you can't power the drive. The only other complaint I have is that the BIOs has been crippled down to just a very few functions compared to an open market computer. For example, you can't set the memory speed or turn xmp off and on. In fact, there are no memory settings at all in the BIOs. Hope this review helps someone else.

I have not installed and used the product. I will return because I’m looking for a mount that will have the TV roughly centered on a wall with a non-center stud. I want to provide a couple measurements that may help others. The current answers are all over the place, both because they don’t specify which model and because I think the design has changed over the years. I have the 22-55 inch full motion model with ASIN B01KBEOL5E, Jan 2023. When fully collapsed against the wall, the bracket that attaches to the Tv is exactly centered (0 offset) over the stud-mounting bracket. So if your stud is off-center, the TV will also be off-center when collapsed against wall. If you push the TV against the wall when the arm is fully extended, there is an offset of 13.75 inches between stud bracket center and TV center bracket center. The base plate that mounts to wall is roughly 11.5 inches tall by 3.25 inches wide by .25 inches deep. The screw holes are are 9.25 inches apart vertically. The distance between the wall and the plate that mounts to TV is 15.25 inches when fully extended. Amazon is not letting me post pics. I think all mounts should include these measurements as part of specs, so we know where TV will end up on wall (not all are centered over stud plate).

Now, when the hero rides in a helicopter, I can actually feel the bass, the thumping of a door closing, the heavy pulsing of some dramatic music. I like it. The bass adds a new dimension to movies, not just for car crashes and explosions, but even voice and background music...just so much. I can hear why awards are given for sound; I can appreciate that much more now. The sub is worth getting.

The Active 2 is sleek and stylish and comfortable. The LTE version offers ability to use basic smartphone features from the watch directly without having to have it tethered to my smartphone so I can leave the phone at home while going for a walk or jog or in the car or locker while doing other workouts. That is a godsend. It activated just fine through Verizon and it linked up easily with my Samsung S21 plus through the Galaxy Wearables app. I hear these watches work best with a Samsung phone for best functionality. The phone is fast and responsive to inputs and while I haven't owned it long yet, it can easily last well over a day on a single charge. I basically upgraded from a Samsung Gear Fit2 and the interface is familiar to me, so the OS is basically an evolution, which is nice so the learning curve is reduced. It is lightweight and has low profile buttons and no thick surrounding bezel make it unobtrusive for general every day use and especially nice for working out. There is one glaring flaw with this watch, however. That is the paltry 4 GB of "storage", of which with a clean, new OS, only about 1.3GB is usable. That may have been sufficient for a basic smartwatch from four or five years ago, and on my Gear Fit2, with its 4GB of storage, it had over 2.5GB of usable storage for music. But for a top end smartwatch with LTE capability, having only 1.3GB of actual usable storage is laughable. You can free up a little bit of space by deleting watch faces, and maybe a handful of apps, although most are pretty useful and don't use much space to begin with, otherwise there's no way to gain more storage. With the available space you might be able to store 150 songs at best, but that leaves no room for adding apps or other options in the future. You shouldn't have to be storage restricted on a device like this and juggle music constantly on and off the device. Plus, just hope future OS updates don't make the installation size larger reducing usable storage even more. It does support Spotify streaming, and if you're a Spotify user that is a good feature especially if you have a decent data plan. But otherwise you will be quite limited in the number songs you can store locally on the phone. I use a lot of ripped live concert albums which isn't readily available on Spotify, and not about to add $120/year subscription on top of an already $120/year add-on for adding my watch to my data plan. Overall it is a very nice watch. Just for a top end smartwatch in 2021 the 4GB storage almost makes it unusable. I am considering the Galaxy Watch 3 instead because it comes with 8GB RAM and otherwise same specs. I just prefer the sleeker look of the Active 2.

I use this case for a workstation with 9 storage drives, and I encountered many thoughtful features when building in this case: 1) Drive cages - The drive cages in the front of the case are oriented such that drives end up with their connectors accessible from the right side of the case. This leaves an pleasantly short and direct path to route SATA power cables from the PSU and SATA data cables from the motherboard. Furthermore, you don't have to worry about anything in the main compartment of the case (the section that houses the motherboard, which is behind the drive cages) interfering with swapping hard drives in and out). 2) Drive trays - It is very simple to install 3.5in drives into the toolless drive trays. The flexible trays have plastic pins on the inner sides that plug into the screw holes of the drive to secure it in place. 2.5in drives sit flush once they are screwed in from holes in the bottom of the tray. The tray's holes are the perfect distance apart, so it is easy to align the drive's screw holes with the tray's holes. 3) Motherboard tray 2.5in mounts - Two removeable foam-padded 2.5in drive trays slide onto rubber mounts behind the motherboard tray for easy installation. 4) Rear-inserted power supply - Being able to remove and insert the power supply from the rear of the case allowed me to simply slide the power supply out to connect an additional power cable when I added more drives to the case. 5) Power supply shroud cable cutouts - This case has many cutouts for cable management. In particular, it has cutouts near the bottom of the motherboard tray and cutouts on the top of the PSU shroud that make it easy to route cables to the graphics card and lower motherboard connectors. 6) Fans and fan controller - The case conveniently comes with all of its fan slots fully populated, so I do not have to buy and install additional fans. Furthermore, they come connected to a series of molex connectors that lead to a fanspeed controller at the front of the case. All you have to do to power the fans is connect the case's assembly of fan wires to two molex connectors from your PSU. 7) Socketed side panels - The side panels are attached to the case by hooking the front ends into slots near the front of the case and popping the rear ends into ball sockets (I don't know the name for such a fastener) near the back of the case. This makes it easy to properly align the side panels with the case when installing them, and it also leaves the side panels flush with the case even without fastening the thumb screws in the rear of the case. 8) Included port plugs - The case comes with silicone (or rubber?) plugs for the front IO ports located on top of the case. Dust and particles really do accumulate in unprotected upward-facing ports over time, so I find it convenient that I do not have to purchase a separate set of plugs. 9) Reversible front hinge - You can change the direction the front panel swings open for your convenience. 10) Noise dampening - both side panels and the front panel are padded with foam. Furthermore, the top of the case has no fan mounts or other openings and is completely lined with foam. This makes my computer very quiet, even when FFmpeg has each of its 22 hyperthreaded cores are under full load. 11) Manufacturing tolerance - I am convinced that this case is manufactured under very tight manufacturing tolerance. When I slotted my graphics card into my motherboard, the holes in my card's PCIe bracket aligned perfectly with the PCIe mounting holes in the back of the case. Furthermore, the mounting holes in all the drive trays are just the right size for screws to fit snugly, making it easy to align a drive's mounting holes with the tray. My list of appreciations is already long, but there are so many more minor things I like about this case, like the visual aesthetics, bottom clearance, and fine fan filters. I haven't discovered anything I don't like about this case, but I hope my review helps you know what kind of building experience to expect from this case. I look forward to this case becoming popular and influencing the design of quiet home workstation cases in the future.

This is the very first time I've ever used a pen display tablet for which I could draw directly onto the screen, so in my case, I may be a bit biased toward praise. For me, the tablet is awesome. Drawing on the screen feels satisfying, and the parallax is minimal (i.e., the tip of the pen is very close to the mouse cursor when moving the pen along the screen) so the accuracy is excellent. I've enjoyed using this tablet so far and am very pleased with it. The tablet does, however, have a few flaws. I've been able to work around them, but they are worth mentioning. The tablet does have fits where it disconnects and reconnects repeatedly. But I have come to find that it only does this if I've left the tablet sitting for a while without working on the piece I have open on it. While I'm drawing on it, it doesn't slip into a disconnect/reconnect fit. That said, this hasn't really been a huge issue for me. My laptop's screen display settings are set to "expand" so that I can use my laptop for other activities (like watching YouTube videos) while having Photoshop open on my tablet screen. So whenever the tablet disconnects and reconnects, once it's done, I'll just open HuionTablet driver (I have a shortcut to it pinned to my Taskbar), go to the "Workspace" link in the tablet buttons tab, and select the tablet screen side as the workspace again. Then things are fine and I continue working. The factory-set calibration of the tablet screen is pretty off. The screen is very dark and a little bit blurry, but I believe these settings are intentional so that the user doesn't end up straining their eyes too much while using the tablet. It's actually felt a bit easier on my eyes and I've kind of appreciated it, but there are ways in which you can adjust the screen settings on it. You can even sharpen the screen as well in its settings. For those who need the colors and gradations in their art to be super accurate, they may not appreciate the factory-set screen settings. There was an instance when I was perhaps moving too fast and the tablet began to glitch out. During that instance, the shortcuts mapped to the tablet and pen buttons were all shuffled around. It took a few seconds for the tablet to get itself back in order again. Turning it off and back on or closing the program and reopening are simple fixes for this kind of mishap, and so far it's only happened once or twice. Sometimes the tablet does seem to freeze up a little, although this is very rare and only lasts a couple of seconds at most. All in all, I'd consider these to be short footfalls, as, in the grand scheme of things, I've otherwise been able to draw with more accuracy and speed than I was with a regular drawing tablet. So to me, it's worth it. For someone who is used to digital drawing but has never had a pen display tablet before, I'd say this one is a fine pick and works well. But for someone who's looking into more serious firepower for their artwork, this one might not quite be up to par.

Beware. According to Seagate, this is an SMR SSHD. It uses a technology to increase storage by layering its strips in "shingles" that, while great for increasing storage capacity, make it potentially run EXTREMELY slowly if you want to edit or rewrite files. Look up SMR drives to see if this is right for you. On a more positive note, SMR isn't necessarily a dealbreaker. I'm using this for a gaming drive and holding all my large storage games on it. I didn't even know it was SMR until I looked it up. For all I've seen so far, it functions normally without noticing any major slowdowns in read/write speed. It appears to use a relatively sophisticated algorithm in tangent with its SSD storage to minimize writes to deeply nested sectors that would require exponentially longer times to write to. That being said. It's my opinion that SMR drives for gaming are a ticking time bomb. The thought that, at any moment, the drive could suddenly need to write something for a game update that requires a drastic restructuring of the disk, rendering it useless for days until it completes, or even worse, completely corrupting a large swathe of files is not worth the stress for me. At the time of writing this review, I am clearing the drive, and will be converting it into a media storage drive for movies and other static media files.

review_text: The USB receiver for this product has major durability issues. I have already gone through two of these sets, and both of them stopped working because of the USB receiver. Unfortunately, Microsoft doesn't have a unifying USB receiver like Logitech, so when the USB receiver breaks, the set is useless. The USB receiver with my latest keyboard started having issues a week or two ago. It would disconnect periodically, and when it did connect, it was usually slow and laggy. I tried a ton of troubleshooting steps on my own (uninstalling USB drivers, trying different ports, and so on), but it didn't solve this issue. The product was still under the three-year warranty period, so I contacted Microsoft to see if I could get a refund. You would think this would be a fairly straightforward process, but Microsoft seems intent on squeezing every last dime out of their customers, even at the cost of customer satisfaction. When I tried to invoke the warranty, their rep first asked me to try a bunch of annoying troubleshooting steps, including plugging the receiver into a different computer. After around 15-20 minutes, we determined that the USB receiver was the problem (even though I knew this going in). Next, the rep asked me to take a photo of the set, including all accessories. I had lost the separate number pad during a move, and I mentioned that I didn't have it. Of course, this caused a ton of issues. He mentioned that I couldn't get a replacement within their warranty terms and conditions if I lost the number pad. I asked him to speak with his supervisor. While I was waiting, I contacted Amazon (who was amazing). I told the rep I was getting the runaround from Microsoft, and that the USB receiver wasn't working. He didn't ask for a photo, for me to follow troubleshooting steps, or anything else. He simply trusted what I said and gave me a credit, even though the purchase took place over two years ago! The problem was solved in 5 minutes. I then left the chat with the Microsoft rep, which still had no resolution 45 minutes in. Microsoft is the worst. Not only do they have a terrible product design with this keyboard (with the single-use receiver), but they're not willing to treat their customers with basic decency if it means they'll lose money. I won't be buying from them again.

These are a great deal. And if you aren't using the WiFi, then they're ready to use. However, if are NOT going to use the WiFi, then why buy one of these? Exactly! So, when using the Wifi, the power draw is too much for the simple power supply capacity and the voltage sags low enough to cause normal operation to stop. I added a 47uF cap to both sides of the LDO (LM1117) and that solved the issue. Digikey has some tiny 0805 Tantalum caps that fit right across the leads and on top of the existing ceramic cap. The picture and sound (even without a soundbar) are outstanding. A large step up from my old 1080p set. The remote with its cursor when you wave it around takes a few minutes to figure out, but it actually works pretty good. Overall, I am very happy with this purchase. I do have a few observations, however: DOCUMENTATION - The documentation is rubbish. You just have to figure out how to put it together, there are only minimal instructions. YouTube videos are your friend. REMOTES - I rather like the remote, but it is rf, NOT ir. My wife just wants basic control; a bunch of buttons on the remote just frustrate her. So, I was happy that her simple old “universal” infrared remote works just fine. ALEXA - The Echo Dot in my living room controls the TV; on-off, mute, volume up or down, and channel change. Again, the worthless documentation slowed setup down, but when I figured out the secret, setup was a breeze. The secret is that there are TWO Alexa paths on this TV. One path is that this TV can BECOME an Alexa - I did NOT need this, since I already have the Echo Dot in the room. The other path is that this TV can be CONTROLLED by Alexa - that is the one I wanted. So, what I figured out was to IGNORE the Alexa choice in the TV setup screen. You need the LG ThinQ app on your Android or iPhone and a login and password on LG’s servers. It helped to enable the LG ThinQ skill in the Alexa app on my phone. After all of that, it guided me through linking Alexa to the app. Once it’s linked, Alexa can control. ADS - To paraphrase the 2001 movie, “My god, it’s full of ads!!!” The TV is connected to the Internet, and it is not shy about plugging products. Also the ThinQ app, although needed for Alexa setup, is mostly junk advertising. LG also tries to collect a bunch of personal information- my recommendation is to give a phony birthday (they won’t proceed without a birthday!!!) and address - zip code, fine, but why do they need my address? From what friends say, the other brands are also pushing ads, so I can’t really grump about LG. That’s my review; I definitely recommend this TV.

I've used these cards in the past, so I'm going to write this review now even though I just received the order today. I have been using Micro Center's store-brand Micro SD cards for years, and have never had one fail. In fact, I was actually planning to make the two-and-a-half-hour drive (each way) to Micro Center to pick up a handful, when lo and behold, there they were on Amazon. Happy day, oh happy day. I use the 256GB Micro Center Micro SD cards in my dual-lens dash cam, recording two simultaneous 1080p streams at 15 Mbps each, and I've never had any problems. That's pretty phenomenal for cards this affordable. The combined write load and temperature extremes make dash cams notoriously tough on memory cards. I bought these 32GB cards for my DEPSTECH DS450 Dual Lens digital borescope, which can only address cards up to 32GB. A quick test showed that these cards formatted and recorded just fine. Your mileage may vary and all that, but long story short, these inexpensive cards have performed just as well as any of the more-expensive ones I've used. I'm happy to be able to buy them on Amazon now rather than making the long drive to Yonkers. Richard

Recently started to using a trackball mouse (about a year plus) and loved it (most of its benefits such less unnecessary hand movement, small foot print, and most of all ambidextrous application. Due to heavy spread sheet works, I still use the good old conventional mouse for quick cell selections, switching tabs, and other boring work related stuffs thanks to strange muscle/brain memories, which I can't easily change. Working from home changed everything - I have a freedom to update my work environment for better productivity as well as ergonomically sound work condition (well, at my own expense). My original "Orbit" is great - no fancy frills, just down to key trackball features plus ambidextrous design (born as righty and trained as lefty). However, I really missed "forward/back buttons" from conventional mouses I have (silly demand). Then I found this "Orbit Fusion". It is literally the device which was developed to satisfy my silly demand (well, not perfectly, I will cover two tiny disappointments later). 1. It has a scroll ring like the original Orbit. If you like your original orbit trackball mouse, you are going to love the same feature in Orbit Fusion. I wish it would have inherited trackball scroll feature from SlimBlade - maybe this is for the next version? Scroll ring is still rough, which might need some break in time (not smooth as scroll ring from the original Orbit). 2. Forward/Back buttons - these were the missing things I have been complaining for the Orbit. With these, I don't need to touch a keyboard or click a back button on the browser/folder. Fair warning: different design means learning curve - all mouses have different button layouts; it will take some time to settle in (no sweat). I need to practice really hard since I am using three different input devices at the same time... All ten fingers will be very busy to catch up these tricks (especially, pinky)... 3. Size - I don't have a gigantic size hand nor a really small hand, but relatively a big hand. This fits under my palm without pushing me too much. I like the low profile design of the Orbit more, but it would be okay with these extra features. Little taller/thicker, but same footprint compared to Logitech MX Master. 4. Wireless Connection - I actually prefer a wired input device (just me with wierd interests thanks to bad experience with wireless connection devices). Sorry this does not support bluetooth connection. However, it is wirelessly connected with a provided dongle, which connection was just a plug-and-play. It even supplies a USB-C adapter for newer devices. 4. Extras: "Battery" is included. I repeat. "Battery" is included. I haven't seen this in years. Not super fancy type, will do the work. Thanks, Kensington!!! There is no port to connect into the computer as a wired input device nor to recharge. Will test its battery longevity (TBD). 5. Trackball - precise, balanced, weighted. I expected a bigger size, but it seems very same compared to its cousin "Orbit". Try to utilize a track ball while working in Excel or any spread sheet application, but very challenging due to pre-existing muscle/brain memories... If anybody has any suggestion to maximize track ball usage in spread sheet works, please share your knowledge, grand trackball master... 6. Wishlist- Fusion is for right hand users only. I tried my left hand, but I can use it same as the original Orbit with one less button. Well, this is my personal wishlist for the perfect input device. It's not a deal breaker at all. Overall, I am very happy to add this to my home office crew. Stay safe and positive. Happy Rolling!!!

It is cute, small light, but I would classify more as a toy projector. Great for kids, or if you just want to travel with it and not worry about damaging it because its less expensive. You do have to mod/add a bunch of stuff to it to get it to do anything, otherwise you kind of just have a weird night light. PICTURE When you attach an external battery via USB mini, it gets very dim for power consumption and the edges of the frame go out of focus very easily. Plug into the wall when possible, or if you take it camping, plug it into a generator for better picture quality. It has "screen door" effect no matter how close or far away the projector is from the wall, so don't expect anything too immersive. SOUND If you use the built in speaker it's all treble and no bass (not to mention fighting the fan sound) so you'll find yourself increasing and lowering the volume constantly. Just plug a decent speaker into it via 3.5 cable. MOUNTING I will say the lightness in weight allows me to mount it anywhere, but again, I had to use camera equipment to mount it, clamp it, or stand it anywhere. Could be used for a lot of creative things if you have a few of them for ambience at a retail space or event. DURABILITY The focus knob is VERY sensitive, it can fall out of focus the moment you take your finger off of it, I imagine after using it a dozen or so times it will only become more loose and harder to stay in focus. MEDIA PLAYER There are no wifi capabilities or apps to play Netflix, Hulu, Crunchyroll, etc built into the actual projector (which is understandable for the price) so BYO Amazon Firestick, or Roku Stick to the party, at least they can power from the USB in the back. VALUE It's pretty good for $60, but considering that you need: - $ external speaker - $ external power - $ Roku/Fire Stick - $ A way to mount it You might want to consider a projector that does at least 2 - 3 of the above for you and simply pay more for it. I also don't understand why Amazon asks about "SHEERNESS" but uh... no, it's not translucent? Does this help anyone???

The pocket is... looser than I expected. You can see in my photos that the top edge of the stretchy fabric is loose enough to gap at the opening. (I removed the SSD and pulled the rubber band away in the second pic so you can see this gap is not a caused by the item or my modification) The fabric gives no tension/resistance and my SSD (Sandisk extreme) slips out easily with even minor movement, like closing, carrying, and taking my computer in/out of my bag. Gravity will keep things in the pocket if dont do any of those things, but in that case I suggest you save yourself a few bucks and just set your drive on your desk. Not sure if I got a dud or if this is how it’s supposed to be, but the pocket edge doesn’t look like this in the product photos so I assumed the fabric would be attached to the back piece with enough tension to lay flat and “hug” whatever is put in there. I was also intending to keep some USB sticks in it, but it’s definitely not secure enough for that! I’m keeping it though, because I found a fix that seems to at least secure my SSD well enough — a strong rubber band around the whole pocket, near the opening. This adds enough tension to keep the SSD from falling out and doesn’t affect adhesion at all. I used alcohol and a microfiber cloth to remove dust and grease from my computer surface and the silicone backing sticks strong even over the rubber band. The rubber band will, however, loosen over time and eventually break, so I’ll have to keep a close eye on that. (A piece of elastic inserted inside that top edge of the fabric would be a better, more durable solution, but I can’t see a way to do this without probably ruining the pocket.) I’m not going to keep USB sticks in there as planned until I thoroughly test (at home) if the rubber band reliably keeps them from falling out. Maybe I’ll add a second rubber band for good measure...
