I'm only giving it three stars because the lubuntu 18.04 software pre-installed in the eEMC is not properly configured. You basically can't configure anything until you create a password for the root account because gksu (or an alternative) is not setup correctly. This is just plain bad practice. You launch config programs from the menu that require root privilege and they fail to work because they require a root password that has not been set. Root passwords are considered bad practice these days, normal distributions properly configure gksu (or whatever) so control-panel code that need root will work properly when launched from the menus. Overall Lubuntu is just plain lame, and despite its alleged "lighweight" design, it is very sluggish with poor UI feedback -- you click something and nothing happens, no acknowledgement of the click, then about the time you think its crashed something pops up. I tried their latest lubuntu-20.04 from the digital-loggers website and it mis-configured the same way. If you don't need the GPIO and other "extra" hardware on the board, its an Atom CPU so you can install any distribution that you like. If you do this and need the extras, be prepared for a long slog as saying the documentation sucks would be complimenting it. Installing a good distribution like Ubuntu-Mate gives you a nice system for the money, I used mine with a Coral TPU to run AI person detection for my security cameras. Supports significantly more cameras than a Pi4 for roughly the same cost. I endorse the hardware, but only if you are skilled in Linux or whatever OS you put on the thing, and aren't afraid of patching to use the "extras" that need non-standard drivers. Edit: I think the GPIO support may be part of the "standard" Atom board support package when you do a "normal" Linux install, but the other extra hardware may need drivers. I haven't looked as I've no use for these, but I have looked for documentation which seems minimal. I know the WiFi works and the Bluetooth seems to (the disable/enable icon appears and toggles when selected) with a standard Ubuntu 20.04 installation. Mine is sitting 10 feet away from my router so in norm weaker signal situations you may need to buy and antenna, I just used it minimally as I was curious if it worked with the standard installation. On my Coral TPY python based AI system I can run the same Python code on both the Pi4B and Atomic Pi, both running Ubuntu-Mate 20.04 distributions. I'm using two fisheye cameras (rtsp streams) with 8 virtual PTZ views processed for detecting "person" using MobilenetSSD-v2_coco. I get 18 fps (a bit over 2 fps per virtual camera) on the Pi4B and 27 fps (a bit over 3 fps per virtual camera) on the AtomicPi. My AtomicPi has been running continuously for over 24 hours without issue, the heat sink is slightly warm to the touch, much cooler than the Coral TPU device, which is still cool enough to hold comfortably. The Pi4B quickly goes into thermal throttling without a fan in this application. I'm upgrading to 4-stars because the hardware performs very well if you install a "normal" Linux distribution on it and the price with the included breakout board is really nice. I'll be ordering another to have as a back up once I fully deploy it to protect my property. The included camera module is just a USB webcam with a non-standard cable connector, and works as /dev/video0 when plugged in and tested with guvcview. If I don't junk it, I'll cut up an old USB2 cable and solder it to the connector and rig up some kind of case so it is generally more useful. The SD slot is very nice, It works like a normal USB external drive and you an insert and eject an SD card same as you would a USB stick. Booting from the SD card works (I used it for the Digital-Loggers 20.04 "distribution") but IMHO you'd be better off booting from the eEMC and using it for extra storage as I'm doing with Ubuntu-Mate. although a USB3 hub and USB stick or external drive would be a better long term option. Edit2: I was wrong about the included camera, its not a normal USB camera, to use it you need some extra drivers to make it look like one. See: digitalloggers/geocam-v4l2 on github. More trouble than its worth to me. YMMV.

I have been comparing different brands and different levels of binoculars. Still am. I'm looking for a set of 8x42's (although I have tried one 7x33). The main criteria I'm using (and I'm discovering their relative importance as I go along) are: 1) Ease of use with eyeglasses 2) Quality of picture (including color, ability to create pop to the image, brightness, and sharpness or crispness). 3) Ergonomics. How easy are they to use in my hands, and how quick is it to lock in the image when putting them up to my eyes? Included in this is the weight of the binoculars. Thus far, I am and have tried the Nikon Prostaff 3S, Prostaff 7S, these Wingspan Skyview, Celestron Granite ED 8x42; and I have also tried the Celestron Granite ED 7x33s. On their way to me are Athlon Midas UHD and Nikon Monarch 5, both 8x42s. While I haven't put this Wingspan model through its entire paces, I saw enough that lowered their value to me almost immediately, largely the sharpness of the image, although the bins have their upsides. And, of course, what works for me may not work for you. It's all very individual. Given the current quarantine recommendations, I don't consider it wise to go to a store and try out different models. Yet this is really important to do for something like binoculars (or a camera). You need to test drive them. So I have ordered a bunch of different ones to see which one I'll end up with. BTW, in the process of researching, my alloted budget has gone up a bit, as I am appreciating the better qualities of better optics. Yet the less expensive Nikons have surprised me. Regarding criterium 1), both the Nikon 3S and 7S are the quickest to lock in an image with my eyeglasses. But they also offer the relative narrowest field of view. Not bad, mind you, but the Wingspan offer among the best in that category by a considerable margin. But that working well with my eyeglasses is one of the reasons why I'm really looking forward to trying the Nikon 5 Monarchs. But this is a review of the Wingspan, so let me speak to their perceived strengths and weaknesses at first glance. They're promoted as using ED (extra low dispersion) glass. This is a reportedly more expensive option to a set of binoculars, as well as multi-coated roof prisms (this has that feature) and dielectric coated glass (these do not have that feature). But in the end, I think the execution is more important than the features. A masterful execution of a set of binocular with fewer cited features is going to be better than one with lots of features but where the execution of those features is not at an equally high level. Nikon, for example, is known for their optics, their glass design. If you see Leica, Nikon, Zeiss, or Swarovski on bins, you're talking the best in terms of the quality of the glass at their price levels. The first thing I did, on a dreary day that today is (overcast and drizzly) was focus on several things around my open backyard and a cemetery I can see from next door. Comparing the Granite 8x42 bins (which have all of the above features including dielectric coating), the Granite made objects really pop. Color, contrast, and light were superior. The Wingspan were okay, but compared to the Granite bins, the Granite rendered objects with more life. It's a feature of better binoculars. It's one of the reasons people spend a lot of money on binoculars. Things you're watching like birds have more light, contrast, richness of color, and detail. But it's sort of unfair to compare the Wingspan Optics Skyview to the Granite, as the Granite retails for double the price of the Wingspan (retailed, that is - still available but no longer being manufactured by Celestron. The Trailseeker model has essentially taken its place). So I tried comparing the Skyview to the Prostaff 7S. One other thing I noticed optically speaking when comparing the Granite to the Skyview, which is important to me, is that the Granite seemed sharper with its detail. The image at the center seemed crisper, and again, with more minute detail rendered. I was sort of surprised that there was such as difference. Not like the Skyview were out of focus, just that the level of detail and crispness to the image was better through the Granite. But this surprised me. Comparing the Skyview to the Prostaff 7S, the 7S were also sharper/crisper. The 7S were also a little bit brighter. Perhaps the Skyview offered a hair more contrast, but the 7S were noticeably brighter. But the sharpness, the detail of the 7S and the relative softness of the Skyview (even with the diopter adjustment) killed the Skyview as an option for me, knowing that I'd easily take the 7S over the Skyview, given my priorities. On its own, I wouldn't complain about the Skyview if I hadn't used the 7S. I expect better performance from a twice-the-cost retail of the Granite. It's just when you put it up against the Prostaff 7S that I think the 7S offer better value. The Wingspan, ergonomically, are on the lighter side. Probably closer to the 7S (the 3S are still lighter). They're compact, too, shorter than the 7s (and about the same length as the 3S). They're easy in the hands. They feel just fine. But for me, even without the ED glass in the 7S, the 7S outperform the Wingspan in normal light. The ED glass might help a bit when you're in darker surroundings, but the 7S without the ED glass is still really good. [Note: I have yet to try ANY of them in extremely dark conditions other than a test I did in a darkened hallway between the 3S and 7S. I put a dollar bill up on a wall. It was much easier to see the bill and the detail through the 7S than the 3S.] Due to the basic sharpness of the glass, the Prostaff 3S are a good budget choice if you just want to be able to see birds in the daytime. The 7S will provide better more exciting color and will be better in lower light (though a couple ounces heavier and with a narrower field of view). With the 7S, color details get exciting. For example, my wife and I were out at the Plum Island (Massachusetts) National Wildlife sanctuary a couple of weekends ago. We spotted a wild turkey nearby (Not the whisky brand, but the real thing.). On a wild turkey, the head is pink, with a robin's egg blue below its eyes. The feathers are black, but with a brilliant pine green/blue almost metallic luminescence. Through the 3S, I could see the bird from about 75 yards away. Switching to the Granite 7x33, the bird's colors became brilliant. The pink and blue on the head just popped. The luminescence of the feathers were vibrant. It was gorgeous to look at. Looking through the almost half the price Prostaff 7S, almost all of that magnificent color was retained for the viewing. It was gorgeous to look through. And then going back to the 3S, I could see the bird, but the bird was sort of just there. The colors lost their boldness and the incredible depth of color. That discovery seeing how birdwatching can go from merely seeing a bird closer up, to being really moved by the magnificence of its coloring interested me in upping my budget. I might end up going for the Prostaff 7S. I'd like to find a pair of bins that have greater field of view, but I'll give that up for the great feel and ergonomics, as long as I'm not giving up exciting optics. I was surprised as to how much better the 7S were visually over the 3S, but both rendered sharp detail. The Skyview were closer to 7S in terms of color, and slightly better with contrast, although not quite as bright as the 7S. But the lack of crispness/sharpness of the Skyview were just unacceptable to me after using the others. You may not notice it yourself using these in isolation. The Skyview are easy to hold and easy to use. I like that their objective lens caps are attached. The ones Nikon uses in their Prostaff models stink. They have a tendency to fall off (and they're not attached, although they are on the Monarch 5). The Skyview is relatively light, and they're compact for an 8x42 model. And maybe absolute sharpness is not THE most important thing to you. I'm guessing that they might possibly be as good or better in low light than the 7S. But I do think that if you can spend not too much more, that you can get a better pair of binoculars than the Skyview. Or at least for my purposes, I have. One last thing, if you look around, you might find a new pair of the Granite 7x33 for close to $200 (and they honestly retailed for $319). The optics are so good that they're about as bright as the lesser cost 8x42 bins in moderate lighting. And the images just pop through them. Ergonomically, they're terrific. They're relatively light, and more compact than any of the others I have tried (as they are 7x33 rather than 8x42).

For people who are experiencing HP reverb G2 disconnect issues, this problem is due to signal corruption because of their lousy cable as well as power loss due to said cable. This USB C board compensates for both. 40-100% higher price than competing boards but after trying out two other devices that simply didn't support my HP Reverb G2, I went to my old standby, Startech. I used to compete with these guys and they make damned great products. What I liked about this product is that like so many of their products, Windows already has the driver because Startech only uses OEM components on their boards. These are the same components used on the motherboards themselves so the OS typically recognizes the board as one of its own. I tested in two different motherboards and in one the drivers had to be downloaded but that was automatic, in the other more modern board, the drivers were already present.

I bought this router in 2014. It is still a great router! If you have an internet package of 300mpbs or less, this will work great for you! No reason to get faster than 300mbps to begin with. 100mbps is way more than most households need! Cable companies love to try to sell you what you don't need! Having more bandwidth does not mean faster speeds! I used 25mbps internet from 2014 to 2017, until my cable company upgraded me for free to 75mbps. No difference. I used to play fast spaced fps games that needed fast speeds (cod, CD, etc.). I was always in the top two players. No lag. Now I have 300mbps, no difference in speed again. Think of the mbps not as speed, but more like a gas tank. If you have a ton of devices being used at the same time, the gas tank gets lower, but, as long as not empty, the speed is the same. Being near empty, or, full, provide the same speed. Anyways, this router suited me well for 5+ years! It was now sent to my daughters college dorm where she uses it. I did upgrade to a new router when I moved to a new and larger home. I have many devices connected (over 30, from Amazon smart plugs and hue smart lights and wireless security cameras and 4 tvs with Amazon Fire devices, and phones, tablets, computers, etc.) and wanted something newer. So, I figured an upgrade was due. Now, if you want a low cost and solid router for 300mbps or less and you have less than say 15 wifi devices. This is the router to get!

review_text: Well, I ordered them since they are advertised to support THX and LDAC. THX is primarily used for movies, so for these to be connected to a home theater you need a bluetooth transmitter that supports LDAC. Of course, you could use aptX (HD), but what‘s the point not to use LDAC which delivers the highest quality audio? After rearranging the RAM sticks the computer would POST but would not accept any input from my keyboard to enter the BIOS. I assumed a setting in the BIOS was causing this so I shorted the reset pins on the board, no change. I removed the CMOS battery, no change. At this point I suspect a bent CPU pin, but after inspection there were no bent pins. I then acquired new RAM sticks with confirmed compatibility with my components with no change. I have attempted to plug my keyboard into each USB port on the device, no change. I have spent 8+ hours troubleshooting the device and now my only culprit is the Motherboard or PSU. review_text: The camera quality was good. The wide angle lens did distort the image (i.e. made straight lines look curved) as you would expect with a wide angle lens. The microphone was very sensitive and worked well. The overall quality was what you expect for the price. I did have problems getting it working at first. When I first plugged it in, Windows would stop working with a BSOD and the computer would need to restarted. I could not get Windows to start (or continue to run) with the webcam plugged in. This issue did not go away until I removed all LOGITECH devices using Device Manager (with the camera unplugged). LOGITECH devices needed to removed in the imaging, sound video and gaming controllers, and the Universal Serial Bus Controllers sections. When removing the devices, also check the box to remove the related drivers if it is present. This installation issue is, of course, a LOGITECH driver problem and is not a fault of this webcam. With this being said, LOGITECH is very common brand so this issue could affect many users. After all LOGITECH devices and drivers were removed, Windows worked fine with the camera plugged in. No drivers needed to be installed. The Windows 10 built-in drivers worked fine.

review_text: I have some pretty good telescopes, and I have a few pairs of the little pocket binoculars that are so common, and quite a few items in between. The problem that I have been tolerating for a long time is that of not having an "optimal" pair of binoculars for routine use. These would have fairly bright optics, fairly good magnification, fairly light weight to carry, a reasonably sleek, non-clunky shape, a moderate size, reasonable sturdiness, and a comfortably sharp focus. I only received these "Byakov" binoculars today, and in addition to all of the above, I find that they also solve the ages-old problem of what to do with the lens covers. It is desirable to protect the lenses well when not looking through the binoculars, but it is always such a pain to pull off the caps, put them safely somewhere, and then be able to take a look. These eyepiece covers attach to the neck strap, so they simply swing out of the way, and the objective lens covers are held by tabs, and they just fold downward, out of the way. Removing the covers is not extremely fast, but it is faster and more care-free. The other items included in the package, the phone camera mount, the tripod binocular mount, and the tiny tripod, are nice to have as well, just in case one wants to use them. No, they are not super sturdy, precision equipment, but they are also not mere junk. For the price, I have no right to say that anything here is less than great. If I were being picky, I would say that, on my instance of this product, the lenses are not absolutely free of distortion, but I can read quite fine print at quite a distance, in a neighboring room lit moderately from a side window. The view is comfortable and clear, and I don't feel that I am being robbed of detail that I want to see. This is in comparison to many cheap binoculars that, when they are in focus, you still can't make out details. Again, for the binoculars that I received, the weight seems good, and the feel of these binoculars is solid, in contrast to what I think I have read from some users. Nothing here is loose or floppy, nothing rattles, and nothing feels fragile, even though the few exposed, hard plastic parts would probably not withstand a high impact, more than one would want to give to a pair of binoculars. The focus dial moves without difficulty, but it also feels smooth and firm, and it brings the view into precise focus. The right eye focus compensator is also firm and smooth, reaching a precise focus and not changing position without effort. A smaller and even more portable size is always preferred, of course, but that would be hard to achieve without losing either magnifying power or brightness. The feel of these binoculars is serious, like a real tool, yet not cumbersome. I don't see a better compromise between carrying convenience and general capabilities than is in this basic design of binoculars, and it is a delight to find this degree of quality at a price that does not make a person reluctant to use them regularly.

This is sold as a display good for gaming but when I hooked this up to my computer it has been nothing but problems. First off, they don't include a HDMI 2.1 Cable. Cables come with every computer monitor standard and if LG wants to compete with that market they need to include a cable. Going to buy one presents you with many cheap cable options, many of which include reviews that say the cables are not what they are supposed to be, so why LG doesn't include a $30 cable with a $1700 TV is beyond me. I can't enable HDR in windows while at 4k so I don't know whether its the TV, Cable, or Computer but LG should have eliminated this variable by including a properly rated 48Gbps cable. Monster cable doesn't sell anything over 27Gbps so I'm very confused as to whether a true HDMI 2.1 cable even exists. Calling LG tech support was very disappointing, after connecting remotely to the TV and being explained the Instant Game Response keeps launching even though it's turned off, they simply passed the buck to Computer Tech Support (Video card manufacturer?) which is not cool. The computer has nothing to do with why the display keeps flashing and whether or not the cable is no good. Include the proper cable with the TV and fix the problem with the Instant Game Response turning on even though it's turned off in the menu. I'm going to give this TV one more try with another cable and than I'm returning it and getting a proper monitor. Lesson learned, if you want something for gaming, get a monitor and avoid the headache. Maybe this is good as a TV but who would want to pay the extra money for game settings that don't even work or might work if you get lucky buying the correct cable online somewhere. (Update: I'm learning that my 5700XT videocard only uses HDMI 2.0. Club3d offers a Displayport to HDMI 2.1 adapter that will fix the 10bit problem but at the lost of VRR. When the BIGNAVI and 3000 Series videocards come out this should address that problem but now I'm learning that the CX model is limited to 40Gbps HDMI 2.1 Input so I'm going to return this for the C9 model unless LG is going to publicly plan on updated the firmware to allow for 48Gbps.)

Write speed: 7.5MB/s Read speed: 118MB/s Read is good. Write at this capacity is ridiculous (bad) (250,000 MB) @ (7.5MB/s) I tested moving a 4k video from SSD on my computer. 4790k 4.4ghz usb 3.0 (3GB) file size. 3,000/7.5s = 400s/60 = 6.6m. it took 6.6 minutes to write a 3gig file. If you move a more complex cluster of files with folders. It will be less than half that speed. The larger the file the slower the drive gets. In layman's terms this would take an eternity to fill the drive to 75% capacity. Approx 7 hours of data transfer. All drives now days should do a minimum of 25Mb/s write. But we are in a revolution of flash memory chips that are in such demand, that USB drivess get the worst of the (binning process) SSD, M.2's and NVME are cherry picked for everything now days. You have to actually spend about $40+ to get a drive that can write at acceptable speeds. (25MB/s+) Examples: Sandisk extreme PNY pro elite Patriot supersonic rage Also for all the computer illiterate's out there.. (Drive size) and (useable size) are not the same. Because a kilo-byte (1,000 bytes) of data is actually measured in (1,024 bytes) so as drives scale up in size. The capacity is exponentially decreased. There is also a buffer in every drive for the operation of the storage controller. So when you get a drive. Its allways less than whats measured. Blame the guys who decided to measure kilobytes in units of 1024 instead of 1000. In layman's terms your drive will have less capacity than what is advertised always. Bottom line this drive is not adequate for its capacity. However if you write small files at a time. And use this as a back-up. This moght work. As long as you need the storage and write to it incrementally. Or just pictures/ music, this should be fine. Just dont expect it to fill up very fast.

We are good with with Amazon Music HD. It shows a Device Capabiity of 24 bit /192 Khz and even most UHD music is at a max of 24 bit /96 khz. review_text: I’ve been using the Antop Outdoor TV Antenna for about three months. I live in Denver, ~30 miles from Lookout Mountain where all the broadcast antennas are located and aimed at the city and front range. We can easily receive 50+ channels out of the air. I have a clear line of sight of the mountain. The Antop Outdoor TV Antenna was very easy to install on the Direct-TV mounting stand that held a satellite dish until November when we cut the cord. The antenna sits on the roof of our house 15’ above the ground aimed directly at Lookout Mtn. Some days the signal using the Antop antenna is great on channels 2 thru 20.. Many more days the signal is lackluster, especially on channels above 20. I have to scan for digital out-of-the-air channels frequently. I can’t use the Smartpass Amplifier that came with the antenna because, with the amp turned on, the signal is so pixelated as to be not viewable. I paid around $50 for the antenna and was hoping for better results than Im getting. I am disappointed and I wouldn’t recommend.

To the company’s credit, they simply replaced the unit immediately at no cost and no questions. I gather that I was not the first person with this problem. Now, about 1yr 9months on the second unit, the automatic sound monitoring function that handles auto-off has failed. The unit now turns off automatically regardless of the fact that sound continues to it while we are watching something or listening to music. Nothing has changed mind you - not the tv, the cabling or connection (which is optical), the TV or player setting for audio. The Zvox 155 just failed. This is very frustrating since this device performs perfectly otherwise.

Let's get it out of the way - this is a cheap radio. Cheap looking, cheap materials, cheap on/off/volume switch, cheap band and tuning knobs, It's priced $10-15 more than it should be. The product photos are altered to make it seem larger than it actually is (but the dimensions listed seem accurate) But it works. There are two main "pros" - the first is that it works. It's not great but it works. Sound quality is average. Reception is average. Everything about it screams poor quality but it works. The second "pro" is that it has a built in rechargeable battery. When you plug in the included power cord (no wall wart so there is that, too) it charges this battery. You can run it off this internal battery for some time. I listened to a baseball game so it will work for at least a few hours. There is no charge indicator. It will also run on 2 D batteries. My experience is that if you put batteries in a radio, they will be dead when you really need it. My assumption is that if you leave it plugged in at least the internal battery will be charged in a power outage. Time will tell. In any case it actually does what I need it to do - let me listen to baseball games while sitting on my deck. I wouldn't use it to seriously listen to music but you could use it for background music. The am fm and shortwave bands all seem to work. Local am/fm broadcasts all seem fine. Shortwave reception is uninspiring and there is no provision for an external antenna. You get what you get. I gave it 3 stars and maybe it only really deserves 2; t it's a cheap radio doing cheap radio things. But it works and I like the internal battery.

This review is for the Wake Up Light Sunrise Alarm Clock for Kids, Heavy Sleepers, Bedroom, with Sunrise Simulation, Sleep Aid, Dual Alarms, FM Radio, Snooze, Nightlight, Daylight, 7 Colors, 7 Natural Sounds, Ideal for Gift sold by Jall Store I needed a reliable clock not tied to my smart phone and it's flaky battery and really wanted to try a sunrise clock but didn't want to spend over $100 to discover I didn't like them. So here I am... Overall, I'm enjoying the concept. The light output is more than enough and the light color range is also nice (soft warm glow to bright white which you can limit when you set the alarm). I initially chose use a 20 minute wake up cycle (light only, full spectrum, no sound), and I've woken a few times just 5-10 min into the cycle (no alarm sound). Absolutely love those days. I've also slept through it because my pillow was over my head... Since, I really can't afford to not wake up on time, I decided to utilize the build in alarm sounds. Glancing through the list, Ocean caught my eye. I though Ocean would be nice, and at first, it sounded fantastic. Crashing waves, rhythmic - not too fast, and not too slow, not high pitched - just a good ocean wave crashing on beach sound. I though I'd found the perfect match to my sunrise - yes, Zen was in my grasp. Then a few seconds into the track the @#$@ seagulls start squawking. Seriously, why? Have you ever spent time around Seagulls, they're loud, obnoxious and they'll steal anything they can carry. That's not what I want to wake up to in the morning. What's next, soundtracks for a crowded beach, or maybe a sinking supertanker blasting it's horn or a lighthouse fog horn at point blank range so my ears can bleed? You had one job... Unfortunately, the other offerings followed the same pattern - all seemed just as harsh (too high pitched, disruptive and not in tune with a soft sunrise IMO). - birds chirping in the morning - yes, I know birds chirp in the morning. At my house, they're in a tree, over 20 yards away and not trying to be reproduced out of an alarm clock speaker less than a foot from my ears. - stream sound (like a steady peaceful river flow sound) - again too high pitched and too fast IMO. - windbells - I'm just going to stop you there and note in this case word combo should be wind CHIMES - as in mid-high pitched chimes and not those lovely lower pitched bells that your verbiage implies - piano music - Not even once in my life have I wished to wake to a piano (or for that matter drums, trumpets or triangles) Ok, I'm a bit over the top on these alarm sounds, but you get the point. I'm not a fan of this part of the clock. There's a lot of opportunity for improvement. My answer was to set alarm 1 with no sound, alarm 2 follows later with sound... If alarm 1 doesn't gently wake me like it should, alarm 2 certainly will, but I'm going to have a rushed morning.. Does it have an FM radio, yes. Will you want to use it - I seriously doubt it. Per JALL's reply in the Q/A section of this product when asked about the Radio: Please know that when you hold the radio button down, the clock will scan all the available stations automatically and save them as P-01/P-02/P-03 and so on ( up to 10 channels ). You don't need to do anything until it finishes the process. After finishing, the clock radio will select P-01 channel by default. If you want to change channel, please hold "+"/"-" to select P-02/P-03 and another channel Just 10 channels? no way to delete unwanted channels to keep scanning the higher frequencies to reach the channel you want? Where I live, 10 channels doesn't even reach the first decent rock or country station. However, I'm pretty sure this isn't the new digital FM frequency tuners, so 10 might just cover it all in a few more years. Despite what I feel are failures in the extra features, from a basic standpoint - an alarm clock that simulates sunrise & a 30 min sunset it works, and it works quite well. Yes, better alarm sounds and a functional radio tuner would have been nice, but I'm still happy with my purchase. They also include a bunch of labels/stickers so you can choose to label the clock controls (or not), and you can choose if you want them to be seen when the lamp is glowing or just put them on the opaque body (other side of the inputs). So, for these reasons, I'll give it 4 stars and keep using it until something better comes along.

Bought a Renewed Dell XPS 9300 laptop in November of 2021, and bought a 4 year Asurion insurance policy for peace of mind. After 2 months, I performed a system update which caused some intermittent issues with wifi connectivity. Rather than research a solution on my own, I reported the issue to Asurion; which after some light troubleshooting over the phone, asked me to send in the laptop. Two weeks passed and I received a notification that Asurion unilaterally decided to keep my laptop rather than fix it, and refunded me the price of the laptop without the taxes I paid, and without the fee I paid 2 short months thinking I was getting 4 years of Asurion coverage. In short, I incurred an almost $400 loss. To add insult to injury, after speaking to Dell after this all transpired, I learned that the issue I reported to Asurion was a common Dell issue caused by a recent system update and could have been easily resolved by changing a single setting in the device manager properties. Checking on the internet confirms this across dozens of independent posts. Between losing the amount I paid for insurance 2 months prior, as well as the taxes paid for the laptop, for a problem what could have been easily resolved, I am left $400 poorer shopping for a laptop in a market where the prices are the same, or even higher. Meanwhile, Asurion keeps the entire premium fee I paid for 4 years or service and keeps the laptop which they can easily flip after making one properties change. Totally unacceptable.

I was looking for a gaming desktop to replace my gaming laptop for everyday use (got tired of disconnecting/reconnecting the laptop when I traveled). When I couldn't find a low-profile desktop in my budget and with the desired specs I turned to mini PCs. The Ace ARM5 ticked off all my boxes: - great chipset with dedicated graphics - tons of expandability - small form factor - good selection of I/O (including Display Port & USB-C) - decent thermals - interesting design (I love it) and RGB lights - GREAT PRICE!!! While my Intel i7 laptop is faster, the difference is barely noticeable in everyday tasks and web browsing. This is the only mini PC I found with a combination of Display Port + USB-C + USB-A 3 ports. Expanding the memory from 16 to 32 GB and adding an additional 1T SSD was super easy due to the magnetic side panel (and only brought my total costs to $600 USD). As for gaming...playing E-sport titles (like CSGO, Fortnite, etc.) is great. I've transitioned to playing AAA titles on my console, so don't need (or want) to play them on this machine. However, I was surprised how great this little PC handled City Skylines. I loaded up my largest save (over 500K population) and the ARM5 navigated around and rendered everything without a hitch. The fan did kick on, but it's so quiet you'll never hear it over your game sounds. In terms of "cons" the power selector is a bit of a gimmick. You'll probably leave in one mode and forget about it. Also, I wish the RGB light patterns you set were remembered when you have to shut down/restart (I eventually just left it as the "rainbow" default). Finally...you'll either love or hate the design. I think it's pretty interesting, but have seen other reviews that can't stomach it. The tented form factor helps keep it cool. and the small footprint (about the same space as a Roku or Fire TV remote) is great for anyone with limited desk space All-in-all this is a great machine at an even better price, and I would highly recommend purchasing it!!!

Out of the box, this camera turns on five times, then turns into a brick without first "activating" it via the smart-phone app. That app is pure spyware. There's no legitimate reason why an app would be required to "activate" (ie "use") the camera. If I buy a camera, I expect to use it, out of the box, without having to install an app, "read and understand" several End User License Agreements, create an account, and expose all of my files, location, phone-contacts, etc to a Chinese spy company. If someone wants to use the app, that's fine, but REQUIRING all of that to use the camera is a deal-breaker for me. Trying to install the app and pair the camera is yet another undesirable headache. Video modes: This camera is supposed to give the Hero-9 (or at least the Hero-7) a good run for the money, but there's no "native" white-balance (a ProTune feature since what, at least Hero-2?). No on-screen zebra-striping or histogram; those features require the app. In manual mode, I can set the shutter and EV, to let the ISO control the exposure, but there's no indication of the current ISO or actual EV on-screen or in the app; this would make it hard to use ND filters under variable lighting. No wide/medium/narrow views, just a wide view that's not as wide as GoPro. There's no way to turn off Bluetooth on the camera. If the camera is on, it's broadcasting a Bluetooth MAC and other unique identifiers. These are just problems I'm finding in the first few minutes. Many of these features that I'd expect on-screen are available via the app, but the excessive app permissions and the *REQUIREMENT* to use the app to "activate" the phone is a no-go; not to mention that I want to use these features without a smart-phone. "Features" like this are pushing me back to GoPro, and other action-cameras that aren't heavily reliant on spyware. The GoPro app may be intrusive, but their cameras work fine without it.

EDIT May 2022: I have to drop the review a star due to a recurrent issue that is now confirmed to be the Deco. What's happening, is that internet speeds via WiFi will randomly degrade for no clear reason. I have three routers active - a TP-Link, the Decos and an Orbi. The TP-Link and Orbi internet speeds remain unaffected, but anything connected wireless to the Deco will experience sudden, unpredictable declines. The reason I know it's wireless is that connecting directly to the switch via Ethernet (which bypasses the Deco completely) returns expected speeds. Rebooting the Deco is the only solution I've found, but that's not sustainable during the mid-day. I guess I'm just old school. But I completely dislike these newer routers forcing you to use a mobile app to configure them. It's fine to provide as an option, but we need to get back to a world where all you need is a computer. The reason this matters is simple. It assumes you're physically close (i.e. so you can connect) to the device, which you logically would be. But what if something goes wrong and you need to dial in remotely (say, for your security system that's on it)? You can't do that with this, at least not without extra hoops. An older router Netgear router did this straightaway without extra configuration and the Orbi also allows you to do it, so I'm not sure why we're moving away from something so logical. It's the same frickin server. Anyway, here are the points. ✔️Mesh coverage is superior to the Orbi, by far. The Orbi tended to start cutting out with some of the satellites; not here. ✔️Speeds are good, but for the most part I haven't had an issue with speeds with any router, really. It's all about placement. ✔️The mobile app interface IS somewhat intuitive (although I think the functions should be on the front screen, not currently connected devices). ✔️It did a better job of figuring out the types of devices. ✔️I have not had any issues with 2.4GHz/5GHz with devices. Everything I've tried to connect has connected...eventually. Most of the problem children are connected via Ethernet though. ❌The initial setup was extremely painful. Part of this wasn't the Deco's fault, it's the cable company's desire to have a matching MAC even though it shouldn't matter. (If you use Cox and run into the issue of it not connecting, just reboot the modem with the Deco plugged in and it should sort itself out. You don't need to match the MAC to the modem's MAC, because they will detect that a router is connected anyway). ❌I had to buy mounts because all you get is literally the puck and a charging cable for each. The mounts allow you to mount the Decos near the power outlet, which frankly should have been in the box. ❌The ports aren't labeled. It may not matter (if it acts like a switch), but they really need to label their ports for in/out. ❌Some devices come in as UNKNOWN and you have to figure out what it might be based on when it was connected. In my case it did this with a cellphone, which is weird, because my main cellphone (A Note 10) was perfectly identified. So that means Deco is keying off a specific field (probably some description field) rather than the standard one every device uses (device name). ❌WPS tends to be finicky. With my printer, it claimed to never be able to connect, yet after a few tries, the printer just automagically got itself connected without my intervention. I'm still not sure how or why; I suspect the Deco was late in acknowledging the new device. ❌The Deco appears to some devices as multiple, conflicting SSIDs rather than a single mesh. Windows picks it up properly, but basically anything that is an IoT type of device (printers, sprinklers, etc.) may get confused and experience connection issues. I still haven't reconnected my robot vacuum as a result of this. ❌With only one port available on the node that's near the modem, I had to string two switches, one for local IoT hubs that didn't support wireless (Phillips Hue, for example), and then ran cabling through an annoying room separator so that the living room had access to Ethernet-based internet for my gaming PC and my PS4 Pro. The PS4 Pro has wireless but terrible signal through it, the gaming PC has a wireless card that doesn't barely work, so Ethernet was a must. I call this out because you'll have to do something similar if you have more than one device that needs Ethernet for your own layout. I considered Powerline Ethernet, but the wiring this place is garbage.

Main Review: I'm primarily a PC gamer but I liked the idea of having a Xbox Series X connected to the same monitor as a companion piece for original Xbox games, 360 games, multi-plats and games that I don't need a lot of horsepower for. My current monitor is an Asus PG279Q which served me well for many years but is HDMI 1.4 which caps out at 1440p/60hz. With the Xbox Series S and X supporting 120hz over HDMI, I decided it was time to look into a new monitor that supported HDMI 2.0. After doing a little research, I decided on going with the XG27AQ since it seemed to be basically an upgraded model of my previous monitor. It supports 1440p at 120h and has VRR, HDR and low latency modes. All of which the Xbox Series X can support. So far, so good. Picture wise, it's very similar to the PG279 but the colors do seem to pop a bit more. The blacks are black and the picture uniformity is very good. I also have no dead pixels out of the box. Build wise, this is a great monitor. I was a little worried that the stand was going to take up too much room or be awkward but it's great. Hefty, sturdy and while a little oddly shaped looks really nice on my desk. The monitor overall looks and feels high end, is well made and has a lot of attention to detail. I will note that the bezel is more grey than black but I think it looks nice and blends in well with my other components. As for the Xbox Series X, it instantly detected that my monitor supported VRR and low latency modes and asked to enable them. I noticed that it said HDR wasn't supported for gaming however. I had to go into the Xbox settings and enable the YCbCr mode and then it detected HDR. One interesting thing to note is that you have a few options for display. You can run the Xbox in 4K and 60hz and even though the monitor is 1440p, it accepts the signal and will allow you to run it this way. It simply downscales to 1440p and looks fine. You can also set it to 1440p and 60hz or what we are here for, 120hz. I saw a few people mention that HDR is locked to 4K but this is not the case. I was able to set it to 1440p, 120hz and was able to get HDR. I tested Assassin's Creed Valhalla which runs at 60fps and everything ran and looked great with HDR enabled. Speaking of HDR, since this is only HDR400, it's not going to blow anyone away or look as good as a high end TV, I was honestly pretty impressed. The HDR is fairly bright and noticeably made Valhalla look rich and have more detail in the lighting and looked preferable to having it off. HDR on Windows is a bit of another story. There's really no reason to run HDR on a desktop. You need apps, games or movies to take advantage of HDR, otherwise it's kinda pointless. I recommend keeping it off for normal use and then you can enable it in-game if a game supports it. And finally, a few minor nitpicks to point out: - I do wish Asus would give a single button to change inputs. If you want to change inputs, you have to go into the monitor menu and fiddle through several sections. One good thing is unlike my previous monitor, it will automatically detect the input. So if I'm playing the Xbox and I power the system off, it will switch back to DisplayPort for my PC if you wait several seconds. I just wish there was a single button on the back of the monitor to switch inputs. Especially since you have 2 HDMI ports and DisplayPort. It's not a huge hassle and it's certainly better than my previous monitor but still more cumbersome than it needs to be. - The inputs are a tight fit. There is a lip on the back of the monitor under the inputs and if you have a HDMI or DisplayPort cable that has a big connector, you might struggle to get it to fit. Thankfully, Asus does include cables but if you are using your own and they are oddly shaped, you might have some trouble. I'm super happy with my purchase so far. If you are looking for a new 1440p 120hz monitor for your Xbox Series S or X, I would certainly add this to your list of options. Or, if you want a great gaming monitor for PC and want to upgrade from the classic PG279, it's a worthy successor. Xbox Update: If you are buying this specifically for the Xbox, there are a few updates and things to note. The Xbox Series S/X both output natively at 1440p so everything looks sharp and great on the monitor. Also, despite being a 1440p monitor, it accepts a 4K/60hz signal so technically, you select 4K as your resolution on the Xbox and it will simply downscale to 1440p. One issue however is 120fps and HDR. For 120fps to work, you have to uncheck the "Allow 4K" box in the Xbox settings. All of the games I have tested that have a 120fps option assume you are playing on a 4K TV so it sends a 4K/120fps signal. Since this is a 1440p monitor and can't accept a 4K/120hz signal (This would require HDMI 2.1), it will convert it to 4K/60hz which the monitor can accept. In order to get 120fps, you have to disable the "Allow 4K" box in your Xbox settings. This will then force 1440p/120fps. One issue with this is that Microsoft for some reason doesn't allow HDR in any resolution but 4K. If you uncheck "Allow 4K", you lose HDR. So in closing, it's not perfect but it's mostly a Microsoft issue. 1440p support is there but it does seem kind of an afterthought. What will have to happen is more games natively support 1440p/120fps instead of sending a 4K/120fps signal and Microsoft needs to allow HDR at other resolutions in a hopeful firmware update.

Since there's currently 2 items on this page please know that this review is for the T30 speakers (item listed as "2.0 with NFC and Bluetooth"). Just like the identical T20's without bluetooth/NFC the T30's offer brilliant sound in a cost effective package. However, most of these units are now manufactured to comply with the European regulation of going into Standby Mode every 10 minutes if it doesn't detect audio to save electricity. Need to grab some lunch from the kitchen? BAM, you lose audio. Need to run to the bathroom at the office? BAM, you lose audio. On your computer reading articles and not playing music? BAM, you lose audio. In older models when speakers went into "Standby Mode" it meant that if it detects audio again it will turn itself back on after a few seconds. However if you use these as computer speakers that delay causes missed windows notifications, missed voip calls ringing, missed calendar reminder beeps, missed email notifications, etc. But these T30's and most of Creative's latest speaker version, what Creative is calling "Standby Mode" is actually AUTO OFF, not a Standby Mode that will turn back on. So every 10 minutes when it goes into "Standby" it DOES NOT wake back up after you ask your pc/tv to start playing sound again. The power light goes off after 10 minutes and you have to physically touch the ON button after 10 minutes for it to work again if you aren't constantly playing music on them. Every. Single. Time. Creative calls that a "feature" to comply with that European regulation for saving energy. I call it an epic design flaw. I confirmed this with Creative customer support. They confirmed that "Once the speaker is in standby mode, you have to manually power on the unit by pressing the power button." Some people have gotten around that annoying flaw and run a vb script with windows scheduler that plays a low level frequency audio file every 9 minutes all day long to keep the speakers awake. It's a great idea, but shouldn't be a requirement to keep your darn speakers on (not to mention people who aren't very computer savvy would struggle to figure out how to do that). This is a shame because the sound quality is great and the speakers look sharp on a desk. Another option to try and keep the speakers on is to connect the T30 via bluetooth to something, but most people only use bluetooth on an as-needed basis since bluetooth technology is very vulnerable to hacking. If you are interested in these speakers for their looks and sound quality, I'd suggest you try buying an older model. Hey CREATIVE, you have an awesome product but REALLY need to make separate model #'s for European sales and USA sales and CLEARLY STATE the ones that have the horrible 10 minute AUTO-OFF feature (make it a toggle switch at least, or several hours not 10 minutes). Us American's would much rather waste electricity than get up to turn speakers on every 10 minutes. True story.

review_text: When the wireless networking game was becoming a ubiquitous household staple, Eero was a crowd funded enthusiast project that solved the dead zones problem limited by your router by allowing you to litter your house with multiple access points that were still connected to the same network. While this existed in the commercial setting, Eero's edge was to simplify the setup for residential users and was a true set-it-and-forget-it solution so every corner in the house got wireless internet on their devices. And it was doing great things, like including HomeKit support and great band steering to utilize people's faster internet speeds, that the name of the game was simplicity and range on the same network (something wireless extenders could not do). The speeds were great, support was great. Then Amazon purchased it. Not only has the trojan horse become more blatant entering your home (if it hadn't already with Echo and Fire devices), but the inevitable cost cutting that comes with company acquisitions would trickle into their lineup. And the Eero "Con" 6e is the official end of what the Eero brand used to represent. Is the setup still easy? It can be but when it doesn't it's extremely frustrating relying on an app to hang up. The market is saturated with mesh wireless systems that have a setup through the app so your options are plentiful. HomeKit has been officially removed (still available on the Pro 6 but on this flagship system it's been removed) just as it did on their other new release, the 6+. And hey, Eero wants to upsell you services in their app that is standard on most other router systems; what a treat on a flagship model. But the real kicker is, it's the actual router and mesh system that is absolute crap. I'm often sitting in the same room of the router or other unit and get poor speeds. It has a lot to do with the lack of a dedicated backhaul band to maintain fast and consistent communication between the other Eero units, which is the whole point of having a tri-band mesh system. The Pro 6 actually has a dedicated band for backhaul, whereas this "intelligently" picks and chooses between the 3 bands. With other mesh systems, you can typically configure around this (Deco and ASUS for example, at the time of writing), but Eero has always maintained that they're smarter than you so it's never been an option. Because the third band in the Pro 6e is a separate and brand new sub-6Ghz band with its own channel frequency, Eero wants to "intelligently" switch between all three bands for backhaul despite the drawbacks on each band. While the sub-6GHz's advantage is considered a pro because its new channels cannot utilized by the previous generation WiFi protocols (essentially giving owners VIP channels that their neighbors cannot utilize or share) so speeds are next generation, the drawback is the range is essentially line of sight. Put this all together and Amazon/Eero believe they can intelligently flip back and forth between 3 bands (slow but long range 2.4GHz; fast but average range 5GHz; fast but poor range sub-6GHz) for you and hope that you'll see full bars and not question why your internet speeds are slow. On the device/client side, that's easy to hide. But the backhaul is something we have zero control over when this connection is slow/poor. And with the Eero Con 6e, you're left with very poor speeds because the backhaul is so poorly handled. I'm in the same room and can barely pull 300 Mbps connection despite having a wifi 6 laptop and phone. This was replacing my Orbi WiFi 6 tri-band, which was consistently 450-500+ Mbps in the same setting. The Pro 6e's sub 6GHz band speed advantage is nullified. And there's no way around this, frustrating me enough to consider the failure of expectation to be an absolute CON. On most routers, I would be able to tinker but Eero won't let me touch this setting, instead focusing on upselling this MSRP $699 mesh system's SERVICES like parental control, DDNS, and virus protection. If you look at Amazon's other acquisitions (Blink, Ring for example) and you'll see this upselling because of cloud storage but with the Eero it's just such a pathetic money grab for something that is available on other routers standard. The router system itself used to be an easy sell for the easy setup but the poor mishandling of the backhaul makes an embarrassing official beginning of the end for this once beloved brand. While I see this could be salvaged according to another reviewer by saying it's better in bridge mode, paying $699 for a wired access point system is frankly ridiculous when you're also giving Amazon/Eero direct access to your internet history to sell. I paid a reduced price for this system but the frustration behind using this is an absolute con. If you're willing to spend this much on WiFi, get ASUS. Or Orbi or Linksys; even Deco is better than this crap. And if you think this Con 6E is just an anomaly for the Eero brand, their 6+ is the other new model so the direction of the Eero brand is clearly to upsell services while removing features. But yay for using your 4th gen and newer Echo dots for extending your eero system (max rated 100Mbps)...

Another reviewer describes this as an action-camera, and that is closer to the truth than the manufacturer's description might lead you to believe. It is entry-level at best. First, the imager is 8 megapixels, so the settings above 8 megapixels are poor interpolations for still images. I would not recommend any of the higher resolution settings at all. The zoom is also interpolated and then digitally cropped to achieve the zoom effect. The image rapidly looses detail, so only a little zooming is tolerable. Dynamic range is very limited as well, so images with bright skies will wash the sky with pure white unless you adjust the exposure for still images. Video does not have much for exposure compensation, so just figure on unsatisfactory bright light videos. Low-light outdoors and most indoor videos are also going to suffer, so don't expect much. If you can live with the wide-angle, short focal-length lens, and shoot only stills and video under cloudy-bright outdoors, or supply sufficient diffused lighting indoors, the results aren't completely horrible. The IR function can be useful at close range, and might be the best application for this little beast. Buy several batteries if you want much shooting time, and plan on relatively short video segments. Fortunately, you can also run on USB power if available. Just experiment in advance so you know the limits. Bottom line, this is priced like a toy camcorder for good reason, it kind of is toy-like. As long as you know the limits and work under those constraints you can have some fun with it. Just don't think it's a "real camcorder", 'cause it's not a real camcorder. Caveat Emptor, buyer beware.

I was very excited to get start with this case but with delays to getting parts i had it sitting. In my closet for months. Four months later and I finally was able to make my build. Let me start with the positives The screen is amazing I strongly recommend if you did get this case to invest a few dollars on wallpaper engine on steam. When you do the internals right its very pleasing. The materials use on the cases are also very sturdy which is great because you might want to mod it. Negatives - borderline disaster levels of airflow. Be aware that you must pay the white paint tax for everything to maximize the effect of the panel my 3080 is black and its makes things very dark on its side of the panel. The whole case has a total of 3 120mm fan slots the rear fan is pretty standard but the two side mounted fans get practically no airflow. I would not run any high end video card and processors in this case with out modifying this case. My mistake was to build with a 5900x and RTX 3080 in this case. The only place to mount a AIO for my CPU was on the side mounted vents. but it does no serve the purpose of dissipating the heat as it has very limited airflow. Due to the cubic pattern ventilation on the side panel. My Adventure with this case: Before modifying this case my temperatures where 85+ after short brief sitting of gaming. I was very concerned with this. So I set off to remedy the situation. First thing I did is measure my clearance between my motherboard and the top of my case. I cut into it and add two 120mm fan slots. This brought great amount of airflow into the case but the case still didn't have enough outbound airflow because the vent holes are terrible for this purpose. In addition the case the side panel gets incredibly hot. I cut open the side panel where the vents would be and covered it with a mesh that would give better for airflow. With the added pressure of the two fans and the better ventilation this dropped my temperatures drastically. 72-75. I do not recommend this case for a beginner or if you don't want to invest time and money on modifying it. If you have lower tier parts that don't put off as much heat then go for it. The product features are good: This hub, and others identical to it, are great for tying a number of devices together, particularly if you want to run the hub some distance from your computer, so need the hub to be powered in order to maintain signal strength (quality/speed). It has on/off buttons for each port, which is nifty so you can power devices down without having to stress the cord or the internal connections unplugging connectors. It also functions unpowered, which can be nifty if you're traveling, and don't mind your computer/laptop pushing the power to your devices. The manufacturing may not be quality, and the customer service is significantly sub-par in my short experience: Unfortunately, the feature to operate without the power adapter can be a bit of a "gotcha", as in my case, I didn't notice for several months that the power adapter did not work properly.. my devices still worked most of the time, and they'd just flicker out occasionally, leading me to suspect cords, devices, computer processing and such. Once I noticed my laptop battery was draining while plugged in, but occasionally recovered and held a charge unplugged, I started investigating for a power draw, and quickly realized the hub was not operating correctly. If I pushed the DC cable into the hub firmly, or held it at an angle, the lights would stay bright, but if I did not apply pressure, the lights would randomly dim or brighten over time/jostling. These symptoms, which I described to technical support on my first contact, indicate that there is either a short in the DC power cable, or the DC plug is not making adequate connection to the port on the hub, or the solder joint of the port on the hub has failed. In other words, this requires a new power adapter connector (as I offered to solder the replacement into place), or a new hub to resolve. Despite describing an even more in depth set of trouble shooting which I used to absolutely identify the point of failure, they asked questions I had directly answered already. That's fairly common with the first line of "techs", so I answered their question, and again pointed out how the symptoms make it clear what the problem is. Others having reviewed this item have reported that their devices would be killed or randomly shut-down by this device. I had a power supply ostensibly killed by it! (Though it could also have been a faulty AC cable.) I have had a laptop randomly freeze or shut down when using this device with its dock. I found the cause - a ground loop! Ensure that both computers who are client to the device are plugged into the *same wall outlet* or same surge protector, and thus having the same source of ground. In some houses, the grounds may have unequal potentials, I believe it is, and electricity may begin to flow from one to another, through the ground leads on your electronics, using this device as a connection! This can kill devices, or otherwise cause supremely vexing misbehavior. Ensure all devices plugged into this device are on the same path to ground (same surge protector, or outlet). I use it with a USB hub, and it is excellent as an inexpensive surrogate for a larger and costlier KVM switch. I recommend writing a script that puts one computer to sleep when it looses several USB devices at once, thus allowing the monitor to automatically switch to another computer's input, for a fully-functioning KVM solution! Now, its chiefest defect, is that the USB out port is not on the back, which I rectified with two USB 90-degree adapters. This defect makes cable management a greater hassle in a setup where the device is permanent. It would also be nice if a keyboard shortcut could trigger the device, or if a small, removable, wired remote were available. Excepting these (significant! - why did I have to loose a power supply over this?) defects, this is a great device. USB 3.0 on it especially is quite lovely to have for its impeccable bandwidth.

These sound OK. The sound is clear with no static. I'm not an audiophile, but I think they lack the bass that my previous pair of Bluetooth headphones had. There are a few problems that make these a little annoying to use. Connecting To Two Devices ------------------------------- These headphones can connects to two Bluetooth sources, but it only connects to one of them automatically. I have paired the headphones with my Windows 10 laptop and Android my phone. When I turn on the headphones, they automatically connect to one or the other device. To connect the other source I have to go into its list of paired devices and click the connect button. I have two other Bluetooth headphones that reliably connected to my two device automatically when I turn them on. Two Audio Sources ---------------------- I have not tested these headphone's ability to handle a call. I have tested multiple audio sources at the same time. It seems to handles two sources quite well, but I believe some of this behavior is up to the software being used. If I am are listening to a song with Amazon Music's (web site) on the laptop, and then start playing a YouTube video on my phone, the audio from the phone does not come through. YouTube silently plays the video with Close Captioning enable. While the video is playing if I pause the song on my laptop, the sound from the video comes through. In contrast, when I'm playing a song on my laptop and then start playing a voice message on my phone, the song on the laptop pauses and the voice mail audio comes through. When I pause the voice mail playback, the song resumes on the laptop. Controls ---------- There's something not quite right about the "Volume Up/Skip Forward", "Power/Pause", "Volume Down/Skip Backward" buttons. On these headphones, I often find myself skipping to the next or previous song instead of increasing or decreasing the the volume. On my two other headphones a quick press of the "Volume Up/Skip Forward" button would increase the volume. A long press would Skip Forward. A very long press would increase the volume by multiple steps. In contrast, with these, headphones a quick press skips to the next song. A long press increases the volume. A longer press increases the volume multiple steps. If I want to increase the volume one "notch", I have to do a long press, but not too long otherwise the volume goes up more than I want, and not to short otherwise it skips to the next song. I find it hard to get the buttons to do what I want. Perhaps I have been trained by my other headphones. I see the logic in these headphone's controls scheme, but I believe the other control scheme is better. Announcements ------------------- These headphones have voice announcements. The female voice sounds natural (not synthesized), but the voice actor has an accent, or English is not her first language... or maybe the voice is synthesized and it is have trouble producing the correct sounds. "Power On" sounds like "Power Ong" "Power Off" sounds like "Power Opf", "Connected" sounds almost normal "ConnecTED", "Maximum Volume" sounds like "Maximum Voloom",

The motion detection was terrible and did not appear when a person or a car moved; it only appeared when it detected only few things. Even worse, I had it set to the highest detection setting and still had this problem. The second worst feature of this camera is the lack of playback, which is a detriment to both the camera and the company. You cannot review the entire footage that is recorded throughout the day. I would love to have a playback feature in this camera so that I could review what it had missed recording. Wyze does much more than this camera; it has better motion detection and can playback footage rather than just giving you what detection video. It's also less expensive, and I already have two Wyze cameras. When compared to what this camera offers, nothing but disappointment and a high price for something with numerous flaws. Not happy with my purchase, considering it just cost me an extra $80 in controllers. *****UPDATE***** Did a bunch of testing today and with the top of the case totally removed everything works fine. I bought two of these. I have Linux on one PC, and Win 10 on the other; both OS's "saw " the drive on connection. The storage capacity is very high for the size of the drive. The transfer rates seem about 15% slower than advertised on a USB 3.0 connection, but that's not really an issue for me. I can still rip a pretty comprehensive backup overnight, so good enough. I have a firewall, but I like having a backup that's physically isolated from my network. I'm running an i7 on a z270 chipset with 32g of ram, a 500mb ssd, and 6tb in spinners in two raid 1's (a 1 gb and a 2 gb) on the Win PC, and the Linux unit is an i5, z270, 16g of ram, a 500 gb ssd, and a 1tb spinner. I've had excellent luck with the WD black series drives, which is all I ever buy for my builds- one of the drives in my bigger PC has almost 35 thousand hours of run time on it (yeah, replacing it soon, but still- no errors, no overheat, no issues at all). I will update this review if I experience any problems, but as it stands right now, I'd recommend this drive to anyone who doesn't need something faster.

review_text: So, this is a very nice hard shell for the 2018 and 2019 models of the MacBook Air. I ordered the "Clear Frost" or whatever they are calling it and its a very pleasant color that is translucent enough to let the Macbook's design features, logos and color be shown off. I've previously had the "crystal clear" hard shell. I think this matte frosted on is a better choice because it seems less fragile and more pliable. The crystal one, seemingly by the nature of the material seems to need to be that more rigid stuff so it can have its gloss and mine lasted less than 2 weeks before developing stress cracks in the corners and then having the mounting tabs start to splinter off. I'm not as thrilled with Ibenzer themselves. This was bought directly from the manufacturer. Firstly, they played the old shipping game. They clearly couldn't deliver the product within the timeframe promised, even with Amazon's current extended delivery windows (why exactly am I still being charged for Prime?). So to prevent cancellation, they created a shipping label on Saturday, and didn't actually deliver the product to UPS until Thursday. its a common tactic in e-commerce, one I personally detest, and it makes me question the business ethics of the vendor. Speaking more to that. This cover is described in the listing as being compatible with the 2020 MacBook Air. But in reality it isn't. It's a misleading statement and practically all the vendors on Amazon are doing the same thing. This was made for the 2018-19 MacBook Air. The 2020 model, while apparently identical to those, in fact isn't. Having received the scissor keyboard upgrade it is about 0.5mm thicker on the bottom. The top shell fits perfectly. On the bottom, that tiny difference keeps the bottom shell from being able to snap on successfully on both sides. Again, business ethics. The case does stay on, with a friction fit, and it does function as protection, so I"m going to keep it until an actual 2020 version is produced. Right now, nobody seems to have a 2020 version of a hard shell. Even InCase, Apple's in-house case company seems to have been caught flatfooted. Either everyone expected the 2020 model to be exactly identical or the Coronavirus caused manufacturing snags, I don't know, but I'm too fastidious about new tech to not have a perfect fit. it just bothers me. [[VIDEOID:ac1dcd2fb8b6e8bb044aaed4a508fc59]] When I saw a WiFi 6/Bluetooth 5.0 PCIe card for under $50 I was skeptical. But with thousands of positive reviews I had to trust the public. I installed this card in my main desktop PC because at the time I thought my internet access point was simply too far away to run a cable. After a week of use, I powered on my PC and noticed the WiFi wouldn't connect. I waited a few minutes and eventually the access points showed up but I had to re-connect manually. The following day it stopped working completely. No access points, no device in Device Manager, nothing even showing up in BIOS. Things I tried: 1.) Re-seated the card and switched USB 2.0 headers 2.) Power-cycled the PC 3.) Uninstalled and reinstalled the drivers multiple times (in and out of Safe Mode) 4.) Uninstalled all other wireless device drivers The 5Ghz never stayed connected (2 walls, 1 floor, and ~40ft), the 2.4Ghz topped out at speeds that flopped between 40Mbps and 80Mbps, and latency was intermittent (adding a fluctuating 20-40ms) - terrible for online gaming. My USB-based NETGEAR AC1200 (A6210) worked much better. The 5Ghz stayed connected and the 2.4Ghz topped out at a steady 110Mpbs. I also used a TRENDnet AC1900 that worked fairly well. This TP Link Archer TX50E was supposed to replace that because I was sick of having a huge 4 antenna monster sitting on my desk (also it didn't have BT or WiFi 6). Alas. In the end, I ran a 100ft Ethernet cable out of the window on the second story of my house, all the way around the building, and back into a window downstairs. TLDR; TRENDnet AC1900 and Netgear A6210 were much better choices for speed and network stability in my case (2 walls, bottom-floor, and ~40ft from access point - plus gaming). The TP-Link WiFi 6 AX3000 (Archer TX50E) was no longer recognized by my PC (BIOS or Windows) after 1 week of use. Solution: Ran an Ethernet cable outdoors and around the house.

review_text: The TP-Link EAP225 is a great product that has brought wifi to my backyard and garden. Once set up, it is good quality (at least out of the box) and subtly perched on the corner of my house roof. HOWEVER, set up for home/residential use was -- as mentioned elsewhere -- a bit tricky (but not impossible). Fortunately, as an ER RN, I'm used to figuring out doctors' incomplete instructions. HERE'S WHAT I WISH SOMEONE HAD TOLD ME: NEED TO PURCHASE: **the TP-Link EAP225 Outdoor Access Point product **a short Cat6 Ethernet cable (to connect EAP225's small white EOP box to your router) **a long Cat6 Ethernet outdoor cable (to use from the EAP225's small EOP box to wherever you wish to place your EAP225 access point antennae) TO SET UP: 1. Connect the small white (EOP) box to your router using the short cable. Then connect the small white (EOP) box to your access point antennae using the long outdoor cable. A green light appears on both when connected and powered. (I set it all up in the house to make sure it works, then threaded the long outdoor cable through my ham radio external outlet to the outdoors.) 2. On your smart phone download the "TP-Link Omada" app. It asks you to "create an account" which consists of an email username and password. 3. Open the Omada app, and on the very bottom choose the "Standalone APs". 4. After a moment, (if you have completed #1 and it is functioning) the app will find and display the EAP225 Outdoor Access Point. Choose this. 5. It asks you to create another username and password. It also asks for the SSID of this product. This info is found on the inside of the access point antennae piece, at the bottom of the enclosure where you connected the cable to it (it is very, very tiny). In a moment, the app confirms that set up is complete! 6. Mount the outdoor access point somewhere high that offers clear visual of the area you want wifi'd (the signal loses strength when blocked by obstacles). That's it!...at least for today. I watched numerous Youtube videos to piece this together, and in each one I noted where an update of the equipment or app tweaked the procedure. But you get the drift -- it's not that difficult if you know the simple ideas behind the setup. AND, as I mentioned, the added range of my wifi was worth an extra Youtube vid. Five stars!

I've had the Yoga C940 now for 4 days and I couldn't be happier with my purchase. I saw it displayed at electronics store and it really seemed to stand out from all the other laptops and ultrabooks there. I took some time researching, mulling it over, comparing it with a lot of others. I almost went with the Lenovo Flex 5 but decided against it in favor of the durable metal case of C940. What got me started on insisting on a 2-in-1 in the first place was me contemplating getting the Samsung Tab S7+ tablet (12"0), which competes for the Apple iPad pro. But by the time you get the tablet and the keyboard case that goes with it, you are shelling out nearly $1,000 just for the baseline model. I love Samsung and Android.... but this is not the most versatile experience. Even Microsoft Office is stripped down. Then I thought, "Why not go with a device that morph from a laptop into a big tablet like the S7+ or the iPad Pro? Plus, I get all the benefit of Windows apps, I can run Android apps (though Windows Your Phone app or even better through Samsung Dex)" That way I'm not spending money on 2 products, but 1.... So began a big search and comparison in the realm of 2-in-1 ultrabooks. As I said, the first one that caught my eye a the electronics store ended up being the one after long decision I bought, the Yoga C940. And I couldn't be an happier. It's lightwight, durable, SUPER FAST (the highest performing SSD and RAM is installed), has a beautiful screen and good battery life. My use is everything except gaming. It's a classy machine all around. Quick observations: * It's very fast. Nothing runs slow on this machine. The specs on the SSD are 3 Gig read AND write speeds, Along with Intel Optane, 12 gig of DDR4 SDRAM and there are no bottlenecks. Apps open rapidly and the machine is smooth all the way around. With the lid closed (sleep) when reopening it is instantly on, just like a smartphone. Tap your finger on the fingerprint reader and you are instantly in. * Screen quality is excellent. I got the 1080 HHD one, rather than the 4K, primarily because I didn't want the extra battery drain with the higher resolution panel. Before I got it I was a little concerned that it would be mediocre. FAR from it.... crisp graphics, nice color range, dark blacks. My eyes are accustomed to my Samsung Galaxy S10+ Super AMOLED phone. There is no let-down when glancing back to the Yoga. I run the screen at about 75% brightness. if i was younger I could get away with less. * Battery Life - I would say 8-9 hours with regular usage, web browsing, writing, media play. I have the Intelligent Cooling turned on and there is absolutely no slow down that I can see. Scale of 1 to 10, I'd give the battery 8.5 * Ergonomics - the keyboard is generously sized and I find it mostly easy to type. It's very, very slight stiff in keypresses, but nothing I can't get used to. I chalk this up more to sturdier quality. * Sound - BEAUTIFUL! I love classical music and it's perfect for that. I love how flipping around to tent or tablet mode does not compromise the sound at all. Hats off, Lenovo, the sound bar design is BRILLIANT. Good, clear well balanced sound for such a small package. * Other modes - very nice. The tent option is nice for media play without exposing the keyboard to food or whatever. I use it in tent mode when preparing and eating dinner. Tablet mode is very nice. Just a nice alternative to sit and enjoy reading, browsing or media consumption. * Onboard pen - what a nice extra feature! And I love how it is neatly stored and charged in the inboard "garage". Overall... this ultrabook hits it out of the park! I highly recommend the Lenovo Yoga C940 for you if you are looking at a compact (without sacrificing screen or keyboard), very durable, fast and versatile ultrabook get it!
