So I figured I would try this cheaper brand for a games drive as nothing of great value would be lost if the worst happened. So Ill start first with pros. This drive was cheaper than my Samsung Pro 980 by around 50 dollars. This drive as well as my 980 pro are both 4.0 drives and my 980 pro beats this drive by an average of 1500mb/s, but after all it was cheaper. I find the speed of the Sabrent acceptable. CONS The install sheet asks first and foremost if you are holding a double sided or single sided SSD. (I don't know why they cant just print off different instructions based on unit instead of a generic sheet but whatever). The heatsink comes with a thermal pad pre attached to the base plate and also one attached to the underside of the heatsink itself. The problem is the 500 GB has chips on BOTH sides but on one side it only has chips coming up about half way. So no matter WHICH directions you follow the thermal pads are going to be under differing pressures. If you follow the single sided instructions and double up on the pads on the base it creates almost too much pressure against the area that has chips on both sides. And if you follow the double sided directions then it doesn't feel like too much pressure where the chips are double sided..but now you don't really have great contact on the other end where there are only chips on one side. I guess it should be no surprise that my 980 pro only runs about 6 C warmer than this SSD with the heatsink. (980 doesn't have heatsink other than "tape" that comes on it from factory) And the 980 pro is on the very bottom so doesn't get the best airflow, I would wonder which one runs cooler just stock. I'll also point out that the m2 screw that came with the sabrent was stripped, BAD. Thankfully I work on a lot of electronics and have a big organizer filled with m2 screws of every length conceivable. Finally, During installation make sure you get your Serial Number if you intend to warranty this. Because even though it doesn't say it anywhere, you only get a one year warranty WITHOUT registration. I have an Aunt who works for the FTC, she said they have to disclose this type of shenanigan's up front which they do not so they may very well be violating CFR and you could potentially leverage this fact into getting service a few years from now, but I wouldn't count on it. If your wanting the whole 5 years better go uninstall it hope the thermal pads dont get messed up and grab that serial. I don't care to be honest. If this SSD dies then that will just ensure I steer clear of anything Sabrent in the future. A good company with a SOLID product shouldn't ever have to really worry about the warranty. So why is Sabrent trying to cloak their policy? Are they expecting a lot of drives to crash after a few years? I am a Samsung fanboy, always have been at least on SSD's that is. I have only ever had to file one warranty claim with Samsung and they honored it even though it was 4 years and 10 months old. NO.QUESTIONS.ASKED The main thing they cared about was that I was below the TBW level, which I was just by a bit. That replacement is still going today in my media PC in the living room. You don't buy something hoping you'll need the warranty on it, but man...that 50 dollar price difference is really looking miniscule now eh. My . 02 cents.

Like many, I had some dead spots in my wifi coverage near the extremes of my house. It's not a big house, but without a bunch of work, I can't optimally place my modem and router. I have been running an Asus RT-AC3100 with no real complaints. I had a second RT-AC3100 as an AiMesh node and it worked well enough for a few months, but then anything connected to that node would start to lose internet. I could reboot the node and get it back, but this would happen again in as little as 24 hours, requiring another reboot. This continued even after I hardwired the node to the main router with CAT6 cable. I decided before I upgrade everything, I'd see if a repeater would fill the need. Not an ideal solution, but I'm tired of trying to fiddle with settings and the off the shelf mesh packages are expensive (at least the good ones are) and come with their own problems. I picked this up on recommendation from DongKnowsTech. He seems to know his stuff and, despite not usually recommending repeaters, he said he had no reservations about recommending or using this particular device. About a month in and things seem to be working just fine. It took a bit to get it setup as a mesh node, but I've had that issue before with other AiMesh devices (it can be *very* finicky detecting new nodes being added, even if wired directly). My dead spot is gone and my guest network is also extended, which I don't think is always the case for nodes. Part of me wonders if I should have just put the money for this into a newer router with a stronger signal, or just have gotten a full blown AiMesh compatible router and made that a node instead, but whatever. This works and I'm happy so as long as it keeps working. AiMesh has come a long way since I first tried it when it became available, but it's definitely a bit of a pain to setup. But Asus firmware is incredibly flexible and full of features once it is. You don't need a cloud account to control your own router locally, which is how it should be. Their support isn't always great, but that's not unique to Asus (i.e, they're about as good/bad as anyone else in this space). Overall, I'd say this is a reasonable solution for dead spots and it gives you WiFi 6 compatibility and options for how to set it up. For <$100, it's worth a try if you need to extend your wifi. Hopefully it lasts.

They project. No one would call them mellow or laid back, I guess if that person were used to something MUCH more intense, like maybe a studio monitor or something. They are essentially even tonally, the highs (which one expects with two tweeters, both pretty small) do not ring out and neither do the lows. The night vision works very well. Night vision in this case is actually an infrared sensitive camera and an infrared spectrum flashlight. The camera does not have an image intensifier tube like a night vision scope. No matter, though, because the Eve cam setup works great. NOTE: as the factory information states clearly, night vision does not work through glass so don’t ask. Read the information. Setup is as straightforward as it can be with this so-called “smart” home stuff. The camera has a pretty strong magnetic base if you can find something made of ferrous metal to stick it to. The power cord is long enough. Unit does not have batteries and must be plugged in all the time in order for it to work, just like your TV. The EVE software can be used to flip the image right side up if you want to hang this camera upside down from the ceiling or similar. Camera can swivel up and down, and sideways on it’s little plastic mounting stalk. The EVE camera is NOT made for outdoor use. The manufacturer website states this clearly and also states somewhere the min and max temperatures and humidity this cam can tolerate. It won’t handle below-freezing temperatures. Couple of drawbacks partly due to Apple failing to put enough thought into their Homekit products. First, the cam can use 5G but apple home kit really only works with 2G so what’s the point? Second, cam is called “HD” and I think I saw reference to 1080P somewhere but this is just not true. The resolution is probably about 320P if that. Third, only one person at a time can view the cam image, I think due to programming mistakes on Apple’s part. If you are viewing the cam image on your phone, another family member cannot view the cam image on his/her phone until you stop. They will get an error message about only one user at a time being allowed. For this price point, the Eve cam does work well. The motion sensing is very reliable and can be used to switch a security light on or other electrical “smart” device. The ability to record or not is nice too. This cam does not have a zoom or variable focus and you cannot tilt and pan remotely like you can on some fancy web cams. No matter, the Eve cam is pretty nice for basic home security. The night vision image almost seems clearer than the normal image. NOTE: I’ve heard recently that Eve might roll out an outdoor version and maybe you want to wait for that. This camera is hardware version 1.0, which is never a good thing as far as mistakes, defects, and bugs, but it still works quite well for something that is just barely past the test phase and into production. If you want a night vision security camera for indoors, or maybe sheltered outdoors if you live in a very mild and fairly dry climate, then you should feel confident about going ahead and buying this camera now instead of worrying about waiting for the next version.

review_text: 8-23-21 Background: I live in Ann Arbor MI, we have 4 4k ATSC 3.0 channels. They are on separate frequencies than their standard HD versions. I use Plex server to share this tuner with my roku powered tvs, cell phones and computers. My last tuner was a quadHD, which worked very well in the winter, but once everything gets leaves, the signal for every channel was unwatchable. One strange thing is that my fox channel is VHF, rather than everything else which is UHF. Installation of this 4k tuner was very simple, plugged it into the network, antenna cable and power, within 2 minutes I could see it within plex. Easily configured it within plex, scanned channels and saw almost double the channels as my old tuner. Including 4 channels that are ATSC3.0. The good: My ATSC 1.0 channels come in almost perfect, huge improvement over my old quadHD tuner. Channel changing is very quick. Picks up channels my old one did not. The bad: ATSC3 uses AC4 for audio, but there is no public codec, so there is no audio on the ATSC3 channels. I will update once there is a codec, and audio. My server is a 64GB, dual xeon 2.6ghz, quatro p400 gpu, 500gb NMVe monster.

Sure, I bought this flash drive to store data...well, a movie, actually...but the glistening, streamlined beauty of it has made me revise my work space. First, I cleared a place on my desk to display its glassy perfection. Then I cleared everything away to give it the attention and focus it deserves. Then I stopped working altogether and spent hours staring at it, mesmerized by its clear, weighty presence. It exerted a zen-like power over me. Now, my allergies have cleared up. My dog obeys me. The cat has given me to understand that she might obey someday, too. I have let my home and garden deteriorate while I meditate on the flash drive's incredible loveliness. The dishevelment and disarray surrounding it have only served to accentuate its beauty as the one spot of dust-free, clutter-free existence in my life. Someday, I may even watch the movie that resides within it. But nothing could equal the pleasure of staring for hours on end at the cube-like transparency of the paragon of flash drives. Nothing.

So to someone that knows enough about computers to know it's running way too slow but not enough to feel comfortable changing parts, this part is easy enough for you. Even if your friend is on the phone for moral support, you can do this. You can change this. I have faith in you. If I can do it, you can do it. And feel free to call for moral support.

review_text: I bought the MR9600 (aka AX6000) before Christmas while it was at 1/2 off the list price. Although there has been a steep learning curve at times, for that price I'm happy with it. Full price, though? I couldn't see paying that at this point. It's a first generation WiFi6 router that, imo, still has some kinks left to work out. What I like: - Better range than my old AC1750 router. In our 2 story house of about 3000sf, we have the router downstairs on one corner of the house with the master bedroom in the upstairs on the opposite corner of the house. The old router couldn't even push the 5GHz network up there, and the 2.4GHz network would usually only get about 20-30 Mbps speed. This AX6000, on the other hand, can pull 150 Mbps on 5GHz in the same location scenario. One of my motives in buying the AX6000 was in it's mesh capability, thinking that I might want to put in some nodes eventually to extend coverage, but with the new router it really just isn't necessary. - I wanted to like the 5GHz/2.4GHz integration (i.e. as configured out of the box you only see one network being broadcast). The router automatically evaluates the connection and switches to the better band (5GHz for best speed, if you are closer, but drops to 2.4GHz for better range if you are too far away). However see the negatives list below for the downside of this feature. What I don't like: - The first big issue I had was routine dropping of older devices from the network. The main culprits being a number of home automation wall plugs and a wifi printer. They would all see the network just fine and set up and operate initially, but within a few hours of first setting up they would drop from the network and not re-connect with anything short of a full setup from scratch again. As noted in many other reviews of this unit that issue was solved by separating out the two bands, which negates the integrated band functionality I previously mentioned I wanted to like. If your wifi needs consist only of newer, higher end devices such as phones and computers then this probably won't be necessary. I, at least, had a hard time figuring out how to split the networks since the router setup app doesn't have a button or anything obvious to automate that. I felt a little dumb when I realized all you have to do is enter a different name for one of the two bands in the router setup and hit save. After that all my devices that wouldn't stay connected previously have now been running fine for many weeks on the dedicated 2.4GHz network, including through many cycles of router's power. - Device prioritization and the routers internal speed test app: This one got pretty wonky for me. The router has an internal speed test app that can be accessed from the routers Admin menu. I had understood that this was the "trunk speed", i.e. that it measured the full bandwidth available to the router, which would then be apportioned to the myriad of devices connected to the router. Each device then would have a speed test result of something less than the router's speed test. However after upgrading my internet service to 1Gbps down/35Mbps up, I kept still seeing 11Mbps up speeds, unchanged from my previous plan's speed test result. (Download speeds were within expectations.) I tried everything I could think of, and finally called the ISP. They claimed my service had been upgraded and it must be my equipment's fault. Finally I got a technician visit. On his specialty equipment he showed full speeds from my modem, but wildly different results when connected to the router. One speed test site would report 40Mbps upload while 3 others would report 1Mbps upload, or sometimes 11Mbps. To his credit, after he left our house the tech came back about 15 minutes later. He'd been searching forum reviews on his phone apparently and found someone who mentioned Device Prioritization as a source of a similar issue for this router. Sure enough, one click of the off button for Device Prioritization and my router's speed test app was reporting full plan upload speeds. Weirdly, though, after turning Device Prioritization back on, the router continued to report full speeds. What's more, speed tests run from our cell phones (which are not on the Prioritized list) ALSO now reported full plan upload speeds. - One other hitch to mention: Older 802.11AC wifi cards might not be able to see this router network at all if they don't have up to date drivers. My work laptop was one such case, but once I got my IT dept to finally update the 3 year old wifi driver they now work together just fine. I have had no other cases of any device having a problem connecting to the AX6000.

UPDATED Have been contacted by the vendor to address some of my issues. - An app can be downloaded from the Emotn store to allow iPhone mirroring without ads - Power supply has been changed to one that doesn't overheat - Vendor recommended a factory reset to solve the slow UI - unlikely to solve it as I'd only done a basic setup and added a couple of apps so there wasn't much to reset --------------------------- Packaging looks nice. It's packed well and everything's in one piece. The remote is similar to a Firestick remote and takes AAAs although batteries aren't included. Firing up the projector it's worth noticing it's not terribly loud. We start at fairly typical Android-ish setup screen where we connect to WiFi and then the launcher comes up. This is Emotn's launcher, not the standard Android or Android TV launcher. Let's get setup... auto-keystone works well enough on the vertical axis and if we want to fix up the corners manually we can do that in the settings. So, so far it's quiet, looks decent, and it's Android based. So far so good. Let's load up some apps because here's where it starts to get a bit strange. Although you can use the Google Play store, Emotn has their own store. As far as I can see this is to basically force specific versions of apps rather than the ones in the Google Play store. For example, the regular Play Store Hulu app won't work so you have to use the Emotn one. Each time you add an app from the Emotn store you get the "this machine is loading an app from a 3rd party, it may not be secure" message which doesn't make you feel great. Whilst we've been noodling around downloading apps we've noticed that we've got plenty of storage to do so (16GB with 10GB free) but the remote's a bit cranky depending on what angle pointing from and the box isn't terribly responsive. In fact it's slow. Very, very slow. But it's cheap and we're optimistic types, right ? So let's play some media. Plugging in the FireTV and starting up Disney+ again we're all good to go. How's the sound ? Not great but not terrible. As for picture settings we're lacking in some contrast so we'll pull up the settings app and change the contrast. The settings app gives you a photo of a girl in a park or similar and it obviously changes as we adjust the contrast. Anything above 50% and whites start to get very washed out very quickly. So we'll leave the brightness sort of where it is and tweak the contrast at least. As for the colour, everything's very green. Let's try "Sport" setting... still green. Let's try another setting... still green. Let's set everything back to default... still green, now low contrast. So you tweak until it's not absolutely terrible and then go back to the Firestick and it all looks exactly the same as it did before. So, we change settings again, go back to the Firestick and it still looks exactly the same. So, because we're inquisitive types, we max out the brightness so that the test picture is completely white then go back to the Firestick and... it's still exactly the same. So any changes we make to brightness or contrast don't actually apply to the HDMI input. Then we notice they don't apply to the launcher either. At this point we aren't happy campers because we can't even change the brightness and contrast on the HDMI input. Oh, and everything's still pretty green. Meh, let's unplug it and move it to a darker area - hold on... why is the power adapter that hot ? Like, scary hot. As for the stated specs of the unit, let's take a look... Contrast ratio : Amazon description says 12,000:1, Emotn website says 3000:1. No way is this putting out a 12,000:1 contrast ratio. Brightness : 250 ANSI. Maybe although that seems a bit optimistic. Projected size and distance : Emotn website says 1.5 to 4.5m with a screen size of 65" to 251". Amazon says 1.5m to 6m with a screen size of 60" to 240". In my case I'm doing 120" at 3.3m. 120 at 3.3m should be pretty easy for a projector with these specs but the focus is a bit rough. Noise : less than 29db. Absolutely not but if you want to tell me it's in the mid 30s I'm ok with that. So let's do some quick pros : - 1080p - Sealed light engine so now worrying about dust, which is nice for a CCC - Auto keystone and decent 4-point manual adjustment is awesome - Super portable, can be battery powered and mounted to a camera tripod - Android with Bluetooth and Wifi so if the included remote dies I can easily hook up something else to replace it - Reasonably quiet Cons : - Colour reproduction isn't great - Focus at reasonable range isn't great - Contrast and brightness can't be adjusted for devices plugged in to HDMI - Contrast is poor - Brightness above 50% leads to significant white blow-out - Android OS is slow and laggy - Google Play store apps may or may not work - Power adaptor runs ridiculously hot, as in "I'm really not sure I should be plugging this in" hot. Ultimately if you want to watch stuff in a dark room at a small screen size (say 60"), at $200 it's fine, but you won't be using a 100" screen in the back yard.

I only gave this 4 stars because it did not come with an original Apple Keyboard nor mouse. It did come with "matching" keyboard (w/number pad) and mouse...both wired...but that is not how it was originally sold. Obviously the supplier found they could make more money by selling off the original keyboard/mouse as separate items. But that is not the main point, is it? How about the computer, itself. Better news...as far as I can tell, the computer arrived in mint condition and started up as if it were a brand new Apple product (same procedure). Initially, I was shocked that the keyboard/mouse were USB-A and the four computer inputs were USB-C...so how was I to plug them in? Well, separate from everything else and floating in the bottom of the box was a small bubble-pack envelope with two USB-A to C adapters. Problem solved...the computer started up beautifully and I am totally satisfied (except for the change-out of the keyboard/mouse as explained). Actually, I don't think the computer was intended to have wired keyboard/mouse otherwise there would be more than four inputs. The computer looks and runs like brand new. Mine is the 8 core (which is a heqq of a deal) with four USB-C inputs, 8Gb RAM, and 256 Gb SSD. Actually, the latter is not a problem because all my "data' (which includes documents and media) is stored either in iCloud or on an external drive....which, for me, makes starting up a new computer much easier since none of that has to be ported over to the new computer. Apple computers comes with a lot of native Apple software (almost all of which I use), but I also have a list of 25 other Apps (many from the App Store) that I use in addition to the standard apps...so getting them loaded takes a while. review_text: First I'll Explain my specs so you know what my computer's purpose is. It's a gaming machine that I also use for work. I had installed all my games on the rocket to gain the best performance and because 2tb was ample to store all of them: Asus X570 Crosshair Hero VIII Ryzen 9 3900x MSI GTX 980 Crucial 1 tb NVME (Replaced with Samsung 2 TB Evo Plus) Sabrent 2 TB rocket (Replaced with Samsung 2TB Evo Plus) Samsung 850 EVO 500GB I had purchased this in the beginning of December for my new gaming rig hoping to save some money and take advantage of the NVMe slots on my new x570 board. The performance was pretty good but from benchmark comparisons to a friends rig I could tell this wasn't as fast as his Samsung's. At the time I weighed the bulk fast storage and cheaper cost over outright speed, and bought a crucial drive that was slower and cheaper but also NVMe at the same too with the sabrent. They both worked just fine but with a little high temps than I'd seen with nvmes before, even though I had ample airflow to the motherboard. The packaging was great and amazon shipped it quickly. Fast forward to June, 7 months later. I start up my rig go to click on a game and it says the target/shortcut is missing. Thinking its a fluke I navigate to the path and realize the folder isn't there, go to file explorer and the whole Sabrent rocket drive is gone. It had failed completely. I immediately opened a ticket with Sabrent and am working with them now to get this resolved (will update this review as I deal with them). I put the Rocket into an NVMe m2 cradle and the drive is completely undetectable and then into another motherboard with the same results. I can only assume the controller on it has died. It gets hot in the cradle but doesn't mount at all and no disk diagnostic tools like crystaldisk or hdsentinel can even detect it. I used a linux based tool and although it couldn't mount I could see the disk information, it only had around 44 hours of power on time total as the drive only got used for games. That same day in a hurry to get my gaming rig working, I dropped some cash and purchased two 2 tb Samsung 970 pros and put them in my rig after they arrived, ran some benchmarks and not only do they run cooler but they score higher in all the benchmarks I ran. I can also tell during installs of all my games and files back to them they get written at a more consistent steady speed and with higher speeds overall. I had really high hopes for the Sabrent 2tb rocket, it worked great for the 7 months I had it till it died. It was around HALF the cost of the Samsung 970s when i purchased them and that immediately caught my eye, but the performance and debacle of it dying 7 months later has led me to distrust the brand entirely for solid state storage. I was lucky I didn't store anything critical on it for work or school. In the end I ended up having to fork over the cost of the Samsungs anyway just to gain peace of mind and reliability. In conclusion, stay away from these drives, having it fail within a year of purchase isn't worth the cheap cost. Data and time is expensive and this brand hasn't proven itself as reliable as its competitors. Save your money and get a Samsung. As for support there's a solid day between responses and I will update my review based on how they respond and how the whole ticket process goes.

I've enjoyed this camera so far but here are some potential downsides or simply things to consider. 1. Batteries: If you won't be able to rely on a solar charger and the camera is going to be mounted somewhere where a ladder is required, BUY EXTRA BATTERIES. The camera comes with one battery with space for another. In my case, a single battery lasted a bit less than 2 weeks. Since I have this camera mounted in a location where a ladder is required to change the battery, recharging the single cell involves setting up the ladder, bringing the battery down to charge for a few hours and then setting up the ladder again to reinstall it. Save yourself the headache of this process and buy at least 3 extra cells and swap them out 2 at a time all at once. This will reduce the amount of times you spend swapping them and double the replacement interval. If you know you'll need batteries that will need to be recharged, factor the cost of extra batteries into the cost of purchasing this camera. This camera is already not a cheap option and paying for 3 extra cells (or probably 4 since most are sold 2 at a time) really changes the cost v benefit of this camera. 2. Network: Most of us will be looking at the battery version because we need to put this camera in a location further away from power cables and potentially your wireless router. Be sure your wireless network is robust enough to push decent signal to the camera or be prepared to buy a signal booster/wireless AP of some kind. Aside from those 2 notes, the picture is clear and the video quality solid once I increased the wifi signal. I love the ease of use of the ring app and easy integration. Honestly, If you can go with a wired camera, I'd really suggest putting in a bit of additional time/money to avoid the battery issues. If it just isn't an option though, I'd recommend this camera only if you buy the battery cells required to support it or a solar charger.

review_text: I have a Brother HL-3140CW color laser printer. Our household was able to print via its WIFI interface for a couple of years. After which, the WIFI interface became intermittent and then failed completely. Since the printer still worked well via its USB interface, I researched print servers. I tried the IO Gear GPSU21 since there were many reviews. I'm happy to say that this unit allows all computers in our the house to share the Brother printer. I didn't give this unit a 5 star rating due to the installation process. The provided instructions (and the instructions downloaded from the IO Gear site) only provide guides for Windows XP/Vista and MAC. My PCs use Windows 7 and 10. Therefore, I had to guess my way through the process. After many failed attempts, I was about to return this product. After one final attempt, however, I finally got it to work. Once I got one PC to print, I got the remaining PCs (and MAC) to print quickly. My recommendation to others is to do the following: 1. Connect your printer to your PC via USB. 2. Install the latest printer driver software for you printer and ensure you can print. 3. In Control Panel, remove the printer (Note: the drivers will remain on the PC). 4. Connect your printer to the IO Gear GPSU21 and connect it to your network via Ethernet. 5. Download the latest IO Gear GPSU21 software and run the setup application. 6. Run the print server wizard application. 7. When asked to select a printer, you may see the printer you deleted (step 3). If so don't select it. Instead select add a printer. You will then be guided through multiple pages. 7a. Select local rather than network printer. 7b. Select LPT1 for port. 7c. Select your printer manufacturer, model and driver 7d. Select the printer in the list with LPT1 port. 7e. Do not share printer. 7f. Do not print a test page since the port setup won't be completed until after the summary page. 8. After this process you can now print from you PC. Setup will be painful the first time, but the print server does work and works well. Now when I print, the document shows up in the print queue only briefly before it prints. This is so much faster then the printer's original WIFI interface.

Absolutely love this case for the 8 hot swap bays on the front and the overall clean look of the SiiverStone CS380B. I purchased it 9 months ago and I'm very happy with the investment. It is great for quick expansion of a home UnRaid NAS set up. Here is my breakdown of the pros and cons to this case: Pros: • Clean/Sleek Silver Stone look. Their design has a certain understated simplicity to it, in my opinion. • 8 hot swap bays with front panel access are perfect for my Unraid NAS build. • Backplane supports both SATA and SAS drives. Updated version now powers with one Molex and one SATA connection. • 2 - 5.25 bays also leave space for future expansion. • Hinged front door has a small magnet to help closure. (No, it’s not strong enough to cause data corruption.) • 2 Old School tubing ports on the rear I/O panel for those that wish to use a liquid cooled radiator set up that won’t fit inside the case. (Steam Punk design coming soon:) • Light weight mid tower makes it easy to maneuver during initial build and mod phases. Cons: • Cable management is rough. I’ve been building systems since Warcraft 3 came out and this one has more challenges than my old Lian Li PC69 • Despite having the specs to support ATX it feels cramped once everything is in place. • Ventilation – This case is not built with airflow in mind. The 2 fans that are mounted to the drive cages are trying to push air through a wall. Very few gaps to get the air over the drives. • Temperatures – With poor ventilation comes increased heat. My hard drives range from 31C to 39C at idle. When running preclear they push 50C I started with spare parts (I5 3750k, z77 extreme4 mb, 16mb ram) added 3 shucked WD 8TB drives (1 for parity) plus an old 480Gb SSD cache drive. The case is ripe for modding to personal needs if you have the time, tools, and ability. Getting ready to drill additional venting into the drive cages and right side panel and swap out the case fans. Added an HBA card for more SATA ports. Also ordered a couple of Icy Dock hot swap cages to go in the 5.25” bays to give me space for 4 more 2.5”drives and 2 more 3.5” drives. 9 months later and the back plane is holing up fine. Upgraded parity drive to 12TB and changed cache to 2 – 1TB ssd drives. I really should have bought a fully modular power supply.

I have fibromyalgia and ptsd and I was using 3 different devices to track my wellness - an Apple Watch during the day, Oura ring to sleep and Coros Apex for exercise. I wanted to consolidate into one device and I’m happy to say I have found it! I love how focused this watch is on recovery and the nervous system. I also love how it doesn’t discourage you when you need to rest, etc like a garmin does. I feel that it really just compares you to your own baseline as opposed to the rest of the population who aren’t dealing with a chronic illness. For exercise, it works great. I’m still figuring out what buttons do what during a workout but I haven’t had any issues. What I also love about it is that it’s pretty minimalist compared to other activity trackers but packs sooo much info and data into the app. You would never know by looking at it how much data it’s collecting. I’ve found the sleep tracking and ANS charge to be the most useful tool for me to take care of myself and you can see correlations between stress and both of these numbers. I also love how you can turn the watch onto do not disturb but the red dot will still appear to let you know you have notifications. Even the Apple Watch couldn’t accomplish this. I will be selling the other devices because I’ve finally found what I’m looking for. The only downside is the straps but I do think this is one of the nicest looking watches on the market.

Great laptop for the price, I don't think you can find a laptop this great at this price point. I have not tried the fingerprint scanner yet. Decently fast boot up times given it has an SSD. Battery life is actually pretty great, too. I am happy with the ports, it even has a USB C port. Screen gets very bright. It also took about 5 minutes to put in an 8GB ram stick in the easily accessible and open ram slot. Some cons of course since this is a budget laptop (these cons can be considered "normal" at this price point): - Full HD display with 1080P screen, however the color quality, especially blacks and other colors is not great. It feels like white is overwhelming compared to other colors. But otherwise at this price point it is OK in my opinion, just that there is a very noticeable difference compared to my 700 dollar laptop. - CPU kind of sucks. I added 8 GB of ram which did make the computer faster, but downloading things or loading times can be slow with the CPU being the issue. However it is tolerable and I am overall happy with the speed for this price point and do not feel I have to crutch on my other high end laptops. - The acer 5 series is usually marketed as "slim", but this laptop is definitely not slim. It isn't bulky though, I think it is very average or more in thickness compared to actual slim laptops on the market. If you have 330 dollars only to spend and are on a tight budget, don't hesitate to get this laptop. If you do purchase this laptop, I would DEFINITELY recommend adding additional ram (I got 8GB ram for 25 bucks at microcenter) since it is super easy to upgrade the ram in this computer, and it made a noticeable difference in browsing, loading, scroll speeds. So. For young kids, it's okay. My boys are both under the age of ten, so they still have low expectations and are easily entertained by this product. The unfortunate thing is that you have to be ultra specific when using commands - and even then, the Alexa AI struggles. For example, if you say, "Read me a story", the Echo Dot will randomly open a book from Audible. And it won't select a new story until it's done reading that book. Let's say that book is something like 365 days of Alphabet Rhymes. Just imagine the torture. I watched my kids repeatedly command their Echo to "Stop! Read a different story." Guess what? The device picked where it had left off each time. This went on until I stepped in and tried to stop the never-ending alphabet rampage. Took a couple tries, but we finally found out that the key command to use is "Cancel." And after some troubleshooting, we found out that the command "Alexa, TELL me a story" has better results in that the AI will list a small selection of short stories for the young audience to choose from. The Freetime thing seemed like a good idea. The Alexa AI alluringly suggested that we could request specific character stories by saying things like, "Alexa, read Cars 2." Haha-ha...ha. Nope. If you request that, Alexa says, "Sorry, I can't find anything on Cars 2/Frozen/Toy Story/etc." So the only way my kids can get the AI to read the story they want is by asking "Alexa, tell me a story" (and even then, it'll only list a few at a time, so the boys have to repeat this process several times before finally hitting on the story they wanted. We have books that we purchased on Audible, and Alexa lists those books when we ask it "What Audible books do we have?" Unfortunately, if we ask it to read one of our Audible books, the AI acts as if it can't find the book...ya know, the one it literally JUST LISTED. And in case anyone is wondering, yes, I have opened the parental permissions and marked our Audible books as accessible for the Echo Dot Kids Edition. Permissions be damned, I guess. Alexa only reads what it wants. Don't even get me started on music. You can ask Alexa to play genres, like "Alexa, play classical music." The AI will oblige. However, if you ask for specific artists (that are available for Amazon Prime members), Alexa will somehow not find the artist. It's very similar to the "read a story" conundrum. The AI suggests that you can listen to your favorite artists, then it claims it can't find them. Pros: This makes a good, two-way intercom for announcing that it's dinner time, bath time, bedtime, etc. This Ech Dot also works great as a speaker through which you can play your music or audio books - so long as you open the Alexa app from your phone and enter the commands on the app to play the desired media on the Echo Dot device. Again, the Echo Dot itself has been playing dumb, so our attempts to directly request that the desired media play on Echo Dot have not worked. The Alexa app on my phone functions though. Upon request, this Echo Dot will amuse your child with a selection of repetitive and lame jokes. Fine for early grade school, but I imagine the novelty will wear off soon. One thing that I appreciate is the way Echo Dot Kids Edition handles sensitive questions. Since this device was going to be used by my children, I tested it by asking a wide range of awkward questions, from "What's the difference between boys and girls?" to "Who is Hitler?" to "Is there a God?" to "How are babies made?" For sensitive questions like these, the AI will gently suggest that the child speak to their parents or guardians. All in all, it's a glorified smart speaker that you can control from your phone, with very limited interactive features. And Freetime is basically useless for the most part, because requesting specific media typically ends in the statement "Sorry, I can find that." I recommend only getting this if you are looking for something to entertain a young gradeschooler while you are studying or working from home.

AUG 2021, the SATA-power cable caught fire. It melted the connection point on the hard drive in the process. Ok... company support - The site says you can 'Request' a RMA without a 'ticket #'... nope - page won't submit without a ticket #. Next = telephone: First call, recording says wait time is thirty minutes to speak with someone. (hung up) Second call only 15 minute wait. Spoke with rep, he asked me to email photos of the damaged power supply and the damaged hard drive. I did so. I get an email saying that since I spoke with a rep they were closing the ticket ..... HANG ON!!! They never gave me the ticket # to submit the RMA request. Third phone call... (insert exasperated sigh) ok, after the third phone call service was what you would expect. RMA approved... return shipping label provided... The replacement they sent was a step up, from 500W to a 600W. In a follow up email they even asked about the hard drive... if I sent them the original proof of purchase... they would what? they did not specify a monetary reimbursement. The cost of the drive is not the primary concern... it's the data loss. Ok, my recommendation... go with the industry leader Seasonic. There are other R E L I A B L E power supplies out there. With a little research and a few more dollars... A bad power supply can kill your entire system. I was fortunate it was only the hard drive (insert angry mumbles) and power supply.

review_text: This is my second Amazfit watch. It may have been a mistake to buy from Amazfit again but time will tell. My first Amazfit watch (BipS) lasted about 18 months and then the battery quickly died going from lasting 14 days regularly to lasting about 3 days overnight then lasting for less than a day to lasting about a minute. The GTS 2... First, the good. The battery life is fantastic!! I used to get about 14 days on my previous Amazfit BipS. I am averaging about 10 days on the GTS 2. That is my primary reason for trying another Amazfit product. No other brand seems to be able to come close to the battery life that the Amazfit watches have. The watch face is bright enough to see outside but is NOT trans-flective like the BipS was. The watch comes with a decent number of sport modes. Sleep tracking seems to be decent and data does get sent to the Zepp app onyou phone or tablet. Now the rest... As mentioned the BipS would reflect sunlight to backlight the face. The GTS 2 is simply bright enough to see in the sun but not near as visible as the BipS trans-flective face was. Like the BipS (and unlike my wife's FitBit), the GTS 2 takes a l-o-n-g time to get a GPS signal. This was something Amazfit touted was improved in the GTS 2.... eh, not so much. Within a few days the watch started complaining about being low on memory whenever starting an activity and suggests syncing. I sync and sync and still get this error every time I start an activity without fail. If you open the Zepp phone app, and there is an update ready, the watch will perform a system update immediately regardless of what you may be in the middle of. "No soup for you!". The Zepp app is not that intuitive. How do you start an activity in Zepp on the phone? A menu option like Home or Enjoy or Profile? Nope. There is an unlabeled gray bat across the bottom that one has to slide up. Even then the only options for activities in this screen are Running walking and Cycling. The bottom line is that IF you want long battery life in he smart watch field, you will need to compromise. I'm taking swing #2 with Amazfit. If I have battery problems again then I will be done with Amazfit and hopefully some other company has gotten their device to last more than a week by then (hello? Fitbit?).

Listen- you paid $40 bucks for this unit, don't expect stadium filling sound or deep, chest pounding bass because it ain't there. Pros: -price -portability -fm radio -blue tooth -external devices (ie external hard drive with music can be attached to the usb hub) -blue lights (if you like them) Cons: -blue lights (if you don't like them), I know today's portable music player fetish seems to be blue lights and such, me personally don't need them, only problem is you can't turn them off (at least as far as I can tell -and it doesn't state such in the instructions) and they obviously take battery energy away (albeit minimally) -not the prettiest looking player in the land, to me it's kind of homely looking but I don't plan on staring at it all day, it's just for outside use. -FM tuner sensitivity. My favorite station is a local college station that plays jazz. Every other radio in my house and car can receive it indoors but this unit can't. Compounding this you cannot 'manually tune' in a station, it's auto-tuning so weak stations get passed up. Also the FM antennae looks very, very thin so it could be prone to breaks if mishandled or accidentally closed forcefully. And once it's broken it could be hard to replace -so keep a metal hanger nearby for plan 'B'. Misc: The unit is well thought out, well operational, and for it's price it's in a league of it's own. Only potential issue is it's made in China, no surprises there and decent, good stuff comes out of there. But in my experience low costing electronic devices tend to work well -at first and depending on the quality of circuitry used it's lifetime can vary from short term to long term. In a nutshell it's crap shot but again, it's $40 so no one's going to shed a tear if it keels over a day after it's warranty expires. -the unit size varies from review to review; some say it's large, others say it's small. I say it's size is relative to your needs meaning it's not a 1980's "on your shoulder" carrying boom box, but then again it's not a small, pocket sized walkman either. The pic attached gives you an ideal of it's size.

I’m giving this item two stars and adding 1 back for Amazon’s quick replacement of the original, defective camera. If Master Tailgaters (MT) had proper QC and a consistent product, I would give it five stars. Unfortunately, they don’t and you will pay a price for their oversight. Bought this item because the price was right and it was the only backup camera that had an “OEM Look” for my venerable 2000 Silverado. I did not want a license plate camera or a surface mount that I would have to find a creative way to install. The MT tailgate handle looked ideal and I was excited to get it. I found the tailgate fitment to be very good. Other reviewers have noted issues in this area so I had concerns prior to installation. The bezel was solid, the cabling was the perfect length, and the connector was small enough that it exited the bottom of my tailgate without issue (no drilling or bending of metal required). This part of the install was a snap. Next came the video/power connections. The harness that came with (defective) Camera # 1 (C1) had green and black wires on the tailgate end of the cable + a fused red wire. The cab end had an RCA video connector and same green wire (no red wire). I deduced that the grn/blk wires were the reverse circuit. The instructions stated this would power the camera. Not true. No mention was made of the red wire. With the reverse circuit and video connections done, the display would switch to the camera feed (grn trigger) but the screen was black. Decided the red wire was important despite not being mentioned so I connected this to 12V but still no joy. Tried Amazon’s tech support option but they were as much in the dark as I was so they sent a replacement camera. Camera # 2 (C2) showed up and I connected it to the truck with and without red wire power. Learned red wire power is required and C1 was defective. Note that harness # 2 was different than the first one and still didn’t match the instructions. Upon seeing C2 work, I had to run ANOTHER cable from tailgate to cab to connect to switched power! Had I known this the FIRST time, it would have saved me a lot of time, aggravation, and very colorful language. Since it is required, it SHOULD ALREADY BE IN THE HARNESS! NOTE: WHAT YOU GET IN THE BOX IS INSUFFICIENT TO COMPLETE THE INSTALLATION! Thanks MT. You’re just…special. Other reviewers have commented on image quality. The resolution of the working camera looked like garbage when I tested it on an HDTV. Sorta Minecraft-ish. However, the image quality on my Kenwood Excelon head unit is fine and I have no complaints on this front. Bottom line: Buyer beware. Assuming you get a functional camera, you can make it work with some effort and the result is satisfactory. Getting from A to B is the challenge. Go in with your eyes open, and you might want to pop for the insurance on this one…

I bought this for my iPad Pro so I could attach devices and hard drives. Many of the cons to this device are not actually the fault of the manufacturer but problems with IOS. First, know this before you buy... Transfer speeds are excruciatingly slow between an external device and IOS. Again, this is not likely the result of the dongle as I’ve seen this complaint with IOS in general, but this dongle does NOT offer anything to accelerate the process. Honestly I’m not even confident that the dongle is USB 3.1 certified. I would doubt it. Second, the dongle does not have a power supply or outlet. Since dongles use the power outlet on the iPad to connect most include a second power outlet on the dongle itself so you can use devices and charge the IPad. This can also speed up transfers because you are not relying solely on battery. Unfortunately this dongle lacks a way to charge the IPad, meaning you either use the dongle or you take it out and charge the device. Third, and lastly, this dongle does not have a magnet nor is it designed to fit onto the ipad. Instead the dongle just hangs off the ipad. Unfortunately the dongle cord is not long enough to even sit evenly on a table. You will always be hanging from the ipad. This cannot be good for the outlet long term. If you can get past these cons then BUY the device. I use it for quick transfers only and so it meets my needs. BUT if you need to have external devices connected to your IPad at all times DO NOT BUY THIS DONGLE.

Sound is good enough for my audiobooks. Battery is meh. Range is adequate. The biggest problem is feature creep. They've put dozens of possible commands based on different states of the phone. Listening to music enables a different command set than not listening to music, for example. In the media playing layer, they've added toggle noise cancelation, toggle transparent mode, volume up, volume down, next track, previous track, power off left bud, and power off right bud into two "buttons". These same "buttons" are non responsive touch sensitive electric contact surfaces. There is no clicky membrane to provide feedback of how many times you pressed the button or whether you're holding down the button. Add to that there is a delay in response of around half a second, so you're never quite sure if you put the right command unless you wait. The "buttons" are activated sometimes when you try to adjust the position of the buds in the ears. There is also a bug that cranks up the volume to the maximum or minimum if you happen to accidentally activate that command. You can't bump the volume up a little. Your options are max volume or mute. But worst of all: the electrically sensitive touch areas are activated by the current in your hair. Your hair. Picture in your mind that you are walking with your headphones on. Your well conditioned hair brushes against the contact surface and triggers the volume up command. The volume on your audio book gets set to maximum and you have to rip the headphones out of your ear to prevent a ruptured eardrum. While fumbling with the headphones in one hand and manually lowering the volume of your your phone in the other, your palm turns off both headphones because there was five seconds of continuous contact with your skin. The transparent mode is nifty, but only works if both buds are on. The buds are not symmetrical and the left bud does not fit in your right ear. I truly hate these things. I believe they are possessed by the spirit of a housefly that I murdered last year.

I have used quite a few PC speakers and intended this to be an attractive upgrade for my gaming machine. These sacrifice appearance for functionality though. First, the wires are stupid. You've got sound control half way between the speakers and the USB and audio jack. Can't think of a more inconvenient place to put it really. The fact that you still need to jack these in because the USB is just powering them is also stupid. The design leaves a nice gap between the speaker and its stand which is a great place for all of your other wires to get tangled and trapped making it a choir to move these around. Also, the base has 4 small pads that would normally prevent the speaker from sliding around but the ones on this thing are plastic, not rubber, so the speaker skates all of the desk at the slightest tug on the wire. Finally, the audio quality is TERRIBLE because the wires are so poorly shielded that even a USB light being plugged in nearby makes the speakers buzz incessantly. If you have an on/off switch on your USB hub, which I do, you'll also be treated to an ear splitting buzz and pop each time you turn the power on or off. Worst speakers I have ever purchased, hands down.

review_text: Seeing this, I had a momentary doubt that it was as advertised. Then I thought, nah, Amazon wouldn't have it if it weren't real. Well, I guess I should have gone with my original misgivings. No fault on Amazon, they have a whole lot of stuff people sell through their site, and someone has to let them know it is crap before they can pull it. That being said, here are the deets: I started to transfer data from an external hard drive to this device. Once the device got to 120GB, transfers started failing. When queried, the device said it contained 120GB of data and had 1.8TB of space remaining, but nothing else would transfer. A quick internet search let me know that it was a low-capacity drive set up to report a much larger capacity than it actually held. I contacted Amazon Customer Service, and a refund was started. I will drop it off today. From now on, name brands only.

Mac support for this product is horrible. I see other reviews that seem like some people were able to get it working but it is anything but plug and play. Here's the experience I went through before giving up, returning, and just buying a different one. I plugged it into my Macbook pro expecting it to work out of the box and it did not. Tried a few different cables to verify it was the adapter and it still didn't work. Then I looked on the UGreen website and downloaded the drivers. The drivers download from mediafire in a .rar format. Macs don't natively support .rar so I had to find a separate program to decompress it and get at the actual .dmg archive containing the driver. Opening the .dmg and running the installer it wanted access to my downloads folder which I initially rejected. It failed so I tried again and gave it the permission it wanted. It failed again and said I needed to disable System Integrity Protection. Disabling that protection requires turning the computer off then turning it back on while holding down a combination of buttons before changing some settings. It was at this point I gave up. So you know, disabling that protection would give the program root access to the entire computer. A program with this access could do a lot of malicious stuff. I'm not saying this driver would or does do malicious stuff, but it should be able to operate without root access for consumer protection. It is a security vulnerability to allow this. There is no reason I should have to do any of those above steps to get a product to work, much less disable System Integrity Protection. I'm a computer scientist and have plenty of experience dealing with file formats, networking, and bios tinkering, but this is too much. TLDR: Many steps are required to get this working on Mac and the driver wants full root access to your operating system (Very suspicious and unnecessary). No consumer should be asked to turn off System Integrity Protection to get a usb peripheral working.

An example of how they differ is I compared the charging of an iPhone 13 Pro at 10% charge with this cable from an Anker 45W USB C wall charger. A proper Anker C94 cable jumped immediately to 9V and proceeded to charge quickly at around 18-20W. Same with the cable that came with the iPhone. This cable stayed at 5V and hovered around 14W. That’s not terrible but it did behave differently. The C94 is supposed to be sturdier in construction and required to protect against over-current. This may not have those protective features. If 64gb is enough for you, then save yourself ~$30 and get he venturer. My use case - I primarily use this to watch videos. I pre-download movies on Netflix and Hulu so I can watch them later without wifi (e.g. on a plane, in my trailer, etc). There are two USB inputs, one HDMI input. I use VLC app to play video files that I downloaded on a USB and it played back just fine. I also plugged in a Roku stick into the HDMI to have the option and it works as well. See my attached image. I tested the battery life by continuously playing a movie on Netflix/Hulu and the battery drain was very consistent over time: about 20% battery reduction every hour. So int total, the RCA played for ~5 continuous hours and then the battery was completely drained. This, IMHO, isn't bad for a relatively inexpensive unit. Please keep in mind the unit was not using wifi and I was not running any other program while the downloaded videos were playing. Overall, I'm quite pleased.

The Pros: This case does exactly what I hoped for. It's well-padded and sturdy with quality construction. It looks like it will hold up to regular use over a long period of time. It fits the 2021 Paperwhite Signature Edition like a glove. I was looking for a case that can be used to stand the Kindle up on a table while reading and it works perfectly as a display stand. The ability to adjust the angle of the Kindle while it's standing is a nice bonus. There is no side-to-side lean like an Origami style case has, and it's very stable while in the standing position. The Cons: The case adds a lot of thickness to the device. I understand that the flip/levering/stand functionality requires additional moving parts and materials that a "standard" book style case doesn't need, but the case makes a pretty tight fit if you're trying to tuck it into your back pocket or coat pocket on the go. The Kindle and case together are almost double the thickness of the Kindle and the "standard" Amazon case. The case does not allow wireless charging. Because the case is so thick, the Kindle must be removed from the case in order to take advantage of the wireless charging capability of the Signature Edition. There is a cutout to allow the USB C cable to be attached for charging. The cover can shift side to side when placed in a bag or pocket. This last item is a fairly specific nitpick, but if you read/listen to your books across multiple devices, it can cause some issues. Because it's so easy for the cover to shift, the magnet that triggers the sleep/wake action will move far enough to wake the device. (The cover only shifts slightly, the screen of the Kindle is never exposed and is always protected) When the Kindle is jostled in a bag, it tends to wake just long enough to connect to the wifi, but not quite long enough to sync to the latest whispersync position. Then, as it's going back to sleep, it updates the whispersync with the Kindle's last read position and overwrites wherever I left off in Audible or on the Kindle phone app. Overall, I would highly recommend this case if you're looking for a case that's durable, easy to hold, and can stand on a table or other surface while reading. Just be aware that wireless charging isn't possible unless the device is removed from the case.

First off, my last PC case was a mid-tower and that felt quite a bit cramped, especially with modern graphics cards getting larger and larger, and CPU air coolers being so damn huge that it takes up the rest of the space in your case. Oh and then there was the hard drives with their cables dangling in the way. Some people are really good at cable management and those people are cool and all, but I wound up with my last case looking a total wreck because I just didn't have any room for anything. Well this case is a full tower so it's much more roomy. Hard drives are actually oriented sideways relative to the front of the case, so the cables aren't in the way and there's enough spots to route cables through that you don't even have to see them if you don't want to. My power supply has all the cables nicely pre-wrapped and it's modular so I can install them as I need them (or don't and save some more space) and combine that with being able to route the cables around the back of the motherboard and the whole thing has a MUCH cleaner look to it. You might almost be convinced I'm now one of those cool guys who can do really good cable management. The glass side panel is tinted a bit, but if you have some fancy internal lights you can still easily see everything. I've got my CPU cooled with a huge Noctua DH-15 cooler and with everything running it barely makes any noise. The hard drive makes more noise than the fans do. I docked one star off the noise level because the hard drive DOES make a lot of noise. I think it vibrates the whole case or something. Maybe if it had some kind of dampening it wouldn't be so bad...but it's still a whole lot quieter than my old Lian Li case. There's also plenty of ventilation holes in the top, front, back and bottom of the case. The top and bottom also has an external air filter held in place by magnets so you can help keep the insides of your case from getting dusty. All in all though, this has been a great case as long as you don't mind the size. I used to prefer the mid towers but I think I enjoy having all this extra room. It has made installing everything much easier.

Hindsight: I wouldn’t have had the storage space for a 10” dobsonian scope anyway, and the portability of this scope will make me want to use it more! Setup was easy. Downloading the StarSense app was simple, mounting and aligning the scope, red dot, and StarSense during the day was a breeze. This evening was overcast but clear dark sky told me I’d have an hour where seeing would improve so I brought it out and started viewing. God I missed this. I haven’t had a telescope since I was a young teenager and there’s just something so nostalgic and calming about sitting back and looking over the craters on the moon. The entire hour was over before I knew it. I’ve attached a low magnification image and a high magnification image just captured through my smartphone because, somehow, no one has posted any images of captures from this scope. Very happy with my purchase, and can’t wait to find some clear dark sky to really test what StarSense can do! 4 stars because I replaced the lenses and diagonal as soon as I held them (plastic pieces that didn’t feel substantial) and even at this price it would be nice to have fine focus adjustment, but other than that for the price I’m very happy.

The headphones worked as expected, for the first 2 months. Then, I developed a pretty severe allergic reaction to them. It took me a couple months to figure out what was causing the reaction, because I wear the earbuds so sporadically, and the reaction was not initially so severe but would last for days after wearing them. (Typically, for me, allergic reactions calm down after removing the allergen pretty quickly -- but not this time! So I thought it must be something environmental.) These headphones caused contact dermatitis in my ear canal and the outside of my ear where the hook wraps around. On the same day as wearing the headphones my ear canals will swell nearly shut, then the itching and oozing starts. My ears leak liquid like crazy for a few DAYS, then it calms down but crusty irritated skin remains. It takes about a week to recover from wearing these. The most frustrating thing is that Apple does NOT stand behind this product. They said that since I did not buy it directly from them I could not get a refund. Clearly, to me, since such a large number of customers are having reactions that make it unusable, the product is defective! I spoke on the phone to Apple for nearly an hour, and after giving them all these details including symptoms and serial number, they were like "Sorry, but there is nothing we can do, call Amazon." Then amazon puts me on hold for a half hour, and are like "sorry, return window closed." This is COMMON reaction. Just google it. Don't risk your ears or your money.

review_text: It's a cheap system, so you get a cheap system. Decent video quality. You can't get the video or pictures that are recorded, off of the recorder. First time Apple watch purchaser here. I tried other cheap(er) watches and kept returning them - no bang-for-the-buck. This is pricey, no doubt about it. Grudgingly coughing up $425 and comforting myself with Amazon's platinum return policy, I decided to give it a go. I'm awfully glad I did. So here's the thing: there's no killer app for me. Truly. No one thing that goes A-HA and makes me love it..... ......BUT, there are tons of little things that, together, are more important than each one individually. - Blood pressure monitor - PulsOx monitor - Walkie-talkie function. I thought this would be a gimmick but it's so damn helpful when I'm trying to remember if I need to pick up eggs at the grocery store - Checking texts without having to pick my phone up each time - Checking Telegram, ditto - Pings from Life360 (an app I pay for) telling me when my family members have arrived/left somewhere so I know if I need to get moving so I can pick them up - A watchface with my next appointment prominently displayed along the bottom - An exercise "ring" sort of thing that eggs me on to: stand up for a minute or two once an hour; exercise at least 45 minutes a day; get in at least 10K steps a day. Again, sounds gimmicky, hell it is gimmicky.... but isn't the old saw that if it's stupid but it works, it ain't stupid? - Tile tracking of my phone and wallet. Push a button and hey, that's where I left my phone - Stronglifts integration so when I'm at the gym I don't have to keep staring at my phone to know when to start my next set. It has haptics. My wrist buzzes, time to stop writing that email and get to work - Haptics in general, which is a much nicer way to wake up in the morning vs. the BLAM BLAM BLAM of the alarm clock. It buzzes your wrist in increasing intensity until you wake up. Seriously a nice way to rise and shine. - Sleep behavior analysis. Tells me if my sleep is getting interrupted, the levels of deep sleep, etc. Not sure if it's even all that overly actionable but it's nice to see and it does sort of course-correct me if I'm only giving myself 4-6 hours of sleep vs. the 7-8 I need - EKG. Yes, you can actually take EKGs of your heart to see if there's irregular rhythms - Fall detection. Hopefully I'll never need it but if you fall and don't turn it off, it calls 911. Nice feature for older folks. - NFC. Instead of bringing my wallet, I have my watch. Touch and go. I haven't tried this yet of all the features so this one may not be ready for prime time, but looking forward to giving it a go. - Set a remote time for my phone camera so I can get in the picture! - Calls on my watch. Never thought I'd use it but I can now live out my fantasies of living in a Jetsons world. Quality is great and it's especially useful when on a conference call when you don't need to speak much. - News flash items. I get critical news from Wall Street Journal, NY Times and Washington Post that I can scroll through - Siri on command. My sole critique is here - you're supposed to be able to "raise to talk to Siri" but it doesn't work well at all. You have to push the little button on the side. Pretty mild criticism, but still on balance it's great because I can say "how's the weather?" or ask a question and boom, instant results TL;DR There's a ton of stuff, each of which is mostly on the "That's nice but not overwhelming" end of the scale that together makes for a great device. I'm happy with it even at the eye-watering price. And like all Apple devices, if it's too pricey for you, wait a year and you'll get it substantially cheaper.

I bought two of these, hoping to push signal upstairs and to the far end of the house. Sometimes, it has worked. But... The biggest problem that I have had was getting a bad IP address through the extender: Though the Netgear router itself seems to hand out proper (192.168.1.x ) addresses, the extender sometimes coughs up a 192.168.0.x address for the client. Customer service was not useful for this problem, and not worth the attitude and overseas gibberish. Now that I have shelved one of the extenders and dumbed down the other, I am occasionally not getting an address from the extender (ie, 169.x.x.x). Do not plan on using the same SSID as the host router (especially with two extenders, which is verboten, since one may try to chain off the other), but using the same id will also complicate problem isolation. For instance, VOIP connections are not clean over the extender, I could only determine this by checking the ssid that my phone was using. Do not buy this extender if you have or plan to buy a WiFi-6 router. It will work (with the above qualifications), but you may find the extra strength & speed of a newer router to actually be significantly faster than using the extender in a given location. I would guess that some of the problems above could be fixed with some software mods; in particular, the ability to lock the extender on a single router's MAC would allow it to share name SSID's in a multi extender environment. Something else will need to be done about the DHCP issue. Netgear also has an attractive "Nighthawk" app for network mapping and device config mods; it has no idea what to do with this device.

Hey - the lights actually work pretty good. But here is the bad: you have to constantly adjust these lights to when you turn them off and on. For example, they don't have an "off switch" you simply dim them all the way out until they are off. Additionally adjusting the white balance is essentially broken as it adjusts the brightness of the warm/cool leds MUCH more than it should. For example when I go 50/50 for warm/cool leds, I would expect that the light output would remain pretty much the same. But in reality the light output dims a whole bunch. So what I end up doing is this constant thing where I (1) change white balance (2) re-adjust light levels (3) change white balance... At certain low level settings the LED lights will actually flicker. The control of the light should have used with a high resolution PWM (pulse width modulation - a digital dimmer) that is standard on most micro-controllers. The problem with the low resolution PWM scheme that is used is that this product will likely have flicker on a lot of cameras. Like what the heck? This product when all the way through the design and manufacture process and they used software logic that is completely bugged out. Did they even test this product with users? Unbelievable! Every single time I want to turn this product on I have to re-adjust both knobs on both lights, so 4x adjustments total. I swear that I have to spend about 5 to 10 minutes to get proper light levels. Instead of dealing with this I just simply leave the lights on all the time. I'm thinking about getting a barrel plug switch just to allow me to shut off the device so that I don't have to re-adjust everything when I want to turn it on. As a software engineer I know exactly how to get this sort of calculation right, which is based on light output calculations of the gamma control curve and using that to set the PWM of the light. The manufactured messed this software up. It becomes apparent as soon as you use this product. Until they MFG fixes this in software (and adds a power switch!) then I suggest people look elsewhere.

What I liked about this soundbar is the dialogue can definitely be heard. You can also adjust the Treble and Bass to your liking while presets are available. The inputs accommodates older and new tvs. It even has an output to connect another subwoofer which is a nice feature. You can use an hdmi arc, optical, but I'm only using the aux connection since that's the only connection available for my TV which is OK for me. As much as I like that I can hear the vocals when I watch a movie using this soundbar, the bass from the subwoofer is extremely lacking. It's one of the reasons I bought this product, but the only way for me to know the sub is working is if I put my hand underneath the sub and feel it vibrate. I originally placed the sub on the floor next to my tv, then I decided to move it next to the couch across the TV. Still, I can barely hear the bass. Since the price was cheap when I bought this soundbar, I decided to buy a 60w subwoofer and it made a big difference. Now it sounds full and I can feel the bass rumbling. If you're looking to hear the dialogue in a movie, then this will work. If you want to hear and feel the bass, then buy something else or get ready to purchase a separate subwoofer.

I purchased the CM-3201 LTE filter hoping that it would fix a problem I had with two channels pixelating, with the signal going up and down just enough (value of 59 - 87, with sometimes as low as 0, out of 100) to cause this. The LTE filter did not solve my problem. The problem exists exactly like it did before. These two troublesome channels are full power and their transmitting antennas are even mounted on the same tower and height as all the other channels that give no problem. However, one thing that should be noted is that although the filter I received states on its glued-on label that it passes the signals in the 5 - 599MHz range (only up to UHF channel 35), it actually passes as high as 609MHz, namely, up to channel 36. There is a channel 36 (not virtual, but actual transmission) in my area and it did not block it; the signal passed right through it. The worded specifications on the Channel Master website states that it passes signals in the 5 - 609MHz range (up to channel 36), this is even though the photo of the filter in the same webpage shows the filter's glued-on label as stating 5 - 599Mhz (as if it blocked channel 36). Channel Master has to fix this inconsistency in specs as well as Amazon. I wrote Channel Master about this and they responded to me that the LTE filter should pass the 5 - 609MHz signals, although they made no mention as to why the inconsistency in the filter's misleading glued-on label. On a separate matter, there is no specification as to any signal loss by attaching this filter, thus, I suppose that there is none. I experimented observing the signal range on my TV and antenna setup, both with and without the LTE filter and on every channel. There was no difference as to signal strength. In summary, I wasted my money, but there was only one way to find out if my problem had to do with the cell phone towers in my area.

I used this as a second monitor connected directly to my MacBook Pro via the USB-C to USB-C cable. The monitor is also connected directly into the electrical outlet via the power adapter. It was working fine for three months then abruptly stopped working even though I didn't move it or change anything. Now, even though it is connected to power and through the USB-C cord, it says "NO SIGNAL" then immediately goes into "POWER SAVING" before it goes to sleep. I've tried unplugging and replugging the cables, and switching to different USB-C ports on my laptop. I even tried using a new USB-C to USB-C cable that I purchased separately. I also tried connecting the monitor to my laptop using the HDMI port -- and none of those attempts work. My monitor is only 3 months old and it's already faulty and unusable. I've seen some Amazon reviews that mention that this has happened to others as well -- where the monitor stops working 3 or 4 months after purchase, so this seems to be a common issue. I've reached out directly to Newsoul to troubleshoot and can update this review with how that all shakes out. But this has been a real disappointment. UPDATE: After a couple days and a few emails back and forth explaining my setup and all the troubleshooting I did, the company agreed that the monitor was broken, and shipped me a new one very quickly. Customer service was fine but now I’m concerned this new one will break after 3 months too. They didn’t explain why the old one broke after I didn’t do anything to it, so we’ll see if this one ends up being a dud too.

I bought this to serve as a repeater (my old one could only do wireless bridging on 2.4 ghz but I wanted one at 5G so file transfers woul be faster). First headache is that you need internet when you first set up the product. You have to go connect it to another router and use its internet connection to help you begin the setup process. Second headache is that you have to create a Netgear account. That's another password to remember. Third headache is that if you want to create a wireless bridge, you have to know exactly where to look. Advanced->Advanced Setup->Advanced Wireless Settings. Then at the very bottom, click on "Use other operation mode." When you click on that, a new section pops up, as well as a purple button disguised as a banner. It's like they don't want you to use this device for a wireless bridge. Fourth headache is that whenever you want to login, it takes a few seconds to look for the internet. If it finds the internet, it makes you log into the Netgear account. If it doesn't find the internet, you can log in via the local account. In either case, you get to look at the same guy/actor's picture while waiting to get to the login screen. I would rather look at a solid background than at that guy's face one more time. Fifth headache is that it seems to start blocking random connections. It is very weird. DNS requests for only amazon.com and www.amazon.com will time out, but I can request the DNS for any other site, including smile.amazon.com. Pings to a server's virtual IP address will be blocked, and I can't ping my computer from the server. If I restart the router, communication resumes for a while until it is blocked again. I've gone through every setting and can't see what could be causing it. The last headache is the worst, especially when you're working from home due to the coronavirus and it starts blocking some of your connections.
