I'm conflicted with this device. I bought it to use the FIRST PARTY Microsoft branded OEM component cables with my original Xbox. And it does that. However that's not all it does. Many games on Xbox aren't HD. The most that aren't, this converter struggles with. Most of the time there are vertical lines either static, or slowly moving left or right. I presume this is some form of interlacing. Even with the Xbox set to 480p, with my AVR and TV stating it's receiving 480p, the lines persist. However, now lets get to why I'm conflicted. I took my Xbox 360 and hooked it up instead. Set it to 1080p. The lines were GONE. I replayed the same scenes that really brought them out. Nothing. Then, I switched the resolution to 720p. Still, completely gone. So then I set it to 480p. The lines were back in full force - now, on the Xbox 360. A shame, as this converter was so close to a home run. Wouldn't practically use the Xbox 360 with component cables anyhow, because it has HDMI. So in the end, it doesn't perfectly do the job I purchased it for. Among other things, the input lag with this converter is either very little to non existent. With my Samsung QN90A in game mode, everything feels snappy and on point. That's coming from someone accustomed to 120/144Hz low response time displays. All in all though, it's not horrible enough to return it. I knew it wasn't a perfect solution, but it will suffice for the time being and will serve for testing/troubleshooting future consoles. As far as a permanent solution for the Xbox original, I have the Chimeric HDMI adapter on the way as it's the end all be all for maximum fidelity on the Xbox - and frankly, a more elegant solution. May update with pictures because everyone loves pictures

Cons: They must have had an internal communication failure between engineering and marketing because nothing about this PCB is 20Gbps capable. The main chip on the PCB is ASMedia's 3142 PCI-e Gen 3 X2 (not X4, which would be required for speeds over 16 Gbps ) to USB 3.1 Gen 2 (not USB 3.2 Gen 2) 10Gbps (not 20Gbps) controller. Windows 10 will automatically install the driver, "ASMedia USB 3.1 eXtensible Host Controller - 1.10 (Microsoft)". That controller has two USB 3.1 outputs, the first of which directly connects to one USB-A port. (on back, furthest from the type-c port.) The controller's second output connects to a hub chip (VL822-Q8, also USB 3.1 Gen 2 @ 10Gbps aggregate) that splits off to the remaining 4 ports. This card can't run anything at 20Gbps and the only way to get 10Gbps would be to only use one port at a time. The orientation on the USB outputs might cause some trouble plugging things in fully when it's used in chassis where the back plate is cast metal rather than stamped sheet metal. My use for this card is in a Dell R720 2U Server. It's back plate is made of thicker metal that prevents inserting the USB-A cables fully (and connect properly with USB 3+) without modification. Pros: Build quality looks good. Windows installs drivers automatically. I can confirm that it's capable of 10Gbps

These are really a triumph of form over function. Starting with the robust little box, which is almost impossible to open. The top part should have "thumb" cut-outs so you can grip the inner part whilst pulling the outer lid off, but it doesn't. A struggle just to get the box open, as the lid is very close-fitting.Inside, the holder/charger is a smooth flattened egg shape, nestled - quite tightly - inside a flattened egg shaped recess in the plastic moulding. There's a bit of a cut-out but the charger is smooth and unless you have sticky fingers, you won't get it out on the first attempt. Once out, the top flips open - but again it's completely smooth and nothing to grip. There is a knack to it and once learnt it's OK... The individual buds are held in by quite a strong magnet, and again it's hard to get a grip to pull them out. There's a button on the bottom of the charger but again, totally smooth and virtually invisible; you certainly couldn't find it by touch alone or in dim light. There are volume / function "buttons" (touch areas) on the buds and again, not marked.So these take a bit of getting used to and can be fiddly, especially at first use.But they're great. Sound quality is great, volume control is great, battery life is ... OK.The associated phone app does virtually nothing as far as I can see. And the name - EarFun - is just cringeworthy.I'm a "newbie" to using ear buds, and still think that people walking down the street talking to an "invisible friend" look totally ridiculous. But I'm an ancient luddite. Certainly these will be used - for instance when I'm working in the garage. I don't need to use them for phone calls; if I take a call, I stop what I'm doing to give the caller my full attention, so holding a phone is no problem. What I am disappointed about - and it's not the buds' fault - is that they don't work well with my Windows laptop. I'd hoped I could listen to zoom webinars etc whilst in the same room as my partner watching TV. But the Bluetooth on my (quite old) laptop is such that unless my head is within 12" of the laptop keyboard, the bluetooth signal fades in and out every 1 - 2 seconds on each bud; much of the time either one or the other is working, but sometimes neither (and sometimes both). A check of the bluetooth signal from the laptop confirms the signal is very weak, so can't blame these buds really.There are cheaper buds on the market, and certainly ones that don't challenge you just opening the box. But these certainly look good and are tactile (and comfy in the ear) and give very good sound reproduction.

review_text: After our original remote mysteriously disappeared (we have children), we ordered this remote as a replacement. It showed up today and we put the AAA batteries in and were attempting to use it to turn on the TV when I felt a pain in my hand. I figured it was just a little shooting pain I get sometimes from work, but then it happened again and I grabbed it with my other hand and realized that the remote was burning hot. We managed to get the back plate off of the remote and saw that the plastic around one of the negative terminals was starting to melt, so we knocked the batteries out and let it cool down. On closer inspection, I noticed that the coils were a little bent out of whack, but I assume that is from the extreme heat. I straightened out the coil and got a new set of batteries just in case there was something wrong with the (brand new) ones I put in. Immediately the heat came back so I knocked the batteries back out before it started to melt again. I'll be returning this immediately. This thing is incredibly dangerous. If it would have worked when I tried to use it, I likely would not have noticed the burning, as that is not where I normally hold the remote. I happened to be holding the bottom of it at the time since I was looking around the TV for a manual button, since the remote wasn't functioning. These things have burnt down houses before. Buyer beware. It gave me a nice burn on the palm of my left hand for the trouble of ordering it, and I still have no way to turn on our bedroom TV.

The newly renamed Zepp app tracks sleep and gives you a nightly sleep score, as well as breaks down your time spent in deep, light or REM stages. It's actually been really helpful in getting me to engage in more mindful sleep practice. The battery life is as advertised, FANTASTIC. I have been putting it on the charger at 30% and i have only had to charge it twice since delivery. The tracking modes I've used for exercise work pretty well. The GPS tracking for outdoor running works really well! I have been very pleasantly surprised by how well it works, actually. It connects in a few seconds, maybe 10-15 at most in a dense urban area, and the few times I've used it running trails the connection works much faster. The app has many features I have yet to utilize, but there is plenty there, including means for tracking a whole slew of physical measurements, calorie counting, water intake, etc. It does basic notifications for texts, calls, has a music controller, but doesn't have a ton of "true smartwatch" features, it's definitely not meant to replace or even stand in for a phone. Received Eero 6 three pack mesh system as a gift. I replaced our aged Airport Extreme/Airport Express router system with the Eero and it dramatically improved both the signal strength and coverage throughout our 3000 sf house, garage, back patio and front porch. We pay for 100 meg service but really only approached that speed on our Mac Books in two rooms. iPad topped out at around 50 meg and iPhones typically about 25 meg. In a couple remote rooms speed was down to 10-12 meg. Now we have 100 meg (or even slightly higher) on all devices in every corner of the house. One disappointment was that the installation instructions were too basic and did not cover common contingencies - despite the fact that the Eero 6 has those capabilities. Our cell reception in the room where our modem is located was not strong enough for the Eero 6 to connect during installation. After 3 failed attempts, I went to the support page on Eero.com and after 20 mins of searching discovered alternate instructions covering when you lack a cell signal. Those instructions worked perfectly and I had the system up and running, and the old routers disconnected in about 15 mins. This could have been just as quick and easy as a "normal" install if Eero had just included this information with the unit. After installation, all units seemed to learn all devices within the first 12 hrs, and now seamlessly hand them off as the device move through the house. Another plus is that it is very easy to move the units to find the optimum locations. You unplug a unit, move it to a new location and plug it in. Within a minute the unit is back locked on. Overall, the Eero 6 system is easy to install and provides fast Wi-Fi with very uniform coverage. I would have given 5 stars if the alternate instructions had been provided with the system.

review_text: I have 3 of these units in all different kinds of configurations, mainly for Roku movies or PS4/PC gaming. The one common thread among them all? They all keep blacking temporarily every 3-8 minutes before the signal comes back. The worst part about it is that I'm not even pushing it to it's stated spec. The specs say it can handle 4K at 60Hz; I'm only pushing 4K at 30Hz and it still keeps blacking out constantly.

While it might look good and the brand is something I know, the unit is not something I would tell someone they should buy. It pulls in a lot of noise on my vehicle, I have to back off the RF Gain and turn up the squelch quite far or it just pulls noise and static. I have been through 2 antennas, mounts and coax cables. The first was a K40 mag mount which you can't use with these radios or the radio fails the TX test due to no grounding on the antenna, the second is a Wilson Antenna and Wilson body mount with a new coax cable, same results with the noise, vehicle running or not it seems to have a very sensitive receive on it. The display is worthless, you can't see it in bright light, you have to literally have the unit facing you to even see anything of the display, I should of bought something old school with a needle rather than this digital LCD screen. Now at night time, the screen looks great, but my work is during the day, so not much good for me.

PROS: The ECM-B1M is an excellent sounding microphone that checks almost every box for a quality shotgun microphone. The super directional mode works very well at blocking out excess and ambient noise around the talent and being able to switch into omni directional is great when turning the camera around for vlogging or showcasing products. Also the fact that this microphone can just connect via hot shoe makes it all the better. I did a comparison between the audio quality of this microphone vs Rode VideoMic NTG vs Deity Duo... and I found the Sony to be the best all around in the super directional mode. CONS: The built-in shock mount allows the microphone to move around a bit to absorb shock when vlogging or moving during video capture. This review is about the Nakamichi Shockwafe PRO 7.1 eARC (7.1.4ch SSE MAX). I bought the Nakamichi to replace a Samsung HW-K950 5.1.4-channel system that I’d purchased new in 2016. It died after almost seven years of service. That system boasted 16 drivers total, four of which were up-firing speakers. It did a decent job of implementing Dolby Atmos. With it, we enjoyed listening to music and to movie soundtracks with their details vibrant and well-presented. While looking for a new system to replace it, I was put off by the price of the latest top-of-the-line Samsung, the HW-Q990C. So, I looked at other Samsung models and those of other manufacturers (JBL, Sony, Bose, etc.) including LG’s offering, the S95QR. In the past, I’d read about Nakamichi products, and reviews of the latest seemed compelling. After seven years, I expected the competition to have caught up with and surpassed 2016 Samsung’s HW-K950. Given the size of my apartment, I chose the Nakamichi Shockwafe 7.1.4ch PRO eARC SSE MAX. What a disappointment! The most important attribute a sound system is the quality of its sound. No matter how much I fiddled with it, I never got anything close to decent sound, let alone the sound of the K950. In a word: it's boomy! Even with the treble topped out, it’s still got far too much volume in the lower range. There’s just no crispness. Also, channel separation is weak. The subwoofer is impressive to look at and it pumps out tremendous volume in the low range. But, its sound just doesn’t satisfy due to the lack of upper range from the rest of the system. In the end, even the bass tends to lack definition. The two rear-surround sound speakers connect to the subwoofer, where their amplifiers are located. They connect via puny 20-gauge solid strand wire, 33-feet long, with RCA jacks at each end. That’s at least 0.6 ohms of resistance just in the wire. Which says: low-power, low quality. I will say no more about them. Yes, the system features an immersive surround-sound effect. Dolby Atmos test videos show the Nakamichi at its best. However, those effects do not outshine the overall poor quality of its audio system. With the Surround Sound feature enabled, the sound stage is greatly widened and feels immersive. However, once again the lack of high-end detail translates to a stage where the elements are blurred. Then, there are more practical considerations. For example, if the audio or video stream changes format, the system drops the audio for four, five or more seconds. At first, it was confusing – did I misconfigure something? Once I figured out what was going on, it ended up being a real irritation: you will lose the first part of the audio of any program when a format change occurs. Nakamichi brags about their Bluetooth 5.0 with aptX HD. However, I heard slight crackling and other effects during audio playback over BT that I’ve not heard with any other devices. Is volume control important? Strangely, using the controls on the remote or soundbar, the volume steps up and down, two units at a time (0, 2, 4, 6, 8, etc.) When changing the volume level over Bluetooth, the steps are four units at a time (0, 4, 8, 12, 16, etc.) However, each graduation is about 6 dB, which, especially, on the low end, is far too large. I frequently found that the sound was either that little bit too loud, or that little bit too soft, and there was nothing I could do about it. All because somebody didn’t want to deliver a control with any finer graduation. On an all-digital system, finer control costs nothing – it’s simply a bad design. And, speaking of controls, most of them lack range. For example, there isn’t a really meaningful difference between full and low settings for center channel volume, treble, back-surround or side tweeters. Finally, there’s the remote control. There is real virtue in being able to control every feature of a device without having to use another smart device, like a smartphone or a tablet. That everything about the system that can be configured is accessible via the remote is pretty cool. However, the Nakamichi remote control is poorly laid out, its instructions are difficult to understand, and the display on the soundbar presents text in a non-intuitive way. I found myself referring back to the manual (on my smartphone), time after time to try to figure out what was being displayed. In the end, it was a whole lot of work for very little reward. Summary: 2016 Samsung HW-K950: 4.5/5.0 2023 Nakamichi Shockwafe PRO 7.1 eARC: 1.5/5.0

Just dipping my toes into DMR and gave this a go as a first hotspot. Kind of wishing I had picked a different one since I spent most of the day getting this going despite having a lot of experience with raspberry pi and radio in general (though admittedly brand new to DMR.) First issue I ran into was trying to figure out which radio/modem to choose in pistar's setup. There's a question about it with multiple different answers and another review that said to use "MMDVM_HS_Hat (DB9MAT & DF2ET) for Pi (GPIO)" which it turns out is correct...but...didn't seem to be working so I questioned it. And when I ran 'sudo pistar-findmodem' it reported as a MMDVM_HS_Dual_Hat even though this is pretty obviously not a dual board. Plus the firmware was v1.3.something and current is up to 1.4 so I decided to upgrade it. But...which TXCO does it have? So I wound up removing the OLED so I could read the package and determined it was a 14.7456 MHz TXCO and flashed it with 'sudo pistar-mmdvmhshatflash hs_hat' Turns out that was right but it still took me awhile to figure it out because first I missed that I had my radio configured for TS1 while pistar was expecting TS2. And second...the sticker on the board said the offset was 500 but that was definitely NOT the case. I finally enabled debug level logging in MMDVMHost and saw that with -500 offset it was hearing something but not enough to decode. And after some experimentation found that -200 got me down to 0.2% BER. Finally Success! Also not sure why it comes with only 2 standoffs to separate the boards and 2 short screws and 2 long screws - but no nuts. I'm guessing they assume you don't need standoffs and long screws on the side with the headers to join the boards as the headers provide the support there. I assume the 2 extra sets of header pins are for the optional OLED/Nextion connections under the LED's. So finally got it working but trying to figure out which "model" it was for config and flashing took way more effort than it should have. And the provided offset was way off. Still gets 3 stars since it does work and was one of the cheapest options with fastest delivery - but looses 2 due to incorrect and lacking documentation as well as coming flashed with the wrong firmware.

To start off, let me just say that I know I reviewed this product already about a week after I first got the cameras set up with like SUPER detailed information but for some reason my old review is now gone so I’ll do a much simpler pros/cons list and let you decide. Pros: - price point: when I bought them, they were marked WAY down. This same set seems to go on sale quite frequently too. - came with two cameras and the ability to add more to the same system. - pretty good visibility/visual quality on the cameras. - fairly easy to set up & easy to understand. instructions although be prepared for a good fight if you’re mounting these into siding. - app isn’t too difficult to figure out, settings are easy to find, app seems to work without issues that I’ve noticed. - cameras came slightly charged so the first time charging only took a couple of hours. - the spot light is actually really bright for such a little light! - when you speak to the app it comes out from the cameras fairly loud - I have mine set all the way up. Cons: - night mode: if there is any sort of bright light source near the cameras that is left on day and night (I.e. my neighbors front porch light) it messes with the auto detection for night mode. My back door camera (pointed at neighbors front door light) stays constantly in black and white mode because it can’t decide if it’s night or not and it only started once the light started being left on 24/7. The street light, although only being on at night, was causing intermittent issues with the night mode detection as well. - weather: I don’t know if it’s the fact that the front of these doesn’t have a smooth face or what, but when it rains water stays stuck on the actual camera lens making it almost impossible to see. - detection: this has been the biggest issue thus far… cameras have a thing that shows you AI filtered events which I can only assume is where the other half of the motion events go to be lost forever. You can not view the clips that were filtered either. If the AI was intuitive you would be able to go in and view filtered events to mark as junk or not which would overall I think improve the camera system exponentially! I have a camera on either side of my house facing a road and one camera will catch a car passing the front and the other camera will not catch the car passing the back or vice versa. - power management modes: my cameras were set to optimal surveillance when I first got them thinking the middle of the road option would be the best and I would run it like that until I had to charge it the best. That being said, the cameras are late to catch movement if someone is walking onto my porch, for example, and then it only record a couple of seconds (usually 10) of them standing there or whatever. Even if the person is actively moving around or talking it will randomly cut off. In the optimal surveillance mode I previously had the cameras in, the clip length is supposed to be able to record up to 60 seconds but I haven’t seen any clips even with people like actively walking around or talking or whatever being that long. It’s like it records long enough to let you know someone was there and that’s it. Really negates the purpose of a camera system in my opinion. Since I’ve had to charge my cameras I changed the settings to custom with the clip length set to 120 seconds and clip interval (although I’m unsure of what this setting truly is for - no clarification in book or listing) to 5 seconds to see if that better fits my needs fully accepting that I will probably have to charge them more frequently with this setting. If there is any significant change in battery life with these settings I will update again if my review doesn’t go missing again. - Battery life: in big bold writing on the box and in multiple places in the listing it advertises 180 days of battery life. My cameras made it 54 days before I charged them. To be fair they were each at ~20 and ~30 percent but the cameras has stopped really catching any events at all once they were between 50-40% so I really couldn’t afford to wait and see how long it took it to actually get down to dead 0. - activity zones: I’m honestly not even really sure what the point of these is at this rate… if you don’t set any it seems to miss a lot. If you set the zone to entire field of view it seems to miss a lot. If you set one specific zone it seems to still only do better at closer distances rather than far. - the app: in order to view live feed you have to click into camera one, let it load, then click out of that camera, click into camera two to let it load - it would make much more sense if you could swipe between the different cameras live feed even if it still needed a second to load, and especially if you have more than two camera linked. Normally not a huge issue but it is annoying but if you were trying to follow someone moving around your house then it would become an issue. If you’re watching the live feed of the camera it will not also record at the same time. If you click the record button while viewing the live feed it saves it to your camera roll and not to the storage for the camera system. - charging: Charging the first time from ~20-~30% it took almost a whole day. The charger that came with the cameras didn’t want to work. I also couldn’t get the cameras to charge while plugging the cord into the home base, I had to plug them into a normal plug in order for them to charge. - audio quality: Audio feed from recordings is mostly hit or miss but I mean overall it’s not awful. Just not great. If I have someone standing on the other side of my porch talking I should be able to hear them clearly and sometimes that’s not the case. Audio quality when you’re speaking to the app is another story… there’s a massive lag in the audio and you can hear yourself talking on the live feed which is kind of hard to talk around - I think the mic picks up on what you’re saying as well as what you’re trying to say so it all becomes really jumbled. The way I’ve been able to get it to work best is to hit the talk button wait a second and then speak slowly and clearly. - distance: it’s weird because it seems like cameras pick and choose when they wanna actually detect motion within further distances. Sometimes it will catch motion further out sometimes it won’t. Another hit or miss thing. - visual quality: to be clear you’re probably not going to catch a tag on a car but I mean if someone is near you’re house you’re gonna be able to see them well enough that the police should be able to have plenty to go off of/use in court. - additional cameras: I’ve seen this price fluctuate a bit but right now they are $69.99 and I’ve seen them go closer to $100 and at that price you might as well just buy this set again and have an extra home base to keep as a spare or whatever. One single camera shouldn’t end up being more expensive bought alone and I haven’t seen a set of just cameras where you can buy more than one either. Conclusion… I paid $169.99 for this set (before tax) and I’ve seen it go as high as $230ish and as low as it is now at $149. If it had been any more expensive then it was when I bought it I would have gone ahead and sprung for a better camera system just because the price difference between this and another better system wouldn’t have been big enough to make it worth trying to go for the cheaper system. Also, if I had the choice today to buy more cameras to go onto this system or spend a little more for a better system with say 4 cameras (what I actually need to properly cover the outside of my home) I would spring for the better system with 4 because of not only better quality but also because the additional cameras seem so ridiculously priced. In the end, if you just want some peace of mind by having the ability to view outside and clips if something important happens and you find this on a good sale then it’s still worth it in my opinion. But, I wouldn’t pay full price for sure. ***as far as the security comments everyone is making I’ve not seen anything about that yet but if I had seen those reviews before I had bought these I also would not have bought them because I wanted a closed system with no subscription to keep things secure. But, then again my set is outside only so I’m not too terribly concerned that anyone who hacked my system would get much info about us other than my tag number so I’m not freaking out about it either. I however, will not be purchasing indoor cameras from this brand as I originally intended now.

Summary: These fit well and are more compact than the Bose SoundSport Free and the higher-end QuietComfort Earbuds. For those who are looking for a nice set of workout buds, these should be a good match with the proper considerations. I would recommend these to active/fitness folks who are interested in an alternative to PowerBeats. If you have any audiophile tendencies, these buds are ok but might disappoint. I was on a quest to find a suitable pair of true wireless earbuds for workouts and walking around. After doing all the prerequisite reading, the Bose Sport seemed like the best option on paper. Despite that, I ultimately chose a different set of earbuds. Here are my impressions. Sound: These buds have a good overall sound profile. However, the bass/low-end is distinct and overwhelming for my personal taste, which leans toward the flat or neutral realm of listening. The wired headphones that I currently use include an AKG Q701 and a Shure SE215. I avoid calling myself an audiophile (and I don’t have $1000 cans), but I have a particular preference for a certain kind of sound (clearly). My SE215s are in the style of In-Ear Monitors (IEM) and isolate better in outdoor settings than the Bose Sport while sounding more neutral. I usually do yard work with the SE215s and tried the Bose for the same task only to find that the latter did not isolate as well. It is important to note that the Sport do not have any kind of noise cancellation like the QC Earbuds. For Bluetooth headphones, I have a pair of Sennheiser HD 4.40. Hooked up to an iPhone, they sound blah. When connected to a device with AptX (not compatible with iPhone), they sound livelier though still mediocre, but I do prefer them over the Bose when using the higher quality codec. I primarily used the Sennheiser for walking around the office/house before looking for a set of true wireless buds. Importantly, the lack of AAC in these is a detractor when listening to music with the phone. The Bose Sport use AAC with the iPhone and sound better than the basic SBC profile. Vocals on the Bose sound pleasant and well-rounded (mids and highs present). In fact, compared to the Airpod Pros (the other set I am considering), the Bose are clearer and more enjoyable in the vocal range. The biggest problem is with the bass. There is just too much of it for someone with flat-sound preferences. If you like a good thump while working out, these might work well for you. If you do have audiophile tendencies, these might be lacking. My personal opinion, too, is that compared to AAC, every other current codec sounds better. Still, if you have an iPhone/iPad, you will want headphones with AAC capability because that is the best we are going to get. In for a penny, in for a pound. Fit: These fit me very well and felt more comfortable than the AirPods. I used the default medium tips and these felt securely tucked into my ears. As noted earlier, they are smaller than the other Bose buds and are less noticeable. They fit better (very subjective, I know) than the AirPod Pros, and I think they look better. Kudos to Bose for this. Battery: So-so. I used them for a few hours (maybe 4-5) and then needed a charge. I have not owned any other wireless buds with a charging case prior to this adventure, so the default 10-hour charge time in the case seems ok to me. Build/Overall Quality: For the price (close to AirPod Pro territory), they do feel premium. The charging case has a nice matte finish and seems sturdy. Connectivity/App: These never dropped a connection while I used them. The Bose Music app seems fine, but it is missing an EQ. This would really fix its core problem for me. Other users have asked for this (check Google for user feedback). Still, these cannot top the AirPod integration into the Apple ecosystem. Final Thoughts: After trying this and the AirPod Pros, I am sticking with the AirPods for a couple of reasons. First, the AirPods are not impressive sound-wise, but they are more neutral than the Bose. Further, the feature set on the AirPods for Apple users is compelling. Works easily with my iPad. Works easily with my MacBook. Has noise cancelling and other Apple black magic. Both have an IPX4 rating (minimal but adequate). If I am going to have a pair of walkaround true wireless earbuds for the sake of convenience, AirPods it is. And, with the current discounts, the Pros are a better deal than the higher-end QC Earbuds. At the end of the day, when I do want to Listen to Music, I will sit in my living room with the Q701s hooked up to my receiver that is piping in 24-bit/96Khz audio from the MacBook. Yes, I am that kind of weirdo.

Successfully set-up two other EUFY camera models (indoor pan & tilt types) using the same EUFY app, same procedure, same 2.4 network, and same Smartphone. That all went well so would indicate my network and phone are not the issues 2. Reloaded the EUFY App to current version 3. Tried two different E40 Solo Pro cameras 4. Tried two different Android Smartphone's (LG & ZTE) 5. Spoke with EUFY customer support and verified the procedure was correct and should work. They suggested turning off mobile data. getting closer to the router, and trying a different phone. Tried all three suggestions. One other reviewer of a similar model (E20) has also encountered the problem. Both the E20 & E40 are new models but use the same set-up app as the other EUFY products. Obviously there is some sort of mismatch involved but I'm at a loss as to what it is. I suspect it has something to do with the new model app code (or camera firmware) & certain phone models. Too bad because the E20/E40 appear to be affordable well-built products with a number of nice features. I gave the product 3 stars on the assumption that it is probably a good product since others have activated it so it "may be" a mismatch on my end. Still, the company needs to investigate and hopefully fix the problem.

I went to college for both Computer Engineering and Computer Science. I am pretty computer literate, and this was the best add-in Non-Raid PCIe Sata Card I could find. It uses one of the only two chipsets that I could find on Amazon (at the current time) that supports the PCIe 3.0 standard that gives up to double the bandwidth of the previous PCIe 2.0 standard. This card uses the ASMedia ASM1166 chipset. The other chipset I found that supports PCIe 3.0 is the Zhiwei JMB585 chipset. Most add-in Sata port cards, that you can find, are usually PCIe 2.0 and only work at half the bandwidth of the new PCIe 3.0 standard. It also runs on an x4 slot, as compared to other options that run on a slow x1 slot. It also has 6 sata ports, supports hot swapping and port multiplier (allows you to connect an external drive bay with multiple drives to one single sata port). You can hypothetically connect up to 30 drives to this card. I have not tried this myself and not sure how well it works. I was going to go with a multi-drive external bay, but the power supply on these external bays do not support multiple high power draw 3.5 in drives. They usually only support multiple 2.5 in drives that require a lot less power. Now the operating system you use is irrelevant in regards to booting up. The boot process is usually initialized by the bios. I had the exact opposite experience of a previous reviewer with regards to booting up the system. I recently upgraded to a mid-range computer system using a Gigabyte B450 Aorus Pro Wi-Fi Motherboard. This is a recent motherboard that was still being sold this last Christmas on Amazon. It has the lastest BIOS version. Despite this, it would not boot to any drive when running it in UEFI mode. I had to use an internal motherboard sata port to boot the system when running this add-in card in UEFI mode. But once I switched to legacy support on the BIOS, it would allow me to boot to any drive connected to any port on this add-in card, including hard drives, blu-ray drives and dvd-rom drives. When running this card in UEFI mode, no drives connected would appear in the BIOS screen, and you would not be able to select any as a boot drive. I been using up to all 6 ports on this card, because I have a lot of hard drives, and it's been very stable and working fine for almost 2 months (I purchased this card in February 2021). I do recommend this card, but you may want to experiment with running it in both legacy and UEFI mode, and seeing which works best on your motherboard.

review_text: Pros: ------------- The board has a lot going on with it. Lots of features, support for many things, its x570, its Gen 4, two m.2 slots, and its practically the only white(ish) x570 motherboard in existence! However, do not use Zen 3 on this board, everything else should be fine though. Cons: ------------- - ALL of my USB ports constantly shut off and back on, to the point where the system is not usable... I even RMA'd my board because of this problem, it had some other issues too, but they sent me back somebodies old used board and said its because of a parts shortage and they couldnt fix the issue. Some of the components on the "old" replacement board show obvious abuse and wear and tear, this replacement board could have spent a year or more in somebody elses computer, and this made (and makes) me very angry! I literally paid full price for a new board but i get an old used one... Regardless of all that, the new board has all of the same problems. I even bought a 3rd party PCIe x1 USB card and am running my USB devices off of there hoping to dodge the boards USB malfunctions, but i have lots of things using USB headers that cant use my card, and they are constantly resetting, and my computer is constantly playing the USB disconnected and reconnected sounds. FYI: The new PCIe x1 card is not working well either due to something else being wrong with the board. Problems with it are also preventing me from using some of my PCIe x1 slots, more on that next. - I'm guessing here, but if you use the second M.2 slot, you can only use one of the PCIe x1 slots (i bought x570 to avoid this problem). Im now stuck using either my Sound Blaster card, or my USB card. At least i believe this is why my other x1 slots arent working? I swapped the cards and only the first x1 slot worked in both situations proving both the sound card and usb card worked fine, but i havent removed the second m.2 drive to test further. Take a look at the picture of my PC and you'll probably understand why i refrain from ever removing anything. I did turn my computer on one time and my sound blaster card just started working, even the strip lights that are plugged into it turned on, everything worked just like its supposed to! But that was only once... out of many many many times turning this thing on and off. - Aura Creator Software is good and bad, i love how customizable it is and the things you can do with it, but i have specific effects running on my RAM LED's and on the rest of the motherboard, but minutes after applying it, they quit... every time, no matter what... So i installed Aura Sync through Armoury Crate. Its way harder to use with less customization options, and i feel like it requires Aura Sync, but that didnt resolve any issues. The animations dont play and all the lights freeze in place after running for a short period of time (like, 1 minute or so). - Every now and then, i feel like my keyboard begins to lag, and all of a sudden a button i pressed on the keyboard begins to repeat until i press it again. This might actually be the result of my addon USB card, but this wouldnt be a problem if it wasnt for the motherboard having usb issues. Removing the USB devices from the card and plugging them back in fixes it, every time, but that's an annoying step i shouldnt have to do, and its only temporary. - Sometimes when i turn my computer off, the power button will not turn it back on. I have to pull the power cord from the PSU and plug it back in. This is one of the reasons i sent the board in to be fixed, but it continues to happen with board #2. This has started to fizzle out and isnt much of a problem now, it might be from the most recent BIOS update. We'll see how this goes. - There's a major lack of white x570 motherboards on the market, and this is the only one that really exists that can even be considered as an option. There are parts that should be white and arent. For example, why is the heatsink on the mosfets silver? Why are the m.2 covers silver? What about the SATA ports? RAM slots? CPU socket? 24 pin power port? PCI slots? etc... I feel like there could have been more white, especially since that would help fill this gap in the market (no white x570 boards). Maybe we need a version 2 of this board since this one is getting quite old and doesnt work for zen 3? - If you buy this and put a Zen 3 processor in it, you will literally be throwing your money away. If you're putting Zen 2 in it, you should be good to go! Conclusion: ------------- I bought this for the AMD Ryzen 9 5950x CPU. I believe the issues with this board are based on the Zen 3 architecture only. Zen 2 CPU's and prior should work fine. Overall, if the USB issues can be fixed, i could live with the rest of the issues. The bios isnt too great but it does get the job done, it has a lot of limitations so if you plan to overclock, you wont get very far. I've upgraded to every iteration of BIOS's they've released for this board and they all have the same problems, but i feel like with each new version (beyond the betas), the USB issues are actually getting worse, not better. The issues with the PCIe ports and USB devices (including addon cards) are very very bad! I think the board needs more white parts and maybe even white panels that can be removed if the customer wanted the black and white theme. USB issue needs to be fixed, more PCIe lanes or better use of them so you can use more than 1 PCIe x1 slot, a better bios would be nice, and even tacking on an extra 50 bucks would be fine for most consumer if the thing would just WORK! I'm currently considering other motherboards to replace this with. I'll probably just 3D print white panels where i believe they should go.

I do not understand why the description says 1080p. Even the Image of the Product has 1080p highlighted. It will only project 1280*768. This is NOT 1080p and it is NOT 16:9. It is 16:10 at best which may seem like a small difference but at 100+ inches diagonal you will get a lot of wasted horizontal space. I must have played around with this thing for hours trying to figure out what was wrong, did I have a setting messed up, maybe my input device was not set correctly. Then I finally started looking closer at the description and it clearly says 1280*768. Aside from this and the fact that I will now have wasted space on my 100" 16:9 screen, the projector is very solid. The picture is clear and the sound is actually pretty good. I had some speakers set up ready to go and when I turned the projector on and played something the sound was so good I haven't bothered hooking them up. I probably still will but the point is you would be OKAY without any. My purpose was for playing video games in my office and not having to take over the living room TV to do so. So I am not watching big time movies or using it as a regular TV watching device. I pull down the screen, turn on the projector, play some PS4, turn it off, roll up the screen and back to the real world. My 3 stars is based on the inaccurate and confusing description. It doesn't help either that many of the Customer Answered questions confirm it is 16:9!! A simple measuring tape and calculator will prove that wrong. 16 divided by 9 is 1.78. Measure the projected picture and do the math, width divided by height. You get 1.67 which is 1280*768. Would love to be proven wrong and shown how to get true 16:9. I will happily update this review!!

I was excited about getting a set of wireless surround speakers because running cables is such a pain. I went through two soundbars but they just couldn’t overpower the sound of the air conditioner in my apartment (it’s noisy). Anyhow... The Good: each speaker has it’s own amp; no central amp/receiver is needed, just the wireless hub. Set up was a snap: unbox, place speakers, place hub, plug everything in, then start the sync process with the app on your phone. The app allows you to estimate the distance from the prime listening position. The speakers were loud enough to overcome the AC. The Bad: the app doesn’t allow you to adjust treble/bass independently, nor does this system support popular compressions for surround. Think of the cool things a full-up amp does, having you put that little microphone in different places while it calibrates itself; this doesn’t do that. The worst part: the sound at higher volumes becomes distorted and you can hear the boxes vibrate. On that, the drivers are in crappy plastic housing that probably contributes to the vibration. This is a little too much cost cutting in my opinion, and had briefly considered disassembling the enclosures and placing them in custom boxes but that was just too much work to recover quality when I could just return them. It doesn’t come with and independent remote control, but most everything can be done on the app. The AppleTV remote seemed to work for the volume just fine.

What a piece of junk. I bought this two months ago as a Christmas gift, and have only given it to the my sister last week. Let me tell ya, it’s one inconvenience after another. Here’s the list in chronological order. 1.) Opened it up, thinking it was bluetooth or had the required cables to connect to an iPhone. Turns out it didn’t and this one is my fault. I should have looked at the reviews. It will only come with an hdmi connector (both ends), and you’ll need a lightning-hdmi adapter if you want to use a wired connection with your phone. It’ll work if you’re only using it for a laptop. If you want to use Bluetooth, you need to buy a dongle that allows connection and attach it to the project. While there’s a USB port, you can’t use your typical charger to directly connect your phone into the projector. 2.) Bought an hdmi-lightning adapter, and it was easy to connect it at first where it’ll ask you to trust the device on your phone like the prompt that you get when you connect your phone to your computer. I don’t know why it requires that, but moving on. Once you accidentally turn off screen mirroring, good luck connect it to the stupid thing again. You’ll either have to reset your iPhone settings, or have to turn your iPhone off and on in order to reconnect. And you will have to do that a lot because it’ll kick you off whenever it decides to. You’d think you’d see it under the screen mirroring options, but nope. It’s not there at all. 3.) Once I got the hang of it, 10 minutes into continuously using it, it made a loud high pitched noise, and the image froze while distorted. No matter how many times I turned both the iPhone and projector on and off, it started doing it one minute into watching a video. I figured it was the adapter I bought. Because you need to power the hdmi adapter with a lightning charger, I thought it wasn’t getting enough power since I used the old iPhone charger that only delivers 5W. Switched it out with a 20W charger and power brick, but nope, still the same result. Then I used my other brick that delivered 65W. This time, the projector lasted a bit longer before doing the same thing as it did before. I give up. Piece of crap. It’s, overall, stupidly useless. You can’t use it. At least the one I got can’t be used. It’s cheap at $90, but you’d expect it function at least. What a piece of junk. I would have returned it if the return window hadn’t closed. Saved you some frustrations. Find a different projector.

Fantastic set! Unlike other products on the market, this is actually two identical units. Each one can accept a DVD. Most other units we’ve seen have one master unit with a DVD, and the other is just a screen. This one allows both kids to watch different shows OR the same show. Very cool. Screen size: VERY large. Crystal clear with vibrant colors. I can’t imagine a better screen. Speakers: Initially I didn’t think I liked them being in the front of the unit, as it makes the footprint larger. Since it’s just the back of the seat, though, this isn’t actually a big deal. Just didn’t think it was as sleek as it could’ve been. BUT, I was actually wrong! Having the speakers in the front is WAY BETTER. The kids CAN hear everything, but the adults up front don’t have to! Amazing difference. The units we had before had the speakers in the bottom. So as the noise projected down and back for the kids, they also projected forward. So the adults had to hear everything as loud as the kids heard it. No good. This configuration is so much nicer. Thank you! Buttons: Being on the front allows the kids to easily start and stop a movie, and switch back and forth between their movie and the other unit’s movie. I recommend purchasing another a/v cord so you can cross wire the two units like I did. That way either kid can switch to the other unit’s movie without having to swap any cords. You can see in one of my photos how there are three things plugged in instead of just the two cables it comes with. That’s why. The patch cord needed is 3.5mm (yup, I just saved you having to research that bit of info). Remotes: They are the same. One remote can control either unit. Just depends which one you point it towards. We keep one in each door so the kids can use them when they want to. But other situations may desire to only keep one in the back, and you can do that too. Opening: This unit is unique in that the door swings up. I show this in a photo. It’s too soon to tell, but I suspect this is an attempt to reduce the one recurring problem we’ve had with 4 different dvd player units over the past 10 years. That problem is the door eventually getting to the point that it doesn’t register being closed. By being a drop door, I don’t suspect this will be as likely of an issue down the road. Time will tell. My one and only gripe: The on/off switch is on the side of the unit BETWEEN the plugs, and is small-ish. It’s not awful, but having a larger switch on top or on a side, or even the bottom would be better. Because it has a battery, you sort of want to turn it off when not in use. You can push “pause”, but the kids typically just turn it off.

review_text: Although I've only had this drive for a couple of hours, I've come to several conclusions. - The capacity is nearly as advertised, just shy of 500gb. At the price paid, that is an exceptionally low price per gb! - The drive write times are relatively slow. I believe that this is a USB 2.0 drive, not the advertised USB 3.0. Using the USB 3 plug on my laptop, the write speed was 12-15mb/sec. Using the USB C plug, the write speed ranged from 12mb to 24mb/sec, with a mean speed of about 22mb/sec. - The capability of using 3 different types of plugs is terrific. However, the build quality is suboptimal. The drive connects to its colored housing by a clip which can be dislodged. My drive came out of its housing the first time I tried to remove it from the laptop plug. Fortunately, it was easy to put it back together. Be careful. Overall, the drive is a good value for the price, but you should buy it with the above caveats in mind. Subsequent review 12/5/20: I can no longer write to the drive. Additionally, folders of photos which were previously written to the drive are now empty. I would give zero stars if possible.

Hello all, I’m a WiFi technician, you can’t expect large results for the price. I can’t go realistically on a vacation for 95% percent off. As I tell my customers in WiFi terminology speed, what you pay is what you get. This is an ok, good, and awesome extender and will do the job for most of you, It’s not about how many devices are connected but really depends for what you use WiFi for and how many use it at the same time. This WiFi extender isn’t mesh, mesh means you don’t have to log off of the Host Router and log into the extender, you stay connected within the same WiFi network. This is not a mesh it’s a basic extender, meaning you have to log off of the host router and log into this none mesh extender meaning it cuts your speeds in half. Mesh extenders do not cut your speeds in half. Also, either mesh or none mesh extenders, I’ll show you how to get top speeds. Download a speed tester on your phone device, I choose Speedtest by Ookla, gives better results. Before connecting the WiFi extender. Do a speed test next to the host internet router, speeds can’t get any better since your next to the host‼️. Now go to the area which is the last place further away from the host router. Do a speed test there. If your speeds were poor or can’t reach, try the next room before closer to the host router. If speeds were better then try connecting the extender there. If extender is not giving good results even though WiFi bars are full try connecting extender in a different area within the room location otherwise try moving the extender a little closer to the host router. This practice will provide top speeds. Never install extender to far away from the host router, this can provide ugly speeds even though WiFi 🛜 bars are full. Now if it’s a mesh extender, same principle applies but don’t install mesh booster to close to the host router otherwise you may be connecting to the mesh extender and will provide slower speeds because host router will always be faster then a mesh or none mesh extender. What can reduce WiFi 🛜 range, water pipes, bricks, concrete, sheet metal, logs, marble etc. If your trying to get better range with top speeds from one room to another and there’s a bathroom in between, water pipes will reduce WiFi. So then try installing extender away from the bathroom. Test as you go. I don’t use speed test to check for best place, I use a WiFi value gauge meter. This never ends in explaining. Most important is you get the point in what I’m saying. Best of wishes to all. If any misspelled words, my apologies, I was texting fast.

I've been using this since April. I usually use KVM switches, but my preferred brand's new Displayport 1.4 models aren't compatible with my Dell WD19TB dock, so I decided to just use my monitor's DP and HDMI ports to switch between computers and something like this plugged into a hub. I had a number of problems with it, but i worked past most of them until recently. I plugged a USB hub into the input for this, and port A into my laptop dock and B into my desktop. My mouse, keyboard, gamepad, and one or two other things were plugged into the USB hub. Note, this is a powered hub so power draw should be a non-issue. 1. Regularly, something would just stop working until I unplugged it and plugged it back in to the hub. I tried a couple different hubs, same model different units and another from a completely different manufacturer, same problem no matter what. 2. It'll auto select kind of randomly. Not as in "it randomly decides to switch inputs," that would be much worse, but I leave my desktop off most of the time. If I do happen to shutdown/unplug this from my laptop dock, it'll sometimes default to switching to the desktop and sometimes won't. Not a big deal, just unpredictable when I'm doing some as simple as rewiring (Shelter at Home/starting to work from home has meant a lot of "what if I moved this..." situations). 3. I decided to alleviate some of these issues by getting a separate, dedicated USB hub switch for my keyboard/mouse/gamepad and plug this into my USB audio DAC. I figured it'd be nice to be able to leave the audio on my laptop dock if I need to switch over to my desktop just for a moment. I got a new Sabrent USB hub that's hire wattage, and plugged that directly into my laptop dock and plugged this USB switcher into that. USB audio would just die before a song finished playing while I was testing it. Plugged it into a USB-C adapter on my laptop dock (it has very limited USB ports), worked for a while, but after ~30-45 minutes stopped again. Right now it's sitting unplugged. I might keep playing with it, I honestly think most of the issues is that it draws power from the host devices it's plugged into. Seems logical, but I think the way it's implemented is bad. If you just need something simple, or you're going to use for a device you don't use frequently, it's probably fine. You may need to futz with it regularly, but it'll probably work for the most part. A few people report that it's blown up their computers... which is why I'm fairly confident it's a power draw problem.

I am happy with this purchase. Very functional, though aesthetics so so. I did have bluetooth connection issues when I first purchased, only to be resolved when I happen to by a new phone. I am no expert, but I suspect having a phone that supports bluetooth 5.2 was the major difference. I bumped up my review stars as I am now functional, but still note my previous issues as I suspect others may have similar issues if you don't have a latest gen phone. Pros: - The drop down mic design is fantastic. If you have to be on work calls (zoom or otherwise), having a really easy way to mute/unmute and to know if you are muted/unmuted is a massively important feature. With this headset I can just throw the mic up or down. - The mic sound quality is as good as I have found. I have earbuds/headsets from Bose, Plantronics, Samsung. In testing on a voice recorder at least, this Jabra headset came across the best. I didn't do any extreme tests of how the mic cancels out background noise, but in a work from home situation it seems sufficient to block the noise of my family behind me. Some of my Bose and Plantronics headsets do this well, but there is something less natural about how your voice comes through the mic, either because of the mic position or how it processes the sound. - The ANC and hearthrough implementation good enough to be useful. My Bose headphones definitely do this far better. But I also have earphones from Samsung where the noise cancellation is useless. On these the ANC is helpful in quieting the fairly loud noise of my heating/Ac units, and that is what I need most of the time. It is not as effective as my Bose headsets in blocking out the broader array of background noise - e.g. my Bose can pretty effectively mute the sound of the television if it is on it NYC street noise, this Jabra headset is less effective there. But again, ANC is good enough that I am glad I have it and better than some other attempts. - The headset feels well built, high quality. - The dongle Bluetooth connection to my computer has been very stable. If I only used this for my computer, then I I would have no Bluetooth complaints. - It almost does Bluetooth multipoint better than all my other headsets - will explain in cons. When working, I can move back and forth from my phone and computer relatively seamlessly. - Not my primary use case, but audio quality is pretty good. - The auto busy light is really helpful. My wife knows when I am on a call and shouldn't be interrupted as opposed to when I am just listening to a podcast or something. - Charging stand is a nice option. - Reasonably light. Cons - Updating my bluetooth issues. I just upgraded my phone to an S22 from an S20. The S22 has the latest bluetooth 5.2 support, while the S20 was 5.0. I have no disconnection issues with the new phone. I am no expert, but I suspect there is some sort of backwards compatibility issue. [PREVIOUS] The Bluetooth connection to my phone sporadically just disconnects. Mostly when not in active use, but occasionally when I am on a call or listening to something. Support offered only the normal repair, reset type advice, which didn't help. I could get a replacement, but seriously doubt this is an issue a replacement would fix. I think this is either a firmware issue, or a backwards compatibility issue (phone has Bluetooth 5.0 but not 5.2? Dunno if that matters). Again, connection to my computer through the dongle is rock solid and when working the multipoint is the best I have used. But I can't have my headset just disconnect from my phone in the middle of a call (worth noting I have no Bluetooth issues on my phone with the 4-5 other earbuds/headphones I use). - Aesthetics - I do wish they could make it smaller. Feels a bit like I am wearing a gaming headset on work calls. Worth it in terms of functionality and there are not smaller options with comparable functionality, but still wish it was smaller. - Comfort - Pretty comfortable for a good while, but after an hour or so my ears hurt

20200229 I want to like it more ... but I'm having a hard time. It has some attractive aspects, particularly that it is made in Texas. The case has many contradictions, such as the shell being sturdy, really sturdy, but the interior foam not so much. This case is great to have for protection that conforms to TSA specs, but it will force you to make some hard choices. Why would you want this case, rather than a regular camera bag? Because airlines are not very friendly, and they don't care who is carrying what, so if you get on the plane, even being a good flyer with only two carry-ons, and there is no room because the people in front of you are not such nice folks, the airline will make you check your bag. The airline won't ask if your bag is more important because it has expensive camera gear, the flight attendant will just order you to check it. They don't care. So, if it gets checked, it needs to be able to be locked, and it needs to be able to withstand the abuse dished out by the baggage handling. Hence, the Condition 1 case. This case is the 22" you-can-carry-it-onto-the-airplane size. That is nice to be able to carry it on, but the foam padding is so thick, don't expect to put very much into the case. The problem is the foam, it is not very dense, and it is the "pluckable" stuff that you customize for the items. Customizing is great, but BEWARE, it is a one-way trip. The foam is pluckable, which means once you've pulled it apart, there is no going back. Also, since the foam is not that dense, you need to leave a lot of foam between each item. I found that anything less than 2 cubes of foam was unworkable, and I tried to leave 3 pluckable cubes where possible. The other problem with the foam is it is not very dense. Not being so dense, more foam is needed to properly cradle the camera equipment. The next big problem is the size. This is not Condition 1's doing, it is the limitation of the 22" max for the airplane. The problem is this limits choices. Optimally, in the pluckable foam setting, it is best to place items vertically. For cameras, this means the lenses going up and down. For pistols, it would mean barrel down (or put another way, not laying things in horizontally). Doing this will get more items into the box. BUT, what lens will fit in there vertically. NOT the Sony G master 70-200. Certainly not the Sigma 150-600. Placing lenses in vertically, I can store a 100mm prime, a 50mm prime, one Sony 24-240 zoom, a camera body, and some incidentals (batteries, cards, and straps). Condition 1, if you are reading, you could have done a very different and much better system for this one box, specifically for camera equipment. Something more like what camera bags use, but just a little heavier. And, Condition 1, get better foam. This stuff is too light, feels like it will disolve in a few years. And, just use solid foam, not the pluckable stuff. The problem with pluckable foam is it will "pluck" by itself. Or, one mistake, and a piece is missing that you cannot put back. Solid foam, a sharpie, and a sharp blade would work much better. Or, as I said, a real padded divider system. ESPECIALLY since you are charging more money for this than some of the larger boxes. 20200312 Update I took the case on a trip. I fits perfectly in the overhead bin, it fills the bin almost completely. The size is just so there is enough slack to get the case in and out. I also took an empty LowePro camera bag with me, which was a good thing, since this case is nearly useless for doing anything outside of a car or an airport. Walking through the airport, the case is a bit unstable. Even the slightest bump or lift in the floor will upset the case, causing it to wobble back and forth. Twice it completely tipped over. Once the case gets off-balance, it wobbles back and forth with increased motion. I have not tested it more, or measured it, but I suspect that the wheel base is not appropriate for the righting arm, so once it is off balance, the motion will increase rather than decrease. Keep a firm grip on it. The carry-behind handle release is not ergonomic. To release the handle (to extend it) you must press on a plastic retainer. This requires two hands. Two hands are not always available when in the airport dealing with other items. Also, the case shape sacrifices interior space for exterior asymmetric reinforcing. The case could have been made to have a bit more room on the inside. Changing the shape of the case would also allow spacing the wheels further apart, which would make the case more stable. Lastly, Condition 1 offers a variety of case sizes. Most of the cases have a price point proportionate to their size. This case is an outlier. Condition 1 charges a premium for this case, it being more expensive than the larger 25" x 10" version. That appears to me to be nothing more than price gouging because this case conforms to the TSA dimension constraints. Overall, the case is adequate, but I will be considering other systems in the future.

Update: FStop Labs, after reading my review below offered to send me another ND8 filter to replace the one that fell off my GoPro Hero 8. I received it today, and appreciate their good customer support. I revised my original rating from 1 star to 3 stars. I will continue to use these filters, and will update this review again in a month or so. I use my GoPro 8 at least 4-5 times every week, and it's always action on boats, mountain bikes, etc. It I never lose another one, I will eventually upgrade my review to 5 stars. The filters themselves are great, and they are certainly easy to take on and off the camera. Original Review: Seems like a great idea - design one set of filters, and then just make an adapter for each camera. The filters are oversize so they will fit cameras with bigger lenses. The adapter snaps onto the GoPro Hero 8, and is secure. The adapter is metal and the filters each have a magnetic border which allows them to snap into place onto the frame. I wondered how strong the magnets would be on an action cam where there could be a whole lotta shakin going on. Today was about my 3rd time to use one of the filters. Before taking off in the boat, my ND8 filter was on the camera. When the battery died and it was time to change it... no filter. Since the mount overhangs the boat, the filter is no doubt somewhere at the bottom of the lake. I also use my GoPro for mountain biking on very rough trails. I didn't even try these filters in that situation because I was nervous about the magnetic hold. There is no rim around the lens adapter. Just a flat filter magnetically stuck to a flat adapter. But I thought the boat would be safe. Not so. Unless you have your gopro mounted on a tripod I don't recommend these filters. They are not suitable for any action.

You would think that a company like IBM would know not to go cheap on such an important component in a computer, especially one touted as a "Gaming Computer", as the power supply, and yet Lenovo has done just that. The provided PSU is 500W maximum which means that it probably won't ever provide 500 watts, but the provided GEForce 3060 RTX requires at least 600 watts to run efficiently, and 750 watts would be even better. The problem is that you have to be very careful what power supply to buy, since the case is small and requires a small form factor PSU. My solution was Corsair SF Series, SF750, 750 Watt, SFX, 80+ Platinum Certified, Fully Modular Power Supply (CP-9020186-NA), with an additional NECESSARY purchase of the COMeap 24 Pin to 10 Pin ATX PSU Main Power Adapter Braided Sleeved Cable for IBM Lenovo PCs and Servers 12-inch(30cm) because the Lenovo motherboard has a 10-pin connector for the PSU. You have to remove the hard drive and hard drive bay in order to get the original power supply out, but fortunately that makes room for the additional cabling. The solution of course would have been for Lenovo to source for a better-powered small form factor PSU, but it's fortunate that the aftermarket provides such a solution. Kudos to Corsair for making the SF series to accomodate these small cases.

review_text: Very nice cameras. Great price,extremely well made and packaged. I am by no means a tech savvy guy but these were very easy to hook up and get running. I like the fact that they're hardwired because my house doesn't get a lot of sunlight and batteries would be expensive and too much trouble. I also don't get great Wi-Fi signal so the fact that it comes with its own DVR and records for a week before automatically resetting is great too. Picture is clear and night vision doesn't miss a trick. I mounted mine on the sides of my house pretty easily but I might add some hopefully helpful hints. First, after deciding the best places for coverage you would like, try to establish a place inside your home that you can plug them in. I got creative and was able to hide the thin power cords in cabinets and other not quite so noticeable places. After deciding these 2 things drill a hole through the exterior wall right where the camera will sit, or as close as possible, in order to hide the power cord and protect it from the elements. My home has vinyl siding and I punched through pretty easily using a 1.25" spayed bit in my drill. They're not very expensive and available at any hardware store. After pulling the large white wires through and plugging in the small power cord I shoved the white wires("pigtail") back into the wall so that only the little power cord was left showing on the inside wall. Next, I wrapped a piece of duct tape around the power cord where it was coming through the wall so I could protect the cord while putting spackle(again hardware store, cheap) to seal the hole(leaving large wires sealed in the wall). Before spackling the hole closed I replaced the insulation from the hole drilling by cutting a rag and stuffing it in. I then spackled the hole and after it was fully dried, sanded it smooth, removed the duct tape and painted it. Another very important step is caulking around the base of the camera outside. If it's not caulked and sealed up it can allow for all sorts of creepy crawlies in your walls as well as poor insulation. Caulking is easy. First, find an exterior latex caulk in a color close to your siding(you guessed it, hardware store, cheap). Next, after camera is securely fastened, squeeze caulk around the base with a caulk gun(hardware store,cheap) and then wipe away excess with a damp rag. It will dry and your home will be secure and protected. Hope this helps you and if you have any questions you can always ask the guy at, you got it again, the local hardware store.

I bought this router to be used as a elevated performance VPN client so I could protect all traffic leaving my home. I understand that I must have an account at an external VPN provider to support my VPN intentions. This device unfortunately also requires an additional login to the manufacturer to be active at all times for the VPN to work. The point of VPN is to limit the eyes-on activity, not add yet another activity identifying account. This router also apparently has intrusive activity in providing it's own unsigned certificates which creates problems with other secure applications that pick up self-signed certificates, blocks their use and creates continuous security alert prompts. The VPN software package supplying both client and server applications is a fee based add on that must be downloaded after router installation. Microsoft roots beginning to show? I am returning this router and have purchased an Asus 2900 that comes complete with the needed VPN functionality, both client and server, without additional cost and does not require any additional manufacturer connectivity.

This monitor does what it’s advertised to do well. When plugged into a PC/laptop as external display, it runs games great at 1440p & 144hz (up to 165hz display port). It also runs certain PS5 games that have 120hz support at 1440p very nicely. The biggest drawback I have found is that console games capped 60fps are a hit or miss on this monitor. This monitor does not do 60hz well for some reason. Obviously 60hz is not its intended function, but many of the older PS4 games, like older CoD titles (which run at 60hz), look terrible on this monitor. There’s ghosting, screen tearing, and input lag, even with the response time set to Level 1 in the monitor’s OS, the lowest value. Even Battlefield 2042, which is a next gen game meant to run at 60hz has ghosting and a slight input lag with this monitor. It’s not a true, smooth 60fps. This wasn’t an issue with the generic 24” 60hz flatscreen I used to play my PS5 on, for PS4 or PS5 games running at 60hz. So if you’re a PS5 owner looking for a “do it all” monitor for your next and last gen titles, you may be disappointed to see your last gen titles don’t run as well as before. Overall, still a good buy and a no brainer for PC users looking for a budget gaming monitor, or next gen console gamers.

I decided to get a TV for my bedroom, and after a lot of research between all the 32” TVs with either built-in Fire or Roku, I decided on this one and am so happy I did. I’m a woman of a certain age - old - and am technologically challenged, but setup of this TV was a breeze, starting with clear instructions on how to take it out of the box. (The screen came in a plastic bag with two handles, and it just slid out of the box.) The picture and sound quality are fantastic. There were a lot of questions in the Q&A section about Bluetooth. I got the 2020 version of this TV, and you CAN connect things with Bluetooth. It’s an option in Settings. I connected AirPods, and they work perfectly. Once connected, the speakers on the TV cut off, the remote’s volume control works on the AirPods, and they stayed paired with the TV so I don’t have to go through the process of pairing every time I turn on the TV. Now when I turn the TV on, the TV’s speakers come on until/unless I take my AirPods out of their charging case; if I put them back in while watching, the TV’s speakers automatically kick in. Couldn’t ask for it to work more smoothly! I have a Mohu Leaf Indoor Antenna on order; it was actually supposed to come today, but when I checked my Amazon orders for today’s deliveries, it’d been changed to next Saturday. No biggie; I know the antenna will work because I already bought one for another TV - picked up 147 channels. I added Roku to get Peacock TV which isn’t available on Fire right now. This is where I made a mistake. After doing what I thought was pretty thorough research, I got the Roku Express. Turns out it doesn’t connect to 5GHz, only 2.4 GHz. It seems to be working okay, but I’ve ordered the Roku Streaming Stick+ which will connect to 5GHz. (Those numbers really don’t mean anything to me. I just know 5GHz = good, 2.4GHz = not so good.) The remote for the TV isn’t exactly as pictured; it has a Disney+ dedicated button instead of HBO Max; okay with me. I wish the remote had lighted keys - that’s my only VERY minor complaint. Other than that, the remote is fantastic - so much so that I ordered the 3rd Generation Fire Stick which has the exact same remote to replace my old Fire Stick (and remote) on the living room TV. I started this journey because I got sick of paying $100 a month to Dish when all I basically did was watch local and network news (and Prime TV). I got the Mohu antenna ($40) for my living room TV which took care of the news. This Toshiba TV is just icing on the cake. I was just THINKING about getting it, but when the price dropped by $50 (to $150), I decided to take the plunge. I ended up getting Hulu (no ads) for $12/mo and Peacock TV (no ads) for $10/mo. After the initial cost of all the hardware I bought, I’ll be saving ~$80 a month, so I’ll be coming out ahead in no time. I’ll probably add more channels/apps in the future, but for now I have plenty of new stuff to watch. I wish I had done this long ago, but I didn’t even know it was possible. Dish was going to raise my rates again (by $25/mo) and I’d just had it, so I started checking into things. To give you an idea of how long I’ve been overpaying, my Dish equipment was so old they didn’t even want it back. I feel so much better now that I’m not paying $100 a month to watch the nightly news AND I have an awesome new TV in my bedroom! Update: I’ve had these TVs (I bought two) for two months. Peacock+ is now available on Fire TV, so no need for the Roku stick anymore. My Mohu Leaf antenna is connected, and is working very well; I can change to the antenna output by choosing the option onscreen. I’m still very happy with my purchases.

I had a Galaxy Active 2 for over 2 years. Then the battery stopped lasting all day (and would drain rapidly and die in the middle of workouts), it stopped synching to Strava, and a host of other issues. So as a replacement I went with the older model Venu which was cheaper now that the Venu 2 has been released. On the whole, I'm very happy with the Venu. Pros: - GPS tracking for jogging is OUTSTANDING. My Active 2 would sometimes lose GPS and mess up my whole run. - Activity and health tracking in general I find to be far superior - heart rate, step count, etc. This thing is a fitness track first and a smart watch second. - Spotify integration for downloading and listening to music is smooth and easy, I found it a little clunky on the Galaxy - Absolutely no problems with touch sensitivity as some have said, and I have a bumper/screen protector on. In fact, I found my Galaxy watch to be TOO sensitive, it would start workouts and do other weird things if I'd just graze my watch with my arm or something. Hasn't happened with the Venu. - Love the look with the silver bezel. Snap a silver metal band on, and it goes from workout tracker to night out at a fancy restaurant Cons: - My biggest complaint is that the bluetooth to headphones is either weak or gets interference or maybe competes with processor time with the GPS or I'm not sure what. When I start my runs, the music goes in and out of my BT headphones for a few minutes before the signal becomes stable. SUPER DUPER ANNOYING. And it only happens on runs, not on other workouts. - It's not an edge-to-edge screen like my Galaxy was, so that took some getting used to seeing the smaller screen not fill the watch face - There's no button to go directly back to the watch face, only a "back" button. So if you're like 4 menus deep and just want to cancel out fully, you have to hit the back button 4 times. Annoying. Generally, the menu layout is also a bit lackluster with common options buried deep (like connecting to said headphones) - Even though fitness tracking is far superior, I found my Galaxy watch did a WAY better job on sleep tracking. Go figure. - It doesn't have the apps the Galaxy does. I really only used one 3rd party app on the Galaxy watch, Golf Pad, and Garmin has its own golf app, so no big loss for me. But if you use other apps you may be disappointed.

IR Camera / Fingerprint sensor: I can't tell you because I'm using LInux and MSI doesn't offer drivers for either of those things. Audio: Very good. Build quality: quite solid and good looking in an understated way. The bottom panel is a little flexible, but you'll only notice when lifting. It otherwise feels pretty nice, not cheap, but not like something machined from aluminum. It's a sacrifice I'm willing to make for weight and price.
