Two things you need to know about this light: 1. It's NOISY. It, itself, makes noise. Also, be careful where you route the USB cable. It is attached to the light, so you can't swap it out for a shielded one. If you route the USB cable around speaker wires or near an XLR cable, the sound from the light (that sounds so dumb but it's true) will interfere with the speakers and you'll have a high-pitched whine out the speakers. That being said, re-route the cable and the noise goes away. 2. It's tall. An odd complaint, but if you have limited desk space, or this goes atop a monitor in a hutch, you may ruin into space limitations. I ended up just bending it forward and it clears my desk hutch. Light seems nice, the power switch is handy, the light has adjustability and it's CHEAP, just be sure you don't invite this noisy neighbor into your sound studio.

I purchased this case because I needed something "different" than the standard rectangular PC box. It is a very nice case but it does have it's problems. Here is what I love and hate and even despise about this case. What I love: It looks great!! If you get the White one, you can paint it any color you want! Roomy interior, Power/USB buttons are on the angled edge making them easy to reach regardless if your cases if forward facing or sideways. Room for 8 fans! USB C port in front. Lighted power button. Plenty of room in the rear to hide those unsightly cables. Glass panels on 3 sides allow you to showcase your glorious "PC Master Race" hardware and RGB lighting (if you're into that sorta thing) And best of all: No finger slicing sharp edges!! (Always exercise size caution when building). What I hate: Only room for 2 SSD or 3.5 inch HDD drives. (You'll need to be creative if you want to add more) No HDD activity light, reset button on the front, combined headphone/mic jack that requires an easy to lose adapter (at least HYTE included it). Front facing USB 3 ports are black instead of blue. This can make it difficult to see witch way to insert USB a devices on the front. Huge GPU's press up against the glass cutting their airflow, so you might need to use water cooled GPU's to avoid overheating. The "Air Filter" Mesh on the top of and side the case fused to the panels and are not removable. They can impede airflow if they get clogged wit dust and require constant attention. You will have to pry them off every few weeks for cleaning. Due to GPU mounting, every expansion card you get will have to be half-height. Long power supplies with stiff cables like the "EVGA Supernova 1300 P+" can cause you problems with you cable management. What I DESPISE: The included PCI-E 4.0 Riser gets in the way when you need to plug in all your cable headers into the motherboard. The PCI-E Riser very difficult to remove and can't simply be removed with a screwdriver without needing to dismantle the lower half the case. The problem is that if you need to upgrade it in the future to 5.0 or need to replace it should it become damaged, it will become a serious headache. The locking tab on the PCI-E slot is VERY DIFFICULT to reach when there is a GPU installed! If you have big hands, you may need to remove your ram or cooler to get at it if you want to replace your GPU.

I have installed several dozen cell phone and tablet screen protectors with only minor complaints - but never have I attempted to fit one inside a bezel - and NEVER will I try again. If I had to do it over again I would do as one person wrote and leave the film on the sheet and just tape the whole thing (at the edges) to the screen. 1) Alignment is difficult as they have you start at one end. You have to get it within less than 1/4 mm or the sides will run up against the bezel. Unlike with a cell phone or tablet, there is no positioning guide to assist with precisely aligning the film. The thickness of the plastic conspires against a gradual peel and stick, 1mm at a time, which works wonders for its thinner cousins. 2) bubbles are inevitable, I think the stiffness of the plastic exacerbates this. Expect to peel back and try again at least 20 times during install. Furthermore due to how thick the sheet is, the bubbles wont go away on their own (some protective films come with micro holes that leak the air bubble over time). The provided cardboard tool does a poor job of removing air bubbles, and rounds over quickly (it is cardboard). I found a credit card with a smooth edge did much better (after the cardboard failed). 3) Peeling back and taking another run at it is very risky as it often results in dust getting trapped in the adhesive which makes the problem that much worse (those bubbles don't go away and the adhesive is not thick enough to encompass them. I don't have a certified clean room - do you? The instructions at the very end mention a steam filled bathroom - that is not a suggestion, it is a minimum requirement. 4) Finally be very careful when peeling it back because too sharp of a bend and it will crease the plastic and then proceed to unstick itself in that area (permanent bubble). Overall this was an exercise in much frustration and left a barely usable end result. I suspect that if I did 10 of them back to back, by the end I would finally get good at it, and have something worth keeping. Practice makes perfect, don't expect the first one to be very usable.

I originally purchased a set of Samsung bluetooth earbuds, but ultimately returned them because the sound quality was abysmal. I also had people complain that my voice wasn't very clear on phone calls. But I will admit that the small size made for a great experience. Fast forward a few months and I decided to give these headphones a try. I already own the wired triple-driver ear buds (which sound AMAZING), and my daughter had a pair of the dual-driver ear buds (which sound VERY GOOD). Well the good news is that these bluetooth headphones have a sound that is about the same as the dual-driver wired ear buds, which is to say it is VERY GOOD...far better than the Samsung ear buds. They aren't as good as the triple driver wired earbuds I have, but for the price I did not expect them to be. The bass is pretty clear, as are the highs. The sound is pretty neutral and leans a little bassy, but not "boomy". Overall listening to music on these is an enjoyable experience and does not feel like a compromise like the Samsung ear buds did. Phone calls are VERY clear. The sound pickup is far better than the Samsung ear buds I had, and probably better than anything else with that design. With these, the microphone is in the wrap-around neck piece, right at the front, so it is more directional to your voice than true earbuds. I ask people on phone calls if they can tell I am talking with headphones on, and nobody has yet been able to tell. The design is the only drawback, as they are not good for anything active. The neck band will bound around too much if you jog, and if you do anything where you aren't standing up (like lying down), the neck band will fall off. So if you are looking to buy these for sporting activities, I'd pass on them. But for "typical" use of walking around, or sitting, they are fantastic. For the money, they are a great buy. The sound quality is excellent, and battery life seems good with them as well. Just know ahead of time the pros and cons of this design.

In the absence/reduction of face-to-face time during this health crisis period, people have become extremely reliant on proxy contact to keep in touch with one another. Having relied on their home security system for years, I was thrilled to learn that Amcrest also had a line of webcams, to connect to the outside world. I’ve relied on my Microsoft LifeCam HD-3000 since 2011 so I saw it fit to upgrade to and test out the modern and affordable Amcrest 1080P HD Webcam (AWC201-B). My old system’s video quality maxed out at 720p (this was HD back in 2011) so I was eager to upgrade to a 1080p system for webchats. Out of the small box, the camera comes in a pretty simple two-piece set-up; a detached plastic material lens-cover and the webcam itself with an embedded 5’9” USB2.0 power/connection cord. I would have preferred to have the lens cover preinstalled or integrated onto the camera instead of it being a separate piece. The lens cover attaches to the camera using a double-sided tape that is preinstalled on the cover itself. The face of the camera is a glass type construction split into three sections. The camera section is in the center with two LED lights mounted to each side of the lens. The microphone receiver is to the left of the lens and the right side just has the manufacture logo printed on it. The backing of the camera feels like a pretty common plastic covering. The stand/clip mount appears to be of the same plastic quality as the camera backing; there is an option to mount the camera on a tripod via a female 1/4” connector on the bottom plate of the stand. The folding clip feels sturdy and the contact points are cushioned with rubber padding to prevent scratching or scuffing. Overall, it’s not a bad looking webcam and it’s all black color scheme will allow it to be integrated easily into any setup. Installation and setup of this camera is pretty straight forward on my Windows 10 system; it’s pretty much plug-and-play. There is no on/off switch on the camera but the two LED indicator lights on the camera will light up when the camera and mic are accessed. The long cable allows for a variety of mounting positions. The camera itself does not have any software to manage it; instead, it is managed via whichever third-party app is used to operate it. Mounting the camera on the top of my computer monitor, it is only adjustable vertically. Horizontal adjustment is only possible by physically moving the entire camera to a different part of the monitor, standing it on the desk, or mounting it on a tripod. The video field of view is 70 degrees so it captures a decent amount of the environment; make sure nothing is in frame - that you don’t want seen. Not surprisingly, this camera’s video quality is an improvement over my old 720p device; but, it’s really nothing to marvel over in today’s world of standard 4K video quality. I tested the camera using the default Windows 10 camera app and OBS Studio. The Windows 10 app does not offer much of anything to adjust the camera settings with. Windows 10’s default microphone setting does not allow for any audio setting changes beyond volume adjustment. OBS offers more but it’s not something most users will know how to tinker with. I originally wanted to be able to use this camera for streaming or content creation but found that it is only really good for the occasional camera user. The video quality is not sharp enough or clear to be able to compete with today’s 4K technology that can be had on most smartphones. The audio quality sounds muffled, does not filter out background sounds, and captures a lot of static wind/air noise. I found that a separate and dedicated microphone and video setup would better suit my needs. However, for webchats and meetings while at my workstation, this product is cheap and decent enough to accomplish those needs. Bottom-line, this is a simple product to use that requires no prior knowledge or experience. It’s fairly affordable, decently constructed, and isn’t too bad of a looker for most average desktop setups/users. Price to performance, I would say that this is a definite 4 out of 5 stars due to a lack of supportive software.

Put it this way--I regretted buying this speaker until I applied the Bass Reducer, now I really like it! The controls are quirky and sometimes unresponsive, but I got used to it. There is a voice after powering up that informs you the device is "DISCOVERING" the bluetooth connection. This voice is obnoxiously loud and I wish I could disable it. The same voice tells me "GOODBYE" when the unit powers down. It's awful. I got this Monster to replace my Oraolo Go, which died after 6 months use. Oraolo's controls are more responsive and reliable ad I see it. Sound quality is comparable after the EQ bass reduction mentioned above. The Oraolo is more comfortable (the Monster is stiff), but that doesn't bother me much. Not sure if the firmware is able to be updated, but fixing the overloaded bass output and getting rid of the annoying voice would make this a 5-star product in my opinion.

review_text: If you hardwire this camera to your car's battery and leave it on parking mode, it will slowly drain your car's battery. There are 4 main factors that will determine if the next time you try to start your car it will be dead. 1. The amount you drive.. If you drive your car a decent amount, to work or to the grocery store, you car should charge you battery enough for the camera not to drain it to death. However, if you have a short commute, you may have a net discharge each day. 2. How often you drive. If you leave your car parked for a few days (hello, pandemic!) The camera may, again, slowly drain your battery if it keeps recording... depending on where you park, which brings us to... 3. Where you park. If you park on a street, in a lot, in a driveway, or in a car port, your camera may be active most, if not all of the day. Leaves, cars, trees, people, and even birds will all cause your camera to turn on. 4. Type of battery. Your average car battery (or starter battery) is not designed to constantly be charged and drained. It is also not designed to steadily run for a long time. It is designed to provide a burst of power to start your engine. Frequent draining without sufficient recharging will shorten your battery's lifespan. You may even see powdery sulfate crystals form on the terminals, or "Sulfation." Some car batteries (dual purpose batteries, AGM batteries) are designed to provide both burst power and sustained power, and dont lose as much off their lifecycle by frequent draining.

I was using this with a 5 drive set-up on both Windows and Mac OS. Windows 10, and Mac OS Big Sur 11.4. The positives: The enclosure is quiet and kept all of my drives cool enough (~80-90 degrees Fahrenheit). USB-C was nice (and rare for this size enclosure at this price), and R/W speeds were ~240 mb/s. The box is fairly small, and the drives were secured without issue. I consistently transferred the connection with this enclosure between two devices, sometimes on the same OS and sometimes on different OSes. Never had an issue with hot-plugging, or OS recognition. That is about the end of the good. The negatives: Cheap materials, even if it is machined aluminum. No soundproofing inside. I didn't need it, but if your drives are loud, then good luck. The most annoying part of this enclosure, though, is the fact that it goes to "sleep", forcing the drives to sleep as well. Sometimes all of them, and sometimes only the ones that aren't in constant use. And there's no way to turn that off. AT ALL. In my Mac system settings, I've selected to "never put the hard drives to sleep" -- so this shouldn't happen. Yet it still happens, and it isn't the OS's fault. This wasn't a problem with my old QNAP DAS, and it isn't a problem with my newer (replacement for this) 8-bay OWC enclosure. For some reason, as many other reviewers have mentioned, this enclosure just puts the drives to sleep. If that doesn't seem like a big deal, read on. Because if you are someone that plans to use this to access media on an HTPC or streaming device (i.e. Plex, Jellyfin, etc.), the drive sleeping is ANNOYING. Videos take minutes to load, sometimes throwing failures that they cannot be played. On other DAS and NAS enclosures, they take seconds (or less) to load. Folders (on both Mac and Windows) take minutes to load with this enclosure, sometimes freezing the OS (or Finder / File explorer) in the meantime as the enclosure slowly wakes up and brings the drives back online. I thought it was going to be a non-issue for me; or at worst, a small issue. But the drives go to sleep every 15-20 minutes (unless you are constantly using/browsing the specific drive that you are needing to access). And even if you use just one drive and that specific drive isn't asleep, the others likely WILL be. It got to a point where trying to load media information on my streaming device would take minutes. I couldn't even scroll through my media because folders were just grey, default icons. I could click on a video and instead of seeing a description, play button, etc, I would be met with a buffering sign because the media hadn't been accessed yet (because it couldn't). It got to the point where I began to expect to see a 'buffering' icon anytime I wanted to access anything on my HTPC. For those of you using Plex, you'll be seeing a lot of blank posters, artwork, descriptions, etc. For those of you doing video work in After Effects or Premiere, good luck. Would not recommend buying unless you plan to use this as housing for your backed-up files, which you plan to access maybe once every few weeks.

First, I will state that my ears physiologically do not take kindly to earbuds of any kind and earbuds like these just often get pushed out. Also, coming from a over-ear, high-fidelity headphones to these earbuds was a serious step down. So, my review is tempered by those facts, but is designed to be fair. These earbuds are hard to position in the ear for clear sound at first, but with some maneuvering, they settle in. The winglets (designed to stabilize the earbuds) are comfortable, but not rigid enough to actually stabilize the buds (a tradeoff for comfort). At first positioning, I found them to be extremely lacking in bass. A repositioning (twisting action) in the ear canals solved that problem, but ended up clipping the high frequency response. That was frustrating. Finding the right position to have balanced bass / treble response was a chore, and when found, still did not perform well enough for a critical listener. If you just like your music loud (at the cost of tonal balance and clarity), then you'll have no problem with the performance. The mic / button performance felt solid in clicking (not flimsy). For everyday use, tooling around general listening / phone call utilization, these headphones are good. And once fitted in, are quite comfortable for long periods in the ear. For critical listening, these are not the choice of earbuds, as they sound no better nor worse than the hard, low-level Apple earbuds.

My house is under 2300 sq feet and only one story. It DOES have very high ceilings and a small loft (that overlooks the dining area) which is where we have our modem and router hooked up (to shoot out over the house). Now I don't know anything about routers and mesh wifi, so I had to do tons of reading on this because my youngest son's room had spotty signal with our old Netgear router because it was the furthest room away from the router. After reading reviews and articles on mesh wifi, I opted to go for this deco m9 model only because PCMag had it rated as the best mesh wifi system for 2020 even though it barely has 323 reviews on it vs the deco M5 model with thousands of positive reviews. Sooo...set up was super easy with the app. If I can do it with my limited knowledge on these things, then ANYONE can do this alone! Once I made one hub a router (hooked up in the small loft to the modem) I then gave my son a hub and placed the last one in my master bedroom. Now here come the problems. My oldest daughter's room is directly below the loft where the Main Hub/router is, and she gets spotty signals! HOW and WHY?? Why is this happening when it never happened with our old Netgear router, which was in the same exact place this new Deco is now?? Considering my house is barely 2300 sq ft, three hubs would be overkill, right?? This gets me pissed off already that PCMag lied to me. This can't be the best mesh wifi of 2020!! Arghhh!! So I then take my hub out of my bedroom, plug it into the dining area...annnnndddd the HUB blinks red. No blue, no green, just red. Next comes a couple of hours of me trying to reach tech support and reading forums and playing around with this Hub. I reset it millions of times, bring it closer to the router to sync it, reset it again, still blinks red. Finally get tech support to chat with me after waiting forever to get a rep, and they have me do everything I've already done. Last resort is to reboot the whole system. And that does the trick. So you'd think everything should be dandy? Nope, my daughter complains that her wifi signal drops all the time and she can barely do homework on her computer. I now have moved the hub from dining area right into her bedroom even though her room is directly below the main hub/router itself. That's just ridiculous. Maybe I should have just gone with the Google Nest that my friend has been raving about. Ugh, if only I didn't have an Alexa already in every other room of the house...would buying the Google Nest wifi even make sense when we are an Alexa family?? I guess I'll have to see if there's any more issues with our wifi before our return window is up! And if I start to get spotty signals in my master bedroom (we are also far from the main router) do I really want to buy another Tp-link Hub for my room??? If it gets to that point, I'm returning this thing back!

I've been using the headset for just over 24 hours. I like the fit, sound quality and apparently mic is good on the other end. One thing that was KILLING me however was I was getting a bad echo (hearing myself speaking into the mic). I eventually found the fix. Another review on amazon wrote about a "side line" issue. This setting does not exist in my version of windows (11); however, I was able to find a "Sidetone" setting. Once I set that to mute, it fixed the problem completely. Here's my fix : find your Logitech USB Headset H540 in sound settings, click it and then select Properties. In the Levels subfolder you'll see "Sidetone". Click the speaker icon or set to 0. Hope this fixes your issue.

So this is basically a motor that pushes out air through one of two nozzles. I purchased this air duster because constantly buying cans of compressed air was getting expensive and I wanted a renewable and eco-friendly alternative. The air duster is pretty impressive, but it absolutely does not have anywhere near the blowing strength of compressed air which was very disappointing, as dust is very sticky and if you can't just blow it off you'll have to spend time wiping it off. As for the actual physical design of the product, I'm very unimpressed. The way the nozzle attaches to the duster does not feel very secure in my opinion, some type of locking mechanism would have been nice to have. My unit came with two nozzles, one that was just a plastic tube and one that had a brush attachment. The bristles on the brush aren't very firm which is good for electronic components, but irrelevant on surfaces like the base of a keyboard because it just won't latch onto dust. Cosmetics, the Amazon listing shows no company branding or logos on the product, but another person's review included a picture with a company brand on it, and my unit came with something similar but for a different company. Not sure if this is just a bunch of different companies that sell off the same product page, but I hope all of their dusters are at least of the same quality. Overall, I wouldn't recommend buying this product if you want something that matches the performance of compressed air cans.

I don't generally leave reviews but I really had to for this. You might be confused by the 4 star rating when I adore this cable, but I'll get to that. Firstly, I'm so happy this thing works! My charging port was a little busted on my iphone, to the point that I always had to angle the cable in a certain way and even then it was a crap shoot (yes is was the port itself and not the cable, even tested it at the apple store). I plug the connecter in and it started charging instantly. No hassle, no jimmying it around or putting two bookends on either side to hold the phone at a 37.3 degrees angle. It just worked! Charging seems quick, haven't tested the data transfer but thats not something important to me. Cable works in all directions, doesn't have to be plugged in a certain way just to connect. Really happy with this purchase. I'll say the main drawback is that the piece that connects to the phone is wider than the actual phone. So much so that the case can't sit flush with my phone. If It becomes an issue I may just cut an insert for it to fit, but I do worry that it may get caught on something and fall out. Pros: * Just works * Came with 8 heads for many different products * Medium and Longish cables * Tiny blue light on cable to help you find it at night Cons: * Piece that connects to the phone is wider than the phone and sticks out * Cable is not braided. The cable seems strong enough, but with travel and lots of movement non-braided cables don't last as long * Magnet could be stronger A braided cable and a connecter that sits flush with my phone would make this a 5/5.

This is an honest review, I hope this helps. Where to even start with the plethora of problems this monitor has. Let’s see , out the box the picture quality and brightness compares to a TV from the 80s had to mess with the graphics cards settings to try to get a better color quality. At first I didn’t notice that monitor went to the dessert because it was covered in dust from the back side, I’m not sure if that was just the packaging not being sealed properly but when I passed a cloth over it , it was dirty dirty. Firmware updating is like getting ready to make a sacrifice, I had go out of my way and buy THREE USB sticks because the monitors is “picky.” Had to download the zip. file directly onto the USB and unpack it in there. A regular 2.0 Sandisk worked for me. But that update didn’t fix a damn thing until a couple of days laters. The main problem was flickering and the signal getting lost and coming back up after a second or two , so you can imagine how annoying that was. Mind you all my drivers where updated G-sync was on and tried it off as well and VRR was also on. That problem went away on its own because i didn’t touch anything on it for a while, which is weird but if you do update and mess around with the settings make sure to unplug the monitor out of your power source and give it a couple of seconds so it can boot up with the right settings you chose. HDR doesn’t work at all when you turn it on it just washes out your picture even worse. Samsung care has been no help at all , first time I tried to reach out there was a language barrier so that was not fun trying to explain what was wrong , second time around they opened up a ticket for me to have a specialist come out , that still hasn’t happened and it been three days now and no one has called out to set up the appoint. It’s a good thing I don’t use this for work. And to have a specialist tell me yup it needs to back and you’re going to have to wait until it gets fixed id rather just return it and go somewhere else. But now it was two new problems , one is understandable and the other one just doesn’t make sense. When pushing the monitor to 240hz and it’s highest resolution it gives your GPU a coil whine, that one is understandable but man my 3090 sounds like it about to fall apart. The other newest problem is that I can hear a popping sound coming out of the right hand side of the monitor . I was going crazy trying to figure out what it was, I had recently bought speakers so I was for sure it was those but nope, unplugged them and the sound still kept going . That’s when I realized it was the monitor. I’m not sure what it is but it’s not the plastic settling in or anything like that because it’s a constant pop, it even happens when the monitor is turned and unplugged!!! For the amount of money this monitor cost it’s just a more expensive regular G9 with the same problems that plagued that monitor. The Neo G9 was just a copy and paste with a little dazzle to make you shell out money. Honestly worst monitor I’ve ever had to deal with. The headaches and time invested are not worth buying this. Please don’t be in denial if you purchased this thing and are having these problems just return it.

The one little drawback to it is that, with all its memory capacity, the SanDisk 128 GB microSD card has room for not just the good memories, but the bad ones too. I would have just as soon forgotten the time when I was 4 years old and I peed my pants at pre-school. But no, there it is, faithfully recorded on my memory card along with all the other memories, bad ones and good ones. So SanDisk, if you could include a memory-filter in the next model of these memory cards, I'll up my rating from 4 stars to 5 stars.

I am completely happy with my new setup. For years, my home network was run by two (2) hard wired Airport Extremes. With the 2nd Airport Extreme extending the WiFi. The past year, as we have started streaming more devices, I was noticing that our two WiFi AppleTVs would start to lag. On top of that, certain areas of the house had terrible reception. It got to the point, it was better to just switch phone to cellular than try to deal with the lag. review_text: I’ve been a huge fan of Garmin for many years. First Garmin was the Forerunner 245 several years ago. In between tried the competition (Withings, Polar) but wasn’t satisfied as they were either lacking in terms of complete overall package or the ecosystem wasn’t as well rounded. Started to get back in more active lifestyle and the integration of Garmin connect with more 3rd party apps (Strava, Zwift), I started to look to return to Garmin. Went with the Venu 2 Plus. Gorgeous screen, good enough battery life, smaller size. Thought I would use the built in speaker more but didn’t. Realized that it didn’t have some of the activities that I wanted, in particular trail running. The 955 dropped and I saw it had more activities, it had more metrics like training readiness, and it had maps. Thought briefly about the Fenix 7 series or the Epix, but didn’t like the weight or the cost. Kept on going back to the 955’s total package of weight, features, and cost. Very happy that I did. Compared to my Venu 2 Plus, it gives me way more data than before. Paired with my HRM Pro the distance tracked is way more accurate. I do a light morning walk/jog on the treadmill in the morning. When I walked with the Venu, it would undercount my distance by 40%. I would have to ensure my arms moved rapidly and over exaggerated for it to count anyway near accurate. When I ran it would overcount my distance by 2x. With the 955 it’s dialed in within the .01 km each time. I love the navigation and mapping. Downloaded a dozen or so local courses and their maps from All trails and each time it’s accurate and redirects me if I’m off. The one thing is that it seems to be overly sensitive to how off track you are, a few steps off and it’ll redirect you. Not a huge deal since I’d rather it keep me on track than let me drift off course. I went for the non-Solar version since I do most of my training in the morning indoors or at night. My outdoor activities are limited to the weekends so I don’t get 3+ hours in the sun to take advantage of the solar charging. I’m getting 9-11 days of charge using for 1.5 hours on average activities a day. Quick to recharge, when it’s low it’ll recharge 50-60% while I’m showering and getting ready after a workout. Great job Garmin!

review_text: [[VIDEOID:4d45e64ae8aef45c800cbb53c6d9c0e7]] Over the past several years I have had a few incidents in parking lots and on roadways that brought me into the market for a dash cam. Another negative point is the JBL software and the app (only tested on Android) which is very heavy and slow to boot up (when it doesn't get caught), and this limits you a lot if you have certain settings loaded on the touch controls, which forces you to use the app to configure others (e.g. if you configure the volume control on a headphone, and the control of songs in the other, you lose control of soundproofing mode / talk throug ), so there is also a lack of greater customization and touch controls (some cheap SoundPeats that I had allowed you to perform many more actions without even having an app), in addition to the fact that there are other options only controllable through the app such as Voice Over in calls or switching between music mode and video mode (aka low latency mode). They also have quite a bit of latency, even in "video" mode, so for gaming and even watching videos they are not the best. In addition, if you integrate them with the Google Assistant you lose the touch controls on the headphones even if they are configured, although with the default controls (not integrated) you can also invoke the assistant with touch controls. For the price they have, if you only want them to listen to music with active soundproofing and you are looking for comfortable in-ear headphones, they are very good. But if you are looking for versatility and fast handling, or use for video games, perhaps you have to look at other models.

I'm updating this review after 18 months of pure hell with this device. Two essential features don't work: sync and heart rate monitoring. Without sync working, you have no way to track your activity and basic functionality is lost. Heart rate monitoring continues to be inaccurate above 120 bpm. They've never fixed that problem. Also, when sync breaks, it takes the battery with it. The battery lasts 2, maybe 3 days instead of 5 or 6 when this happens. And it happens frequently. And when it happens, the watch dies unexpectedly, leading to further frustration. What makes it worse is their support organization, even the 2nd-tier support are unable to follow up with these fundamental issues. There's no path for their support organization to raise issues with engineering to get these issues addressed. I wish Fitbit would wake up and fix these basic issues. But it appears they abandoned this product. --- I had a Fitbit Ionic before this and it was excellent. I was expecting this to be an upgrade with all the new features, but I'm extremely disappointed in the most basic functionality of this watch. The ECG feature is nice if it gives peace of mind, but not at the expense of a daily fitness tracker. This is where the Sense falls short: * Poor HR tracking - often off by 10 to 40 BPM, especially when exercising (!!!) * Poor sleep tracking - often fails to recognize several hours of sleep a day * The band is hard to adjust and tough to fasten * Poor touch screen performance - it's often unresponsive to swipes and touches * Sync fails daily - "Can't sync your Sense" Sadly, I didn't notice the HR discrepancy at first since the Ionic was almost always dead on and I expected the same. However, this caused me some anxiety as it started to get way off from what I was expecting. It's high during resting and low during exercise. I compared both the Ionic and Sense to a professional-grade ECG device. The Ionic is close, the Sense is not. The Sense generally reads much higher (+5 to +10 BPM) than my actual HR at rest and much lower (-20 to -30 BPM) while exercising - either of which makes the device useless. At least a couple times, I couldn't reach my target HR only to find out it was the Sense! I've tried every remedy on Fitbit's website and have worked with multiple support agents on this. There's a forum topic on their site detailing the exact thing I'm seeing, yet every support agent I've talked to failed to raise the issue to engineering and have every customer go through the same pointless exercises to fix it. Maybe the physiology of some people makes the Sense fall short, but the Ionic seems to have solved this. This is likely to be one of the few things I return. I'm not hopeful Fitbit fixes this before my return window expires since people have been experiencing the same thing since October. Thus far, Fitbit hasn't even acknowledged there's a problem, much less a solution.

I ordered a set of these and returned them because they didn't power on. I was sent replacements and same thing. I knew the power cables worked and the SATA cables were functional. What I didn't know is that if you have an older power supply, alot of SATA power cables will send a 3.3v signal down pin #3 which with these (and many other enterprise grade drives) which would force drives with Power Disable feature to get stuck in a hard reset condition preventing them from spinning up. I pulled out the pins and cut #3 off, put it back in and it worked fine. Another option is a 4 pin molex to SATA adapter as they tend not to have power on that specific pin

Unfortunately, it arrived with the spider vane bent. Usually this isn't a big deal for a newtonian/reflector but in my case it was preventing the scope to achieve collimation. Collimation would last until the go to track a target. I will update the once I receive the replacement one. The mount itself, it's ok even though the scope is too much for the tripod. If it's extended all the way, it shakes like if it were on a subway. Probably better to move it to a surveying tripod. The red dot finder does it job. Once it's aligned it's very easy to find a target. Something you'll only need to do a few times when you're aligning the scope (2/3 star align). Solar system alignment isn't the greatest. I tested this method with Jupiter and Saturn. The go-to failed to track the Moon and Mars by 5 degrees. The eyepieces are ok for entry level eyepieces. The 25mm is go to find targets or to observe "bigger" DSOs. Recommendations 1. Learn how to collimate your scope. There are a lot of videos that can help with this. This is something that you just do before enjoying the scope and the night sky. Don't be intimidated by it. It's very easy to do. 2. Ditch the batteries and get a power supply adapter. The one below works like a charm. https://www.amazon.com/gp/aw/d/B08BHS4X44?psc=1&ref=ppx_pop_mob_b_asin_title 3. Get a 2x barlow, start with something cheap to get started while you learn the sky. On the good days (night) a barlow will allow you to get "closer" to the planets and moon. Something like an svbony 2x barlow: https://www.amazon.com/SVBONY-Barlow-Multi-coated-Internal-T-thread/dp/B07ZDMJ81F/ref=mp_s_a_1_6?dchild=1&keywords=svbony+2x+barlow+lens+1.25+inch&qid=1604271152&sprefix=svbony+2x&sr=8-6 4. Once you get the hang of it, get wide angle eyepieces. You can start with low cost ones to get started and experience the differences. The svbony gold/red line will cover you on this one, and you won't lol the budget wine this starting out. https://www.amazon.com/dp/B07C6LRCNN/?coliid=I18EQHISUTYBQ4&colid=H3KWCP7HB0AU&psc=1&ref_=lv_ov_lig_dp_it You can also get a zoom eyepiece. This week come in handy if you decide to try astrophotography with a cell phone. https://www.amazon.com/SVBONY-Telescope-Eyepiece-Astronomic-Telescopes/dp/B07XZ6DY18/ref=mp_s_a_1_1?dchild=1&keywords=svbony+zoom+eyepiece+1.25&qid=1604271463&sprefix=svbony+zoo&sr=8-1 5. Make your own power tank out of SLA batteries. This will come in handy if you go to a dark site. https://www.amazon.com/dp/B00KQX5EDO/?coliid=I1RLG3HDA89BA&colid=6GQJJHRIP7QB&psc=1&ref_=lv_ov_lig_dp_it 6. If you're completely new, get Turn left at orion. Should probably be acquired before buying the scope. You'll learn a lot about the sky with the book. https://www.amazon.com/Turn-Left-Orion-Hundreds-Telescope/dp/1108457568/ref=mp_s_a_1_1_sspa?dchild=1&keywords=turn+left+at+orion&qid=1604271720&sprefix=turn+left&sr=8-1-spons&psc=1&spLa=ZW5jcnlwdGVkUXVhbGlmaWVyPUEzSkwxVkYxUlQxMkg1JmVuY3J5cHRlZElkPUEwMTQ2MDExMzYzQlhRR1RGOUcwWSZlbmNyeXB0ZWRBZElkPUEwODcyMDgxVjVSNlg5QVZXSFJLJndpZGdldE5hbWU9c3BfcGhvbmVfc2VhcmNoX2F0ZiZhY3Rpb249Y2xpY2tSZWRpcmVjdCZkb05vdExvZ0NsaWNrPXRydWU= 7. review_text: I needed a KVM to share keyboard, monitor, and mouse between two PCs. I settled on this. It seems like even in 2021, KVMs are overall bad. By the time I filter out the ones with obsolete connectors such as VGA, and ones that have HDMI but fail to support high resolutions and refresh rates, there is not much left. The ones that remain often have concerning reviews. I opted for a KM switch instead - I hook both PCs up to the monitor directly and use the monitor input to switch between them. That way I get 1440p/144Hz, guaranteed. This switch handles the keyboard and mouse flawlessly so far. It even has two extra ports if I need to plug anything else in. In that regard, it is more like a USB hub that connects to two PCs. I have not plugged anything in that requires more speed than a keyboard or mouse, such as a flash drive or USB hard drive. I am only reviewing its use as a KM switch. My only two gripes are its size and power. First, it is small and light. Very small, very light. It does not stay put on my desk. I have to wedge it in between other stuff to keep it from falling off the back of my desk. Second, it allegedly works without using the included power cable. When I do not use the power cable, the mouse does not work. Plug in the power, the mouse works. Just plug in the power cable. It seems like other products have similar issues, so I will plug it in to power and call this one a draw. Anyway, this works very well for my use case and I can easily recommend it if your needs are the same.

Good: Lots of positive reviews regarding the sound quality. But, the Law of Diminished Return applies. For example, while the Ananda is double the price of the Denon AH-D5000, but I consider the sound to be 10/15% better, not considerably better. The silver looking grill appears to be metal and the ear cup appears to be harden reinforced plastic. Very detail sound & separation of the details Bad: While I bought it here, NEW from Hifiman. The shipper just slapped a shipping label on the retail box, no shipping box. The retail / leather box arrived dirty, scratched and unsealed. When I opened it, the headphone was filthy, lots of dandruffs inside both ear cups. One ear cup even had two short hairs in it. See pics Bad headband design. The headband deep scratches / damages itself under normal use!! Scratch marks got deeper and more apparent after a few days. Ugly: I compared it to another Ananda, very close serial number / about 50. Both the headband feels and the sounds are considerably different! This one has a much looser head band / little clamping force. After many test tracks, the sound is consistently dull and lacks sparkle. I prefer the sound of the other Ananda. Personally, I prefer speakers over headphones because the deep bass and 3-D sound allow me to feel the music better. While I really did not expect the Ananda to beat my speakers, Ananda did sound more detailed which presents another side of the music and a different feel. Quality, fit and finish, and packaging are a big disappointment. I have higher expectations for headphones that is a quarter of the Ananda’s price. (One can study apple or oneplus's packaging) Even the fancy leather looking box is poorly designed. It’s useless after you take out the headphone. While the box looks big, it is a tight fit. In order to store the headphone in it, you have to unplug the wires and shrink the headband. It is a chore and not sure how long those plugs and the head band will last if you do it frequently. The self-scratching headband is so terrible and I don't recall any cheap headphones that even comes close. Whoever picks up this headphone will have to see two deep scratch marks from the band.

review_text: This device spent a really long time sitting on the floor in a semi-unpackaged state because it was obvious from its raw proportions that this device is a bit ungainly and indeed, in its assembled form it is way out of proportion to its utility. Actually, its over-wide stance detracts from its ultimate utility because its large foot print reduces the places it can easily be set up and used. Side to side this is approx. 34" wide; it should have been 30". This H-frame table top camera mount is designed to enable one to take photographs from directly above an object. It essentially facilitates product or specimen photography by enabling one to suspend a camera from a central tab or arm so that its lens look out at an object directly below its aperture. Once attached to the central tab, one has the ability to adjust its focal length by approximately 5 inches through the use of a friction bind created with a thumb screw device much like one finds on the attachment device of tripod. In addition, the central tab can be moved approx. 8 inches to either side in two inch increments also by use of a thumb screw that screws into 8 additional screw holes on the horizontal bar. Thus one camera can be affixed in nine different places on the horizontal bar, approximately 16 inches from side to side. The horizontal bar can also be affixed at five different heights with holes approximately four inches apart running from the very top of the H-frame arms which stand approximately 28" high. Finally, the camera body itself can be attached to either side of the central tap which also acts to increase the focal area one's camera has the run of, backwards and forwards by about 4-5 inches. Despite being very simple to assemble, one finds that with just a couple of minor tweaks, this device would be far, far more user friendly. First off, as mentioned the device is too wide. It could have been made only 30" and it would work a lot better and also be easily handled. Also, its simple design incorporates the use of simple thumb screws to hold it together meaning that one necessarily does a lot of screwing and unscrewing of thumb screws to make any adjustments which is a tedious and a bit inconvenient. A more complicated but vastly superior solution would have been to use springloaded pins that could set and released by pulling on them thus enabling rapid and easy adjustments rather than the rather awkard procedure one is forced to use that requires one to hold the thing together while trying to seat the threads of the thumb screw in a screw hole. Being able to simply press in a button or pull on a spring loaded knob in order to "glide" the apparatus up and down or side to side would be ideal. Incidentally, despite the use of "Glide" in its name, this thing does NOT glide, nor does it have any gears. Neverthess, despite its underwhelming design and its overwhelming width the thing does actually work to hold one's camera directly over an object in order to to specimen or product photography, and it has a couple of arm attachments that may be used to hang a light or backdrop off of, as special lighting is definitely called for in order to use this to its maximum effect. Another thing one will want is a remote camera trigger, and also a camera that has an adjustable display that allows one to lift it off the back of the camera to reveal the screen to the photographer as it is impossible to use the camera's view finder once it is affixed to the center tab. As stated, this is both reasonably robust and well-made so that it doesn't feel like a waste of money, but one wonders if the narrower stance and a better thumb screw or fastening system would have made this a five star acquisition. As it stands now, due to its awkward design dynamics which limit its utility and ease of use causes it to rate only 3 stars.

In open air the Pi3 will run about 65C. If I stop all of my camera monitoring and graphics while the Pi3 is mounted to the back of the display, the temperature drops to 65C within a few minutes. This is with a heatsink only on the CPU for cooling. I'm going to add a fan and see what happens. review_text: I have been using an iHome product for several years, but got tired of the buttons and LEDs failing on multiple models, so this time around, I was determined to *not* buy another iHome, especially after reading some of the reviews on their newest models that talk about the same issues. (e.g. their TimeBoost iBTW41) After a month, I am pretty happy with the i-box Glow Pros: * The snooze button has raised bumps - simple, but very important! * The wireless charger has worked pretty well . . . only once I woke up and the phone wasn't fully charged, so now I'm careful to make sure the phone is centered on the dock. * I like the ability to use/see the phone while it is on the charging dock * No functionality is obstructed when the phone is on the charging dock like some other units * I like the night-light (glow) feature, but wish it would remember my color choice * It has the ability to turn clock LEDs all the way off * The built in sound effects is a nice touch, e.g. white-noise, water, birds, frogs Cons: * The buttons can be a bit confusing, probably not enough buttons, as they tried to re-use buttons for multiple purposes, and sometimes not consistent, e.g. use "next" button while updating the time, but use the "Alarm" button while updating the alarm time. * You can't change clock brightness during snooze. I sleep with the clock LEDs off, but when my alarm goes off in the morning, I usually snooze it several times. I am *not* able to turn the clock back on while snoozing (again re-use of the same button) * Similarly, if you are falling asleep to music on a timer, be sure to set your wakeup alarm first, otherwise same button problem * Waking up to sound effects is OK, it starts softly, but gets a bit too loud pretty quickly. I don't think there is a way to set the max volume in this mode. Also the sound loop is pretty short. In the end, waking to the sound of a trickling stream of water is not as relaxing as you might expect. e.g. my reaction waking up to it the first time was, "Yikes, what's that noise?!" * The sound quality not as good as iHome * The radio reception not as good as iHome * You have to manually set the time on this unit * The buttons feel a little cheap, snooze button has a strange double-click feel towards the back * Not too much difference in the clock LED brightness levels (4 levels + all the way off) * LED time is relatively small from across the room (but this is understandable given the space taken up by the vertical phone dock) The list of Cons looks long here, but I am being nit-picky just for your information. Overall, I am glad I purchased this, and still glad I selected it over any iHome model. I plan to update this review if there are ever any reliability issues. Update after 2 months: I find my phone *not* fully charged once or twice a week, even though I am careful to center it (iPhone Xs) on the dock. Maybe offset left or right would be better? I don't know. :-(

like almost all 'usb dacs' this one will show ground loop noise from your computer. if you pause on a song and turn the volume all the way up, you'll hear a squishing noise, as a high pitched randomly shifting sound. again, normal speaker listening will be fine. I mention this just as a point of info, for those that might want a dead quiet system. this isn't it. I have not tried to mod this yet, but I suspect that if I can find an spdif serial link between usb rx and dac, I could insert a pulse transformer and isolate them. I've tried using the cheap usb isolators but they refuse to work faster than usb1.1 and this dac NEEDS full usb2.0 support. for the heck of it, I also bought the topping d30, which does have 2 spdif inputs to choose from along with usb. the usb input is noisy due to ground noise on the d30, just like this dac, BUT if you use toslink fiber, it breaks the ground and you are noise free. many motherboards (not laptops, usually) have optical spdif out, so that's a way around the noise. I also tried coax spdif from my usb/spdif dongle to the d30 dac's coax input. still noisy! because, again, almost all usb/spdif dongles dont isolate ground. I then inserted a diy pulse trafo between the source and the dac and the noise was GONE! just like the toslink opto link, no ground leak and no noise. its a lot cheaper to buy a pulse transformer and insert that between coax spdif lines than to try to isolate usb!! for those that needed to know this, here you go. the usb inputs on both this and the d30 dac are noisy, but if you go with spdif and isolation, you will be noise free.

I ordered these renewed PA7017 (AV1000) units to replace a pair of AV600 units I'm using to connect a POE router to my main gigabit data switch in my house. The POE serves four hardwired IP cameras, so the powerline connection needs to handle streaming video 24/7. As measured by the TP-Link Utility, my AV600s were giving me about 120 to 130 Mbps. I went with the renewed AV1000 units to save a few bucks, figuring that they would be open-box or returned units that didn't meet the customer's needs. What I received were the OLDER PA7010 (AV1000) units, which are not the ones pictured and are much larger than the PA7017 Nano units. They are so large that they block other outlets when I install them where my AV600s were. They were also in pretty rough condition, looking like they had been in use for a long period of time. Finally, I only got one ethernet cable with the pair, not the expected two cables. On the other hand, these PA7010 units did work and did pair with each other quickly. According to the TP-Link utility, my power line connection has jumped up to a steady 210 to 220 Mbps, an increase in speed of over 65%. In fairness, the older PA7010 units sell for more than the newer PA7017 units, but I really wanted the newer Nano form factor and the most recent hardware/firmware. I'm on the point of returning them and spending the extra $12 to get a brand new set of PA7017s.

I've lost count of how many TP-Link mesh wi-fi kits I've set up! They're easy to install right out of the box, and while they won't beat the fastest mesh wi-fi kits out there, once up, they tend to stay up very reliably as long as the electrical power stays on. (After a power failure, they recover autonomously.) I have set up many mesh wi-fi systems for my residential consulting clients, and a few a few very small business ones. Most of those installations don't go smoothly. Netgear Orbi, which the industry pundits keep raving about for its raw speed, has consistently been the most difficult to set up, with very long boot times and many false starts per node. Linksys Velop is better, but it still typically takes 2-3 attempts for each node before it connects. Eero is quicker, but I nearly always end up doing it the hard way, by entering the nodes' serial numbers into the app to it locate them. (Linksys and Netgear, you might want to add that option to your apps...) But every TP-Link Deco system I've ever set up, which includes this one, the M5 and the M9 Plus, has gone like clockwork. The nodes boot up much more quickly than their competitors, and usually connect right up on the first try. TP-Link wins again on overall reliability. My experience with Netgear Orbi is that the nodes have trouble staying connected to the system. It doesn't seem to matter how far a satellite node is from the base unit; all seem equally prone to dropping their connections. And when they drop, it can be a serious pain in the neck to get them reconnected. I've had to reboot them multiple times, and even reset them to out-of-box condition. Linksys Velop isn't much better in this regard. In one extreme case, a client's Velop system dropped one node, reassigned that node's identity to a different one, and I had to reset the entire set to out-of-box condition in order to recover. Eero doesn't seem to mess up that badly, but I have found that clients with Eero systems occasionally need to unplug all their Eero access points and then plug them back in. TP-Link Deco systems, on the other hand, seem like the Energizer Bunny: they just keep going and going and going. I don't remember ever being called back to a client's home or office to fix one. So, why would you want to purchase any of those other systems? In a word, performance. TP-Link Deco systems, including the S4 that I'm rating here, go up easily and are rock-solid reliable, but they don't win races. The fastest TP-Link Deco system, according to independent testers who have published their results, is the Deco M9 Plus, which reportedly outperforms even their new Wireless AX systems, and even that won't outperform the latest Orbi and Velop systems. The TP-Link Deco S4 is decidedly middle-of-the pack. The Deco S4 kit that I just purchased and installed delivered 215Mb/sec on the 5GHz channel when I tested it. That's far better than the system it was replacing, so I don't expect the client to complain about it, but that's nowhere near the 1Gb/sec cable Internet connection to which the first unit was connected, the signal only had to travel about 30 feet and through two drywall walls, and I was less than 20 feet from a node when I ran my test. Performance on the 2.4GHz channel was rather disappointing to me - only about 45Mb/sec - but again, that's a lot better than the client was getting from their old system. Note that the performance I was measuring was more than enough for what most people do with wi-fi, including web browsing, e-mail, A/V streaming and even sharing large files, but Orbi, Velop and Eero all typically deliver better throughput with their Wireless AC and AX systems. So, the bottom line is that if you just need steady, rock-solid wi-fi that goes up easily and stays up reliably, The TP-Link Deco S4 and its cousins are all great choices. If you need blistering performance no matter how hard it is to get and no matter what you have to put up with to keep it going, then look elsewhere. Personally, I'm sticking with TP-Link.

ASMedia chip makes it 5 * for me. The main review is in the next paragraph, some instructions and fine points follow. I have now owned this for 5 months and used it many times. Perfect performance with enough speed. I have used it for backup, and offline cloning. The documentation is not stellar but it's OK. The feel is solid; cables for power and USB seem snug in their sockets, but do not nudge them! The ASMedia chip has a good reputation, so I think ongoing operations will be smooth. I am using two 2TB enterprise HDDs, which tend to run a bit hotter than consumer drives. Using crystaldiskinfo and crystaldiskmark In a room about 20 degrees C., I am seeing temps below 32 degrees C during the most intense long duration use and benchmarking tests . Sequential read/write speeds from a screaming fast NVME SSD equipped computer are of about 190 and 400 MB/s on a USB 3.0 port. Disk to disk cloning is faster. I like this a lot! NEVER PLUG IN OR REMOVE A DRIVE INTO/FROM THIS DOCK WHILE ANOTHER DRIVE IS MOUNTED (through this dock) ON YOUR COMPUTER. It warns you about that in the friendly manual. TO USE AS DISK CLONER: DO NOT connect the USB cable!!!!!! 1: plug power into wall and dock and ensure that switch is OFF 2 insert BOTH drives making sure that you do not need the data on the target drive, 3: power on the dock, 4: press the not-so-accessible button on the back labeled start for three seconds and release, 5: briefly hit the same button and a tiny blue led at the bottom front of the unit (can be a bit hard to see) will flash under "25%". That led will go solid and the next one will flash (under 50%) as cloning progresses. When the 100% LED is solid, turn off switch and remove disks. FOR USE CONNECTED TO A COMPUTER (like backup or file transfer): 1: plug power into wall and dock and ensure that switch is OFF. 2: plug USB cord into host computer and dock, 3: plug drive(s) into slot(s) 4: power on the dock. In windows 7 I did typed disk into the computers search box (magnifying glass in taskbar), found the app to partition the new disk and used that app to initialize it. It automatically named with the disk manufacturer's name. To disconnect: 1. Use the "safely remove hardware" button in your taskbar, 2.: when you get an OK to remove notice, turn switch off, 3.: remove disks. 4.: Unplug power and USB. BTW to use the "safely remove hardware" button in the taskbar I had to go to "my computer", right click the disk, hit properties then policies, and optimize the particular drive for performance rather than for removal. In the default (optimized for removal) setting, the disconnect button in the taskbar did not work; when I tried, it always said the drive was in use.

Hot and ground cables are smaller than the specified 4ga. Approximately 3/16" in diameter and high strand count puts it around 8ga. (The higher the gauge, the less current the wire carries.) Cut ends of both appeared too silvery to be copper, outer surface of strands appears to be copper. Ground cable and speaker wire were tested with small butane torch. Both failed test and aren't copper. Strands curl quicky and green florescence is only a flash as the plating burns off. (Appear to be aluminum plated with copper.) Wires and cable are non-magnetic. One of the brass colored 4ga fittings was filed. Brass coloration continued beyond normal plating depth. Fitting was tested with torch, surface and filed areas oxidized and discolored consistent with brass. No folding or slumping occured. Brass colored fittings appear to be actual brass. Fuse holder contains 60amp fuse. This is not acceptable for, at best, the carrying capacity of 8ga wire at 12volts. Aluminum wire often has corrosion problems when not specially connected to standard wiring systems. This corrosion can cause fires. In addition, aluminum lacks the malleability of copper and will crack, over time, when subject to vibration or bending such as found in a automobile. Other cables, wires, and fittings not tested as enough information was collected to judge that product deviates far enough from description to pose a hazard to the unaware end user. There are likely other flaws. The insulation had a strange smell when torch testing and may not be flame retardant and/or use plastics that outgas in an unacceptable manner. Basically, the cables are undersized for the fuse and will degrade over time. Other flaws may be present as callous disregard for the user is present. Cables will catch fire before the fuse blows. This is likely to occur while vehicle is in use. This fraudulent and negligent product could easily result in property damage, personal injury, and even death.

The Kasa Smart Video Doorbell Camera is packed with features. A beautiful camera that records in up to 2K video. The motion detection and optional sound detection are great. There is no “bubble effect” with this camera either. The night vision does a great job. As with other doorbell cameras, you can adjust the activity zone to pick up motion in the areas you want. The motion and sound sensitivity can be adjusted also. It has two-way audio that’s pretty decent for the overall cost of this doorbell camera. It also has preset responses you can choose to use when needing to speak to a visitor or intruder. Notifications can be activated to receive them on your phone or tablet. The doorbell button LED or status LED can be turned on or off also. The biggest feature that attracted me to this doorbell cam was that it doesn’t require a subscription to save video. You can install up to a 124GB mini SD card to store video. Of course, if you want to subscribe to Kasa Care you can more easily access your cameras video and it allows for 30 days of saved video for $3/mo. or $30/year for one camera. $10/mo. or $100/yr. for up to ten cameras. Otherwise you will have to use a screen recorder while playing your video to save it to your phone. The camera has a 24 hour continuous video recording option, so even when nothing is detected it will still be recording. This option can be very useful, but will fill the SD card quickly. The chime is good. It doesn’t have a huge variety of pre-loaded chimes, but it has a pretty decent selection. The doorbell can be paired with more than one chime at one time, but unfortunately I haven’t been able to find where an additional chime can be purchased separately. The only issue with the Kasa Smart Video Doorbell has been that it’s prone to disconnecting from the network quite frequently. I have been communicating with TP-link support due to this issue and they have been very helpful and responsive. Gaby at tech support is super! She was able to send me another Kasa Doorbell Camera very quickly after troubleshooting my original camera. Update: USE THE JUMPER WIRE! This is what is causing everyone's disconnecting issues! I skipped the jumper wire installation also and after receiving the new doorbell from Arlo Tech Support still had disconnecting issues. I did some more troubleshooting and found that the existing doorbell chime not only was buzzing, but the chime connected to the doorbell was randomly moving up and down. I then searched online to find out if the lack of a jumper wire being used could be the cause of all the issues. Bingo! The jumper wire allows for the doorbell camera to be fully charged by the doorbell transformer at all times. This is needed due to the power it requires to keep the camera functioning. Without the jumper wire, the electric current fluctuates to the doorbell and at times will not be enough to keep the camera operating properly or the wireless connection steady. Since installing the jumper wire all the issues cleared up and even the doorbell microphone sounds clearer. The wiring video in the Kasa app shows the jumper wire installation, but doesn't tell why or if it is needed. I have adjusted my star rating to 5 stars and highly recommend this affordable, feature packed video doorbell!

The Meshforce M3s is the complete version of their M3 router system. While the M3 is a single router, the M3s includes three units, so you have everything you need. Nothing else is required to set up a mesh WiFi network. On the back of each unit, there’s two Gigabit Ethernet ports. As with most routers, one of these is for connecting to your home’s cable modem. An Ethernet cable is included in the kit for this purpose. The other port on each can be used for connecting PCs, game consoles, and other Ethernet-capable devices. To set up the system, choose one of the M3 routers to act as your “main” unit. This is the one you’ll connect to your cable modem. Next, download the My Mesh mobile app, which is free on Android and iOS, and follow the install instructions. Like most modern routers, the M3s Suite is a dual-band system. This means that it supports both 5GHz and 2.4GHz WiFi signals. The 5GHz channel provides up to 867Mbps of bandwidth, or just shy of full Gigabit speeds. The 2.4GHz channel adds an additional 300Mbps, pushing you over a Gigabit when you’re on both bands. After you’ve set up the M3s system, you can use the My Mesh mobile app to adjust a variety of settings. Perhaps the most commonly-used feature is the parental control option. There, you can set specific permissions for specific devices. This way, you can ensure that each of your kids has an age-appropriate online experience and you can also set bedtimes for individual devices. Overall, this is a great mesh network for the money. It is very easy to setup and this 3 unit system can cover up to 6000 square feet, but is expandable if more units are purchased.

review_text: *Edit* I took this on a week long vacation, and with my experience with my commute as well; have been noticing issues hard to ignore. - The battery, even when I turn off, seems to drain quickly, lasting about 4-7 days. In addition, it takes ~4-5 seconds to power down with the power button, if the manufacturer reads this, make it an “on/off” switch like the Logitech. - The charging pogo pins have proven to be rather annoying to have to charge with the case open, and the magnets need to be placed just right, I’d sacrifice a larger case to get USB-C charging, or a side pogo pin charging if possible. - The magnets are just not strong enough to hold the iPad in place. I like the iPad 10 generation folio keyboard case design where it uses a plastic and magnet combo to keep the iPad back attached to the case, while the hinge is still operational. - Make the keyboard layout a 6 row keyboard with function keys. I’ve gotten used to the 5 row keyboard and having to press the ‘control’ key for the 3rd set of symbol keys, but it’s still taking longer than expected to acclimate. Overall, I’m still keeping the keyboard, as it beats carrying my Logitech keys-to-go and Apple Smart Cover combo, or the larger and even heavier keyboard cases that are in the market (I personally don’t need the trackpad that manufacturers are adding to their keyboards). This keyboard has good key strike travel and still hits the right spots for me (compact, all-in-one, good keyboard feel), but if Hou can fix even 2 of the 4 issues I have, I’d gladly pay $100 for this keyboard. I was hoping after more than a year that the iPad mini 6 has been out, more well named vendors like Zagg and logitech would have a smart folio keyboard for the iPad mini 6. I tried one of the generic clamshell keyboard case with trackpad and backlit keys, but the performance was so inconsistent, and the keyboard layout was just too different to get used to, as well as the added weight. I ended up going back to my Logitech and Apple Smart Case until I saw this case in my Amazon feed. With the Hou keyboard, I purchased once I saw the other reviews, as it's close to the look and feature of the Apple Smart Folio Keyboard. I like the relatively slim keyboard, similar to my Logitech keyboard. The key travel is nice and feels solid. I don't miss the backlight, and the keys seem easier to remember for the placement. Since the keyboard layout is quite small, they had to integrate some standard keys to toggle with the Control key, (_, -, +, =, {, }, [, ], ", ', ?, and /) After a few minutes, I was able to mostly touch type these keys. I do wish the spacebar was longer, but it's manageable. Not sure about the pogo pin charging cable, and will have to see if there are replacement options if needed. The power button is easy to press, but hard to see if you don't know where to look. The hinge tilts to a max of 90 degrees from the case to table, giving the screen about 45 degrees tilt. One negative I have is how the magnets do not seem as strong as the Apple Smart Keyboard and I could see the iPad slip off the case if given enough of a nudge. I do take care of my items, but wish the connection was as strong as the Apple case. Overall, I am very happy with the keyboard case so far, as it gives me a small keyboard folio that is relatively slim and light, compared to what is available right now.

You have to kind of pay attention to the center of weight of your case when sliding it in, otherwise , if you have a vertical gap , which I'll get to next, you run the risk of the case tilting up or down. The bad and bizzarre, it seems the width and height adjustment are limited by spaced holes , at least vertically that you can only use to tighten down. Unless I'm misunderstanding something, your case may or may not fit snugly against that metal flap, depending on it's dimensions, and you are limited by those spaced screw holes to tight it down. My case doesn't align with a hole that makes that metal flap snug against the side and worse, there is about a 1" vertical gap because those screwholes would only line up with the tightening bolt with the 1" gap. Another hole up, and I would run out of vertical space to slide the case in. Just a bizarre design, if in fact the thumbscrew bolts are supposed to go into holes on the chasis. Maybe I've got it misfigured though. I have no idea what this little red arrow pointing down to a vertical hex screw is even supposed to be for, since their is the vertical thumbscrew right above it for tightening the heigth of the mount. Really bizarre! My case is basically just balancing itself in the mount. Kinda precarious! Made worse by the fact that I mounted it with 4 long stainless steel bolts from the topside of the desk and countersunk them with nuts on the underside to make it basically 'hang suspended'. The advantage of this, is because the mount is very heavy duty, it can hold a very heavy case, like mine , with no sweat. Much more secure that the much small included wood screws they include for under the desk mounting. So that makes me happy. Plus I bought one of those heigth adjustable desks, so it was critical that the pc and all it's cables move with the desk to not risk damaging a cable and keeping things neat and tidy.

I have tested one from this batch. These have the inductor marked "100". The first thing I find wrong is that it shuts down when the input voltage exceeds 18 volts. I was going to use a laptop charger to supply it's input voltage, but now I got to find something with a lower voltage. I did not damage the part supplying up to 24 volts but it did not run either (output was set to 12 volts). NOTE: You must somehow disable the pot if you want to use one of the fixed outputs. The manufacture intends that you cut the tiny trace that shorts the adj pads. That's hard to do. If you are not getting the right voltage when you are using the fixed output it is because this trace has not been cut. The other option is to remove the adjustment pot with a soldering iron. Someone suggested cutting the top off the pot. That did not work for me, I had to completely remove the pot to get the right output. I have not done any load testing or noise measurements yet, but I have with other models I have purchased with the same design. Those were very good, but these might vary, since they already do not meet one of the specs. I have found that the ic used on the board is not the one used in the original design. The good ones have the IAGCK marking on the ic (very hard to see). These have DKAAF, and I cannot find a spec sheet for that part. Use at your own risk.

This product is not worth the price you are paying. It seems like it was thrown together at the last minute and not well thought out. Sure it works for what it is intended and the modular features are nice, but there are so many small things that seem easily fixable. Pros: - Modular Design is really nice since you can run maintenance on a single pi without taking the whole thing apart - It is technically "Enclosed" but you can forget about controlling airflow outside the individual PoE fans - OLED Display and Power buttons are a nice touch Cons: - Fans are loud and poorly put together. I have already had three fans whose ball bearings have worn down and cause very loud irritating sounds. - The inserts that hold each pi are not lined up correctly making it difficult to screw in the front screws - The display code needs to be compiled and manually installed (I have no problem with this, however, there are some people who might have a difficult time with this if they don't have a linux/coding background) I would like to see an install script - The PoE hat needs a micro USB for power as well. It only has USB Type C. - There are only two options for fan control -> Full blast, or no fan. - There is no SSD module. UCTRONICS has custom SSD modules for other racks they sell, but this one would benefit greatly from having one. They have a newer model for the same price, so I am hoping they fixed all of the cons with that model.

review_text: This is a gorgeous looking screen. I needed a flat screen, and from using Samsung Quantum Dot monitors I figured I would give it a shot. Hardware Unboxed gave it a great review.. For this reason I needed a very good flat screen for work and play. Pros: very vibrant The screen looks and and is reactive like a premium monitor. Very low latency 165 Hz Flat Almost no IPS glow No dead pixels Excellent color reduction after calibration. Amazing for gaming. I prefer the more square shape, compared to the elongated 27" monitors Vesa mount compatible PS5 compatible for down scaling 4K. MSi has done a fantastic job with this. Viewing angles Cons: Plain looking box. I'm used to nicer packaging. Bland, but practical stand. Lighting on the back of the monitor is pretty lack luster. Plastic casing is ok Needs some calibration to make it look better out of the box. It's overly vibrant, but easily adjusted from the OSD to make it look great for gaming and daily use. I would recommend a tool if using it for photo work. The MSI Gaming OSD software had to be uninstalled from the pc as it did not recognize going from 1 MSI monitor to this. I am very impressed with this monitor. The screen looks great, and is fast and responsive. My gripes are very minor, as the frame and boxing materials are very bland. I was hesitant after reading the reviews about dead pixels, but experienced none. IPS glow is practically non existent I would definitely recommend this for gaming, productivity, and photo/video work. I was deciding between this, LG IPS monitors, Dell/Alienware, and the Samsung G7. It does take a powerful GPU to hit 165Hz.

review_text: These headsets are a game changer for me. Using them is such a pleasurable experience! It's important to understand the advantages and disadvantages: 1) These go outside your ears. Sounds is transmitted through the bones and some through the ears. This allows you to hear your music without canceling the ambient noise. As long as the environment noise is low, the experience is fantastic. If you are riding a bike by the freeway though, the noise will easily overpower the music and ruin your experience. 2) Because the ears are not covered, using them for calls gives you an amazing experience, where it feels almost as if you were talking to the other person in front of you. I cannot stress enough how much better these are for calls than regular in-ear headsets. I use them daily for all my conference calls and would not change them for anything else. The built-in microphone also uses bone conduction and works very well and reliably. I gave it 5 stars for noise cancelation meaning cancelation of everything but your voice. Of course outside noise cancelation for what you hear is non-existent. 3) Fit is excellent. These will NOT fall from your ears, even if you are working out. I have some issues with them itching the back of my ears sometimes, but in general they are far more comfortable than anything else I've tried. 4) The controls work very well. The only gripe I have is that press and hold of the left button is supposed to let me use Siri but I have not been able to make that work. 5) Battery life is very good and they charge fast. 6) They have multi point pairing. This is an awesome feature that allows me to use them at the same time with my iPhone and my computer. It is not perfect, but works as expected most of the time. Sometimes I just have to turn them off an on to have them re-connect, but that is easy to do. Overall, just a great product. As long as your audio expectations are met, you will be very happy with them. I just wish they were a bit cheaper...
