review_text: When I set out to buy a monitor initially, I was just looking for something I could put next to my main LCD panel to act as a spot I could move apps to when needed. I started to go down the rabbit hole of portable monitors, and was not terribly impressed with most of the ones I saw, until I came across this one. It fits my needs perfectly. After using this monitor for a few days I have successfully connected it to my main computer. The color range is vibrant, the blacks are fairly black (there is a HDR mode but I found it tends to wash out the color when enabled...might work better for other scenarios). Because this screen has the connectors on the side, I can quickly swap out the mini hdmi with one from my Raspberry Projects and so far I have had no issues outputting HDMI from the Pi3, Pi4, and PiZero1/2. The look of this monitor stands out among the other ones I saw on Amazon. One thing I especially like about the aesthetics is there is no huge branding badge on the monitor. It looks instead like the top half of a Macbook (I have a wireless LG keyboard/pad combo that fits perfectly on the bottom flap of the cover. The magnets on the cover are pretty strong and attach to the monitor on both sides, so is still easy remove when needed if a VESA mount or tablet stand is preferred. There are a few accessories you can request after receiving this product and registering it which is a nice touch. And helps complete the kit depending on your workflow. The inputs are sufficient. You'll have a mini HDMI in as well as USB-C. There is another USB-C as well in case this is used so you can supply power to the device still. Both ports appear to be fully connected so no hassle remembering which one to use. Also, sticking to standards is a nice touch, as I don't have to worry as much about a proprietary power source (although they do strongly suggest using their adapter and cables for the best results...it's a 5v 3a output power adapter from what I can tell). The LCD menu options are also fairly complete for a low to mid range monitor. You have brightness, contrast, color control, sharpness, DCR, power saving, temp, low blue light, Free Sync, and even aspect ratio just to name a few. Oh, and also having built in speakers is a plus. They're not high end, but decent enough to get the job done. The only con I have so far, which is not really a big issue, is the rocker switch for the LCD menu. And that's only a personal preference. I tend to like a full wheel style input button (like a volume button) for side mounted switches like this. But that said, it still gets the job done and works well...and once I set up all my prefs I haven't had to go back to it. All in all, very pleased with this purchase. It's portable so can go where my electronics projects are. It's clean, stylish, and works beautifully next to my main monitor. It displays well and even has good performance for gaming (no difference from my main monitor). This is definitely a project I will be recommending to friends looking for a flexible duty every day small monitor.

I purchased the dual displayport model here. This is an 11 star review of it. I switched out a similar and working KVM Trendnet model TK-240DP model for this one, hoping for an improvement in the displayport bandwidth to get to higher refresh rates, while also loving that remote switch. The Trendnet model is capping out at 2x1080@59Hz, and this model has support for the dual 1440@144Hz my monitors and I need. After an initial struggle getting the item to work, and the complimentary 2 star review that followed, support from the seller (qeesun) reached out to me and offered to help troubleshoot. It was quickly determined that I must have gotten a dud and a replacement was sent out unreasonably fast. 2 days later I had a new one, was up and running in 20 minutes, and I'm thrilled to say I finally got exactly the KVM I've been looking for, for like, over 3 years. The chat support I received was excellent. 2 Displayport monitors are now running 1440x2560@59.9Hz on the laptop side (the max my Dell dock can do), and then with one poke of the remote switch I'm running them both 1440x2560@144Hz (Nvidia gsync-variable, no issues there either) on the desktop side. Switchover varies from 2-4 seconds, in line with the trendnet kvm. The monitors "feel" the disconnect during switchover, so there's some window rearranging to do each time I switch over, just like with the previous kvm. I'm already accustomed to it. There's ZERO heat coming off of it after this first 5 hours of continuous duty, unlike the trendnet model which runs mildly warm to the touch. I knew the remote switch would save me some cable clutter, but man it freed up a TON of desk space, far more than I imagined it would. I was resistant to the idea that this didn't have analog audio switching at first. But now that I have a basic 1/8" y adapter converging both PC signals into my audio receiver, I quickly realized that I should have been doing it this way all along. If I'm on my desktop tending to a personal email, my laptop can still ding when I'm about to be late to a pointless work meeting. Even if I change my mind on the y adapter, there's still room to put a USB to 1/8 audio dongle on the front side of this kvm and do all the audio routing through USB. I might even buy a spare I like it so much. Game changer for all you WFH gurus like me.

review_text: I bought this sound bar for purpose of being a speaker. But it makes a set of privacy destroying demands for no good reason: * I cannot use this without installing the app. Ok, I reluctantly did that. * I cannot use the app without creating an account. It is a SOUND BAR. But still, I reluctantly did that too. * It asked me for permission to know my location. I denied it of course. It is a SOUND BAR! It does not need to know my location. Without granting it permission to read my location, I still could not use the app. And hence I cannot use the sound bar. This was finally too much to consider. I am not going to tell a sound bar my location so I can use it as a SOUND BAR. In the user interface, I did click on "Why does this app need my location?" (or words to that effect). The resulting explanation made no sense. I then tried to use it without the app, but could not. I am a computer security professional and researcher. So I can confirm the common sense conclusion that most everyone would come to anyway: There is no good excuse for a SOUND BAR to make any of these demands. Perhaps there is additional enhanced functionality that would be enabled by these extra permissions --- though the explanation offered by the app made no sense. But even if true, the sound bar should still have its basic functionality --- all I needed --- without these privacy destroying permissions. These privacy destroying "requirements" were also not disclosed in the description. Hence I am returning.

This item has been a game changer by making it a lot easier to tailor car and bedroom cell phone holders to my needs. Took awhile to find these bc I didn’t know what they were called (Are they called 17mm Ball adapters? LOL) but I’m sooooo glad they (this!) exist! What do they do? The two pieces - a ball-prongs and nut - convert a 17mm ball into a 1/4” screw. Mainly bc I use a pop-socket at center/back of my cell phone case, the choices of cell phone holder arm-supports (aka “arm-support”) became limited. The magnetic plate/magnetic arm combo type didn’t work well bc the plate could only fit in the lower section of my cell phone case and bc the center of gravity was so low, my phone would fall to the floor. So, I decided to retrofit my own design using available parts :P I began with a 17mm ball connected to an arm with a cell phone holder-clamp (aka “clamp”) except that the clamps either weren’t easy to use (I couldn’t easily remove my phone) or it just wasn’t strong enough to hold onto my iphone7 plus. After using the aforementioned arm-supports/clamps for some time, I longed to find a better cell phone clamp (which I did find which worked well); however, dreams are dreams and working without this adapter all that time meant that I had to adjust the entire arm-support with every adjustment. Ultimately, the perfect item would allow my ball mounts to connect to better higher quality clamps. of finding an item such as this (plus an additional ball connector) to connect the various arm-supports with the cell phone holder-clamps so that I would have greater flexibility in adjusting the ball joint connected to the clamp rather than to have to adjust the entire arm-support. (I hope this makes sense bc I have no idea of the correct words to describe these items.) This item comes in a pack of one. I ordered two, one for my night stand phone arm-support and one for the suction arm-support hanging from the windshield of my car. This intermediary device allows me (in most cases), the freedom to adjust the cell phone clamp (the part holding my phone) rather than having to adjust the entire arm-support (the arm connecting the clamp to the windshield/headboard). Connections (example): 1- Car windshield 2- Suction 3- Cell phone arm-support with plastic ball joint end 4- This adapter with 1/4” screw adapter 5- Hot shoe mount with 1/4” screw adapter (aka hot shoe mount 360 degrees swivel mini ball head 1/4 tripod screw adapter for camperas, etc) 6- Cell phone clamp 7- Cell phone Build quality is really good and connections work mostly well. Perhaps bc it is made of plastic, the prongs that surround the 17mm metal ball don’t hold onto the ball as tightly as I’d like even though I’ve hand-tightened the locking nut down as hard as possible without stripping the plastic threads, it can still rotate if pushed hard enough to slip. So if anything, making the prongs a little thicker with a thicker locking nut might help reduce that slight slip is my humble suggestion. If your cell phone employs a pop-socket like mine does, this special adapter might be able to help you devise your own cell phone holder too, just like I did!

Hooked up with existing Netgear modem - install process appeared simple with downloaded Netgear app on the phone. That's where the challenges started. During the installation process the app continually disconnected from the router. At first I thought it might be an app issue - tried to work with it for considerable time as each attempt I seemed to get just a bit further in the install setup before the wifi signal dropped and I had to start all over. After more time than I care to admit trying to trouble shoot it myself I broke down and called the tech support line. Over an hour wait - finally got rep on the phone who did a good job but had me work around the problem of the wifi dropping (ethernet direct into the router from a PC). Finally got the setup complete after an hour or so on the phone with them. Minutes after the call was finished the wifi dropping issue started once again. A call back had me #7 in the "cue". 90 minutes later I finally hung up and called it a night. Next day I called back and with a 30 minute wait was relatively quickly served. Rep once again was technically good and had good customer service skills. A good experience when you speak with someone. After re-installing all the firmware and resetting things to factory defaults etc. and another hour on the phone she concluded it was a hardware issue and the router would need to be replaced. Netgear then sends a notice - for a quality return you can pay for the freight and send in the router and upon receipt they will send you a new one. Meaning you are without a router for an undetermined period of time as they work it through their system. Alternately - you can give them a credit card and pay $30 to have a new one overnighted to you with a pre-paid return label to send the defective one back. I filled out their paperwork and begrudgingly paid the $30 to get a modem overnighted to me. Now salt in the wound - I get an email tonight that I need to send photo proof of the serial number on a product I have registered with them as mine and provided earlier photographic proof of purchase of the item - so the shipment was delayed and will not ship until after the weekend. Unbelievable - Netgear is far too large an organization to offer this poor of a customer experience. I'll be searching for alternate brands moving forward. Stay away if you have any concerns about having to deal with anything customer service wise.

I purchased this radio for my 2001 Dodge RAM diesel truck. My main goal was to add Bluetooth capability so I could listen to podcasts and make/receive phone calls. I also considered going with several possible Apple CarPlay capable units but steered away from those because all the decent ones were relatively expensive and double DIN which would require cutting the subdash and the dash bezel. Then I saw this on special for $40 on Black Friday and ordered it since it didn't seem like I could go too wrong for that amount. To summarize i got about half of what I wanted, I can listen to podcasts and internet radio but can't make phones calls due to the fact that it has an internal mic and my truck is very loud (see below). I like the backup camera more than I thought. So all-in-all I think I got my $40 worth but will most likely replace it with a model that has an external mic option at some point. I installed it myself. I ran into a couple of issues during installation. 1) The instructions stated that I needed to connect the backup input to an orange wire on the radio harness but there was no orange wire. I searched the Amazon questions and found a couple that had response from the manufacturer stating that in the absence of a orange wire, the pink wire should be used instead and there was one of those. It worked. 2. The gauge of the wire on the radio harness is pretty small so I had trouble trying to tap the wires with 14-18 guage T-splices. I ended up stripping a section on the truck wire, wrapping the radio wire to make the connection and then putting on a lot of electrical tape to attempt to seal it. So far I have not had any problems with these connections. 3. I also had to use the Antenna Control output as the on/off control for my crossover amp. That worked fine. The good: - I like the backup camera. It is clear and bright. It wasn't originally something that I cared that much about now that I have it I use it. - The Bluetooth connection seems pretty good, my phone seems to reconnect quickly each time the radio starts up. Which is often, see annoyances. The radio does not show any information about what is playing on the phone like many other radios do. It just shows the phone name. The skip controls seem to work fine as well as the Answer and Hang Up controls. Annoyances: - The USB port does not work. I have tried different cables and phones but have never received an indication that the phone is charging nor an indication from the radio that it sees the phone. - The touchscreen does not work. There are several touchscreen-looking controls on the screen but when I try to press them nothing happens. I went back and verified that the product description states that it is a TFT screen. My guess is that some internal wiring harness to the front of the radio is disconnected or shorted and that is causing but the TFT and USB problem. - As far as I can tell this unit does not support an external mic. There is a mic built into the front panel of the unit but it does not work well in my noisy diesel truck. This is very unfortunate since one of the things I wanted was to be able to make calls but can't while the engine is running. This one issue is probably what will force me to replace the unit in the near-ish future. - Whenever I shift into reverse the radio or Bluetooth stops playing. It does display the backup camera but whatever function the radio is currently doing stops. I have never seen this on any other stereo. Not only does it do this when I want to back up but most of the time when I shift from Park to Drive since I have to shift past Reverse to get there. - The 3 button preset does not seem to work reliably. Most of the time when I push it nothing happens, occasionally it will switch to the preset. The others seem to work fine. - The stereo powers down while the truck starter is engaged. For most vehicles this would probably not be noticed since you just get in and turn the key immediately to the Start position. However for a diesel I first put the key in the Ignition position to charge the cylinders. This could take from a few seconds to a minute on a cold morning, then I move the key to the start position. So given this and the "shut-off in Reverse" issue I mentioned previously the radio/Bluetooth usually starts and stops playing 3 times before I get on the road which is a little annoying. I have considered trying to alleviate this with a couple of capacitors, one on the power input and one on the backup input but I have not tried this yet. Oddities - In 12 hour mode, the clock displays 00: for twelve P.M. So if it 15 minutes past noon, it shows 00:15 which I have never seen before. - It took me quite a while to figure out how to get to the Settings menu. The operating instructions in my box seemed to be for a different model. Anyway if you are in the same boat, you need to hold in the Volume button to get to the Settings menu where you can set the time, pair with a phone, etc.. If you just push it and release you get an audio setting menu which lets you set the set the Bass, Balance, etc. - I have been through the menus multiple times but cannot figure out how to un-pair a phone. I guess it's not a big deal but it seems like something someone might want to do.

First, for all these application, no raw format. The only stream is MJPG, where hardly a single pixel has the same value as the raw image. Useless. The frame rate is not adjustable, so choose a size, and you get ONE default frame rate. I have used SharpCap with dozens of cameras, and even the cheapest camera will give you a complete set of properties for SharpCap (any camera control software) to see what the camera is capable of. USB 2 is a waste. That is why they only give MJPG lossy streams. Every setting drops frames. No exceptions. And this interface board cannot support ANY of the frame rates. I ask for 30 and I get 19.5. Ask for 15 I get 13.1. Ask for 640x480 at 8 fps and it gives 7.7 and drops frames like crazy. What this tells me is the Arducam made a USB camera interface card that is not standard, is vastly underpowered, expensive, and comes nowhere near exposing the full range of capabilities of the IMX477 sensor - which is what it was supposed to do. AmCap.exe that you download from ArduCam has no digital signature. So it could be spam ridden. It is the worst camera capture tool I have seen in a long time. My conclusion is that ArduCam is not ready for any of the application areas I mentioned, except with lots of hacking and fiddling and spending. MJPG only, why bother? This is the right idea - have a universal USB and wireless interface to MIPI cameras. But ArduCam came nowhere near the mark. I am just very disappointed. I feel like I have been scammed. USB3, full support for all the properties and capabilities of MIPI sensors. Raw formats, regions of interest, 1000 fps regions of interest. NO losses in transmission. NO fluctuating intensities. I tried this with the Raspberry Pi HQ Camera Module. Maybe this ArduCam interface works only with ArduCam IMX477 Camera Board.

I am so glad I bought this instead of an iWatch. Sure, there may be some functionalities missing, but I don't need a watch that replaces my phone. I was looking for a watch that would track my health, sleep, and have a quiet alarm - this watch does all of this perfectly, while having a battery life superior to Apple's. I charge my watch once every 10-14 days, for about 20 minutes. I wear my watch every day and use it to track my steps, heartbeat and sleep. However, there are some things I wish could be improved. CONS: - Scratches Easily: I've had this watch for about one week and there are already a lot of scratches on the screen. I wear this on my non-dominant hand, and do my best to avoid scraping it against surfaces. However, there are giant scratches. I've had my iPhone for about 3-4 years without a screen protector, and I have 1-2 scratches on the screen. Not sure how screen durability compares to iWatch. - Slow Response: When I turn my wrist to look at the time, the display turns on a solid 2-3 seconds afterwards. Doesn't sound like a lot, but it can be really irritating after a while. - Touch Screen Sensitivity: Sometimes I need to press a little harder than normal or swipe multiple times to get a response - Bluetooth: For some reason, my watch doesn't automatically connect to my phone unless I open the app. It makes it basically impossible to control my music with my watch unless I open the Zepp app first, and wait a minute for it to connect.... for like 3 hours PROS: - Worth The Money: A $100 watch that lasts 2 weeks, tracks health, fitness, and sleep? And connects to phone to give alerts on texts and set alarms? It's a watch that doesn't replace your phone, but acts as an extension. - Alarms: I struggle with waking up in the money and constantly ignore audio alarms. I had my doubts about a vibrating alarm, but it definitely works for me! I love the smart alarm option – waking you up during light sleep within 30 minutes before the set time. I actually don't feel completely horrible when I wake up at 7 AM now. - Remote Camera: This is such a minor feature, but I was so happy that you could "click" your phone camera remotely. When you open this app and press the button, it simulates the sound button on the phone, and takes a photo. Great for timer photos and tripods! - Watch Face Design: There are many watch face designs, but my favorite is the default one. It shows you all your stats in one place: time, date, power, steps, calories, heart rate and weather. - Small Wrist Friendly: As someone with smaller wrists, I was pleasantly surprised by the size of the watch face and the band size adjustments. My wrist is about 2 in (5 cm) wide, and the watch face is *the perfect size*. Not ridiculously mini that it's hard to seen the screen, but also not giant, that covers my entire wrist. The band also has 12 holes to allow for a wide range of band adjustments. - Easy to Clean: Yes. This watch is waterproof. It feels so wrong to shower and swim with it on, but it definitely works. It's so easy to clean the band and screen, that there's no worry of getting it too dirty.

This unit is OK for the price, but only barely. I had read that inside was a replaceable 18650 Lithium Ion battery and that is why I bought it. I didn't mind that the reviews suggested maybe under 2 hours play time. When it came time to switch out the battery after maybe 2.5 hours play time, opening the case was tricky. I removed 5 screws and still had to find the hidden several "catches" to open the case. Each made me feel like maybe I would never get it back together again. Once inside, I discovered one of those flattish Lithium Ion batteries that was possibly replaceable, but certainly not as commonly found as the 18650. My fancy 18650 charger/tester/reconditioner and spare batteries would be useless here. Also, once inside the case I immediately noticed there is only one speaker. It seems well built and provides decent sound, but is not loud enough to picture this unit as a party sound source. Positives: Sound quality is reasonable for a monaural tiny speaker. The rechargeable battery works, but not for long... The pairing with blue tooth headset went seamlessly. The unit seems well built. The speaker seems high quality. The accessories provided are of reasonable quality and function as well as expected for an under $60 product. The oversampling or whatever they call it in the description works just fine. I accidentally pushed my unit off the table and it hit the floor full on the edge. There was no hesitation or interruption of the sound. I have carried it around the house and yard with me with similar flawless result. I don't know if this is a comment about my cheap blue tooth head set, or this unit, but the distance I can walk from the unit before losing signal is well over 40 feet, even around a corner. Negatives: Not stereo as advertised. Volume is lacking. You won't be able to hear this in most cars beyond maybe recognizing the song. If you are wanting to listen to audio books, do not buy this unit. I get play time of about 2 CDs per battery charge. Charging time is SLOW, maybe a couple of hours. I need to comment on the questions and answers about being used by the visually impaired. While, no, there are no raised shaped marks on the buttons for self-learning without the instructions, the instructions are clear. Even though I am not visually impaired, once I have learned the button placement on a unit, I really don't look at it except to read the track number rarely. I certainly don't look at the buttons to turn on the unit, start, pause, stop, fast forward, back up, or change the CD. I don't see any issues with a visually impaired person using this unit if there is somebody to read the instructions and help the individual learn the button placement. The on/off button is a tactile slide. Even the charging should go easily enough in the dark. Comment for the reviewers that say the unit won't pair with their car: Read the instructions, or even the product description above. This unit will not pair with a car. To use it in the car, use the included AUX cable and connect it to your AUX port in your car if you have one. This will allow you to use this through the car's amplifier and speakers. The blue tooth connection in this unit is one way, out only. It cannot receive incoming blue tooth signals from your car (or headset) i.e. volume control. I suggest plugging in the charging USB while in the car, too. Overall comments: If you want a CD player to play audio books, this will work nicely if you are going to use it in a place where it can stay plugged in except for occasional room changes when you will use the battery. If you intend to play music, you must use the wired, or blue tooth headphones for stereo sound or sufficient volume for comfortable listening. I am not going to return this, but I am disappointed that it is not as advertised. My hope was to use this on my lawn mower to listen to audio books. The poor volume, even at maximum with head phones on maximum are far too low for mowing. Battery life is also an issue for me for mowing. It will be fine to use near the bed and on the charger for audio book listening.

The Arteck keyboard is a pleasant exception to that. It is extremely strong, due to the metal cover on it. Beyond that, The exceptionally clever design allows it to be paired with multiple devices simultaneously. It comes with its own USB dongle to plug into a PC, Mac, or even a Smart TV. Now you should know that this is not a full sized clickable type keyboard. There is no numeric keypad on one side and the keys are small “Chiclet“ style keys, that only have a short throw travel. [[VIDEOID:24c6d2e5535cc5228343e102556bda97]] For the price, it's still a good buy. A lot of improvements over the previous model I had, though some of the same flaws still, and 1 step backward. The mobile app lets you record your route, DVR or download recordings to your mobile device, and control the dashcam from your mobile device (or at least change settings). Not recommended to modify dashcam settings or functions while driving regardless, of course. The picture seems clearer. The night vision option is arguably better, yet I found myself wanting a little bit more artificial brightening for the night vision. This is STILL an excellent and easy-to-install option if you want a back-up camera on your car, with an even larger display on this model, although I can guarantee that the suction cup mount will fall, and I honestly ended up using glue to keep it up, once I found the right spot. That's not a knock on this suction cup as it's a knock on all suction cups, but if you are worried about resale, or have a lease, the suction cup can work for awhile. Including a mount option that hangs off the mirror would be better for many. You'll have to glue or use gorilla tape or both to keep the rear camera up. The dashcam records excellent video, again arguably better, and has some quick preset options, and better power management options. That said, the parking monitor is unlikely to last more than 2-3 hours or so in my experience, and you probably want some external battery with a foldout solar panel if you want that option if your car is parked at work or something. A lot of the above criticisms are ones I had of my previous model, except for the artificial brightening of the rear camera, so there are improvements. But this new model has 1 major step backwards in my opinion, which a firmware upgrade should be able to solve. The old headlight alarm would sound once, and had a clear, decently loud sound (okay, could have been louder). The new headlight alarm is such a quiet odd tone that you could easily miss it, except for the fact that it will keep going off, even when you have your headlights on. I recommend 2-3 headlight alarms at most when the camera has external power going to it, and using a different and louder tone. I personally don't care if you reuse some existing tone in the camera. But it's honestly so annoying that I'll likely shut off this feature, which sucks, because it's a really nice safety feature for anyone with an older car whose headlights don't turn on automatically. I'd still recommend it, but a firmware upgrade to address some of the above issues, if possible, and inclusion of a mount to hang it from the rear-view mirror would make this a great buy. This is a physically well made cable with an inline converter. It does not really fully match the description or the included leaflet and if you leave default settings you will get disappointed. However there are things this is good for. There is a nice color rendition when set correctly. 1. On the HDMI side the EDID information (that is send to the device "projecting" video to it) identifies as 1280x720 60Hz. There are a few other modes listed, but this is the native resolution. There is no benefit of forcing the projecting device to a higher resolution. 2. On the UVC end - the usb capture device: 2A) The device correctly sends brightness, contrast and saturation settings - color representation look natural with them. 2B) The device default capture resolution is set as 1920x1080, which is suboptimal - the image is smudged and stretched, again this is not the native resolution and you will want to change it. 2C) There are 3 resolution that you want to use for capturing images that don't look terrible: 2C1) 1280x720 60Hz MJPEG - there is ghosting and artifacts on sharp edges/text, so anime/cartoon material is not recommended. natural images(photos) show less perceptible artifacts. 2C2) 720x576 25Hz YUV2 - this is PAL resolution turned into progressive video. Can be captured without artifacts - e.g. use this for a SD material in PAL - something like an old camcorder, older console like the Gamecube, VCR deck or a OTA STB in EU. 2C3) 720x480 30Hz YUV2 - this is NTSC resolution turned into progressive video. Can be captured without artifacts - e.g. use this for a SD material in NTSC - something like an old camcorder, old CCTV camera, VCR deck, your aging Nintendo WII (with the HDMI adapter) or for one of those funky OTA converters. 3) Audio There is no audio in the UVC capture device - the included leaflet only instructs you to set up the UVC capture device in OBS - you will not get audio that way. When setting the source, select a separate audio device and select the separate USB audio device that appears. 4) Encryption the EDID block indicates that the device can support encryption, though at the resolution it is good for, that is not needed. For the price this is an ok device if you keep it within the above limits.

I found not ever SATA adapters work with Linux and the raspberry pi. Reading the reviews, people mentioned this works, so I bought it. And it does work perfectly. Previous one I bought before this didn’t, would get stuck at boot. It’s a chipset issue. Anyways this one has UASP, which increases speed, and more importantly in my opinion, TRIM, which basically means, whenever you store something in your SSD, if there were bits of data in that location marked/flagged as deleted but bits of 0s and 1s still present inside, TRIM will just write over it. Without TRIM the driver would first zero out all the bits then insert the new data. This maximizes an SSD’s write cycle limitation. Unfortunately TRIM is a hardware feature, so any cable/adapter that does not implement it, won’t get to take advantage of it.

Bought this 4TB SSD for my DJ performance laptop to store media files. My idea was to not have to use an external USB drive for my files. After installing the drive, I started transferring media files to it. For unknown reasons the drive would simply disappear from the system. This seemed to occur most frequently when I'd attempt to move a large folder of several hundred gigabytes (using TeraCopy). Part of the way through the move, the drive would vanish. Restarting the system didn't find the drive. But, if I got into my BIOS, usually it was at least recognized there, but sometimes not. Without making changes in the BIOS, if I saved and restarted, the drive would sometimes magically appear. Thinking it was a driver issue, I updated all drivers for my system. (LEVEN does not seem to offer any firmware updates to its drives.) This seemed to have resolved the disappearing drive issue. Until the drive vanished in the middle of a wedding reception. That was it. It is now relegated to an external USB enclosure. I swapped it out for a high capacity spinner which will no doubt be 100% more reliable. So, I highly recommend this drive if you want to install it in an external usb drive case to have on hand just in case. But, if it's your bread and butter, there are better options. Look for a drive that has a DRAM controller built-in.

review_text: I am by no means an audiophile, but I know what I like and what sounds good to me and I am seriously impressed by these Earfun Air 2 earphones. I've now been using these for 4 weeks as my daily earbuds, they're that good and I own more premium and expensive ones from some big brands.The design of the earbuds is very much like that of the Apple AirPods with the stems, which is the first pair of this style I've owned as all my other pairs are of the in ear design. I found these extremely comfortable to wear even for prolonged use and I didn't suffer from any ear fatigue after 4 hours of constant use. I used the pre installed medium silicone tips, but there are also other sizes bundles in the box if these aren't right for you. The earbuds are gloss white in colour with a silver strip with the Earfun branding on, this has a slightly matt finish to it giving slightly more grip when you handle them.To get the most out of these earbuds the first thing you need to do is download the Earfun Audio App available from both the Google Play store or the Apple App store. Once you have downloaded the app you can connect it to the earbuds where it opens up a world of customisation, from EQ setting to what you want to assign to the touch controls, which is a great feature and not something that is always available on other brands. The app also has a find my earbuds feature again something many rivals don't have.The touch controls work well, although as the touch sensors are at the top of the buds I did on occasions accidentally activate them when just moving them in my ears.There is no ANC here, which isn't a surprise given the price, but there is a good amount of passive noise cancellation due to the excellent fit of these earbuds. But what they lack in ANC they make up for in their ability to play Hi-Res Audio and LDAC codecs which produce outstanding sound quality from supported sources.There is also a game mode which can be turned on via the app, this worked well in my test of playing games like pubg mobile, I could certainly identify where enemies were coming from easier and although not groundbreaking as lots of competitors have similar features it's a nice addition.The call clarity from these earbuds is much better than on some of my other pairs, with clear, crisp voices both received and transmitted.Battery life is fantastic, I've only charged these once so far in 4 weeks of mixed usage and charging is on par with many others.Value wise these are amazing and how Earfun has crammed so much tech into these and kept the price so low is astonishing as at the moment the black version can be snapped up for £35 and the white for £40 which is an absolute bargain and makes these so easy to recommend.

review_text: With the advent of 4GB and 8GB Raspberry Pis, and their improvements with I/O and USB, I decided to finally build a power and space efficient homelab for personal improvment. I'm glad I chose this as an integral component of the build. What I used: * The black-and-green Cloudlet case * 6 Pi 4s with PoE hats * 2 SATA SSDs * Ubiquiti ES-8-150W switch * Ubiquiti ER-X router * Mikrotik dual-radio access point The Good: * Quarter-inch acrylic is rigid and resists breakage * The modular 'blades' can hold Raspberry Pi 4s and SATA SSDs without issue * You can see the reflections of the Pi LEDs in the acrylic, making the whole thing look even more fancy * The green blades are UV reactive, so a blue LED or light will cause them to softly glow * The fans are -quiet-. I can barely hear the thing while sitting next to it with all four fans running! * There's plenty of room underneath the blades for a small router, AP, or power cables for the Pis if you don't want to PoE. The Bad: * The blades are a bit fragile, given their thin profile, and the bendable parts are prone to snap if you're not careful. Fortunately, c4labs ships spare ones with the kit! * The power connectors on the fans are on the long side. Since I'm using a power-over-ethernet board on my Pis, the result ends up putting pressure on the next blade over when installing them in the case. They're standard Dupont connectors though, so I don't see any way to fix it other than replacing them with lower profile (and probably more expensive) connectors. Something I have the tools and experience to fix, but others may not. Make sure you take this into account when planning your build. The unexpected: * The Cloudlet case bolts perfectly to the wall-mount ears on the Ubiquiti ES-8-150W powering the whole shebang. I just made sure to add large washers to prevent the acrylic from cracking. For the back two mounting holes, I used standard brass standoffs to make sure the Cloudlet case rests level on the switch. This made the build so much more clean and portable. In Conclusion: Thanks to C4Labs, my tiny homelab (the "micro-rack") is portable, space efficient and adequate to my needs. I'm really glad they make a product like this. If I ever want to expand my homelab for more compute, it'll be easy to bolt another one of these to a new switch and add more Pis!

I have owned a variety of Bose headphones over the years, but my favourites by far were the Bose Soundsport Bluetooth Wired headphones. So much so I had two pairs which lasted ages and when I heard they were going to discontinue them I bought one last pair so I could have a set for another few years. I used these headphones mostly down the gym, running, rowing, or even at work as a gardener, so it is safe to say I lead an active lifestyle, but most importantly I want a set of headphones that are durable, sound great, comfortable and also fit perfectly so that despite moving around they do not pop out at the slightest moment.So when my beloved last pair of soundsport gave up the ghost a few weeks ago I figured it was time to look around at the options and figured that because I was so impressed with how the last set of Bose headphones I owned, I would trust them again and go with their latest set of earphones.After owning them for two weeks and giving them a good trial they are not up to standard, but come at a much higher price also.Let’s start with the app which you need to download to get connected and also change the various settings. At first it looks very glossy and lots of cool gadgets, but as other reviewers have stated it is a little glitchy and after only a few minutes it crashed on me and wouldn’t connect. (NB I have the latest software update on my phone so it is not like I haven’t the latest version to work alongside the app).Secondly the sound. The immersive sound is very impressive and it has three settings; the first to leave as is per the recording, the second if you are to sit still the sound stays very central in your head, and the third, movement which allows you to move your head around and be active and the sound follows you around, it really is very impressive. But… I found at times it cuts out returning you to the off setting which jolts you back to a different sound and feel and then returns a second or two later thus resulting in this very odd and uncomfortable listening experience as it reverts back and forth.Next up the fit. And this is the worst of the lot. As I said before, having had the Bose Soundsport headphones, and yes they are larger in comparison for in-the-ear headphones to these, but the fit is magnificent. These come with three different fittings, and I have tried all three and a cross variety of the three because I am aware that my ears might be ever so slightly different in shape/size by the slightest millimetre and so it is worth trying to figure out what is best for you. I tried all of these and despite this the fit just didn’t feel quite right. When out running they jump ever so slightly in the ear but because of the noise cancelling features it sounds like someone is jabbing something in your ear, like a ‘thud, thud, thud’ with every step you take.The disappointment I have for these is overwhelming, especially at the premium price. I don’t know how Bose can make something that is worse than a previous product and get it so so wrong. I guess if you are sat at a desk or sitting at home listening to music these might be good, but I just want a pair of headphones that are designed for exercise and aren’t a set of cans to put over your head, but have the listening experience to boot.I will most certainly persevere with these, mostly because I have to now having spent a small fortune on these, but they are a huge disappointment based on previous headphones bought by Bose.

review_text: This is a review of the gofanco PRO-Matrix44-SC. It is a 4x4 HDMI matrix switch with auto downscaling from 4K to 1080p. Now that I've gotten everything working, it is fine and it works as advertised. But getting there was an adventure. I'll start by noting that the 4K to 1080p downscaling works quite well. It does appear to output real 4K to compatible devices while 1080p displays connected to the same input receive a 1080p version of the signal. The conversion causes no apparent lag or unnecessary quality loss. In fact I am able to use AI upscaling on an Nvidia Shield TV with a 1080p display this way, and there is still a noticeable visual improvement. Whether it would look just as good in native 1080p output mode without the upscaling and downscaling, I can't say. The built-in web interface is very crude, not feature-complete, and the device doesn't actually adhere to the HTTP protocol, which may complicate attempts to integrate it with third party software. I did not try the cloud interface, instead opting to block the matrix from accessing the internet. Now the problems. My first remote control didn't work at all. I reseated the battery half a dozen times and tried it once with the battery flipped over the opposite of the labeled orientation. I even tried a different new battery of the same type. What boggles my mind is that when I looked at the remote's IR LED through a cell phone camera, I could see it clearly lighting up when I pressed buttons. Yet the HDMI matrix did not respond to it. No response through the built-in IR receiver and no response through the external plug-in IR receiver. By the way, here's a tip: Don't try to peel off the protective plastic layer from the IR receiver window on the matrix box. I just ended up accidentally unseating the hard plastic window and pushing it inside the unit. (the remote still didn't work with this window out of the way) So I contacted gofanco support and with a little back and forth we concluded that the remote was likely defective. They mailed me a new remote, which worked. Then for giggles I tried the new remote's battery in the old remote. Suddenly the old remote worked just like the new one. I swapped the batteries between remotes several times and both remotes worked every time without a hitch. But my third-party battery with equally good voltage still did not work in these remotes. What the heck?! Unfortunately that wasn't the end of the problems. The day the replacement remote arrived, I discovered that output 2 on the matrix didn't work at all. Gofanco support wanted me to try uploading the latest firmware onto the matrix. The exact same firmware version it had shipped with. I humored them and ordered a USB to serial adapter so I could upload the firmware. Here's another tip: if you get a serial adapter for this HDMI matrix, get one with a male DB9 connector (exposed pins) and male screws to the sides of the connector. Some USB to serial adapters have female DB9 connectors and/or female screw holes on the sides. Anyway, the firmware upload did not solve anything, so Gofanco support instructed me to return the defective HDMI matrix to Amazon. The replacement matrix arrived today and all inputs and outputs work properly. The remote control was no better than the first one. It didn't work until I fiddled with it and reseated the battery way too many times. But once it started working, it stayed working (so far).

I originally wrote this review for five stars, but after using it for a few weeks I have to decrease it to three stars. I've been struggling to find an external SSD that works correctly with macOS Catalina. Some of the others have awful reviews, poor performance, and in general don't work correctly. Crucial is the first one that works. First, the read speeds are as advertised (and twice as fast as SanDisk or Ravpower portable SSDs). I needed a solid state external drive on APFS for Final Cut, and this drive works tremendously for that task. Formatting is a breeze since this doesn't come with bloated unremovable partitions like Ravpower, so the process was painless. The cons are that the write speeds suffer greatly due to a lack of DRAM, which would assist with maintaining drive speeds for large copy jobs. Because of this, the write speeds often plummet to difficult to use speeds if copying large files. To copy 180gb would take about an hour at the speeds I am seeing on my drive. To be honest almost all the drives available aren't up to par, and this is a market that is severely lacking in suitable devices. This one does the job if you don't need to rely on it for copying large amounts of files to the drive quickly. If you're using it to read files, it's perfectly adequate.

review_text: GET FAMILIAR WITH ARMOURY CRATE this is very important. Recommended operation is Silent or Turbo mode when plugged in. On battery use Silent mode and use the iGPU mode to disable the Geforce card. (By doing this you should get up to 6+ hours of light work with the 2nd screen on, maybe 8-10 light usage hours with only one screen. Potentially an all-day laptop for work and school if you do this.) There's also noise cancelling mic tools and some other stuff in the Crate. DOLBY ATMOS IS YOUR FRIEND this is also very important. Movie mode is very good for a lot of content, but I put it back on Music or Game when not watching something. No webcam, no Thunderbolt, no fingerprint, MicroSD reader but not full size SD, no optical drive. 1080p not 1440p or 4k. sRGB color is good but not same as full Adobe color on the 4K. However the 4K/120 model is rarer than unicorns. I use the display at 100% scale. Main screen does not take touch or pens. Poor battery life when using the Geforce, this is normal for any laptop. Has dual mic plus good noise cancelling, works well with external webcam. Empty slot for an extra m.2 2280 SSD if you need a lot of space for videos, games or other material. Bottom screen easy to organize, super useful. Full 10-finger touch input works well with Android. Supported by Microsoft Surface Pen and the Wacom Bamboo 2 smart pen, this can improve your work flow a lot....or you can just hand-sign a photograph before sending it to grandma. There is a hardware button to disable 2nd screen entirely to save battery. There are software keys to keep the mouse inside the upper screen, and to disable the keyboard for safer pen usage on the lower screen. Keyboard lights up, colors can be set, touchpad is small but decent. Touchpad turns into number pad, makes an acceptable substitute most of the time. Laptop body is strong, not very heavy, designed for excellent cooling without a stand, designed to work well as a desktop replacement. Has video, physical internet (ethernet), and a USB type A on the back for classic desktop usage. Extra type A sockets, audio jack and power input go on the left away from touchpad and right-handed mouse users. Audio jack is high quality and connected to an ESS Saber audio chip. Four speakers plus virtual surround work very well... Everyone already knows the R9-5900HX is a very fast processor for a laptop, both in simple and heavy tasks. Not everyone knows that ARMOURY Crate can better tame the chip to work at whatever level you want it to, either more power or quiet and efficient. The video chip is Geforce RTX 3080 high-performance type (16GB video memory instead of 8GB on Zephyrus g15, max 130W vs max 100W on same g15). This can give you 15-20% more performance. In comparison it has more memory than a desktop 3080 (10GB) and it performs similar to a desktop 3060Ti or 3070. It is suitable as a workstation using the Studio drivers, or as a gaming machine using the Gameready drivers. There are other systems with up to 150-165W on the same video chip if you must have that last fraction of performance. All games run on this machine, most in Full HD Ultra or even better. There's plenty of other stuff to cover but for me the important parts were what I listed above. If you ask about things like frame rates I will say Yes it plays every game, and with a high power 3080 you really won't have to worry about exact numbers in most games.

review_text: This HRM works great initially. I use it with my Garmin Forerunner 735XT and it worked flawlessly for about 12 months, using it 2-4 times a week on 1.5 hr bike rides. The HRM stopped working after a year so I figured the battery needed replacing. First off, the micro screws are a major headache to take out initially as they are super tight and small. I actually broke my micro screw driver trying to get the screws out. To get the screws out I has to clamp the HRM to a work bench then take my broken screw driver and put the head into a drill. Once I got the screws out and battery replaced, the HRM still didn’t pair with my watch. Tested a second battery and same result. I read another review that talked about the backing not pushing the battery down enough due to the small self tapping screws not clamping down enough after battery replacement. I pushed the battery down by hand and sure enough, the HRM paired. I tried several thicknesses of pads I had laying around for the case to push the battery down correctly and finally settled on the combination shown in my review photo. This is the only way to get this HRM to work after a battery replacement. Trouble is now, I screwed the screws in and out a dozen times to figure out how to get the battery replacement to work and I don’t think the screw heads and self tapping surface will take another round after this battery dies. Hopefully my trial and error will help someone. Bottom line is this HRM won’t last more than 3-4 battery replacement cycles even if you follow my lessons learned from trail and error. The battery replacement is a major design flaw with this HRM (are you listening Garmin?) Someone else's review said it well about Garmin HRMs - plan on having to buy a new HRM every 1-2 years and consider it Garmin's yearly tax on allowing you to use their watch. 5 stars for first year of use, one star for battery replacement and longevity.

I'm a long time Fitbit customer. I previously owned Versa, and Versa2. Prior to that I had a couple of Pebble smartwatches. So I quickly upgraded to Sense when it became available. All the features I love about Fitbit watches, sleep stats, fitness stats, continuous heart rate, notifications, are there and working very well. Initially I found the new UI a bit confusing. Not having the physical 'Back' button on the watch set me back a bit. I struggled for a while on how to get back to the watch face from various situations. Things improved much better when I eventually discovered the "VIRTUAL BACK" button. If you gently press the middle left side of the watch, it gives you a haptic feedback and puts you right back to the previous screen. Otherwise most existing features work similarly. Swipe to the left, you get the application list. Swipe down you get the notifications. Swipe up you get the enhanced fitness statistics as well as weather widget and EDA widget. Fitness stats have been broken into two: CORE and ADVANCED. You have to load the ADVANCED stats separately if you want to see it all. NEW FEATURES: If you swipe to the right, you get the most commonly used settings. 'Do not disturb', 'Sleep', 'Always on', 'On when arm moves' buttons as well as watch face dimmer and music volume. These are very useful to have easy access to. I'm keeping the 'Always on' mode on at all times and turn off the 'On when arm moves' setting. This way I can always see the time at a glance and use the 'virtual back button' to light up the watch face when I want. I put my watch to sleep mode before going to bed. I use the virtual back button to wake the watch up and turn off the sleep mode when I wake up. With these settings, my battery lasts about 5 days. ECG: This is an app in the application list. When you want to take your 30 second ECG, you start the app, place two fingers on the watch face corners and let the watch measure your ECG. After 30 seconds measurement, the watch tells you if you had a-fib during the 30 second time it took the measurement. It doesn't continuously monitor your heart rate looking for a-fib. I guess the idea is when you are not feeling well or having heart palpitations, you will manually start this app and measure it. SKIN TEMP: The watch measures your skin temperature while you sleep and compares it to your baseline temperature. The idea is that a large variation in your sleep temperature may be an early indication that you are soon to get sick. EDA: Allows you to relax and measure your stress level for two minutes at a time. Afterwards it gives you a number indicating your stress level. You can also log your mood periodically and the Fitbit app keeps track of it. I find this feature marginally useful if at all. CHARGER: The new charger is much smaller and slimmer than the old versas. It has four small pins that connect to the watch on the back side. It reminds me of those old pebble watch chargers, where after a while dirt and sweat got in between the pins and contact with the watch became difficult. I had to frequently wipe clean the charger and the backside of the watch with wet wipes so that it could continue to charge. It remains to be seen if this new charger will develop those same problems as old pebble watches. I was hoping for touchless charge, like those of apple watches. Unfortunately not in this release...

review_text: This was my first gaming mobo since 2013, and I already had some knowledge on how to build a PC, so didn't rely too much on user manual/resources. NOTE: Despite the box having a sticker saying it was ready for Ryzen 5000 series CPU's, the BIOS date was from Aug 2020, meaning I had to use Q-Flash to update the bios. Many folks may get caught up on the fact that they wouldn't expect to be purchasing a mobo with BIOS this old, especially since the pre-installed BIOS were not compatible with Ryzen 5000, despite the sticker suggesting otherwise. Q-Flash made it very easy to update the BIOS, but I wanted to note this to help others that may have issues, as if you are using a Ryzen 5000 series CPU, YOUR PC WILL NOT BOOT until you update BIOS. I had to manually uninstall the drivers that come with the mobo and install the generic windows 10 audio driver. All is working fine now, but I wouldn’t expect this to be an issue. I wasn't sure which brand to jump back into after being out of the gaming PC world for a bit, but given the good experience, I will use AORUS going forward.

Overall I really liked this board. You can get most of the features in boards half the price, but this one has the water monoblock which is very, very cool looking. With hardware this expensive, they need to make you fall in love with the design because if it's just specs it's not enough to justify the price. With that said, the aesthetics of this board are great. I appreciated the amount of cables, extras, packaging, and the premium feel of the whole experience. It was very enjoyable to unpackage and build onto this motherboard. Now for the quirks - Either they don't work or are mislabeled in the manual, but BOTH of my RGB headers on the board itself didn't work. There are two sets of RGB headers, 1x aRGB and 1x 4-pin RGB per section, with a jumper available to select the appropriate voltage (so 2 aRGB headers, 2 4-pin rgb headers, and 2 jumper switches). I set the aRGB active on the top, and that aRGB device didn't work, and I set the 4-pin RGB active on the bottom, and that didn't work on that device either. For both of these RGB devices, I had to use the included fan controller. One theory I have is that the board can only support one type of RGB at once, so you cannot mix and match. The lighting on the board is standard RGB (non-addressable). This was pretty disappointing. The product images show a beautiful gradient on the lighting of the board. You can't actually light it that way! On the PCB RGB, you have about 12" of an LED strip that can only be one color at a time. I feel like this is a big opportunity that they missed. The lighting for the mobo RGB headers can only be set in pairs. You can control both the RGB (or aRGB) headers with the same color simultaneously, but they cannot be set independently. Again, this kinda sucks. Small issue, but one of the cables for the fan controller had a wire pulled out from the connector. I was able to get around this, but you'd think it would have been caught in quality control. The fan controller itself is pretty cool. Unlike most competitor offerings, it supports 8x aRGB, 8x 4-pin RGB, and 8x fan control all at the same time and independently. It will be difficult to cleanly route 8 of the ribbon-wire connections, I ended up daisy chaining RGB devices and consolidating to 5 ports on the controller. One major problem I had to overcome was that the USB connection cable between the fan controller and the mobo is very short, I think just 15cm or so. It severely limits where you'll be able to mount the fan controller. This is impactful, because if you're utilizing the controller then you have up to 8 fan/rgb leads, plus two temp leads, plus usb input, and it's hard to manage that much cabling if you can't optimally choose where you want to mount it. Onto the software. It's not good. RGB Fusion is a buggy mess. Smart Fan doesn't control your system fans, only the controller fans. Oddly, "System Information Viewer" is the program you need to use to change system fan curves. You cannot access the controller fans within System Information Viewer. You control system fans within SIV in a section called.... Smart Fan. It's confusing, and frankly Gigabyte needs to spend the time and money to get it right like ASUS has. It's a bad experience when someone is configuring their PC for the first time to have to endure the sheer terrible design and bugginess that is RGB Fusion. To reiterate, you cannot control all of your fans in one place. You need to control your system fans (i.e. mobo fan headers) in one program, and your fan controller fans in a different program. They're both Gigabyte programs, and for a strange reason one is called Information Viewer. If any of your fans are non-PWM, you can voltage control them. But you can only do that in BIOS. It was frustrating to attempt this through SIV, because it doesn't work there. Only within BIOS can you change the fan control scheme. I have the fancy Gskill RGB trident royal RAM in gold. RGB fusion thinks this is a non-addressable RGB element, and will only do static color things. You can disable the control in the software, but that will override any lighting configuration you do in the Gskill lighting software. The solution is to go into the RGB Fusion software folders, and delete the .dll's that reference "DDR". This will trick RGB Fusion into not attempting to control the RAM. Lastly, the Gigabyte App Center is also terrible. Updates fail multiple times in a row, and when updating system software, it automatically attempts to download (and install!!!) a google toolbar for IE and Norton antivirus. Really bad bundling, Gigabyte. Overall I like the board. It has quirks, and the Gigabyte software suite is poor quality, no nice way to put it. With those things in mind, this is the best mobo for the z390 out there. That was worth it to me. I would never consider a low end Gigabyte now, knowing how bad their software is. EDIT: I originally had this at 4 stars, but now I'm making it 3. The 10gb/s ethernet jack stopped working when I swapped out my router (??). The other port on the board works fine. The Gigabyte software is too poorly designed to actually update this driver - every time it searches for new driver, the Aquantia 10gb ethernet driver shows up, attempts to installs, pretends like it does, but doesn't actually install the new driver. EDIT2: I need to drop another star. Another issue - even though it says this nowhere in the manual, only one of the two temp sensors on the motherboard can be used by the fan curve BIOS functionality. Also note, I had to put ALL of my fans on the motherboard headers and stop using the included fan controller. The software was just too spotty, and I was tired of my fans running at 100% speed sometimes because the software stopped working. I really just need to reiterate, and hope that GIGABYTE listens - GIGABYTE, your software is absolutely terrible. Please feel free to contact me directly if you need examples, screenshots, steps to reproduce, etc. I like the hardware you guys make, but you need help with your software. I might eventually record some videos of the sheer badness that is Gigabyte's software.

Given the explosion of wireless cameras recently in the market, I wanted to purchase a premium product to test out. This had my hopes up pretty high until I tested it out the last 3 months in an outdoor setting with some nighttime traffic. Base station indoors. Two cameras outdoors (25ft and 50ft distance to station). A few positive things to note - - Easy set up - Clean user interface - Crisp daytime 4k video - Camera firmware and updates are automatic and managed seemlessly by Arlo - The AI categorization algorithm is pretty good - Probably the best wireless 4k stuff on the market today Real challenges that need to be addressed that introduce a lot of maintenance and friction: - Stock battery life is pretty terrible. I have to charge these up every 10 days, even though I only use them for nighttime purposes in a medium traffic parking area. And you can forget any type of real distance between the camera and the base station, it kills the battery. Arlo could have packed a bigger battery into the box for the price being paid, but really cheaped out here. Instead they want you to buy a bigger battery separately. That's bad product strategy. If you want to be the best WIRELESS camera, it starts with the battery life. It's already one of the most expensive cameras on the market... why would you cut costs here? - Charging is absurdly slow, and the battery indicator is terribly inaccurate and a guestimate at best. It takes 8 hours or more to bring a camera up to full charge by cable... again... I ask why for such a small battery? Cellphones with bigger batteries charge in two hours or less. Yes, you can buy a separate charging station, take down the camera, pull the battery out and charge the battery in a station... but again why? This is wireless device... battery life and power management are foundational to product success... how did you mess this up Arlo? The cellphone industry already figured this out for you. - These are IoT cameras that connect to Arlo's own servers through the smarthub that acts as a gateway. They cannot be directly connected to on your local intranet. Everything goes through Arlo's servers and cannot be operated without passing data over the internet. The only way to access any manage the cameras is over their website. And you MUST have a good internet connection. Even the local storage in the smarthub must be accessed through the internet, or the SD card pulled and put directly into your computer. Arlo claims this is for security reasons, but I'm not 100% sold on this approach. The smarthub is just a locked down wifi router... There should be better ways to do this without requiring data to go through Arlo servers. - Motion detection is good, but more problematic, the video often cuts short of activity actually occurring - If you are expecting to capture license plates with this... not happening unless it's pointed right at the car 10 ft away max. I believe this is because of the 180 degree ultra-wide lens on a 4k sensor. Effectively, expect the same clarity of video as a 2k 130 degree camera that just covers a lot more area. - The video CODEC used to record and store videos is proprietary, which is completely unnecessary given the widely available, open source, and free codecs that are well known and used throughout the industry. You must purchase the video coded separately for Microsoft Edge or Google Chrome, and it doesn't even work with Mozilla Firefox. This also means you can't share videos with others unless they buy the codec as well. - The wireless connection is still WiFi protocol and susceptible to basic WiFi jamming and interference. It really needs a different secure wireless method. (To be fair, there are not a lot of alternative wireless methods in the industry yet. Just know it's ultimately a WiFi camera.) - Subscription is pretty much a requirement for functionality to be worth anything. Though, the price point is such that if you are forking out money for this camera, the subscription price shouldn't be your biggest concern. All that said, this tech is far better than what was on the market just 3 years ago. Given Arlo's apparent strategy, they are making it work and proving to be innovative. The only reason I bought this was to test out viewing my 3D .mpo photos shot on a Fujifilm W3 3D. I also bought the Lume Pad to compare. One can view .mpos on a third party app: sView Image Viewer. $700 is expensive, but I don't know of any other 3D lenticular tablet. The tablet comes with two pre installed 3D apps: IQH 3D Player for videos, Sight3D for images. The 3D lenticular screen is reasonably sharp but the viewing angles are still difficult to get. When you do get the right angle, the 3D is decent but always a little ghosting. Other than the Leia player app on Lume Pad, there is no downloadable app that I know of that can natively display .mpos on this display. That there isn't a universal 3D standard file format and recognizing software is the biggest problem with 3D. When I initially played the youtube app, I wasn't able to get 3D from SBS. Eventually I discovered I had to find and run a pre-installed app called 3DFV first. Then when you run the youtube app, you can watch SBS videos in 3D by selecting a tab overlay on the left. Unfortunately, this overlay only shows up on the youtube app and the google chrome app. Compared with the Lume Pad, the IQH3D has much better HD resolution. Lume Pad's 3D is kind of easier on the eyes, but less 3D and looks like 480p all the time. Lume Pad's 3D also distorts more. Lume Pad has a much better dedicated software ecosystem experience, able to simulate 3D on 2D videos even! It's a shame IQH3D doesn't have the same 3D software ease. Side Note: PROMA The hardware is virtually the same as the ProMa tablet being sold direct from China. I returned this and later bought the ProMa Tablet because it comes with free keyboard case. The software layout is also slightly different but also sView shows the files you're browsing on the side in a transparent overlay. It also comes preinstalled with a screen protector. All in all, if you're thinking about testing, go amazon and return. If you're thinking about keeping, GO PROMA! 3D Tablet Comparison Lume Pad vs. IQH-3D (Pro Ma King Tablet) IQH-3D – Lenticular Tablet (Bigger looking image) (Looks better with Lumix) Pros +FULL resolution, like native HD +Slideshow on sview +Brighter Cons -Poorer viewing angles (more ghosting) -No Native .MPO support (Must Convert to SBS or use sView image viewer to view .mpos) -No Auto Brightness SBS Conversion process: open stereophoto maker File>Multi Conversion Select MPOs or make file of only MPOs (Output File Type: Side-by-Side JPG) (Output File Setting>Image Quality: 99) Output Folder>(where you want it) Convert All Files Confirm Conversion Start: Yes Copy to tablet (Download and) Open sview app>Tap on folder>sdcard0>select Images, Mix images & videos Select 3D mode: Cross-eyed Lume Pad – Light Field Tablet Pros +Native .MPO support: Leia Player +Better 3D Viewing Angles? (~less ghosting) +Better Software Ecosystem, Interface, Buttery +Better Color (Deeper reds) Cons -Lower resolution 3D, like 480p. Very screen doorish. -NO Slideshow Overall, I decided I preferred Full Res lenticular 3D over easier viewing angles lower res and slick feeling of Lume Pad. I returned the IQH3D and bought the PROMA directly from the China brand site.

review_text: I selected this battery as what I deemed to be the least sketchy aftermarket I could find, that also could be shipped in two days or less. I didn't have to have it fast, but I don't ever like buying direct from other countries and waiting weeks for a shipment to arrive. Price wasn't important to me, but NinjaBatt's price is excellent. Also, there's a nice touch I think is not included with similar products from other manufacturers: There's a sheet of heavy gauge clear PVC on the top and bottom of the battery. One covers the adhesive, the other acts as a spine to keep the battery segments together while sliding the battery into place during the most critical step of the install process. Once you're sure the battery is located perfectly, you can peel off this spine - the second piece of plastic on the top. I had to reposition the battery a bit, and this support piece made that much easier. The adhesive doesn't fully adhere until pressure is applied, so that helps as well. I followed the ifixit guide, which can be found by searching google "battery replacement macbook pro mid 2014 A1494", and it worked fine. I added an extra step because it made sense to me: After going through the install process, I turned on the laptop, connected the charger and made sure the battery had reached 100% capacity. No, I don't mean checking for "100%" next to the battery icon at the top of the screen. I went to about this mac > system report > hardware > power. Then I compared "Charge Remaining (mAh)" to "Full Charge Capacity (mAh)". The first time I checked, these numbers were not equal, even though the percentage at the top of the screen read "100%". About 10 minutes later, I reopened the system report and the latest snapshot showed them to be equal. (truly full charge) With battery capacity at true 100% full charge, I immediately closed all apps and shut down the Macbook. Then I disconnected the charging cable. About a minute later, when I was sure it was completely shut down, I reset the SMC: first hold down shift-control-option keys on the left side of the keyboard, all at the same time. Continue holding those keys and add the power key. Now hold all four of those keys down for 10-12 seconds. (Run a stopwatch on your phone or keep an eye on a clock with a second hand to be sure.) After that, I booted up the Macbook, and left it unconnected. Use the laptop until battery is around 5% before charging again. Then charge until full. Repeat this 2-3x and by then the system should be calibrated to the battery and fully utilizing available charge. In some cases, this means the battery will seem to discharge more rapidly than expected until the third or fourth cycle. Then it should last about as long as a new stock battery. From then on, charge and discharge in the 30-90% range when not leaving the laptop connected to power. If you typically leave your MBP connected all the time, set a reminder to do a monthly discharge down to around 30% before reconnecting. In short, this battery works, but I never paid attention to the discharge rate of this laptop. If it gets me through an hour of work before I board a flight, I'm fine. I'll be charging again before I'm in the air, and everywhere else I go there's always AC receptacles.

In a nutshell:Things I liked:+ The overall quality. Everything about it, from the angled USBC cable, to the charger itself, to even the wall plug... they all feel of the highest quality.+ The wireless charger itself feels exceptionally well-designed. It feels like a premium product, not only in the materials that they've used, but also the weight and the way in which everything is cleverly hinged and angled. It feels like it has been carefully designed to give you the maximum charging options in a very compact unit.+ Charging performance, as you'd expect, is really good. Charging performance is not noticeably affected by charging multiple devices at once.Things I didn't like:- The price is extremely high. £100 for a wireless charger and wall plug is very much the top end, even though this is a branded product. To be fair, similar premium chargers from UGreen and Belkin tend to be priced in a similar price range.Do I recommend it?Yes, although with one or two caveats.If you want a very good quality mobile wireless charger that's great for taking away with you and will charge your iPhone, your AirPods and your Apple watch all in one, this is great. If that is specifically your use case, you probably won't find a better wireless charger than this.If you're less bothered about the brand name, there are some unbranded chargers at around £30-£50 that will perform as well as this. However, they will not feel as premium.If you want a wireless MagSafe phone charger that's also capable of charging higher-powered devices, you might want to look at the UGreen MagSafe charger. It is around £30 more, but I've tested it and have found it to be excellent, providing up to 100 watts of wired charging power in addition to the angled MagSafe phone charging plate. It has no specific AirPod or watch charging functions though.If you want a charger that is likely to stay in the same place (for example, by your bedside) you might want to look at some of the Belkin charging stands which are very expensive (about £140), but do look very good - although I will say that I haven't tried those, so I just don't know if they're going to be quite as good.But for what this Anker charger specifically does, I don't think you'll get anything better.

I purchased this display after seeing a coworker using a portable monitor. They're a great solution to the not enough screen space problem. The physical size of the display is almost identical to my 16" MacBook Pro. Actually it's slightly smaller, thinner and much lighter. From a portability point of view, it's perfect. Easy to carry in my messenger bag. The display itself is beautiful. The glass screen is 100% of the front. Very elegant looking. The rest of the casing is nicely made with the feeling of good, solid construction. The protective case is ok looking and should do an adequate job protecting from scratches. As a monitor, the picture is gorgeous. Bright, very crisp. To my eye, it's comparable to Apple's retinal display. It's worth noting that macOS scales the picture 1920 x 1080 @ 60hz. I don't know why or if it effects all content or maybe just fonts. Looking at the selection of monitors with the same 4k resolution on Amazon, there are many choices. Actually, this is among the most expensive because of the touchscreen. The product description implies that the touch feature works on laptops. Sadly, it only works on windows laptops. There is absolutely no touchscreen feature on a Mac. For this reason, I will probably return the monitor and either purchase a less expensive model without touchscreen or model with a touchscreen that works with Apple laptops. There are several other observations that may be important to some buyers. The display has stereo speakers. They are tiny and underpowered. Sound quality is good enough for laptop feedback tones, but you wouldn't want to listen to music except at the lowest volume levels. Anything louder than ~50% sounds awful. I tried to watch a movie on the display and didn't have good luck. Playback was jumpy as if the USB and/or monitor refresh rate couldn't keep up. I'm not a gamer but I can't imagine they would have a good experience. The product description mentions iOS. So, I plugged the monitor into its included power brick and directly into my iPhone 8. I was not able to get anything to appear on the screen. Finally, this monitor is power hungry. While the monitor is powered by my laptop, fans constantly run at medium speed. Also, the charger does not replenish the batteries although they don't drain either. You can run both the laptop and monitor off of batteries. I would expect less than 2 hours with the monitor and more than 8 hours without.
