I want to highlight that the 7 outlet units (non USB) are rated at 1440 joules vs the 6 outlet units that are rated at 1080. For that reason, I always purchase the 7 outlet units since there's no cost difference. Surge protectors that are rated below 2000 joules are good for basic home electronics like consumer grade printers, modems, air purifiers, and phone charging stations. For expensive home entertainment electronics, gaming consoles, and home servers, you need units rated at 2000 joules minimum. I recommend APC's backup batteries as those regulate power fluctuations as well. Surge protectors are not designed to last indefinitely. You should replace them every few years. If a surge protector is more than 5 years old or looks damaged, you need to replace it. If your building experiences frequent brownouts or blackouts, then you should replace them 1-2 years. My only complaint is the cord is off-centered. It sits a tad right of the outlet instead of dropping straight down. However, the 6ft cord is plenty long and wrapped in thick insulation. The unit has dual LED lights. One indicates that the unit is operating within parameters, and the other indicates that the power flowing into the unit is grounded. If either of the LED lights is out, there's either a problem with the unit or possibly the building's power. I highly recommend these surge protectors. I've used APC surge protectors and backup batteries for years with no issues. They offer excellent performance for the money.

I currently own a Garmin Instinct Solar 2 and the Crossover Solar. The Garmin Crossover Solar is my favorite smart watch to date. I use it for monitoring my daily health and fitness. I have owned the AW 1,3, 5 (stainless steel), 7 (titanium), and Ultra. As much as I enjoy using the Apple Watch series, Garmin provides me my health metrics from the watch without aftermarket apps. I don't like having to continually depend on my iPhone to see my health metrics. Garmin allows me to connect through their app on my phone, web browser, tablet, etc. Garmin also plays friendly with 3rd party providers such as Strava as to where the AW I have to manually sync my data with Strava. I run, bike, weight train, walk, stand up paddleboard, do yoga, and a variety of other activities. The Garmin gives me a readiness score to help prevent over training. I also like that it continually monitors my vitals, stress, sleep levels (quality of sleep), etc and determines whether or not I should take a break from my exercise. Proactive health and fitness are my lifestyle. I can also compare my fitness/performance levels to other Garmin users, and it provides me insight and feedback... the AW does little of that. For example, I can look up on the Garmin Connect site and see my age group and how I compare to other Garmin users for distance, pace, etc. for an activity. I also like to save coordinates while hiking, on trips, etc. I have the Garmin Explorer option to pull up waypoints. It's convenient sharing my data with other people as to where the AW only allows me to share a screen shot of my workouts with some data. I noticed that the AW does not record stand up paddleboarding as an activity or exercise. The Garmin does, while also recording my route on a map… pretty cool. I wore both devices and found that the Garmin is a bit more accurate running indoors on a treadmill compared to the AW Ultra and Crossover/2. I finish my distance right on point with the treadmill as to where the AW ultra at one mile is .15 to .25 miles off typically; yes, I’m familiar with the calibration process (deleting old calibration… 20 min walk/run outdoors). The Ultra and series 7 (watches used at the time of comparison to the Instinct 2 solar and Crossover Solar) also counts a bit more steps with basic wrist movements as to where the Crossover/2 do not. Once my Garmin gets to one mile, I can calibrate it to match what the treadmill says and it's good to go. The AW is great to generally observe data regarding health, but the lack of feedback is concerning. Also, I do like to check maps out on my adventures or saved coordinates on a map. If I save coordinates on the AW, it is a bit more extensive to pull things up on a map as to where the Garmin side of things just does it. I feel stuck on the AW viewing travel data/waypoints. The Garmin Connect app on my iPhone has all my data in one location. The AW, I need three different apps. Apple has a ways to go on the health/fitness side of things. I see them getting there in the near future and I can see myself eventually getting back on board once things catch up... assuming they do. I will miss closing rings and competing with family/friends on an Apple Watch, but the Garmin is much more on point for my daily lifestyle. I kept trying to convince myself the Ultra would be adequate, and I greatly enjoyed having cellular/music while out on runs, but I'll stick to bringing my phone at this point. I do have a AW5 that I can occasionally use for cellular when I do not want to carry a phone on me. Choosing between the two for my lifestyle, Garmin is ultimately the platform I am choosing to stick to for my active lifestyle of monitoring my health and fitness. I forgot to mention that I like that the Crossover’s display is always on with physical hands and I can glance at it. I’m not a fan of the limited battery life of the Ultra and I’m not sold on the always on display or OLED... just a preference of mine. One other point I’d like to leave is I like the plastic polymer casings on the Instinct/Crossover series. The titanium and stainless casing show scratches like crazy on the Apple watches (aluminum too… my children have the SE and series 5 aluminum, which we keep cases on). The polymer-fiber casings on the Instinct hardly show any where and tear… just mentioning that for those who are a little OCD such as myself. My Instinct Solar 2 has been seen a lot of wear and tear and still looks nearly new despite having scratches (these scratches are matte and hardly noticeable… one must go out of there way with angle lighting, etc. to even see a glimpse of anything)… my point is the polymer-fiber ages well and has seen its fair share of knocks and use in an active lifestyle… my Apple watches patina hard over time and look banged up. I’ve used cases on my Apple watches in the past and they seem to just add to the wear and tear. Aging gracefully and not concerning myself with aesthetics and durability is another win on the Garmin for me with daily use. ————————— Well, my minute hand became loose on the watch. I noticed another person had this issue on a Reddit forum. Amazon made an exception past the return date and authorized a return for me, which I greatly appreciate. I’ll being opting for the Garmin 955 Solar and will definitely miss this watch. I just don’t trust the longevity of the mechanical aspect of this Watch given that I’ve come across others having this issue. Had this issue in reliability not been an issue of mine, it’d still easily be one of my most favored watches I’ve owned to date… there’s nothing like it out there… ——————13MAR23———— I decided to try another watch… same issue (reference photos of watch at the 2oclock and 7oclock position. I decided to keep it because I like the fit and practicality of the watch so much and I guess this may just be the nature of the watch unless there’s a bad batch out there. I contacted Garmin about the issue and the rep said this does not seem “normal.” I’ll test the replacement. If I have the same issue I’ll likely keep the watch although the loose minute hand is a bit of an annoyance. I tried the 955 Solar… a great option too around the same price. The screen is much easier to read indoors on the Crossover Instinct Solar compared to the 955 Solar and the battery life is much better on the Instinct Solar… the Solar option on the 955 doesn’t seem to benefit the battery life much, but on the instinct Solar there is a significant difference for my daily use scenario… especially when running/biking outdoors.

If I hit Menu again from there to look at the setting again, it is set back to NARR. - Same behavior for SFT-D and OFFSET settings. The strange thing about this is... if I've programmed the radio with CHIRP, the offsets actually seem to be working. I can talk on SOME of my local repeaters fine. But in the relevant settings menu nothing seems to be set 4. Finally, the reason I say SOME above is because this radio is not hitting about half of my local repeaters. I have tested with both of my other handsets on the exact same antenna and they hit them all fine. I have tested it with my SWR/Power meter and it's definitely putting out 8W, but I've seen reports on these having a lot of spurious emissions... I think this may be the case with mine. 5. I am having seemingly random cutout of reception - audio will become chopped up and I can't make out anything. Has only happened on 1 repeater channel so far and was able to confirm it was not the repeater. I may request a refund or an exchange

review_text: I had this watch for a week and couldn't continue using it.. Since I used a cuff to measure the higher blood pressure, I'll go with that reading. • Pulse: This seemed accurate. • Watch Face: I loved that I could customize this. However, a couple of days into setting it, the face reset--and I didn't update this on my phone. I'm also not aware of a way to update this directly from the watch so I'm not sure how it reset. • Battery life: I had to charge it about 4 days in. • Workout modes: I was impressed with the amount of different modes, but there's no catch-all "workout" mode. I couldn't track any classes I did, which was disappointing. The app for the smart watch doesn't sync or integrate with any other apps. I've previously used other apps where it'll at least sync with Google Fit, but this doesn't. Overall, it's hard to trust stats on a phone that don't seem accurate. It may also be tricky to return this item after purchasing, since this a third-party purchase through Amazon.

As of October 10/2021, the Thetis FIDO2 Bluetooth key works reliably and quickly over USB in limited testing with Google, Microsoft and Yahoo. However, the Bluetooth has poor range as compared to other keys I own including the Google Titan Bluetooth key or the Feitian AllinPass K33 Security Key (USBc + Bluetooth with fingerprint sensor) or the Authentrend ATKey.Card (USBa + Bluetooth with fingerprint sensor). My computer is a few feet away from my work table. With this, I have to get up from my seat, place the key directly next to my computer and then activate it. Then, leaving the key in range of the computer, I must return to my seat to type in the PIN, then get up once again to tap the key to confirm. In addition, the handshaking/communication over Bluetooth is significantly slower when compared to directly plugged in and to a lesser extent when compared to the other Bluetooth keys mentioned above. Authenticating over Bluetooth works fine with Microsoft and Yahoo, but fails with Google accounts (tested on Windows 10 with Firefox and Chrome) with the message saying "Can't read your security key. Please try again." Plugged in works fine. Did standard troubleshooting, including deleting the key from my Bluetooth devices and repairing it; then trying other Windows computers. So where does this leave us? The Google Titan Bluetooth is missing FIDO2 (can't be used with Microsoft/hotmail), but works with Yahoo and Google. Battery life is good - lasting weeks to months. Feitian AllinPass K33 Security Key (USBc + Bluetooth with fingerprint ) works Microsoft/hotmail and yahoo, but not Google (I have tried and failed) . As per Feitian's website, it weirdly supports FIDO2 but NOT FIDO U2F. Not as good as the titan ble with battery life, but still decent. Do note that the pure UsbA and UsbC keys without bluetooth such as the Feitian K26 and K27 support both FIDO2 and FIDO U2F (I do not have experience with these). Authentrend ATKey.Card (USBa + Bluetooth with fingerprint sensor) works fine with Google, Microsoft and Yahoo both over USB and Bluetooth. However, it has silent battery drain or significantly lower battery life when compared to the aforementioned competition. In addition, it has a weird annoying bug when the battery is fully drained - it has to be charged for about 5 minutes before it becomes functional. Yes, this means that one must spend 5 mins watching the blinking red led while it is plugged in your computer's UsbA port to go away before it becomes operational. Overall, my current preferred bluetooth key is the Authentrend ATKey.Card and my preferred USB alone key is the ATKey.PRO (these have fingerprint sensors). I like the Atkey.PRo's design of putting finger pressure in the direction of port orientation rather then perpendicular which may result in port damage (like most of the competition including the just released Yubikey Bio). That said, I believe there is room for improvement with Bluetooth FIDO2 and FIDO U2F keys, and would like to see proliferation of the more secure Level 2 keys.

Setup was SUPER easy. Senors work fine, not perfect. Customer service has been great. However, the system and the siren pad need work. The siren pad is the worst part of this system. First, it's not very loud. If the TV is on upstairs, you can barely hear the siren downstairs. If it's off and your upstairs, it is still quieter then the vaccum cleaner. When standing next to the siren, again it's not very loud. It should be loud to the point you can't be next to it and you should be able to hear it upstairs with no problems. When the system senses something, it takes 2-3 mins before the siren goes off. This is an issue in that it talks telling you to disarm the system which would just lead a thief directly to it. Then all you have to do is unplug it and it is completely down. Yes, it will still send you an alert to your phone but big deal, by the time you do something about it, the thief is gone while drawing NO ATTENTION to your house. The purpose of an alarm should be to deter a thief IMMEDIATELY upon entering you home. That doesn't happen with this system. The simple fix for this would be to have a rechargeable battery in the base just strong enough to sound the siren for 5 mins once it gets unplugged. Also, like most wifi based systems, when your power is out or your wifi is down, this system will do you no good. Again, it will still send alerts to your phone but nothing AT your house to deter any thieves. The batteries in the sensors are pretty weak. They've only lasted a couple months before having to replace them. Hopefully the new batteries will last longer. The discount they claim they will help you with DOES NOT fully offset the price of the monitoring service; especially since the cost of the monitoring service KEEPS GOING UP. With the monitoring service, I'm not always available to speak on a phone. So if you can't/don't answer, their service will send the police. I've already had a few false alarms happen and that would cause the police to come out unnecessarily. After a couple of those, the police/city will charge you. So in regards to my title, if you have this system WITH A SEPARATE battery powered camera system, I think you would be very well setup. If the alarms go off, you could simply check the cameras to determine the real need of getting the police out. The best reason to have a separate camera system is that if the thieves disable the Kangaroo system, you've still got camera backup. Most thieves are under the impression there would only be one system and once they defeat it, they would go in with a false sense that they are good to go. ****UPDATE**** Over the course of 5 days since my review, the whole system has failed. The siren pad is changing modes on its own. Two more of the Entry and Motion sensors have stopped working and won't reset. I sent customer service an email and they clearly are too lazy to look up my account to see what I bought and what is going wrong. They can't even read the entire email!!!! Total garbage. Wish I could get my money back but of course the system failed after the return window closed.

You also must use an external player for CD's and Mp3's (played from computer or dedicated MP3 player) connected to 3.5mm cable AUX port. Will not play MP3 files from flash drive plugged into USB port. Wished I had my hands on the specs before buying because the user's manual states 60Hz-18kHz frequency response so forget low end bass as well as trusting YouTube sound samples that post frequency response graphs and record with binaural mics. The W-King does have smooth rounded and punchy bass with non-EDM drum tim-tom hits retaining good bell tone which means they carefully designed the roll off bass octaves below 60Hz to not sound boxy and thonky like the old boomboxes in the '80's. The W-King maintains a well balanced sound with most music styles but it does not have as big a sound as the YouTube samples suggest. EQ effect has two settings, one enhances vocals and higher frequencies to come across louder with more clarity, the other setting is more compressed and a bit muffled. I didn't hear an increase in louder, deeper bass between the two EQ settings but that could be due to the songs I was playing. But it does explain why most of the YouTube sound test videos samples electronic digital music with its clean digital waveforms and balanced sound. Even though they're not portable my Boston Acoustic small satellite mains with small boxy subwoofer I bought at Salvation Army for $6 back in 2004 has much more fuller and lower end bass for its similar small size but with murky highs. I get better clarity with the Boston Acoustics on my Spectrum digital cable box analog output where the highs sound normal. The advantages of DSP streaming I guess, but every cable channel has somewhat different sound dynamics, some better, some worse so its the signal, not the speakers at fault which also applies to the W-King. Give it a clean balanced signal and it will deliver it. The W-King's 12in. long enclosure box has main drivers about 7 inches apart that pretty much cancels out any stereo effect when listening for L/R cross channel reflection and wide pan stereo presence where it just ends up sounding like a very loud mono speaker. I test panned left to right channels using my MacMini's Sound Pref settings to confirm it's a stereo signal but I had to have my ears inches from the mains to be sure. Just to be clear this stereo sounding mono applies to all boombox speakers in this class. Directional frequencies in mains have to be spread out at least 3 ft apart to hear the stereo effect from a reasonable distance. You certainly don't want to listen to these W-Kings at loud volumes standing 3 feet away. It's downright uncomfortable. At least at loud volumes they deliver a clean signal. I didn't hear any scratchy noise in the highs as it is with most boomboxes cranked up loud at my local park. The W-King is a VERY GOOD AND LOUD outdoor MONO sounding speaker with very little distortion but lacks low end bass. It's also built of solid construction. The "big-ness" of the sound is just not what I expected going by YouTube sound tests. I'm going to keep the W-King for reference purposes as someone who is fascinated with audio reproduction technology improvements in the past decades.

review_text: When I came to enter my review, I saw reviews from 2018 complaining about the software. I guess things have changed . I just transferred 8.2 GB from a Surface Pro 3 to a Surface Pro 7 in 7 minutes. The cable has an activation code for the software, which I downloaded from Barvura to each computer. The code activated the software (NOT just a 30-day free trial) on each machine and both machines recognized the cable. The software asks what kind of task you want to complete (moving data from one computer to another and syncing data between two computers are two tasks I remember seeing). When I selected transfer data, it immediately gave me a window asking if that computer was old or new computer. Then it presented a window showing the folders it would transfer. I glanced at the list and then started the transfer. Seven minutes later it was done. I can go back and try again, this time selecting any folders the program didn't automatically choose, but I doubt there will be much to do there. The only possible issue is the program stops when it finds a conflict (and it WILL, see below) and awaits your decision. If you walk away, the transfer sits awaiting your return. No big deal, unless you are moving 1TB of data and want to be productive somewhere else in the meantime. The conflict it found was it's own install program on the two Surfaces, noting a conflict between slightly different install times. When I clicked ignore, it raced on ahead. No hesitation to recommend this product. The easiest data transfer I've ever done between two computers. BY FAR.

review_text: I literally tried 6 router/modem combos. Each one kept slowing down requiring a reboot nearly daily. ISP ran new cabling, came to our house 3 times, and each time couldn't figure out the problem. I even tried a Motorola branded one I couldn't mount on the wall. Here's the trick: Go to your web browser, type in 192.168.0.1 and log in to your router settings. Default username is 'admin', password is 'password', unless you changed it when you set it up. Go to advanced in all the menus until you find channel, there's 2 places. I forget the exact procedure but you need the advanced menu for each. Go to wifi channel and view the colored bars. All the wifi signals in your vicinity will be displayed. Hover your mouse over each bar, and yours will be there somewhere in the list. If it shares a channel with another network, such as an extender or a neighbor, set it to an unused channel. I should add that the factory default for what channel your router uses is AUTOMATIC which is the cause of the problem. Just select an empty channel from the drop down menu and make sure it switched by rebooting and checking. Keep in mind a factory reset (the one you do with a small wire through the hole at the rear) will set it back to "auto". Also keep in mind these are idiot proof, bc if you accidentally change something you're not supposed to mess with a factory reset (default) will put everything back to the way it was when you took it out of the box when new. This took me over a month and a lot of frustration to figure out, but trust me when I say isp techs are the luck of the draw and I dealt with a half a dozen throughout my problems and not even one made this suggestion. Including Netgear. It worked for me!

It's hilarious how they advertise that you don't need to wet the contacts before putting on the monitor. The hilarious part of that is that wetting the contacts would be far less frustrating than dealing with this device as it comes. This device has two major problems, which I'm calling dropdowns and dropouts. Drop downs means that it randomly miscalculates the heart rate, and places it at a significantly lower BPM than it should be. Dropouts means that it completely disconnects at random times. The drop-downs tend to happen when the device is on your arm, and your arm is below your heart in some sort of compression exercise. The dropouts happen during other types of compression, mostly twists in yoga. Another issue is the syncing. The device regularly will go into a state where it flashes blue and red, won't sync with anything, and won't even turn off at all. In this situation, the only two options are to let the battery drain, or plug it into the charger. I've never let the battery drain, and don't even know how long the battery would last, because this situation happened so frequently that I have no choice but to just go ahead and charge it to get it out of the situation. I've tried this HRM in all of the six different available configurations, and multiple times each. I've tightened the band, I've loosened the band. I've tried on a full charge, I've tried on a low charge. This thing is the single most annoying piece of tech I have ever had to displeasure of using. I mustered up the strength to give it three stars, because it does technically track heart rate and sync with devices most of the time. It just doesn't do it consistently enough to deserve anything more. If I had read this review before buying, I would not have bought.

I wasn't sure what to expect from this T86DVR model - the least expensive front & rear dash cam with both Android Auto & CarPlay. So far, I'm very happy with it after a month of use. The wide and not so tall aspect looks really nice atop my dash and doesn't obstruct my view. All the wires are hidden so it looks nicely integrated. Power is through a 12V to 5DC USB converter hidden behind the factory head unit. The hardest part of the install by far is cleanly running the wire from the rear camera to the dash. The internal speaker and the FM transmitter sound was fine for navigation and calls but not that good for music. Using the Aux output to the car's amp is much better. Android Auto (version 9.0.x) is working really well, including Coolwalk features. I have had a few random disconnections but only when my spouse was in the car with her iPhone. Maybe her phone is trying to connect to CarPlay which causes the AA disconnects? In any case CarPlay works perfectly well for her when she drives the car. The dash cam quality is pretty good, both front and rear. It's quite nice now to have a backup camera that has really good night vision. The best part is being able to keep my phone in my pocket and having it connect wirelessly to Android Auto (or CarPlay) and automatically bringing up navigation map using Android Driving Mode. No longer do I have to make a run back to the car to get my phone off the dash. Lastly, I had some questions I needed help with and contacted USManju@163.com. I received very prompt and helpful replies and videos from Irelia in customer support. UPDATE: Lowered the rating due to not being able to have a phone conversation while driving, even with the windows up. People simply can't understand me due to the audio breaking up. Voice commands are spotty as well. Calls through Android Autp do work OK when I pull over and stop and the engine still running. Obviously when stopped the ambient noise level is quieter, but this suggests this unit's microphone is quite poor at any noise cancellation above a certain level when driving.

The usual flashy lights that come with gaming computers and a multitude of fans should keep everything cool. The power supply is under the bottom fans along with the SSD which I also find a bit odd. You better have a clean room, with HEPA filters, filtering other HEPA filters when installing this thing, along with nitrile gloves so not a single drop of oil from your hands gets on the adhesive while installing this thing. I will say I was hopeful, the way it comes with a plastic tray/sleeve you set the tablet in looks really well done. Unfortunately, unless you're cleaner than surgeon, you're going to get dust, dirt, particles or something stuck on the screen before you can put the protector on it. Once you peel back the sticky sheet, it's like a magnet/black hole to attract anything and everything that could be floating in the air at your home. You could go over the screen a thousand times before trying to apply the protector, but once you peel that over, it's like the scene from Avengers Endgame where Dr Strange opens portals for everyone - except all the people are dust and dirt. Plus, the protector is a few millimeters smaller than the screen, so unless you want it to be off by a bit & cover up things like the camera and light sensor, you'll do the thing where you place it down, lift it up, place it back down, lift it back up, and do that over and over until you get it kind of straight. The problem with that, is again - dust, dirt, and any small, tiny hairs within a 3 city block radius are attracted to the screen adhesive side. Something will get stuck under the screen, guaranteed, and it will drive you absolutely insane. It's like the thing magically teleported under the glass. At least it comes with a little screen wiper thing for getting the air bubbles out, which works pretty well. The problem is, unless you're wearing nitrile or latex gloves, when you get skin oil from your hands under the protector and on the adhesive, that isn't an air bubble, it's oilly residue. That doesn't spread out with the wiper thing, and will stay there until you take off the protector. You really, really do need to either surgical scrub your hands before touching this thing, or better, wear some nitrile/latex gloves while putting it on. It makes it harder because if the sticky part of the screen touches your gloves it sticks like crazy, but at least you don't get oil on it. I really, REALLY wanted to like this thing, but I fell victim to it again. Maybe it's just a spigen thing, but I tried one of their screen protectors for my Nintendo Switch and my Pixel 2 XL cell phone, and they did the EXACT same thing. Noticeably smaller than the screen so hard to line up & apply straight, extremely susceptible to skin oil that won't ever go away. Also for the Nintendo in particular, when you apply & undo to try and get it straight, one corner of the protector will never stick to the screen again. It's such a shame, because spigen makes really good cell phone cases, and I figured their screen protectors would be just as high quality. Nope :/ So basicallly, if you have a clean room that surgery could be performed in, the ability to cover every millimeter of your body with PPE to prevent any foreign particles or dust to enter the application area, and can magically nail the placement of the protector first try when sticking it on the screen, give it a shot. There's always the chance that it's just me - that I suck at doing these things, which is always possible lmao, but when it happens again and again, with multiple devices and multiple products, it doesn't feel like it's my fault in the slightest. Good luck!

review_text: I'm a die hard 3D fanatic. I've been through it all ( started with 13 Ghosts in a movie theater as a child). Through the years, I've experimented with 3D tech as it progressed. From flickering active glasses to the passive, movie theater style approach . I still have a 3D computer monitor and TV, though they're not set up at the moment. I even have 2 Nintendo 3DS units which was quite an accomplishment being the first, truly mainstream product that did not require glasses to view 3D, and finally, the ultimate 3D experience was/is VR using the Oculus Rift/Quest systems. Yes, it is quite the tech, but wearing the headset is not something you'd want to do for long periods, as it can become uncomfortable , and I don't always like the feeling of cutting off my real world surroundings. Fast forward to 2021. I had my eye on the Lume tablet, but not at the original price. I already had an iPad Pro which is pretty unbeatable. When I saw the $299.00 price tag (April 2022), it was a no brainer. I always wanted an android tablet as an alternative anyway. The flexibility of the Android OS goes beyond IOS, making it a helluva lot more interesting for tinkerers and people who love to customize! Well, I'm happy to say, this tablet is beyond my expectations.. Look, if you didn't grow up with 3D tech, and expect Jason Vorhees to jump out of the screen and slice you, then you're not meant for this. Go play in VR insead. When you understand going in, the limitations of 3D, then you'll love this. The 3D is gorgeous, but the tablet's native resolution (2D), will drop dramatically to accommodate the 3D mode (just like it does with passive glasses displays on TVs ). The display will sometimes be dimmer in 3D, but it varies with each app and its contents. 3D Photos look amazing and you hardly hardly notice the dimming, where as some games it's quite obvious, but again, depends on the app. Speaking of which, the game library is not large yet (I think they're around 100 titles at the time of this review). Some games utilize the 3D intelligently and will leave you impressed, while others are too basic or simply not good. Gameloft's Asphalt racing & Architect are both samples of top quality on all levels, and there are few other 3D gaming gems hidden among the crop; I'm still going through them. Now for some REAL hotness: I just installed Citra, which is a 3DS emulator with an option for Lume 3D. It's still an early version, but quite a number of games already work excellently! Having 3D on a sharper, larger screen with 3DS gaming - are you kidding me? This is amazing. What I find most impressive are the videos and photographs. It's like, some objects look almost as if they're protruding 4" off the screen. This baby can convert 8K 2D youtube videos to 3D in seconds , or at most, a minute. There's so much to try out on youtube and other social media platforms , that you'll realize, there just isn't enough time in a day. The app is called LeiaTube, which is part of a suite of Leia 3D apps including one where you can even take your own impressive 3D photos and videos with the dual lens camera. Some of the other pre-loaded Leia apps for the Lume include a viewer for manipulating thousands of 3D objects, mind-blowing community photos and dozens of well-done educational videos covering a wide range of topics, each pretty lengthy! Explore everything from the human body, to heading back in time to ancient Egypt, all in 3D of course. Want to watch blockbuster 3D Movies? You can head to Leiaflix and for $1.99, you'll have a mini 3D theater right on your lap, and the results are impressive and even more exciting is an app on Google Play called Jellyfin. You also have to download the server software for PC or Mac as well as a custom video player made by a talented individual (check the Leia forums). Now you're able to REMOTELY watch your own 3D videos (and 2D) from your Lume tablet from anywhere in your home over wifi. It's Amazeballs! The tablet uses a USB type C connector. If you purchase one of those multi inputs to C adapters, you can add a hard drive, USB flash or SD cards so you'll be able to transfer items from your expansion storage to the Lume, or you can download Total Commander, and remotely transfer PC/Mac files to the Lume and the reverse. All from your bed. And finally - two things that are MAJOR surprises -- beyond the 3D itself are the sound and picture quality. When using the tablet in normal 2D (like any Samsung tab), the picture quality is unreal - it actually gives the iPad screen a run for its money. I mean, this display almost approaches OLED - with crisp, bright and bold colors, and a rich black level. As far sound, we're talking Dolby Atmos. It's the richest sound I've ever heard on any mobile device, and the build quality is solid, like a tank. So, take away the 3D, and you have one killer tablet on its own. Head to the Google Play Store and go crazy! I hope enough units sell so this unique tablet gets the support it deserves.

I wanted to love this product. It was cheap enough and I have had some real good experiences with TP-Link. Unfortunately I would not have a good experience with the Deco X20. Set up was easy. Plug one of the devices into your ISP modem and turn it on. The device automatically configured itself and within minutes I had internet. Then you plug in the remaining devices and they connect automatically to the main unit. I was able to get internet all the way to my garage with is about 2000 square feet away. I was happy at first - the first day. The very next day I experienced no internet although my laptop was stating I was connected to my network and I had full bars. Still was not able to browse the internet. I waited for about 10 minutes and then had to reboot the main TP-Link device. After a few minutes, internet was restored. This happened a few times during the day. So the reports on internet dropping are accurate and correct. I also noticed that streaming video was heavily pixelated and would buffer quite often. Speed tests showed less then half of what I was paying for. Since this is not a tri-band router, I never expected to receive my full bandwidth, but I never expected less than half. Yet even at 50Mpbs, this should have been more than enough to stream 4K. And I was averaging between 30-50Mbps. I began looking for rules in the router that may help alleviate the issue. I turned on QOS and gave my Roku priority. Yet this did not solve the issue. Then I turned off all the anti-virus protection that comes defaulted on. And then I saw an improvement. There is no fine tuning of the AV, its either off or on. So I was not happy that I needed to turn off an included feature just to improve my streaming picture. I also had my Xbox wired to my main Deco device. I found out that when I went to download a game from the Microsoft store, my download would begin and then stop. Wired, I was getting less than 1Mbps!! At this point I began to troubleshoot the equipment. I never had streaming issues or wired download issues with my previous Router. I removed the Main deco unit and swapped it with one of the slave units. I tested my speed and network again and found no improvements. Still had streaming issues and still could not download On a wired connection. I connected my laptop directly to my ISP modem and tested internet. I had maximum speed and no issues downloading via my Ethernet cable. I measured the speed both on wireless and wired. One expects the speed on a wired connection to be better than a wireless connection. Yet in my case it was the reverse. My WiFi speed was always greater than my wired speed. I called TP-Link and they had me do pretty much the same troubleshooting I had already done. In the end they wanted me to install a BETA firmware to see if this would resolve my issues. BETA? No thank you. I was not going to spend one more minute with a device that obviously had issues. I immediately ordered the EERO Pro Mesh Tri-Band routers and the difference is night and day. Trust me when I say you want a Tri-Band router. Speeds are almost as high as what you are paying your ISP for, and my wired connections and blazingly fast. My WiFi out in my garage is amazing and I could not be happier with the EERO. The TP-Link Deco X20 is their V1. Wait for the V2 of this product which inevitably gets a release when TP-link revolves hardware issues. In its current state of V1 I could not recommend this product to anyone.

These Paradigm SE Atoms are simply fantastic! Crystal clear sound at any volume, rich, full sound, solid Canadian build quality. They really open up at mid/high volume levels, but still sound above average for the price point at low volumes too. The woofers take a bit more time to break in as they are pretty stiff, but bass is super tight and accurate right out of the box. The aluminum tweeters add a surprising amount of brightness for paradigms, and really have impressive extension and clarity up top. These monitor se atoms really excel in the mids, which are just glorious and buttery smooth. Think Elac b5/b6 but better. Bass is deep and full as well, although true bass heads may want a bit more. Outstanding for music, but also better than expected for tv and movies as well. I have always loved the mid-rich, full, clean, balanced sound of Paradigms and these SE Atoms don’t disappoint. The smooth extension of the highs from the aluminum tweeters really is a pleasant surprise too. I’m using them in a 2.0 set up for mostly music and occasional action movie. You can compare these to the Klipsch RP line, Infinity Reference, KEF, Elac, and others in this price range like I did side by side and the Paradigms win easily for me. Their silky smooth mids, clarity, volume, and non-fatiguing sound are unbeatable at this price. Highly recommend. I like them so much I bought 2 pairs! True entry level audiophile sound at a bargain price.

review_text: 4 Stars - I have 2 Blink Mini’s linked to a Module2. I have them mounted inside and pointed toward the outside through windows. The cameras were fairly easy and painless to set up. I like the small size of the cameras and that they don’t have batteries to maintain or that can swell and fail over time. The picture quality is excellent daytime and low light. I can’t comment on infrared night time picture quality, as I have disabled the infrared and LEDs to prevent reflection on the window glass. The app needs improvement. It’s good that you are able to block out zones where you don’t want to detect motion, like normal traffic on the street. However, this doesn’t work at night as it will trigger cars in the zones blocked from monitoring. Not just some, but all cars at night will trigger recording in the blocked zones. It’s good that you can enable and disable individual cameras easily from the home screen of the app. However, I wish they would make it so you could silence the notification from individual cameras without disabling the motion detection and recording easily from the home screen. The only way is to go deep into the app settings to turn off the notifications for all cameras. I tried the Beta test of the instant notification which would be good, however, it negates the ability to delete clips directly from the notification, which I like when the clip is of the mail carrier or the neighbor’s cat that likes to hang out at my house for some damn reason. When I turned off the instant notification, I noticed that the cameras stopped picking up any motion, so I deleted and re-linked the cameras to the app and this fixed the problem. There is a way around it. First I disable alexa and turn the wifi off. Then I turn on the airplane mode, do not disturb, and portrait orientation. Then I turn on the text to speech on my book and use the on/off button to switch off the screen. Basically I eliminate every distraction from solely doing text to speech. Since I primarily want to move easily between reading and listening to text to speech I don't miss using alexa, and I suspect it is the attempt to multi-task that switches off the text to speech. The portrait orientation is important, if the fire is trying to switch between orientations with auto rotate it will turn off the text to speech. Also I use old fashioned earbuds that plug into the device with a wire so I don't know if blue tooth would also need to be turned off. Using this method I'm able to listen to text to speech as long as I like which important when I want to use it on long drives plugged into my car radio. Just in case you're having trouble finding it, the text to speech voice option is under Settings>Device Options>Keyboard & Language>Text to Speech to select the voice you want to hear. I’m so glad I decided to step up from the 12600T I was planning on using to the 12600K, which is the cheapest Intel CPU that has the efficiency cores. I was nervous at first, because my plan was to build a low-ish power, 100% passively-cooled, internal GPU, no moving parts PC for use in my bedroom, where my previous computers were annoyingly loud. I used a Noctua NH-P1 passive cooler and a Seasonic PX-500 fanless PSU, and my system is not only 100% silent, it turns in impressive benchmark numbers and never gets close to throttling temperatures even after sustained Cinebench runs. I run my system at -130 mV, with no overclocking, and CPU power consumption peaks at about 100 W, while idle CPU power consumption is less than 2W. My heatsink never gets too hot to touch with my bare hand in daily use. The only thing preventing my system from being a high performance gaming PC is the lack of dedicated GPU, but the internal GPU is more than enough for me to run four simultaneous instances of BlueStacks 5 to play my favorite mobile game, and fast enough to run Diablo III and EVE Online with medium settings. The Core i5-12600K is roughly competitive in performance and price with the AMD Ryzen 7 5700X.

There are definitely some things to like about this mouse, but the movement of the trackball itself within its socket is not smooth. (UPDATE: It broke in with time and some effort.) Pros: + Very nice feel in the hand. I like the shape and the very fine bumpy texture. + Tilting scroll wheel is nice; I use it for copy/paste since horizontal scrolling is available through scroll click + mouse. + Mouse customization software is decent, and allows buttons to map to arbitrary key combinations such as Ctrl+Shift+Z (up to 3 keys at once). You can save multiple setups, so that one can be used for browsing and another for gaming or photo editing. Unfortunately you have to open the Mouse Assistant to switch between these. There is a Presentation Mode option which lets you use a mouse button to enter a special Presentation Mode, but it's more limited and can't press whatever keys you want. + Back and forward buttons are easy to use. I have seen reviews on Youtube complaining that they're not; if you look closely they have changed the button shape to address that problem. Cons: - The button on the far right is awkward to use. Trying to hold it down while moving the mouse almost always results in my accidentally clicking with one of my other fingers. Admittedly this is a muscle memory thing; I can right-click-and-drag and left-click-and-drag without making a mistake, but if I try to far-left-click-and-drag, it's hard for me to not accidentally press down with all my other fingers too. - I have gotten occasional missed clicks, where I felt the left mouse button click but it doesn't happen on screen. It's pretty infrequent. - The mouse customization software can't control the acceleration setting, just the sensitivity. - The whole physical trackball setup seems poor, as I elaborate below. All the nice aspects of this mouse seem like attempts to compensate for poor pointer control. I use the back and forward buttons on this mouse because actually pointing to the back or forward button on the browser is harder than with my previous mouse. I use the scroll wheel because pointing to the scroll bar would be an absolute pain. The extra button on the right - which dials down the sensitivity - would be completely unnecessary if the trackball would move at small speeds without jumping. I recommend turning your computer mouse sensitivity all the way down and using the high DPI setting (as well as the high accuracy mode on the bottom switch). The jumpiness in the cursor movement is caused as your applied force hovers around the coefficient of friction at slow speeds. As long as you're spinning the ball a bit faster, movement is quite smooth, and you get fairly comfortable and accurate mouse control; there's nothing wrong with the sensors. But it's no gaming mouse. I've got the settings at a place I'm happy with, but doing an online mouse test I hit almost half as many targets as my old mouse (a logitech Marble Mouse). Another piece of software that helps is Custom Curve, which lets you change the shape of the mouse acceleration curve. The idea is to dampen slower mouse movement, so that the initial jump that happens as you try to un-stick the trackball only moves the cursor a few pixels. That way you regain fine control in small regions, and when moving the mouse faster you can still get most of the way across the screen with one glide. This certainly makes the mouse more pleasant, but it hasn't actually improved my score on mouse accuracy tests; the acceleration makes me less accurate targeting areas from across the screen. I think the problem is from a couple sources. The trackball is designed to have a bit of stick, perhaps so that it doesn't keep freely spinning if you give it a push; they wanted it to only move when your hand is on it. (I like to be able to "throw" my trackball; it's generally how I spin around when playing a game.) Getting hand oil on the ball helps a bit, but even with hand oil on the surface, as you rub your fingers over the ball you will feel your fingers stick and slip against the surface, making a low squeak like a hand on rubber. This stick and slip is precisely what happens to the mouse. The other issue is that the bearings, the little points of plastic and/or ruby that support the trackball, are arranged in a way that creates smooth vertical movement, but doesn't provide the same amount of friction (or lack thereof) for horizontal movement across the screen. This asymmetry is almost more annoying than the friction in the first place. Still, the trackball is the larger problem, and I'm going to try replacing it. I fully expect replacing the trackball to give me a quite pleasant mouse, provided I choose a good replacement. But that doesn't mean this product deserves very many stars. UPDATE: I replaced the trackball with a 34mm ball bearing just to see how that would work out. The bearing wasn't a very good trackball, and seemed to be slightly large, creating some friction. However, after using the bearing as a trackball for a day, and rolling it around rather roughly, re-inserted the original trackball and found that it suddenly didn't feel awkward to click on small buttons, select text, etc. Over the past few days I've done a few other things, like placing a little lubricant on the ball and generally rolling it around and trying to break it in; but using the bearing is what pushed it over so it's suddenly working acceptably. I repeated the mouse test and was able to get the same score as with my old mouse. (Returning to the mouse test over and over has been a huge help. It's much more revealing than ordinary tasks.) I'm still a bit concerned about the occasional glitch in the left mouse button, but I may actually keep this mouse.

review_text: The Apple power supply is seemingly the poorest designed product which Apple has produced in recent years. It is a poem of design over function, built to pair nicely with the macbook pro, it actually seems designed to degrade after months of light use. The insulation first begins to crack, and then the outer insulation continually fails and falls off, revealing the bare cabling.. On the section near the adapter, it is mechanically horribly designed, ensuring that high stresses will be placed on the conductive inner wiring, which mechanically fatigue and being to fail. This reduces the conductive pathways from the power supply to the cord, and increased resistance can lead to increased thermal loads which in turn contribute to increased failure of the wires. It's as if Apple doesn't include any material or mechanical engineers on the design team and just chose to make a power supply that looks nice but fails at multi-year intervals, forcing consumers to buy a new one.

review_text: I ordered these after seeing stellar reviews of their sound quality on a number of sites and Flossy Carter's channel. I have been using the Sony WF-1000 XM4s since June. Before those, Sennheiser Momentum True Wireless 2, along with the Galaxy Buds Pros. I also previously tried the Bose, Klipsch, Cambridge Audio and others (not the Airpod pros - I no longer have an iPhone). While the sound quality was the best I have heard (when using the same BT codec for comparison), I ended up returning them for several reasons. First, I could never get a good fit or seal with the included ear tips as well as my own personal favorite ear tips I have used since I bought the Anker Soundcore Liberty 2 Pros a few years back. I have a big head and ears, and I could never get a consistent seal with the B&Os using any tips. They would come lose easily if I moved pretty gently, like bending over to tie my shoe. I know a lot folks recommend the Comply tips. I tried those, too, because I have a bunch of those in their largest size. I have never liked them because they don't stay in my ears. and my experience with the B&Os was the same. Second, despite not giving a good seal, they started hurting my ears after 1-1.5 hours of use. So much so, I had to take them out. Because the foregoing reason are personal, you may not have the issues I experienced. Third, the app and controls are primitive. Why is there no single tap control? Everything is a minimum double tap or double tap and hold. And there is no way to set a control to skip to the next or previous song. Many earphones allow you to customize your controls to your liking (the Sennheisers, the Galaxy Buds, the Sonys [to some degree]). Most of them allow you to control both volume and skip forward/back from the touch controls. Not these. And the volume adjustment feature, double-tap and hold, reacts way too fast, such that you almost always increase or decrease the volume more than you intended. There are also no audio cues to confirm that you have done anything when you tap the buds. Fourth, the sound is stellar, when you use the apt-x codec. For buds that also offer the apt-x codec, the B&Os are superior (ex. SennheiserMTW2, but not by much). The sound stage is broader and the image is clearer, although there is a fair amount of harshness on higher notes of challenging instruments like trumpets. A lot of reviews suggest that these sound better than the Sonys. That may be true in some comparisons (like maybe if you se the old SBC or AAC codecs), but I didn't do those comparisons because I always use the highest quality codec offered on any buds. So, if you have an iPhone, the following will not matter since Apple only offers AAC. HOWEVER, these two buds don't offer the same higher quality codecs. The Sonys offer LDAC but not apt-x, while the B&Os offer apt-x but don't offer LDAC. The LDAC codec was developed by Sony, but it has licensed it out for free to all the phone and DAP manufacturers. It supports significantly higher data throughput rates than apt-x, but the tradeoff is definitely a less stable connection than apt-x. For me, the long and short of it was that the Sonys on LDAC sound noticeably better on most tracks than the B&Os on apt-x. Using my same ten HD and Ultra HD test tracks from Amazon Music, which span classical (symphonic and quartet), jazz, hip-hop, rock and African, the Sonys sounded better than the B7Os on 8 of the 10 tracks. They were more musical and balanced and gave a greater sense of air/resonance around each of the instruments. I returned the B&Os for the unexpected discomfort and lack of a good fit. But for forty+ percent more than the price of the Sonys ($399 vs. $278, and the Sony are now starting to get discounted), even if they were comfortable and gave a good seal, I would still not buy them. Bottom line: if your phones supports apt-x but not LDAC and, like me, your highest priority is sound quality, get the B&Os, assuming you can tolerate the idiosyncrasies of the controls/app and are willing to spend. If your phone supports LDAC (all Galaxy phones, for example), save the money and app frustration and get the Sonys. If you have an iPhone, you should probably stick with Airpods because of the inexplicable AAC-only requirement of the Apple ecosystem. And please let me know if Apple starts prioritizing sound quality over premium pricing (maybe by allowing the $550 Airpods Max to support some better codec than AAC?).

For the $37 I paid for this (50% off), I love it. I wanted something primarily to be a Bluetooth speaker but that also charged my phone and had a clock, and I wanted it to be pretty. I also didn't want to spend over $50, so I knew I wasn't getting a miracle. But I'm overall very satisfied! Here are my thoughts after a few days of use: PROS: - It's truly gorgeous. The mirrored screen (which is a true mirror!) is so luxe, and the rest of it is simple, clean, and black. Visually it looks like it cost way more than I paid for it and would be worth the $75 original listing price. - You can turn off the display entirely, which is great for nighttime. - The speaker sound is great. Not mind blowing or anything, but it does the job. - When the phone is placed correctly on the wireless charger, it charges my iPhone more quickly than other off-brand ones do. CONS: - While the display can get quite bright, for some reason it automatically dims after a few minutes. You can get it back to full brightness by clicking the O button, but if you're playing music at the time, doing that pauses it. I'm not sure why the display can't stay at full brightness permanently, especially while it's plugged into the wall as mine is. - When playing through Bluetooth, the "BT" symbol only stops blinking when you first connect a device and when your music is paused. When music is playing, it blinks continuously. I find this a little infuriating. - If you've been using Bluetooth but your device has been disconnected for a while, you have to cycle through all the Modes to reconnect, which results in some annoying beeps as you go through the Aux and Radio settings. - It's a bit hard to see the symbols on the buttons, and they aren't intuitive. I'll get used to it over time, but it's a little annoying at first. - You have to place your phone *very* carefully in the right spot to get it to wirelessly charge. Also, if you're playing music through your phone, it will pause briefly when you place your phone on the charger and again when you pick it up. This may be the case with all Bluetooth chargers though... - The clock has already lost a minute since I got it 2 days ago. - The aux port seems somewhat unnecessary these days. I wish it were a USBC port instead. Overall, I would have been very happy paying up to probably $55 for this, but not more. If you're looking for a good speaker/clock/charger on a budget and this one is on sale, I definitely recommend!

My Complaint: I thought I was buying a new product, I suppose I bought this case used and wasn't paying attention. This product came unboxed, no product information such as C.O.O. [country of origin], California warning, et al. I am bothered by the sticky residue on the entirety of iPod Touch case. It gave me a feeling that it was in the 'sell' pile from some hoarder's house. If my son gets sick from whatever contaminate that is stuck to this case, who do I contact for retribution? WHO! Pic 1: Unknown sticky residue on the touch screen overly. Pic 2: Damage or manufacture defect on the back plate in the camera lens overlay near the inner edge. Pic 3: Outside view of the port bank (speaker port, charging port, 3.5 headphone jack port). No damage. Pic 4: Inside/behind the port bank. Port cover feels like silicon, plugs have tiny built-in gaskets to seal. No damage. Pic 5: Scratch on the touch screen overlay in the upper right side of the Home Button dimple. Pic 6: What the back plate looks like overall. My Overview After treating the case with 70% Isopropyl Alcohol and a water rinse it looked fine. Crisis averted . . . I hope. This iPod touch case fits 7th Gens. It feels rugged & watertight and is difficult to open gently[as it should], especially tough to remove for those who don't have fingernails. There is a sealed gap on the right side of the port bank that helps with opening. If you aren't careful, the device will be vulnerable to water; So, give the port plugs a firm press to close completely flush. Since there wasn't any product packaging or information provided in the shipment, I've not water tested the case (so please test the case empty, duh). Water protection should not be a problem if it slips in the shower, bathtub of water, or any shallow watery hole and quickly snatched out. The touch screen overlay is a flexible film that will neither protect the screen from impact on surfaces that aren't; In addition, it does not rest directly on the iPod screen. The space between the touch screen & the film should be enough room for tempered glass screen protector. Thank you for reading my review, I know it was a lot for such a chintzy item.

My first Surface Pro 7. Very nice design and I like it because you could install any apps like a regular computer. It works out of the box at first, but after I installed the Windows updates I start having screen freezing up issue. No matter you are browsing the web or typing in MS words it would freeze up. Very annoying. I could return it to exchange for another one. But, I ending up calling MS tech for the issue. I spent hours with Microsoft tech. It was the Intel Graphics refreshing issue! If you having the same problem that I had. You need to download the Intel Graphics Command Center app and install it. After installed. Open up the Intel Graphics Command Center app. Under "Power", select "On Battery" turn off Panel Self Refresh to "OFF" and do the same to "Plugged In" to "OFF", then exit it out. I hope this would help others that having the same problem.

review_text: I bought two of these and they appear very well made. Our Comcast entry coax had to be replaced and I asked the repair person if these GDTs could be installed. She said if a Comcast person finds one installed, it would be removed as it's "not compatible with our system." Spare tubes. Several sources claim these last years unless subjected to catastrophic or extreme exposure to lightning. I emailed the Chinese XH firm via Amazon for replacements but never heard back. Replacements are available from DigiKey Part No. 495-4669-ND and the price is $1.80 each. The reason I started digging is lightning struck near our gatehouse and damaged two Comcast Modems and our fax modem, two computers - one a server - and a monitor - about $10K damage.

I purchased a Ubook 11.6 a few years ago. As you can see from my original review (see below) I had mixed feelings about it (except for the keyboard, which I flat-out hated). Nonetheless, I went on to use the Ubook 11.6 for several years as my treadmill device for work. I found that it adequately handled my day-to-day activities of web browsing, video meetings, and working in the Microsoft Office 365 suite. Recently I had the opportunity to put the newest version of the Ubook – the Ubook X 12 – through its paces. (See pictures for unboxing experience.) As the name implies, the Ubook X 12 has a slightly larger screen, but perhaps most important of all, it had a fully functional keyboard! I was so happy to see that CHUWI was able to resolve the earlier issues with the Ubook 11.6 keybaord. As in the case of the Ubook 11.6, the Ubook X 12 keyboard attaches magnetically to the base of the tablet. No Bluetooth involved. The keyboard also serves as a protective cover when you fold it up. How does the Ubook X 12 compare to high-end Windows tablets? Aesthetically, it looks very nice. When I was testing it, I had it sitting next to an HP Elite X2 G4 – a tablet costing many times more than the CHUWI. Glancing back and forth they looked very similar – you certainly can’t tell the Ubook X 12 is a lower-cost model by looking at it. Having said that, there are differences on the inside. Whereas high-end tablets use Intel Core I5 or I7 processors, the Ubook X 12 employs a 4-core Celeron-series processor. There’s no shame in that. The Celeron is an able workhorse – it is certainly able to run the usual array of work and student applications. I even fired up a resource-intensive graphics program (Krita), and it ran fine (although it did take more time to load than on a Core I5 or I7). I didn’t have much luck with the battery-driven (battery included) two-button stylus. Yes, it worked. But I personally don’t like the feel of a rubber tip on slick glass, and I had some issues with consistency of strokes. However, you should probably consider that to be my personal problem; I see other reviews where the reviewers are happy with the Ubook X 12 as a drawing tablet or for note taking. So, it might just be me. What’s the bottom line? If you are looking for a tablet to handle web browsing, video meetings, and mainstream productivity applications, the Ubook X 12 is a bargain. ORIGINAL REVIEW OF UBOOK 11.6 FOLLOWS I bought the U Book to replace an aging Microsoft Surface Pro 3 that could no longer handle the job of being the secondary work computer I use when on my treadmill. For work, I need to run Outlook, Teams, Chrome, Evernote, and typically one or more office apps (e.g. Word, Excel, or PowerPoint). My Surface Pro 3 only has 4MB of memory which just isn't enough room to fit all the apps. So I had a memory problem - not a CPU or disk space problem. I wanted a low-cost solution, so the U Book was attractive to me. It had the memory allocation I was looking for (8MB) and sufficient CPU power and storage. So I went for it and bought the package that included a keyboard and a pen. Now let's get to the love/hate part of the review. The tablet itself is very nice - it falls into the love category. The kickstand is sturdy and adjustable. The screen is nice. It has a good range of ports (2 USB-As, 1 limited-use USB-C, one micro-HDMI, and a headphone port). The ports are somewhat awkwardly arranged, but then again, it's hard to find a great place for ports on a tablet form factor. In terms of meeting the needs to run my applications - it's worked just fine. The CPU consumption runs higher than it was with my Surface Pro 3, but then again the Intel Celeron is not exactly Intel's top-of-the-line processor. I was fully aware of that at the time of purchase. The keyboard (with integrated touchpad) falls into the hate category. I don't mean casual hate either - I mean full-on, pick-it-up-and-throw-it-out-the-window hate. I found the touchpad to be completely unusable. The keyboard would lose connection as I was typing and would therefore drop characters right and left. DON'T GET (OR USE) THE KEYBOARD. I ended up using a bluetooth keyboard and extra mouse I had lying around the office - and I'm quite happy with the result. I received a pen in the package, but have no opinion on it (other than it uses hard-to-find quadruple A (AAAA) batteries). I haven't tried to use it for drawing. I did use it as a stylus and it worked. So what's the bottom line? I do see this as an incredible value. This was an under $400 solution when everything else I looked at was over $800. Just don't expect to get more than what you pay for - and you need to know what you are going to use this device for before you buy it. This is not a gaming system or a high-end media manipulation platform. However, it's an excellent solution for middle-of-the-road business applications or casual web browsing.

Let me start by saying that overall, this is a good head unit, but it is NOT straight plug and play. A lot more similar to turning your phone screen on than it is to turning your phone on after you've turned it off completely. -Backup camera works immediately, even if the unit isnt fully booted yet. -If you use the "Chat With Us" option on their website, they are very responsive. Just remember, they are in china so you might be reaching out to them in the middle of the night. The Bad: -If the unit is too warm, the screen will blink until the unit cools down. I'm eventually going to look into installing a PC fan in the dash to run whenever the stereo is powered. This does go away once the car cools down and only happens if you run the stereo after the car has been sitting in the sun. - 4 of the clips were just slightly too wide and had to be shaved down. It took me quite a while to figure out that this was the reason I couldnt get it to push in all the way, since they do appear to line up and it wasnt until I noticed some marring on the dash clip holders that I took out my calipers and measured. -Unit did not come with the correct backup camera wiring harness for my xv crosstrek. I'm not unfamiliar with 12 volt wiring, and after a few hours of research, I was able to figure out what wires on the factory harness needed to go to what wires on the provided stereo harness. You can see my attached photos for reference, but basically I made 4 jumper cables (you can hardwire if you want, i prefer not to mess with the stock wiring). Using the cables, I attached the black power ground from the aftermarket camera harness to pin 15 on the factory harness, the black camera ground to pin 16, the yellow signal wire to pin 8, and the red power wire to pin 7. Hopefully this helps someone.

I like many of Beelink's mini computers and the SER design especially. I find the SER5 very handsome and I like the fact that the 5600H is in an all-metal case (most are plastic), which matters to me because there's no "inner frame" of metal. All-plastic cases (other than the grills) without any inner metal skeleton worry me, though I have to say that visually there's' almost no difference between the SER's that have plastic shells and this metal one. One thing: If you allow this thing to run at 35-45 watts, it's going to get hot and noisy if you do things (like play games) that ramp up the CPU/GPU. This can be avoided in two ways: First, I think that because people have complained about noisy fans in mini PC's, the builders have ramped back their fans. They run them just enough so that the CPU's stay "in-space" but that doesn't prevent the NVME SSD from heating up and I don't like how hot the thing is. HOWEVER, if you do into the BIOS and ramp up the fan speed just a little bit it makes a huge difference, and the fans on this system have a very nice 'lack of sound' - even when they ramp up you hear more air-movement noise than anything else. Incidentally, if you unscrew the bottom cover and (gently, as there's the SATA cable to be careful with) look inside, you'll notice that the fan isn't doing anything for the NVME drive and RAM. For casual use that won't matter, and the Kingston NV1 drives run slow (as NVME drives go), but while there is mesh on both the left and right sides, there's nothing to cause air movement, as the fan doesn't pull from that side of the motherboard. If you want to be able to run with no concerns, and you aren't adding a 2.5 SATA drive, I'd suggest removing the bottom cover and setting this on something that allows air to enter from the bottom. Doing that significantly reduces the temps seen for the NVME drive (and RAM also). I have mine sitting on a Marane fan unit (USB) set to low and I can stress this thing for hours and nothing gets above the low 30C's except the CPU, which is less sensitive to high temps than the other components. One concern: As much as I like these little things, and as much as I think Beelink will try to do the right thing: If something happens that can't be easily fixed (say a fan goes bad as happened to me with one) and it happens after the 30-day Amazon return, you will have to send it to China to be repaired as Beelink isn't quite large enough to have any facilities in the US. So imagine the time and cost and hassle of returning a system to China for repair. This is replacing a 7-year-old Intel NUC and that little machine is still going strong. review_text: Where do I start.. The good: picture quality is good. Both day and night. With the spotlight, night vision is great but you don't get much distance. Very little lag time when live streaming to your phone. That's it. The bad: Motion detection. The camera only records when motion is detected. Problem lies when the motion it detects is literally only the traffic driving by. And even that is spuratic at best. I can walk into the driveway, open the door to my truck, drop the tailgate, unload the tools, get back in the truck and drive away with no detection at all. The the neighbor drives by on his way home and motion detected. I tried with and without zones. People only or all motion. It just doesn't matter. I played with sensitivity. It just is so spuratic. Almost never did it record me getting into my truck but occasionally picked up my truck as the tail lights pull out of the driveway. Usually it would detect a person if a dog was there but not if a person didn't have a dog. It missed the FedEx guy dropping a package at my door. Then it missed me taking the package. Then it got the solicitor selling solar panels but not until I opened the front door. Battery.. I understand that when it detects the cars driving by the battery won't give you 6 months but I only got 4 days on one camera. The other 3 including one 2 pro add on with 360 day battery were down to 3 out of 4 bars after just 10 days so the math says maybe a month would be expected. Then there's the footage. On the setting it was on it should have recorded for 1 minute every time an event was detected. Instead I got anywhere from 7 seconds to 24 seconds with one 58 second recording when absolutely nothing was there. I had high hopes and it just didn't pan out.

note that this is only a dual core i3 which is probably fine for a lot of things but you will almost for sure have to replace the hard drive with an SSD if you want anything approaching usable performance in Windows nowadays. I don't know if the hard drive is just way worse than most, or if that's just how slow hard drives are, but this computer went from almost unusable to pretty darn quick with just the change to an SSD. Unfortunately you can't upgrade the RAM, but 8 gigs is fine for what I need. it is nice that this has a discrete graphics card and it's a little bit better than some of the integrated solutions, but at this point I think an iris pro is actually better overall if you're trying to find some sort of graphics option on a machine of this size. I mostly use this for zwift or watching movies on our TV so for me it's perfect. just because it has that radeon does not mean that it's going to be a gaming machine so don't expect it to be.

*Edited Feb 5 & 7, 2020 " I have to change my rating from 5 stars, to just 2 stars. I would not buy again, and I don't believe anyone else should, either." Jan 6, 2020 - I received the unit today. Installation was so simple, it's a smart design. I installed 4x 10TB Seagate Iron Wolf hard drives, all were instantly recognized and worked flawlessly. USB 3.0 speeds were fairly quick, moving 3 TB of data from one drive to another within the enclosure in under 8 hours, consistently 95- 100 MB/s. The external material is primarily aluminum, and very good for cooling. The photos (and other reviews) had me assuming it were plastic, and not great for cooling. The fans are adjustable with a dial at the base, at full speed are fairly noisy, but even at half speed they move *ALOT* of air through the enclosure. I see in some reviews there are reports of these fans dying, if so, I can see it being an issue. But I also see they are a standard size, and I like the unit enough to be willing to replace them if that becomes an issue. The power supply is a stand alone AC adapter with an IRC 320 C13 connector (your standard PC power cable that runs from the PC power supply to the wall power plug). This is very nice, because it means 1/2 of the power cable is cheap and widely available in the event you need a replacement. However, the power transformer itself is made of lower quality plastic and I imagine will be the first component to die. It looks and feels very cheap, especially compared to the overall excellent build quality of the enclosure itself. For a day 1 experience, this is a pretty fantastic USB enclosure. If it goes awry or malfunctions in the next 6 months, I will return and update this review, and I will certainly do my due diligence and be aware of a better AC adapter for the unit, as I am fairly sure that is the "weak link" (and the corner cut to get this unit down to under $80 at the time of my purchase). At this time, I am very, very happy with my 40 TB external box! Feb 5, 2020 - The fans died tonight. It is less than 3 DAYS out of the return window. Pretty odd timing. The drive temperatures were FAR higher than they should have been at idle, when the fan died it really got way hotter than I had expected, and put the drives in serious danger. It isn't worth the risk. After this, I have to change my rating from 5 stars, to just 2 stars. I would not buy again, and I don't believe anyone else should, either. **Feb 7, 2020 - The fan itself was actually fine. However, the power port on the PCB itself no longer supplies power to the fan. So, basically, the fan cannot *BE* replaced without also replacing the power supply for the fan. $17.99 https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B009OXTWZI/ref=ppx_yo_dt_b_asin_title_o01_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1 Photo is of the actual fan, installed to the device (with a chrome fanguard I already had, the one that comes with the fan is very professional looking... so I couldn't, in good conscience, use that for this). Everything works, again. I now require 2 AC plugs to power it, but on the upside, the fan keeps blowing even when you shut the drives off, cooling them off after use, where the original left them as they were.

review_text: I had the Tozo NC9 earbuds which I initially enjoyed. However, they began to have issues after several months, and when I requested warranty replacement, TOZO insisted instead that they send these NC2 with the stipulation that I review them to get a refund of the cost. Since other persons were having trouble with the NC9 also, I agreed. (TOZO "purchases" good reviews on many products in this manner, by offering to refund the product cost in exchange for a review. Don't be deceived by good reviews on any TOZO product, they've been traded for.) As for these NC2 earbuds, Pros: IF (that is a BIG IF) you can get decent noise isolation, the sound of music ONLY from these is quite good for my taste. TOZO added wireless charging back to these, and that was appreciated. These two things are unfortunately the only good things I can say about them. Cons: Fit is super uncomfortable and clumsy. No matter what cuff size I used with the buds, maintaining any noise isolation was nearly impossible and they actually make my ears hurt, something I’ve never experienced with any other buds before. While the sound quality of music is good, speech is so muddy that it’s difficult to understand. Even the recorded voice telling you which mode you are in sounds bad. They are completely unusable for calls or Zoom meetings. They distort voices to the point of being unintelligible. BT connection has issues with interference that I haven’t seen with other products. When I go walking, the sound cuts out when I get near a power line. Again, never noticed it with other products. Though the case includes wireless charging, the buds are inserted into the case in an unnatural orientation. When you remove a bud from the case, you have to adjust it in your hand before you can even attempt to insert it in your ear. Kind of a small detail, but just another frustration with these. Despite the Airpod appearance (which to me is goofy and would have kept me from ever purchasing these *to each his own*), I really had high hopes for these. Active noise cancellation gives such an improvement to music quality, and I really enjoyed the NC9. But, active noise cancellation is ineffective with these buds because of the fit and inability to maintain noise isolation. Add to the poor performance of the earbuds, the negatives of a company with illegitimate practices, and 1 star is all they deserve.
