The Arris SurfBoard G34 advertises that it is compatible with Comcast Xfinity internet service provider. IT IS NOT as I will now explain. I bought the modem router early in 2022 The modem router would drop the signal from Comcast periodically. This would happen once a day if not 2 or 3 times a day. I would retrieve the signal by rebooting the modem router. This would take 5 or 10 minutes which was aggravating, especially when I was involved with an online class or meeting. The technical details are that for 9 or 10 months I worked with Coimcast and Arriss to resolve the problem. This involved talking with Comcast technical support 5 or 6 times, in which they would tell me that nothing was wrong; that the upstream QAM power level was correct for the model modem router that I had. This level was between 40 and 41. They further said that the problem was with the modem router and that I should call Ariss. I called Arriss about 3 or 4 times. Each time they would tell me that the upstream QAM power level had to be between 45 and 61 for the modem router to work properly. More calls to Comcast. After the fifth or sixth call, I was able to talk to Comcast Advanced Technical Support. This involved 3 calls. They acknowledged the problem and tried to fix it on their end in the first two calls. Nt succeeding, they said that the problem could only be resolved by sending a technician to my house. The technician came and set the upstream QAM power level to a little more than 44. He indicated that increasing it further would damage the signal from Comcast. Thinking that would be enough signal boost to eliminate the problem. But, that night, the modem dropped the signal 3 times. Obviously, the problem hadn't been fixed. Realizing that the advertisement for this modem router was false, I returned the modem router to Amzaazon. I have not communicated this false advertisement to Ariss or the FCC yet, but I wasted 9 or 10 months of my time determining the solution to this problem.

At that point its displayed the mb firmware version as 0301 which won't support later Ryzens. I downloaded the latest firmware version (4204) to a USB drive and used the ASUS Renamer.exe to give the firmware file the correct name expected by the BIOS FlashBack feature on the mb. The USB drive goes in the USB port just below the Ethernet port. With the power off I used the BIOS Flashback button to update the firmware to version 4204. Booted up, got the BIOS flash screen, pressed F2 and got the page telling me to press F1 and it hung up again.. ASUS recommended to remove everything from the mb except the CPU, it's fan and the ATX connections from the power supply to the mb. Had to use a graphics card to see it boot to the BIOS splash screen, pressed F2 and then F1 and hung up. I've tried everything and can't get beyond the BIOS splash screen, press F2 and then the screen telling me to press F1 to modify the BIOS settings. I only have a wireless keyboard and mouse and they are both found as it boots to the splash screen. In researching I found one person with the same problem had an old PS2 keyboard that let him change his BIOS but I don't have a wire keyboard or a PS2 keyboard. I've spent hours on this mb and ZERO. I have 8GB of DDR4 ram that runs at a lower speed but the mb sees the ram and the ram passes the mb test. I've ordered 16 GB of DDR4 3200 ram so I'll try that. Second Update - I bought new Corsair DDR4 3200 memory thinking the old DDR4 2400 could be the problem but it wasn't. I bought two 8GB RAM modules in a pack and one is to go in DIMM-A2* and the second in DIMM-B2*. Either module works fine DIMM-A2* but when the second module is added to DIMM-B2* the CPU won't boot to BIOS. Using one 8GB module in DIMM-A2* boots up into the BIOS and hangs. I've tried different graphics cards, different video cables, a Ryzen 2200G, a Ryzen 5 2600x and the minimum setup of motherboard, CPU with cooling fan, the graphics card, a wireless mouse/keyboard and all of the components pass the motherboard test LEDs but the BIOS never responds to me pressing F1 to modify the BIOS. I've given up and let Amazon know I want to return the board. I've used ASUS quite a few times and I've never had such a hassle. I'm now ASUS gun shy!

Excellent noise cancelling — much better than the first generation, and to my ears it’s just as good as (if not better than) AirPods Max. The Find My functionality works perfectly (especially with the speaker to play sounds from the case) and the lanyard loop is a nice addition as well. You can also see the battery status of the case and AirPods when the case is closed (even works on iPad).My favourite feature is the new adaptive transparency mode, which is phenomenal in blocking out loud sound to let music / calls / audio through, but still let you be aware of your surroundings. Note that the feature needs iOS / iPadOS 17 or macOS Sonoma. However, if you set the long press gesture to switch between (any mode) and adaptive transparency on a device with a supported OS (such as iOS 17), the AirPods will use adaptive transparency when you toggle to it from the long press to the stem even when paired with an OS that doesn’t officially support it (such as macOS Ventura).At least with the USB-C case version, on macOS Ventura the icon in the menu bar when the AirPods are connected is not of the AirPods Pro, but of generic headphones. You also can’t set adaptive transparency from the menu bar toggle. I don’t use the personalised volume (I want to set the volume myself) or the conversation awareness (I prefer to take the AirPods off when talking).The one weird thing that has happened is that when talking on a call whilst in noise cancelling or adaptive transparency, when I hear my voice it sometimes sounds robotic and somewhat metallic? It’s a bit strange and doesn’t happen too often — could be a firmware issue or that my pair has a problem (inclined to think the former).Overall excellent product, and if you can get them at a discounted price below £200 then go for it! I definitely recommend.

This review is for the MSI Review Rebate Program. I was looking to upgrade my 8 year old MSI motherboard to a 10th gen board. That board was solid for me, so I decided to stick with MSI, rather than Gigabyte. (Plus, the Gigabyte 10th gen boards were more expensive.) While I'm not a hard-core gamer, I do plan on playing games with this PC. As I don't really care about RGB on the board, I opt'd out of the Gaming Plus board for this cheaper Pro model. From what I can tell RGB is the only notable difference in the two. Edit - 8/8/20: The ALC1220 audio codec on the Gaming Plus board is supposedly better than the ALC892 on this Pro board. The Gaming Plus board also has an S/PDIF audio connector. As the MSI web site says, this is a well-constructed board. I could tell just by taking it out of the box. Installing a board is installing a board - pretty straightforward, if you've done it before. The user guide is pretty decent for being a foreign-based company - i.e. English instructions are pretty good. Plus, there is a lot of good detail in the manual. One thing they could improve on in the install instructions is providing clarity on CPU power. Instructions imply you need the 8 pin and 4 pin power connectors, but you only need the 8 pin, unless you are going to do some very serious CPU overclocking. (multiple articles on the internet on this) I'm using an NVME card as my primary storage. Installing that under the FROZR shield was a piece of cake, especially since multiple m.2 screws are included. When the board booted, it had no problems with the NVME card or any other component for that matter; the board just booted up fine. Something I find slightly odd... when booting up, the logo displays, but the options to boot into BIOS or Boot Manager only blip on the screen for .5 seconds. I'm not sure if this is because I have a fast NVME drive and CPU, or if its a flaw in the design of the board. I installed Windows 10 (2004) on this PC. I seem to be having some issues with the onboard Realtek audio drivers. When I try to install the latest from the MSI site, they don't seem to stick - the Microsoft drivers stay there. I called MSI tech support and they couldn't really figure it out. So, I'm hoping either Microsoft or MSI comes out with a patch for this. I personally think Dragon Center is a bloated piece of software. It installs multiple components that do not apply to me - e.g. mystic lighting. Also, the "scenarios" feature I found to be harmful, in that as soon as you click on a scenario, it changes your BIOS settings (e.g. memory speed). On the surface, that sounds like a good idea. However, the scenarios customization does not allow you to customize key aspects (like memory speed). You have to go back into BIOS. It turns out Live Update is all I really needed, so I uninstalled Dragon Center and downloaded Live Update from the MSI web site. (It is not on the install disk included with the motherboard.) Everything considered, this appears to be another solid board from MSI at a decent price-point. Update (8/7/20): While the initial install of the Realtek drivers did not work well (install package kept reinstalling), I did eventually get it to work by cancelling out of the reinstall. Part of the issue was that I originally got a bad tech support person at MSI. His immediate and only advice was to reinstall Windows, which I had just installed. He didn't bother to understand the issue. When I later got someone who knew better, he clarified that only the "Sound, video and game controllers" device shows an updated driver. The devices under "Audio inputs and outputs" still show an older Microsoft driver. This is how it is supposed to work according to MSI. Audio is working fine, which leads me to a point... I'm not clear what the "Audio Boost" feature does. The sound from this board is no different than what I got from my 8 year old MSI board. BTW - Both times I called MSI tech support I waited less than 5 minutes and both techs were clearly English-speaking - likely in the US like me.

Admittedly still adjusting to this keyboard and layout. I’ll likely have less problems with it once the adjustment period is over. So I’m lending the review a star, as I assume 4 stars is where I’ll settle eventually. Given that the keyboard is made for an apple product, I’m unsure why they couldn’t use the apple keyboard layout for CMD and ALT. Many keyboards products made to be interchangeable with Apple and non-Apple products use the traditional, non-apple layout of the command key closer to the spacebar, but if you’re not changing between the two, it can be pretty maddening. In general, I find this a fault with Apple, but for the sake of a keyboard made exclusively for an Apple product, I have some questions. My biggest issue is the backlight. Yes, it has a backlight. Yes, the backlight can change between various rainbow settings. But the backlight only works while you’re typing. If you’re writing something and you stop to think for more than 3 seconds, the backlight goes off. it’s actually ten seconds, but it’s still too short a time period. As someone with ADHD, the light going on and off is very distracting. I also don’t love that the keyboard has to be charged separately. The Magic Keyboard is charged with the iPad; There’s no need for a second charger. So, the keyboard needs a secondary charger, you shouldn’t use the iPad’s USB-C charger unless you don’t plan to use this keyboard for very long, and the device doesn’t come with a long USB-C cord, so you have to buy one separately, or you have to take out your iPad to continue using it while the keyboard charges, or else stop using the iPad while the keyboard charges. Which is relatively frequently. For background: My only problem with the Magic Keyboard is that the angles are fixed—you have very limited range. If you bought an iPad so you can draw AND write, while it’s super easy to take off the iPad from the Magic Keyboard, you’d have to put it in a separate protective case or go without a case completely while drawing. I got this keyboard to allow me to use my iPad for both purposes. I’d be able to do that well with this device if it didn’t need to be charged separately and the backlight issue, like I said, can be fairly distracting. The Magic Keyboard also doesn’t have a slot for the Apple Pencil. It can still charge, but the pencil is free-floating and can easily fall off. I always like the idea of a keyboard cover, but the reality of them isn’t worth the trouble. This comes with one, if that’s your thing. Things I like about this case: They’re right about the swivel. That works great. I like that it has a designated place to hold an Apple Pencil while it’s not in use. The placement allows the Pencil to charge, but is also protective of the pencil: it’s not going to fall off while using this case. The buttons are easy to use. The volume buttons are covered, the power button is not, weird choice, but all right. The iPad charging port is easy to access. It is easy to remove the iPad and put it back in, and the hinges don’t slip throughout the day. The keyboard is the perfect amount of clacky. If you like the barely-there style of Apple’s keyboards, this product isn’t going to be your favorite. I like the clicky clacky though. The touchpad works with most (probably all) quick gestures related to the ipad. The minimizing gesture can be elusive, though. Other than the minimizing gesture that takes you from app to Home Screen, all the other gestures seem to work just as well as the Magic Keyboard. The keyboard shortcuts, I’m not mad about. I don’t use the device-specific shortcuts often, but I frequent the iPad shortcuts, things like ‘play next’ and the volume controls, often when I’m working. This is something I don’t remember the Magic Keyboard having.

Project S - Midi (mid size) This case does what you ask - the size of a receiver and fits right into your tv stand as you'd want. It fits comfortably and does what it needs to, but with major problems from my experience with it. Pros: 1. Excellent HTPC box for gaming rigs 2. Fantastic design ideas, and looks 3. Enjoyable building as you can remove the entire rig from the case and build it out simply and comfortably. Cons: 1.Thin walls on the inner chassis 2.While it supports a 240mm AIO, the Kraken X52 COMPLETELY blocks the hole to run the CPU EPS connector. With some custom sleeved soft cables, perhaps you could squish it through, but I was forced to run my cables across the motherboard like a peasant. 3. Alignment of the screw holes for the PSU did NOT line up - only 3 screws fit 4. HDMI cable is blocked by a random L shaped area on the back, resulting in me having to squeeze it in before securing the inner chassis to the external. Makes no sense 5. PSU is completely exposed and offers no option for cable management except a tiny cutout that cannot accept thicker sleeve cables. 6. Designed for numerous drives...without options. Instead of allowing you to mount a 240mm radiator in the front instead of drives like most cases with removable drive cages, it just becomes wasted space you end up just filling with excess cabling 7. PSU is not pushed up against the bottom of the case, resulting in no gap between the PSU and motherboard, which prevents front panel/USB connectors from being easily routed to their desired location through extra holes like most quality cases 8. No dust filter on front intake for some reason, but there are filters on every other side, even the left which has no fan options, but can support a 3.5in drive only (again, for no reason should this not be interchangeable) 9. Due to all of the above issues, thermal capabilities are limited. Simply removing the top glass reduces thermals by 10c. An option with a vented top and/or fan mounts in the front would significantly improve the case. There's a reason smaller cases have dedicated ventilation for GPUs. I'm sure I have a couple more gripes, but that's a LONG list of cons, but I don't hate this case. It's going without a top panel in my entertainment center, and should be adequate. Disappointed that I can't run it with the glass with a high end build, but it is what it is.

review_text: I had my eyes on an Aero 15 for a while and I finally decided to buy one when it recently went on sale. Here's my review of the Aero 15. PROS: 1. It's a good looking laptop. Slim, light, very thin bezels, metal all around, solid feel. 2. They advertise the internal component manufacturers and everything is top shelf (except for Killer Wi-Fi...). Samsung display, Samsung memory, Grizzly thermal compound, Intel SSD drive, etc. I wish all manufacturers were doing this. 3. Available with OLED 4K display. Not many "gaming" laptops offer this. While gaming in 4K is probably out of the question on the 1660 Ti, one could use a lower resolution for gaming and use 4K for work and media consumption. 4. Great assortment of ports, including Thunderbolt 3 (rare on "gaming" laptops). 5. Free M.2 internal slot for extra storage, upgrade-able memory. 6. Big battery. 7. Very competitive price for the specs. CONS: 1. The laptop arrived with a defective display. On the black boot-up screen pixels would randomly fire up. Once booted up, there were flickering lines and bands randomly appearing on the screen. I noticed it within the first 3 seconds after powering up. What kind of quality control does Gigabyte have these days? 2. I didn't like the keyboard at all. The first thing I noticed was that the keys were very stiff. I have never typed on a stiffer keyboard, and I've typed on many keyboards. But the worst thing about this keyboard is that they crowded the keys together! At first I couldn't figure out why it feels so wrong, and then I measured it (left edge of Q to right edge of P). Compared to 2 other laptops and a desktop keyboard, the key sizes were the same, but the keys were slightly crowded together horizontally. I suppose they really wanted to make the numpad keys the same size as the others. Then they had to crowd the keys to make the keyboard fit. My other full keyboard laptop has narrower numpad keys, and I've seen that done on other laptops too. As a touch typist I am very disappointed with this keyboard. 3. This keyboard has very bright RGB lights. Even on the lowest brightness setting I found them too bright. 4. There are no indicator lights for power, disk activity, battery charging, caps lock, num lock. I can only assume that the same people who botched the keyboard decided we don't need those anymore. 5. The RGB lit keyboard only lights up the primary key functions. The secondary functions are not lit. This was not a big deal for regular typing, but for things like adjusting brightness or volume you better have a flashlight handy because those symbols are not lit. I find this ridiculous. 6. Minor keyboard complaint: since this is more of a versatile laptop and not a purely "gaming" one, I wish they didn't use the ridiculous font they used on the keys. 7. Coil whine. Annoying non stop coil whine. 8. In CPU stress tests one core would heat up significantly more than the others, by as much as 10 degrees C, most likely due to bad thermal paste application. Another QC failure. Gigabyte had a good thing going with the Aero line. They found a good niche in the market for a premium versatile laptop. The laptop is very well spec'd and priced but the product was ruined for the sake of symmetry and who knows what other design principles only other designers would care for. The lack of quality control is quite obvious, too. I really wanted to like this laptop but I just couldn't, so I returned it.

The nominal 64GB drive has a true capacity of 61524148224 bytes, or 61.52GB, or 57.31GiB, or 120164352 sectors of 512 bytes each. This is before any partition table or filesystem is created. I created a FAT32 filesystem on the drive, and sequentially wrote 60 files of 1.00GB each, containing encrypted zeros (effectively, random data). The total time was 4744.81 seconds (including the sync command), for an average rate of 12.6MB/s. Non-sequential writes would be slower, but 12.6MB/s should be considered the maximum possible write speed of the drive. On reading back the files, the first 52 files were error free. After that, the drive failed, and seemed to reboot its controller repeatedly. I noted that the drive was too hot to touch, even through its plastic case. I disconnected and reconnected the drive, and the rest of the files verified correctly. The overall read speed was 142MB/s when there weren't any errors. All these tests were done with the drive sitting in open air, at 72 degrees F ambient temperature. Reading a huge amount of data off the drive should be done carefully, in shifts, to avoid overheating it. Idling and write accesses don't seem to make the drive overheat, but the metal connector always feels uncomfortably warm after unplugging it, even if you hardly do any operations. Note that I did all these tests on a USB 3.x superspeed port. If you use a USB 2.0 or USB high speed port, your speed will likely be limited to 30MB/s. I removed 1 star for lying about the capacity (3.9% is missing from the advertised size), and another star for lying about the write speed (it claims to be 10 times faster than a 4MB/s USB drive, which is 40MB/s, but it actually can't write faster than 12.6MB/s). I still gave 3 stars, because it is faster than other USB flash drives I've tested of similar capacity.

review_text: I wanted and needed this product to work. If you’re like me, you found a stack of disks in storage that may or may not have something valuable on them. It’s been well over a decade since you had a computer with a floppy drive, so to the rescue comes this little 3.5” USB drive. You might get lucky and get access to all your files, but most likely you’re going to find issues like claims the disk is not formatted or some files can be copied and others not. You might be thinking that the disks went bad in storage, which is totally possible. But what I found over dozens and dozens of disks is that only about 1% were actually bad disks. This drive is just inconsistent in reading disks. I ordered another 3.5” drive from a different brand and found them to be physically identical. Ironically, what one drive couldn’t read, sometimes the other could. A lot of work to try to recover old digital photos from one of those early 3.5” disk-based cameras. How can I be certain it is the USB 3.5” drive and not the disks? In nearly all the cases of being unable to read the disk or a particular file, the original digital camera had no issue reading that same disk. So here are my tips for getting your files back and hopefully never having to deal with a floppy disk again. 1. Don’t give up on the disk. 2. Try another drive. 3. Wait an hour, a day, etc and try again, sometimes just 10 minutes later the disk was readable. 4. If you happen to have one of those old floppy disk cameras, try using its copy disk feature and copy the questionable disk to another disk… sometimes this worked. 5. If it’s really important, or you just don’t have the time to waste with all of the above, try to get ahold of an old computer with a 3.5” drive and move your files via that computer to USB drive, CD or even cloud storage if it can connect online. I believe this 3.5” USB drive is no substitute for those originally built for name brand computers.

This is a OEM Garmin suction mount, it comes in a Garmin retail box. But it is much better than the 'standard' OEM Garmin suction mount that is included with a Garmin GPS. This one has a 7.0cm cup-diameter; the standard suction mount has a 5.4cm cup-diameter. Also, this one has a post that is a bit longer and the whole unit is of a more solid and more sturdy construction. Garmin sells it as an add-on accessory to be used with the larger 7" GPS units to provide them with 'extra holding power.' But this suction mount will fit almost all Garmin GPS units, new and old alike, as almost all of them mount to this standardized 17.2mm diameter swivel ball. My unit is a Garmin nüvi 255W (in the product line-up back in 2010) and the swivel ball fits the unit perfectly. Nice and snug, but still swivels well. I've used the 'regular'-sized mounts for the last decade, since I bought the GPS unit, and I can tell you that this 'large' suction mount has a ton more holding power; I could feel it even as I initially mounted it on the windshield. My experience in owning no less than six of the 'regular'-sized mounts over that decade -- some OEM Garmin, some third-party aftermarket -- is that they barely last two years before the suction efficacy totally fails. My guess is that eventually the suction cup warps (from sun or heat or popping off/on or whatever) just enough so it can no longer hold a seal. But I've got a feeling this large one is going to hold up longer. We'll see. UPDATE: It lasted about 13 months before it started refusing to stay suctioned-up to the glass. Every morning I would come to the car and it had fallen off. Before that, though, it was rock-solid on the glass from Day 1 -- much, much better than all the smaller non-OEM ones I've owned. Take note I am in the Southwest and this suction cup saw service through a VERY hot summer, many days over 110 degrees. That may have accelerated its demise. I bought another one, we'll see how that one goes. ASIDE: Other things I have learned about living with these suction cups: (1) The ones with the clear suction cups hold well but will turn into goop under heat and run down your windshield and drip onto to your dashboard. (2) You CAN 'shim' a loose Garmin swivel ball with a ring/halo of electrical tape. It's an imperfect & aggravating solution, but it will keep the GPS from drooping/flopping face-down and will hold it to any adjusted position. (3) If you want to try to 'glue' your suction cup to your windshield, the best substance I have found to use for that is Permatex Clear RTV Silicone Adhesive Sealant. It's about $7 a tube at most auto stores. If you apply not-too-much not-too-little around the diameter of the suction cup as you mount it to the windshield, it WILL extend the life/hold of the mount and it won't turn into goo. But the silicone is a pain-in-the-butt to remove from the windshield when the time comes, requiring multiple applications of lighter fluid plus a lot of initial loosening then scraping with a single-edge razor blade. YMMV.

The box arrived and my excitement was furthered. It was a slim box and everything packed nice and neat! As I unboxed it my confusion grew a little bit. Instead of a standard power cable with various video ports in the TV itself, this thing is complicated with a control box. I suppose it could be to simplify the wall art idea (i.e. 1 fewer cable coming out of it maybe?) But in pursuit of this engineering miracle, the brilliance of Samsung introduced unnecessary complexity - there's a giant cable that must be connected from the TV into the control box. Your power and HDMI, etc. then plug into it thus adding an additional connection point that could fail. Anyways my somewhat complicated setup was complete! I installed the batteries into the oddly shaped remote control Then, with my excitement reaching a crescendo that could only culminate in the beautiful "SAMSUNG" blue and white image splashed on the screen that I so eagerly anticipated, all that remained was the simple, final push of the power button. With a measured flick of my right thumb, this newfound pleasure would be mine! AND..... Nothing. A little red light flashed on the remote. "Hmm" I thought. I flicked again. Nothing. After a third flick brought no change I checked all the connections, un-doing and re-doing in the overly specific and risky order that apparently is required of such an amazing engineering marvel. I plugged and unplugged the power. Flick. Nothing. Being a veteran of years of PC support, I seemlessly and ever so carefully moved the unit to another power outlet. Triple checked the connections. Flick. Nothing. DOA. Patience worn thin, frothy anticipation turned completely flat like a 3-day old beer, I packed up the unit and sent it back never to buy one of these again. Turns out my experience was like that of the 1995 film "Waterworld". Couldn't wait to see it, couldn't have been more disappointed once I did (in fairness the movie projector actually worked at the theater and at least I did see Waterworld, but still...). Sometimes even Samsung, the Kevin Costner of electronics can't thrill you. Save your money. This thing is probably cool when it works. That is, if you can ever power it on.

I was expecting an experience more akin to Siri on the apple watch where you can raise your arm and say "Alexa..." not fumble on the screen, or press a button to wake the watch, then hold the same button to wake Alexa up. The watch does have an "offline" assistant built in that allows you to open the watches many apps with voice commands (so the watch is listening!!!), but it only recognizes the built in apps like "compass", "flashlight", "heart monitor" etc. strange it doesn't recognize the allegedly "built in" Alexa app as one you can open with voice as that would at least allow: "Open Alexa" and then you ask your question. Summary - smart watch - it's amazing. Portable Alexa - disappointing.

When I opened these I was expecting another pair of budget wireless earbuds, but happily I was very mistaken! The case is well built, with a convenient slim size and rounded edges. The hinge is very solid and closes with a nice snap (this is where a lot of lower quality models fail). The buds sit in nice moulded cavities and stay in place even when inverted and shaken around!Pairing with my phone was effortless. In terms of comfort they are excellent, sitting firmly in my ears with little adjustment needed. The default tips fit me fine, but there are 4 other sizes included if you need them. I wore them for a good 4 hours straight without any noticeable discomfort.In terms of battery life I haven’t been able to run them dead, so can’t give figures, but I would definitely say they are equal to or better than the competition.On to audio quality. These use the LDAC codec for high fidelity streaming, a feature missing from many lower end headphones, and it definitely shows!In Rachid Taha’s Barra Barra the percussion wraps all around with a clear soundstage, I’m able to pinpoint the individual instruments clearly. The electric guitar is warm and central, coming straight down the middle like a freight train, and the vocal sits clearly on top. I was even able to pick out some atmospheric synth elements that I’ve never noticed before. When the drums come in later in the song the kick is tight and powerful, underpinning the track beautifully.In Armand Van Helden’s I Want Your Soul, the kick is once again powerful without being overwhelming. The hats skip around with plenty of space to hear the detail of the reverb. The main bass synth fills out the low end without overpowering the drums. When the chorus breaks things do get a little muddy, the vocal is clear, but there is so much going on in the lower mids that I don’t think the drivers can quite maintain separation.Honestly I was blown away by the performance, I did not expect quality like this at the price point. Are they reference headphones? No (but honestly would do the job in a pinch). Are they fun? Absolutely. Anyone would be happy with these as daily drivers.My only real issue (and a minor one at that) is that these things block pretty much all external sound and there is no passthrough, so for me are more suitable for home and office listening that walking on busy streets. I like to be able to hear my surroundings while out and about. To be clear, this is the nature of the beast and not a criticism, but something to be aware of.In short, these are excellent. Highly recommended.

After spending time with these cameras I've found them to be a "you get what you pay for situation." They are still one of the few bullet style cameras that require no drilling into the mirror or body, but they are not adjustable and are generally mediocre quality. Pro: + No drill design with enough stickiness on the cord to keep the visible parts in place. + Easy to wire up and includes a toggle switch to invert the image. They are mislabeled as a "gridline" setting. + Body mounted design is hard to find these days, this is one of the few that is compact, no drill, and a decent price. Con: - You get what you pay for in the image quality department. There is noise and banding not found on other cameras that remind me of an old school CRT display. - No IR or visible illumination so night time visibility would be poor without street lights, head lights, etc. - Wiring is cheap, toggle switch is too. Longevity will be a concern here, especially if you consider this an added eye in your blind spot. - No gridlines and no clear way to add that through another device. This means that you can only look up and down just so far...this may not be important to some, but it is very important to me for what I use the camera for. Overall, I am happy with this camera. I purchased this product because it was cheap and would allow me to install blind spot cameras triggered by the turn signal. I contacted the seller about buying a different switch but was told that was the only option. Additionally, the instructions are horribly inadequate. I had to sit with my car in pieces touching wires together trying to figure it out for myself. If you ask for help you'll just be told to look at the pictures. Hopefully this will help Red 12v wire - tapped to cig lighter power Black ground - tapped to cig lighter ground Brown "monitor" - reverse signal TO head unit Grey "rear" - reverse signal FROM vehicle wiring harness (do not connect to with brown, it goes from car to box then box to head unit) Yellow "left" - connect to left turn signal in door (I used a multimeter to test each wire going to the side mirror with the turn signal on) White "right" - same as yellow but for other side I connected the camera power wire to the extension wire (rca plugged in and red wires soldered together) then by the box I did the same thing (red to red) and you don't need the ground wire by the box I also connected the front camera to my head units front camera option instead of to the box It works decently - there is some lag when you turn the signal on but that's to be expected. Sometimes it goes to a blank reverse signal for no reason. For the price it's not too bad (this would be unacceptable if this were more than 50 bucks) Hopefully that was helpful - you'd think if I can write instructions that the person/company making money from this product could too.

review_text: I had very low expectations for this cheapest of 4K TVs and I've had otherwise great experience with other LG display products. I was only looking for the cheapest utility display as a test output for 4K video products I install so I had low expectations. This TV didn't even meet my low expectations. This TV was clearly designed for the Hospitality industry where in-room video experience is not a high priority. Anyone who has stayed at a hotel and couldn't the contrast right on the in-room TV will know what I mean. I do not recommend this as a buy. The same device was also marketed as a Westinghouse model. The first one actually had the Westinghouse branding on it even though it was in an LG Carton and had LG firmware. Ooops!!! I guess the QC at the refurb company didn't pay attention to the bezel when this was renewed. But that's more humorous than anything else. Just know that LG makes this exact same model for other companies so shop around under the different brandings for the best deal. Even the model numbers are almost identical although the menus are different depending on which version of the WebOS software they burn into the firmware. I bought this refurbed and I'm glad I didn't pay full price. Had to exchange the first one due to the fact that the internal brightness enhancement (BEF) filter had shifted causing a wrinkled look to the display. Amazon took care of it but it took two weeks to get it all settled. If you do buy this, go for the extended warranty. Whatever you do, don't even think of buying it new. It's significantly cheaper to buy the refurbed unit and get the extended warranty. The factory new warranty is only a year anyway and you are likely going to need it as I did. All in all, the refurb company who packaged this did an effective like-new packaging in that the plastic was properly shielded with Nitto film although the internal styrofoam was cracked indicating that the carton had taken a huge hit despite the fact that there was no exterior damage to the box. This might explain why the filter had shifted. The replacement TV came in a similar box but it was obvious that it had been unboxed before shipping as the factory tape was not present and it had been re-taped at least twice based on the two different type of box tape that was used. The replacement TV however had none of the display defects the first one had. As far as the product itself goes, there are no pros to this TV so only the cons. * Horrible, horrible menu. Too complicated for the average non-audio professional. Confusing menu layout and just impossible to do a quality calibration and I have software and tools to do this. I'm not sure what a consumer would do to calibrate it. * Without calibration, the picture is horrible at best. I wouldn't use this as my primary display. Maybe as a video for a welcome sign in a lobby or perhaps to play cable TV in a waiting room but definitely NOT as an everyday TV. Even with professional calibration tools, the electronics just isn't up to snuff. As an example, if you increase Brightness you sacrifice contrast. Blacks look washed out and colors are not consistent with even cheaper TVs and Monitors that I have in my shop. So reds that are displayed on this TV look pink of you calibrate for blue and likewise if you calibrate for reds, the blues are sacrificed. All in all, an indicator of just cheap engineering. LG could probably fix this with a firmware upgrade but don't count on it. This product was clearly shipped before it was ready. LGs higher end products don't exhibit this. * The gaming functions are a joke. Using it as a monitor you quickly learn that the color gamut of the display is held back by some awful interface electronics. Although its supports HDR, LG clearly didn't work out the bugs in their design and this just feels like a product rushed before fully testing the firmware. * The display has a protective covering plastic covering which causes further reduction in clarity due to internal reflections. It looks a lot worse the closer you get to the screen. It would be OK if one could remove this but I saw no obvious way to do this and I didn't want to void the warranty. I may change my mind and try to disassemble the bezel after I've had the TV for a while but the out-of-box view was horrible. * The remote control is a joke. It's needlessly cramped buttons make it impossible to use. Now one could use a third party remote to solve this but that adds more cost. Plus the symbols on the remote are confusing at best and their illogically placed. My other LG TVs had remotes with generous sized buttons, this one was clearly penny-pinching design compromises. So they save $0.02 to just create a bad initial impression. Not a smart move on LG's part. * The smart functions are also a joke. The menus are slow as molasses and the response times are horrific. I hooked up a Roku stick to it and that remedied the problem there but why even bother putting that function inside the TV if the processor driving the WebOS interface is too under-powered.

If you're expecting a cheap computer you'll be satisfied, but there's a few quirks you should know about. The computer has 64GB EMMC storage built in and a removable 64GB SSD, not one large 128gb drive. The OS is installed to the internal storage by default but I recommend copying it over to the SSD because its about double the speed. Before doing anything crazy like reinstalling the OS, use a program like DoubleDriver to back up the drivers that come pre-installed, as I found the touch driver provided from the Jumper website doesn't seem to work right like the one it comes with, and windows will not detect it or the hinge drivers automatically. Even though the device has USB C it doesn't seem to be fully compliant. For one the included charger is a dumb one that ONLY outputs 12v, so I wouldn't recommend risking your phone or other devices plugging into it. The good news is it DOES work with other USB C PD chargers, but instead of 12V it will want 15V. My USB PD car charger which is more than capable of 15v does not like it and won't charge the laptop unless its off for some reason. USB power banks will not charge it unless they are capable of 15V over USB C which most small ones are not. If you know what you're doing my solution to this PD charging issue was to cut the included charge cable and put a "USB-C PD Trigger Module" capable of 12V on the other end, this DIY adapter will trick PD power banks into thinking the device wants 12V and send the raw 12V into the laptop charge port like the wall charger does.

Buyers should be aware that the Treble and Bass knobs are very fragile, they may be made from egg shells. In the 7 years I have this radio 2 knobs one Treble and one Bass knob have broken. At $19 each knob, total $38 for knobs that should never have broken in the first place, that seems like a lot. Shipping was approximately $13 exorbitantly high for such a light weight and small knob to ship, each time a knob broke. I still don't know how either knob broke, I think over time the cheap plastic just became brittle and they just fell apart. Poor quality for important control knobs. The sound quality with the Aux. hole in the back is much lower quality sound than from the radio. I tried listening to Pandora thru the Aux. input and it sounded terrible. This radio is a solidly built, for the most part, storm radio with good AM/FM, Weather & 2 Meter Band reception. I think with an analog screen it would eat less battery. It does eat D batteries, so you better have a good supply of D Batt's before the storm sets in. For this reason, I feel this Radio is best used when plugged into AC power. I used this during Hurricane Sandy black out and many Black outs over time and it pulls in the signal very well. The reception is the radio's strongest asset. The mesh screen has started to rust over time, not sure why, since it has never been exposed to direct rain. I had higher expectations from a radio in this price point and was not expecting the problems I have had and the poor customer service that has been provided for what I consider a manufacturers defects. I would love to have given the C Crane a 5 star rating but, had to deduct one star for weak plastic that will fail over time and another star for their poor customer service. If I had known in advance about the knobs being prone to breakage, I would have purchased another radio.

review_text: I've only used it for three short trips out and back, so 6 "legs." It's never stayed mounted for more than about 10 miles. I have a phone with a suction mount that has been on for years, yet this one has trouble staying put for 10 minutes. I'm not sure why this one so horrible, maybe because it is really small to hold a 7" GPS? But the back of the GPS is set up in such a way only this mount will "work". It's a round piece that goes into the back of the GPS, then a little ball that pops into the suction mount. It's fallen off glass, then a very smooth flat metal part of the dash, and on the dash itself which is like a rosewood paneling with a glass like surface, that my phone mount has been suction mounted to for years. And the way the mount is, I don't know how I could make some Velcro stick to a surface, and the GPS. But the on button is on the back of the unit, so how would one turn it on if it's velcro'd to the dash? It's just a horrible design. But even in testing, if you mount it to glass at home, once you arrive back home, it will have fallen off the glass. And I live in TX, not CA, so there's no shaking going on at my house; It's not a mobile home, brick homes don't move much even in windy conditions. The routing does not take you to the truck entrance like it advertises, at least not the three I've used it for, had I not known where to go, it would have been costly, time and mileage. In addition, every GPS I've used takes me back to my yard via highways which drop me on local roads less than one mile from my yard. This one wants me to get off and drive 4.6 miles through neighborhoods, which although trucks are "allowed," through trucks are not. As a local I've taken that way before when there was a crash on the highway, but even then, only when the highway is either backed up really bad or closed. All this to make the trip 1.2 miles shorter, although it would add close to 30 minutes to the trip with all the stop lights, depending on the time of day. Also the app slows down the internet, I keep getting messages from my phone about its incessant pinging, and in 3 of my 24 days of data usage, it's responsible for 10% of my total data usage. I have learned over the years that (small, portable) external hard drives are not particularly trustworthy, and most of them last at most a couple of years before they stop being readable. For that reason I always keep two permanently connected to my computer, each running a sequential backup every hour or so. I know that sooner or later I'll have to replace one, but I feel fairly confident that the second one will continue to work at least until I get the replacement. This particular Seagate drive, however, was doubtlessly the worst so far, as it lasted less than three months. To add insult to the injury, I found out that Seagate's first-level support is abysmally incompetent. The first technician that responded informed me, quite cheerfully, that they'd make sure to make me very satisfied, although no, they would not replace the unit because they did not ship to Puerto Rico. On strongly worded WTF-get-me-your-manager later, I was told that of course they would ship me a replacement, and gave me the instructions to request an RMA online. The only form, again, did not accept addresses from Puerto Rico, so more communications time had to be wasted so that the second-level technician force-entered the address into their returns system. I was also cheerfully informed that all replacements are refurbished units. Lastly, while I was in the process of sending the drive back to Seagate for replacement, I was sent another message cheerfully informing me that my case was being closed due to "lack of response". Another WTF message was required to receive a last cheerful "clarification" that what they meant was that because the replacement was already being processed, they would proceed to close the support ticket. I did get the replacement unit, and it does appear to be working, but I have only had it running a couple of weeks. We shall see. If it's within my power and I can help it, however, I will definitely avoid getting another Seagate drive ever.

The charge on my AirPods Pro Buds doesn't last the entirety of my long-haul flights or overnight if I wear them to sleep. Buying a 2nd set of AirPods to always have a charged pair on hand seemed excessively expensive and indulgent. These Beats Studio Buds do the trick for less than 1/3 the price of my AirPods. For my purposes, the Beats Studio Buds work out great. The sound quality and noise-cancelation features of the Beats Studio Buds are just a step down from my noise-canceling AirPods Pro Buds. With the Beats Studio Buds, I hear a little more of what's happening around me which is disappointing, hence the 3 stars. However, I wouldn't give the AirPods Pro noise canceling feature more than 4 stars. Neither brand of Buds holds a candle to my Beats over-the-ear noise-canceling headphones. For sound quality, I get some weird feedback if I'm laying down and the Beats Buds rub against my pillow, whereas I've never had that problem with the AirPods Pro, hence 4 stars for Beats Buds vs. the 5 stars I would give to the AirPods Pro. The battery life is almost identical for both brands, which IMO is subpar in both brands of Buds, so I would give them both 3s. I would rather have slightly larger buds that held a charge longer than the tiny buds I'm constantly searching for when I drop them on the floor or into various crevices. The charge on both brands of Buds lasts about the same amount of time, which equates to about 4-5 hours of usage per set. For my very long-haul flights of 10-15 hours plus airport time, my Airpods are recharged again by the time my Beats run dry, and then my Beats are recharged if the 2nd Airpods charge gives up. Most planes have USB ports, but I have yet to find one that does more than trickle charge, which means my iPhone must get the USB port so it doesn't die when I'm watching shows, listening to music and podcasts, or reading on my Kindle app. So I can't recharge my Buds of either flavor while I'm using my phone. Fortunately, the charged-up cases get one set of buds back in action by the time the other set dies, and I can often get enough of a 2nd recharge on my Airpods to last until I reach a 'real' recharging location.

I bought this computer for my roommate on Black Friday so it was a great deal. I've read most of the reviews for it here on Amazon so I had some expectations about how it would work. I credit the nvme SSD with making the performance snappy with this computer. And you can easily upgrade the SSD to a larger capacity if you want. There is also an empty bay for a 2.5 inch sata SSD but you need to purchase a cable and mounting bracket for it. Overall a decent computer for many people who don't need a high powered machine. Recommended. Note: I just updated it to 22H2 and the Disk Cleanup utility has been moved. The only way I can find it is with the search box on the task bar. (I have since found it in Start>All Apps>Windows Tools.) Update 1/13 - I've spent even more time with this machine and I will say it rivals my Acer Aspire 5 which is saying something. At the current price of $245 from Amazon it is over $110 cheaper than the Acer Aspire 5 so it is a best buy in my opinion. The Asus VivoBook 14 is a great computer. Update 1/16 - I discovered why people are getting low wifi speeds using Ookla Speedtest. The computer comes set to only utilize 802.11n rather than 802.11ac that it is capable of. Go to Device Manager, Network Adapters and double click on Realtec Wireless LAN. On the advanced tab Wireless Mode set to 802.11a/n/ac. Then Task Manager shows that 802.11ac is being used. It's too bad the computer didn't come set to use 802.11ac out of the box.

I bought this ahead of a trip to use it while transporting a Travel Trailer 800 miles back home. I opened it at a hotel, away from my home wifi connection. This started the comedy of errors. 1. Do Not plan on using this without first checking for any map and OS updates while connected to your home wifi, which in my case was 9GB. The unit can't connect to Hotel Wifi that requires webpage confirmations, so therefore the update could not be installed via Hotel Wifi. This limitation is idiotic, given I'm connected to the unit via Bluetooth and should be able to transmit the data that I download via my phone connected to hotel wifi to the GPS unit. I could not. So this inability could lead into the second problem. 2. The unit did not recognize an address that has been present for 70 years. I tried every address format including punctuation and spelling out road names and the state name - but it just didn't recognize anything. Google maps, however, recognized it and guided me there to the pickup location without fail. This leads to problem 3. 3. The Search Function is inconsistent. I attempted to search for "IKEA", a fairly prominent business establishment... Or so I thought. The unit could not find any businesses by this name. I keyed in the actual address of the IKEA that I wanted, and the unit recognized the address and suggested "IKEA". How is that possible? This occurred for several search queries. I ended up having to find the address of my destinations via Google Maps on my phone and transcribing then to the GPS unit, which felt duplicative and frustrating. I ended up keeping Google Maps open on my phone just in case, and I'm glad that I did. Read on to the next problem. 4. The route guidance is not sufficient; here is what happened. I input my address (given the first and second problem). The unit told me to drive on an adjacent road for 183 miles. Wow. Within 1 mile I was at an intersection that required either a left or right turn, but the unit did not indicate that I had to turn left or right. Being in San unknown city, I didn't know which turn would keep me on this road/highway. Google Maps however knew that the turn was present and guided me to stay to the left and turn left at the light. It should have known there was an intersection and instructed me as to which lane to use, and instructed me to turn left. It was a 2 two lane intersection and I needed to know to stay in the left lane. This failure to be informed is somewhat forgiveable in a car, but not when you're towing 33 feet of trailer and an indirect turn could be disastrous. Because of these 4 issues, I'm completely dissatisfied with this unit. I'm returning it and searching for another unit. Garmin really let me down. This unit is completely useless.

In this case there is an unremoveable drive cage on the bottom next to where the power supply goes. Pros: -Relatively inexpensive telephoto with a good range of focal lengths -very, very light, and reasonably small -great image quality if you can get enough light -great stabilization to stop MY movement/wiggle at slow shutter speeds. Cons: - f/8 aperture at 400mm is just too small to get fast shutter speeds in anything but bright sun - overall small aperture seems to reduce accuracy and speed of AF on tricky subjects - the great IS won't stop the subject's motion (not really the lenses fault, just not how IS works), so f/8 and the resulting shutter speeds cause issues when shooting sports/action I have very mixed feelings about this lens. On one hand, it is great for the price, the Image Stabilization is awesome, and it is much smaller and lighter than other similar lenses, like the much, much more expensive EF 100-400 F4-5.6. The downside is the small aperture, narrowing to f/8 at the full 400mm, and you really need to stop down one or two notches from there if you want maximum sharpness. As such, you end up running pretty high ISOs if you want to keep the shutter speed high to stop action, and the noise resulting from the higher ISOs starts to rob sharpness. This issue isn't too bad on a sunny, cloudless day--but be prepared to drop shutter speed and crank up the ISO in less than perfect conditions. Forget shooting anything moving indoors, or in the morning/evening. I found this out when I was trying to photograph the action at a local airshow--it was a somewhat cloudy day, and I just couldn't get enough light to run anything but wide-open, with ISO 1000+ to get even 1/500 shutter--resulting in blurry AND noisy pictures unless everything came out just right. On top of that, it seemed like it was missing focus a lot, probably due to the small aperture. My camera focuses just fine on fast movement with other lenses. Don't get me wrong, this lens is awesome for landscape, portrait, anything where you can get everything to hold still, and you can even shoot action on a very bright, sunny day. But if you want laser-sharp photos of things moving fast in anything but perfect light, be prepared to pony up the cash for an EF adapter and an L-series lens, or use a faster, shorter lens and hope you have enough resolution to crop in. I'm not sure what niche this lens is supposed to fill. For a beginner who is trying to save some money, the RF 24-240 is a better all-rounder, or the Tamron 18-400 if you want a one-lens-for-everything. For the enthusiast or semi-pro, the 24-240 is still better at the low end of the range, and anyone seriously trying to shoot telephoto in imperfect light would be much better served by one of the large-aperture 70-200 L-series lenses or the EF 100-400. Ultimately, I sold this lens and spent about twice as much on a used EF 100-400mm F4-5.6 L IS II, which is superior in every way, besides weight and size.

Screws to get to the battery compartment. If your batteries go dead, you have to undo several screws to reach the battery compartment. What genius thought this was a good idea? Why not just have the same cover you use to get to the SD card slot also let you get to the batteries? Who designed this? I genuinely would like to know. 4. Poor build quality. I assume Vilros has no quality control. Another review here says there are 6 screws you have to undo to get to the battery compartment. Are there? Not on mine. They did not mold the plastic correctly so one of the screws cannot even reach the threads. So they give you 6 screws but only 5 actually work. The 6th screw you might as well keep as a backup in case you lose one because it doesn't actually fit in the hole. 5. Can't secure the fan in place. The fan is held in place purely by friction. No screws at all. It might move out of place if you drop the case, and I often accidentally move it when trying to open the case, making me have to position it again. A very strange decision. Notice here I did not complain about it requiring batteries or you needing a USB adapter. These are also lazy decisions, but I sort of expected it. If those were the only "issues", I wouldn't have anything to complain about. But the issues with this thing are nonstop. I bought this because it is the only case I'm aware of like this. I wanted an all-in-one unit for my Pi that was similar to how older computers were, with the keyboard and computer as one unit. This is the only product like this I'm aware of, except maybe that Pi 100 case, but they do not sell that case separately, nor does it have the ability to add a fan like this one does. To my knowledge, this is the only case like this, which surprises me since this seems like such an obvious type of case to make, it'd be one of my first ideas. This is a great monitor for a single PC but anything beyond that is problematic. My new job gave me a MacBook Pro and that's when all my problems started. As other reviews already mentioned, there is no software available for anything other than Windows. Even though I was able to connect my Mac to the monitor, the functionality is very limited. None of the functions that come with the Display Manager application are available. The only way to scale the screen is to decrease resolution which makes everything very blurry, so it's either that or a magnifying glass. The volume cannot be controlled by the connected device. None of the cables included with the monitor accommodate USB C type connection so I had to buy a separate set of cables. I now have my other PC and my Mac connected to this monitor with a shared mouse and keyboard, but switching between sources is a real pain. I set up two of the monitor frame buttons to serve as source shortcuts, which is convenient. However, the buttons are hardly visible, especially if the room light is not bright so you end up having to poke around with a finger to find one of these buttons. Once you successfully switch from one source to another, they behave completely differently. For example, if I switch from my Mac to my PC, the Mac seems to recognize that the extended monitor is no longer connected and is able to switch to a normal mode moving all the application windows back onto the native screen. This behavior is different when I switch from my PC to the Mac. My PC continues to act as through there is an active second display and it does not switch back to being the primary. I have to actually disconnect the cable for that to happen. All in all, I would definitely recommend this monitor for a PC but if you are a mac user, or if you have a mix, I'd look for something else.

review_text: Despite other reviews warning that the Samsung T7 SSD runs hot, I bought it based on the assumption that it would do so only under heavy use, such as large video file transfers. I use it to store and process raw and JPEG photo files, which it does at significantly higher speed than my previous external hard drive. It's also dead silent, vibration-free, and trouble-free (so far). I have discovered however, that even when it's not in use the resting temperature hovers around 100 degrees F (41 degrees C). This will of course depend on the ambient room temperature. The cooler the room or the larger the heat sink you set it on, the cooler it will run. It also has a built-in protective circuit that will reduce transfer speeds if the heat approaches 48 C (118 F). I have yet to experience this, but it's good to know the T7 is unlikely to die without notice. That said, if the heat aspect makes you nervous you should probably consider something else.

Videographers and Photos use massive amounts of storage. The best way to deal with them on a budget is to setup network file shares with a JBOD setup. We were using G Drive Thunderbolt 3 10TB Enclosures connected to mac pros running server OS. The G Drive Thunderbolt 3 10TB Enclosure is quite expensive, $500. They have a 5 year warranty and they're good for it. What I've noticed is these enclosures tend to fail, but the 3.5" hard drive inside is still fully functional. Pulling the drive voids the warranty, however sending the whole unit in on a warranty replacement takes up to 2 weeks and they will replace it with a new drive, and it's burdensome to copy over 8-9+ TBs of data, 18 hours in a perfect scenario. These enclosures will work on a straight swap with the G Drive Thunderbolt 3 10TB Enclosure's hard drive. The only way the drive was recognized in my case was to use the enclosed USB 3 cable, not the usb c/ thunderbolt 3 even though those are supposed to be interchangeable. However this may be the lack of the 2013 Mac Pro thunderbolt 3 support without using the Apple dongle to convert thunderbolt 2 to 3. In any case, $55 was well worth the cost! I have not found a way to purchase a G Drive empty Enclosure that's fully compatible that makes financial sense.

review_text: This is a follow up review for me. I purchased this as a replacement for my old messenger bag when I was changing jobs and wanted to treat myself to something nice. The bag is room, it has good capacity to hold your laptop, files/notepads, pens and pencils with a hand pocket on the rear. These were all great features I really enjoyed with the bag. But I have to lower my rating on the bag for a few deficiencies that really stand out. The first one that I noticed was that I was seeing staining on my pants! When I wear khaki's or light colored pants if the bag rubs your legs (this is going to happen if you have more than a short 2 minute walk) the dye used for the leather will transfer to your clothing. The next concern was after having the bag for 6 months the carry strap failed and broke. I know...someone is saying to themselves, "But did he overload the bag!" The answer is no. My bag load was a standard Think Pad style notepad, a 5 subject notepad that I use to take notes, 3 pens, 2 pencils and a Sharpie. If that sounds close to what you might put in your bag that should help give perspective. Don't want to dissuade anyone from the bag because it is nice...just consider purchasing the optional insurance that can be purchased if you do...you may just need it.

review_text: Summary about the NVME SSD Legend 800 2 Tb model: The manufacturer ADATA misleads customers by claiming that the model has 256-bit AES encryption and that user data is protected. This is not true. There is no instruction for this feature. It is impossible to find any information on the manufacturer's website or anywhere on the Internet about how the encryption feature should work and how to check the security of user data. Support on the manufacturer's website and the store selling ADATA on the Amazon platform ignore, and no comments on this issue. I recommend that Amazon remove this product from sale and issue a warning to the seller and the manufacturer, as the product's technical description is inaccurate. I spent a long time deciding which NVME SSD M.2 format to buy. There are many options: major brands like WD, Crucial, and Samsung, as well as countless smaller brands. The price for 1-2 Tb models is roughly the same, but most do not have an encryption feature, making the product more expensive. I decided to take a risk and choose a second-tier brand that, in addition to similar speed and durability characteristics, indicated the presence of 256-bit AES data encryption in the description, which is critical for me and the reason I started upgrading my old Crucial SSD, which does not have this feature. Imagine my surprise when the Legend 800 2 Tb model had no encryption! Not only is there no instruction provided with the product that explains step-by-step how to set up the disk at first launch, but there is no such instruction on the ADATA manufacturer's website. Who did they make this product for? Telepaths, who are supposed to guess how to install it themselves? In the proprietary ADATA SSD ToolBox application, which is designed for managing and setting up all ADATA disk models, there is no corresponding functionality for encryption setup or even an indicator of whether it is working. I spent two days of my life trying various methods described in the instructions of other manufacturers, such as Kingston and Samsung (which have instructions on this matter), but these methods did not work. I tried to enable encryption through the BitLocker program included with Windows 11 Pro, but the ADATA SSD did not launch the built-in encryption on the chip. All of this is evidence that the claimed functionality of having built-in encryption on the chip in the ADATA Legend 800 2 Tb model does not correspond to reality. The company should either release a refutation and make a publicly available step-by-step manual on how to set it up or sincerely apologize to customers for the deception. Until this, I will no longer buy ADATA

I have an older TV that has a usb port that doesn't provide adequate power for the poorly designed resource hog of a product the amazon fire stick is. As a result, trying to use that port to power the fire stick is problematic at best. Often times the device will struggle to boot up, or will flash the display off and on periodically while operating. This product is advertised to fix exactly this problem - to use a battery to store power, and offer a boost when more power is being demanded. It is hard for me to measure whether or not this product made any improvement since the problem is temperamental with or without it. But I tried everything, and found that even with this product, I frequently have problems and have to frequently restart the fire stick (which is an agonizingly slow process) due to flickering problems, or it getting stuck and freezing up. I eventually got to the point that it wasn't worth fighting this fight anymore, and I've run an inconvenient cable to plug the fire stick into a powered outlet with the included adapter. The power problems have completely gone away as a result, although now my fire stick continues running and streaming away even when I turn the TV off since it's plugged in 24/7, which makes using the sleep mode on my TV inconvenient since I'd really rather it automatically turn off. Bottom line is, from my observance, this cable made absolutely no difference. The battery did not offer the needed boost to allow my fire stick to be powered from the TV. I think this product is a pure scam, with the hope that people will just think it improved a temperamental situation, when in reality it's just a power cable with a battery that does nothing. I'd recommend staying away from fire sticks completely if possible - if roku is an option for you, my roku stick never had a problem being powered on the TV's usb port (although it was an older stick). It's too bad that the roku is limited compared to the fire stick, although part of that is amazon's fault. Amazon's complete pulling of support on streaming twitch to devices other than a fire stick is a completely unethical power play! Not only has it forced people to replace roku sticks if they want to watch twitch streams, but it has noticeably reduced viewer counts for streamers. Such a short sighted move....it'll sell a few extra sticks, but it will cost them way more in viewers.

The headphones come packaged in a nice blue gift box with the charging case and a set of different sized ear tips. The charging case is compact and lightweight, but ultimately feels a little bit cheap. One strange design choice is that it has a USB-C male cable attached to it instead of a USB-C female port - I am not sure if that would be an issue or would be more convenient than needing to carry a separate cable, but it’s worth noting. In terms of design the earbuds are not anything special and are just large bulbous pods sitting in your ears, though the do have a nice chrome JLab logo on them. The earbuds use Bluetooth 5.2 (not the latest 5.3) - Battery life is rated at 42+ hours total without ANC, with 9+ hours with each earbud - I’ve not personally tested this but it seems a little overestimated.The paring process was not seamless - the earbuds connected to the app quickly but they did not actually pair with my phone - I had to go into the bluetooth settings and manually pair them first. Now in my Bluetooth menu I have JLab ANC and JLab ANC-App, which I think is a poor implementation as other companion apps don’t work like this.Out of the box, the built in first EQ preset (JLab Signature) sounds pretty bad - the second EQ preset (balanced) sounds even worse. Switching to EQ preset 3 (Bass Boost) improves the sound a lot, as it adds much needed low end to the sound signature whilst removing the harsh tinny upper range, making these passable. Unfortunately, when you’ve got Active Noise Cancelling enabled, it really negatively affects audio quality and reduces clarity by a noticeable amount, pretty much destroying the sound with a crunchy filter over the top of it. It does cancel out noise fairly well, but degrades your listening experience with it.Overall, due to the active noise cancelling (the main selling point of these earbuds) destroying the sound quality, I can’t honestly give more than a 2*. Without using ANC and using the bass booster EQ preset, then I would give them a 3*. There are much better implementations of active noise cancellation available, and for the price point there are better sounding alternatives.

This laptop is a great buy for the money, especially considering you're getting 16GB of RAM and a 6-core processor. Overall a solid package marred by a few shortcomings that may or may not matter to you. Pros: * Price to performance is unbeatable * Comes with 16GB of RAM (dual channel) when most laptops at this price point only get 8GB * Very fast processor that handles just about anything you can throw at it * Pretty good graphics for integrated - lets you play a lot of games at lower settings if that's your thing * Fairly rigid construction and the plastic has a nice soft coating that feels good in the hand * Responsive touchpad * Plush, backlit keyboard with plenty of travel * 1080p screen is plenty sharp for this 14-inch panel - no issues with reading text or watching videos * Speakers get loud and are clear until you get super high ( >80% volume) * Touchscreen works well * Comes with a free pen (battery included) * SSD can be replaced in the future if you need more space * Battery life is respectable - I'd say 7-8 hours if you're surfing the web and watching some youtube videos on a battery-friendly power mode * Fingerprint reader is fast and pretty accurate (works on the first try 9 out of 10 times) Cons * Screen is dim compared to higher-end laptops (or even Intel variants of the same laptop). At 250 nits, you'll likely have no issue using it indoors (which 99% of us are), but know that you will likely have it maxed out all the time, which will impact battery life. * Plastic build. While the build quality feels solid, it's still not going to be as sturdy/rugged as a metal body. Expect to hear a few tiny creaks and groans here and there if you're moving it around a lot (like using on the couch). * Heavy if using as a tablet. This is par for the course with most 2-in-1 laptops. Defects * My unit came with 1 dead pixel. * Coil whine. I hesitate listing this as a defect since it's present on most laptops to some degree, but I think it's loud enough to put here. On battery, my unit has a bit of coil whine. It isn't too audible unless I am in a dead silent room. When charging, the coil whine increases to a noticeable volume. Something to consider if you plan on leaving yours plugged in a lot. * Audio popping. Before and after any sound is played on the laptop (e.g., streaming a video online), I can hear an audible "pop" come from the speakers. It pops once before any sound is played and then pops 2-3 times after the sound is finished playing. It appears to be a driver/Windows power management problem. Essentially, the speakers turn themselves off to save power, so anytime a sound is played, they turn on (causing a pop) and then afterwards turn off (causing a few more). "Just mute the sound" I can hear you say. Doesn't work. Even on mute, the speakers will turn themselves on and off if they think there may be audio on a given web page or application. This results in hearing tiny pops randomly while using the laptop. I spent hours diagnosing and troubleshooting this issue, even going as far as editing the registry. No dice. This appears to be a software issue, but I don't know if this is a Lenovo Windows problem. Either way I have been unable to find a solution that fixes the issue. Conclusion I ultimately returned the laptop. If the defects above were not present, I would be typing this review on the Lenovo and be perfectly content knowing that I got a really good deal on what is a very capable machine. I hope the coil whine and audio issues aren't impacting a lot of people who buy this laptop. At the end of the day, I'm just not confident that my luck would change with a replacement unit. I'll likely snag one of the other AMD Ryzen laptops coming out in the latter half of this year. UPDATE: I found a fix to the audio issue. I'm not 100% on the order of operations, since I changed a lot of things, but if you are experiencing issues, try this: 1. Go to device settings > Sounds, video, and game controllers 2. Select the RealTek audio device and right-click to update the driver 3. Choose browse my computer for drivers 4. Choose let me pick from a list 5. Install the High Definition Audio Device drivers (restart if asked) 6. Go to the registry editor and type "Computer\HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM" into the box at the top. Hit enter. 7.Hit ctrl + f to bring up search and type "PowerSettings" Hit enter. 8. You should end up in a subfolder of 0001 or 0002. Click on the parent folder (the 0001 or 0002 folder) and look at the DriverDesc field. Find the one that says "AMD High Definition Audio" 9. Now go to the PowerSettings subfolder for that one. 10. Modify the "ConservationIdleTime" file to be all zeros: (00 00 00 00) and click OK. 11. Audio issue should be fixed now, but restarting the laptop is a good idea. 12. I then went online and downloaded the latest AMD drivers. Just google "amd ryzen 5 4500u drivers" and it should be the first results. Click Drivers and Support at the top of the page and download the software. 13. Restart the laptop after installing the AMD updated software. Hope this helps someone. In light of this, I am ordering a replacement unit to see if I can get one without dead pixels and coil whine. Leaving rating at 3 stars since no one should have to go through all this with a brand new machine. UPDATE 2: Happy to say the replacement unit has no dead pixels and much reduced coil whine. Will be keeping it. The audio popping issue was still present, so it does appear to be a driver issue. Did the same fix as the first unit and seems fine now. Hopefully future drivers will fix it for good.

review_text: It fits the MacBook Pro M1 Max but is not 100% flash—there is about a 1mm extrusion. This doesn't bother me as I won't snag on the edge. However, you can feel the edge of the adaptor if you run your fingers along the edge of the laptop. The build quality is good—plastic for the most part with an aluminum finish on the outside. Removal of the SD card is easy using your nails, and the same can be said for the adaptor itself... although it is a little tighter. This is a USHII-rated adaptor so the advertised max speed is 312MB/s. The card reader in my M1 Max is rated the same. I have yet to use a card that meets the max-rated speed. The read/write speeds are way below advertised speeds. I use this with a SanDisk Ultra 400GB microSD XC 1 card. This class 10 card is supposed to run at 120MB/S max, but never does. In its provided SD adaptor—37MB/s Write, 81 MB/s Read. In the BaseQI adaptor—35 MB/s Write, 89 MB/s Read. The BaseQI is slightly slower but negligible. I won't really know if the BaseQI lives up to its speed classification until I find a microSD card that meets the same rating. Essentially, this is a functional solution to adding and keeping a microSD card in your MBP, especially if you move your laptop around much. It keeps the card safe and it won't catch or snag as you move about. However, if you need high speeds for your microSD card, keep looking elsewhere. Jet Drive is an option but the price is much higher, and you don't have the option to change SD cards as needed. I use this for storage of my music files and it works okay. I will keep using this until another option becomes available (other than Jet Drive). I don't regret this purchase as this is my only option and it works, but consider your need for speed before buying.
