review_text: What Worked Well: 1. Application of the protector is very easy with handholding stickers on both ends. You can really get it lined-up perfectly if you’re patient. It also resulted in the most bubble-free installation I’ve ever had on any screen protector *ever*. Zero bubbles, zero dust, and completely on-point. 2. The fitment is very good. There’s a very small and uniform gap between the bezel and the edge of the protector, and the notch for the front camera was cut very tightly. 3. It cleans-up nicely. One swipe with a microfiber cloth, and you’re pretty much good to go. 4. It feels pretty robust. Sure, it’s not going to take a sledge-hammer, but I feel like if I dropped my keys accidentally over the screen, we’d be in good shape. Things to Take a Look At: 1. It’s a matte anti-glare screen protector, but it only reduces glare and diffuses it throughout the whole panel. So, instead of seeing the reflection of the lightbulb, you get a white haze spread across the entire screen. It’s more of a “light diffusing screen protector” than “anti-glare.” However, it does this REALLY WELL. The overhead lamp above my desk is visible like I’m looking at it in a mirror without the protector, and with the protector, the whole screen just glows white from the light without a specific point of illumination. 2. Unfortunately, the light diffusing also diffuses the light from the panel itself, so your text is a LOT less clear than without it. This is the bane of anti-glare layers, but it seems particularly harsh here. NOTE: I’m using this on a 2021 iPad Mini (Gen 6), and that has a very small screen with very small fonts. Because the fonts are so small on this layout, the effect of the light diffusion is probably worse than if it were a larger screen. As such, the iPad Mini screen *really* takes a hit in display quality with the protector on. 3. The Apple Pencil feel is not much different than that of the original glass. The pattern of the glass isn’t aggressive enough. Sure, you don’t want it to sand down the tip of your Apple Pencil, but you do want it to feel like it has SOME drag at least. It’s there, but it’s almost imperceptible, and it’s definitely not at the level you’d call “paper like” or “paper feel.” The only real difference I can note is that the CLUNK-CLUNK sound of the Pencil on the glass as you write is dampened/deadened well with the protector, but it doesn’t really change the feel much, and that, to me, *is this product’s critical disappointment.* If I have to suffer with the tremendous loss of screen quality, I should be more than making-up for it in enhanced Pencil feel. In short, if you want an anti-glare screen protector for your iPad Mini, this is a fine and reasonably priced choice if you aren’t getting it specifically for enhanced Apple Pencil feel. If you are, I might keep looking.

I always wondered if this item would truly do it's job. Some of the reviews have not been favorable and some are. Now I have real world experience with this Surge Protector. My signal comes in via coaxial to the modem which is connected to old Asus router I was using as my wi-fi access point. This Asus Router was connected, via an Ethernet cable, to an expensive Cisco Commercial Router. I parked the APC Surge Protector at the end of that Ethernet Cable and then plugged the other end of the APC into my commercial router's WAN. It sat there for quite a while and I had no idea if it was actually going to work. Sometime in the last week the coaxial cable coming into my home experienced some type of surge (probably lightning) that ran up the line to the modem, then through the Ethernet Cable connected to the Asus Router, through the outgoing Ethernet cable connected to the APC Surge Protector. That surge evidenced itself as follows: Burnt connections in the outside coaxial cable as well as my inside coaxial cable running to the alcove where my equipment is installed. It then proceeded to fry the modem (owned by the ISP, so no harm no foul) thru the Ethernet Cable (which was also burnt out) connected to the Asus Router. It fried the Asus Router then and ran down the Ethernet cable with the APC Surge Protector at the end which was connected to the Commercial Router. Bottom line is the lightning strike took out everything (including Ethernet Cables) all the way up to the APC Surge Protector. It protected that router as well as my expensive CAT 6 cabling throughout the residence. In other words, the APC Surge Protector DID IT'S JOB.

review_text: This is my fourth Ticwatch and I'm happy to say, they keep finding ways to improve it. Coming from the Ticwatch 4G from 2019, this one is still quite an upgrade. Here's why: -battery life - Not only is there a bigger battery included, there's also a new processor that is more battery efficient. I'm easily able to get 2 days battery life with my normal use. But wait, there's more. If you use the mode where you have to touch the screen to wake the AMOLED, you get even more battery life(up to 4 days in my case). What this means is when you lift your watch to see the time, the screen stays on the low power LCD with a glowing backlight so you can see it at night. If you get a notification buzz and lift your wrist within a few seconds, it activates the AMOLED like normal. To me, this is much more practical as I rarely use my smartwatch apps and only lift my wrist to see the notification or tell the time. -Weight and size - I've tolerated the size of the Ticwatch Pro for the past two years. It's always been a little thick though, and my previous watch was the Samsung Galaxy Frontier S3, which in my eyes was the perfect size to fit under my long sleeve cuff. This Ticwatch is significantly thinner though and fits just as good as my old Samsung did. What's crazy is it still looks the same as the previous design too. The weight is also noticeably less, which is also a good thing. On paper it's 11g lighter, but some of the weight difference is in the wristband too. -Android wear - I've always struggled with Android wear because it just plain runs like crap. But with this new processor, it's SO MUCH BETTER. Far less lag than before, so I'm a lot less frustrated when trying to get my music going while GPS is tracking a run. Screen - The always on screen has more on it this time and looks slightly more professional. Slightly... The rearrangement of the date and making the battery life more subtle were nice touches. Here's what I didn't like and why I docked a star: - the charger - If you've owned previous Ticwatches, you've probably had the magnetic dock, which has pins that interface on the back of your watch. This time, the dock is replaced with a small magnetic dongle. The problem is, it's too freaking small and is susceptible to being knocked out of place. I find myself spending a good 30 seconds just making sure it's connected properly, only to find that the connection fails the second I place it on the table. I've also tried connecting it with the watch face down, which seems to work better, but is problematic in order to see if the watch is actually charging(impossible while face down). What ultimately worked was 3D Printing a dock of my own. It's on Thingiverse if anyone else has this problem. I've had trouble with the docks in the past watches, but this is a step backwards for the Ticwatch. They really need to step it up with this on the next version and maybe consider wireless charging. -The LCD screen - Minor complaint but the LCD screen is oh so slightly darker than the previous versions. The result is slightly worse contrast which makes it a little more difficult to read in a darker room. The backlight makes up for it, especially in completely dark rooms where it was always impossible to read the time, so there's at least that. In the day time, you won't know the difference though. -the wristband - It looks great, but the wristband just feels cheap to me. It's probably because it weights almost nothing. I think it'll last a while but only time will tell. Very minor complaint though, because it still looks better than the last one. I miss the leather/rubber combo look though(I think that was two versions ago). Complaints aside, this is still the best Ticwatch. In the future, I hope they improve the charger. I would also like to see a 4G version launch alongside the non-4G version so I can make a choice without wondering if the other version is coming(customer service refuses to tell me if there's a 4G version of this hardware specs coming). If they leave everything else alone, I'll be perfectly happy to keep upgrading in the future.

review_text: [[VIDEOID:3ddc6a970850e298eea427d3061b9ff]] For reference: I have been using capture cards for recording Video Games and recently for streaming ever since the Dazzle HD back in 2009, and I have upgraded twice since then. My most recent capture card was the Razer Ripsaw but that is being sent in under warranty, and I may be looking for a new one if necessary. I then stumbled on a random comment of someone using a cheap capture card and that it worked out for them, which led to me wanting to see if capture cards were finally cheap enough for anyone to try making. The Device Itself: The box is small cardboard, only containing the device, a manual, and protective cardboard packaging. It’s a small dongle device a tad larger than a USB stick with an HDMI port out the other end. Reasons to Buy This: Quality: Good, better than expected. The video it exports is is decoded in MJPEG, gives you more compressed video than YUY2 or other formats that current capture cards use, but in return taking up less bandwidth over USB. It will require some CPU power to have the preview running. I also think about 6GB of ram was being used just having OBS open, using almost half of mine. MJPEG is usable, but looks a bit compressed when looking through the preview window. It is very usable though and I played all of Paper Mario Origami King through the preview window, only sometimes having trouble with attack timings. I have attached several screenshots of the OBS settings menu and what options you are able to select. YUY2 is available in format setting but resulted in footage stuttering on my end, so it seems only MJPEG is officially supported. The device only supports recording up to 1080p 30fps recording or 720p 60fps. There is also 4K passthrough at 30FPS without HDR (there is no passthrough to TV function, by this sentence I mean you can plug in your 4K ps4 and be able to view the preview and record at 1080 30 or less). Don’t buy this if: You want dual-channel audio. First of all, it was hard to figure out how to get audio to work at all. I have attached a screenshot but basically the capture card shows up as a microphone device in your computer’s sound settings. Then you have to set your capture card to use a custom audio device and select that new sound device. The audio plays in mono. I was also having an issue with **I also had an issue with audio monitoring would slowly Desync. Using OBS’ audio monitoring setting I would hear the gameplay, but over time it would slowly go out of sync with video. Though, streaming and recording audio would be perfectly fine! Only I was out of sync! I was able to get around this by going into Windows Sound settings and the capture card’s audio device and selecting “listen to this device”. The only problem would be whenever the console is turned on, I would still hear it through the PC but at least it never went out of sync this way. TLDR: This is the better price point capture card with just downgraded features: namely MJPEG video, 1080p30/720p60 limit, Mono Audio, and no passthrough cable. And currently, there is a lack of capture cards on the market due to COVID (unless you plan on paying that price-hike for a used one). This price point is very tempting for people wanting to get into video recording/streaming at a cheaper pricepoint.

The primary reason for the low rating of this inexpensive reconditioned PC is that four times it randomly rebooted. On the plus side, the company who did the reconditioning reached out to me via email with an offer of assistance (via a form letter that I believe to be sincere), and then a second email offering a replacement PC shipped express. I am a retired IT manager, and based on my experience, the problems are such that the device could not be repaired in the field and needed to be returned. Please be aware that perhaps Amazon itself has to share in the responsibility for dissatisfaction with this particular unit, in that the description may be inaccurate or perhaps designed to cover a wide range of potentially available reconditioned items. I have a good deal of sympathy with the reconditioning company on this particular unit. Below this paragraph I have listed the specific problems with the PC. The last issue (random reboots) is a fundamental, non-fixable in the field problem with this PC. I strongly suspect that the rebooting problem is why the PC came to be reconditioned in the first place, and again I strongly suspect that the reconditioning company did not experience the problem while in their hands, and after doing software updates, testing and packaging, sent it to me. Intermittent problems such as this are troubling for all involved, and I have some sympathy for the reconditioning company in this respect, as well as for the description issues mentioned above. Problems with New Desktop PC The day that the PC was received • The picture on Amazon shows a vertically oriented PC (it stands up); what was shipped was a horizontally oriented PC (it sits flat). This is not a real problem, just what was received was not what was pictured. • The product description on Amazon describes the drive system as a 120G SSD + 1T, and yet in another place the web site describes the drive system as a 2T hard drive. This PC was selected for purchase in part because of the SSD described in the product description. It does not have an SSD drive. This is not a major problem but is an incorrect product description which is disconcerting (and time consuming when trying to find the SSD using software). The next day during which the setup was mostly completed • There was one instance where a blue screen with a big Error Message suddenly appeared on the monitor, and the PC had to be manually rebooted. This should have been a major red flag. The next day when switching over to a new monitor and beginning to use the PC • The picture on Amazon as well as the product description shows that the PC has an HDMI port. This PC was selected for purchase in part because it was described as having an HDMI port, both in the product description and in the picture on the web site. The PC received did not have an HDMI port, which required the emergency purchase of an adapter and a cable. Now even those expenditures were wasted (see below). • Worst of all, four times while actively using the PC the monitor went totally black. All four times when the PC came “back to life” the display on the monitor displayed the opening screen (the one where you input your PIN). This indicates that the PC was (randomly) rebooting, and the lack of reliability is totally unacceptable.

I deducted one star because there isn't a subtitle button on the remote, you have to go into the menu to turn it on and off, hugely inconvenient for that quick change. I deducted another star for not having a display button I find useful. On the Sony bluray the display button shows a few things, it shows the video bit rate. That shows me the quality of what I'm watching. I find that important for videos I've made and edited. It shows the bit rate of the audio. Those few things are game changers for me.. Another disappointment is the digital audio output, it only has toslink. Optical cables are far too delicate and the slightest kink and they're toast. Digital coaxial is the only way to go. The cable is far more versatile and vastly more durable and far less money achieving the same or better quality. Knowing what I know now I would have picked a Sony and said forget matching brands. I did like it fits under the TV so I don't have to put it elsewhere.

review_text: It took me about 3 hours to install the printer on the network. Once installed it is fantastic and a very flexible printer and scanner, particularly for the price. There are no Mac installation directions - you're on your own. You cannot download any of the Mac software from Pantum because your Mac will identify it as malware and not install it. So, you'll need your own scanner software - my prior printer/scanners software worked great. In the absence of Mac instructions the wifi button on the printers dashboard screen is a red herring - it has nothing to do with your network setup - it's only relevant to mobile setup. The key breakthrough after hour 2 was connecting the printer via the enclosed cable to my Mac then once connected to the printer by cable navigating to the printer page. From there you can get to a screen where you get a page (looks like something from the 1990s) that allows you to identify your network and enter a password. The next step, again there are no included instructions, is to reset the printer not to print 2 sides of the same page for documents. This is an apple design. Since the printer has the latest design for Macs it is set to work with the standard Mac two sided default setting. You'll need to search youtube or the Internet - you have to navigate into Terminal and enter a series of commands to reset the printer across your network. It's not terribly difficult and nostalgic as you are essentially back in a late 1980s DOS environment. If Pantum would include some simple directions for Mac Users I imagine this would have been a 20 minute install exercise. The printer also has its own network, which makes printer from your mobile devices very simple as well. It's a simple setup process that is described on a sticker on the printer. This is when you use the network button on the dashboard screen. Unfortunately, it created confusion for me because in the absence of any Mac instructions, I thought that was the actual network setup. Just ignore it when connecting to your network. It's a separate process for mobile only and you still have the two sided printer process to reset. I'd give the printer a 5 star if there had been some simple instructions for Mac. There is extensive documentation for Windows users. Great value, great printing and scanning, and if you like puzzles a great install process. For me, a paragraph of instructions would beat the puzzle experience.

This is a review for the LG 34WQ73A-B, which appears to be a recent release (9/2022, review written 12/2022). I wasn't sure how this would hold up to my current monitors: an LG UltraFine 5K 27", an LG 4k 27" and an Alienware 34" with the same resolution (gaming, 144hz). I went with the 34WQ73A-B because it has an IPS panel and my other LG IPS 4K and 5K screens have very good color accuracy and my MacBook renders text to both very well. I didn't need a high refresh for gaming, just 60Hz for office work as a software developer working in design systems. I have this placed next to my 5K UltraFine, which makes it easy to discern where it is a step down (pixel density). That said, it holds up well and is very comparable to my Alienware 34" at the same resolution. Font smoothing isn't as ideal as the 5K, but it looks good enough to not bother me at all. I use it for Zoom meetings, browser windows, and also code editing. I still prefer the 5K for previewing output (web development work on the front-end) but I'll use this just as well when the details/colors don't matter too much. I picked this up at a good price and I see it dipping even further as I write this, but no regress for what I paid. I could have returned it and gotten a lower price on a second order, but why bother. I'm happy for what I paid. The retail price is a fair value so anything less than that (and it goes for much less) is absolutely a steal. I had also considered stepping up to a 38" monitor for 2-2.5x as much but I couldn't justify the price difference. It would have been the same pixel density, and only going to a 5K2K monitor at 38-40" would have been a real improvement, but those cost around 4-5x as much. Like I said, next to a 5K 27" monitor, it holds up and I'm not disappointed one bit, it does what it sets out to do very well. I also compared its HDR performance next to my 5K and it held up really well (see the first photo with both displays). I had to turn the brightness to 100%, and made sure the HDR options were enabled. It was slightly less bright than my 5K, so I intentionally lowered the brightness on my 5K to match it better; the 5K was at 100% initially which was probably too bright for everyday use in the first place. The 5K at around 50% brightness matches the 34WQ73A-B at 100% brightness, so I feel like the 34WQ73A-B is a relatively dim monitor best suited to medium to low light settings. I don't work in a bright room, I keep my lights low and warm, so this is not an issue. In a bright space with lots of sunlight, it could be more of an issue, so keep that in mind. It probably wouldn't matter with good contrast, but darker images might not show up as well. If I could call out any other cons, it would probably be the backlight bleed. One photo shows approximately what you would see in a dark room (I turned off the lights) and the photo with a brighter backlight bleed is from the camera auto-exposing to a higher degree. It does not look like the brighter photo but it's still a good photo to show what the backlight variance is like. In everyday use, it's not a problem. I think it would handle a movie just fine even with dark scenes, it would just fall short of what an OLED TV panel could do. Again, if you research what a panel like this can do, I think this is going to deliver on what it should be capable of. At the current price point, it's one of the best values I've ever had in all my monitor purchasing. Each of my four monitors all fill a slightly different expectation and I'm pretty happy with my two setups for gaming (27" 4K + 34" 3440x1440 144Hz) and office (27" 5K + this LG 34" 3440x1440 60Hz). I think this is ideal as a value-oriented office monitor and you'd have to spend 5x as much to really have a noticeable upgrade in the ultrawide format.

Background: I'm looking for a replacement for Bluedio Victory headphones which I've had for years, but have experienced some issues with. I also have Soundcore Liberty Pro 3, Spirit X2's, and on my PC a FiiO K3 DAC with FiiO FH5 and Sennheiser HD599s. My biggest complaints with headphones that I've had is either build quality and comfort (headbands not having padding, clamping force is too strong). The Q45's have neither of those problems. Yes, they have a lot of plastic, but they don't feel cheap. Yes, the headband padding is maybe less than others, but it still feels cushy enough. The clamping force is strong and firm, like on ATH's M50X, but that makes them uncomfortable over long periods for me. I find the Sennhesier HD599's to be hands down more comfortable, but the Q45 is still solidly "good." The ANC on the Q45 is also pretty good, I'd put in on par with the Liberty 3 Pros I have. They seal against your head pretty well and that also contributes to the isolation. Unfortunately, the sound quality I can only describe as mediocre. I'd put them on par with my Soundcore Spirit X2's, they just sound flat and not in a good way. Bass is poor, which I found surprising. I'm not a fan of too much bass, but for me even the Q45s are very weak in this area. For some reason, snare drums sound very sharp and a bit unpleasant to my ears. I'd say this is accurate to real life and the sound is very clear, but it's also not an issue I've had with any other headphones. Additonally, the sound stage sounds distant. Plugging them in by cable to a FiiO K3 DAC does little to resolve the sound issues. To be fair, the sound quality is not horrible, it's just very average. I can tolerate that on my Soundcore Spirit X2's because I mostly use them outside walking, listening to podcasts. When I put on headphones I am usually planning on listening to music, and want a very full sound. The Q45's don't deliver that, and I'll probably stick with my Bluedio Victory's until something better comes along. A couple other pros I want to point out on the Q45: uses a standard 3.5mm cable on both ends, which is great in case the battery dies and you ever lose your cable. Controls are easy to find and use. They're pretty lightweight. The band is covered well and prevents hairs from getting snagged easily. If it wasn't for the "meh" sound quality, these would be absolutely outstanding headphones.

For a buck fifty ($150.00), you get what you pay for. I film a weekly open mic night at a local restaurant. The venue is outdoors on a covered stage in good weather and indoors in the dining room during inclement weather. This camera makes the transition well. At first I filmed indoors and it automatically went into night vision mode and I didn't like the result of that evening's taping. I tried to utilize the remote control features via the app and it was completely useless. The app is very basic and offers little control and the lag time is horrendous. So that feature was useless to me. The next issue I had was that it chops up the files in 13 minute (12:59) increments. So that created more editing time for me on the onset due to having to combine files in my editor. I learned to hit (double tap, actually) the Stop/Record button at the end of each set as most performers do not run past 10 minutes or so. It performed well in low light at first, inside was great and when we had afternoon sunlight while outdoors, the video quality was good. However when the evening light faded and we went to using the stage lighting (which is minimal but equal to the inside lighting) the picture would get dark and grainy and just didn't look good at all. After using this camera every week for a year now, it had developed dark lines that scroll down the display when filming and are present in the finished video file making the video completely useless to post on YouTube. This past two weeks the camera has developed a sound in the audio that sounds like a metronome accompanied by a lot of hazy static. I now have two nights of completely useless video that looks and sounds horrible. Fortunately I also file a separate angle with another better quality camera for close up and fade shots that I can at least edit and use. I have learned to always have two cameras filming at all times. I am grateful for this camera, it has taught me that cheap cameras deliver cheap audio and video. Cameras need to be properly stored and transported and handles with care when filming. Although I have not had a major bump, drop or crash incident with this camera, I did keep it in a hard case in my truck with all the other equipment and it gets hot in Texas, which may have caused the problems I'm experiencing. I have also been able to learn some techniques and it helped me decide whether to continue to pursue this hobby or not without having to shell out a lot of money. The second camera I purchased is a Q2n Handy Video Recorder 4K. It was a bit more costly, but it's much better quality both audio and video. Today I broke down and bought a used reconditioned Cannon Vixia HF G40 for $500.00. I'm anxious to see how well that performes.

I really, really wanted this dash cam to work. It had good reviews online, over 2,700 Amazon reviews when I bought it, with a 4.5 star rating. I also have several stalkers actively harassing me, and so far their minimally invasive measures have been enough to keep the police from arresting them. I've bought dash cams in the past, but they only showed the straight ahead vantage point, and I was lucky if I could get a single license tag number off of the footage, much less a face to prove anything. This dash cam seemed to be exactly what I've wanted for the past 20 years, but then the first one I ordered had issues, then the replacement had issues. The first unit's rear view camera didn't work, and neither did parking mode unless the camera was physically moved to wake it up. And yes, that's with motion detection on, which means it's supposed to record when it sees motion. I called Amazon support to see how to get the rear camera to work, but there wasn't anything else I could try -- it's just the one cable. And so Amazon ordered a replacement which came quickly. Meanwhile I'd asked a question of the Amazon community about how to get the rear camera to work, and someone said that the one cable sort of snaps into place. Well, I tried that and was actually able to get the rear camera to work, although the original unit's cables didn't snap together and you had to moosh them together pretty hard to get it working, which didn't seem right. The new unit did work with the rear camera, and the cable did snap in. There were little plastic notches in both cable ends to sort of guide you as to the orientation, and you had to be sure that they fit together to fit it in right. But then... after I set the resolution to the highest setting, the new unit stopped recording. I had footage of me putting the new dash cam in the window and changing its settings, but nothing after that when I got home. This was disappointing, as there was something happening along the road that night that the police would have appreciated seeing. And so I wondered whether it was because I hadn't connected the rear camera yet, or if the thing just doesn't record on the higher resolutions. And so I went about testing the camera after the rear camera was hooked up at different resolutions. I was able to get some footage, but the kicker is, the camera apparently lost my time setting, and so the 1st and 2nd round of tests are hard to figure out and I have to redo them. I can't say yet whether this 2nd dash cam is going back to Amazon or not. However, the parking mode does work better on the newer unit, though probably not well enough to prove it if a stalker is driving past my house 10 times a day. And I noticed something about the night vision in the new unit -- it seems to work via infrared, because you could see a part of my bra's outline in one of the interior videos I reviewed. I was wearing a dark blue shirt at the time with a printed image on it that made it impossible to see my bra under regular light. However with this dash cam's night vision, you could see the straps and upper part of the bra well enough to know it was there. That's if you turn on the cabin footage, which unfortunately I need to do because sometimes one of my stalkers breaks into the van and spends a lot of time there. Though he'd probably take the chip out and erase it, knowing his past history. (That's an issue mentioned by another reviewer -- the footage stays on a chip in the dash cam until you remove/replace it, it isn't uploaded to the cloud, though it generates so much footage that an upload wouldn't be practical. That means if someone smashes your windows to steal something, if they notice the dash cam and steal that, too, then you've lost your footage of the break-in.) I also ended up buying the VanTrue brand chips because it had a high capacity and is fast enough to handle video. Overall, I'd say that the quality of the electronics is iffy, but if you can get the features to work, it's great. I'm looking forward to hooking up my laptop to the big screen TV to see how many license tags I can read that way. I also saw a man who looked like one of my stalkers while the thing was running, and I want to find that footage to see if I can prove he was there. This thing just might help me get a restraining order and scare those guys off! If it can do that, it'll be worth all the money and trouble to get it to work, and then some.

In 2020, Garmin made a change to this strap that is either intentionally environmentally unfriendly, an impractical choice made by a product person or engineer who has never had to replace a battery, or just lazy... I shall explain. Since the early aughts, I've owned many, many HRM straps. I've had straps from Polar (okay), Wahoo (they always break at the snaps), CooSpo (they sell these on here, the last one I had ate batteries unless you took them out), and a few from Garmin. I actually had the last generation of this strap (pre- September 2020, per their site). As far as HRM straps go, I came back to the Garmin strap because it is the most comfortable and does seem to last the longest. I usually get a few battery changes out of each HRM strap, but some cocktail of sweat (I have higher sweat salinity levels, per testing... medical condition thing) and dust always makes them go kaput after 18-24 months. I don't like that aspect, but I try to wring as much life out of them as I can. I've never had an issue pairing this strap and have used it with an Edge 530, Zwift (both via Bluetooth and ANT+), and a Fenix 5x. I know some people have issues with pairing, etc. Never had one. And I find the chest straps to be more reliable than the wrist based sensors in Apple and Garmin watches (sweat seems to cause issues with the LED sensors). So, yes, this is probably the best strap I have used. However, the decision in September 2020 to move from the #00 Philips screws to Torx T5 is some mid-70s Detroit automotive nonsense. Torx can be fine in many applications. On paper, the splines should provide more grip. But anyone who has worked in a bike shop or with small parts using Torx screws knows that they are very, stupidly, easy to strip. In the T5 size they strip almost instantly. It is very hard to get the splines to line up and for the head of the wrench to stay in the screw. The first time I replaced the battery on the post-September 2020 HRM-Dual strap, the screws stripped almost instantly. I was careful, but the tiny bit of Loctite or whatever threadlocker I suspect the screws were dipped in made the splines strip almost immediately. The combination of soft steel of the screw (they are made from steel, you can check that with a magnet) and the hardened steel of a wrench, leads to "chewy chewy, metal dust" fun. I had to press the the head of the wrench into the screw, while driving the sensor against my palm, just to get enough bite (I was probably cutting new splines) to get the screws to drive back in. The second time, it was much, much worse. I had to do the same move to loosen the screws. It was slow and awkward. Then when I finally released them, one fell to the floor. I swept over the concrete floor with a retrieving magnet and just never found it again. Le sigh. I resorted to jamming the other screws in, then wrapping the whole sensor in electrical tape. Here's the fun part: I had to do this to the last one when one of the screws similarly went walkabout. The electrical tape will hold, but for most people, this would be binned and they would buy a new strap. This is just the stupidest idea. It ruins an otherwise fantastic product. So, dear reader, when this strap dies, I am going to ship all of my dead Garmin products (I have others, but some of their stuff is amazing) back to Garmin's Olathe, Kansas headquarters. They can figure out how to dispose of the garbage they have produced. In summary: negative stars. Do not buy. Shame on Garmin. Boo!

review_text: I was excited about the Feitian K33 to begin with, it seemed like it had everything, nfc, ble, usb, FIDO2, and biometrics. Reality was a bit different. FIDO2 Passwordless is going to be awesome for consumers and corporations... once it is widely used. The problem is, no one supports it as MFA/Passwordless yet other than Microsoft via Azure AD or Windows Hello. I did not test against AAD because I don't have an Azure tenant to play with. I only found one solution that consistently works with Hello, this wasn't it. First, almost all existing implentations are 2FA (pin +key) only, not passwordless. I haven't found a password tool that allows anything other than Yubikey that also does auto fill. They problem I have with the Yubikey 5 is that it relies on presence rather than a specific piece of info. (Think thumbprint to open your phone vs just a double tap). No, fingerprints aren't perfect, but at least a bad actor has to put some work in on a fingerprint scanner. 2. You really don't need it with most smartphones. It's either built in or readily available with authenticator software and can be set up as the security token itself in some cases, in other cases, software running in a secure environment, handles all of the FIDO work. BLE too. 3. Poor battery life makes the ble functionality pointless. Needs separate cable to charge or use as usb device. 4. Sharp metal edges at external band interface not comfortable. 5. Feels flimsy. 6. Supports parts of Fido2 specifications, but doesn't have CTAP1 for backwards compatibility with U2F. No HOTP. No TOTP. 7. Not recognized as a Windows Hello compatible thumb print reader.

review_text: My rating falls close to a 1.5 for multiple reasons: For starters, this headphone is marketed and sold as an ANC (Active Noise Cancelling), Over-Ear headphone. Typically, headphones like these are targeting people who buy them for travel (i.e. a plane ride) but also are helpful in any public space. Please keep this in mind for the rest of my comment. From the inside out, these headphones cannot hold their own with any other pair in the price range. I purchased my pair when they were 57% off, bringing the total from $350 to $160 (including tax), but I cannot in good conscious recommend them for either price bracket. Comparing them to the most common headphone in the $350 bracket, the Sony XM4 (and newly the XM5) are a essentially the opposite side of the spectrum when it comes to all qualities. They clearly lose the battle for acceptable headphones to buy for $350, but some could make a case for the discounted price. Everything I found wrong with the Beats (most to least important): - Sound quality is mediocre. I attribute this to the old design (nearing 3 years) and old parts (Apples W1 chip is long outclassed by the newest chips) With that said, I am also no audiophile (someone who has a keen skill/desire for high quality sound) but I can make general observations about the sound quality from the Studio3's. I can't give an super detailed review of the sound quality because I only listened to ~3 songs and maybe 2 videos. But I can say is the trope that "Beats just overbass their headphones" isn't true. I can't say what you find as a proper balance of bass, but to me it seemed fined and not too far one way or the other. But you can tell that the timbre wasn't all that it could be. For the MSRP listed, this should not be case, even for an old design that was adopted and revamped by Apple. - ANC, one of the primary marketing points, is horrible. This is comes from a variety of reasons other than just poor build quality, after reading into the making of the Studio 3's, Beats tried making an early "adaptive" ANC by changing the way sound is measured, processed, and then cancelled. However, it fails completely and everything from your fingertips rubbing together at arms length, to a pencil dropping behind a closed door is essentially the same with/without ANC on. The only different is bass is slightly toned down, you don't feel like constantly pressure that other ANC headphones give (kinda like you're in an airplane at max altitude), but you hear a slight "woosh" constantly. - As mentioned before, build quality as a whole is terrible. Straight out the box, the right earcup is crumpled a towards the bottom because of a poorly designed folding mechanism that squishes the earcup against the headband as it's packed into the case. The earcups themselves have this cheap, fake leather look and feel, the stitching is far apart and looks poorly made, the earcup foam is obviously cheap, it easily compresses (therefore there's a lot of air) but then refills as if the foam itself isn't compact but just large pockets of air (meaning the foam itself is low quality), and the size of the earcups is very small for over-the-ear headphones. So if you happen to be ok with everything I mention, having medium-big ears will already make the experience impossible to begin with. The top headband, a common weakpoint that's overlooked in headphone design, has literally no cushioning. They didn't even use the foam from the earcups, it's rubber on the outside (when slightly damp or if it just came off someone's head) feels comparable to a pencil eraser. There is a little give to the headband but the material underneath is too thin for me to discern from just pushing down. After wearing the headphones, straight from the box, you could start "feeling" the headband begin pressing into your head after ~1 hour, then feel that annoying soreness after ~1.5 hours of total listening. Once again, considering travel or just extended use would be expected of a $350 headphone, there were too many bad choice they let slide. With the buttons provided on the headphone, there is one good but a few bad things. Firstly, Beats Studio3 happen to be one of the few headphones in this bracket that have a distinct power button. But the action button and touch pad are the main concern I found. A lot of online reviews will say the action button (the beats logo) feels cheap and totally disrupts the hearing experience, but I can't say I completely agree. I do like a tactile button, but the button provided has a distinct and somewhat loud click. It doesn't inherently sound cheap nor satisfying to me, but that's partly subjective. However, you can hear the click very clearly when you are wearing them so if that's something you dislike, and you'd prefer a touchpad then be aware of that. One of my most concerning observations for the build was the Micro USB charger in the headphones. A lot of online reviewers bash on the cable that's provided to charge the Studio3 pair, but I don't mind that they were able to pack some ginormous cable because I can plug in the USB A into a nearby port for close charging. However, the choice for Micro USB charging as a whole is a bad idea to me. Micro USB is getting very old now, being outshined by Lighting and USB C when it comes to things like charging speed, data transfer speed, etc. But my main concern is durability. Again, a $350 pair of headphones should essentially guarantee you multiple years of use. I didn't fully test the battery life of the pair, but over my years of use with Micro USB I know that the cable itself can corrode but most importantly if the input port (like the one that built into the headphones) doesn't have good glue to hold it to the plastic inside of the earcup, then the port can pop out can render the charging useless. In the first example of the cable breaking with time, I'm sure a lot of people have old Micro USB cables laying around, but if the input port falls out, then you will be forced to use the provided AUX cord for the headphones (can't listen to portless devices like modern iPhones). - All the other complaints were at least somewhat merited regarding an expensive headphone. But this one is mostly based on aesthetic. Of these entirely subjective points, the most relatable would be the bulky carrying case the headphones come in. It's very wide and rounded, so it definitely won't sit in a backpack or carry-on without taking up unnecessary space. But if the case was designed to be wider/longer but slimmer (like the Sony XM4's) it could slide into thinner pockets without stretching out the bag. Also, forcing the headphones into a smaller but thicker case is what causes that earcup compression problem I mentioned earlier. The scale of the headphones looks off. From product pictures to models wearing them, the headphones look really nice and stylish. I bought the matte black pair, and I was excited to see how they looked. But they pair overall seems smaller than what you expected (like how I briefly mentioned the small earcups). The overall look seems like it could only give that proper "Beats" look on certain people with specific head sizes/shapes. If you happen to find this pair on sale, don't really care too much about noise cancelling, want a listening experience that is good but you don't mind if it isn't groundbreaking, but want a pair of headphones for more of the luxury aspect, then it wouldn't seem like a bad deal to buy these.

review_text: This router... is fine. If your internet speed is 500 mbps or less, this router will work great. However, if you have gigabit internet or higher, stay away from this thing. In comparison, the Asus GT-AX11000 (older, but similar product) did around 650-700mbits. Moving downstairs (2-story house), made things much worse. This TP-Link pushed around 140mbits through the walls... while the Asus pushed ~315 mbits in comparison. The clean inner design is also wonderfully clean, but not built to allow easy upgrades. For instance, I wanted to install another 4TB SSD drive, but it was extremely difficult, since there's no access to the power unit, and the SATA slots on the motherboard are almost impossible to get at without taking the system apart. But all-in-all, I'm very happy with this rig! EDIT: In the meantime, I've had to revise my opinion and lower the rating to three stars. The reason is because the instant I (accidentally) hit a button on the remote that is included with the rig, the fan lights came to life. I tried everything to get them to either turn off or return to the default setting. Nothing has worked, and none of the RGB control software I downloaded was able to change a thing. Also, as described above, it's almost impossible to access any of the components in order to upgrade or maintain the system. You would need extremely tiny hands to get at the SATA ports or RGB headers. I originally wanted to tear out the HDD and replace it with an SSD, and then add a second or even third SSD, but I'm afraid that's almost impossible without taking the whole machine apart. If you're someone who never opens the case and leaves the system as is, you will probably be very happy with it. It's very silent and runs very smoothly. Update 3/22: I am updating my review by lowering the rating to 3 stars due to the disappointing performance in the past few weeks. The camera app initially has a feature called "smart push" where you can fine tune the motion detection notifications and define a "hot zone". These are great features and it worked well, until it was cut off after 30 days. You must sign up to the monthly fee of minimum $3/mo and that was what I did. However, after the smart push was restored the software no longer functioned as before. The delay in notification seemed longer and sometimes none at all. It used to detect my cat coming to the front door waiting to be let in but now it rarely detects it and when it did there is a event and video recorded but no auditable notification sent. I followed the instructions and sent several feedbacks on the failed events but so far no resolution. Most of the cameras on the market today require a server connection and a custom app in order to work. The delay in response and failed notifications could be caused by the server communication latency and bug in the app where one of the updates made it worse. I have returned 3 other cameras for the same reason and I thought this one was an exception but no more. Since I missed the return window I will probably cancel my smart push subscription and move the camera to a different location where I only need basic motion detection. -------------- I selected Dzees camera by accident. Few months ago I bought a camera of a different brand and it did not work very well. The motion detection was spotty at best and the phone app, vicohome, would crash often. I googled the issue and got a link to Dzees support and they actually helped diagnose the problem and suggested I try their app. I did and it worked flawlessly since. When I needed a 2nd camera, I went to my Amazon history and tried to get the same camera but it got redirected to a different camera so I bought it. It had a different app but worked well for couple of months then started to have the same spotty motion detection and software issues. I tried to use Dzees app but it won't connect to the new camera. I returned it and tried 2 more cameras, each with a proprietary app, but none worked the way my 1st camera did with the Dzees app. I then tried to search the Dzees name to see if they also makes cameras (I thought they were just software) and found and bought this one. It did not disappoint me. The support is excellent. The firmware in the camera gets updated regularly. The app is easy to use with no constant pressure to buy the cloud storage or flooded with ads. There is a short delay between the motion detect event and the actual notification. I think this is due to the fact that a remote server (the cloud) is used for all camera functions. Depending on the location of the server and how it is set up, the delay can be significant or none at all as in the case of the other failed cameras I returned. The camera has an internal battery and needs to be charged through a micro-USB connection so if the camera is close to a wall socket then a USB charger will work well. If not (as in my case) I had to run a line from my 12v garden lighting and add a converter to get it to 5v. The line is active only at night so during the day it is running on battery. It works well so far. Overall I am very happy with the purchase. My cat too as he can again come to the front door and be detected and be let in.

I purchased a Motion+ earlier this year, but that speaker had horrible distortion with high frequency sounds. You could hear the crackling most with high range piano music. I had to stop listening to music because the cellophane-cracklying sound was so distracting. Anker's advice was to tweak the speaker by adjusting the equalizer settings in their app. I read the privacy policy and did NOT want that app on my phone. No, Anker, you may not have that degree of access to my phone just for me to be able to use your speaker I've already paid for. Another big problem I had was the quality of mid notes. Playing orchestral pieces, the mids were almost non-existent. I kept thinking something was wrong with my digital music. I tried my phone and my tablet. Super-quiet, almost impossible to distinguish mids. Then I hooked up either device (phone, tablet) to my wired speakers. Full-bodied, rich, engrossing sound. So it was the Anker Soundcore Motion+, not my music. But I kept reading glowing reviews of the Motion+ and watching YT videos singing its praises, so I broke down and bought another unit to pair. I thought if I could simulate stereo, the sound quality would be much better. Problem 1: I'd be sitting at my desk playing music quietly when out of the blue the volume would crank up to max on its own. I wouldn't have touched my phone or the speakers. Nearly vomited up my heart from that scare. Problem 2: Bluetooth kept cutting in and out no matter the music source. The speakers wouldn't maintain a stable connection with each other even on the same desk with my phone RIGHT next to the master speaker (blue BT light). Nothing I tried--turning off ALL wifi in the house, turning off my phone's cellular, even reconfiguring my entire home to use ONLY ethernet for internet (no wifi or cellular signals at all) and turning off ALL other Bluetooths in the house--made the speakers' "stereo" connection stable. After listening to song after song skipping and stuttering badly every few seconds or minutes, I bit the bullet and returned the Motion+. As I had these problems with multiple Motion+ speakers, I won't be buying from Anker again. But what most disappoints me is all the rave reviews on this speaker. First, the sound quality is nothing to write home about. It's OK for a cheap BT speaker, but doesn't rival my 10-years-old Bose wired desktops--tiny 4-inch boxes that pump out far richer sound across the whole spectrum. No, I'm not a "Bose person." I just really like the sound of these old but faithful speakers. Mediocre sound quality isn't a price I'm willing to pay for glitchy "new" technology (BT) and wireless convenience. As I'm reading in other 1-star reviews that others have had the same BT problem with their Motion+ speakers (and a lot of other BT speakers), I'm going to stick with inconvenient-but-they-work wired speakers until BT technology is actually as good as current wired technology. I really wanted to like the Motion+. It's a bit heavy and big, but since I wasn't planning on moving them a lot, I appreciated their stable heft. And they're tasteful looking speakers (except for the fingerprint magnet rubber casing). But low sound quality and unreliable BT connectivity were deal killers for me.

Causing a range of actions from replying the high pitch into the ear louder, through to completely stopping all sound including playback for a second. Wind resistance is terrible, they can’t handle cancelling out the sound of wind at all, actively replaying wind noise into your ears.“Aware mode” suffers too, sometimes muffling speech of others initially so you miss the first words of a sentence, despite other sounds passing through fine at the same time. When speech does come through, it's really robotic/tinny in sound, not realistic at all.“Immersive mode”, one of the things Bose seems so proud of, on a couple of occasions left a strange effect when changing between modes. The closing and opening feels cheap too.I got these in the sale at £220. They certainly aren’t a £300 pair of headphones, they aren’t a £100 pair. I’d be frustrated but unsurprised at the £50 mark.I got these because I had two pairs of AirPod Pros go distorted in 3 years, the first pair replaced under warranty. But they never had any of these problems! My AirPod Pro's noise cancelling, pass through and connectivity were always on point, showing it can be done with small ear buds. Bose just seems to have failed to make a good product.Refund started, I’ll spend the money on some new AirPod Pro 2’s and just bite the eternal Care Plan cost to cover any distortion.(Update) AirPod Pro 2s are equal in sound quality to me as an average user, also about equal on comfort, but far superior in every other measure in this review.

Garmin produces pretty good GPS units, with one serious flaw: batteries, and power in general If you want to use non-rechargeables, don't mind always carrying a spare set, and aren't trying to record a track log, this may not bother you too much. Baterry life is decent, but if you use the GPS as much as I do, you will go through a lot of them. But if you want to use rechargeables and/or if you want to be able to record a complete track log (with no gaps where the GPS ran out of power and you didn't notice for an hour), you will will be very disappointed with Garmin. And this battery pack just pours salt in the wound. First, most (if not all) current Garmin GPS units automatically turn off when you unplug the power source. That means that if you want to be sure of a complete log of your hike/bike ride/etc., you need enough charge in the batteries to last the entire trip. If you try to plug in the GPS to a power source and the plug happens to get disconnected accidentally, there goes your recording. Same situation if the batteries didn't have a full charge to start and run out partway through. A decent option would be to be able to use rechargeables, plug in the unit to charge before a trip, and be confident it will last the whole time. However: a) you can only charge this official Garmin "battery pack" internally; all other rechargeables have to be removed and charged in a separate charger; and b) these are pretty lousy batteries; they don't have a great capacity to start, and they don't last long before losing much of their charge And the real salt in the wound is that Gamin completely gouges you for these poor-quality rechargeables. They are way more expensive than standard AA rechargeables and their performance is much worse. If I could at least use good-quality rechargeables and charge them internally, I'd be much happier. This seems like a very transparent ploy by Garmin to try to squeeze more money out of their customers, basically getting customers to pay extra for the privilege of dealing with Garmin's poor design choices in the GPS units themselves. And worse, it's not even a good battery. If it were a top-shelf rechargeable, I could justify it like the "Apple premium" -- you have to pay more for the official accessories, but at least you get something good for your money. It's a shame to ruin so much good engineering in a product with such stupid decisions in one key area.

review_text: The Panasonic RB-M700B, has 2 touted features XBS Bass(Enhanced Boomy Bass) and Active Noise Cancellation (ANC] The headphones are plush and very comfortable. They have an open air design unlike many headphones in the “Bass” arena. This headphone disappoints on many levels. The ANC feature is toggled on/off via a toggle on right ear phone with all other controls. The XBS feature has 4 levels. It’s advertised incorrectly on the specs. XBS can be set to Off/Low/Medium/High. The Bass is the kinda of thumping, sub that is becoming more popular. The closest models that I compare it to are the Sony wh-xb900n or Skullcandy Crusher ANC. So the really bad, most important fact is if you have XBS enabled, whatever bass this achieves is completely turned off in you enabled the ANC. It is the most ridiculous ANC feature for “Bass” headphone. The sound is much warmer than the other 2 heaphones mentioned. Most particularly the highs(treble)are not bright. That’s not my style. If you enjoy having a muffled, 2khz- 16khz and want some bass this might be the model for you. Personally I find this model to be very overpriced for such a disappointing ANC Bass headphone. If you like a warm sound, open air with reasonable added bass I’d recommend the lower RM-M500B. That model lacks the ANC feature and has a supposed longer playtime battery life. These are big bulky headphones that don’t collapse in any way, and don’t come with any type of case. Your money is much better spent on the feature rich Sony’s or if you want rattling bass go for the Skullcandy Crusher ANC. I listened to all the headphones with Premium Tidal, Deezer HIFI, and Spotify. I personally can’t choose between the Sony and the Crusher ANC so I have them both, for different listening experiences. I would strongly avoid this whole new line of headphones by Panasonic.

After dealing with an old network card for the last few years, I decided it was finally time to upgrade. I defaulted to familiar brand names like ASUS and TP-Link, but every card was averaging $50. Not wanting to drop 50 bucks on a card, I looked at this network card, which provided Bluetooth 5.2 and WiFi 6E at a much more approachable price, so I place and order and patiently wait. This card KILLS it. The Bluetooth range on this thing is way beyond my expectations, I can walk to every space in my apartment without interruption. Visually, it's not much, but not too many people care about that. Installation is easy if you know what you're doing. Please be sure to install the drivers BEFORE adding the card to your motherboard for the smoothest experience. I highly recommend disregarding the disc inside the box since most modern PCs don't have a disk drive. Instead you can install your drivers by downloading them from Intel's website (just google for AX210 drivers and it should be the first result). Don't forget to connect the 9-pin USB cable to the card into the motherboard to enable Bluetooth capability. After that, you're fully set to connect to your everyday WiFi and/or Bluetooth needs. Overall, this card works perfectly for a reasonable price. Save yourself money and buy this.

review_text: I bought this switch to make it easier to switch a keyboard, mouse, and camera between a PC and a MacBook. The external switch button was ideal because it allowed me to use nano-tape to mount the switch and button under the desk (with the button positioned right next to the desk controls). Being USB-C native was also a big help, since other (less expensive) switches have not worked properly with my MacBook. Unfortunately, this switch also has a major problem - it expects both computers to be powered on or it will not switch inputs. So if I turn off one computer and try to use the other the next morning without turning them BOTH on first, I am unable to switch the inputs. I also have a dedicated power cable (which is micro-usb for some reason) running to the switch and the light is clearly on... but the input-switching button itself does not actually work unless both computers are turned on. Unfortunately, I don't know of any better options out there. Unless you want to get a regular USB hub and manually swap USB cables to switch inputs, this switch is probably as good as it's going to get. It's just a shame that it's so poorly engineered that it requires both inputs to be live in order for the input-switching to work. It's like... IOGEAR: your switch had ONE JOB. And you failed at that. AND you charge 5x more than any other switch to boot. That's not acceptable.

review_text: Speaking as a cable technician for one of the larger companies out there, this runs cooler (less heat produced, more efficient with electricity) and more stable (doesn't drop off nearly as easily due to low dBmV or low MER signal issues) than the rental Ubee, Technicolor, and Arris models my company "includes for free with your package". And yes, the AQM also works with the Cisco CMTS we use are our hubs currently, at least in my city that I work in. I bought one myself in December, it's been running a server without interruptions. Of course any line damage or RF leakage issues will still need repairs, but I've seen it more than once with weak signal on the coax (sometimes even negative dBmV levels from the tap), but yet this modem stays locked on without issues. That's impressive, and only one or two rental model modems we offer (which are exclusive to business class, not residential customers) gets close to that feat. Any one-star reviews you see here are likely going to be significant leakage issues inside or outside the home, almost never the modem itself with a well-made model like this MB8600. If the manufacturer changes who is designing & making this (i.e.: no longer Motorola engineering), I will update this review. Until then, 5-stars and my non-official (can't speak on behalf of the company I work for of course) but personal experienced-based approval.

review_text: This is a great and affordable product, useful to anyone shooting film or videos or adverts or magazine spreads. It's basically a big round ring that permits you to face it with any one of five different reflective surfaces. In any camera lighting scenario, indoors or out, the reflective surface can be held by a crew hand, or mounted on a tripod, to bounce extra light upon your subject, right where you need it. review_text: The bottom plate is made of plastic. I had brand new Pi4, Canakit 3.5A power supply with PiSwitch, and a high capacity SD card from Microcenter. System was running fresh first-time installation of reptroPie 4.6 (image obtained from developer's official website). It melted just in minutes of use. And the bottom plate is really close to SD slot on Pi4, the plastic piece of case pushed and squeezed SD card while it was melting and expanding, which caused physical damage to SD card too. SD card was validated on PC before use. The issue only started after it ran on the Pi in this case. I first thought it was a defective SD and actually got a replacement with customer support. And the second card ran into exactly the same problem. It was physically damaged by the melted case, and it totally melted inside the adaptor when I tried to reformat and recover the SD. I also realized that the daughter board that came with case took control of USB-C port which also happens to be the power input for the board. By scroll this reviews, so many people reported defectives HDMI port or USB-C malfunction. Some had the same issue that SD cards being toasted after adapting their daughter board. Here is my suggestion about this case. Don't buy it, because its daughter board is controlling USB-C with power supply. Don't mess around the power supply, it can cause actual physical damage. It kind reminds me of Nyko switch dock. It seems like just a USB-C to HDMI adaptor with power on it. Then it toasted motherboards after Nintendo post the 5.0 firmware update... My point to the story is that, again, don't mess around with the power supply. A lot of things aren't as simple as it seem to be. Most negative reviews here are complaints for their daughter board. It is even being mentioned in a lot of 5 stars positive reviews. Don't trust this company to control your power supply when they cannot even figure out how to transmit video signals or data.

The numbers of issues faced with this defective product has been extremely frustrating and caution a prospective buyer of this DOCSIS 3.1 modem to reconsider. Do yourself a favor, choose another brand Modem or Gateway. For what it's worth, I manage an enterprise network engineering team of 14 network engineers. I possess 6 current Cisco certifications. I had a need to expand my home network by installing a new layer 2 switch into my basement where I didn't have network cabling. I did, however, have a nearby ceiling-mounted access point providing strong wireless connectivity. So I bought this to connect to the switch so it can connect to my home's network thereby allowing all devices to still be hardwired to the switch with no need for each device to connect via WiFi. It works OK for this purpose. No issues except I cannot get faster speeds than FastEthernet/100Mbps even though all layer 1 links have negotiated GigE port speeds. I use iperf on linux boxes for internal speed testing. It seems like this wireless bridge somehow uses its wired port as a FastEth interface. I can get faster speeds on my raspberry Pis using their internal wifi over this wireless bridge. But again, it works great other than the speed issue. But the far bigger concern to me is that I noticed this device sends traffic to Chinese IP addresses. My firewall was allowing the traffic at first. With this device only needing to be a layer 2 bridge on my network, it has no business talking to anything in China. I created a DHCP reservation based on its MAC address so it always receives the same IP and then I blocked all traffic from its IP address going to the internet. Prior to the block, the only traffic I observed going to the internet was NTP and ICMP traffic, but I still would be wary of this thing. If this was developed by an American company, it would be coded to use NTP from North American sources rather than Chinese sources. But it constantly tries to ping something in China as well as tries to NTP sync to something in China. This tells me it's not just manufactured in China, but the software devs work in China also. And as a network guy, I do not trust it with my data. I'll still use it because I know how to block it. But if you don't have the ability to block it on your network from reaching out to the internet, be aware. I'm going to put this device on a different internal zone on my firewall so I can observe its traffic and what it's trying to talk to internal in my network.

review_text: I bought this primarily to use for sound for my computer, but it's also hooked to my flat screen TV. It's connected by Bluetooth to the laptop. The only way to defeat this is to turn the volume on the amp to 0 whenever you turn it or the computer on. > The volume control dial has no pointer, so you can't tell where it's set. The indicators in the other dials are just notches...difficult to see. I think i can solve those problems with a bit of white-out. > The EQ function is of little use. Some of the settings seem to be of no use for any application. The 2 i use most are "Jaz" (boosts high and low frequencies) and what appears to say "nO .-" which i assume is the flat setting. Overall, it was a good deal IMO. Excellent sound, easy to hook up and it takes up very little space on the desktop. Update 11/7/20; The unit has begun randomly shutting down. I have a love/hate relationship with Wyze’s security cameras. I love the low cost of their cameras. It’s easy to install and setup. No subscription is required (but with limitations)! Live view, for the corded cameras, loads very quickly. I hate the significant notification delay when the camera detects motion. I’m talking about up to a minute delay (at times 2-3 minutes)!! So don’t expect to be able to speak with anyone through the camera because they’ll be gone by the time you get notified of their presence. I get a lot of false alerts. The camera detects “motion” from moving shadows and headlights at dusk. I live in the center of two busy streets so it’s difficult to aim the camera away from the passing cars on either side. At night, I’ll get notifications of every car that passes because of their headlights. During the day, adjusting the detection sensitivity reduces the amount of false alerts from cars. Error code 07 occurs a quote a few times which prevents video playback of an event. I also get missed motion detections. I had an amazon delivery today (March 26 at 10:18am) and 2 cameras failed to detect the driver. My last notification for the day was at 8am so it wasn’t caused by the “cool down” limit. The camera also has a short cord so you’ll need to purchase their extension kit if you don’t have an outlet within 5 ft of your installation spot. I also own 2 wireless outdoor cameras. One is installed on the side of the house without a nearby exterior outlet and the other camera is in front of the house on a tree that is roughly 15 ft from the house. Two weeks after installation, the battery percentage is at 80%. The live view loads a lot slower when compared to the wired cameras. It takes 15-20 seconds to load live view whereas the wired cameras load live view within 5 seconds.

I bought this to keep an eye on the backyard of a 2nd residence. This is quite a large yard and I read reviews saying it worked for pretty big areas so I was hopeful. It actually works best as a way to see what's happening at any given moment since you can see the live feed anytime you want. But as a detector, it was disappointing. I tried different motion sensitivity because for the first couple of days I would get notifications constantly and nothing was there, resulting in the same view every time I got an alert. Maybe the leaves of the tree moving, or the water or shadows on the ground were activating it, I don't know, but I never saw anything other than an empty yard. I turned the sensitivity down slightly and then got nothing, even when walking in front of the camera. I could watch the live feed from the camera with someone walking in the yard and I wouldn't get any alert. With the sensitivity up all the way up and in bright daylight it does work much better if there is something *actually* in the area, but it only alerts you at the start of the motion. So if someone is in the yard for 10 minutes, you will only see the first moments they are detected, nothing else, which seems odd. Night vision is disappointing. Maybe it needs to be in total darkness- I do have some landscape lights that perhaps messes it up. Either way,. when it did send motion notifications it was pointless because you can't see anything other than whatever lights may be nearby. Another issue-lost power for a moment and somehow that made it so the micro SD card wasn't formatted anymore. Reformatting it is a process; you have to remove the camera from wherever you have it, unscrew 2 screws on the camera to get to the micro SD, put it in an adaptor, reformat and then put everything back together again. A real hassle and not something that should happen just because power goes out. We had a couple of cool shots when birds flew right in front of it, but other than that it really wasn't worth it. Will be looking for another option.

As I have owned this unit for little more than a week, this is strictly a short-term evaluation of its out-of-the box performance. This MYPIN 4K media player is a very compact (only 3"x3"x0.5") unit which looks well-made and solid with a black anodized metal casing. I specifically bought this unit to remedy to the limitations of the media player functions of my Roku 3, specifically its inability to play files of certain video (such as .avi) or audio (such as Dolby or DTS) formats. On the positive side, I can certainly say that my primary goal was achieved. This unit has been able to detect and play flawlessly any kind of audio and video file (including subtitles) of whatever size (up to 6GB) I have been able to throw at it. This unit also has no problem detecting and reading the 5TB external hard drive disks on which I store my various programs. It is advertised to be able to read up to 8TB but I have not yet been able to verify that.. On the negative side, this unit does has several shortcomings. As far as I am concerned, the main shortcoming is that program navigation is very awkward and clunky. Moving from folder to folder and file to file is not smooth and often takes repeated pushes of the remote command keys. Also, within a given folder, if you navigate forward past the last file it will come back around to the first file but it will not let you go backwards from the first to the last file. Finally, while this unit can navigate downwards from menu to folders to files, it seems unable to do so upwards and, once you navigate out of a file it goes directly back to the root menu without giving you the opportunity to stop and explore the intermediate folders. Similarly, the setting of the video parameters (language track, subtitles, etc…) with the menu key is very awkward and requires each parameter to be set individually one at a time as each push of that key only allows the adjustment of a single parameter. Another shortcoming is that the power supply to that unit seems awfully touchy and it will not accept any AC convertor but the one provided with the unit, which could be a problem if you lose that one or need to replace it. Even once properly plugged in and operating, the unit seems very susceptible to either video program loss or even complete power shut-off if you try to move it or sometimes only touch it. I do not know if this problem is a default particular to my unit or not. Therefore, all in all, this unit does exactly what I wanted it to do but it is very temperamental and somewhat frustrating to operate. We'll see how long it will perform.

I was very excited to get the Shure headphone as I loved the sound quality of the SE846 and I would really want a headphone with nice sound quality & ANC. I got the Bose QC35-II before, I loved their ANC & phone call performance but the sound was not my preference, plus, the hinge got loosened after about 3 weeks of use, that's why I returned it (Thanks for Amazon's return policy). Then when Shure has this released, I just couldn't resist myself to get this right away. I have seen reviews before about the huge hard case it comes with, which I thought it'd be inconvenient to me to carry around later if I commute back to work every day when the normalcy is back. I still wanted to get my hands on it just because of the sound quality that I can expect from Shure. It didn't disappoint me on that, of course, the ANC or phone call performance are not as good as Sony WH-1000XM3 or Bose 700, I'd still have kept it if the multipoint bluetooth connection failed after nearly 3 weeks of daily use. Since the pandemic began, I have been working from home using my TV/computer/cell phone together, so having a headphone that can connect my TV/computer & cell phone together is a huge plus for me, this way I wouldn't miss a call from clients or zoom meeting with coworkers. After using it for about 3 weeks, it suddenly stopped doing so, even I had it connected to both devices, the headphone wouldn't play back/pick up where it stopped yet both devices showed paired to my headphone. I was unable to control it to end my call or play my music/TV sound, I have tried to reset it or back to factory setting, none of them worked. I also tried to contact customer service to get this resolved and nothing changed. I assumed I was bad luck & had a defective set, now I'm not sure if I should try my luck again to get another pair or give it a try on the B&W PX7 or wait for Sony XM4 (and hoping they would provide a complete multipoint connection). All in all, the sound is great, ANC & call audio can be better to compete with other competitors like Sony/Bose, and if EQ adjustment from the app can be applied to audio played from other apps (like Tidal) instead for music played from its app only, I would give this a 4 stars if I had a good set.

Within that period you can imagine the stress i was going through. Fortunately, without more explanation customer support replied 3 days later saying that the issue had been fixed and i needed to restart the app. Sure enough, I restarted the app (hard down swipe) and the crypto were back on my account. I was able to fix the problem myself by installing the app on a spare tablet i have. I synched the tablet to the app and it started generating the barcodes again. I deleted the Safepal app on my iPhone and reinstalled. So now the Safepal app is working on both my iPhone and tablet. I followed up with Safepal for an explanation as to why these glitches happened and to let them know that it causes unnecessary stress and monetary losses. I never heard back from them. At this time I can honestly say that I cannot trust Safepal app/wallet due to these unpredictable glitches and piss poor customer service. It can happen at any time and of you’re not lucky as I was, your crypto may be gone. I actually ended up writing this review as I was on amazon looking for a new crypto wallet. In all fairness, since I’m subscribed to different crypto groups, in my despair I asked around to other people whether they’ve had these issues. They seem to be uncommon. But bear in mind that all the glitches I went through can potentially lock you out of your crypto permanently. As I have researched more wallets and read reviews, it seems that crypto wallets are susceptible to glitches. What is unacceptable, it’s the inability for the user to call a phone number and talk to customer support. I understand that the price tag on the Safepal is very attractive but Personally, I can’t wait to put my S1 in the trash.
