I used two of these cards to install two used e-bay Toshiba 800 GB U.2 NVMe drives into a Dell R720xd server. The adapters themselves are great, no problems fitting either the drives or into the PCI slots. After all, they are just simple cards with nothing but a U.2 socket, some holes for screws to anchor the drive (the screws that come with the cards are too short, thankfully I have a lot of hardware from old dead computers laying about), and a single very small surface-mount device (probably a resistor), and traces to connect the socket to the card edges. On first startup I was a bit disappointed when my new to me NVMe drives didn't show up in bios or the Dell hardware inventory manager program that runs at cold boot. I thought I wasted my money because after all Dell says in their documentation this particular server does not support NVMe on the PCIe buss. But I kept playing with them and finally figured it out. The drives have their own BIOS/Management software that loads as the very last thing after all of the firmware BIOS, iDRAC, RAID card, etc setup programs run and just before the OS boots. I just configure boot mode to UEFI and both drives came right up. Ubuntu on install recognized them and I set them up as software Raid 1 and it is running lightning fast. The gui is ready for sign-on in about 30 seconds when the OS finally starts booting, which is quick indeed compared to the 2 or 3 minutes it used to take booting from the RAID array. A bit of an overkill for a home-lab VM host machine but it is my toy, it was fun, and anytime I add hardware and it works (especially when Dell says it won't) is a reward in itself. So all told about $160 on ebay for the two NVMe 800 GB drives and about $60 for these two cards and I've got a nice hot-rod server!

With all that being said; a lot of other reviews for trackers say that it’s not accurate or updated real time either. I do feel safer that he has the AirTag on. I would recommend as maybe an extra security BUT NOT TO BE RELIED ON COMPLETELY for pets! Spoiler Alert: Long Review follows. Here's a summary: - Pros: Good picture quality, battery function, app features, complete kit with accessories - Cons: Poor wifi, poor SD card space management I bought as an impulse purchase with a $29 discount with Brad’s Deals code. Came as a very nicely equipped kit, including mounts and a Silicone skin cover. I already have a Wyze Cam Pan so most of my experience with this Reolink will be in comparison to that, not just in terms of the camera features and capabilities, but also the apps and setup procedures. Make sure before setting up the camera & app that you're in a good spot for your 2.4 Ghz wifi AND that your phone is also connected to the same 2.4 Ghz network. Will not set up if your 2.4 and 5 Ghz networks have the same SSID. I found I had to turn off the 5 Ghz frequency on my router temporarily to force the phone to connect via 2.4 Ghz. The app has a lot of features and configuration settings, much more than the Wyze app. But sometimes it's not clear what they do. Install the app on your phone, scan the QR code on the back of the camera, and it takes you through the rest of the steps. Somewhat easy setup that only requires setting a password for the device itself. It will ask you to set up an account but unlike Wyze, you do not need to set up an account if you don’t want to (and I don't). You won’t have cloud capability without an account; I don't care. One particularly nice but potentially useless feature in the app is the Display --> Quality settings. For each diusplay mode (Clear and Fluent), you can set the desired resolution, frame rate, and maximum bitrate (bps). But why wouldn't I want all of these set to their highest potential? You can also set up Push Notifications, email alerts, and also option it to sound an alarm when motion is detected. I haven't set up any of these but I dabbled with the email alerts - again it doesn't rely on the cloud service, but you do have to put in your own email account's ID and password. Not sure how I feel about that. Slightly wide field of view. I took it outside to try different locations. It’s sensitive to Wi-Fi signal strength especially if you want an HD image. (That is one of the reasons I bought it, isn't it?) I decided I didn't want to commit to any drilling and mounting, so I let it sit for a while. Eventually I just stood it on a shelf in my laundry room so I could spy on my cats' litter box. For this, it actually works well, but I could do the same with a USB-powered Wyze Cam for $20. The camera has motion-detection (unlike the Wyze which also has sound detection). It does have PIR (Passive Infrared) motion-sensing, which I'm just learning about and could be useful in dark conditions. (I don't know if turning on PIR will turn off motion detection by the imaging sensor.) You can adjust the sensitivity of the motion sensing so it doesn't trigger more often than desired. But it doesn't give much guidance about what setting to use under what conditions, it seems to be largely trial-and-error. But as currently set it will detect my cats coming in, and even when they (or I) walk past the door. In lieu of cloud recording, I inserted a cheap 32GB micro-SD card, which works fine. However even with only event recording (it does not have continuous recording), the SD card fills up fairly quickly. I don;t know if it has a "rolling overwrite" feature where it overwrites the earliest recordings when space runs out. You can have the option of recording audio, which would obviously use even more space but why wouldn't you want this? However you can set the (minimum) duration of recording post-detection to either 8, 15, or 30 seconds. This can help save space, especially if you have it pointed at an area which has high traffic. (Wyze only has 12 second recording duration, or continuous recording.) If the camera continues to detect motion beyond the minimum set, it will continue to record for as long as motion is detected. HOWEVER, you cannot delete individual events, or select events to be deleted. So, for example, it recorded me spending several minutes of vacuuming, but because I cannot deleted this event, it stays on the SD card taking up space until I either format the SD card entirely, or the camera at some point in the future deletes this recording (but not before deleting other recordings prior to it). Wyze, on the other hand, will let you go in and delete individual events that you do not wish to keep. Event playback works OK; for the given day it will show events on a "bar graph" which you can scroll through and then select to view. You can take a photo snapshot during playback, record a snippet from an event, or save the event recording altogether to keep for later. It also lets you view at 0.25x, 0.5x, and 1x speeds. I wish it had an option to view at speeds greater than 1X. The included battery has its own micro-USB port for charging, either by the solar panel or the included USB wall charger. However the camera will not operate without the battery. It slides onto the back of the camera and clicks into place, much like the battery pack on a cordless drill. It can be removed for charging, or can be charged while in-place. The battery already had 58% charge out of the box, but they recommend to charge from a USB outlet before mounting. It comes with its own USB wall charger and cord, but I found I was also able to charge it with a regular 1A USB charger I had laying around (I think it was a $1 charger). I found a USB charger that delivers only 0.4A, so the next time the battery discharges, I will try that one to see how quickly it recharges (if at all). The battery life is largely driven by the motion detection, recording, and also playback through the app. The app does calculate and graph the amount of time used for these functions so you can see daily power consumption, and make adjustments to these settings if the battery runs down too quickly. I do like the rechargeable battery; I could see that it's a nice option to have in case the power goes out. The solar charging panel has a nice design, with a long cable and its own detachable mounting bracket. I thought at first it was useless but as of late I notice that it has been maintaining the battery at 98% or better. (Again, this can be affected by the motion detection, event recording, and of course the amount of sunlight available.) It has a nice long cord with a micro-USB end that plugs into the back of the battery itself, and a small sleeve to cover the connection and protect from the elements. I have the panel in my window facing west so it usually gets several hours of direct sunlight, but over time the battery will still discharge faster than the solar panel can charge it. Frankly, I think the better option is to get just the Argus Pro without the added cost (between $40 - $60) of the solar panel. One could either remove and recharge the battery every so often (maybe weekly), perhaps spending that money on a 2nd battery to swap out. Or, if one must have an outdoor solar charger to charge the included battery, there are plenty of others on Amazon to choose from that have been vetted and reviewed. (I don't know but I think it would have to provide at least 2.0 Ah / 2000mAh of charge, which I think may be asking a lot.) Or better yet, buy a cheaper camera (again, such as a Wyze for about $20) without a n included battery, then research and buy a solar-charged power bank that has its own built-in battery to power the unit. Again, I could only see needing to use a solar charger if one were putting this (or any other camera) in a tree or somewhere else outdoors away from electricity. Otherwise, I think I'd just drill a hole, run the USB cord, and plug in a wall charger from inside. My biggest gripe with this camera is the poor wifi connection. My Wyze Cam Pan is connected to the same 2.4 Ghz wifi signal, is farther from my router, and rarely if ever has issues connecting when viewing the live stream or recording playback through its app. Most, if not all, of my other devices in the house connect solidly and have fast throughput. This Argus Pro, on the other hand, is almost directly beneath the router in my home, but I still get a "Connection failed" error message approximately half of the time. I don't even know how this could be effective outdoors where wifi range is even more limited. When it fails to connect, the status and configuration features are also inaccessible. Even when it does connect, it is a poor enough connection that the app will sometimes prompt you to switch from "Clear" (1080p) to "Fluent" (640x480) display mode. (Again, why did I buy a 1080p camera if it wants me to switch to 640x480?) These two complaints, the ineffective yet expensive solar charger and the poor wifi connection, are the main reasons I knocked this kit down to 3 stars.

What arrived 3 days later was a part of the firestick package, the gizmo that goes in the HDMI port on the TV in an envelope. I had prepared the defective firestick in a sealed package, awaiting pickup by UPS. Before UPS arrived, the partial Firestick showed up. It looks to me like it was taken from a refurb bin and sent to me, as if that was a suitable replacement. I chatted, called, emailed: they will not send a replacement complete Firestick in the package, like it was when I bought it. It looks like I have to make do with whatever they send me. Computer was delivered quickly and was well packaged. Everything initially seemed to be in order when I removed it from the box, although the internal packaging (inside the pc case itself) was not present, which raised the possibility that this unit had been previously unpacked and returned. Nevertheless, it looked ok so I carefully checked that all cables were well seated and that there were no obvious issues inside the case, then connected the peripherals (monitor, keyboard and mouse) and powered it up. The initial motherboard screen appeared normally, but was followed by a message to select the correct bootable device. I've built plenty of PCs and am reasonably familiar with how the process works. So I checked the BIOS settings. They were correct with the SSD selected as first boot device, but I changed settings (re-ordered boot order, etc.), tried booting (no go), and then returned everything to the original, correct, settings, and tried booting again. None of which made any difference. So I opened up the case - both sides of it - disconnected the SSD cables, reconnected them and ran through attempted boots after each disconnection/reconnection iteration. No love there either. At this point the problem was 99% certain to be a bad cable, bad SSD, or iBuyPower didn't install the OS. Next stop was a call to iBuyPower's tech support to be sure I hadn't missed anything. And this is when we go from a 3 star unfortunate purchase to a 1 star "screw these guys forever" situation. Tech support. What a nightmare, what a joke. It took me five calls with their broken menu system to ENTER A QUEUE as the first four calls disconnected at random times in the process (e.g. entering "2" for having bought the system from a retailer actually caused the call to disconnect - I did that twice). On the fifth call I finally managed to enter the general customer support queue. Waited it out for 30 minutes, got a human being on the phone, and he transferred me to the tech support wait line. After an hour of listening to the tech support auto-repeating hold message, without a countdown timer or any message about my position in the line, and the call disconnected. Called back again, re-entered the queue and this time I left my number for a callback. We'll see what happens, but I'm not hopeful. Bottom line, iBuyPower delivered a dud product and the process of fixing it is an absolute goat rope. They just don't seem to be a competent organization. So understand that when you buy a PC from this company you are rolling the dice. Maybe most of the computers they sell are put together correctly. But if you happen to get a bit unlucky (e.g. if Amazon sends you a previously returned unit without correcting the issue for which it was returned) then you are in for a miserable experience.

review_text: Jan 31, 2023. Don't do it!! First off this model is now 5+ years old! I bought this camera in 2017 (at this exact same price) for the occasional cruise vacation and casual snorkeling photos with the thought that if it got lost, broken, stolen, whatever, not a big deal. It was a spur of the moment purchase as I was about to leave on a trip and I just wanted something delivered fast and cheap but I did not do any homework. I got both, fast delivery, and cheap. Beyond that, total frustration. I hate writing bad reviews and feel many people write them more from "user error" or "lack of patience" to read the instructions and a lack of general knowledge of the product. This is not me. This item, I tried to like it, I tried really hard. I read all the ching-lish instructions and before you write me off as being a stupid boomer techno nube, I am 54 and work in technology now, was the high school yearbook photographer, worked a few years in a pro camera shop, studied cinematography in college, I have owned, seen, and used MANY different types of analog, digital, still, and motion/video cameras over my ENTIRE life -- used the whole range from cheapest "point and shoot" to the most expensive "wide formats" -- I know a little bit about cameras, not a pro, but not ignorant and have way above average knowledge. I've used this camera on several (4-5+) trips and it is always a pain in the neck to figure out how to use it, each and every time, because it is not intuitive at all. The times when I have figured out how to use it, it is capable of taking a decent enough picture (for a cheap camera), but it is always such a challenge and I am always wondering if I am getting what I think I am getting and often I don't. I just got home from a trip this time only to find out that I did not get a single photo of my reef snorkel in Roatan and then I accidently wiped it in the effort of looking for my photos. I had managed to get my old pics copied off before, but it still should not have been that easy to wipe. If you are getting older and need reading glasses the menus on this thing are impossible to read without them. Most of the time I am missing the action while messing with the camera. The buttons are not only NOT intuitive, but backwards from what you would expect. The power button is also the "mode" button so frequently I would end up power cycling and rebooting it when trying to get it into right photo mode. In addition, the longest it can go is 5 min before it shuts down, so I would try and snap random pictures just to keep it "awake". On every power up (intentional or not) it is a wait of 10-15 seconds for it to reboot and get the screen up to "ready" just to try and get it into the right mode as it always wakes up in video mode instead of "still" photo -- which is fine if you always do video, but bad for snapshots or any other mode. It won't "wake up" in the mode that was used last which is totally frustrating to always have to futz around with menus just to snap a picture. I'm done! I got some good underwater pics with it a few years ago when in a kayak in shallow clear water with the remote trigger. Back when I was nearsighted and could see the tiny icons, the menus/buttons were confusing --even when I could see them --- and after cataract surgery it is now totally hopeless to try to see and figure out what mode it's in or what it's doing -- especially in the water, cheaters are required. I write this as I am now shopping for a real camera as this is a stupid frustrating toy and I am usually patient and very forgiving of cheap stuff that works. This works, just really bad software and design. Size and waterproof fine -- just agony to use. Hope it was not too much of a rant. After 5 years, I'm done. (insert mic drop here!)

Worse of all, I hear my breathing & foot steps...it's very stressful. I need to look into that. But overall, I am thrilled with this purchase.

After 30 miles of weirdly consistent misdirection over familiar roads with easy routes, the humor faded and the annoyance rose. My wife & I shut it down and pulled the plug. Initially I'd supposed the bad directions derived from local map anomalies copied from Google, and my selected tolerance for including routes with dirt roads. But that explanation soon proved inadequate. Want some examples? 50 yards short of joining a rural highway which would bridge a river en route in 3 miles, Ms. Cargad demanded we turn onto a dirt lane running briefly parallel. When I declined she insistently demanded we turn back and obey the goofy turn imperative for the next 5(!) miles. Our destination was on the left side of the highway. After finally accepting our veto of the last commanded turn, she began directing us to turn right(!) on every dirt road for 8 miles till we arrived at our left turn driveway--at which time she told us our destination was still 1,000 ft. ahead. On the return trip we set an (easy) destination on second highway onto which we would turn left in 14 miles. As before, the projected route was initially mapped correctly and accepted. But after 9 miles, the Cargad lady began ordering right turns at every road intersection. That was when our patience ran out. I'd really had hopes for this GPS. My initial experience with TomTom had been great--until it was "upgraded" into senility by the removal of 43 US states to accomodate reduced information on the remaining five. My Garmin experience was only slightly better: a glitchy, obtuse machine with a poor touch screen, but it remains at least consistent because I refused to upgrade it. (The maps are a decade out of date.) So I had high hopes for this Chinese replacement with a cheap price and a surfeit of bells & whistles. After sending it back to its maker, I'll probably gamble again with the familiar bad domestic choices and hope for something better than the dubiously "refurbished" TomTom I returned several years back for behavior (mildly) similar to what I described above in the Cargad GPS.

I have many devices, but I needed a faster means to transfer data between a QNAP TS-451, a spare pc media server, and my main work computer. I do 3d rendering which is process and resource intensive, and because I have so many large files and projects, I sometimes work off of network shares and back up to them. The latest PC/media server had a built-in 2.5g port, and I picked up two 2.5 G USB adapters for my older work PC and my NAS. This switch bridges the connections between those. Now my file transfers are way faster between these tree systems and I experience far less lag when loading assets over the network. The one slowdown/bottleneck I experience is from an older 7,200 RPM SSD drive. I hit around 140-150 connecting to that. Otherwise, for real performance you will want NVME drives which will gain you 250+. Keep in mind, I believe 2.5 G is only really useful in either work situations or where large transfers of files are done on a regular basis. Very few people including myself have Internet speeds that are faster than 1 gigabit so it’s likely not going to make your internet or even most household devices any faster.

review_text: The sound quality is really good, the noise cancellation is excellent and the fit is superb. That said, the Android app, as other reviewers have mentioned, is diabolical. I can seldom get the earbuds to connect within the app, even though they are working fine connected to the phone the app is running on (Samsung Note 10+). Then there is the lack of multi-point connectivity which may be a deal-breaker. Perhaps I was spoiled by my previous Technics EAH-AZ60 earbuds... those would connect to my laptop and phone and automatically pause any media being played on the laptop when a call came in on my phone, which I could answer with a tap on either earbud. With the Bose QC II earbuds, you're forced to pause what's playing and disconnect the earbuds from the laptop, dig out the phone to answer the call and faff about trying to reconnect Bluetooth to use the earbuds on the call. That said, it can remember 7 devices and the earbuds speaking out the name of the connecting device is a cool touch - it's just a real shame it's such an awkward task which is nigh on impossible to do before the incoming call is forwarded to voicemail.For someone who is mainly interested in using the earbuds with a single device and wants great sound and possibly the best noise cancelling on the market (judging by reviews - I haven't tried a whole load of different manufacturers or models myself) then this may be for you. However, for someone who wants to use the earbuds on a laptop with YouTube, Teams, Zoom etc. as well as a phone or two, and have that experience be seamless, then these probably aren't the device for you. The app is also dreadful, although you can operate these largely OK without interacting much with it. I'm in two minds as to whether to return these and get a different make - possibly the Technics EAH-AZ80 which can do 3 device multi-point (although I wasn't super-impressed by the reliability of my AZ60s) or the Sony WF-1000XM5s which can do two device multi-point.

review_text: You see a lot of reviews here that say laptop breaks down after using it for 1~2 years, and thermal throttling is the extremely likely culprit for all those reviews. The left side of the screenshot was taken while running a 360p YouTube video. 6 watts of energy use by CPU and that was enough to push the CPU temps to 86 Celcius (or 186.8 Fahrenheit), as shown in pic #1. Clearly there is no way a computer can play Netflix or YouTube everyday and still work fine 3 years later taking an abuse like that for years. There is a Quality Control Pass sticker on one of the screws which I suspect voids warranty if removed, but I went ahead and opened up the internals anyway. I found that the only thing that transferred heat from CPU to copper heatsink was a flimsy cheap 0.5mm thermal pad, but nothing pushing heat to outside the laptop, as shown on picture #2. I replaced the CPU dye's thermal pad with Arctic MX-4 thermal grease and also put a generic cheap 6W/mk 1.5mm thermal pad between the copper heatsink and the laptop's metal casing. This resulted in the right side screenshot of my zero throttle, cool CPU temperature while running 1080p Youtube video. Obviously the laptop chassis is way hotter because it's being used as a gigantic heatsink, and by using thermal headroom for performance rather than longevity, the lithium battery's exposure to high temps might be a concern after a year or two. Once I took care of the thermal throttle issue, everything about this laptop has exceeded my expectations for the $320 price point. Screen color, touchpad&keyboard responsiveness, battery life, etc. are all great. I like how there is an option to either use USB C for charging, or a dedicated charging port for charging on a portable device like this, but at the moment, I only use USB C for cable management. Performance is also very responsive for everyday uses but only after the DIY thermal grease&pad. UPDATE: I decided to take off another star because I found a glitch where if the computer goes to sleep and wakes back up, the keyboard does not work at all unless it's shut down completely and restarted. Updating to Windows 11 (yes it's supported) fixed the keyboard glitch but unfortunately this makes the laptop less responsive than the Windows 10 Pro it originally came with.

Overall, this product is severely lacking. My goal for this product: Replace Windows Media Center, and use this box for over the air (antenna) recording of broadcast TV, with playback via Roku app. Recordings stored on an attached external USB HDD. Search Feature: The search feature does NOT work for OTA (broadcast) programs. This is not yet documented (support says they will document it now, however). Impact: if you want to type in say "Judge Judy" and ask the box to record all new episodes - you can't do it that way. You must find the program you want in the guide (what channel? what time?) and then schedule the program to be recorded. You can select only new airings. This is immature - a Tivo in 1999 could do this - it's 2020 now, and this product can't. Pause of live TV: you cannot pause a live program. Let's say you have nothing setup to record yet, and are watching some program and want to pause it -- you can't. You can only pause programs that have been already recorded. I'm not sure if you can pause / rewind / fast forward a program that is currently recording or not. Impact: This is immature - a Tivo in 1999 could do this - it's 2020 now, and this product can't. Handling of scheduling conflicts: I do not see any area where I can define which program is more important... Example, if I want three shows to record at the same time, which one will not be recorded? What will happen if it misses the scheduled airing, will a future one be recorded instead? Who knows. I'll eventually find out. Impact: you may expect your favorite show to be recorded, and then come to find out it was not recorded, and may never be recorded. This is immature - a Tivo in 1999 could do this - it's 2020 now, and this product can't. Picture quality: It's acceptable, but color accuracy seems worse than on Windows Media Center. Setup: The setup process is somewhat poor, and poorly documented. You're going to need a computer, a phone, a Roku (or similar product if you want to playback on a TV), storage (USB HDD). On your phone, you install the Sling App, and then are asked to login -- you cannot signup for a Sling account from your phone, you must leave the app and sign up using a browser. Why? Who knows. This is silly, but whatever. After you login to your Sling account, you can detect the AirTV and link that to your account. Scanning for over the air is quick. User Interface: Average / Poor. Recordings are not displayed in a very appealing way. Windows Media Center and Tivo were light-years ahead of this. Reception: I'm not quite sure yet -- I think it may not be as good as my old Silicon Dust tuner was. Overall: The Good: No reoccurring subscription required for DVR & guide. The Bad: No search. Poor setup. Poor interface. Immature product. Not up to the standard of WMC or Tivo. Conclusion: Too soon to tell - maybe I'll keep this cheap box, maybe I'll return it and try out a Tablo next. Update: 2/2/2020: When you have a program scheduled, it may not show in the scheduled section, but will show that it is recording in the grid, this is likely because you said new episodes only, but there is no way of knowing. Sound: Audio quality is poor. A guest said "What is wrong with your TV?". Lowering rating. Strongly considering a Fire TV Recast.

review_text: First off, I have done a few home based set ups of modems, routers and wireless devices. I'm not a professional but can follow directions, if given. This review is based off my needs, the most important one was a device that had an ethernet port where I could use a sim card from a jetpack. The same need that may have brought you to this device. I currently have 2 jetpacks, both with unlimited packages (plan is only $10 each). The ethernet port option is the only thing this unit is good for, here is what I experienced-- *The wifi signal is extremely weak. If this unit is in the same room, fine. Move it to the next room over. Not so great. My wireless devices would pick up my router across the yard in my garage or the one on the lower level of my house before this one. This causes hiccups for my wireless devices and everyone knows how annoying that is. I thought I could have 1 internet device upstairs and 1 downstairs. Nope. *Because of the 1st issue above I decided to try a wifi mesh system, this unit being the base. Thinking I could use this to feed all my wireless devices such as my Amazon Fire Sticks, Kindle and echo devices, etc. Noting that typically I only have 1 device running at a time. I just have devices in every room. That did not work either. The unit showed internet signal and connection but would intermittently keep cutting off connection to the base wifi mesh unit. I hooked up my wifi mesh unit to another router to test it and it worked seamlessly. Tells me again that this issue is with this product. Note that I did turn off wifi signal on this modem as recommended by the manufacturer when using a mesh system. Long story short, if you keep this unit in 1 room for wifi and can run an ethernet cable directly to your device then it's fine. Anything beyond that it is useless. Am I missing something in a set up? Possibly, but that would require advanced skills that most users wouldn't have. This unit has its perks but also has it's downside. Hopefully this helped explain them. You can take away with what your needs would be.

review_text: This dashcam is... I dunno, I had stopped looking into them a few years back, every one of them had some issue or other. This one, though, is SOLID in terms of what it delivers: a very solid forward and interior "cam team in the head unit, and a tail that leads to the rear-facing camera. All three deliver on fairly high quality crisp video - if I ever take my car to Russia I can probably make one of those Youtube or TikTok videos where something crazy happens captured by the ever-vigilant dashcam! In terms of the feature set, it delivered nicely on the night vision, and while I didn't have a 256GB microSD for testing, I was able to use a 32GB unit, which did come in handy - I can confirm the video looping feature also works well. Other untested features: I didn't try the shock test - getting into an accident to see if it records was kind of out of scope, just to tell you guys about it. ;) And I just haven't yet had an occasion where the parking feature kicked in, so I cannot comment on that. I was very leery of this camera at this price for three video capture units... But it truly lives up to the task. Of course, there IS the downside of just installing it in your car - depending on how your existing mirror/dash setup works, or how easily you can run cables through your own vehicle... Well, let's just say for testing purposes I let it "all hang out" to see it in action ASAP. And like I said, once installed, it's great at its job. The trick is, now I have to find a way to hide the cable to the rear cam (my car is pretty new, and I don't want to muck it up too much... And I wish I had more options for powering the whole thing - anything that full-time occupies my cigarette lighter is a bummer for me. I'm sure if I were more handy, I could somehow splice it in directly to the wiring harness fairly discreetly, and hide all the cables. But, if I were in a rental car on a trip, say, or I started driving for Lyft or something, this would be a great economical solution to covering my bum in both the event of an accident, or any issues that could happen in the interior. So, that's the deal: for me, this is definitely a keeper, because I am starting a new job with a fair amount of road miles ahead. But even for the occasional driver, if you were already thinking "dashcam", and you don't want to hunt around for the cheapies that fall apart, or just face front, are missing a rear cam or night vision, etc... THIS is a great choice, and I think it will be a great value. Of course, I'll update if that's not the case, but this is good vibes so far!

It's freaking annoying. - Didn't try the HDMI port, as my desktop has a dedicated GPU to drive my 4K. At this point, I had rated it 4 stars. - MacBook: - Plug this into my M2 MBA, and everything seems to work, as long as I don't use the 100W PD port. - Using the HDMI at 4K UHD / 2160p60. Don't care, it's a pain. If I use one of the cheap HooToo USB-C hubs prevalent on Amazon, those work with either controller unlike this Anker. For the Mac case, I think this owes to me replacing my Mac's charger with one of Anker's GaNPrime chargers and an Anker 100W PD cable. Not rewiring my desk to try Apple's charger, as I've already had issues with this hub. While I think this hub could be handy if I found myself on a long trip with just a MacBook, for my desk setup switching between a PC and a MB, it just doesn't cut it. I bought this camera to use indoors although this can be used outdoors as well. This is wireless so it makes it easy to just mount it anywhere and it also comes with a pivoting mount which is super convenient to get the perfect angle you want Packaging: The packing is big due to the size of both the camera and the hub. The packaging is also super tight and not easy to remove the contents. I had a hard time getting the stuff out of this Hub: I own the Blink, Wyze, and now this Amcrest wireless cameras, and both Amcrest and Blink need a Hub. However, the Blink is a wireless hub and only needs to be plugged into power and can connect to your WiFi. Amcrest on the other hand needs a wired ethernet connection and also needs to be plugged in so in my mind is not super convenient in order to place the device. Both Blink and Amcrest have USB ports on the hub however not sure what the Amcrest port does as it did not recognize my USB drive, however, I can use Blink for expanded storage Wyze does not need any kind of hub, so you can place the camera anywhere, although the Wyze Cam V2 needs to be plugged into a power outlet in order for it to work as it doesn't have its own battery Setup: Wyze cam v2 is the easiest to set up as you only need to plug it in, install the app and the camera can be setup Blink on the other hand requires to undo the plate, read a barcode and then install batteries to make it work. Amcrest is similar to where you need to first register the hub and then the camera. Installing the rechargeable battery in the camera is easy but the mechanism feels flimsy App: App for both Wyze and Blink are easy to operate and you can fine-tune the camera settings to your liking example settings up motion zones etc Amcrest you cannot do that and the app is not convenient to use. The app shows cloud storage and micro SD, however the camera does not have any micro sd slot so you would need to go for cloud storage which is paid option Storage: Both Wyze and Blink support on-camera storage. Wyze has a micro SD slot and Blink has built in storage which can be expanded by using the USB port on the hub. Amcrest - i did not find any such option and the usb port does not recognize my 32GB USB drive for extra storage Image Quality: The picture quality on all the cameras is great and all support Full HD 1080p resolution. The best picture quality and night vision goes to Wyze and then Amcrest. Blink night vision is average. Amcrest also allows you to choose Standard or Full HDas an option and you can record the clip or take a snapshot. Not sure where does the system store it but it is super annoying to find the clip. As the snapshot or recording is not stored in the camera itself, you need to go back to the main page in the App and then go to Account Settings-> My saved files in order to access the files You can setup maximum of 6 cameras with the Amcrest hub and Wyze does not have any such limit Build Quality: The Wyze Cam v2 and Blink are made out of plastic and feel cheap as compared to Amcrest which feels smooth and premium and well built overall. But that also adds to the bulk and Amcrest is heavy as compared to the others. Battery Life: Wyze is a powered camera so it is not required to charge or the batteries to be replaced but it is pain to run the power cord into an outlet. And you will need to find a long one. Blink takes Lithium batteries similar to AAs but Amcrest comes with a hefty rechargeable battery which is supposed to last 6 months but subject to usage. Its been 10 days since I fully charged the battery on the Amcrest camera however it is down to 77% already and I dont even have Motion detection on. I just use it indoor to monitor what the kids are doing. Overall: If you are looking for a security system that you can install and will give you max features and value for money - I would suggest Wyze or Blink. If you need indoor cameras, I would still recommend Wyze or Blink due to the convenience and price point. Amcrest for the features and quality is not worth the money in my opinion but from image quality and night vision perspective the camera delivers.

The speakers were easily combined and won't fall apart. There are also foam feet pads to protect the desk from scratching. Sound quality is a downgrade from my 10 year old speaker. This is one of the cheap options on amazon for a speaker and if you need a speaker and tight on money sure buy it. But for anyone trying to add LEDs to their set up or trying to get sound quality and base for their setup don't bother with Redragon. Conclusion: I am by no means a expert, I am a competitive gamer building a budget setup. I knew opening the box that I bought a cheap speaker and wasn't expecting top tier sound quality and was still disappointed. The cables are messy and NEED to be hidden. The LEDs aren't bright nor light up the whole area. There was no manual in the box. I do not recommend this product. Spend more money for a speaker that gives you what was advertised.

review_text: Just installed my Eero system - the app / set up is very easy. Saw an immediate improvement over my ATT fiber supplied router/modem. The speed tests I ran while standing stationary near the first device confirmed 50-100 Mbps increase over the ATT router. BUT my second Eero node is centrally located in a dead zone in my 1500 sqft home, but I cannot get my devices to connect to the second Eero node. The problem, I have quickly learned, is that my devices don't like to switch between nodes as I move throughout the house - they just stick with the original node until connection completely fails. Apparently this kind of "stickiness" is common among consumer grade mesh systems, and a notorious problem with iPhones. I finally managed to connect to the second Eero node a couple times and ran speed tests - when connected to the second Eero node, I saw a huge speed improvement, but again - it's almost impossible for my devices to switch to the second node because the first node's signal is strong enough to cling onto, but not fast enough to solve my dead-zone problems. Frustrating.. this is marketed as a simple solution to Wifi issues, the box even says "never think about Wifi again." I have already spent more time thinking about my Wifi than I've ever wanted to and I'm no closer to a solution. UPDATE 1: I discovered that my firmware was not up to date on the Eero nodes, after the update I’m having much more success switching nodes as I move throughout the house. It still takes a little long than I’d like, but it’s switching to the second node before my network speeds drop too significantly. Upgrading from 2>3 stars, I’ll give it a few weeks and update again.

review_text: I bought this in June to carry on a hike of the Foothills Trail. Got it setup and tested at home before leaving, including getting the satellite subscription. On day one of the hike, device worked perfectly, except it went through battery life faster than expected. The battery was drained from a full charge in one day. No worries, I brought a power bank for this purpose. Day two, started with a full charge. Device will not send and receive messages, not does it appear to be transmitting location information. Battery was dead by 8:00pm. Once again charged battery to full overnight. Day three, still won't send or receive anything, battery went dead by lunchtime. Recognizing that constantly recharging this brick is bleeding my power bank dry and now having to rely solely on my phone for navigation, I throw this junk into my backpack and don't touch it again for the rest of the seven day hike. If I'd needed to activate the SOS feature on this device, I'd be dead on a mountainside right now for all the good this device would have done me, because there certainly wasn't any cell service there. When I got home, I plugged it into a wall charger to see if it had stored the tracking data it had never sent, and discover it will not hold a charge nor will it power on at all. I've basically got a $350 paperweight with a pricey service contract attached. And Garmin really makes it tough to figure out how to modify your subscription. I'll never waste my money on anything with the Garmin name again, and I suggest you do the same.

This is the first hybrid IEM I've listened to, and I hope others do not provide this tone/timbre. Above all else, what matters to me most in music reproduction is natural sounding music, or at least my perception of natural. These do not sound natural. In fact, I would describe the sound as artificial or even sterile. There is no decay to the notes, so the sound is very crisp with almost a metallic color to the sound. I can see why some would like them, because at first listen it creates a perception of detail and resolution. I tried all the tips and filters, and the stock seemed the worst to me. The "reference" filters are the opposite of their namesake. I've invested a good amount of money in audio equipment over the years and the "reference" filters sound the least reference of anything I've ever purchased. I tried so hard to love these listening to every possible tip/filter combination I could think of and had at my disposal, because I love the clean look and they were very comfortable for me. I enjoyed the fact that I could move about without having to worry about them losing their seal. I returned them, because in the end it's the sound that matters most. I've listened to much cheaper headphones that sound better.

The Logitech (LG) has a gap between the function keys and device cradle that make LG quite a bit bigger than it should be. - (see image where I stacked JC on top of LG) Weight: - JC weighs less, and the difference is noticeable. - JC 24.8 oz. - LG 28.9 oz. - LG has a more balanced weight, while JC feels front heavy (on the spacebar side). Buttons (size and shape) - Both keyboards have buttons that are about the same size. The size is fine for both. - LG has a more traditional "sqround" shape (which is what I prefer). - JC has circular shape, which seems strictly worse than sqround, and I can't think of any advantage to having circle rather than sqround. Circle buttons feel like a typewriter if that's what you're looking for. Buttons (sound): - There is a true difference of sound here. LG keys are too loud. JC is noticeably more quiet. Even typing softly on the LG I couldn't make it quiet. - (see video comparison) Device cradle: - Similar enough that I can't tell any difference. No issues, except that depending on the size/case for your device, it may not fit in the cradle with the case on. Bluetooth - Both are easy to pair. - Both are easy to switch between channels. - LG has 3 channels while JC has just 2. Power: - LG uses 2 AAA batteries, which it came with. - JC uses an internal/rechargeable battery. - I'd prefer replaceable batteries like in the LG since it means I could potentially use the keyboard for the rest of my life if it doesn't break otherwise. Eventually, the internal battery of the JC will probably deteriorate and then the device will be a brick. Winner: - For me it's the Jelly Comb B046. It's smaller and weighs less. I like to walk around the park and dictate emails, notes, etc. into my phone recorder app. It has gotten very cold, so I thought it would be a good idea to get a Blue Tooth headset, connect it to my Android phone in my pocket and hands in gloves for my evening stroll.Based on Amazon Reviews, I bought the JLab Go Work Wireless headset.I tried it on my computer first, and after faffing about with settings (which is always the case with Blue Tooth) , the sound quality was very crisp, very clean . I tested the microphone via Audacity, and after fiddling with the settings, got excellent recording quality.So I put on my gloves and connected the headset to my Android phone (which I set in a pocket) and went for my walk. I dictated about 45 minutes worth of emails etc. before I went home. Down loaded the audio files only to find 45 minutes of faint rustling.I couldn't believe it. I tested the headset on the phone, discovered that the waveform was barely 5 db! I spent an afternoon searching the internet trying to figure out if it was problem with the headset or a problem with the phone. I finally found the Android built in EQuing and boosted it as high it would go. Absolutely nada.I even called JLAB tech support, all the nice agent could suggest was that I boost the volume toggle on the earphones, which, as I expected, boosted playback but did nothing for the microphone.A few more futile hours on the Internet, and I came across an obscure Reddit post that explained the problem.Google has deliberately crippled Android so that you can use an external mic, such Blue Tooth, or wired, at a reasonable volume ONLY on phone calls and Google apps. Microphone input to ALL other third-party apps (such as Zoom or WhatsApp voicemail) will be throttled down to 5 db or so (as people using these apps have discovered much to their dismay). Google claims this undisclosed passive-aggressive throttling is for "security" reasons.The JLab Go Work seems like a very nice headset, but through no fault of JLAB;s, is unfortunately not fit for MY purpose. 5 Stars for the Headset itself and sadly,1 Star, as for me it is now a very lovely paperweight.,So on the average I'm giving it 3 Stars.If anybody knows of any phones that will allow a Blue Tooth mic to record regular levels of a signal please let me know. I will be very grateful.

I had a strange issue with my Xfinity service where I use TIVO and cable card. On certain HD channels I would see pixelation and channel degradation to the point where it was un-watchable. I thought it was my TIVO Bolt or even the cable card which Xfinity provides but since the signal problem only affected specific channels I determined this had to be the incoming signal. So, as a last resort before calling Xfinity (ugh) I decided to try this amplifier and install where it comes into my house. I also bought new 6 foot coax cables and some 75ohm terminators to cap off any unused ports around the house as well as on this amplifier. If you don't cap the empty ports off they can act as an antenna and could result in more noise on the channels or even a visit from Comcast due to excessive broadcasts into the air. FCC requires Comcast and others to prevent this as it could interfere with other users systems. I figured for a few bucks I would just purchase a pack of 5 terminators and cap off the unused ports and avoid any issues plus do the job correctly. They simply screw on to the coax port....nothing complicated. I removed my existing splitter and installed this amplifier (which is also a splitter), a couple of terminators for unused ports and connected the incoming Comcast cable and the power adapter. This amplifier DOES REQUIRE an OUTLET nearby as it is powered to help deal with less than ideal incoming signals from Comcast (or whatever service you have). I've seen a lot of posts about this issue from many people using various services so this is NOT just a comcast issue. Keep in mind, this will boost the INCOMING SIGNAL to compensate for signal loss but it CANNOT FIX AN ALREADY BAD INCOMING SIGNAL. It will simply boost whatever is coming into your house. If the signal is low or poor for other reasons like bad cabling from their incoming box to your house then this likely won't do much other than boost a bad signal. For our issue, it was specific HD channels during evening hours when usage was likely higher on Comcast's systems and there was no indication the signal coming into our house was bad across the board. Only for a handful of channels. I don't know if Comcast can do anything about specific channel's signals or not but I didn't want to deal with them if I could avoid it as involving them is always a headache and they rarely make anything better and often create other problems in my experience. They always want to blame our cabling or router or whatever and I can do the same things their technicians would do in order to troubleshoot issues. In this case, I seem to have found the solution thanks to other postings so I wanted to detail my issue too. Ideally, it would be nice if customers could call Comcast and get them to fix it but in many posts I've seen their solution is to do exactly the same thing...install this amplifier, terminators, etc. to resolve the issues for customers. Clearly, they want to avoid having to run NEW OUTSIDE CABLING and digging up a yard and so on and I am sure most customers don't want that either unless the cabling is found to be truly bad, broken, cut, etc. Then it is worth it but for this random pixelation issue on only certain HD channels at certain times of the day this seems to resolve it. So far we have not seen any additional pixelation issues on the problem channels and our HD channels are as clear as ever. Again, buy this amplifier, a 5 or 10 pack of 75 ohms terminators to cap any unused ports in your house (i.e. where cable ports are in your rooms) as well as on the amplifier itself and make sure you have an outlet nearby to power the amplifier. The best location is where it comes into the house. Good luck!

I originally bought the MB882SP-1S-1B and used it to install a new SSD in my iMac. When I got everything wired back up and tested the drive, the machine wouldn't recognize it. Nothing. Nada. So we worked backwards and removed all the components one by one and tested those. The old drive was dead, the new drive was working fine and formatted for OS, thermal heat sensor good to go... that only left this converter/enclosure. We came to the conclusion that the clamshell design that is supposed to push the connections from the new hard drive into place when you close the box did not work well enough to really push it all the way in. We tried bending the metal at the back to get it to have more tension. Nothing. Still no hard drive found when we booted the machine. As a last resort, and hoping we were right about the enclosure being the issue, we ordered the MB882SP-1S-3B, since that enclosure allows you to manually push the hard drive on to the connections yourself. Tried it the moment it arrived - clicked the connections into place, closed the machine back up, turned it on and boom, there was the hard drive. I have to imagine that a LOT of people would give up after they saw that the hard drive wasn't being recognized. Or they would at least assume something was wrong with the drive or wiring. Nope. It's the stupid clamshell enclosure design. DO NOT BUY THE 1B MODEL. Buy the 3B or at least another brand or version that doesn't have such a terribly executed mechanism inside that doesn't allow you to connect the hard drive on your own.

You have to choose one of the two unless you use a voice assistant. However not being able to control volume isn’t a big deal to me. What is a problem is that I can’t pause and play unless that earbud is assigned that function. The capacitive touch buttons are ok. They are a little bit finicky especially if your hands are wet. Final thoughts : These right now go for about 200$. For that price these buds are not worth it. For android users there are plenty options that are better than this at this price. I use two of these in my home theater. For a 14'x20' sealed room with a cement floor it is probably overkill and I no longer have set to over 30-40%. The company actually recommended dual PB2000s for my size of a closed room. But the most expensive subwoofer is the one you have to upgrade, so I went with dual PB3000s. I would have even gone larger, but the small size (about 2' cube) and weight {about 75#) made them not too intrusive. They were purchased here on Amazon from secondary source with condition of "new, other". There was a discount because of "box damaged". Indeed both subs had a 6" hole in the outer box. On the other hand, the subs appeared to be completely sealed in original packaging with absolutely no evidence of prior use, not even a fingerprint. Very happy with the extra savings. There are numerous reviews stating that these PB3000 overperform for their woofer size (13"). The cabinet weight at 75# is manageable without a dolly or more people. At the same price point you can get a much larger and heavier (150#) Hsu 15' sub, or a Monolith 15" sub but your back will thank your and your ears wont detect a difference. Plus, the SVS subs have a better finish and have phone app control (that I rarely use now that set up how I like it). These overperform because of the split wound coil on the woofer, the latest in subwoofer design. I turned these up to near maximum volume once or twice when I first bought them and it is thunderous. My whole 3500 square foot house was thumping and rattling. Not really useable at those levels. But in my placement in a basement home theater they give fantastic impacts. My old sub was a 1990s Mirage dual 12" 400 watt continuous power. It gave me a headache, and I rarely used it. The modern more powerful subs are much LESS harsh and easier on your ears with no headache even at loud volumes. I hear the port makes it easier on your ears compared to a sealed sub. Also, subs from about 10 years ago or more are "boomy". They typically have a single frequency and volume that is either "on" or "off", kind of like intermittently firing a bazooka in that they sound the same each time and are somewhat annoying. Modern subs are much better able to show a range of frequencys and volumes that make them blend in much more. Even with my home theater adjusted to augment the base it is much less obvious than with my old subwoofers. They trigger for subtle bass throughout the movies but when the time comes they will blow your socks off and make you grin like you are 10 years old. The PB3000 is rated 800 watts or 1600 wats RMS. I have 2 of these, two 1000 watt amplifers for Buttkickers, and a 500 watt receiver all on the same 1500 watt circuit. I watch movies at louder than average at -18 volume with the bass +3-6 DB. I have never blown a fuse. I have had it so loud that was worried would break the windows at sound levels that cannot be endured for very long. I have read elsewhere that 2 pb5000s at 1500 watts continuous each have been put on the same circuit without a problem. Not sure how this is, perhaps because of much capacitor energy supply greatly lowers the average power requirement, but don't worry so much about the watts on the circuit. Your ears will bleed long before you blow a fuse. I took the feet off so they slide around on the carpet easily. My luxury house has mice, and I am worried because I know there is nothing preventing them from going into the subwoofer port and hanging out. The metal grill looks fantastic but is not remotely rodent proof as it leaves a 2" gap between the grill and the port. This has not been a problem. The phone app is nice to fiddle with when you are first setting it up. Receiver subwoofer setups are a complicated mess that can take you a week to fine tune. In short, make sure you buy 2 identical amps to get rid of dead spots, knowing that your subs wil be smaller. Secondly, add 30' to the speaker distance for the sub so the longer to develop shockwave will hit at the right time. Finally, do a "sub crawl", or place your speakers in the corners of the room (second best), or along a wall (at the least). SVS has made its name on subwoofers. If you are going to buy another brand, kindly make sure it is on "The List" of recommended subs at subwoofer101.com. At least 90% of subs just don't cut it and will have the dreaded boominess without LFE (low frequency effects). Remember, the most expensive sub is the one you have to upgrade later. This sub is great because of the fantastic output for its size and weight, as well as its premium finish and phone app control.

I bought these antennas for my Mofi 4500 Wifi router, installed in my travel trailer, when used for long-range Wifi as WAN. The trailer positioned about 50 feet from the router, and the signal goes through 4 walls. With the two original 5dBi onmi-directional whip antennas, I got a signal of 44% to 50%. The signal was so degraded, that the wifi signal was mostly useless, taking 30 seconds to show a google search result, and dropping and re-connecting regularly. Then, I installed these two 9dBi directional panel antennas, I got a signal of 91%, and a steady signal and web page results showing instantly. You can say, the difference is like night-and-day. Before buying I read-up on wifi antennas, the various types of antennas, how they work and how they perform. I learned that the dBi number refers to 'gain' and the more gain the better the signal, but it's not increasing the signal level as much as it is concentrating it in a particular direction. A small 3dBi antenna sends the signal out in all directions, up down, forward backward, left and right. It doesn't matter how you position it, as it radiates in all directions. A longer 7dBi or 12dBi whip antenna, when positioned vertically, narrows the beam to the horizontal plane, and doesn't send any signal up and down. Then a "panel" antenna is designed to send the signal in the direction the panel faces, with a fairly narrow conical pattern, about 30 to 60 degrees wide. This type of antenna is ideal for me, because I am trying to get wifi signal from a single AP in a particular direction. I simply aim both panels at the AP. This has the *added benefit* of rejecting interference. Interference is a bigger problem than most people know, as the 2.4GHz spectrum is becoming more and more crowded with Wifi, Bluetooth, cordless phones, microwave ovens, and garage door openers in cars and homes. That's why I found a LOT of variability in my wifi throughput. During the day, it had poor throughput, and was constantly dropping but in the evening it was fast and solid. In both cases, signal was the same 44%-50% and nothing changed or moved - so what caused this variation? Interference. When more people are using the 2.4GHz spectrum, throughput is very poor, but when other people stop using it, the throughput is suddenly better. When I scan for Wifi, I see about 20 access points in homes around me. That is potentially a lot of interference from other networks. But with a directional antenna, it concentrates power in the direction I want, and rejects everything else. Thus the directional antenna is the KEY to wifi performance. These antennas from Alfa Networks are good quality. Alfa is a decent Taiwanese company that makes quality radio equipment. I have no doubt that this antenna is properly designed and built, and works as specified. The outside of the box clearly shows the response pattern for this antenna, and I am sure it performs exactly as described. It certainly worked for me. Now as to those reviewers who said this antenna "doesn't work" I think they don't understand about how to properly make use of an antenna like this. Maybe they didn't know that a whip antenna is somewhat directional, and this panel is even more directional, and in either case, the antenna must be properly aimed. For this panel, the 'alfa' logo is the 'front' of the panel and must be aimed at the target, but if the logo faces away, then you get no signal. I wish this was clearly explained on the box, so that non-technical users can get good results. But the fact is, that most antenna products don't explain this, which is why so many people get such variable results. One other issue with this panel - it only rotates 180-degrees. So there are some directions it cannot face. But you can get around it by rotating the screw mount to get the other 180-degrees of movement. Weird, but it's workable. I noticed that most users buy this antenna for flying drones. It is excellent for that application! But you must aim the panel at your drone. While a whip antenna must be pointed perpendicular to the drone, the panel must aim the face of the panel towards the drone. Then, the whip will work well, but this panel will work even better. Now you can easily see why this antenna is probably not suitable for your home wifi router. To cover all areas of the house, you need an onmi-directional antenna, and the one that came in the box is probably the best choice. But if the AP and client are both fixed, (as in my situation) or the equipment is always aimed towards the target (as with a drone) then it makes sense to use a high-gain directional antenna, like this alfa panel. Good luck - with the mysterious world of antennas, you're going to need it.

We are an apple family and the speeds on the iOS devices is excellent at a range of 10 feet. we average over 400Mbps. Walk just slightly further from the router and that speed drops to less than 30Mbps. Why? because the devices switch from 5Ghz to 2.4Ghz band. We have multiple iPads and iPhones all exhibiting the same problem. That's when you realize how little control EERO gives you over the settings. No ability to turn on and off the 2.4Ghz band. No ability to reserve devices by Mac address onto a particular band. If you are going to remove all options from the user's control, then you better be better than EERO is currently exhibiting. And when you have to really get deep into EERO, you realize how much the user interface sucks. There is no browser based interface for EERO. I would stay away from this product. I feel ripped off and now have $500' dollars worth of equipment sitting in a drawer collecting dust.

The Sandisk 128GB dual drive comes formatted as FAT32 with an Android APK file and PDF manual in the root drive, explaining how to install app on phone. 118GB available space. I used the Microsoft Windows Media Creation tool to download and format this drive for Windows 11 setup. It created a 32GB partition and after 4GB install has 28GB free for swap files and driver additions.. however the rest of the drive was unallocated space. Run Disk Management and create a Simple Volume in NTFS to create an 84GB partition. Then backup your data so that it can be transferred to a formatted drive/system. My beef with this device is speed. I have a brand new system: Z690/i7-12700KF/32gb/3070Ti/usb 3+3.2 headers. I get a hard motherboard fail if I try to stick the USB-C end of this device in. BIOS hard stopped on reboot to tell me there was a USB OVERVOLTAGE error and would not reboot until I removed the drive. With the other 'blue' end plugged into a blue 3.0 port I am getting 30MB/sec at the start of a transfer and 10-15MB/sec for most of the long haul. It took me over an hour to copy 44GB of files to the fresh NTFS partition. I really expected much more performance, considering it's rated at 150MB/sec. By contrast my NVMe PCIe x4 SSD is 750MB/sec to copy videos from one folder to another. This USB device is the bottleneck.

This board is very nice. Linux (Ubuntu Jammy) installed just fine. I did not try Bluetooth or WiFi, but the audio, ethernet, video, and hardware monitoring (CPU and NVME drive temperatures, etc) all worked. The i5-13600K runs great on it, though it is recommended to tweak the CPU Lite Load values down a bit to get cooler temperatures without sacrificing performance. One major issue I had. The M-Flash BIOS update over USB just did not work. I tried EVERYTHING. 9 different USB sticks of varying size. Tried in all 8 ports (the 8 in the rear and the two in the front panel). FAT32 vs NTFS. Putting the BIOS file in the root directory. Putting the BIOS extracted folder in the root directory. The motherboard just refused to recognize it. Finally, I got it to work by putting another M.2 NVME drive into the motherboard, formatting it to FAT32, sticking the BIOS file in there, and running M-Flash. This finally worked as M-Flash found the drive with the BIOS file. So crazy that the only way I got it work was not even a documented method. I may keep a FAT32 partition on one of my drives to do BIOS updates in the future, since I doubt I will ever get the USB sticks to work. If it wasn’t for the BIOS issue, I would have given this 5 stars, but I had to knock a star down for wasting me hours.

Your device is WiFi only, therefore you will find no IMEI # and you will not be able to add WiFi hot spot thru a cellular provider. In conclusion, I recommend purchasing from another seller since this smarty pants treats their customers poorly when asking for clarity on a product.

Here we go. I'm setting the printer up, in exact accordance with the manual except where otherwise stated. I pull out the 'cassette' (input tray) as instructed, and the whole thing just comes out. There's nothing actually holding it in place. The cover at the front of the cassette also just falls off with the lightest touch. None of this actually seems to be held together, it just sort of sits together, at least until touched. This does not fill me with confidence. I load a piece of paper in for the print head alignment, as instructed. Immediately I'm hit with an error message: paper jam. Not a good sign. I pull the cassette all the way out (literally detaching it from the printer, since there's nothing connecting the two together) and can see the paper back there. The printer is tightly grasping it while admonishing me to remove it. We engage in tug of war for a few moments. I am victorious. I place the paper back in and push the cassette back in (I have to reach a little way into the machine to prevent the paper from slipping under the cassette as I do so). The printer resumes its print head alignment. What happens next is that it outputs the piece of paper with nothing printed on it. I just get my blank piece of paper back. The printer proceeds to make all manner of noises for the next five minutes, while the display states "printing - 1 minute remaining." Finally, printer realizes there's no paper. I'm too afraid to open the unit and see what has been happening for the last five minutes while I've been hearing what I assume to be printing noises. I load the paper into the cassette again. This time, it begins to output the blank page again, then takes it back, then outputs it and takes it back a second time... and then, finally, to its credit, I get the printed page, which I am prompted to scan. No problems with the scan. Next, the display ominously tells me that Canon "would appreciate your cooperation" in allowing the printer to send them data about how I am using the printer. I am given the option to refuse this. When I select this option, I am promptly informed that since I did not consent to having my data scraped, I will not be able to use web services (at least, until I change my views on privacy and allow the data scraping). Failing to see how the two things are related in any logistical sense, I can only presume this is punishment for my intransigence. From this point, the instructions go on to explain how to connect a smartphone or PC via Wifi, omitting mention of the USB Type B port in the back of the printer. Since I am banned from using web services, a USB connection seems to be my only option. No USB cable was provided with the printer, although curiously in 2021, a fax cable was. No problem however, as I came prepared with my very own USB cable. Let's see if my Windows 10 machine can recognize the printer without me needing to download Canon's own drivers, which will no doubt oblige or encourage me to also install some proprietary software I don't want and will never use. Immediate success! Okay, I'm very happy about this. Windows found the printer instantly - I didn't need to prompt it at all, and was able to print a test page on the first go. And it was fast. Colors are displayed correctly, everything appears to be aligned correctly. This was better than I had been anticipating, given the earlier paper jam and flimsiness of some of the parts. I'm going to wrap up my review here, but I will update if anything changes. I recommend getting the four year protection plan, not based on my experience with this machine but on home printers in general, because they rarely last that long.

review_text: I am so annoyed. This item has multiple issues and is a poor design. I brought 3 Ring stick up cams and solar panels. So got 3 gutter camera mounts (this product) and 3 gutter solar panel mounts (Aobelieve brand). First the 2 gutter mounts (solar and camera) are similar except the solar bracket is on top and the camera bracket is facing downward which makes sense. BUT the design is 10X different. The solar panel gutter mount has a long screw for the camera and based on a ball swivel joint for a full 360 degree adjustment. Not this camera mount. All 3 of my camera gutter (this product!!!) mounts had long screws that were too short and would not tighten the unit to the gutter. I had read some reviews of this but thought it would not happen to me. Some guys said they went to Home Depot and brought longer screws. My solution was to cut up an old door mat that was rubber and thick to act as a placer or wedge to fill the gap so the long screw would tighten and hold in place. . The above issue was with the mounting screws to the gutter. The real issue was with the main screw that attaches to the camera. it was too short. When screwed in the camera was at an angle. To align the camera straight up and down, you would have to unscrew and back off the camera (unsafe). So when screwing the camera onto the screw all the way, the camera would be at an angle. Un-screwing the camera 1/2 or 3/4 a turn would only leave a partial connection and risk it falling out. Next like on a tri-pod, you have another screw nut that you are supposed to use to tighten against the camera to lock the screw in place. Well this screw nut was too small to tighten with your fingers. the screw nut was very small and my fingers could not reach the screw nut. it was too small (I do not have big / fat fingers!!). My solution here was to remove the screw nut completely so I could screw the camera in all the way. Then when I had to back off (un-screw the camera) to make it up and down and not at an angle, I would see how much space is needed and place washers to fill the gap. Lastly, the screw that I discussed above is connected to 2 things. One will move up / down and the other left to right. This is ONLY 2D, not 3D. Note I mentioned the solar panel gutter bracket was based on a 360 degree ball socket. This camera gutter mount is NOT. Poor design. So you are limited on the angles you can adjust your camera. The good news, the Aobelieve gutter mount for the solar panel will actually work for the Ring camera too. All you have to do is un-screw 4 small screws that hold the bracket on top of the unit and re-attach it on the bottom so the bracket is pointing downward. this took me less than 2 minutes. First the Aobelive solar panel gutter mount has full length screws to attach to the gutter. The main screw into the camera is long enough to go in fully and the screw nut to tighten to the cameras is large enough anyone can manually tighten. Did I say, it also is based on a ball and socket design to give you full 360 degree adjustment. This product does not have that. i am going to return these and do not believe all the short one line reviews that say this product is great.

I purchased this keyboard cover sold by The Deal Source and shipped by Amazon—this is very different from sold by Amazon and shipped by Amazon! I received an obviously used product because it did not match one I had previously bought in person. Here are some things that were missing (also see pictures): 1. There is a plastic bag that should be around the keyboard inside the box. 2. There should be a plastic ring around the camera hole protecting the buttons. 3. There should be a removable plastic sticker along the bottom edge of the keyboard. 4. (Most important) There should be a white serial number sticker underneath the side of the case that wraps around the iPad. Logitech customer service cannot help you without this serial number. As for the item itself, this is the cheapest "Apple-approved" keyboard cover for the iPad Pro. I like it better than their own keyboard folio because it wraps all the way around (including keeping the pencil secure) and because its switch keys feel like I'm actually typing. Well, after a year and a half with this system (8 cameras) all I can say is that it's a wash. It was reasonably priced, but it's left me wishing I had spent more on somebody else's better quality system. I'll address the DVR first. It has many shortcomings. The software features are clunky, and lacking any settings for any sort of WiFi IPC range extender. This is AN IMPORTANT OMISSION. The antennas are fixed and not detachable or extendable. The beeper on the unit is loud and obnoxious, and cannot be disabled, forcing me turn off automated maintenance. There is only one internet port ( more on this in a sec) As to the cameras: In WiFi mode, they do not even come close to their maximum stated range. Expect HALF the stated number, with poor signal strength and thus poor frame rates as a result at the half range number. The adjustment screw for changing the camera angle is TOO SHORT. It barely has any thread engagement, is painted black, falls out easily during adjustment and is easily lost (ask me how I know). I had one of eight camera fail 6 months in, replaced free by ZOSI (more on that in customer service). At the highest resolution, you cannot make out a car license plate at 20 feet. The included ten foot extension antennas did NOTHING to improve the signal. Don't waste money on them. The camera power supplies will cover of both sockets of a two prong outlet. This is important consideration in an outdoor installation with outdoor outlets up to the latest code with clear plastic covers. You will NOT be able to close the cover if you plug in off the bottom socket, and the power supply will be exposed to the elements. In all other respects I have found the cameras adequate, with decent image quality and night vision range. They have stood up to the weather pretty well. But IF you want to hard wire these via Ethernet cable, you are going to have to buy a switch because the DVR only has one port. Multiple cameras, plugged into the switch, and then the DVR, which a can only presume will work. As to customer service, it's polite, but difficult. Obviously you are talking to someone in China. They like to debate you and get you to try a whole lot of things to fix your problem. One thing at a time, one e-mail at a time, ONE E-MAIL PER DAY. Some of them had me going outside in bad weather, up on the ladder, back and forth until I just told them I wasn't going to do everything they demanded over a period of days.To make things worse, It was often a different agent whom I had to start over at the beginning with. After several days of this nonsense, taking photos of the camera, serial numbers from the DVR, QR codes etc, they sent a new camera for the one that failed. I am not saying they were not polite, they were just doggedly inefficient and troublesome to communicate with. There is no manual included, and what they tell you to download is more like a quick start guide. That's insufficient. So if you are on a tight budget, you might look at Zosi. But otherwise I'm not sure I recommend it based on the performance claims that seem vastly inflated.

So, I decided to bring the G7 down to nothing, but as I played (and watched the scale slowly sink), when it reached "2%" it suddenly started charging. I turned the computer off and checked it periodically and lo, it was charging. I waited until it it reached 100% and started playing a game. But, (and this is a good but..), it maintains it charge a LONG time, I go weeks playing the old Battlefield 2 games, old Dooms, Fighter Ace and a few others and this thing keep clickin' along. But, wait (and use it on something unimportant) let it get to 2%, get off it and let it do it's thing. It'll continue to charge as you use it at that point. Not sure what the 2% deal is, My other PC's stay around 100 with the "stock" packs. But for something like a dedicated gaming computer... it does fine. I wouldn't trust it (hence the 4 rating) for a work or family laptop.
