Used this watch for a year before writing a review. First off, it's smaller than the normal size Suunto watches (e.g. spartan ultra), and that unfortunately results in a substantial reduction in battery life - it is about 1/3 to 1/4 of the normal large size watch. You can barely get 5 days out of this battery after a year. It used to get about 8 days new. Compared to the larger watches, the display of this watch is really round (no notch at the 6 o'clock position), but unfortunately the resolution is lower and the software isn't really well adapted - e.g. reading notifications is considerably harder as Suunto kept the icon size the same and text is only in the lower half of the display. The display is also a fingerprint magnet, but fairly easy to read. The new watch face introduced with the 9 renders properly both in standby and in active mode on this watch (in contrast with the big one on which is horrible). Colors are still limited and for example you won't get the yellow color used in all marketing materials. Also the bezel around the display is ridiculously large for something from 2021. The leash while on the shorter side has a space saving locking mechanism with a socket and pin that seems to be adequate and the material is nice. Sleep detection is somewhat inaccurate, some days up to a couple of hours and complete lack of detecting/tracking naps. O2 saturation detection is complete and utter joke. It is broken - it works once in a blue moon, like literary I have it set up to do constant during sleep but when I go to see it, the reading is often over 20 days old. Trying to trigger it manually is unreliable, as there is no interaction - it's up to the watch to show you an old inconsistent reading or try to obtain a new one and fail. Even when it somehow manages to get the O2 reading, it would be disturbingly low - often in high 80s, while other watches and medical devices would read 97-99 at the same time. The resource measurement is also inaccurate - you remove the watch and put it back on after a minute and somehow you have "gained" 15-20% of resources. You also don't get to see the details of why the watch decides what your current resource level is. On iPhones the Suunto app won't sync your heart rate data with the health app. The sports features work adequately and well most of the time, and the watch is quick to get a fix if it was recently synced, but if not, getting a fix can take more than 30 minutes, even when both gps and glonas have been enabled. Compass works well but it's harder to see on the smaller screen (mostly due to how large the bezel is). Navigation on the current track could have also benefited from a slightly narrower bezel. The interface and accessing different features is very easy to use. There is only one function overload which is the long press of the center button and you get a great visual feedback for that. Something that Suunto has broken on this watch is the ability to select time zone by name - you only have the time zone offsets, and while it has gps, it can't sync the time with the gps or figure out the time zone automatically. For the price of this watch, I wish it worked a little better, especially with sleep and o2 and had better battery life. Correcting the other minor annoyances would have been good as well.

The monitors are excellent quality, exactly what I was looking for to take on the road with me and work remotely. I love them and I'm glad I made the purchase. Since my partner also works remotely, we bought two of these so that we could have the flexibility of each of us using one, OR one of us using both. He also loves that he can use the display modes to mirror his screen to a customer sitting opposite him. All of this functionality works great. However, when using TWO of these to connect to your laptop and have a three-monitor setup, there are some caveats that weren't very clear (or I underestimated) upon purchase. They do work, and the quality and function is pretty good, but it is very bulky. As it does clearly state in the instructions, the mounting setup requires that it rests on a flat surface. It is NOT capable of supporting two monitors without tipping over your laptop, unless they are resting on something for support. This makes it difficult to work on any soft or angled surface (such as your lap, or on your hotel bed, or even on an angled laptop tray). Each monitor has to be connected separately, so there are cables running around every side of your computer. Also, only one powered USB-C can be connected at a time. After hours of trying to find some sort of dock with two, video capable, powered USB-C connections, I learned this is a limitation of the technology, but I found it rather irritating that they seem to go out of their way to omit this from the instructions. In any case this meant that the second monitor was not plug and play as I'd hoped; I had to call corporate IT and have the drivers installed to run the second monitor from a regular USB connection. Overall, I would absolutely buy these again. The quality was so impressive for the size that I almost feel bad giving them 4 stars instead of 5. However, the manufacturer differentiates these from others by advertising the ability to connect two of them at once, so IMO they need to work on making that setup a bit cleaner - or at a minimum, be more transparent about how it will work in practice.

I’m a long time Turtle Beach user and in this case Gen 1 Stealth 600z I wanted to like these Gen 2s, I really did. USB-C is nice. Aesthetics are improved. However I am returning them. Here’s my condensed takeaway. Connection issues. The mic will sometimes randomly disable itself, requiring a full power down and power on. The headphones will still work though. Awkward during game/lobby chat. There seems to be no rhyme or reason it happens. It’s just random. I’ll admit it doesn’t happen often though. Also sometimes turning the headset on does not turn it on despite getting the confirmation beeps: no audio. The headset seems to be fussy and doesn’t quite know what it’s doing at times. Sound. Don’t bother with the reviews saying X sounds better than Y and vise verse when it comes to these models. The long story short is there’s no perceptible difference. They’re both fairly affordable gaming headsets. Anyone who says there’s a big difference doesn’t know what they’re talking about. I’m an audiophile and i’ll tell you the sound is just “good enough.” nothing more nothing less. And they’re roughly in the same ballpark in terms of sound quality. Comfort. If you use these Gen 2s after the Gen 1s, you’ll notice the ear cushions on the Gen 2s aren’t as open as the Gen 1s so you’ll sort of hear yourself as if you were plugging your ears which can be disorienting when you talk. It’s an odd sensation. Also the cushions on the Gen 2 seem to be made of a stiff foam. While not uncomfortable the foam does squeak as you move your head and/or adjust the mic boom or volume buttons. Also the volume and mic wheels on the Gen 2s are awkward. I’m often confusing one for the other. Another awkward thing is as you switch through the sound modes on the Gen 2s, there’s no audio cue to announce the mode you’re in. All there is is a beep and you kind of have to guess what mode you’re in. Simply put I prefer the Gen 1s but wish for the USB-C and easier to control mic boom of the Gen 2s.

The reason I purchased this particular radio is that I owned an old Grundig YP400e that was so old and beat up it was time to replace it. However, I could only spend about fifty dollars. I knew the quality of Grundig radios and this one had the very stable digital shortwave frequency range that I wanted. So far, I'm happy with the purchase. The physical quality is just the level of quality that I expected from them. It is a radio that, even with just the whip antenna, is sensitive enough to reach out and grab FM, AM, and Shortwave stations. The Bad: I only said it would reach out and grab FM, AM, and SW stations. Only those three because, for whatever reason, I cannot get mine to go into Longwave no matter how many times I press the AM/LW button. Is it just mine or the entire production? I don't know. I don't listen to LW and, as far as I know, there isn't really anything down there except beacons. So, I don't miss it and I didn't get it for that, so I'm not disappointed. I think it might be the software, or programming, or whatever because sometimes it takes three or four presses of a button for the radio to switch over or to turn on. It won't do anything unless the screen is lit. Odd, but alright. The Good: Other than the two Bad issues, the radio works just fine. The FM and local AM reception is very good. Listening to a FM station about twenty to thirty miles away isn't a problem. In my West Texas house here in the high plains I can get WBAP 820 from Dallas, TX just fine after the sun goes down. It is a very sensitive radio. Everything else in the radio works just fine as it was designed to do. For the world traveler, the time zone knob is an easy way to change the radio's clock to the local time zone. Just open it up and turn the knob to the appropriate time zone and you're good to go. Just make sure to set the clock to the local time zone first by reading the manual. The physical build of the radio, as in the outside case itself doesn't seem to be fragile to me. It's built tougher than you think. Because it's designed to be used by a traveler it's built to take a little bit of a beating. Shortwave Reception: I put this in a separate section. This is a very sensitive radio that will pick up stations even with the short whip antenna. Reason is, and this is just a guess, is due to the DSP and some type of signal amp inside. Again, just a guess. Because the radio seems to be adjusting itself for the best reception. The volume will lower, or detune, during frequency changes. When it settles on a frequency, the signal will come back as if you're increasing the volume. So, that's why I say that. I could be wrong. But it is very stable. There is no drifting in the signal. So, you will get stations with just the whip antenna. However, there are some things to keep in mind about shortwave reception. Shortwave is AM, or Amplitude Modulation. Same as local AM, just higher frequencies. Therefore, shortwave is susceptible to interference from other electronics, or RFI. Such as: Computers, power strips, wall warts, fluorescent lights, TV's, power lines, etc. If you are in a metal building it will effect the incoming signal and not for the better. Such RFI interference will increase the background static, so turn off everything you don't need while listening to shortwave. It will help. Another thing to keep in mind is atmospheric propagation. Good stations to start off with is WWCR and WRMI, in my opinion. I say that because both of them have day time and night time frequencies that are transmitted specifically for North American listeners. Shortwave station antennas aren't omnidirectional, normally. They usually point in either one direction or two directions such as East and West or North and South. Take BBC for example. I can't here it in the USA because they don't transmit in my direction. So, no matter how good of an antenna I put up I can't receive a station that's not pointed in my direction. Normally. That's why stations such as WRMI have maps on their website which shows transmitter direction and signal strength. Shortwave radio signals are susceptible to the time of day, atmosphere conditions, and even sun cycles. Some stations will work better at night while some work better during the day. I would suggest for anyone wanting this radio, or any radio for receiving shortwave, to do research regarding shortwave propagation. Another to look up is RFI and why such electronics can add static to an AM radio. With that said, let me say this. Because this radio doesn't have an external antenna jack it helps to use a clip-on antenna. Like the CCrane roll-up portable. Personally, I made one from a long length of 18 gauge wire and an alligator clip. A length of wire of about twenty to twenty-five feet crimped to an alligator clip then attached to the whip antenna will definitely help the reception. When not in use, just roll it up and put the antenna away in your pocket along with the radio. Keep in mind that when adding antenna length, not only will it increase the radio signal but also the static. So, it may not seem like it's working. But if you change the display to show dBu and dB you can see the difference. I have a simple wire antenna strung out on my roof and when I clip that to the radio the signal can jump from a 40 dBu to around 70 or 80 dBu on the display. But it also increases the static to 25 dB as well. If you are just starting out in shortwave listening: For starting out, this is a good quality very stable non-drifting digital radio. It would help to research AM Shortwave propagation and RFI electronic interference. It will help someone just starting out to understand why you might not be able to get a station even if you are on the correct frequency. For example: Where I am in West Texas panhandle I'm at 3200 ft. above sea level. Out here the land is just like the people and the language...flat straight and goes on forever. So, with an elevation around 3200 ft. I could get signals better than someone who lives in a valley surrounded by mountains close to sea level. And to understand why turning off electronics will help reception by decreasing the level of static the radio receives thus being able to hear the station better. And be inventive with your antenna. Almost any length of wire crimped to an alligator clip will work as an antenna. Remember Slinky? Look up Slinky antennas on Youtube. Or a metal tape measure screwed onto the alligator clip. Be creative, do research, and happy listening. Update 2-7-21: I got the radio on the 26th of January and immediately put in the batteries. With the radio on for a good few hours each day and the display light on constantly half the time the batteries lasted ten days. Update 3-20-22: I've had this for a year and I've found out something about this radio. It's about the tuning knob and how it changes frequencies. The way you change frequencies quickly is by turning the tuning knob quickly. If you want to change the frequencies slowly then you turn the tuning knob slowly. Well, we have a saying in our household. "Nice in theory, horrible in practice." That method of fast scrolling through frequencies is a nice idea but for one problem. It doesn't work that well after the tuning knob gets worn in. At first it worked just fine, however, as the tuning knob gets used and worn, the programming has a hard time defining when is slow tuning and when is fast tuning. Because it gets worn the system will often see the knob and halfway between notches and will rapidly change frequencies. Even when tuning slowly, the system will think you want to fast scroll through frequencies. There's nothing really wrong with the tuning knob itself even as it wears in with use. The problem is how that worn in knob interacts with the auto slow to fast frequency change feature. This makes getting to the frequency that you want almost like rolling the dice. Sometimes you'll get to it just fine and other times it will keep fast scrolling with no way to slow it down to get to the one you want. So, in my opinion, it was a nice idea but after a while, after a bit of use, it almost becomes unusable because the system is scrolling through frequencies too fast that you can't land on the one you want to listen to. The radio itself is fine, but it would have been better to put a button that selects fast or slow scrolling rather than an automatic feature that is problematic the more it gets used.

It got stuck because without realising, when you use the buttons, you push them in further. Luckily the smaller rubber wasnt to my liking, so I changed it for the bigger ones. You have to be careful. Careful because I couldnt feel it in my ear. Luckily someone I knew was in the foyer of my block of flats. It's cold out so had a hat on, dark so I wore my headlamp, and windy so wore a bigger coat. Was very comfortable and snug over my earphones and I plodded along. I got home and saw the bloke, so being polite tried to turn the right earphone off, you have to actually press the button. I was thinking it would just turn off, which it did, but I pressed skip, which skipped to the next song, so pressed it again, did the same thing, then a longer press, that turned it down, double clicked it. I could see the bloke talking but couldnt hear him, so I was desperately trying to turn the things off, it didnt happen, so pulled it out of my ear instead. Then saw the rubber had gone, couldnt feel it in my ear, so was scouring the floor for it, as I was doing that, the bloke told me in was in my ear. It was lodged right in. Enough for him to say he'll get a tooth pick and he'll get it out for me. I took my gloves off, and luckily could grab the edge of it with a pinch of my nails.I wouldnt have known where it was, because it didnt do anything to my hearing, so would have had trouble if I had had a bath or shower, bed. That would have got lodged right in the inner ear.Then, this is irrelevant, bu, was trying to put it back on and it flicked into the blokes face and onto the floor..... I Facebook statused all this, so all is abit of fun. Havent got a like yet, but, hopefully it makes someone remember I exist.Was lucky, be careful that they're fitted on properly. Have a happy new 2024

Okay, so I'm going to try and really dive into this purchase and give a good idea of what you're getting into if you purchase. Being upfront, the computer suited my needs okay, and over-all I'm reasonably satisfied, but there are some large caveats that I think people should know prior to purchasing. The computers themselves seem to run fine. I purchased two for my wife and I to game on. They run the games we've played on them and the settings on each game seem to be running better than average. They both run Dayz on high settings which was maxing out PS4 and causing frequent game freezes on a much lower set of settings. My main complaint is in how some things are set up and on how some things are advertised. The first thing you need to realize is that the computer is "game ready" in name only. The information in the listing says it includes mouse, keyboard, Wifi and Bluetooth. Being fair, with the Wifi and Bluetooth there is kind of an advertised caveat that is there, but you have to be reading carefully to catch and I missed it. The keyboard and mouse you get are, frankly, trash. That wasn't a deal breaker for me, and I was pretty much ready for that out of the gate and bought equipment from the start to address that problem. The main thing I ran into almost immediately was the lack of pretty standard "gaming" equipment integrated into the machines. Bluetooth. Who want's wires? We certainly didn't. We game from our couch and have two TVs in our front room, one on top of the other so we can play side by side. There's maybe 10 feet between us and the TV (It's actually closer, but I'm giving the benefit of the doubt). There is no integrated Bluetooth in the machine. "Bluetooth" connectivity is added by a dongle that must be plugged into a USB port, and frankly, that dongle is an embarrassment. It won't even reliably cover the 10 feet between my couch and TV. It seriously would not work, so I had to buy new ones. There's another $16. Wifi? Same deal. No integrated wireless card, so again, USB dongle. Guess how well that worked? Yeah, it would drop the very strong Wifi signal in my house constantly (seriously, my smart TV sitting right next to the computer has full wireless bars and never drops Wifi). Guess how well an online only game handles even a three or four second drop in Wifi connectivity? So there's another purchase. This time, $30. BUT! Guess what, and this is the major point of contention I have with the system. All the USB ports are USB 1.0. Current generation is 4.0. 1.0 supports transfer speeds of 1.5Mbps (1996's premier technology) where as 4.0 supports 40Gbps and 3.0 supports speeds of 3Gbps readily. Not a huge deal, I thought, I'll buy a new USB card, along with the wireless card so the internet will actually work without dropping the game. I went with 3.0 because frankly everything was starting to add up and there's a steep price difference between 3.0 and 4.0. Another $20. So, with all my additions in hand, I open the computer... and find there's only 1 open PCI slot on the motherboard. That means there's physically no way to add both the wireless card the system really needs along with the USB upgrade the system also desperately needs. I opted to go with the USB upgrade, thinking that maybe the better USB system would carry the wireless better. Nope. Wireless still absolutely sucks. So yet another purchase, this time for a wireless extender I can plug into the wall at the TV which has ethernet cables I can plug into the computer. There's another $90. That means there's at least an additional $100 in hidden expenses (not counting keyboard and mouse which I went big on so I'm not counting those costs here) just to be able to make the machine function so that I don't have to have everything physically wired and sit within cable distance of my router and the computer itself. That's not to mention a few quality control issues. The biggest is that when I opened the case to add the USB card, I found the extra hot graphics card had not had the protective film removed, which was not flapping loose inside the box. Secondarily, both units started out with the RGB setup which lights up the front of the case in what I would say is kind of an annoying way, but which I know a lot of people really like. That worked well on both units through the first couple of weeks, but has since completely gone out on my wife's unit, while mine continues to work. Not a deal breaker for me, but something that makes me nervous for the long-run prospects of the machine. Thirdly, and I'm not sure if this is just overload with the crappy USB ports or a genuine problem, the USB ports were unstable. Part of the reason that the Wifi and Bluetooth were so bad was that the dongles were actually disconnecting from the computer randomly. Even the keyboard would do it, making a super loud dinging sound and popping up a message on the screen that the new device had been recognized and was ready to use. Are the computers a good deal? For me, probably yeah. I have the disposable income to have all the little things adjusted (minus the single open PCI slot which really annoys me) and all the extra little additions. Usually however, when someone is buying a refurbished or discounted item, every penny counts and for those people, I feel bad if they buy this computer. If that's you, should you still buy the computer? Probably. It was, by far, the best value for hardware I found on Amazon and with a few sacrifices it will get you on most games. Be prepared to be wired into the computer directly and just forget about using anything wireless. Then save up your pennies and dimes and get the upgrades necessary. Overall, definitely an "Average" product, and thus the 3-star overall rating.

review_text: I bought the cheaper version because it's the same monitor with a cheap stand; since I was mounting it on a flex arm the stand was not important. This is a very nice monitor for the money. It is a VA rather than IPS, so the colors are more vibrant, and the reduced viewing angle of VA monitors is not really noticeable unless you're going to use it as an off-center secondary monitor. PRO's - Very reasonably priced - A LOT of screen real estate, you can fit about 50 icons on your task bar. - High refresh rate, very smooth scrolling. - At a little over 12 lbs. it's light enough to work well with flex arms and the VESA mount was easy to attach by myself. - I find the joystick settings control easier to use than the usual pushbutton array. CON's - It does cut off the active application indicator bar on the task bar at the bottom of the screen; as you can see, my solution was to simply place the task bar on top. It took some getting used to, but it works. - If you're using it with 1080p monitors the Windows text is a little small. Still readable just smaller than the other monitors. If it's your only monitor you can always change the Windows settings - No G-Sync support, but I don't do a lot of gaming and the Nvidia studio drivers work great. - You might need a bigger mouse pad, it's long way from edge to edge :) BOTTOM LINE If you've always wanted a widescreen but didn't want to spend over $500 this is the way to go. It's cheaper than the cost of two comparable 1080p monitors, has more screen space and with the curvature is an immersive pleasure to look at.

Honestly after finding all that, I really do love the way it looks, but that process and having to manually run the software every time I want to see it. It leaves a lot to be desired.

these headphones are pretty decent! i bought them as a gift for my friend who didn’t have headphones with a mic (headset). we play video games and use discord to communicate. i also stream on twitch, so it’s important that people can hear my teammates/guests properly, and i’m glad to say that these headphones work relatively well! the connection is easy and they’re essentially plug n play. they’re light and work wonderfully to conform to any head shape. here’s where i become rather cranky, but i’ll try to control myself: the microphone lacks a bit of the low end, but the mids are relatively nice. the only issue is that this headset’s mic picks up a LOT of breathiness if it exists: people in my chat were complaining that it sounded like my buddy was eating his microphone, when in fact he was just breathing normally but exhaling through his nose as he laughed at jokes and whatnot. i recommended that he keep the microphone either just above his nose, or at his jawline in order to reduce the chances that his mic picks up sounds that aren’t desirable. furthermore, the impedance of the mic on this headset is INSANE—i had to turn him up to 200% volume on discord and THEN add like 10dB of gain to my discord track inside OBS (i have separate tracks for discord, music, gameplay audio, etc). this was a huge problem for me as a customer because i know it doesn’t take that much from a company to make a mic *not* do whatever it was. however, he did seem to enjoy the way that the headphones sounded. i can’t say that id fully recommend these, but they would probably work best as a decent backup option if all else fails. i use Bose QC35II headphones and a Rode Procaster mic, and i’m so glad i went that route instead. but if i had to go back and do it over again with ONLY the option of buying a headset, i might up my budget to about $150 and go for Fnatic headset, or the HyperX Cloud Flight (shroud’s headset). the Fnatic is actually like $70 or so, but i would still highly recommend it over this one. for the casual gamer who doesn’t care so much about pristine audio quality in any capacity and just wants something to get the job done, this could be for you. otherwise, i would personally look elsewhere to fit my needs.

Mixed feelings concerning my purchase of the Kindle Paperwhite. I find the Kindle to be transportable and easy to read. The screen is functional, but clumsy. Battery life is still under evaluation since I’m a new user of Kindle’s. And the book cover I purchased works well. The physical human factors, i.e., ergonomics, of the Kindle are quite nice. What I find clumsy with the Kindle: The major disappoints are based on my personal needs - the reasons why I purchased the Kindle. I require the ability to reference a lot of technical material, e.g., books. Which is why I purchased the Kindle. It allows me to transport and access more reference books easily. Unfortunately, too many of my math books couldn’t be downloaded on the Kindle. That’s a major disappointment and defeats the purpose of the buy. It is my hope that that deficiency is corrected in the near future. All Amazon purchased ebooks should be compatible with the Kindle. If not, that incompatibility should be easily communicated before purchase. Book downloads appear to be manual. When the system sync’s it should automatically download and load the books. My Paperwhite doesn’t do that automatically. I had to literally download each book individually. Add that to poor screen response and you see the problem. It’s a pain for users with many books, repetitive, and time consuming. Screen response is slow and clumsy. Too slow for, supposedly, the latest generation Kindle. Moreover, touch screen response is fickly. May I suggest the designation of specific spots on the screen to activate certain commands like bookmarks? You have to hit the screen just right. Add to highlight and dictionary function is very clumsy with poor response. Overall, Out of five I give the Kindle a 3 rating. I am a little disappointed with its functionality considering the length of time the product has been on the market. These problems should have been rectified.

These are so close to perfect, but unfortunately FAIL IN EVERYTHING. First off, sound. I'm an audiophile, so sound is important to me. Audio reproduction from these speakers is not exact, but pretty good. Yes, the bass is lacking, but that is to be expected from ALL small speakers. No noticeable distortion except when maxing out the volume. Again, volume is pretty good for such small speakers. Definitely loud enough to overpower conversations, but without bass, you definitely won't "feel" the music. So why only 2 stars? I bought the pair because I needed low-latency stereo speakers for watching videos. These are advertised as being low latency, connecting 2 for separate left-right stereo sound, and even connecting multiple speakers for "full stereo in multiple rooms, areas, inside and outside" (quote straight off the OontZ website). Unfortunately, these UTTERLY FAIL to deliver these promises/lies. (1) First of all, the low-latency only works with OontZ Bluetooth Adapter made specifically for this Ultra 4th Gen. It is not compatible with the Bluetooth industry-standard aptX Low Latency or FastStream. Thus, the aptX-LL Bluetooth adapter I bought specifically for these was worthless. Furthermore, their proprietary low latency isn't as good as aptX-LL, so I am still distracted by out-of-sync lips when watching videos. (2) After buying the OontZ Bluetooth Adapter, I discovered that the low latency does not work in stereo (i.e., one speaker plays left while another plays right). Instead it only supports "surround" mode where every speaker plays both left and right. Thus, if something moves left to right, you hear it everywhere, not moving left to right. If two people on screen are talking, you don't hear one from the left and one from the right like you would in normal movie dialog, you hear both people everywhere. "Full stereo in multiple rooms" is an outright lie because every speaker plays both left and right. There is no stereo separation. (3) The only way to get true left-right stereo is to have the LEFT speaker plugged in with a wired audio connection. (Left is not ideal for me.) That's correct--STEREO MODE DOES NOT WORK WITH BLUETOOTH. But there's more--to setup stereo mode, you then have clear/forget both speakers' Bluetooth connections, then press and hold the Play button on the left speaker, then press and hold the Play button on the right speaker. EVERY TIME. PITA. (4) Volume on multiple speakers only controls that one speaker. While this might be ideal for different rooms, it's a PITA when the speakers are in the same room, particularly when they're hooked up as stereo. If I need to talk to someone, I can't just grab the nearest speaker and turn down the volume. I have to also go the other speaker and manually turn that one down, then do the reverse when the conversation is over. But now the speakers are out of sync--one could be higher or lower than the other...or maybe it just seems that way in this part of the movie/music. No wait...it's not. Oh, it is. Or not...? Ugh. So then I usually have to pull out my phone and use the OontZ app. The app lets you sync volumes. However, you have to start the app, wait while it searches for nearby speakers, select the speaker, go the menu, choose Volume, then Sync and change the volume--even though you pressed the Sync button and the two volume bars become one, it doesn't actually sync until you actually change the volume. Again, PITA. And note even if you select sync in the app, using the volume buttons on the speaker unsyncs them again. TL;DR Low latency is a lie. Stereo is a lie. If you just need one speaker and don't care about out-of-sync videos or stereo, this Oontz speaker might be acceptable. If you're looking for a multi-speaker setup, avoid these crappy Oontz speakers.

I've been very happy with this watch as an upgrade from my Writings Steel HR. Unboxing and setup was simple. Tutorials within the app walk you through each feature of the watch. ECG. There's an activation process for the ECG function depending on where you live. I had to take one ECG reading and wait for the feature to be unlocked. The app explains exactly what's happening and why. It took a couple hours before I could view my ECG results, and after it's activated the results are instantaneous. It will only categorize your heart rhythm if your heart rate is between 50 and 100 beats per minute. All of my readings within that range have been categorized automatically. HEART RATE. Accurate when compared to my previous watch, a Withings Steel HR. I checked that watch against a pulse oximeter and got similar results. ScanWatch takes your heart rate every so often and displays a reading in the app for every half hour. STEPS. Again, I get similar step counts compared to my Steel HR, which was similar to my previous Fitbit. Steps are graphed in the app for every half hour and totaled for each day. The ScanWatch also counts the number of floors of stairs you climb, and they show up in the app similar to steps. BLOOD OXYGEN SATURATION. Taking your blood oxygen saturation (SpO2) manually is simple and returns a percentage in 30 seconds. It also takes your SpO2 during the night and averages it for you each morning if you enable that feature. BREATHING DISTURBANCES. The watch uses the blood oxygen saturation sensor to determine if you're breathing well at night. The section where you activate this feature warns you that it will shorten the battery life, and it definitely does. One night's sleep with the feature on "Always On" mode took 15-20 percent of my battery, which is a lot considering it should last 30 days on a charge. I changed this to the recommended "Automatic" setting and will have to wait and see on the battery life. FITNESS. I haven't used the fitness features of this watch yet. I've used the fitness features of the Steel HR and this watch is the same. It doesn't have built-in GPS, so you'll need to have your phone on you to track your location on a walk or run. My experiences with this feature have been good. The ScanWatch should be no different; I'll update this review if my expectations aren't met. BATTERY. My experience with my Writings Steel HR's 25-day battery life was always solid, so I'm expecting the same from the ScanWatch's 30-day claim. Some of the features I've activated might shorten it slightly, but I'll update this review if it doesn't meet my expectations. NOTIFICATIONS. The Withings Health Mate app monitors your phone's notifications and calls to alert you via your ScanWatch with a little vibration and text snippet on the watch screen. This feature can be enabled on a per-app basis, so you'll only be notified by the apps you want. DESIGN / COMFORT. The ScanWatch feels durable, has a stainless steel case and fluoroelastomer band. The FKM band is much more comfortable than silicone; it feels similar to leather but is waterproof and a little stretchy. I've found the watch to be very comfortable after wearing it a few days. The stem is easy to twist and click, and makes navigating the menu much easier than the Steel HR's single push button. The sapphire glass is nice and clear. The packaging is pretty Spartan and has very little instruction. I found it nice and clear, but I can see where other reviewers were disappointed. OVERALL this is a great watch I'd recommend to anyone wanting a smart watch experience with long battery life and classic styling.

Oh boy, where do I start? For about 9 months I have been searching for a new pair of earbuds. Got the AirPods Pros in March of 2021. Loved the sound of the ANC and transparency mode But, they would fall out of my ears when I sweat. They were almost the perfect pair of earbuds but fell short because of the slipping. So I went searching for earbuds, Sennheiser momentum, Jaybird, Jabra elite, Skull candy, Powerbeats pro, Sony XM3 and XM4, Bose QC and Sport, Galaxy buds, etc. Then these Beat Fit Pro got released and I was overjoyed. They had the wing tip so they could stay in my ears. Overjoyed by the compatibility with my IOS devices they are basically Airpod pros without the stem and with the fin. So I bought them. PROS: ANC and Transparency are the same as Airpod pros USB C charging Slightly bigger case so still pocketable H1 chip Cool colors CONS: Hurts your ears if you have smaller ears or even medium sized ears. Tried every ear tip. not made for extended use. Not Wireless charging The case is cheap. WHITE BUZZING NOISE IN LEFT EARBUD! ARGGGG the main reason I am returning this is because of a white buzzing noise in the left earbud. I did my research and others have the same problem. And no I am not crazy, I have very sensitive hearing and can hear the quietest of sounds. The sound is hard to describe but it sounds like an electronic part is beeping in the left earbud. This can be heard with ANC on and off, Transparency on and off. If you can’t hear really quiet sounds or high pitched frequencies then this isn’t a problem for you but BEWARE. The other reason is they hurt my ears. The wing tip is too firm and causes pain and discomfort after 10 min of use. I tried every ear tip but it doesn't matter. I didn’t get any of the other earbuds I listed above because I didn’t want them to fall out of my ears so I am super sad that these are so uncomfortable. If you have big ears then this shouldn’t be a problem either but keep in mind. Additionally, They are not very light. The AirPods pros you can almost not even feel them but the beat fit pro you can clearly feel them. So after my failed attempt to replace my AirPods pros with these it seems like I will stick with the AirPod pros. I am super disappointed that these did work out. Trust me fellow earbud fanatics, I have done my research and these fail to beat the Airpod pros even with them major flaw of slipping out. Don’t just follow the trend, do your own research and decide for yourself. What I would suggest is to take your money elsewhere or wait until something else is released.

review_text: We've had this unit for around a year and have tried to like it but it is just junk. I don't know whether it's the recast solely or the combination of the recast and FireTV stick. We have wifi over cable, so data rate around 60Mbps and internal wifi speed at 64Gbps, but this thing is constantly pausing (buffering, I assume), especially during playback of recorded programs, so it shouldn't even be gated by our cable internet speed since this is broadcast TV that the recast is recording. The latest annoyance is during fast forward thru commercials, it loses audio. The only solution seems to be to shut it off and restart it. There are many other annoyances too numerous to list trying to get it to play back recorded programs. Compared with a cable or satellite DVR it fails miserably. We had a ChannelMaster DVR+ that received and recorded over-the-air TV which was on par with cable/satellite DVR, but unfortunately ChannelMaster discontinued the product, no longer supports it, and it has some internal electronic issues that have developed with age; that was our motivation to switch to Recast. After a year tho', I'm about ready to dump the Recast and try TiVo. It just shouldn't be that hard to get this right! Also an update... When you're looking at the reviews, sort by "most recent" rather than the default. Eye opening. While if you look at the star rating, it appears to have around 50% 5-star, when sorted by most recent, the one and 2-star ratings abound. Problems with deleting old, recorded content, pausing and having it go back to the home screen, etc., etc., are a common problem. It's clear that it takes a while for users to discover all the problems with Recast and realize that this product is just broken. With all the bucks poring into Amazon, they should be able to do better. They really should just take this product off the market until they work out the bugs!

First, the stuff that's great: I use this monitor primarily for work and a bit for gaming. If you write code all day, the HDR effect is great. Bright text on dark background is very crisp, and reduces eye strain, especially when working in a dark room. Colors needed some mild tweaking, but, overall, everything from video to games to text looks incredible. Now on to the main issue: This monitor experiences the occasional "screen blanking." Going by other reviews, it's not obvious what this means, so let me clarify. When using the monitor, on occasion, the screen will go blank (black, nothing displayed). This is *not* the same as the screen simply turning off, since you can still open the monitor settings menu, so it is specifically the input from your PC/laptop/device that is no longer rendered. When this occurs, the blank screen will usually flicker on and off until the content on the screen changes (e.g. switch to a different window, or seek to a different time in a video on YouTube). Turning the monitor off, waiting ~15-30 seconds, and turning it back on again will often resolve the blanking issue. Sometimes you need to repeat this process a couple of times. Once the monitor turns on and *doesn't flicker*, it tends to also continue to not flicker (at least until it goes into sleep mode or is turned off again). Combined, these "symptoms" lead me to believe that the issue is with the video input processor inside the monitor. When the monitor turns on, it *sometimes* boots into this broken, crash-prone state. When in this state, some combination of video input data (e.g. specific pixels in specific locations on the screen) will cause the processor to crash, causing the screen to go temporarily blank while it reboots. When it reboots, if the input data on the screen hasn't changed, it can crash again, leading to a loop where the screen appears to blink on and off. I think turning the monitor on and off for 15-30 seconds amounts to a "hard reboot", rather than whatever the monitor hardware is doing when it "soft reboots" when the video input processor crashes. So, to summarize... this issue is extremely annoying, but also manageable. I've run into the same issues with other LG 4K monitors, although their latest 4K TVs don't seem to experience it, likely due to some long-overdue hardware upgrades. If you're thinking of buying this monitor... I can't recommend it as-is. Either go with one of the other options, or wait for LG's 2021/2022 versions and check the reviews to see if this issue persists. If you already have this monitor, I don't think replacing it with the same model will fix anything for you, but hopefully the turn-off, wait, turn-on thing can help you manage this ridiculous bug.

Before I say anything, I have WD drives that date as far back as I can remember. If things change I will update my review. So, as many others have said (not just here) this drive gets major praise, but just like many others, my drive arrived DOA. So I installed in my PS5, which was ridiculously easy, even if youve never done it, first timers will find any nvme drive easy to install. PS5 couldnt initialize it properly and froze at 13%, tried a few more times after reseating it and same thing. My PS5 has had zero problems since ive owned it. Now, at this point I pop it in my PC. Which it does see it (exactly like the PS5, so nothing new), but thats it. Cant initialize it (incorrect function in disk management) which is where everything ends. If you cant initialize ANY DRIVE then thats as far as it goes, you cant do anything. Im sure theres plenty of others where there drives are fine still, and i just got a faulty one. (I will still try the replacement which is a month wait mind you). I dig WD products cause ive never had their HDs die in my lifetime time. Where as my seagate experience ive only had one survive and its currently on its way out. This isnt just limited to PS5 as reviews suggest but to PC as well. Digging deep into the history of this product, it had (and still has) major firmware issues, and if you cant initialize it, then you cant update the firmware. Hope this helps anyone doing their due diligence. UPDATE: Amazon pulled thru much quicker and was no longer a month wait. So 2nd time around, I just avoided the PS5 at first, since the first thing I wanted to do was test on PC and update firmware immediately. This one did all that no problem, then installed in PS5 and formatted no problem. Its only been 5 days but I really did some good PS5 gaming length tests and the drive works great. Im a little worried in the long run for PS5 tho, this drive runs around 36C (not gaming with the default heatsink) in my well cooled PC, which is fine but i might look into a better heatsink. You really dont want to go above 70C. Now lets mention the tiny nvme PS5 compartment basically: higher speeds, higher temperatures, leads to lower life span. review_text: I live in an old cheese factory which has been converted to a single family home. In a word, it is huge. Two stories, 1450 square feet on the main (upper) floor, more than that in the lower floor, which is where the factory was. Much of it was built in the 1890's, with more added on later. There are concrete walls, tree trunks as support beams and a long steel I-beam that was built in a more "modern" phase of additions. Needless to say, the wifi on its own isn't great. The router is centrally located, but still only does well in the kitchen, living room, and dining room, which are all pretty open to one another. There is a TV in the room on the other side of the wall where the router is and I can't watch Hulu on the TV, as it is always buffering. Forget trying to stream anything in the family room on the lower level. I placed the Wifi range extender in my basement with line of sight to the TV in the family room and now have excellent reception in both rooms. I'm overjoyed. Setting it up was so simple, too. Just plug in the range extender in the room where the router is and wait for it to boot up, then press the WPS button on the extender, then the router and wait for them to "talk". Then plug it in near where you need better reception. I have mine about equally distant from the two rooms where I needed improved reception. I don't think I could be any happier unless it came with another 20 gigs of Internet!

Edit 11/24/2021 Well, I got the Cambridge Audio DacMagic 100 and replaced this Fosi Q4 DAC, and it didn't make as much difference as I thought it would. The Cambridge Audio unit is much larger, heavier, and runs off wall current so it doesn't need to be turned up all the way, and it doesn't have a volume knob. I think there is a bit more openness between instruments and perhaps more bass, but the difference isn't nearly as profound as I thought it might be. So, if you need a DAC and you're on a budget, this looks like an outstanding choice. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Well I ordered a Cambridge Audio DAC, but it got put on backorder for weeks and I couldn't wait to try a DAC between my laptop and my HiFi system, so after a bit of research and a lot of impulsive shopping I ordered this DAC just to see what it could do. I'm absolutely amazed at what I am hearing through my Naim integrated amplifier and my grand old KEF 104.2 speakers. Here are the setup details. First of all, this DAC consumes two USB ports on the laptop, one for power and one for sound. It was "plug and play" on my Windows 10 (all updated) laptop. It shows up as an audio device called "Headphones (HiFi Audio)." Once I had confirmed that my laptop recognized this DAC, then I powered the DAC and my amplifier (Naim Nait XS2) and connected the RCA outputs from the DAC to the HDD input of the amplifier. (It really doesn't matter which RCA input I use, but others were taken.) I powered the DAC and the amplifier up and made sure the laptop was sending to the DAC. At first the sound was very faint. In summary, I found I have to turn the DAC to full volume, and use a two-to-three foot high quality RCA interconnect cable to get this DAC to sound good. Since it's running off the USB on the laptop, this didn't surprise me much. It needs all its power to send a signal of sufficient strength through the RCA outputs. So, I keep the DAC at full volume and still have the volume on the amplifier and the computer to alter the system volume with. That is fine. I never tried headphones or any inputs other than the USB. I did like the ability to cheat and pump up the treble a bit with the DAC. This British amp doesn't have tone controls, and the idea is that if you use a quality source you're not supposed to need them ever. Still, it was fun playing with the bass and treble knobs on the DAC. Now, it will be interesting to see how this DAC compares to the Cambridge Audio DAC, if and when I get it.

review_text: I bought this as a cheap capacity upgrade for my boot drive. I immediately started seeing slowness on bootup, while browsing, total system choking while moving larger files, and other odd performance issues. I ran some tests against my existing drives and found some odd results: The below are sustained write tests at 10 second intervals: This drive (SP 1TB 3D NAND): 371, 4, 157, 189, 4.9, 307 MB/s My other SSD (Crucial MX100): 445, 458, 461, 454, 443, 452 MB/s My primary M.2 (Adata XPG SX8200 Pro): 1337, 876, 866, 876, 865, 871 MB/s I found this odd, the drive was peaking at 371 MB/s and frequently dipping down to single digits, which would explain the slowness and choking while moving files. I tested on other data and power cables to be sure those weren't the culprit, and ended up replacing it with a Samsung 860 EVO and ran the same tests again without changing any settings or cables in my PC: This drive (SP 1TB 3D NAND): 420, 11, 11, 11, 11, 11 MB/s Samsung 860 EVO: 467, 468, 475, 473, 472, 472 MB/s This means either this SSD is failing miserably, or is somehow uniquely interacting with windows power management settings as others have mentioned. I did not touch those settings, and all of my other drives are performing as expected, so there is something inherently wrong with the SP drive that causes it to drop to such low transfer speeds. Bottom line: I would not recommend this drive, especially when you can get a Crucial for barely $5 more, or Samsung for $10-15 more and have significant performance gains with no troubles.

review_text: SECOND UPDATE: After seven months use A description of my many problems with the AXE-11000 is below. The good news is, once firmware 3.0.0.4.386_45850 was released AND I replaced my RT-AC88U mesh node with a second AXE-11000, I haven't had further problems. I continue to avoid using the bandwidth monitor and other advanced features in case of trouble. I can't say anything good about ASUS's responsiveness to my problems (or others on their forums.) After submitting many feedback reports using the router's built-in trouble reporting mechanism, and updating a thread on their forums about my crippling problems, the only contact I ever had from ASUS was one asking if I had ever used the feedback uploader (because they don't read anything carefully.) I'm finally satisfied with this purchase, and I've had equally bad experiences with NetGear's high-end home routers. If I had this to do over, I would have waited until the product had been shipping a year before investing in it. A $550 home router should work well at launch -- not require regular factory resets for most of its first year in service. UPDATE: After three weeks use Upon configuring the new GT-AXE11000 in AiMesh with an RT-AC88U, I experienced severe glitches which eventually became so bad that many of my devices could no longer connect -- including super common devices like a Roku Ultra, Macbook Pro, and Ring alarm base station. EVEN ONE WIRED DEVICE COULDN'T GET A DHCP ADDRESS although it could receive broadcast traffic. A factory reset corrected all of these problems. I'll try AiMesh again after a future firmware update. I had horrible results with the OEM firmware version 3.0.0.4.386_42489 on the main AXE11000 node and another 386-release on the AC88U mesh node. For now, I changed my review to 2/5 stars since advertised functionality malfunctions severely; and because the ASUS forums are experiencing some kind of multi-day login problem, which prevented me from getting help from the ROG community. ORIGINAL REVIEW BELOW ASUS markets this router to gamers, but as a remote worker, I appreciate the powerful bandwidth monitoring and advanced configuration options of ASUS routers. I've included numerous screenshots of the router GUI to let it speak for itself. I've been eagerly awaiting the AXE11000 for many months. As a long-time ASUS customer and owner of a 6-year-old AC3200 router, I wanted to update to the latest model, but held out for WiFi 6E support on the new 6GHz band, which will provide more RF spectrum for the next generation of wireless devices. Having used the router for just 24-hours so far, I can say performance around my suburban home is slightly better than with my previous model; and upgrading to the AXE11000 resolved a strange compatibility issue I had with my Ring alarm system. So far, zero problems with the AXE11000. The features that set this router apart from its competition are so numerous, it feels silly to list them: Powerful NAT & Firewall features, Dual WAN, VPN feature, Dynamic DNS client, site survey w/ time-series logs, configurable smart steering, and the AiMesh system put ASUS routers way ahead of anyone else in the prosumer & gamer segment. I'll recommend ASUS 6E routers to everyone once they're able to offer models at more price points, but for right now, if wireless network performance is critical to your remote work and other household needs, consider this an investment just like periodically updating to the latest mobile phone or laptop. While expensive, it is well worth the price.

I recently upgraded my spectrum plan and my old Netgear router N7000 was not able to keep up, lotsa drops, devices having IP address issues, intermittent connection, daily router resets etc. So was in the search for a newer Ax routers, ideally a tri-band but since the prices were sky high, i opted for the dual band AX. Narrowed it down to the Asus AX-3000 and Linksys AX3200 , it is almost $40 cheaper compared to the ASUS and also has good range and higher gig support. 3200 compared to 3000. Pros- compact with no antennas bulging yet the range is better than older Netgear R7000. ( whole house is being covered with 5ghz). The speed i am getting over the air is almost 80% of my what my plan calls for, wired it might get 100% of advertised speed. ( over the air speed is always less than wired connection) Very easy to connect to my spectrum provided modem, did over the air firmware update once i got into the router. ( was super easy from opening the package to connecting my devices, renaming SSID and security PW, enabling Guest network etc took in all about 10-12 mins) So far about 18 devices are connected and have had no issues with dropped network, IP address clash, internet slowdown etc. Browser interface is very simple like i remember back in 2005 linksys used to have. Nothing much has changed, its very basic with not much of hoopla. Cons- The guest network can be turned on but cannot change the SSID. (it is a subset of your router ssid with a dash and guest next to it. ( netgear n7000 gave you the option to name your guest ssid) The guest network when connected using the setting of your phones, it takes you to browser PW login. Just like in the cafes and free WIFI commercial estblishment. The BIGGEST DRAWBACK for me is Linksys app on ios, it does not support this router as yet as this is an E series router, hopefully will get support in future but CS wasn't sure when since this is fairly new router. ( hence only 4 stars which i will update when there is mobile app support to manage the wifi). FINAL THOUGHTS -For the price and features available, it is worth the money, very simple but basic browser router configs. But it does an excellent job of connecting your devices either on 5ghz or 2.5 ghz with blazing fast speed and so far have not had any issues that i was experiencing with my older router.

If this was anywhere near $100 I'd probably give it 1 star. It's annoying to setup and use, and the quality of the video is just ok. Given that it's $69, typically with a deep discount from that, it's at least a possible option if you want something cheap. The issue several other reviews have talked about with it sometimes recording, sometimes not, is definitely true. I have figured out how to work around it though. The problem seems to be when you turn the key to on, but don't start the engine right away. If you wait even for a few seconds it causes a slight interruption in the power supply, which can reset the camera. It shouldn't, that's a known issue that every dash cam should be able to handle, but this one can't. So what I do is just unplug the thing after I park. When I get in the car I wait until the engine is running to plug it back in. This has worked 100% of the time. You can tell on the display if it's recording or not by whether there's a little red dot near the upper left corner, blinking on and off. If you don't see that it's not recording. Just unplug it, let it turn off, wait 30 seconds or so and plug it back in. If you're willing to live with that it's a decent cam.

I backed off the timing of that RAM a bit and got it booting, but it was still not stable and failed memory diagnostics every time, and random reboots were and issue. So I returned it and purchased this one instead. All problems went away! Not only is it booting and rock solid stable at the XMP settings, but I was also able to loosen the timing a bit and clocked it up to 3600MHz which seems to run perfectly fine. That said, there's VERY little difference even in synthetic benchmark scored from 3200 to 3600, so I left this at the stock XMP settings and rolled with it. I've stress tested it for hours with Prime95 and Aida64 with zero issues. Maybe I got lucky and got a good pair of memory with this one, but I certainly do recommend it based on my results now, and on my past experiences with Crucial memory over the years. I have used the Archer AC1750 for a good number of years now, and it was time to upgrade. With an iPhone SE and work computer now supporting Wifi6, and plenty of devices in use during the pandemic, it was time to upgrade to the latest standard. My biggest concerns were MU MIMO performance during concurrent sessions, and range. I am happy to report that this router has handled everything we've thrown at it so far, even with my measly 100Mbps plan. I get good coverage for my < 1500 sq ft apartment, even on opposite ends of the router placement. My only complaint is the limited QoS features and inconsistent placement in the UI: you have to enabled QoS and set maximum bandwidth (which caps at 1000 Mbps FYI, the 1500 is a summation of multiple bands), and then head to a specific device in the devices page to enable high priority. That's all you can do. For the price, other than the UI confusion, no complains or issues thus far! TP-Link is a solid choice for the budget minded. I am a power user in other areas, but don't see a need to drop big bucks for other brands when I get great performance from TP-Link.

[[VIDEOID:974070c819a8d41fd170ca476d471a10]] I rarely write reviews unless a product is terrible or amazing, and unfortunately this product is absolutely appalling. Garmin is a trusted by airline pilots for their reliability and accuracy, so I took this trust to mean that they would release a highly competent dashcam, and bought three of these units. The problems start with the fact it is incredibly difficult to pair an iphone to the device - expect to waste 30-40 minutes going backwards and forwards with bluetooth and wifi settings before you can connect the phone. Don't expect, by-the-way, once the device is paired, it will stay paired, or reliably connect to your iphone - it won't. Expect to spend 30-40 minutes reconnecting devices every time you want to use the iphone app. This is the least of the camera's problems. The worst part is the picture quality, and specifically the ability to read license plates from video footage. You can't. Multiple times we've wanted to report an incident to the police, only to find that the footage is so grainy, it is impossible to read a license plate, even for a car almost on your front bumper. The videos look like VHS tape rendered onto YouTube from the 1980s. We bought these cameras to create a safe environment for our teenage kids and they are worse than useless. I now question their competence or reliability in the sky if they are prepared to push such a poor quality product to unsuspecting consumers. In the attached footage, watch the white truck zoom past on the right, and go on to scrape the side of a Lexus SUV. No chance of getting the license plate of any of the cars, despite their immediate proximity.

I purchased three different size connectors and I installed them into my arcade cabinet (You can see that in my photos) The biggest issue was, which drill bit do i buy? And what size drill bit do i need? But i figured it out and i'm giving you the info to make this easier. I bought a hole saw drill bit. Very low cost and it works good. _____________ Drill bit info and links: _____________ 1. Dual USB 3.0 30mm (1-3/16"): https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B07R7TJ78V _____________ 2. USB 3.0 / 3.5mm audio (https://www.amazon.com/dp/B072KGMJ5N) 30mm (1-3/16"): https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B07R7TJ78V _____________ 3. Dual HDMI (BATIGE was out of stock, so i ordered this one from overseas) 38mm (1-1/2"): https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B07RB4LCZK _____________ 1. and 2. (USB3.0 ports) The usb ports fits slightly loose in the hole made. I locked it in place with the plastic nuts provided and it's locked into place now. Doesn't move. 3. (HDMI ports). 38mm, i pushed it in all the way, it was 99.9% flush with the wood. I had to use a hammer to give it a little tap to get it 100% in. I didn't have to use the plastic nut because it was a tight fit but i put a plastic nut on it to make sure it doesn't move. _____________ NOTE.... IMPERFECT HOLES: _____________ My holes were NOT perfect. They were close to perfect. Probably my fault. A tiny bit of the edges of the holes were chipped due to the hole saw. It might have been my fault. You have to try to drill perfectly straight in. THE FIX: My wood is black, i used a black sharpie marker to touch up any imperfections in the edges of the holes cut. And now it's fine. These adapters will slightly cover up imperfect holes but not fully. That's where the black marker came in handy. _____________ ALSO NOTE... Drill direction _____________ The 38mm hole saw can be removed by hand, by turning it in one direction. So it has threads. If you drill in the wrong direction. You will strip the metal threads and you'll break the bit. (i know because i did that accidentally) i had to buy a 2nd 38mm drill bit that's when i realized the mistake. Once i changed the direction of the drill. It cut really well. _____________ ADDITIONAL INFO: _____________ Steps i took.... 1. I tested the drill bit by making holes in foam core (photos included) you can probably test using cardboard boxes. 2. I made my own template using, pen, paper & a ruler. Drew my dots on the paper with a pen, I then cut into the little dots using an exacto knife. 3. The wood is black so....I used a white sharpie paint permanent maker to color a dot into those little holes i cut. Now i have perfectly aligned dots. And i can see where to aim the drill bit. Marker i used: https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B00E1NXVH6 4. I did the opposite side holes by simply flipping the template paper horizontal, so it's the reverse direction. Draw new dots with the marker. My template paper: I used the straight clean edges of printer paper to help me align things. I made the top and right side of the paper hit the top and right edges of the wood. When i flip the paper, now i do the same with the top left side of the wood. And you're DONE! _____________ If anyone is wondering why i put 4 HDMI ports into the front of my arcade machine. It's for a 4 port bliss-box for all my retro controllers. Player 1,2,3,4

Set-up tip #1 (this was not clear in the instructions): When adding whatever type of sensor (magnetic, infrared, etc), be sure to send the synchronization test trigger signal *WHILE THE UNIT IS MAKING THE CONFORMATORY 3, 5, OR 7 CHIRPS*. Put another way, after you plug & unplug 7-times to allow addition of a magnetic sensor, the main speaker makes 7-chirps ... this is key... while it makes those chirps, trigger the magnetic sensor IMMEDIATELY! If you wait until after it stops chirping, the unit will NOT accept the sensor & it will just be a frustrating process where you assume, incorrectly, that the unit is defective. You must walk through the 3-5-7 chirp programming procedure for each and every unit. You cannot do the 5-chirps, for example, and expect to program all two infrared sensors at the same time....you've got to go through the process two times total. Otherwise, its an insanely bargain unit that works fine for very basic "scare the intruder off" type protection.

Before purchasing. I read the other reviews and thought "why not give it a try" I'm sure glad I did. It's a great laptop at a great price. Just be aware of a few things if you do end up getting this one, see below... I bought this knowing that I would need to upgrade the RAM right from the start, so I purchased a single 16GB module along with the laptop. Trust me it'll do you some good. I also added a second SSD since it has an available extra M.2 slot. The laptop arrived the next day after purchase, in a bigger box so you don't know what's actually inside. For me that was a good thing (nosy neighbors). Upon unboxing I turned it on, got online and registered it with Asus. You get a one year accident drop protection warranty when you do. Then I shut it down and proceeded with the upgrades. Upgrades are easy on this machine. Simply flip bottom side up, unscrew 14 or so screws, carefully remove the back cover (plastic pry tool helps) and you have access to the RAM and SSD's. It comes with 8GB RAM soldered on the motherboard and one open slot to add more (up to 64GB) for a total of 72GB of RAM, but a 16GB module will do for most people. My laptop shipped with an Intel nvme SSD at 512GB of storage. The specs are pretty decent for it. I added a second SSD as a storage/installation drive for games so they don't use up the main OS drive. Put everything back together and proceeded to do a clean install of Windows 11. If you do this remember to download the Intel IRST drivers or you won't see the SSD's upon initial installation. Back up and running, downloaded the Asus drivers and programs for it from their website and then downloaded some games to play. Under heavy gaming or tubo mode, the fan does get loud but not unbearable... nothing compared to other high end gaming laptops. Surprisingly, it runs pretty cool. The RTX3050 ti graphics card runs smooth, even when playing Genshin Impact or Overwatch on max settings on a 4k 144hz HDTV, the wifi 6 card is fast and holds the connection stable between laptop and router, and although there's no RGB backlighting, the single color backlit keyboard does great for night gaming. It's thin, lightweight and not as bulky as a more expensive gaming laptop, but it's exactly what I wanted and needed. The price was great, the fit and finish is good, easy to upgrade, and most of all, it suits my needs perfectly. I would definitely recommend and buy another one, especially from Asus.

What I am using for: I have this in between a high quality Bluetooth receiver and my amplifier in order to provide the ability to apply simple equalization to all of the audio output from my iPad to my HiFi. It has many other uses in terms of placement in a system. ** More detail below, but update after having this for a week. I am super pleased. It does just what I hoped and does it very well. I recommend this highly. I have a Auris Blume HD Long Range Bluetooth 5.0 receiver connected to my amplifier. It has both analogue and digital out. I play music from my iPad through the Audi’s receiver into my HiFi system. I have eclectic music tastes spanning decades, and wish much of the older music (pop, rock, etc.) had a fuller sound and more bass on the low end. Much of the current music has loads of it (maybe too much for some things. I wanted a way to be able to switch the sound profile of my HiFi by merely using the remote. And this totally does the job. Here’s how: I connected the analogue signal out from the Auris Bluetooth receiver (which, by the way, accepts the high quality ACC data from an IOS device and it (the Auris) has an exceptional DAC in it). My amplifier does also. I took this Rolls equalizer and put is in between the output from the analogue outs from the Auris and the amplifier. My amplifier does not have a tape monitor switch I could use for this function (looping the equalizer) but I have the optical/digital out from the Auris going into the TV in on the amplifier accepting digital input and the analogue from the Rolls into the CD input on the amplifier. I set the lowest and highest frequencies up just a bit on the Rolls to have ot function, essentially, as a loudness compensation, with a little more oomph on the bass the added bump on the treble. Now, I can switch back and forth between the TV input (just the label for it—it’s the optimal signal from the Auris, from my iPad) and the CD input (the analogue signal from Auris modified by the Rolls settings) and can instantly switch my sound to a fuller one for certain older music, or for when I want a loudness type function for listing at lover volume. This all works perfectly because, as they note, the Rolls will accept input from anything that is line level analogue and send it on to your amplifier with your modified sound. Wonderful. The rolls seems very well made, sturdy. Someone noted how small it is. It does not seem that small to me. The knobs are reasonable size, have very “feelable” detents for knowing where the neutral is, and they seem to all adjust exactly the ranges that are specified (I tried testing this in a simple way with a test music album). This works. It has many possible uses and it perfectly does what I had hoped it would. It also has a kind of cool retro look to it, which I like a lot.

I purchased this camera because all of the reviews (here and elsewhere) said it had drop-in plug-n-play support for Linux. I'm using Ubutnu 20.04 LTS. When I plugged it in, it failed to work. After a day of debugging, I found the problems. 1. It requires the kernel driver uvcvideo.ko. The good news is, this comes installed by default. The bad news is, it's blacklisted by default (do not start up) in /etc/modprobe.d/uvcvideo-blacklist.conf. Comment out this blacklisting so that it will start up. 2. (And this is the one that killed hours.) Even with the correct drivers, it did not work. The audio worked, but there was no video and no /dev/video# device. The problem: this hardware does NOT support USB3; you must use a USB2 port. It also does not work if you plug it into a hub -- even a powered USB hub. You must plug it directly into the computer's USB2 port. (I suspect that it's very finicky about power requirements.) If you have a newer compute that does not have a USB2 port, then do NOT get this camera. If all of your USB ports are in use and you use USB hubs for peripherals, then do NOT get this camera. 3. The camera is capable of resolutions up to 1920x1080. HOWEVER, as a USB2 device, you'll be lucky if you get 12fps at that resolution. I got it for simple video chats that only need 640x480, which can do 30fps. (If it were a USB3 device, then we could start talking 60fps and higher resolutions.) 4. Manual focus and no lens cover. There's a tiny red light that indicates when the camera is on. There is no indicator for when the microphone is on. On the plus side: the image quality is very crisp (after adjusting the manual focus). And, after figuring out the USB2 issue, obs studio immediately detected the device as a video source.

review_text: I own a Samsung Galaxy Watch4 Classic, and wear it daily. I found the Tozo S2, with a discount code, and made the purchase. First off - it looks and feels like a high-quality device. Smooth, glossy, and finely finished. It's about teh same size, shape, and heft as my wife's Apple Watch 7. The Tozo band is excellent, far better than the band that came with my Galaxy watch. I actually wore both watches for two days, one on each wrist, and found the Tozo to be just about on par with the Galaxy for counting steps and measuring my HR. Both watches notify me of emails or texts about the same, though the icon on the Tozo shows a Gmail icon when I get Outlook emails... Note: I can answer calls on my Galaxy, but not on the Tozo. The battery life on the Tozo greatly exceeds that of my Galaxy, by days! The only criticism I have is that the Tozo Fit app on my phone is somewhat basic at this time. I expect it to be come more robust over time, especially with including more watch faces. Overall, a great buy for someone who wants to upgrade from their older Timex watch or earlier smart watch to an affordable, modern, attractive smart watch.

This review is after usage of the X25D Defender in the field for the last 3 months. It was used multiple times per week and in some cases multiple times per day. I also use the AT24Pro Dreamer by the same company and have for over a year. I purchased the X25 for the horizontal ability of the tripod head mounting. The horizontal system works fine but if you have a full frame camera you will need to splay the legs out extra wide ( which you can - good feature) or you will need a weight bag of some sort as the tripod at full height or even lower does not perform as stable with a full sized camera on the head when horizontal. The other factor which make the X25 my lesser choice for use of the two is the fact that the legs have to be unscrewed to extend vs the AT24 which have the flip levers for extension. Serious time waster to have to unscrew legs. Don't care if all the big names use the system it's a big waste of time in the field. The clip release on the 24 is 5 times faster. The release knob to raise the center column is better on the 25 by design and on the 24 it's once again a knurled knob which in the field ( or cold) is an absolute frustration. Just hard to unscrew, hard to reach and just a bad design choice. If you have no need of the horizontal feature of the 25, buy the 24. It will probably be just as stable as the 25 even with a full size body. Put the clip drop legs on the 25 and I's get one in a heartbeat. There is also a carry bag included w/both. My suggestion is drop sending the bag and reduce the tripod price accordingly. All in all both are very good values for the money but the shortcomings in design on the 25 make it my last choice to field carry, especially in cold weather.
